antichresis: An agreement by which a debtor gives a creditor the use of real property to be able to pay interest and principal of the debt.
antichrist: A denier or opponent of Christ. Specif.: A great antagonist, person or power, expected to precede Christ's second coming.
antichronical: Deviating from the proper order of time. Antichronically, adv.
antichurch: Opposed to the church; against the Christian institution.
anticipant: Anticipating; expectant; with of. Wakening guilt, anticipant of hell. Southey.
anticipate: act in advance of; deal with ahead of time
anticipates: third-person singular simple present indicative of anticipate
anticipating: present participle and gerund of anticipate
anticipation: The commencing of one or more tones of a chord with or during the chord preceding, forming a momentary discord.
anticipative: Anticipating, or containing anticipation. Anticipative of the feast to come. " Cary. Anticipatively, adv.
anticipatory: Forecasting; of the nature of anticipation. Owen. Here is an anticipatory glance of what was to be. J. C. Sha irp.
anticlassical: Opposing or rejecting what is classical.
anticlastic: Having to opposite curvatures, that is, curved longitudinally in one direction and transversely in the opposite direction, as the surface of a saddle.
anticlericalism: The opposition to political influence of clerics.
anticlimactic: of or relating to a sudden change from an impressive to a ludicrous style
anticlimax: A sentence in which the ideas fall, or become less important and striking, at the close; the opposite of climax. It produces aridiculous effect. Example: Next comes Dalhousie, the great god of war, Lieutenant-colonel to the Earl Anticlinal anticlinal, a. Etym: [Pref. anti- + Gr.
anticlinal: The crest or line in which strata slope or dip in opposite directions.
anticline: A structure of bedded rocks in which the beds on both sides of an axis or axial plane dip away from the axis; an anticlinal.
anticlinorium: The upward elevation of the crust of the earth, resulting from a geanticlinal.
anticlockwise: in a direction opposite to the direction in which the hands of a clock move
anticoagulant: medicine that prevents or retards the clotting of blood
anticoagulation: the administration of an anticoagulant drug to retard coagulation of the blood
anticoherer: A device, one form of which consists of a scratched deposit of silver on glass, used in connection with the receiving apparatus for reading wireless signals. The electric waves falling on this contrivance increase its resistance several times. The anticoherer can be used in conjunction with a telephone.
anticommunist: Opposed to the tenets of communism.
anticompetitive: Acting to hinder or obstruct competition.
anticonformity: A form of individualism that is an active rejection of conformity
anticonventional: Rejecting conventions; opposing what is conventional or mainstream.
anticonvulsant: a drug used to treat or prevent convulsions (as in epilepsy)
anticorrosive: An agent that prevents or stops corrosion.
anticyclone: A movement of the atmosphere opposite in character, as regards direction of the wind and distribution of barometric pressure, to that of a cyclone. Anticyclonic, a. Anticyclonically, adv.
anticyclonic: of or relating to or characteristic of the atmosphere around a high pressure center
antidemocratic: Opposed to the tenets of democracy.
antidepressant: any of a class of drugs used to treat depression; often have undesirable side effects
antidiabetic: a drug used to treat diabetes mellitus
antidiarrheal: a drug used to control or stop diarrhea
antidicomarian: A member of a Christian sect, active from the rd to the th century, who refused to accord any special status to Mary, mother of Jesus, and rejected the doctrine of her perpetual virginity.
antidiuretic: a drug that limits the formation of urine
antidoron: A piece of ordinary leavened bread, taken from remnants of loaves used for the Eucharist, which has been blessed but not consecrated; distributed in churches that use the Byzantine Rite.
antidotal: Having the quality an antidote; fitted to counteract the effects of poison. Sir T. Browne. Antidotally, adv.
antidote: a remedy that stops or controls the effects of a poison
antidromic: conducting nerve impulses in a direction opposite to normal
antidromous: Changing the direction in the spiral sequence of leaves on astem.
antielectron: an elementary particle with positive charge
antiempirical: Going against what is empirically true.
antienzymatic: That inhibits the action of an enzyme
antievolution: Opposing the teaching or espousal of evolutionary theories, often specifically the Darwinian theory of natural selection
antievolutionist: A person who believes, or argues, that evolution does not take place.
antifascist: Opposed to the tenets of fascism; antifa.
antifeminist: someone who does not believe in the social or economic or political equality of men and women
antiferromagnetism: magnetic field creates parallel but opposing spins; varies with temperature
antiforeign: Opposed to foreigners or to what is foreign.
antifreeze: a liquid added to the water in a cooling system to lower its freezing point
antifriction: Something to less ea. Tending to lessen friction.
antifungal: any agent that destroys or prevents the growth of fungi
antigen: any substance (as a toxin or enzyme) that stimulates an immune response in the body (especially the production of antibodies)
antigene: An oligonucleotide that attaches to a specific gene and suppresses its action.
antigone: (Greek mythology) the daughter of King Oedipus who disobeyed her father and was condemned to death
antigonon: Any of three American vines, of the genus Antigonon, including the chain of hearts and the coral vine
antigonus: a general of Alexander the Great and king of Macedonia; lost one eye; killed in a battle at Ipsus (- BC)
antigrammatical: Opposing or flouting the rules of grammar.
antigua: the largest of the islands comprising Antigua and Barbuda
antihelix: The curved elevation of the cartilage of the ear, within or in front of the helix. See Ear.
antihero: a protagonist who lacks the characteristics that would make him a hero (or her a heroine)
antihierarchical: Opposing a hierarchy or hierarchies in general.
antihierarchy: Opposing a hierarchy or hierarchies in general.
antihistamine: a medicine used to treat allergies and hypersensitive reactions and colds; works by counteracting the effects of histamine on a receptor site
antihypertensive: a drug that reduces high blood pressure
antiking: One who declares himself king in opposition to a reigning monarch, especially in an electoral monarchy.
antiknock: suppressing or eliminating engine knock in combustion engines
antilegomena: Certain books of the New Testament which were for a time not universally received, but which are now considered canonical. These are the Epistle to the Hebrews, the Epistles of James and Jude, the second Epistle of Peter, the second and third Epistles of John, and the Revelation. The undisputed books are called the Homologoumena.
antileveling: Opposing the elimination of disparities between the haves and the have-nots in society.
antillean: Of, from, or pertaining to the Antilles, the Antillean people or the Antillean language.
antilles: a group of islands in the West Indies
antilocapra: type and sole genus of the Antilocapridae comprising one species
antilog: the number of which a given number is the logarithm
antilogarithm: The number corresponding to a logarithm. The word has been sometimes, though rarely, used to denote the complement of a given logarithm; also the logarithmic cosine corresponding to a given logarithmic sine. Antilogarithmic, a.
antilogous: Of the contrary name or character; opposed to analogous. Antilogous pole (Eccl.), that pole of a crystal which becomes negatively electrified when heated.
antilogy: A contradiction between any words or passages in an author. Sir W. Hamilton.
antimacassar: A cover for the back or arms of a chair or sofa, etc., to prevent them from being soiled by macassar or other oil from the hair.
antimachine: Opposing the political machine of a region
antimask: A secondary mask, or grotesque interlude, between the parts of a serious mask. Bacon.
antimasque: A comic or grotesque dance presented before or between the acts of a masque.
antimaterialism: Any belief system that opposes philosophical materialism.
antimatter: matter consisting of elementary particles that are the antiparticles of those making up normal substances
antimere: One of the two halves of bilaterally symmetrical animals; oneof any opposite symmetrical or homotypic parts in animals and plants.
antimetabolite: an antineoplastic drug that inhibits the utilization of a metabolite
antimetropia: An extreme form of anisometropia in which one eye is myopic and the other hyperopic.
antimicrobial: capable of destroying or inhibiting the growth of disease-causing microorganisms
antiministerial: Opposed to government ministers or ministries.
antimonate: A compound of antimonic acid with a base or basic radical.
antimonial: Of or pertaining to antimony. n. (Med.)
antimoniated: Combined or prepared with antimony; as, antimoniated tartar.
antimonic: Pertaining to, or derived from, antimony; said of those compounds of antimony in which this element has its highest equivalence; as, antimonic acid.
antimonide: Any compound of antimony with more electropositive elements.
antimonious: Pertaining to, or derived from, antimony; said of those compounds of antimony in which this element has an equivalence next lower than the highest; as, antimonious acid.
antimoniureted: Combined with or containing antimony; as, antimoniureted hydrogen.
antimony: An elementary substance, resembling a metal in its appearance and physical properties, but in its chemical relations belonging to the class of nonmetallic substances. Atomic weight,. Symbol, Sb.
antinational: Antagonistic to one's country or nation, or to a national government.
antinationalist: Of, pertaining to or supporting antinationalism.
antinaturalism: The view that the natural world and the social world are different, related to antipositivism.
antineoplastic: any of several drugs that control or kill neoplastic cells; used in chemotherapy to kill cancer cells; all have unpleasant side effects that may include nausea and vomiting and hair loss and suppression of bone marrow function
anting: The practice of some birds of rubbing live ants or occasionally other items into the feathers, possibly as a means of controlling parasites.
antinode: (physics) the point of maximum displacement in a periodic system
antinomian: Of or pertaining to the Antinomians; opposed to the doctrine that the moral law is obligatory.
antinomic: Exhibiting or pertaining to antinomy; contradictory.
antinomy: A contradiction or incompatibility of thought or language; in the Kantian philosophy, such a contradiction as arises from the attempt to apply to the ideas of the reason, relations or attributes which are appropriate only to the facts or the concepts of experience.
antinormal: Antagonistic to or causing deviations from that which is considered normal.
antinovel: A novel that deliberately avoids the typical conventions of the novel, such as a coherent plot and protagonist.
antioch: a town in southern Turkey; ancient commercial center and capital of Syria; an early center of Christianity
antiochian: Pertaining to Antioch us, a contemporary with Cicero, and the founder of a sect of philosophers.
antiorgastic: Tending to allay venereal excitement or desire; sedative.
antioxidant: substance that inhibits oxidation or inhibits reactions promoted by oxygen or peroxides
antipapism: Opposition to papism (the Roman Catholic pope and Roman Catholicism).
antiparallel: Running in a contrary direction. Hammond.
antiparallelogram: A quadrilateral in which the pairs of nonadjacent sides are congruent, but in which two opposite sides intersect and are therefore not parallel.
antiparliamentarian: Opposing parliament or rule by parliament.
antiparticle: a particle that has the same mass as another particle but has opposite values for its other properties; interaction of a particle and its antiparticle results in annihilation and the production of radiant energy
antipasto: a course of appetizers in an Italian meal
antipathist: One who has an antipathy. Antipathist of light. Coleridge.
antipeptone: A product of gastric and pancreatic digestion, differing from hemipeptone in not being decomposed by the continued action of pancreatic juice.
antiperiodic: A remedy possessing the property of preventing the return of periodic paroxysms, or exacerbations, of disease, as in intermittent fevers.
antiperistasis: Opposition by which the quality opposed as quires strength; resistance or reaction roused by opposition or by the action of an opposite principle or quality.
antipersonnel: designed to inflict death or personal injury rather than material destruction
antiperspirant: an astringent substance applied to the skin to reduce perspiration
antiphilosophy: An antitheoretical metaphilosophy critical of a priori justification aiming to dissolve misconceptions that traditional philosophy makes.
antiphon: a verse or song to be chanted or sung in response
antiphonal: Of or pertaining to antiphony, or alternate singing; sung alternately by a divided choir or opposite choirs. Wheat ly. Antiphonally, adv.
antiphonally: In an antiphonal manner; in the manner of an antiphon.
antiphonary: A book containing a collection of antiphons; the book in which the antiphons of the breviary, with their musical notes, are contained.
antiphone: The response which one side of the choir makes to the other in a chant; alternate chanting or signing.
antiphony: alternate (responsive) singing by a choir in two parts
antiphrasis: The use of words in a sense opposite to their proper meaning; as when a court of justice is called a court of vengeance.
antiphrastic: Of, relating to, or exhibiting antiphrasis.
antipodal: relating to the antipodes or situated at opposite sides of the earth
antipode: One of the antipodes; anything exactly opposite. In tale or history your beggar is ever the just antipode to your king. Lamb.
antipodean: Pertaining to the antipodes, or the opposite side of the world; antipodal.
antipodes: any two places or regions on diametrically opposite sides of the Earth
antipodism: A form of foot juggling where the juggler lies on his or her back, usually on a sort of chair.
antipole: The opposite pole; anything diametrically opposed. Geo. Eliot.
antipooling: Opposing or banning associations of rival railroads.
antipope: One who is elected, or claims to be, pope in opposition to the pope canonically chosen; esp. applied to those popes who resided at avignon during the Great Schism.
antiprostate: That counters a disease of the prostate
antiproton: an unstable negatively charged proton; the antiparticle of a proton
antiprotozoal: a medicinal drug used to fight diseases (like malaria) that are caused by protozoa
antipruritic: a substance that relieves or prevents itching
antipsychotic: tranquilizer used to treat psychotic conditions when a calming effect is desired
antiputrefactive: Counteracting, or preserving from, putrefaction; antiseptic.
antiputrescent: Counteracting, or preserving from, putrefaction; antiseptic.
antipyretic: Efficacious in preventing or allaying fever. n.
antipyrine: An artificial alkaloid, believed to be efficient in abating fever.
antiquarian: Pertaining to antiquaries, or to antiquity; as, antiquarian literature.
antiquarianism: Character of an antiquary; study or love of antiquities. War burton.
antiquary: Pertaining to antiquity. Instructed by the antiquary times.
antiquate: To make old, or obsolete; to make antique; to make old in sucha degree as to put out of use; hence, to make void, or abrogate. Christianity might reasonably introduce new laws, and antiquate or abrogate old one. Sir M. Hale.
antiquated: Grown old. Hence: Bygone; obsolete; out of use; old-fashioned; as, an antiquated law. Antiquated words. " Dryden. Old Janet, for so he understood his antiquated attendant was denominated. Sir W. Scott.
antique: In general, anything very old; but in a more limited sense, arelic or object of ancient art; collectively, the antique, the remains of ancient art, as busts, statues, paintings, and vases. Misshapen monuments and maimed antiques. Byron.
antiqueness: The quality of being antique; an appearance of ancient origin and workmanship. We may discover something venerable in the antiqueness of the work. Addison.
antiquer: A person who finishes furniture or objects so they have the appearance of an antique, either for decoration or to perpetrate a fraud.
antiquity: the historic period preceding the Middle Ages in Europe
antirational: Lacking or (especially) opposed to reason and rational thought.
antireligion: Opposed to or acting against religion
antirheumatic: Serving to prevent or counter rheumatism.
antiroyalist: One who opposes royals or royalism.
antirrhinum: a genus of herbs of the family Scrophulariaceae with brightly colored irregular flowers
antisceptic: Someone who is opposed to scepticism.
antiscience: Opposed to science and scientific progress.
antiscion: The mirror image, or shadow, of a planet, based upon a line of reference which is the axis of Cancer/ Capricorn (the position of the sun at the solstices).
antisepsis: Prevention of sepsis by excluding or destroying microorganisms.
antiseptic: A substance which prevents or retards putrefaction, or destroys, or protects from, putrefactive organisms; as, salt, carbolic acid, alcohol, cinchona.
antiserum: blood serum containing antibodies against specific antigens; provides immunity to a disease
antiskid: Designed to increase friction, and thereby reduce the possibility of skid. (of a surface)
antisocial: Tending to interrupt or destroy social intercourse; averse to society, or hostile to its existence; as, antisocial principles.
antispiritual: Opposing or harming what is spiritual.
antistatic: Preventing the buildup of static electricity.
antistrophe: the section of a choral ode answering a previous strophe in classical Greek drama; the second of two metrically corresponding sections in a poem
antistrumous: Good against scrofulous disorders. Johnson. Wiseman.
antitank: designed for defense against armored vehicles
antitheism: The doctrine of anti theists. Antitheistic, a.
antitheistic: Of, pertaining to or espousing antitheism.
antithesis: An opposition or contrast of words or sentiments occurring in the same sentence; as, The prodigal robs his heir; the miser robs himself. " He had covertly shot at Cromwell; he how openly aimed at the Queen. "
antithetic: sharply contrasted in character or purpose
antithetical: sharply contrasted in character or purpose
antithrombin: A small molecule that inactivates several enzymes of the coagulation system.
antithyroid: having the effect of counteracting excessive thyroid activity
antitobacco: Opposed to tobacco, often specifically to either the tobacco industry or public smoking.
antitoxin: an antibody that can neutralize a specific toxin
antitragus: A prominence on the lower posterior portion of the concha of the external ear, opposite the tragus. See Ear.
antitrinitarian: Rejecting the Trinitarian doctrine that God subsists as three distinct Persons in the single substance of the Holy Trinity.
antitropous: Displaying, of, or pertaining to antitropy.
antitropy: A disposition of opposed, asymmetric leaves where a pair of leaves displays bilateral symmetry.
antitumor: used in the treatment of cancer
antitussive: any medicine used to suppress or relieve coughing
antitype: That of which the type pattern or representation; that which is represented by the type or symbol.
antitypical: Of or pertaining to an antitype; explaining the type. Antitypically, adv.
antivenin: The serum of blood rendered antitoxic to a venom by repeated injections of small doses of the venom.
antiviral: inhibiting or stopping the growth and reproduction of viruses
antler: The entire horn, or any branch of the horn, of a cervine animal, as of a stag. Huge stags with sixteen antlers. Macaulay.
antlered: Furnished with antlers. The antlered stag. Cowper.
antoecian: Of or belonging to the point on the globe of the same longitude but the opposite latitude.
antoinette: A female given name from French; best known for the ill-fated French queen Marie Antoinette.
anton: A male given name from Latin.
antoninianus: A silver coin used during the Roman Empire, equal to two denarii.
antonio: A male given name from Italian.
antonomasia: The use of some epithet or the name of some office, dignity, or the like, instead of the proper name of the person; as when his majesty is used for a king, or when, instead of Aristotle, we say, the philosopher; or, conversely, the use of a proper name instead of an appellative, as when a wise man is called a Solomon, or an eminent orator a Cicero.
antonomastic: Pertaining to, or characterized by, antonomasia. Antonomastically, adv.
antony: Roman general under Julius Caesar in the Gallic wars; repudiated his wife for the Egyptian queen Cleopatra; they were defeated by Octavian at Actium (- BC)
antonym: A word of opposite meaning; a counterterm; used as acor relative of synonym. C. J. Smith.
antonymy: the semantic relation that holds between two words that can (in a given context) express opposite meanings
antorbital: Pertaining to, or situated in, the region of the front of the orbit. n.
antrorse: Forward or upward in direction. Gray.
antrum: A cavern or cavity, esp. an anatomical cavity or sinus. Huxley.
antrustion: A vassal or voluntary follower of Frankish princes in their enterprises.
anu: Babylonian god of the sky; one of the supreme triad including Bel and Ea
anucleate: Which does not have a nucleus.
anunnaki: any of a group of powerful Babylonian earth spirits or genii; servitors of the gods
anura: One of the orders of amphibians characterized by the absence of a tail, as the frogs and toads.
anurous: Destitute of a tail, as the frogs and toads.
anus: The posterior opening of the alimentary canal, through which the excrements are expelled.
anvil: the incus. See Incus. To be on the anvil, to be in a state of discussion, formation, or preparation, as when a scheme or measure is forming, but not matured. Swift.
anxiety: A state of restlessness and agitation, often with general indisposition and a distressing sense of oppression at the epigastrium. Dunglison.
anxiously: In an anxious manner; with painful uncertainty; solicitously.
any: To any extent; in any degree; at all. You are not to go loose any longer. Before you go any farther. Steele.
anybody: Any one out of an indefinite number of persons; anyone; any person. His Majesty could not keep any secret from anybody. Macaulay.
anyhow: In any way or manner whatever; at any rate; in any event. Anyhow, it must be acknowledged to be not a simple selforiginatederror. J. H. Newman. Anyhow, the languages of the two nations were closely allied. E. A.Freeman.
anyone: One taken at random rather than by selection; anybody.
anyplace: at or in or to any place
anything: In any measure; anywise; at all. Mine old good will and hearty affection towards you is not.anything at all quailed. Robynson (More's Utopia).
anythingarian: One who holds to no particular creed or dogma.
anywhither: To or towards any place. De Foe.
anywise: In any wise or way; at all. Anywise essential. " Burke.
anzio: a town of central Italy on the Tyrrhenian Sea; the Allies established a beachhead at Anzio in World War II
aonian: Pertaining to Aonia, Boeotia, or to the Muses, who were supposed to dwell there. Aonian fount, the fountain of Aganippe, at the foot of Mount Helicon, not far from Thebes, and sacred to the muses.
aorist: A tense in the Greek language, which expresses an action as completed in past time, but leaves it, in other respects, wholly indeterminate.
aorta: The great artery which carries the blood from the heart to all parts of the body except the lungs; the main trunk of the arterial system.
aortic: Of or pertaining to the aorta.
aoudad: An African sheeplike quadruped (the Ammo tragus tragelaphus) having a long mane on the breast and fore legs. It is, perhaps, the chamois of the Old Testament.
aouellimiden: A subgroup of the Tuareg people.
apa: A title used for male clergy or saints in the Coptic Church.
apace: With a quick pace; quick; fast; speedily. His dewy locks did drop with brine apace. Spenser. A visible triumph of the gospel draw apace. I. Taylor.
apache: any member of Athapaskan tribes that migrated to the southwestern desert (from Arizona to Texas and south into Mexico); fought a losing battle from to with the United States and were resettled in Oklahoma
apaches: A group of nomadic North American Indians including several tribes native of Arizona, New Mexico, etc.
apagoge: An indirect argument which proves a thing by showing the impossibility or absurdity of the contrary.
apagogic: Proving indirectly, by showing the impossibility or absurdity of the contrary.
apair: To impair or become impaired; to injure. Chaucer.
apalachicola: a river in northwestern Florida formed by the confluence of the Chattahoochee River and the Flint River at the Florida border
apanthropy: An aversion to the company of men; a love of solitude.
apar: South American armadillo with three bands of bony plates
aparejo: A kind of pack saddle used in the American military service and among the Spanish Americans. It is made of leather stuffed with hay, moss, or the like.
apart: separated or at a distance in place or position or time
apartheid: a social policy or racial segregation involving political and economic and legal discrimination against people who are not Whites; the former official policy in South Africa
apartment: a suite of rooms usually on one floor of an apartment house
apastron: That point in the orbit of a double star where the smaller star is farthest from its primary.
apathetic: showing little or no emotion or animation
apathy: Want of feeling; privation of passion, emotion, or excitement; dispassion; applied either to the body or the mind. As applied to the mind, it is a calmness, indolence, or state of indifference, incapable of being ruffled or roused to active interest or exertion by pleasure, pain, or passion. The apathy of despair. " Macaulay. A certain apathy or sluggishness in his nature which led him. to leave events to take their own course. Prescott. According to the Stoics, apathy meant the extinction of the passions by the ascendency of reason. Fleming.
apatite: Native phosphate of lime, occurring usually in six-sided prisms, color often pale green, transparent or translucent.
apayao: A province of the Cordillera Administrative Region, Luzon, Philippines. Capital: Kabugao. The province was created from the partitioning of Kalinga-Apayao.
apc: a drug combination found in some over-the-counter headache remedies (aspirin and phenacetin and caffeine)
apeak: In a vertical line. The anchor in apeak, when the cable has been sufficiently hove in to bring the ship over it, and the ship is them said to be hove apeak.
aped: simple past and past participle of ape
apelike: being or given to servile imitation
apennine: Of, pertaining to, or designating, the Apennines, a chain of mountains extending through Italy.
apennines: a mountain range extending the length of the Italian peninsula
apercu: A first view or glance, or the perception or estimation so obtained; an immediate apprehension or insight, appreciative rather than analytic.
aperea: The wild Guinea pig of Brazil (Cavia aperea).
aperient: Gently opening the bowels; laxative. n.
aperitif: alcoholic beverage taken before a meal as an appetizer
apertion: The act of opening; an opening; an aperture. Wiseman.
aperture: The diameter of the exposed part of the object glass of ateles cope or other optical instrument; as, a telescope of four-inch aperture.
apery: the act of mimicking; imitative behavior
apetalous: Having no petals, or flower leaves.
apetaly: The condition of having no petals
apex: The end or edge of a vein nearest the surface. Apex of the earth's motion (Astron.), that point of the heavens toward which the earth is moving in its orbit.
aphagia: loss of the ability to swallow
aphakia: An anomalous state of refraction caused by the absence of the crystalline lens, as after operations for cataract. The remedy is the use of powerful convex lenses. Dunglison.
aphakial: Pertaining to aphakia; as, aphakial eyes.
aphakic: of or relating to or afflicted with aphakia
aphaniptera: A group of wingless insects, of which the flea in the type. See flea.
aphanitic: Resembling aphanite; having a very fine-grained structure.
aphasia: inability to use or understand language (spoken or written) because of a brain lesion
aphasic: Pertaining to, or affected by, aphasia; speechless.
aphelandra: Any of the tropical evergreen shrubs in the genus Aphelandra
aphelion: That point of a planet's or comet's orbit which is most distant from the sun, the opposite point being the perihelion.
apheliotropic: Turning away from the sun; said of leaves, etc. Darwin.
aphemia: Loss of the power of speaking, while retaining the power of writing; a disorder of cerebral origin.
apheresis: The dropping of a letter or syllable from the beginning of aword; e. g., cute for acute.
apheretic: relating to or formed by or consisting of aphaeresis
aphesis: The loss of a short unaccented vowel at the beginning of aword; the result of a phonetic process; as, squire for esquire. New Eng. Dict.
aphetic: Shortened by dropping a letter or a syllable from the beginning of a word; as, an aphetic word or form. Aphetically, adv. New Eng. Dict.
aphid: One of the genus Aphis; an aphidian.
aphlogistic: Flameless; as, an aphlogistic lamp, in which a coil of wire is kept in a state of continued ignition by alcohol, without flame.
aphonia: a disorder of the vocal organs that results in the loss of voice
aphonic: being without sound through injury or illness and thus incapable of all but whispered speech
aphorise: to speak or write in aphorisms
aphorism: A comprehensive maxim or principle expressed in a few words; asharply defined sentence relating to abstract truth rather than to practical matters. The first aphorism of Hippocrates is, Life is short, and the art is long. " Fleming.
aphorismic: Relating to aphorisms, or having the form of an aphorism.
aphorist: A writer or utterer of aphorisms.
aphoristic: terse and witty and like a maxim
aphrodisiac: That which (as a drug, or some kinds of food) excites to venery.
aphrodisian: Pertaining to Aphrodite or Venus. Aphrodisian dames C. Reade.
aphrodisiomania: An abnormal enthusiasm for sexual pleasure
aphrodite: The Greek goddess of love, corresponding to the Venus of the romans.
aphthartodocetae: A sixth-century non-Chalcedonian sect who believed that Christ's body was always incorruptible and only perished by Christ's conscious willing decision.
aphthong: A letter, or a combination of letters, employed in spelling aword, but in the pronunciation having no sound. Aphthongal, a.
aphyllous: Destitute of leaves, as the broom rape, certain euphorbiaceous plants, etc.
apiary: A place where bees are kept; a stand or shed for bees; abeehouse.
apical: At or belonging to an apex, tip, or summit. Gray.
apiculate: (of a leaf shape) having a short sharply pointed tip

appurtenance: That which belongs to something else; an adjunct; an appendage; an accessory; something annexed to another thing more worthy; in common parlance and legal acceptation, something belonging to another thing as principal, and which passes as incident to it, as a right ofway, or other easement to land; a right of common to pasture, an outhouse, barn, garden, or orchard, to a house or messuage. In astrict legal sense, land can never pass as an appurtenance to land. Tom lins. Bouvier. Bur rill. Globes. provided as appurtenances to astronomy. Bacon. The structure of the eye, and of its appurtenances. Reid.
appurtenant: Annexed or pertaining to some more important thing; accessory; incident; as, a right of way appurtenant to land or buildings. Black stone. Common appurtenatn. (Law) See under Common, n.
april: the month following March and preceding May
aprioristic: A priori; based on hypothesis rather than experiment.
apron: a garment of cloth or leather or plastic that is tied about the waist and worn to protect your clothing
aproned: Wearing an apron. A cobbler aproned, and a parson gowned. Pope.
apropos: of an appropriate or pertinent nature
apse: a domed or vaulted recess or projection on a building especially the east end of a church; usually contains the altar
apsidal: Of or pertaining to the apsides of an orbit.
apsis: One of the two points of an orbit, as of a planet or satellite, which are at the greatest and least distance from the central body, corresponding to the aphelion and perihelion of a planet, or to the apogee and perigee of the moon. apsu: father of the gods and consort of Tiamat
apt: To fit; to suit; to adapt. " To apt their places. " B.Jonson. That our speech be apted to edification. Jer. Taylor.
apter: comparative form of apt: more apt
apterous: Destitute of wings; apteral; as, apterous insects.
apterygiformes: a ratite bird order: flightless ground birds having vestigial wings and long bills and small eyes: kiwis
apterygote: Any insect of the order Apterygota.

aptest: superlative form of apt: most apt
aptian: A subdivision of the Early (Lower) Cretaceous epoch.
aptly: In an apt or suitable manner; fitly; properly; pertinently; appropriately; readily.
aptness: a disposition to behave in a certain way
aptotic: Pertaining to, or characterized by, ap totes; uninflected; as, aptotic languages.
apus: A genus of fresh-water phyllopod crustaceans. See Phyllopod.
apyrase: Any of a family of enzymes that catalyze the hydrolysis of ATP, releasing phosphate and available energy
apyrexia: The absence or an intermission during a bout of fever.
apyrexial: Relating to apyrexy. Apyrexial period. " Br ande & C.
aquacade: An entertainment consisting of swimmers and divers performing to music
aquaculture: rearing aquatic animals or cultivating aquatic plants for food
aqualung: a device (trade name Aqua-Lung) that lets divers breathe under water; scuba is an acronym for self-contained underwater breathing apparatus
aquamanile: A ewer or jug-like vessel, shaped like an animal or human figure, used for washing the hands.
aquamarine: A transparent, pale green variety of beryl, used as a gem. See beryl.
aquanaut: a skilled worker who can live in underwater installations and participate in scientific research
aquaplane: rise up onto a thin film of water between the tires and road so that there is no more contact with the road
aquarelle: A design or painting in thin transparent water colors; also, the mode of painting in such colors.
aquarian: One of a sect of Christian in the primitive church who used water instead of wine in the Lord's Supper.
aquarist: A person who maintains an aquarium.

aquarius: (astrology) a person who is born while the sun is in Aquarius
aquatic: Pertaining to water growing in water; living in, swimming in, or frequenting the margins of waters; as, aquatic plants and fowls.
aquatone: An offset printing method using a gelatin-coated zinc plate to print type, line illustrations, and fine-screen halftones.

aqueduct: A canal or passage; as, the aqueduct of Sylvius, a channel connecting the third and fourth ventricles of the brain.
aqueous: similar to or containing or dissolved in water

aquiculture: a technique of growing plants (without soil) in water containing dissolved nutrients

aquiferous: Consisting or conveying water or a watery fluid; as, aquiferous vessels; the aquiferous system.
aquilegia: a plant of the genus Aquilegia having irregular showy spurred flowers
aquiline: curved down like an eagle's beak
aquinas: (Roman Catholic Church) Italian theologian and Doctor of the Church who is remembered for his attempt to reconcile faith and reason in a comprehensive theology; presented philosophical proofs of the existence of God (-)
aquitaine: a region of southwestern France between Bordeaux and the Pyrenees
aquiver: In a state of excitement, trepidation or agitation; quivering.
aquosity: The condition of being wet or watery; wateriness. Huxley. Very little water or aquosity is found in their belly. Holland.

araba: A wagon or cart, usually heavy and without springs, and often covered.
araban: A polysaccharide composed of arabinose residues

arabian: Of or pertaining to Arabia or its inhabitants. Arabian bird, the phenix.

arabis: annual to perennial woody herbs of temperate North America, Europe and Asia: rockcress
arabism: An Arabic idiom peculiarly of language. Stuart.

arabized: simple past and past participle of Arabize
arable: Fit for plowing or tillage; hence, often applied to land which has been plowed or tilled.

aragon: French writer who generalized surrealism to literature (-)
aragonese: Of or pertaining to Aragon, in Spain, or to its inhabitants. n. sing. & pl.

arain: A member of a large Punjabi Muslim agricultural community.
aralia: any of various plants of the genus Aralia; often aromatic plants having compound leaves and small umbellate flowers
araliaceae: mostly tropical trees and shrubs and lianas: genera Panax and Hedera
aram: the biblical name for ancient Syria
aramaean: of or relating to Aram or to its inhabitants or their culture or their language
aramid: Any of a class of strong, heat-resistant synthetic fibres, used in aerospace and military applications.

arawakan: of or relating to the peoples who speak the language of the Arawak

arca: type genus of the family Arcidae: ark shells and blood clams
arcade: a covered passageway with shops and stalls on either side

arcadian: (used with regard to idealized country life) idyllically rustic
arcana: Specialized knowledge that is mysterious to the uninitiated.
arcane: Hidden; secret. The arcane part of divine wisdom. Berkeley.

arccosine: the inverse function of the cosine
arccotangent: the inverse function of the cotangent
arch: Any part of a curved line.
archaebacteria: considered ancient life forms that evolved separately from bacteria and blue-green algae

archaeological: related to or dealing with or devoted to archaeology

archaise: to give an archaic appearance of character to
archaism: the use of an archaic expression

archaizer: One who makes archaic, as by using an archaic style.
archaizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of archaize
archangel: A term applied to several different species of plants (Angelica archangelica, Lamium album, etc.).
archbishop: A chief bishop; a church dignitary of the first class (often called a metropolitan or primate) who superintends the conduct of the suffragan bishops in his province, and also exercises episcopal authority in his own diocese.

archchemic: Of supreme chemical powers. The archchemic sun. " Milton.

archduke: A prince of the imperial family of Austria.

archepiscopal: of or associated with an archbishop

archery: the sport of shooting arrows with a bow
arches: pl. of Arch, n. Court of arches, or Arches Court (Eng. Law),the court of appeal of the Archbishop of Canterbury, whereof the judge, who sits as deputy to the archbishop, is called the Dean of the Arches, because he anciently held his court in the church of St. Mary-le-Bow (de arcubus). archibald: A male given name from the Germanic languages.

archiepiscopal: Of or pertaining to an archbishop; as, Canterbury is an archiepiscopal see.
archil: any of various lecanoras that yield the dye archil
archilochian: Of or pertaining to the satiric Greek poet Archilochus; as, Archilochian meter.
archimandrite: A chief of a monastery, corresponding to abbot in the Roman Catholic church.

archipallium: the olfactory cortex of the cerebrum
archipelago: a group of many islands in a large body of water
archipterygium: The primitive form of fin, like that of Ceratodus.
architect: someone who creates plans to be used in making something (such as buildings)

architeuthis: A genus of gigantic cephalopods, allied to the squids, found esp. in the North Atlantic and about New Zealand.
architrave: the molding around a door or window

archiver: One who, or that which, archives.
archives: collection of records especially about an institution
archivist: A keeper of archives or records.

archlute: A fretted and double-necked stringed musical instrument with a large body, double courses in the bass, and two sets of tuning pegs.

archonship: The office of an archon. Mitford.
archontate: An archon's term of office. Gibbon.
archoplasm: The substance from which attraction spheres develop in mitotic cell division, and of which they consist.
archosaurian: of or relating to reptiles of the subclass Archosaur ia

archpriest: A chief priest; also, a kind of vicar, or a rural dean.
archtreasurer: A chief treasurer. Specifically, the great treasurer of the german empire.
archway: A way or passage under an arch.
arcing: present participle and gerund of arc

arcosolium: A tomb in an arched recess in a wall.

arctangent: the inverse function of the tangent

arctoidea: A group of the Carnivora, that includes the bears, weasels, etc.
arcual: Of or pertaining to an arc. Arcual measure of an angle (Math.),that in which the unit angle has its measuring arc equal to the radius of the circle.
arcus: a whitish deposit in the shape of an arc that is sometimes seen in the cornea
ardea: type genus of the Ardeidae: large New and Old World herons
ardeb: a unit of dry measure used in Egypt
ardeid: Any member of the family Ardeidae, the herons, egrets and bitterns.
ardennes: a wooded plateau in the Champagne-Ardenne region of France; the site of intense fighting in World War I and World War II
ardently: In an ardent manner; eagerly; with warmth; affectionately; passionately.
ardour: feelings of great warmth and intensity
arduous: characterized by effort to the point of exhaustion; especially physical effort
are: The present indicative plural of the substantive verb to be; but etymologically a different word from be, or was. Am, art, are, and is, all come from the root as.
area: The superficial contents of any figure; the surface included within any given lines; superficial extent; as, the area of a square or a triangle.
areal: Of or pertaining to an area; as, areal interstices (the are asor spaces inclosed by the reticulate vessels of leaves).

areaway: a passageway between buildings or giving access to a basement

ared: simple past and past participle of aread
arefaction: The act of drying, or the state of growing dry. The arefaction of the earth. Sir M. Hale.
aren: first-person plural simple present of be
arena: The area in the central part of an amphitheater, in which the gladiators fought and other shows were exhibited; so called because it was covered with sand.
arenaceous: Sandy or consisting largely of sand; of the nature of sand; easily disintegrating into sand; friable; as, arenaceous limestone.
arendator: In some provinces of Russia, one who farms the rents or revenues.
arenga: a genus of tropical Asian and Malaysian palm trees

areolate: relating to or like or divided into areolae

areology: The scientific observation and study of the planet Mars's geology; geology of Mars.

areometric: Relating to, or measured by, an areometer.
areopagite: A member of the Areopagus. Acts xvii.

ares: (Greek mythology) Greek god of war; son of Zeus and Hera; identified with Roman Mars
aret: To reckon; to ascribe; to impute. Chaucer.

arethusa: any of several bog orchids of the genus Arethusa having or showy flowers
arew: In a row. All her teeth arew. " Spenser.

argali: wild sheep of semidesert regions in central Asia
argan: A tree of species Sideroxylon spinosum (formerly Argania spinosa), of southwestern Morocco, particularly prized for its oil.

argemone: any plant of the genus Argemone having large white or yellow flowers and prickly leaves and stems and pods

argh: Expressing annoyance, dismay, embarrassment or frustration.

argiopidae: spiders that spin orb webs; cosmopolitan in distribution
argive: Of or performance to Argos, the capital of Argol is in Greece. n.
argo: The name of the ship which carried Jason and his fifty-four companions to Colchis, in quest of the Golden Fleece.
argol: Crude tartar; an acidulous salt from which cream of tartar is prepared. It exists in the juice of grapes, and is deposited from wines on the sides of the casks. Ure.
argon: A substance regarded as an element, contained in the atmosphere and remarkable for its chemical inertness. Rayleigh and Rams ay.
argonaut: A cephalopod of the genus Argonauta.
argonauta: A genus of Cephalopoda. The shell is called paper nautilus or paper sailor.
argonne: A long strip of wild mountainous woodland in northeastern France, approximately km ( mi) east of Paris.
argos: an ancient city in southeastern Greece; dominated the Peloponnese in the th century BC
argosy: A large ship, esp. a merchant vessel of the largest size. Where your argosies with portly sail. Do overpeer the petty traffickers.
argot: A secret language or conventional slang peculiar to thieves, tramps, and vagabonds; flash.
argued: simple past and past participle of argue
arguer: One who argues; a reasoner; a disputant.
argues: third-person singular simple present indicative of argue
argufies: third-person singular simple present indicative of argufy
argulus: A genus of copepod Crustacea, parasitic of fishes; a fish louse. See Branchiura.
argument: The quantity on which another quantity in a table depends; as, the altitude is the argument of the refraction.
argumentation: a course of reasoning aimed at demonstrating a truth or falsehood; the methodical process of logical reasoning
argumentative: given to or characterized by argument
argus: A fabulous being of antiquity, said to have had a hundred eyes, who has placed by Juno to guard Io. His eyes were transplanted to the peacock's tail.
argyle: a design consisting of a pattern of varicolored diamonds on a solid background (originally for knitted articles); patterned after the tartan of a clan in western Scotland
argyll: a covered gravy holder of silver or other metal containing a detachable central vessel for hot water to keep the gravy warm
argyria: A condition caused by excessive exposure to chemical compounds of the element silver, or to silver dust, the most dramatic symptom of which being that the skin turns purple or purple-grey.
argyrodite: a rare steel-grey mineral consisting of silver and germanium and sulfur
argyrol: An antiseptic compound of silver and a protein.
arhat: a Buddhist who has attained nirvana
aria: An air or song; a melody; a tune.
ariadne: beautiful daughter of Minos and Pasiphae; she fell in love with Theseus and gave him the thread with which he found his way out of the Minotaur's labyrinth
arianism: The doctrines of the Aria ns.
arianist: an adherent of Arianism (the belief that Jesus Christ was not truly God)
aricine: An alkaloid, first found in white cinchona bark.
arid: Exhausted of moisture; parched with heat; dry; barren. An arid waste. " Thomson.
aridity: a deficiency of moisture (especially when resulting from a permanent absence of rainfall)
ariel: A name for the city of Jerusalem, the claimed (and de-facto) capital city of modern Israel, and the claimed capital city of modern Palestine.
aright: Rightly; correctly; in a right way or form; without mistake or crime; as, to worship God aright.
aril: fleshy and usually brightly colored cover of some seeds that develops from the ovule stalk and partially or entirely envelopes the seed
arillate: (of some seeds) having a fleshy and usually brightly colored cover
arillode: A false aril; an aril originating from the micropyle instead of from the funicle or chalaza of the ovule. The mace of the nutmeg is an arillode.

arioso: In the smooth and melodious style of an air; ariose.
arises: third-person singular simple present indicative of arise
arising: present participle and gerund of arise
aristippus: A male given name from Ancient Greek, of historical usage.
aristocratic: belonging to or characteristic of the nobility or aristocracy
aristocratical: belonging to or characteristic of the nobility or aristocracy
aristocratism: The principles of aristocrats. Ro milly.
aristodemocracy: A form of government in which power is shared between the people and the aristocracy.
aristogenesis: A type of orthogenesis that operates by means of a creative principle.
aristolochiaceae: family of birth worts (including wild ginger)
aristolochiales: order of plants distinguished by tubular petaloid perianth and inferior ovary
aristology: The science of dining. Quart. Rev.
aristophanes: an ancient Greek dramatist remembered for his comedies (- BC)
aristotelian: Of or pertaining to Aristotle, the famous Greek philosopher (- b. c.). n.
aristotelianism: The philosophy of Aristotle, otherwise called the Peripatetic philosophy.
aristotelic: Pertaining to Aristotle or to his philosophy. Aristotelic usage. " Sir W. Hamilton.
aristotle: one of the greatest of the ancient Athenian philosophers; pupil of Plato; teacher of Alexander the Great (- BC)
arithmetic: the branch of pure mathematics dealing with the theory of numerical calculations
arithmetical: Of or pertaining to arithmetic; according to the rules or method of arithmetic. Arithmetical complement of a logarithm. See logarithm. Arithmetical mean. See Mean. Arithmetical progression. See Progression. Arithmetical proportion. See Proportion.
arithmetization: The treatment of mathematics by methods involving only the fundamental concepts and operations of arithmetic.
arithmetize: To treat (a mathematical system) by methods involving only the fundamental concepts and operations of arithmetic.
arithmocracy: A form of government where decisions are made based purely on the numerical majority of supporters.
arity: the number of arguments that a function can take
arius: a Greek who was a Christian theologian active in Alexandria and who was declared a heretic for his doctrines about God (which came to be known as Arianism) (?-)
arizona: a state in southwestern United States; site of the Grand Canyon
arizonan: a native or resident of Arizona
arjuna: (Hindu mythology) the warrior prince in the Bhagavad-Gita to whom Krishna explains the nature of being and of God and how humans can come to know God
ark: The oblong chest of acacia wood, overlaid with gold, which supported the mercy seat with its golden cherubs, and occupied the most sacred place in the sanctuary. In it Moses placed the two tables of stone containing the ten commandments. Called also the Ark of the covenant.
arkansan: a native or resident of Arkansas
arkansas: a state in south central United States; one of the Confederate states during the American Civil War
arkose: A sandstone derived from the disintegration of granite or gneiss, and characterized by feldspar fragments. Arkosic (#), a.
arlene: A female given name originating as a coinage.
arles: An earnest; earnest money; money paid to bind a bargain. Arles penny, earnest money given to servants. Kersey.
arm: To provide one's self with arms, weapons, or means of attack or resistance; to take arms. " 'Tis time to arm.
armada: A fleet of armed ships; a squadron. Specifically, the Spanish fleet which was sent to assail England, a. d.
armadillo: burrowing chiefly nocturnal mammal with body covered with strong horny plates
armageddon: (New Testament) the scene of the final battle between the kings of the Earth at the end of the world
armagnac: dry brandy distilled in the Armagnac district of France
armament: All the cannon and small arms collectively, with their equipments, belonging to a ship or a fortification.
armamentarium: the collection of equipment and methods used in the practice of medicine
armature: A piece of soft iron used to connect the two poles of a magnet, or electro-magnet, in order to complete the circuit, or to receive and apply the magnetic force. In the ordinary horseshoe magnet, it serves to prevent the dissipation of the magnetic force.
armband: worn around arm as identification or to indicate mourning
armchair: A chair with arms to support the elbows or forearms. Tennyson.
armenia: a landlocked republic in southwestern Asia; formerly an Asian soviet; modern Armenia is but a fragment of ancient Armenia which was one of the world's oldest civilizations; throughout years the Armenian people have been invaded and oppressed by their neighbors
armenian: Of or pertaining to Armenia. Armenian bole, a soft clayey earth of a bright red color found in Armenia, Tuscany, etc. Armenian stone. (a) The commercial name of lapis lazuli. (b) Emery.
armer: One who arms, or supplies weapons.
armeria: shrubby or herbaceous low-growing evergreen perennials
armet: A kind of helmet worn in the th, th, and th centuries.
armful: As much as the arm can hold.
armgaunt: With gaunt or slender legs. An armgaunt steed.
armhole: a hole through which you put your arm and where a sleeve can be attached
armiger: Formerly, an armor bearer, as of a knight, an esquire who bore his shield and rendered other services. In later use, one next in degree to a knight, and entitled to armorial bearings. The term isnow superseded by esquire. Jacob.
armigerous: Bearing arms. They belonged to the armigerous part of the population, and were entitled to write themselves Esquire. De Quincey.
armilla: A ring of hair or feathers on the legs.
armillaria: genus of edible mushrooms having white spores an annulus and blue juice; some are edible; some cause root rot
armillary: Pertaining to, or resembling, a bracelet or ring; consisting of rings or circles. Armillary sphere, an ancient astronomical machine composed of an assemblage of rings, all circles of the same sphere, designed to represent the positions of the important circles of the celestial sphere. Ni chol.
arming: A piece of tallow placed in a cavity at the lower end of as ounding lead, to bring up the sand, shells, etc., of the sea bottom. Totten.
arminian: Of or pertaining to Arminius of his followers, or to their doctrines. See note under Arminian, n.
arminianism: The religious doctrines or tenets of the Arminians.
arminius: Dutch Protestant theologian who founded Arminianism which opposed the absolute predestinarianism of John Calvin (-)
armipotent: Powerful in arms; mighty in battle. The temple stood of Mars armipotent. Dryden.
armistice: A cessation of arms for a short time, by convention; atemporary suspension of hostilities by agreement; a truce.
armlet: a band worn around the arm for decoration
armload: As much as can be carried with one, or a pair, of arms
armlock: A wrestling move in which the opponent's arm is held immobile.
armoire: a large wardrobe or cabinet; originally used for storing weapons
armonica: A musical instrument made of blown-glass bowls mounted on a spindle turned originally by a foot pedal, and played with wetted fingers, producing an ethereal sound. Technically, it is a crystallophone.
armorer: a worker skilled in making armor or arms
armorial: Belonging to armor, or to the heraldic arms or escutcheon of afamily. Figures with armorial signs of race and birth. Wordsworth. Armorial bearings. See Arms,.
armorica: The north-western part of ancient Gaul, corresponding to modern Brittany.
armory: A thick plain silk, generally black, and used for clerical. Simmon ds.
armour: tough more-or-less rigid protective covering of an animal or plant
armoured: protected by armor (used of persons or things military)
armoury: a place where arms are manufactured
armozeen: A thick plain silk, generally black, used for clerical garments.
armpit: The hollow beneath the junction of the arm and shoulder; the axilla.
arms: Anything which a man takes in his hand in anger, to strike or assault another with; an aggressive weapon. Co well. Black stone.
armstrong: United States astronaut; the first man to set foot on the Moon (July, ) (-)
army: a permanent organization of the military land forces of a nation or state
armyworm: noctuid moth larvae that travel in multitudes destroying especially grass and grain
arne: A male given name from the Germanic languages occasionally used in English.
arnica: A genus of plants; also, the most important species (Arnica montana), native of the mountains of Europe, used in medicine as anarcotic and stimulant.
arno: a river in central Italy rising in the Apennines and flowing through Florence and Pisa to the Ligurian Sea
aroid: relating to a plant of the family Araceae
aroideous: Of or relating to the aroids.
aroint: Stand off, or begone. Aroint thee, witch, the rump-fed ronyon cries.
arolium: A median lobe into which the pretarsus expands in an insect's leg.

See under Vinegar.
aromatic: A plant, drug, or medicine, characterized by a fragrant smell, and usually by a warm, pungent taste, as ginger, cinnamon spices.
aromatise: to fill or impregnate with an odor
aromatize: To impregnate with aroma; to render aromatic; to give a spicy scent or taste to; to perfume. Bacon.
aromatized: simple past and past participle of aromatize
arose: The past or preterit tense of Arise.
around: by a circular or circuitous route
arousal: The act of arousing, or the state of being aroused. Whatever has associated itself with the arousal and activity of our better nature. Hare.

Grasping his spear, forth issued to arouse His brother, mighty sovereign on the host. Cowper. No suspicion was aroused. Merivale.
arouser: someone who rouses others from sleep
arouses: third-person singular simple present indicative of arouse
arousing: present participle and gerund of arouse
arow: In a row, line, or rank; successively; in order. And twenty, rank in rank, they rode arow. Dryden.

arpen: Alternative form of arpent (old unit of measure)
arpent: a former French unit of area; equal approximately to an acre
arquebus: an obsolete firearm with a long barrel
arquebusade: The shot of an arquebus. Ash.

arracacha: A South American plant grown as a root vegetable, Arracacia xanthorrhiza
arrack: A name in the East Indies and the Indian islands for all ardent spirits. Arrack is often distilled from a fermented mixture of rice, molasses, and palm wine of the cocoanut tree or the date palm, etc.

arraigning: present participle and gerund of arraign

arraigns: third-person singular simple present indicative of arraign

arranged: disposed or placed in a particular kind of order
arrangement: an orderly grouping (of things or persons) considered as a unit; the result of arranging
arranges: third-person singular simple present indicative of arrange

arrayal: The way something is arrayed or laid out.
arrayer: One who arrays. In some early English statutes, applied to an officer who had care of the soldiers' armor, and who saw them duly accoutered.
arrear: To or in the rear; behind; backwards. Spenser.
arrearage: That which remains unpaid and overdue, after payment of a part; arrears. The old arrearages. being defrayed. Howell.

arrestment: The arrest of a person, or the seizure of his effects; esp., aprocess by which money or movables in the possession of a third party are attached.
arrhenotoky: The production of male offspring by parthenogenesis.
arrhythmia: an abnormal rate of muscle contractions in the heart
arrhythmias: plural of arrhythmia, which can refer to types of arrhythmia, cases of arrhythmia, or episodes of arrhythmia.
arrhythmically: In an arrhythmic manner; without a fixed rhythm
arriccio: A layer of plaster laid slightly coarsely to provide a key for the intonaco.
arride: To please; to gratify. B. Jonson. Above all thy rarities, old Oxen ford, what do most arride and solace me are thy repositories of moldering learning. Lamb.

arrish: The stubble of wheat or grass; a stubble field; eddish. The moment we entered the stubble or arrish. Blackw. Mag.

arrives: third-person singular simple present indicative of arrive

arroba: a unit of weight used in some Spanish speaking countries

I hate not you for her proud arrogance.
arrogant: having or showing feelings of unwarranted importance out of overbearing pride
arrogantly: In an arrogant manner; with undue pride or self-importance.

He arrogated to himself the right of deciding dogmatically what was orthodox doctrine. Macaulay.
arrogated: simple past and past participle of arrogate
arrogates: third-person singular simple present indicative of arrogate
arrogating: present participle and gerund of arrogate
arrogation: Adoption of a person of full age.
arrose: To drench; to besprinkle; to moisten. The blissful dew of heaven does arrose you. Two N. Kins.

arrowhead: An aquatic plant of the genus Sagittaria, esp. S. sagittifolia, named from the shape of the leaves.

arrowlike: Resembling or characteristic of an arrow.

arrowy: Consisting of arrows. How quick they wheeled, and flying, behind them shot Sharp sleet of arrowy showers. Milton.
arse: The buttocks, or hind part of an animal; the posteriors; the fundament; the bottom.
arsenal: A public establishment for the storage, or for the manufacture and storage, of arms and all military equipments, whether for land or naval service.
arsenical: Of or pertaining to, or containing, arsenic; as, arsenical vapor; arsenical wall papers. Arsenical silver, an ore of silver containing arsenic.
arsenicate: To combine with arsenic; to treat or impregnate with arsenic.
arsenide: A compound of arsenic with a metal, or positive element or radical; formerly called arseniuret.
arseniosiderite: A monoclinic-prismatic mineral containing arsenic, calcium, hydrogen, iron, and oxygen.

arshin: An obsolete Russian length unit, equal to. centimeters, or inches.
arshine: A Russian measure of length = ft. inches.
arsine: A compound of arsenic and hydrogen, As H, a colorless and exceedingly poisonous gas, having and odor like garlic; arseniureted hydrogen.
arsinic: Of, related to, or derived from an arsinic acid.
arsis: The elevation of the hand, or that part of the bar at which itis raised, in beating time; the weak or unaccented part of the bar; opposed to thesis. Moore.
arson: The malicious burning of a dwelling house or outhouse of another man, which by the common law is felony; the malicious and voluntary firing of a building or ship. Wharton.
arsonic: Of or pertaining to arsonic acids or their derivatives
arsonist: a criminal who illegally sets fire to property
arsphenamine: A phenolic amine derivative of arsenic that was used to treat syphilis (under the trade name of Salvarsan).
art: The second person singular, indicative mode, present tense, of the substantive verb Be; but formed after the analogy of the plural are, with the ending -t, as in thou shalt, wilt, orig. an ending of the second person sing. pret. Cf. Be. Now used only in solemn or poetical style.
artefact: a man-made object taken as a whole
artel: A Russian or Soviet craftsmen's collective.
artemia: A genus of phyllopod Crustacea found in salt lakes and brines; the brine shrimp. See Brine shrimp.
artemis: (Greek mythology) the virgin goddess of the hunt and the Moon; daughter of Leto and twin sister of Apollo; identified with Roman Diana
artemisia: A genus of plants including the plants called mugwort, southernwood, and wormwood. Of these A. absinthium, or common wormwood, is well known, and A. tri dentata is the sage brush of the rocky Mountain region.
arteria: a blood vessel that carries blood from the heart to the body
arterial: of or involving or contained in the arteries
arterialise: to change venous blood into arterial blood
arterialize: To transform, as the venous blood, into arterial blood by exposure to oxygen in the lungs; to make arterial.
arterialized: simple past and past participle of arterialize
arteriography: A systematic description of the arteries.
arteriosclerosis: Abnormal thickening and hardening of the walls of the arteries, esp. of the intima, occurring mostly in old age. Arteriosclerotic (#), a.
arteriotomy: The opening of an artery, esp. for bloodletting.
artery: One of the vessels or tubes which carry either venous or arterial blood from the heart. They have tricker and more muscular walls than veins, and are connected with them by capillaries.
artesian: Of or pertaining to Artois (anciently called Arte sium), in france. Artesian wells, wells made by boring into the earth till the instrument reaches water, which, from internal pressure, flows spontaneously like a fountain. They are usually of small diameter and often of great depth.
artful: marked by skill in achieving a desired end especially with cunning or craft
artfully: In an artful manner; with art or cunning; skillfully; dexterously; craftily.
artfulness: The quality of being artful; art; cunning; craft.
artha: One of the four aims of human life in Indian philosophy, along with dharma (righteousness), kama (desire), and moksha (liberation). The concept is variously translated, with translations including meaning/purpose/goal and wealth.
arthen: Same as Earthen. An arthen pot. " Holland.
arthralgia: pain in a joint or joints
arthritis: Any inflammation of the joints, particularly the gout.
arthrodia: A form of diarthrodial articulation in which the articular surfaces are nearly flat, so that they form only an imperfect ball and socket.
arthrodial: Of or pertaining to arthrodia or to an arthrosis
arthrodire: Any member of the extinct order Arthrodira, armored jawed fishes that flourished in the Devonian period.
arthrodynia: An affection characterized by pain in or about a joint, not dependent upon structural disease.
arthrogastra: A division of the Arachnida, having the abdomen annulated, including the scorpions, harvestmen, etc.; pedipalpi.
arthrology: That part of anatomy which treats of joints.
arthromere: One of the body segments of Arthropods. See Arthrostraca. Packard.

arthropomata: One of the orders of Branchiopoda. See Branchiopoda.
arthropomatous: Relating to, or characteristic of brachiopods of the order Arthropomata
arthrostraca: One of the larger divisions of Crustacea, so called because the thorax and abdomen are both segmented; Tetradecapoda. It includes the amphipoda and Isopoda.
arthrotomy: The surgical incision of a joint.
arthur: elected vice president and became st President of the United States when Garfield was assassinated (-)
arthurian: Of or pertaining to King Arthur or his knights. J. R. Symonds.
artiad: Even; not odd; said of elementary substances and of radicals the valence of which is divisible by two without a remainder.
artichoke: Mediterranean thistlelike plant widely cultivated for its large edible flower head
article: One of the three words, a, an, the, used before nouns to limitor define their application. A (or an) is called the indefinite article, the the definite article.
articled: Bound by articles; apprenticed; as, an articled clerk.
articulable: Capable of being pronounced or expressed distinctly in speech.
articular: Of or pertaining to the joints; as, an articular disease; an articular process.
articulata: One of the four subkingdoms in the classification of Cuvier. It has been much modified by later writers.
articulate: An animal of the subkingdom Articulata.
articulated: consisting of segments held together by joints
articulates: third-person singular simple present indicative of articulate
articulating: present participle and gerund of articulate
articulation: A joint or juncture between bones in the skeleton.
articulator: One who, or that which, articulates; as: (a) One who enunciates distinctly. (b) One who prepares and mounts skeletons. (c) An instrument to cure stammering.
artifact: A product of human workmanship; applied esp. to the simpler products of aboriginal art as distinguished from natural objects.
artifice: A handicraft; a trade; art of making.
artificer: A military mechanic, as a blacksmith, carpenter, etc.; also, one who prepares the shells, fuses, grenades, etc., in a military laboratory.
artificial: contrived by art rather than nature
artificiality: The quality or appearance of being artificial; that which is artificial.
artificially: not according to nature; not by natural means
artillerist: A person skilled in artillery or gunnery; a gunner; an artilleryman.
artilleryman: A man who manages, or assists in managing, a large gun in firing.
artiodactyl: of or relating to or belonging to mammals of the order Artiodactyla

artisan: One who professes and practices some liberal art; an artist.
artist: a person whose creative work shows sensitivity and imagination
artiste: One peculiarly dexterous and tasteful in almost any employment, as an opera dancer, a hairdresser, a cook.
artistic: relating to or characteristic of art or artists
artless: simple and natural; without cunning or deceit
artlessly: In an artless manner; without art, skill, or guile; unaffectedly. Pope.
artlessness: The quality of being artless, or void of art or guile; simplicity; sincerity.

binoculars: an optical instrument designed for simultaneous use by both eyes
binode: A double point of a surface whose tangent cone consists of two different planes.

binotonous: Consisting of two notes; as, a binotonous cry.

biogeographical: of or relating to or involved with biogeography

biological: pertaining to biology or to life and living things

biomass: plant materials and animal waste used as fuel

Dryden.

bodyweight: The weight or mass of an organism.

Bookkeeping by single entry, the method of keeping books by carrying the record of each transaction to the debit or credit of a single account. Bookkeeping by double entry, a mode of bookkeeping in which two entries of every transaction are carried to the ledger, one to the Dr., or left hand, side of one account, and the other to the Cr., or right hand, side of a corresponding account, in order tha Italianmethod.
