choriomeningitis: a cerebral meningitis with cellular infiltration of the meninges
chorion: The outer membrane of seeds of plants.
chorionic: of or relating to a chorion
chorisis: The separation of a leaf or floral organ into two more parts.
chorizont: One who challenges a widely held assumption of authorship for a major work, especially one who believes that the Iliad and the Odyssey were not written by Homer.
chorograph: An instrument for constructing triangles in marine surveying, etc.
chorography: the mapping or description of a region or district. The chorography of their provinces. Sir T. Browne.
choroid: resembling the chorion; as, the choroid plexuses of the ventricles of the brain, and the choroid coat of the eyeball. n.
chorology: The science which treats of the laws of distribution of living organisms over the earth's surface as to latitude, altitude, locality, etc. Its distribution or chorology. Huxley.
chortle: A word coined by Lewis Carroll (Charles L. Dodgson), and usually explained as a combination of chuckle and snort.
chorus: A band of singers and dancers. The Grecian tragedy was at first nothing but a chorus of singers. Dryden.
chose: A thing; personal property. Chose in action, a thing of which one has not possession or actual enjoyment, but only a right to it, or a right to demand it by action at law, and which does not exist at the time in specie; a personal right to a thing not reduced to possession, but recoverable by suit at law; as a right to recover money due on a contract, or damages for a tort, which can not been forced against a reluctant party without suit. Chose in possession, a thing in possession, as distinguished from a thing in action. Chose local, a thing annexed to a place, as a mill. Chose transitory, a thing which is movable. Co well. Blount.
chosen: Selected from a number; picked out; choice. Seven hundred chosen men left-handed. Judg. xx.
chott: A dry salt lake, in the Saharan area of Africa, that stays dry in the summer but receives some water in the winter.
chough: A bird of the Crow family (Fregilus graculus) of Europe. It isof a black color, with a long, slender, curved bill and red legs; also called chauk, chauk-daw, chocard, Cornish chough, red-legged crow. The name is also applied to several allied birds, as the Alpine chough. Cornish chough (Her.), a bird represented black, with red feet, and beak; called also aylet and sea swallow.
chouicha: The salmon of the Columbia River or California. See Quinnat.
chouse: To cheat, trick, defraud; followed by of, or out of; as, to chouse one out of his money. The undertaker of the afore-cited poesy hath choused your highness. Land or.
choused: simple past and past participle of chouse
chouser: Agent noun of chouse: one who chouses.
chouses: third-person singular simple present indicative of chouse
chow: A prefecture or district of the second rank in China, or the chief city of such a district; often part of the name of a city, as in Foochow.
chowchow: Consisting of several kinds mingled together; mixed; as, chowchow sweetmeats (preserved fruits put together).
chowder: A dish made of fresh fish or clams, biscuit, onions, etc.,stewed together.
chowderheaded: Stupid; foolish; lacking in common sense.
chowry: A whisk to keep off files, used in the East Indies. Mal com.
chowtime: The time when food is eaten; a mealtime.
choy: A surname from Korean or Cantonese.
chremsel: A fried dumpling made of matzo meal and filled with fruit, typically prunes, and eaten on Passover.
chresard: The portion of the water in a sample of soil that is available to vegetation (e.g. plant roots)
chrestomathic: Teaching what is useful. A chrestomathic school. " Southey.
chrestomathy: A selection of passages, with notes, etc., to be used in acquiring a language; as, a Hebrew chrestomathy.
chris: A diminutive of the male given names Christopher or (less commonly) Christian.
chrism: a consecrated ointment consisting of a mixture of oil and balsam
chrismation: The act of applying the chrism, or consecrated oil. Chrismation or cross-signing with ointment, was used in baptism. Jer. Taylor.
chrismatory: A cruet or vessel in which chrism is kept.
chrisom: A white cloth, anointed with chrism, or a white mantle thrown over a child when baptized or christened.
christ: The Anointed; an appellation given to Jesus, the Savior. It is synonymous with the Hebrew Messiah.
christcross: The mark of the cross, as cut, painted, written, or stamped on certain objects, sometimes as the sign of o'clock on a dial. The fescue of the dial is upon the christcross of noon. Old Play. Nares.
christella: any of several tropical ferns of the genus Christella having thin brittle fronds
christen: To baptize and give a Christian name to.
christendom: the collective body of Christians throughout the world and history (found predominantly in Europe and the Americas and Australia)
christened: simple past and past participle of christen
christening: giving a Christian name at baptism
christens: third-person singular simple present indicative of christen
christian: relating to or characteristic of Christianity
christianity: a monotheistic system of beliefs and practices based on the Old Testament and the teachings of Jesus as embodied in the New Testament and emphasizing the role of Jesus as savior
christianize: To adopt the character or belief of a Christian; to become christian. The pagans began to Christianize. Latham.
christianized: simple past and past participle of Christianize
christianizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of Christianize
christianlike: Becoming to a Christian. A virtuous and a Christianlike conclusion.
christianly: In a manner becoming the principles of the Christian religion. Sufferings. patiently and Christianly borne. Sharp.
christie: prolific English writer of detective stories (-)
christina: A female given name from Ancient Greek.
christine: A female given name from Ancient Greek.
christlike: Resembling Christ in character, actions, etc. Christlikeness, n.
christmas: An annual church festival (December ) and in some States al egal holiday, in memory of the birth of Christ, often celebrated by a particular church service, and also by special gifts, greetings, and hospitality. Christmas box. (a) A box in which presents are deposited at Christmas. (b) A present or small gratuity given to young people and servants at Christmas; a Christmas gift. Christmas carol, a carol sung at, or suitable for, Christmas. Christmas day. Same as Christmas. Christmas eve, the evening before Christmas. Christmas fern (Bot.), an evergreen North American fern (Aspidiumacrostichoides), which is much used for decoration in winter. Christmas flower, Christmas rose, the black hellebore, apoisonous plant of the buttercup family, which in Southern Europe often produces beautiful roselike flowers midwinter. Christmas tree, a small evergreen tree, set up indoors, to be decorated with bonbons, presents, etc., and illuminated on Christmas eve.
christogram: A monogram that forms an abbreviation for the name of Jesus Christ, traditionally used as a Christian symbol, such as the chi-rho.
christology: A treatise on Christ; that department of theology which treats of the personality, attributes, or life of Christ.
christopher: Christian martyr and patron saint of travellers (rd century)
chroma: chromatic purity: freedom from dilution with white and hence vivid in hue
chromaffin: Having an affinity for (and thus being stained brownish yellow) by chromium salts.
chromatic: Proceeding by the smaller intervals (half steps or semitones) of the scale, instead of the regular intervals of the diatonic scale.
chromatics: The science of colors; that part of optics which treats of the properties of colors.
chromatid: one of two identical strands into which a chromosome splits during mitosis
chromatin: Tissue which is capable of being stained by dyes.
chromatism: The state of being colored, as in the case of images formed by a lens.
chromatolysis: The dissolution of the Nissl bodies in the cell body of a neuron.
chromatophilia: The property of a cell that readily stains with an appropriate dye
chromatophore: A contractile cell or vesicle containing liquid pigment and capable of changing its form or size, thus causing changes of colorin the translucent skin of such animals as possess them. They are highly developed and numerous in the cephalopods.
chromatoplasm: The part of cytoplasm that contains pigment.
chrome: Same as Chromium. Chrome alum (Chem.), a dark violet substance,(SO)Cr.KSO.HO, analogous to, and crystallizing like, common alum. It is regarded as a double sulphate of chromium and potassium. Chrome green (a) The green oxide of chromium, CrO, used in enamel painting, and glass staining. (b) A pigment made by mixing chrome yellow with Prussian blue. Chrome red, a beautiful red pigment originally prepared from the basic chromate of lead, but now made from red oxide of lead. Chrome yellow, a brilliant yellow pigment, Pb Cr O, used by painters.
chromed: simple past and past participle of chrome
chromesthesia: a form of synesthesia in which nonvisual stimulation results in the experience of color sensations
chromic: Pertaining to, or obtained from, chromium; said of the compounds of chromium in which it has its higher valence. Chromic acid, an acid, HCr O, analogous to sulphuric acid, not readily obtained in the free state, but forming well known salts, many of which are colored pigments, as chrome yellow, chrome red, etc. Chromic anhydride, a brilliant red crystalline substance, Cr O,regarded as the anhydride of chromic acid. It is one of the most powerful oxidizers known.
chromide: Any of various cichlid fishes found in Asia.
chromite: A black submetallic mineral consisting of oxide of chromium andiron; called also chromic iron.
chromium: A comparatively rare element occurring most abundantly in the mineral chromite. Atomic weight. Symbol Cr. When isolated it is a hard, brittle, grayish white metal, fusible with difficulty. Its chief commercial importance is for its compounds, as potassium chromate, lead chromate, etc., which are brilliantly colored and are used dyeing and calico printing. Called also chrome.
chromize: To chrome; to treat with chromium.
chromogen: Vegetable coloring matter other than green; chromule.
chromogenic: Containing, or capable of forming, chromogen; as, chromogenic bacteria.
chromolithograph: A picture printed in tints and colors by repeated impressions from a series of stones prepared by the lithographic process.
chromolithographic: Pertaining to, or made by, chromolithography.
chromolithography: Lithography adapted to printing in inks of various colors.
chromone: ,-benzopyrone, a derivative of benzopyran with a substituted keto group on the pyran ring
chromonema: The central coiled filament of a chromatid upon which the chromomeres lie
chromophane: A general name for the several coloring matters, red, green, yellow, etc., present in the inner segments in the cones of the retina, held in solution by fats, and slowly decolorized by light; distinct from the photochemical pigments of the rods of the retina.
chromophile: Any cell that can be easily stained.
chromophore: Any chemical group or residue (as NO
chromoplast: plastid containing pigments other than chlorophyll usually yellow or orange carotenoids
chromoplastid: A protoplasmic granule of some other color than green; also called chromoleucite.
chromoscope: A device that adds colours to a monochrome image or adjusts existing colours to appear more natural
chromosomal: of or relating to a chromosome
chromosome: One of the minute bodies into which the chromatin of the nucleus is resolved during mitotic cell division; the idant of weismann.
chromosphere: An atmosphere of rare matter, composed principally of incandescent hydrogen gas, surrounding the sun and enveloping the photosphere. Portions of the chromosphere are here and there thrown up into enormous tongues of flame.
chromotherapy: A form of alternative medicine involving the therapeutic use of color and light.
chromotropism: orientation relative to a colour stimulus
chromotypography: Color printing: the printing of text in colour.
chromous: Of, pertaining to, or derived from, chromium, when this element has a valence lower than that in chromic compounds. Chromous acid, abluish gray powder, Cr O.OH, of weak acid properties and regard as anacid.
chromule: A general name for coloring matter of plants other than chlorophyll, especially that of petals.
chron: A period of time between two geomagnetic reversals.
chronaxie: The minimum time over which an electric current must be applied in order to stimulate a muscle fiber or nerve cell.
chronic: being long-lasting and recurrent or characterized by long suffering
chronical: Chronic. Partly on a chronical, and partly on a topical method. J. A.Alexander.
chronically: in a habitual and longstanding manner
chronicle: The two canonical books of the Old Testament in which immediately follow Kings.
chronicled: simple past and past participle of chronicle
chronicler: A writer of a chronicle; a recorder of events in the order of time; an historian. Such an honest chronicler as Griffith.
chronogenesis: The development of a group of organisms over time
chronogenetic: Relating to chronogenesis (or to chronological age)
chronogram: Belonging to a chronogram, or containing one.
chronogrammatic: Relating to, or containing a chronogram
chronograph: an accurate timer for recording time
chronographic: Of or pertaining to a chronograph.
chronography: A description or record of past time; history. Bp. Hall.
chronological: relating to or arranged according to temporal order
chronologize: establish the order in time of something
chronology: The science which treats of measuring time by regular divisions or periods, and which assigns to events or transactions their proper dates. If history without chronology is dark and confused, chronology without history is dry and insipid. A. Holmes.
chronomancy: The divination of the best time to do something, or the determination of lucky and unlucky days.
chronometer: A metronome. Box chronometer. See under Box. Pocket chronometer, a chronometer in the form of a large watch. To rate a chronometer. See Rate, v. t.
chronometric: Of or related to chronometers, clocks and other timekeeping devices.
chronometrically: In a chronometric way, following the principles of chronometry.
chronometry: The art of measuring time; the measuring of time by periods or divisions.
chronon: A hypothetical quantum or particle of time.
chronophotography: An antique photographic technique from the Victorian era which captures movement in several frames of print.
chronoscope: An instrument for measuring minute intervals of time; used in determining the velocity of projectiles, the duration of short-lived luminous phenomena, etc.
chronoscopic: Of or relating to a chronoscope or chronoscopy.
chronoscopy: The measurement and study of extremely small time intervals by means of a chronoscope.
chrysalid: Pertaining to a chrysalis; resembling a chrysalis.
chrysalis: The pupa state of certain insects, esp. of butterflies, from which the perfect insect emerges. See Pupa, and Aurelia (a).
chrysanthemum: A genus of composite plants, mostly perennial, and of many species including the many varieties of garden chrysanthemums (annual and perennial), and also the feverfew and the oxeye daisy.
chrysarobin: A bitter, yellow substance forming the essential constituent of Goa powder, and yielding chrysophanic acid proper; hence formerly called also chrysphanic acid.
chrysene: One of the higher aromatic hydrocarbons of coal tar, allied tonapthalene and anthracene. It is a white crystalline substance, CH, of strong blue fluorescence, but generally colored yellow by impurities.
chrysippus: A male given name of historical usage, notably borne by Chrysippus, an Ancient Greek Stoic philosopher of the Hellenistic period.
chrysoberyl: A mineral, found in crystals, of a yellow to green or brown color, and consisting of alum inia and glucina. It is very hard, andis often used as a gem.
chrysolite: A mineral, composed of silica, magnesia, and iron, of a yellow to green color. It is common in certain volcanic rocks; called also olivine and peridot. Sometimes used as a gem. The name was also early used for yellow varieties of tourmaline and topaz.
chrysomelid: brightly colored beetle that feeds on plant leaves
chrysopa: A genus of neuropterous insects. See Lacewing.
chrysophane: A glucoside extracted from rhubarb as a bitter, yellow, crystalline powder, and yielding chrysophanic acid on decomposition.
chrysophanic: Pertaining to, or derived from, or resembling, chrysophane. Chrysophanic acid (Chem.), a yellow crystalline substance extracted from rhubarb, yellow dock, sienna, chrysarobin, etc., and shown to bea derivative of an anthracene. It is used in the treatment of skin diseases; called also rhein, rheic acid, rhubarbarin, etc.
chrysophyllum: tropical American evergreen trees or shrubs
chrysophyte: Any golden alga of the class Chrysophyceae
chrysoprase: An apple-green variety of chalcedony, colored by nickel. It hasa dull flinty luster, and is sometimes used in jewelry.
chrysosplenium: genus of widely distributed semiaquatic herbs with minute greenish-yellow apetalous flowers
chrysothamnus: genus of low branching shrubs of western North America
chthonian: Designating, or pertaining to, gods or spirits of the underworld; esp., relating to the underworld gods of the Greeks, whose worship is widely considered as more primitive in form than that of the Olympian gods. The characteristics of chthonian worship are propitiatory and magical rites and generalized or euphemistic names of the deities, which are supposed to have been primarily ghosts.
chthonophagia: A disease characterized by the impulsive consumption of dirt, observed in some parts of the southern United States as well as the West Indies.
chubasco: A violent squall with thunder and lightning, encountered during the rainy season along the Pacific coast of Central America and South America.
chubby: Like a chub; plump, short, and thick. Chubby faces. " I.Taylor.
chuck: To call, as a hen her chickens. Dryden.
chuckhole: a pit or hole produced by wear or weathering (especially in a road surface)
chuckle: A short, suppressed laugh; the expression of satisfaction, exultation, or derision.
chuckleheaded: Having a large head; thickheaded; dull; stupid. Smart.
chuckling: present participle and gerund of chuckle
chuckwalla: a herbivorous lizard that lives among rocks in the arid parts of southwestern United States and Mexico
chucky: A diminutive of the male given name Chuck, related to Charles.
chud: To champ; to bite. A. Stafford.
chuddar: a cloth used as a head covering (and veil and shawl) by Muslim and Hindu women
chufa: A sedgelike plant (Cyperus esculent us) producing edible tubers, native about the Mediterranean, now cultivated in many regions; the earth almond.
chuffy: Fat or puffed out in the cheeks.
chugalug: To swallow (a container of beer etc.) without pausing.
chugger: An aggressive or invasive street fundraiser, especially a private contractor working on behalf of a charity.
chuhra: A member of the Chuhra caste in India
chukar: A bird of species of partridge native to central Asia (Alectoris chukar).
chukchi: a member of an indigenous people living on the Chukchi Peninsula
chukka: a shoe that comes up to the ankle and is laced through two or three pairs of eyelets; often made of suede
chukker: (polo) one of six divisions into which a polo match is divided
chum: A roommate, especially in a college or university; an old and intimate friend.
chumminess: the quality of affording easy familiarity and sociability
chummy: (used colloquially) having the relationship of friends or pals
chump: A short, thick, heavy piece of wood. Morton. Chump end, the thick end; as, the chump end of a joint of meat. Dickens.
chumpish: Like a chump; foolish and incompetent.
chumship: The condition of being chums; friendship.
chunk: A short, thick piece of anything.
chunter: To speak in a soft, indistinct manner, mutter.
chuppah: The canopy over a Jewish couple during their marriage ceremony.
church: To bless according to a prescribed form, or to unite with in publicly returning thanks in church, as after deliverance from the dangers of childbirth; as, the churching of women.
churchianity: Any practices of Christianity that place a larger emphasis on the habits of church life or the institutional traditions of the church than on theology and spiritual teachings of Jesus; the quality of being too church-focused.
churchill: English general considered one of the greatest generals in history (-)
churching: The ceremonial blessing of a woman who has given birth.
churchite: A supporter of a particular church.
churchlike: Befitting a church or a churchman; becoming to a clergyman.
churchly: Pertaining to, or suitable for, the church; ecclesiastical.
churchwarden: an officer in the Episcopal church who helps a parish priest with secular matters
churchwoman: The female equivalent of a churchman.
churchy: Relating to a church; unduly fond of church forms.
churchyard: The ground adjoining a church, in which the dead are buried; acemetery. Like graves in the holy churchyard.
churidars: tight trousers worn by people from the Indian subcontinent (typically with a kameez or kurta)
churn: A vessel in which milk or cream is stirred, beaten, or otherwise agitated (as by a plunging or revolving dasher) in order toseparete the oily globules from the other parts, and obtain butter.
churned: simple past and past participle of churn
churner: The vessel in which cream is churned to make butter.
churning: moving with or producing or produced by vigorous agitation
churr: A vibrant or whirring noise such as that made by some insects, as the cockchafer, or by some birds, as the nightjar, the partridge, etc.
churrus: A powerfully narcotic and intoxicating gum resin which exudes from the flower heads, seeds, etc., of Indian hemp.
chut: A repeated short, low vocal sound made by guinea pigs, thought to express interest or curiosity.
chute: A warm or spicy condiment or pickle made in India, compounded of various vegetable substances, sweets, acids, etc.
chutney: a spicy condiment made of chopped fruits or vegetables cooked in vinegar and sugar with ginger and spices
chuvash: a member of a people of Turkic speech living in the Volga region in eastern Russia
chyazic: of, or derived from chyazic acid
chylaceous: Possessed of the properties of chyle; consisting of chyle.
chyle: A milky fluid containing the fatty matter of the food in astate of emulsion, or fine mechanical division; formed from chyme by the action of the intestinal juices. It is absorbed by the lacteals, and conveyed into the blood by the thoracic duct.
chylifaction: The act or process by which chyle is formed from food in animal bodies; chylification, a digestive process.
chylifactive: Producing, or converting into, chyle; having the power to form chyle.
chyliferous: (Physiol.) Transmitting or conveying chyle; as, chyliferous vessels.
chylification: The formation of chyle. See Chylifaction.
chylify: To make chyle of; to be converted into chyle.
chylopoetic: Concerned in the formation of chyle; as, the chylopoetic organs.
chyluria: A morbid condition in which the urine contains chyle or fatty matter, giving it a milky appearance.
chyme: The pulpy mass of semi-digested food in the small intestines just after its passage from the stomach. It is separated in the intestines into chyle and excrement. See Chyle.
chymosin: an enzyme that occurs in gastric juice
chymotrypsin: An endopeptidase enzyme that cleaves peptides at the carboxyl side of tyrosine, tryptophan, and phenylalanine amino acids.
chytrid: Any fungus of the phylum Chytridiomycota.
chytridiaceae: a family of aquatic fungi of order Chytridiales
chytridiales: simple aquatic fungi mostly saprophytic but some parasitic on higher plants or animals or fresh water fungi; sometimes placed in class Oomycetes
chytridiosis: A disease associated with the presence of chytrids.
ci: being one more than one hundred
ciao: an acknowledgment that can be used to say hello or goodbye, from Italian
cibarium: A pouchy space in front of the mouth cavity of some insects, used to store and chew food.
cibol: A perennial alliaceous plant (Allium fistulosum), sometime scalled Welsh onion. Its fistular leaves are used in cookery.
ciborium: A canopy usually standing free and supported on four columns, covering the high altar, or, very rarely, a secondary altar.
cicada: Any species of the genus Cicada. They are large hemipterous insects, with nearly transparent wings. The male makes a shrill sound by pecul ar organs in the under side of the abdomen, consisting of apair of stretched membranes, acted upon by powerful muscles. A noted american species (C. septendecim) is called the seventeen year locust. Another common species is the dog day cicada.
cicala: A cicada. See Cicada. At eve a dry cicala sung. " Tennis on.
cicatricula: The point, in the yolk of an egg, from which the embryo is formed.
cicatrise: to form a scar, after an injury
cicatrix: The pellicle which forms over a wound or breach of continuity and completes the process of healing in the latter, and which subsequently contracts and becomes white, forming the scar.
cicatrization: The process of forming a cicatrix, or the state of being cicatrized.
cicatrize: To heal or induce the formation of a cicatrix in, as in wounded or ulcerated flesh. Wiseman.
cicatrized: simple past and past participle of cicatrize
cicely: Any one of several umbelliferous plants, of the genera Myrrhis, Osmorrhiza, etc.
cicero: Pica type; so called by French printers.
cicerone: One who shows strangers the curiosities of a place; a guide. Every glib and loquacious hireling who shows strangers about their picture galleries, palaces, and ruins, is termed by thema cicerone, or a Cicero. Trench.
ciceronian: Resembling Cicero in style or action; eloquent.
ciceronianism: Imitation of, or resemblance to, the style or action Cicero; a Ciceronian phrase or expression. Great study in Ciceronianism, the chief abuse of Oxford. " Sir P. Sidney.
ciceronianist: One who writes in the style of Cicero.
cichlid: freshwater fishes of tropical America and Africa and Asia similar to American sunfishes; some are food fishes; many small ones are popular in aquariums
cichoraceous: Belonging to, or resembling, a suborder of composite plants of which the chicory (Cichorium) is the type.
cicisbeo: A professed admirer of a married woman; a dangler about women.
ciclatoun: A costly cloth, of uncertain material, used in the Middle Ages. His robe was of ciclatoun, That coste many a Jane. Chaucer.
ciconia: type genus of the Ciconiidae: European storks
ciconiiformes: order of chiefly tropical marsh-dwelling fish-eating wading birds with long legs and bills and (except for flamingos) unwebbed feet: herons; storks; spoonbills; flamingos; ibises
cicuta: a genus of poisonous umbelliferous plants, of which the water hemlock or cowbane is best known.
cid: Chief or commander; in Spanish literature, a title of Ruy Diaz, Count of Bivar, a champion of Christianity and of the old Spanish royalty, in the th century.
cider: The expressed juice of apples. It is used as a beverage, for making vinegar, and for other purposes.
ciderkin: A kind of weak cider made by steeping the refuse pomace in water. Ciderkin is made for common drinking, and supplies the place of small beer. Mortimer.
cienega: A marshy spring where groundwater bubbles to the surface.
cif: Initialism of cost, insurance and freight.
cigaret: finely ground tobacco wrapped in paper
cigarette: A little cigar; a little fine tobacco rolled in paper for smoking.
cigarillo: small cigar or cigarette wrapped in tobacco instead of paper
cilantro: parsley-like herb used as seasoning or garnish
ciliary: Pertaining to the cilia, or eyelashes. Also applied to special parts of the eye itself; as, the ciliary processes of the choroid coat; the ciliary muscle, etc.
ciliate: a protozoan with a microscopic appendage extending from the surface of the cell
ciliated: having a margin or fringe of hairlike projections
cilice: A kind of haircloth undergarment. Southey.
cilicious: Made, or consisting, of hair. A Cilicious or sackcloth habit. Sir T. Browne.
cimbal: A kind of confectionery or cake. Nares.
cimbalom: A type of concert hammered dulcimer used primarily in the music of Central and Eastern Europe.
cimbia: A fillet or band placed around the shaft of a column as if to strengthen it.
cimbri: An ancient tribe that invaded southern Europe between and BCE, generally thought to have been Germanic (though they could have been Celtic) and associated with Jutland and northern Germany.
cimbric: Pertaining to the Cimbri, an ancient tribe inhabiting Northern germany. n.
cimex: A genus of hemipterous insects of which the bedbug is the best known example. See Bedbug.
cimicifuga: small genus of perennial herbs of north temperate regions: bugbane
cimmerian: intensely dark and gloomy as with perpetual darkness
cincholoipon: The carboxylic acid -[(R,S)ethylpiperidinyl]acetic acid formed by the oxidation of cinchonine
cinchona: A genus of trees growing naturally on the Andes in Peru and adjacent countries, but now cultivated in the East Indies, producinga medicinal bark of great value.
cinchonic: Belonging to, or obtained from, cinchona. Mayne.
cinchonidine: One of the quinine group of alkaloids, found especially in red cinchona bark. It is a white crystalline substance, CHNO, with abit ter taste and qualities similar to, but weaker than, quinine; sometimes called also cinchonidia.
cinchonine: One of the quinine group of alkaloids isomeric with and resembling cinchonidine; called also cinchonia.
cinchonism: A condition produced by the excessive or long-continued use of quinine, and marked by deafness, roaring in the ears, vertigo, etc.
cinchonize: To produce cinchonism in; to poison with quinine or with cinchona.
cinchonizing: present participle and gerund of cinchonize
cinchophen: An analgesic drug used to treat gout in animals (and, until the s, in humans, when it was found to cause liver damage).
cincinnati: a city in southern Ohio on the Ohio river
cincinnus: A form of monochasium in which the lateral branches arise alternately on opposite sides of the false axis; called also scorpioid cyme. Cincinnal (#), a.
cinclus: type genus of the family Cinclidae
cincture: The fillet, listel, or band next to the apophyge at the extremity of the shaft of a column.
cinctured: Having or wearing a cincture or gr idle.
cinder: a fragment of incombustible matter left after a wood or coal or charcoal fire
cindery: Resembling, or composed of, cinders; full of cinders.
cindy: A diminutive of the female given name Cynthia and Lucinda; also used as a formal female given name.
cineangiocardiography: An imaging technique that uses videography to capture the passage of a contrast agent through the chambers of the heart.
cineast: An enthusiast of film and the cinema.
cinefilm: Any of various obsolete film formats, including mm,. mm, mm, and Super, formerly much used for making home movies to be viewed on a projector.
cinema: a theater where films are shown
cinemagoer: One who visits a cinema in order to watch a film.
cinematheque: A film archive with small cinemas, screening classic and art-house films.
cinematic: of or pertaining to or characteristic of the cinema
cinematize: make a film of or adopt so as to make into a film
cinematographer: One who exhibits moving pictures or who takes chronophotographsby the cinematograph. Cinematographic (#), a. Cinematographically (#), adv.
cinematography: the act of making a film
cinenchyma: laticiferous tissue, consisting of irregularly branching and anastomosing vessels
cinerary: Pertaining to ashes; containing ashes. Cinerary urns, vessels used by the ancients to preserve the ashes of the dead when burned.
cineration: The reducing of anything to ashes by combustion; cinefaction.
cinerea: The grey matter of the brain
cingalese: A native or natives of Ceylon descended from its primitive inhabitants; also (sing.),
cingulum: (anatomy) an encircling structure (as the ridge around the base of a tooth)
cinnabar: Red sulphide of mercury, occurring in brilliant red crystals, and also in red or brown amorphous masses. It is used in medicine.
cinnabarine: Pertaining to, or resembling, cinnabar; consisting of cinnabar, or containing it; as, cinnabarine sand.
cinnamate: Any salt or ester of cinnamic acid.
cinnamene: Styrene (which was formerly called cinnamene because obtained from cinnamic acid). See Styrene.
cinnamic: Pertaining to, or obtained from, cinnamon. Cinnamic acid (Chem.), a white, crystalline, odorless substance. CH.CHCH.COH, formerly obtained from storax and oil of cinnamon, now made from certain benzene derivatives in large quantities, and used for the artificial production of indigo.
cinnamomum: Asiatic and Australian aromatic trees and shrubs
cinnamon: aromatic bark used as a spice
cinnamyl: The hypothetical radical, (CH.CH)C, of cinnamic compounds.
cinnoline: A nitrogenous organic base, CHN, analogous to quinoline, obtained from certain complex diazo compounds.
cinquain: A five-line poetic form which consists of,, then syllables.
cinque: Five; the number five in dice or cards.
cinquecento: The sixteenth century, when applied to Italian art or literature; as, the sculpture of the Cinquecento; Cinquecento style.
cinquefoil: The name of several different species of the genus Potentilla; also called five-finger, because of the resemblance of its leaves to the fingers of the hand.
cinura: The group of Thysanura which includes Lepisma and allied forms; the bristle tails. See Bristletail, and Lepisma.
cion: See Scion. The cion overrule th the stock; and the stock is but passive, and giveth aliment, but no motion, to the graft. Bacon.
cioppino: An Italian-American shellfish and tomato stew.
cipher: A character which, standing by itself, expresses nothing, but when placed at the right hand of a whole number, increases its value tenfold.
ciphered: simple past and past participle of cipher
ciphony: The process of encrypting telecommunication signals, as to prevent information from being intercepted by an enemy or competitor.
cipolin: A whitish marble, from Rome, containiing pale greenish zones. It consists of calcium carbonate, with zones and clou dings of talc.
cippus: A small, low pillar, square or round, commonly having an inscription, used by the ancients for various purposes, as for indicating the distances of places, for a landmark, for sepulchral inscriptions, etc. Gwilt.
circ: An amphitheatrical circle for sports; a circus. T. Wart on.
circa: Approximately, about, around (typically in relation to time)
circadian: of or relating to biological processes occurring at -hour intervals
circassian: Of or pertaining to Cir cassia, in Asia. n.
circe: (Greek mythology) a sorceress who detained Odysseus on her island and turned his men into swine
circean: Having the characteristics of Circe, daughter of Sol and Perseis, a mythological enchantress, who first charmed her victims and then changed them to the forms of beasts; pleasing, but noxious; as, a Circean draught.
circinate: Rolled together downward, the tip occupying the center; aterm used in reference to foliation or leafing, as in ferns. Gray.
circle: An instrument of observation, the graduated limb of which consists of an entire circle.
circled: Having the form of a circle; round. Monthly changes in her circled orb.
circler: A mean or inferior poet, perhaps from his habit of wandering around as a stroller; an itinerant poet. Also, a name given to the cyclic poets. See under Cyclic, a. B. Jonson.
circling: present participle and gerund of circle
circuit: To move in a circle; to go round; to circulate. J.Phi lips.
circuital: Of or pertaining to a circuit.
circuited: simple past and past participle of circuit
circuiter: One who travels a circuit, as a circuit judge. R.Whit lock.
circuitous: Going round in a circuit; roundabout; indirect; as, acircuitous road; a circuitous manner of accompalishing an end. Circuitously, adv. Circuitousness, n.
circuitry: electronic equipment consisting of a system of circuits
circuity: A going round in a circle; a course not direct; a roundabout way of proceeding.
circular: an advertisement (usually printed on a page or in a leaflet) intended for wide distribution
circularise: to canvass by distributing letters. Syn. circularize.
circularity: The quality or state of being circular; a circular form.
circularization: circulating printed notices as a means of advertising
circularized: simple past and past participle of circularize
circularizer: A device for making a laser beam circular.
circulary: Circular; illogical. Cross and circulary speeches. Hooker.
circulate: To cause to pass from place to place, or from person to person; to spread; as, to circulate a report; to circulate bills of credit. Circulating pump. See under Pump.
circulated: simple past and past participle of circulate
circulates: third-person singular simple present indicative of circulate
circulation: The movement of the blood in the blood-vascular system, by which it is brought into close relations with almost every living elementary constituent. Also, the movement of the sap in the vessels and tissues of plants.
circulator: One who, or that which, circulates.
circulatorious: Travelling from house to house or from town to town; itinerant. Circulatorious jugglers. " Barrow.
circulatory: Subserving the purposes of circulation; as, circulatory organs; of or pertaining to the organs of circulation; as, circulatory diseases.
circuline: Proceeding in a circle; circular. With motion circuline. Dr. H. More.
circulus: A social group of reptiles where there is interaction and personal exchange between individuals.
circumagitate: To agitate on all sides. Jer. Taylor.
circumambages: Instances of indirectness or deviousness in speaking or writing: circumlocutions.
circumambiency: The act of surrounding or encompassing. Sir T. Browne.
circumambient: Surrounding; inclosing or being on all sides; encompassing. The circumambient heaven. " J. Armstrong.
circumambulate: To walk round about. Circumambulation, n.
circumambulating: present participle and gerund of circumambulate
circumambulation: The act of walking around something in a circle, especially for a ritual purpose.
circumbendibus: A roundabout or indirect way. Goldsmith.
circumboreal: comprising or throughout far northern regions
circumcised: Of a man, having had the foreskin of the penis excised.
circumcision: (Roman Catholic Church and Anglican Church) feast day celebrating the circumcision of Jesus; celebrated on January st
circumdenudation: Denudation around or in the neighborhood of an object. Hills of circumdenudation, hills which have been produced by surface erosion; the elevations which have been left, after denudation of a mass of high ground. Jukes.
circumduce: To declare elapsed, as the time allowed for introducing evidence. Sir W. Scott.
circumduct: To contravene; to nullify; as, to circumduct acts of judicature. Ayliffe.
circumesophagal: Surrounding the esophagus; in Zool. said of the nervecommissures and ganglia of arthropods and mollusks.
circumference: To include in a circular space; to bound. Sir T. Browne.
circumferential: Pertaining to the circumference; encompassing; encircling; circuitous. Park hurst.
circumflex: To mark or pronounce with a circumflex. Walker.
circumflexion: The act of bending, or causing to assume a curved form.
circumfluent: Flowing round; surrounding in the manner of a fluid.
circumfuse: To pour round; to spread round. His army circumfused on either wing. Milton.
circumfused: simple past and past participle of circumfuse
circumfusile: Capable of being poured or spread round. Circumfusile gold. Pope.
circumgestation: The act or process of carrying about. Circumgestation of the eucharist to be adored. Jer. Taylor.
circumgyrate: To roll or turn round; to cause to perform a rotary or circular motion. Ray.
circumgyration: The act of turning, rolling, or whirling round. A certain turbulent and irregular circumgyration. Holland.
circumincession: The reciprocal existence in each other of the three persons of the Trinity.
circumjacency: An area circumjacent to another; surroundings, environs.
circumjacent: Lying round; borderong on every side. T. Fuller.
circumlocution: The use of many words to express an idea that might be expressed by few; indirect or roundabout language; a periphrese.the plain Billing agate way of calling names. would save abundance of time lost by circumlocution. Swift. Circumlocution office, a term of riducle for a governmental office where business is delayed by passing through the hands of different officials.
circumlocutionary: Articulated in a roundabout manner; tautological or with repetitive language.
circumlocutory: Characterised by circumlocution; periphrastic. Shen stone. The officials set to work in regular circumlocutory order. Chambers's Journal.
circumnavigate: To sail completely round. Having circumnavigated the whole earth. T. Fuller.
circumnavigated: simple past and past participle of circumnavigate
circumnavigating: present participle and gerund of circumnavigate
circumnavigation: The act of circumnavigating, or sailing round. Arbuthnot.
circumnutate: To pass through the stages of circumnutation.
circumnutating: present participle and gerund of circumnutate
circumnutation: The successive bowing or bending in different directions of the growing tip of the stems of many plants, especially seen in climbing plants.
circumpolar: About the pole; applied to stars that revolve around the pole without setting; as, circumpolar stars.
circumradius: For a given geometric shape, the radius of the smallest circle or sphere into which it will fit.
circumscribe: To draw a line around si as to touch at certain points with outcutting. See Inscribe,.
circumscribed: subject to limits or subjected to limits
circumscribes: third-person singular simple present indicative of circumscribe
circumscribing: present participle and gerund of circumscribe
circumscriptible: Capable of being circumscribed or limited by bounds.
circumspect: Attentive to all the circustances of a case or the probable consequences of an action; cautious; prudent; wary.
circumspection: Attention to all the facts and circumstances of a case; caution; watchfulness. With silent circumspection, unespied. Milton.
circumspective: Looking around everi way; cautious; careful of consequences; watchful of danger. Circumspective eyes. " Pope.
circumspectly: In a circumspect manner; cautiously; warily.
circumspectness: Vigilance un guarding against evil from every quarter; caution.forces circumspectness on those abroad, who at home are nursed in security. Sir H. Wot ton.
circumsphere: A sphere that is circumscribed about a polyhedron and touches each of its vertices
circumstance: Condition in regard to worldly estate; state of property; situation; surroundings. When men are easy in their circumstances, they are naturally enemies to innovations. Addison. Not a circumstance, of no account. Under the circumstances, taking all things into consideration.
circumstanced: Placed in a particular position or condition; situated. The proposition is, that two bodies so circumstanced will balance each other. Whew ell.
circumstances: a person's financial situation (good or bad)
circumstant: Standing or placed around; surrounding. Circumstant bodies. " Sir K. Digby.
circumstantiable: Capable of being circumstantiated. Jer Taylor.
circumstantial: Something incidental to the main subject, but of less importance; opposed to an essential; generally in the plural; as, the circumstantials of religion. Addison.
circumstantiality: The state, characteristic, or quality of being circumstantial; particularity or minuteness of detail. I will endeavor to describe with sufficient circumstantiality. " De Quincey.
circumstantiated: simple past and past participle of circumstantiate
circumstantiating: present participle and gerund of circumstantiate
circumterraneous: Being or dwelling around the earth. Circumterraneous demo uns. H. Hallywell.
circumvallate: To surround with a rampart or wall. Johnson.
circumvent: To gain advantage over by arts, stratagem, or deception; todecieve; to delude; to get around. I circumvented whom I could not gain. Dryden.
circumvented: simple past and past participle of circumvent
circumvention: The act of prevailing over another by arts, address, or fraud; deception; fraud; imposture; delusion. A school in which he learns sly circumvention. Cowper.
circumventor: One who circumvents; one who gains his purpose by cunning.
circumvents: third-person singular simple present indicative of circumvent
circumvolant: Flying around. The circumvolant troubles of humanity. G. Mac donald.
circumvolution: the act of turning or winding or folding around a central axis
circumvolve: To roll round; to cause to revolve; to put into a circular motion. Herrick.
circus: A level oblong space surrounded on three sides by seats of wood, earth, or stone, rising in tiers one above another, and divided lengthwise through the middle by a barrier around which the track or course was laid out. It was used for chariot races, games, and public shows.
cire: A fabric with a glazed finish.

cleverly: In a clever manner. Never was man so clever absurd. C. Smart.
cleverness: The quality of being clever; skill; dexterity; adroitness.
clevis: A piece of metal bent in the form of an oxbow, with the two ends perforated to receive a pin, used on the end of the tongue of aplow, wagen, etc., to attach it to a draft chain, whiffletree, etc.; called also clavel, clevy.
clew: To move of draw (a sail or yard) by means of the clew garnets, clew lines, etc.; esp. to draw up the clews of a square sail to the yard. To clew down (Naut.), to force (a yard) down by hauling on the clew lines. To clew up (Naut.), to draw (a sail) up to the yard, as for furling.
clews: the cords used to suspend a hammock
clianthus: any of various shrubs or vines of the genus Clianthus having compound leaves and pea-like red flowers in drooping racemes
click: To make a slight, sharp noise (or a succession of such noises),as by gentle striking; to tick. The varnished clock that clicked behind the door. Goldsmith.
clicked: simple past and past participle of click
clicker: One who as has charge of the work of a companionship.
clicking: The sound or action of a click.
clicky: Resembling a click; abounding in clicks. Their strange clicky language. " The Century.
client: A citizen who put himself under the protection of a man of distinction and influence, who was called his patron.
cliental: Of or pertaining to a client. A dependent and cliental relation. Burke. I sat down in the cliental chair. Dickens.
cliented: Supplied with clients. The least cliented pettifiggers. R. Carew.
cliffhanger: a contest whose outcome is uncertain up to the very end
clifford: A habitational surname from Old English.
clift: A cliff. That gainst the craggy clifts did loudly roar. Spenser.
clifted: Broken; fissured. Climb the Ande clifted side. Grainger.
climacium: Any of the genus Climacium of tree mosses
climactic: Of or pertaining to a climax; forming, or of the nature of, ac limax, or ascending series.
climate: One of thirty regions or zones, parallel to the equator, into which the surface of the earth from the equator to the pole was divided, according to the successive increase of the length of the midsummer day.
climatic: Of or pertaining to a climate; depending on, or limited by, aclimate.
climatologist: One versed in, or who studies, climatology.
climatology: The science which treats of climates and investigates their phenomena and causes. Br ande & C.
climatotherapy: The relocation of a patient to a different climate so as to aid recovery from or management of a condition.
climax: A figure of which the parts of a sentence or paragraph are so arranged that each sicceeding one riseTribulation work eth patience, patience experience, and experience hope a happy climax. J. D. For bes.
climb: To ascend or creep upward by twining about a support, or by attaching itself by tend rills, rootlets, etc., to a support or upright surface.
climbed: simple past and past participle of climb
climbs: third-person singular simple present indicative of climb
clime: A climate; a tract or region of the earth. See Climate. Turn we to sutvey, Where rougher climes a nobler race display. Goldsmith.
clinamen: The unpredictable swerve of atoms, introduced as a concept by Lucretius to defend the atomistic doctrine of Epicurus.
clinandrium: An area at the tip of the column of orchid flowers, beneath the anthers.
clinanthium: The receptacle of the flowers in a composite plant; also called clinium.
clinch: To hold fast; to grasp something firmly; to seize or grasp oneanother.
clinching: present participle and gerund of clinch
cline: American geneticist who succeeded in transferring a functioning gene from one mouse to another (born in )
cling: To adhere closely; to stick; to hold fast, especially by twining round or embracing; as, the tendril of a vine clings to its support; usually followed by to or together. And what hath life for thee That thou shouldst cling to it thus Mrs. He mans.
clingfish: very small (to inches) flattened marine fish with a sucking disc on the abdomen for clinging to rocks etc.
clinginess: The state or condition of being clingy
clinging: present participle and gerund of cling
clingstone: Having the flesh attached closely to the stone, as in some kinds of peaches. n.
clinic: One who receives baptism on a sick bed. Hook.
clinical: relating to a clinic or conducted in or as if in a clinic and depending on direct observation of patients
clinician: a practitioner (of medicine or psychology) who does clinical work instead of laboratory experiments
clinicopathologic: Relating to clinicopathology, that is, both the clinical symptoms of a patient and the results of laboratory (especially pathology laboratory) tests, as in clinicopathologic correlations or a clinicopathologic conference.
clink: To cause to give out a slight, sharp, tinkling, sound, as by striking metallic or other sonorous bodies together. And let me the canakin clink.
clinker: turn to clinker or form clinker under excessive heat in burning
clinking: like the light sharp ringing sound of glasses being tapped
clinkstone: An igneous rock of feldspathic composition, lamellar in structure, and clinking under the hammer. See Phonolite.
clinocephaly: a congenital defect in which the top of the head is depressed (concave instead of convex)
clinochlore: A monoclinic-prismatic mineral containing aluminum, hydrogen, iron, magnesium, oxygen, and silicon.
clinoclase: A mineral composed of a basic copper arsenate
clinodiagonal: That diagonal or lateral axis in a monoclinic crystal which makes an oblique angle witch the vertical axis. See Crystallization. a.
clinology: The study of the deterioration or retrogression of an organism after maturity, especially, the correspondance of the form or function of one organism that has deteriorated due to age with the undeteriorated mature stages of degraded organisms from the same group.
clinometer: An instrument for determining the dip of beds or strata, pr the slope of an embankment or cutting; a kind of plumb level. Dana.
clinometric: Pertaining to, or ascertained by, the clinometer.
clinopinacoid: The plane in crystals of the monoclinic system which is parallel to the vertical and the inclined lateral (clinidiagonal) axes.
clinopyroxene: Any pyroxene that has a monoclinic crystal structure.
clinton: wife of President Clinton and later a woman member of the United States Senate (-)
clintonia: any temperate liliaceous plant of the genus Clintonia having broad basal leaves and white or yellowish or purplish flowers followed by blue or black berries
clintonite: A calcium magnesium aluminium phyllosilicate mineral of the margarite group of micas.
clio: The Muse who presided over history.
clione: A genus of naked pteropods. One species (Clione papilonacea),abundant in the Arctic Ocean, constitutes a part of the food of the greenland whale. It is sometimes incorrectly called Clio.
clip: To move swiftly; usually with indefinite it. Straight flies as chek, and clips it down the wind. Dryden.
clipboard: a small writing board with a clip at the top for holding papers
clipeus: A shield worn by soldiers of ancient Greece and Rome.
clipper: A vessel with a sharp bow, built and rigged for fast sailing. Clipper-built (, a.
clipping: an excerpt cut from a newspaper or magazine
clipsheet: A sheet of news, features, and similar material distributed to newspaper publishers for convenient inclusion in their publications.
clique: A narrow circle of persons associated by common interests orfor the accomplishment of a common purpose; generally used in abad sense.
cliquey: Having the characteristics of a clique.

clitellum: A glandular swelling in the epidermis of some annelid worms; it secretes a viscous fluid in which the eggs are deposited.
clitoral: of or relating to the clitoris
clitoris: A small organ at the upper part of the vulva, homologous to the penis in the male.
clitter: to make a shrill creaking noise by rubbing together special bodily structures
clive: British general and statesman whose victory at Plassey in strengthened British control of India (-)
clivia: Any plant of the genus Clivia, native to southern Africa.
clivis: A neume representing two notes descending.
clivus: Part of the cranium at the skull base, a shallow depression behind the dorsum sellae that slopes obliquely backward.
cloaca: The common chamber into which the intestinal, urinary, and generative canals discharge in birds, reptiles, amphibians, and many fishes.
cloacal: Of or pertaining to a cloaca.
cloak: To cover with, or as with, a cloak; hence, to hide or conceal. Now glooming sadly, so to cloak her matter. Spenser.
cloaked: having its true character concealed with the intent of misleading
cloakroom: A room, attached to any place of public resort, where cloaks, overcoats, etc., may be deposited for a time.
clochard: A beggar or tramp, especially in France.
clock: To ornament with figured work, as the side of a stocking.
clocker: A person who clocks (illegally winds back the milometer of) a motor car
clocking: the time taken to traverse a measured course

clocks: European weed naturalized in southwestern United States and Mexico having reddish decumbent stems with small fernlike leaves and small deep reddish-lavender flowers followed by slender fruits that stick straight up
clockwise: Like the motion of the hands of a clock; said of that direction of a rotation about an axis, or about a point in a plane, which is ordinarily reckoned negative.

cloddy: Consisting of clods; full of clods.
cloff: Formerly an allowance of two pounds in every three hundredweight after the tare and tret are subtracted; now used only in agen eral sense, of small deductions from the original weight. Mc Culloch.
clog: become or cause to become obstructed
clogged: thickened or coalesced in soft thick lumps (such as clogs or clots)
clogger: One who, or that which, clogs.
clogging: Anything which clogs. Dr. H. More.
cloggy: Clogging, or having power to clog.
cloister: To confine in, or as in, a cloister; to seclude from the world; to immure. None among them are th rought worthy to be styled religious persons but those that cloister themselves up in a monastery. Sharp.
cloisterer: One belonging to, or living in, a cloister; a recluse.
cloisterly: Characteristic of, or suitable for, a cloister.
cloistral: Of, pertaining to, or confined in, a cloister; recluse. Best become a cloistral exercise. Daniel.
clomb: simple past and past participle of climb
clon: a group of genetically identical cells or organisms derived from a single cell or individual by some kind of asexual reproduction
clonal: of or relating to a clone
clone: a group of genetically identical cells or organisms derived from a single cell or individual by some kind of asexual reproduction
clonic: Having an irregular, convulsive motion. Dunglison. Clonic spasm. (Med.) See under Spasm.
cloning: a general term for the research activity that creates a copy of some biological entity (a gene or organism or cell)
clonk: The abrupt sound of two hard objects coming into contact.

cloop: The sound made when a cork is forcibly drawn from a bottle. The cloop of a cork wrenched from a bottle. " Thackeray.

clop: make or move along with a sound as of a horse's hooves striking the ground
cloque: A fabric with an embossed design
clos: Acronym of common Lisp object system.
close: The interest which one may have in a piece of ground, even though it is not inclosed. Bouvier.
closed: not open or affording passage or access
closefisted: Covetous; niggardly. Bp. Berkeley. Closefisted contractors. Hawthorne.
closehauled: Under way and moving as nearly as possible toward the direction from which the wind blows; said of a sailing vessel.
closely: in a close relation or position in time or space
closemouthed: Cautious in speaking; secret; wary; uncommunicative.

closeout: a sale intended to dispose of all remaining stock
closer: The last stone in a horizontal course, if of a less size than the others, or a piece of brick finishing a course. Gwilt.
closes: third-person singular simple present indicative of close

closet: a small private room for study or prayer
closeted: Not open about one's sexual orientation, romantic orientation, or gender identity.
closeup: a photograph taken at close range
closing: approaching a particular destination; a coming closer; a narrowing of a gap
clostridium: spindle-shaped bacterial cell especially one swollen at the center by an endospore
clot: A concretion or coagulation; esp. a soft, slimy, coagulated mass, as of blood; a coagulum. Clots of pory gore. " Addison. Doth bake the egg into clots as if it began to poach. Bacon.

clothes: Covering for the human body; dress; vestments; vesture; a general term for whatever covering is worn, or is made to be worn, for decency or comfort. She. speaks well, and has excellent good clothes. If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole. Mark. v.
clothesbrush: a brush used for cleaning clothing
clotheshorse: A frame to hang clothes on.
clothesline: A rope or wire on which clothes are hung to dry.
clothespin: A forked piece of wood, or a small spring clamp, used for fastening clothes on a line.
clothier: a merchant who sells men's clothing
clothing: See Card clothing, under d Card.
clotho: the Greek goddess of fate who spins the thread of life
clotted: Composed of clots or clods; having the quality or form of aclot; sticky; slimy; foul. The clotted glebe. " J. Phi lips. When lust. Lets in defilement to the inward parts, The soul grows clotted by contagion. Milton.
clotter: To concrete into lumps; to clot. Clotter ed blood. Chapman.
clotting: the process of forming semisolid lumps in a liquid
clotty: Full of clots, or clods. Clotty matter. " Harvey.
clou: Something which holds the greatest attention; the chief point of interest.

clouding: the process whereby water particles become visible in the sky
cloudless: Without a cloud; clear; bright. A cloudless winter sky. Bankroft. Cloudlessly, adv. Cloudlessness, n.
cloudlet: A little cloud. R. Browning. Eve's first star through fleecy cloudlet peeping. Coleridge.
clough: An allowance in weighing. See Cloff.
clout: strike hard, especially with the fist
clove: imp. of Cleave. Cleft. Spenser. Clove hitch (Naut.) See under hitch. Clove hook (Naut.), an iron two-part hook, with jaws overlapping, used in bending chain sheets to the clews of sails; called also clip hook. Knight.
cloven: from Cleave, v. t. To show the cloven foot or hoof, to reveal adevilish character, or betray an evil purpose, notwithstanding disguises, Satan being represented dramatically and symbolically as having cloven hoofs.
clovered: Covered with growing clover. Flocks thick nibbling through the clovered vale. Thomson.
cloverleaf: an interchange that does not require left-hand turns
clovis: king of the Franks who unified Gaul and established his capital at Paris and founded the Frankish monarchy; his name was rendered as Gallic Louis' (-)
clown: To act as a clown; with it beclowns it properly indeed. B. Jonson.
clownish: Of or resembling a clown, or characteristic of a clown; ungainly; awkward. Clownish hands. " Spenser. Clownish mimic. Prior. Clownishly, adv.
clownishly: In a clownish, undignified, or foolish manner; absurdly, ridiculously.
clownishness: The manners of a clown; coarseness or rudeness of behavior. That plainness which the alamode people call clownishness. Locke.
cloy: cause surfeit through excess though initially pleasing
cloyed: simple past and past participle of cloy
cloys: third-person singular simple present indicative of cloy
cloze: based on or being a test of reading skill using the cloze procedure
club: Any card of the suit of cards having a figure like the trefoil or clover leaf. (pl.) The suit of cards having such figure.
clubbable: Suitable for membership in a club; sociable. G. W.Curtis.
clubby: befitting or characteristic of those who incline to social exclusiveness and who rebuff the advances of people considered inferior
clubfoot: A short, variously distorted foot; also, the deformity, usually congenital, which such a foot exhibits; talipes.
clubhand: A short, distorted hand; also, the deformity of having such ahand.

clubhouse: A house occupied by a club.
clubman: A man who attends a social club.
clubroom: The apartment in which a club meets. Addison.

clubs: third-person singular simple present indicative of club
clubwoman: A woman who is a member of a club.
cluck: To make the noise, or utter the call, of a brooding hen. Ray.
clucking: The noise or call of a brooding hen.
clue: A ball of thread; a thread or other means of guidance. Same as clew. You have wound a goodly clue. This clue once found unravels all the rest. Pope. Serve as clues to guide us into further knowledge. Locke.
clumber: A kind of field spaniel, with short legs and stout body, which, unlike other spaniels, hunts silently.

clumpy: Composed of clumps; massive; shapeless. Leigh Hunt.

cluniac: A monk of the reformed branch of the Benedictine Order, founded in at Cluny (or Clugny) in France. Also used as a.
clunk: a heavy dull sound (as made by impact of heavy objects)
clunking: the sound of a horse's hoofs hitting on a hard surface

clupea: type genus of the Clupeidae: typical herrings
clupeid: any of numerous soft-finned schooling food fishes of shallow waters of northern seas

clusia: an aromatic tree of the genus Clusia having large white or yellow or pink flowers
cluster: To grow in clusters or assemble in groups; to gather or unite in a cluster or clusters. His sunny hair Cluster'd about his temples, like a god's. Tennyson. The princes of the country clustering together. Foxe.
clustered: growing close together but not in dense mats
clustering: a grouping of a number of similar things
clutch: The hands, claws, or talons, in the act of grasping firmly; often figuratively, for power, rapacity, or cruelty; as, to fall into the clutches of an adversary. I must have. little care of myself, if I ever more come near the clutches of such a giant. Bp. Stilling fleet.
clutching: present participle and gerund of clutch
clutter: To crowd together in disorder; to fill or cover with things in disorder; to throw into disorder; to disarrange; as, to clutter aroom.
cluttered: filled or scattered with a disorderly accumulation of objects or rubbish
clyde: a river in western Scotland that flows from the southern uplands into the Firth of Clyde; navigable by oceangoing vessels as far as Glasgow
clydesdale: One of a breed of heavy draft horses originally from clydesdale, Scotland. They are about sixteen hands high and usually brown or bay.
clydeside: The area along the River Clyde around the Glasgow council area, Scotland, possibly also including places such as Clydebank.
clyer: A swelling of the lymph node of cattle
clypeastroid: Like or related to the genus Clupea ster; applied to a group of flattened sea urchins, with a rosette of pores on the upper side.
clypeate: Shaped like a round buckler or shield; scutate.
clypeola: Any brassica of the genus Clypeola
clypeus: The frontal plate of the head of an insect.
clysmian: Connected with, or related to, the deluge, or to a cataclysm; as, clysmian changes. Smart.
clyster: A liquid injected into the lower intestines by means of asyringe; an injection; an enema. Clyster pipe, a tube or pipe used for injections.
clytemnestra: (Greek mythology) wife of Agamemnon who had him murdered when he returned from the Trojan War
cm: a metric unit of length equal to one hundredth of a meter
cnemial: Pertaining to the shin bone. Cnemial crest, a crestlikeprominence on the proximal end of the tibia of birds and some reptiles.
cnemis: The section of the leg from the knee to the ankle; shin.
cnida: One of the peculiar stinging, cells found in Coelenterata; anematocyst; a lasso cell.
cnidaria: A comprehensive group equivalent to the true Coelenterata, i.e., exclusive of the sponges. They are so named from presence of stinging cells (cnidae) in the tissues. See Coelenterata.
cnidarian: radially symmetrical animals having saclike bodies with only one opening and tentacles with stinging structures
cnidocell: An external ciliary process of a cnidoblast
co: Abbreviation of Colorado: a state of the United States.
coacervate: Raised into a pile; collected into a crowd; heaped. Bacon.

coachbuilder: a craftsman who makes the bodies of motor vehicles
coached: simple past and past participle of coach
coacher: one of the side at the bat posted near first or third base to direct a base runner.
coachman: A tropical fish of the Atlantic ocean (Dutes auriga); called also charioteer. The name refers to a long, lash like spine of the dorsal fin.
coact: To force; to compel; to drive. The faith and service of Christ ought to be voluntary and not coacted. Foxe.
coacted: simple past and past participle of coact
coaction: Force; compulsion, either in restraining or impelling. Sojth.
coactive: Serving to compel or constrain; compulsory; restrictive. Any coactive power or the civil kind. Bp. War burton.
coadapted: Adapted one to another; as, coadapted pulp and tooth. R. Owen.
coadjutant: Mutually assisting or operating; helping. J. Phi lips.
coadjutor: The assistant of a bishop or of a priest holding a benefice.
coadunate: United at the base, as contiguous lobes of a leaf.
coadunation: Union, as in one body or mass; unity. Jer. Taylor. The coadunation of all the civilized provinces. Coleridge.
coadventure: An adventure in which two or more persons are partakers.
coag: See Coak, a kind of tenon.
coagency: Agency in common; joint agency or agent. Coleridge.
coagent: An associate in an act; a coworker. Dray ton.
coaggregate: To aggregate along with another material
coagulability: The quality of being coagulable; capacity of being coagulated. Ure.
coagulated: Changed into, or contained in, a coagulum or a curd like mass; curdled. Coagulated proteid (Physiol. Chem.), one of a class of bodies formed in the coagulation of a albuminous substance by heat, acids, or other agents.
coagulates: third-person singular simple present indicative of coagulate
coagulating: present participle and gerund of coagulate

Coagulation is generally the change of an albuminous body into an insoluble modification.

coaita: The native name of certain South American monkeys of the genus ateles, esp. A. paniscus. The black-faced coaita is Ateles ater. See illustration in Appendix.

coaler: A vehicle, especially a ship, used for carrying or supplying coal.
coalesce: fuse or cause to grow together
coalescence: The act or state of growing together, as similar parts; the actof uniting by natural affinity or attraction; the state of being united; union; concretion.

coalfish: The pollock; called also, coals ey, colemie, colmey, coal whiting, etc. See Pollock.

coaly: Pertaining to, or resembling, coal; containing coal; of the nature of coal.
coalyard: A yard where coal is stored.
coaming: a raised framework around a hatchway on a ship to keep water out

coarse: of textures that are rough to the touch or substances consisting of relatively large particles
coarsely: In a coarse manner; roughly; rudely; inelegantly; uncivilly; meanly.
coarsen: To make coarse or vulgar; as, to coarsen one's character. Graham.

coarser: comparative form of coarse: more coarse
coarsest: superlative form of coarse: most coarse
coassist: To jointly assist or to provide an additional source of assistance.
coast: To slide down hill; to slide on a sled, upon snow or ice.
coastal: Of or pertaining to a cast.
coaster: a resident of a coastal area
coastguard: a military service responsible for the safety of maritime traffic in coastal waters
coasting: Sailing along or near a coast, or running between ports along ac oast. Coasting trade, trade carried on by water between neighboring ports of the same country, as distinguished fron foreign trade or trade involving long voyages. Coasting vessel, a vessel employed in coasting; a coaster.

coat: put a coat on; cover the surface of; furnish with a surface

At the same time coercion is not negatived by the fact of submission under force. Co actus volui (I consented under compulsion) is the condition of mind which, when there is volition forced by coercion, annuls the result of such coercion. Wharton.

It might indeed, at that time, have been not improperly called a most important political institution. The coffeehouses were the chief organs through which the public opinion of the metropolis vented itself. Every man of the upper or middle class went daily to his coffeehouse to learn the news and discuss it. Every coffeehouse had one or more orators, to whose eloquence the crowd listened with admiration, and who soon became what the journalists of our own time have been called a fourth estate of the realm. Macaulay.
