convince: To overpower; to overcome; to subdue or master. His two chamberlains Will I with wine and wassail so convince That memory, the warder of the brain, Shall be a fume.
convincement: Act of convincing, or state of being convinced; conviction. The fear of a convincement. Milton.
convincer: One who, or that which, convinces; one who wins over by proof.
convinces: third-person singular simple present indicative of convince
convincing: causing one to believe the truth of something
convincingly: in a convincing manner; in a manner to compel assent.
convive: To feast together; to be convivial. There, in the full, convive we.
convivial: Of or relating to a feast or entertainment, or to eating and drinking, with accompanying festivity; festive; social; gay; jovial. Which feasts convivial meetings we did name. Den ham.
conviviality: The good humor or mirth indulged in upon festive occasions; aconvivial spirit or humor; festivity.
convocate: To convoke; to call together. May (Lucan).
convocation: An assembly of the clergy, by their representatives, to consult on ecclesiastical affairs.
convoke: To call together; to summon to meet; to assemble by summons. There remained no resource but the dreadful one of convoking aparliament. palfrey.
convoked: simple past and past participle of convoke
convoker: One who convokes or calls together.
convokes: third-person singular simple present indicative of convoke
convoking: present participle and gerund of convoke
convoluted: Having convolutions. beaks recurved and convoluted like a ram's horn. Pennant.
convolution: An irregular, tortuous folding of an organ or part; as, the convolutions of the intestines; the cerebral convolutions. See Brain.
convolve: To roll or wind together; to roll or twist one part on another. Then Satan first knew pain, And writhed him to and fro convolved. Milton.
convolved: simple past and past participle of convolve
convolvulaceous: Of, pertaining to, or resembling, the family of plants of which the bindweed and the morning-glory are common examples.
convolvulin: A glucoside occurring in jalap (the root of a convolvulaceous plant), and extracted as a colorless, tasteless, gummy mass of powerful purgative properties.
convoy: To accompany for protection, either by sea or land; to attend for protection; to escort; as, a frigate convoys a merchantman. I know ye skillful to convoy The total freight of hope and joy. Emerson.
convoyed: simple past and past participle of convoy
convulsed: simple past and past participle of convulse
convulsion: An unnatural, violent, and unvoluntary contraction of the muscular parts of an animal body.
convulsionary: Pertaining to convulsion; convulsive. Convulsionary struggles. " Sir W. Scott.
convulsive: Producing, or attended with, convulsions or spasms; characterized by convulsions; convulsionary. An irregular, convulsive movement may be necessary to throw off an irregular, convulsive disease. Burke.
cony: A rabbit, esp., the European rabbit (Lepus cuniculus).
coo: A peculiar whistling sound made by the Australian aborigenes as a call or signal.
cooch: The hootchy-kootchy, a type of erotic dance.
cooee: A long, loud call used to attract attention when at a distance, mainly done in the Australian bush.
cooing: present participle and gerund of coo
cook: To make the noise of the cuckoo. Constant cuckoos cook on every side. The Silkworms.
cookable: That can be cooked; suitable for cooking.
cookbook: A book of directions and receipts for cooking; a cookery book. Just How: a key to the cookbooks. Mrs. A. D. T. Whitney.
cooke: United States journalist (born in England in )
cooked: having been prepared for eating by the application of heat
cookhouse: a detached or outdoor shelter for cooking
cookie: any of various small flat sweet cakes (biscuit' is the British term)
cooking: the act of preparing something (as food) by the application of heat
cookout: an informal meal cooked and eaten outdoors
cookshop: An eating house. A subterranean cookshop. " Macaulay.
cookstove: a stove for cooking (especially a wood- or coal-burning kitchen stove)
cookware: a kitchen utensil made of material that does not melt easily
cooky: A small, flat, sweetened cake of various kinds.
cool: A moderate state of cold; coolness; said of the temperature of the air between hot and cold; as, the cool of the day; the cool of the morning or evening.
coolant: a fluid agent (gas or liquid) that produces cooling; especially one used to cool a system by transferring heat away from one part to another
cooler: That which cools, or abates heat or excitement.if acid things were used only as coolers, they would not be so proper in this case. Arbuthnot.
coolheaded: marked by calm self-control (especially in trying circumstances)
coolibah: Any of a number of eucalyptus trees of central and northern Australia, in particular Eucalyptus microtheca.
coolidge: elected vice president and succeeded as th President of the United States when Harding died in (-)
cooling: Adapted to cool and refresh; allaying heat. The cooling brook. " Goldsmith. Cooling card, something that dashes hopes. Cooling time (Law), such a lapse of time as ought, taking all the circumstances of the case in view, to produce a subsiding of passion previously provoked. Wharton.
coolish: Somewhat cool. The nights began to grow a little coolish. Goldsmith.
cools: third-person singular simple present indicative of cool
cooly: (ethnic slur) an offensive name for an unskilled Asian laborer
coomb: A dry measure of four bushels, or half a quarter.
cooncan: A game of cards derived from conquian, played by two or more players with one or two full packs of cards.
coonhound: any of several breeds of hound developed for hunting raccoons
coonskin: a raccoon cap with the tail hanging down the back
coontie: A cycadaceous plant of Florida and the West Indies, the Zamiaintegrifolia, from the stems of which a kind of sago is prepared.
coop: To confine in a coop; hence, to shut up or confine in a narrow compass; to cramp; usually followed by up, sometimes by in. The Trojans coop et within their walls so long. Dryden. The contempt of all other knowledge. coops the understanding up within narrow bounds. Locke.
cooper: One who makes barrels, hogsheads, casks, etc.
cooperating: present participle and gerund of cooperate
cooperation: The association of a number of persons for their benefit.
coopered: simple past and past participle of cooper
coopery: Relating to a cooper; coopered. Coopery vessels made of wood. Holland.
coordinating: serving to connect two grammatical constituents of identical construction; and so is or' in will you go or stay?'"
coordination: the skillful and effective interaction of movements
coordinator: someone whose task is to see that work goes harmoniously
coos: third-person singular simple present indicative of coo
coosa: river that rises in northwestern Georgia and flows southwest through eastern Alabama to join the Tallapoosa River near Montgomery and form the Alabama River
coot: slate-black slow-flying birds somewhat resembling ducks
cootie: a parasitic louse that infests the body of human beings
copaiba: an oleoresin used in varnishes and ointments
copalm: The yellowish, fragrant balsam yielded by the sweet gum; also, the tree itself.
coparcenary: Partnership in inheritance; joint heirship; joint right ofsucession to an inheritance.
coparcener: One who has an equal portion with others of an inheritance. All the co parceners together make but one heir, and have but one estate among them. black stone.
copart: To share. For, of all miserias, I hold that chief Wretched to be, when nonecoparts our grief. Webster.
copartner: One who is jointly concerned with one or more persons in business, etc.; a partner; an associate; a partaker; a sharer.the associates and copartners of our loss. Milton.
copastor: One who shares the role of pastor with another person.
copatain: Having a high crown, or a point or peak at top. A copatain hat made on a Flemish block. Gas coigne.
copatron: A joint patron; a patron of the same person or organisation.
cope: The top part of a flask or mold; the outer part of a loam mold. Knight. De Co lange.
copeck: A Russian copper coin. See Kopeck.
copenhagen: A sweetened hot drink of spirit and beaten eggs.
copepod: Of or pertaining to the Copepoda. n.
copepoda: An order of Entomastraca, including many minute Crustacea, both freshwater and marine.
copernican: Pertaining to Copernicus, a Prussian by birth (b., d.), who taught the world the solar system now received, called the copernican system.
copernicus: Polish astronomer who produced a workable model of the solar system with the sun in the center (-)
copesmate: An associate or companion; a friend; a partner. Misshapen time, copesmate of ugly Night.
cophetua: A man who falls in love with a woman instantly and proposes immediate marriage.
copied: simple past and past participle of copy
copier: One who copies; one who writes or transcribes from an original; a transcriber.
copihue: An evergreen climbing plant, Lapageria rosea.
copilot: a relief pilot on an airplane
coping: The highest or covering course of masonry in a wall, often with sloping edges to carry off water; sometimes called capping. Gwill.
copious: Large in quantity or amount; plentiful; abundant; fruitful. Kindly pours its copious treasures forth. Thomson. Hail, Son of God, Savior of men! thy name Shall be the copious matter of my song. Milton.
copiousness: The state or quality of being copious; abu dance; plenty; also, diffuseness in style. To imitate the copiousness of Homer. Dryden.
copist: A copier. A copist after nature. " Shaftesbury.
coplanarity: The state or characteristic of being within the same plane.
copland: A piece of ground terminating in a point or acute angle.
copley: American painter who did portraits of Paul Revere and John Hancock before fleeing to England to avoid the American Revolution (-)
copolymer: a polymer consisting of two or more different monomers
copolymerization: The polymerization of multiple monomers to form a copolymer
coportion: Equal share. Myself will bear. coportion of your pack. Spenser.
copout: a failure to face some difficulty squarely
copped: Rising to a point or head; conical; pointed; crested. Wiseman.
copper: the boilers in the galley for cooking; as, a ship's coppers.
copperas: Green vitriol, or sulphate of iron; a green crystalline substance, of an astringent taste, used in making ink, in dyeing black, as a tonic in medicine, etc. It is made on a large scale by the oxidation of iron pyrites. Called also ferrous sulphate.
copperhead: A poisonous American serpent (Ancistrodon conotortrix), closely allied to the rattlesnake, but without rattles; called also copper-belly, and red viper.
copperish: Containing, or partaking of the nature of, copper; like copper; as, a copperish taste.
copperplate: a graceful style of handwriting based on the writing used on copperplate engravings
coppersmith: One whose occupation is to manufacture copper utensils; awork er in copper.
coppery: Mixed with copper; containing copper, or made of copper; like copper.

copr: Abbreviation of confirmation of permanent residency.
copra: The dried meat of the cocoanut, from which cocoanut oil is expressed.
coprecipitate: To cause, or to undergo, coprecipitation.
coprecipitation: The precipitation of an otherwise soluble substance through the precipitation of another substance.
copremic: Relating to, or suffering from, copremia.
coprocessor: An additional microprocessor used to supplement the functionality of the central processing unit, performing tasks such as floating-point arithmetic (floating-point unit) or graphics calculations (graphics processing unit).

coprolalia: an uncontrollable use of obscene language; often accompanied by mental disorders
coprophagous: Feeding upon dung, as certain insects.

coprosma: Any of the plants in the genus Coprosma.
coprostanol: A stanol formed from the biohydrogenation of cholesterol
copse: A wood of small growth; a thicket of brushwood. See Coppice. Near yonder copse where once the garden smiled. Goldsmith.
copsy: Characterized by copses. Copsy villages. " Copsy banks. " J.Dyer.
coptic: Of or pertaining to the Copts. n.
copts: An Egyptian race thought to be descendants of the ancient Egyptians.
copula: The word which unites the subject and predicate.
copulate: Joining subject and predicate; copulative. F. A. March.
copulating: present participle and gerund of copulate
copulation: The act of coupling or joining; union; conjunction. Wit, you know, is the unexpected copulation of ideas. Johnson.
copulative: Serving to couple, unite, or connect; as, a copulative conjunction like and.
copulatory: Used in sexual union; as, the copulatory organs of insects.
copy: Manuscript or printed matter to be set up in type; as, the printers are calling for more copy.
copybook: a book containing models of good penmanship; used in teaching penmanship
copycat: someone who copies the words or behavior of another
copygraph: A contrivance for producing manifold copies of a writing or drawing.
copyhold: a medieval form of land tenure in England; a copyhold was a parcel of land granted to a peasant by the lord of the manor in return for agricultural services

copying: From Copy, v. Copying ink. See under Ink. Copying paper, thin unsized paper used for taking copies of letters, etc., in a copying press. Copying press, a machine for taking by pressure, an exact copy of letters, etc., written in copying ink.
copyist: A copier; a transcriber; an imitator; a plagiarist.
copyread: edit and correct (written or printed material)
copyreader: an editor who prepares text for publication
copyright: The right of an author or his assignee, under statute, to print and publish his literary or artistic work, exclusively of all other persons. This right may be had in maps, charts, engravings, plays, and musical compositions, as well as in books.
copyrighted: (of literary or musical or dramatic or artistic work) protected by copyright
copywriter: a person employed to write advertising or publicity copy
coquet: To attempt to attract the notice, admiration, or love of; to treat with a show of tenderness or regard, with a view to deceive and disappoint. You are coquetting a maid of honor. Swift.
coquetry: Attempts to attract ad moration, notice, or love, for the mere gratification of vanity; trifling in love. Little affectations of coquetry. " Addison.
coquette: A tropical humming bird of the genus Lophornis, with very elegant neck plumes. Several species are known. See Illustration under Spangle, v. t.
coquetting: present participle and gerund of coquet
coquettish: Practicing or exhibiting coquetry; alluring; enticing. A pretty, coquettish housemaid. W. Irving.
coquille: seafood served in a scallop shell

cor: A Hebrew measure of capacity; a homer.
cora: The Arabian gazelle (Gazella Arabica), found from persia to north Africa.
coraciiformes: rollers; kingfishers; hornbills; hoopoes; motmots; bee eaters; todies

coracobrachialis: The smallest of the three muscles that attach to the coracoid process of the scapula.
coracoid: Pertaining to a bone of the shoulder girdle in most birds, reptiles, and amphibians, which is reduced to a process of the scapula in most mammals.
corage: See Courage to Canterbury with full devout corage. Chaucer.
coral: The hard parts or skeleton of various Anthozoa, and of a few hydrozoa. Similar structures are also formed by some Bryozoa.
coralberry: North American deciduous shrub cultivated for it abundant clusters of coral-red berrylike fruits
coralline: Composed of coral lines; as, coralline limestone.
coralloid: Having the form of coral; branching like coral.
coralloidal: resembling coral; coralloid. Sir T. browne.
corallorhiza: genus of leafless root-parasitic orchids having small purplish or yellowish racemose flowers with lobed lips; widely distributed in temperate regions
coralwort: A cruciferous herb of certain species of Dentaria; called also toothwort, tooth violet, or pepper root.
coranach: A lamentation for the dead; a dirge.
coranto: A fast-paced dance which originated in France.
corb: An ornament in a building; a corbel.
corban: An alms basket; a vessel to receive gifts of charity; a treasury of the church, where offerings are deposited.
corbeil: A sculptured basket of flowers; a corbel.
corbel: A bracket supporting a superincumbent object, or receiving the spring of an arch. Corbels were employed largely in Gothic architecture.
corbelling: A series of corbels or piece of continuous corbelled masonry.
corbicula: A bee's pollen basket; in honeybees and close relatives, the corbiculae are located on the outer (lateral) surface of the hind tibia.
corbie: A raven or crow (typically Corvus corax).
corchorus: The common name of the kerria Japonica or Japan globeflower, ayellow-flowered, perennial, rosaceous plant, seen in old-fashioned gardens.
cord: Any structure having the appearance of a cord, esp. a tendon or a nerve. See under Spermatic, Spinal, Umbilical, Vocal.

cordax: A lascivious dance featuring in Ancient Greek comedy.
corday: French revolutionary heroine (a Girondist) who assassinated Marat (-)

cordel: Spanish chain, a traditional Spanish and Mexican unit of distance equivalent to about. m.
cordelle: A twisted cord; a tassel. Halliwell.
corder: One who prepares wood as cordwood.
cordgrass: any of several perennial grasses of the genus Spartina
cordia: tropical deciduous or evergreen trees or shrubs of the family Boraginaceae
cordial: Any invigorating and stimulating preparation; as, a peppermint cordial.
cordiality: Relation to the heart. That the ancients had any respect of cordiality or reference unto the heart, will much be doubted. Sir T. Browne.

In making it the ingredients are mixed into a paste with the addition of acetone and pressed out into cords (of various diameters) resembling brown twine, which are dried and cut to length. A variety containing less nitroglycerin than the original is known as cordite M. D.
cordlike: Resembling or characteristic of a cord.
cordoba: the basic unit of money in Nicaragua; equal to centavos
cordon: The coping of the scarp wall, which projects beyong the face of the wall a few inches.
cordovan: Same as Cordwain. in England the name is applied to leather made from horsehide.
cords: cotton trousers made of corduroy cloth
corduroy: Trousers or breeches of corduroy. Corduroy road, a roadway formed of logs laid side by side across it, as in marshy places; so called from its rough or ribbed surface, resembling corduroy.
cordwain: A term used in the Middle Ages for Spanish leather (goatskin tanned and dressed), and hence, any leather handsomely finished, colored, gilded, or the like. Buskins he wore of costliest cordwain. Spenser.
cordwainer: A worker in cordwain, or cordovan leather; a shoemaker.
cordwood: firewood cut and stacked in cords; wood sold by the cord
cordyceps: Any of the fungi of the genus Cordyceps, a genus of endoparasitoid sac fungi.
core: A body of individuals; an assemblage. He was in a core of people. Bacon.
coredeems: third-person singular simple present indicative of coredeem
coreference: the grammatical relation between two words that have a common referent
coregonidae: soft-finned fishes comprising the freshwater whitefishes; formerly included in the family Salmonidae
coregonus: type genus of the Coregonidae: whitefishes

corer: That which cores; an instrument for coring fruit; as, an apple corer.
corespondent: the codefendant charged with adultery with the estranged spouse in a divorce proceeding
corf: A native or inhabitant of Corfu, an island in the Mediterranean sea.
corgi: either of two Welsh breeds of long-bodied short-legged dogs with erect ears and a fox-like head
coriander: An umbelliferous plant, the Coriandrum sati vum, the fruit or seeds of which have a strong smell and a spicy taste, and in medicine are considered as stomachic and carminative.
coriandrum: small genus of annual Mediterranean herbs
coridine: A colorless or yellowish oil, CHN, of a leathery odor, oc curing in coal tar, Dip pel's oil, tobacco smoke, etc., regarded as an organic base, homologous with pyridine. Also, one of a series of metameric compounds of which coridine is a type.
corineus: A prodigious warrior and the eponymous founder of Cornwall in British legend.
coring: present participle and gerund of core
corinne: The common gazelle (Gazella dorcas). See Gazelle.
corinth: the modern Greek port near the site of the ancient city that was second only to Athens
corinthian: Of or pertaining to the Corinthian order of architecture, invented by the Greeks, but more commonly used by the Romans. This is the lightest and most ornamental of the three orders used by the Greeks. Parker.
corinthians: Either of the two books in the New Testament of the Bible that are written as epistles to the people of Corinth and which are attributed to Paul the Apostle, Sosthenes and Timothy.
corium: Armor made of leather, particularly that used by the Romans; used also by En lish soldiers till the reign of Edward I. Fosbroke.
cork: close a bottle with a cork
corkage: The charge made by innkeepers for drawing the cork and taking care of bottles of wine bought elsewhere by a guest.
corked: having acquired an unpleasant taste from the cork; as, a bottle of wine is corked.
corker: (dated slang) a remarkable or excellent thing or person

corkwood: The tree producing the ali gator apple.
corky: Consisting of, or like, cork; dry shriveled up. Bind fast hiss corky arms.
corm: A solid bulb-shaped root, as of the crocus. See Bulb.
cormel: A small corm that develops at the base of an existing corm.
cormophyte: Any plant having a proper stem or axis of growth, which is distinct from its leaves, phyllophyte

corn: A thickening of the epidermis at some point, esp. on the toees, by friction or pressure. It is usually painful and troublesome. Welkome, gentlemen! Ladies that have their toes Unplagued with corns, will have a bout with you.

cornball: A ball of popped corn stuck together with soft candy from molasses or sugar.
cornbin: A bin for the storage of corn.
corncob: The cob or axis on which the kernels of Indian corn grow.
corncrake: A bird (Crex crex or C. pratensis) which frequents grain fields; the European crake or land rail; called also corn bird.
cornea: The transparent part of the coat of the eyeball which covers the iris and pupil and admits light to the interior. See Eye.
corned: (used especially of meat) cured in brine
cornel: The cornelian cherry (Cornus Mas), a European shrub with clusters of small, greenish flowers, followed by very acid but edible drupes resembling cherries.
cornelius: A male given name from Latin.
cornell: United States actress noted for her performances in Broadway plays (-)
cornemuse: A wind instrument nearly identical with the bagpipe. Dray ton.
corneous: Of a texture resembling horn; horny; hard. Sir T. Browne.
cornercap: The chief ornament. Thou ma kest the triumviry the cornercap of society.
cornering: present participle and gerund of corner
cornerstone: a stone in the exterior of a large and important building; usually carved with a date and laid with appropriate ceremonies
cornerwise: With the corner in front; diagonally; not square.
cornetcy: The commission or rank of a cornet.
cornetfish: slender tropical fish with a long tubular snout and bony plates instead of scales
cornetist: a musician who plays the trumpet or cornet
cornett: An early horn wind instrument used in European music of the medieval, Renaissance, and Baroque periods. Not to be confused with later brass instrument.
cornetto: A trumpet-like wind instrument used in European music of the medieval, Renaissance, and Baroque periods.
corneum: the outermost layer of the epidermis consisting of dead cells that slough off
cornfield: A field where corn is or has been growing; in England, afield of wheat, rye, barley, or oats; in America, a field of Indian corn.
cornflower: A conspicuous wild flower (Centaurea Cyanus), growing ingrain fields.
cornhusk: the husk of an ear of corn
cornic: Pertaining to, derived from, or resembling, the dogwood (Cornus florida).
cornice: Any horizontal, molded or otherwise decorated projection which crowns or finishes the part to which it is affixed; as, the cornice of an order, pedestal, door, window, or house. Gwilt. Cornice ring, the ring on a cannon next behind the muzzle ring.
corniche: A road built on a ledge (cliff), especially along water (a river, sea, etc).
cornicle: A little horn. Sir T. Browne.
corniferous: Of or pertaining to the lowest period of the Devonian age.(Seethe Diagram, under Geology.) The Corniferous period has been so called from the numerous seams of hornstone which characterize the later part of the period, as developed in the State of New York.
cornification: Conversion into, or formation of, horn; a becoming like horn.
cornigerous: Horned; having horns; as, cornigerous animals. Sir T.Browne.
cornish: Of or pertaining to Cornwall, in England. Cornish chough. Seech ough. Cornish engine, a single-acting pumping engine, used in mines, in cornwall and elsewhere, and for water works. A heavy pump rod or plunger, raised by the steam, forces up the water by its weight, in descending.
cornpone: cornbread often made without milk or eggs and baked or fried, typically a southern US dish
cornrow: One of a set of rows of tightly braided hair close to the scalp, forming a hairstyle, of African origin.
cornsheller: A machine that separates the kernels of corn from the cob.
cornstarch: Starch made from Indian corn, esp. a fine white flour used for puddings, etc.
cornu: A horn, or anything shaped like or resembling a horn.
cornuate: Horn-shaped, as with a bicornuate uterus.
cornucopia: A genus of grasses bearing spikes of flowers resembling the cornucopia in form.
cornus: a rosid dicot genus of the family Cornaceae including: dogwood; cornel: perennial chiefly deciduous shrubs or small trees of temperate regions of northern hemisphere
cornute: To bestow horns upon; to make a cuckold of; to cuckold. Burton.
cornutin: A poisonous organic compound derived from ergot, the spur of rye and other grasses.
cornuto: A man that wears the horns; a cuckold.
cornwall: a hilly county in southwestern England
cornwallis: commander of the British forces in the American War of Independence; was defeated by American and French troops at Yorktown (-)
corny: Strong, stiff, or hard, like a horn; resembling horn. Up stood the cornu reed. Milton.
corody: An allowance of meat, drink, or clothing due from an abbey or other religious house for the sustenance of such of the king'sservants as he may designate to receive it.

corollary: Having a corolla or corollas; like a corolla.
coromandel: The west coast, or a portion of the west coast, of the Bay of bengal. Coromandel gooseberry. See Carambola. Coromandel wood, Calamander wood.
corona: The projecting part of a Classic cornice, the under side of which is cut with a recess or channel so as to form a drip. See illust. of Column.
coronagraph: A telescope that has an attachment which blocks out the direct light from the sun or other star, allowing examination of the corona and the detection of exoplanets.
coronal: Of or pertaining to the shell of a sea urchin. Coronal suture (Anat.), a suture extending across the skull between the parietal and frontal bones; the frontoparietal suture.
coronary: Resembling, or situated like, a crown or circlet; as, the coronary arteries and veins of the heart.
coronation: the ceremony of installing a new monarch
coroner: An officer of the peace whose principal duty is to inquire, with the help of a jury, into the cause of any violent, sudden or mysterious death, or death in prison, usually on sight of the body and at the place where the death occurred.
coronet: The upper part of a horse's hoof, where the horn terminates in skin. James White.
coronilla: A genus of plants related to the clover, having their flowers arranged in little heads or tufts resembling coronets.
coronis: In Greek grammar, a sign sometimes placed over a contracted syllable. W. W. Good win.
coronoid: Resembling the beak of a crow; as, the coronoid process of the jaw, or of the ulna.
corotate: To rotate in conjunction with another object
coroutine: A piece of code that performs a task, and that can be passed new input and return output more than once.
corozo: any of several tropical American palms bearing corozo nuts
corporal: A noncommissioned officer, next below a sergeant. In the United states army he is the lowest noncomissioned officer in a company of infantry. He places and relieves sentinels. Corporal's guard, adetachment such as would be in charge of a corporal for guard duty, etc.; hence, derisively, a very small number of persons. Lance corporal, an assistant corporal on private's pay. Farrow. Ship's corporal (Naut.), a petty officer who assists the master at arms in his various duties.
corporality: The state of being or having a body; bodily existence; corporeality; opposed to spirituality. Dr. H. More.
corporally: In or with the body; bodily; as, to be corporally present. Sharp.
corporas: The corporal, or communion cloth. Fuller.
corporation: A body politic or corporate, formed and authorized by law toact as a single person, and endowed by law with the capacity of succession; a society having the capacity of transacting business as an individual.
corporatism: control of a state or organization by large interest groups
corporeal: Having a body; consisting of, or pertaining to, a material body or substance; material; opposed to spiritual or immaterial. His omnipotence That to corporeal substance could add Speed almost spiritual. Milton. Corporeal property, such as may be seen and handled (as opposed to incorporeal, which can not be seen or handled, and exists only in contemplation). Mozley & W.
corporeality: The state of being corporeal; corporeal existence.
corporeity: The state of having a body; the state of being corporeal; materiality. The one attributed corporeity to God. Bp. Stilling fleet. Those who deny light to be matter, do not therefore deny its corporeity. Coleridge.
corposant: St. Elmo's fire. See under Saint.
corpse: A human body in general, whether living or dead; sometimes contemptuosly.
corpus: A body, living or dead; the corporeal substance of a thing. Corpus callosum (k; pl. Corpora callo sa (-s Etym:(Anat.), the great band of commissural fibers uniting the cerebralhemispheries. See Brain. Corpus Chris ti (kr Etym:(R. C. Ch.), af estival in honor of the eucharist, observed on the Thursday after trinity Sunday. Corpus Chris ti cloth. Same as Pyx cloth, under Pyx. Corpus delicti (d Etym:(Law), the substantial and fundamental fact of the co mission of a crime; the proofs essential to establish a crime. Corpus luteum (l; pl. Corpora lutea (-. Etym:(Anat.), the reddish yellow mass which fills a ruptured Grafianfollicle in the mammalian ovary. Corpus striatum (str; pl. Corpora st riata (-t. Etym:(Anat.), a ridge in the wall of each lateral ventricle of the brain.
corpuscular: Pertaining to, or composed of, corpuscles, or small particles. Corpuscular philosophy, that which attempts to account for the phenomena of nature, by the motion, figure, rest, position, etc., of the minute particles of matter. Corpuscular theory (Opt.), the theory enunciated by Sir Isaac newton, that light consists in the emission and rapid progression of minute particles or corpuscles. The theory is now generally rejected, and supplanted by the undulatory theory.
corrade: To erode, as the bed of a stream. See Corrosion.
corradiate: To converge to one point or focus, as light or rays.
corral: A pen for animals; esp., an inclosure made with wagons, by emigrants in the vicinity of hostile Indians, as a place of security for horses, cattle, etc.
corrasive: Corrosive. Corrasive sores which eat into the flesh. Holland.
correal: Under joint obligation (applied to an obligation in which the parties are severally liable).
correct: Set right, or made straight; hence, conformable to truth, rectitude, or propriety, or to a just standard; nnot faulty or imperfect; free from error; as, correct behavior; correct views. Always use the most correct editions. Felt on.
correctable: capable of being returned to the original condition; not necessarily permanent
correctify: To correct. When your worship's plass ed to correctify a lady. Beau & Fl.
correcting: present participle and gerund of correct
correction: the act of offering an improvement to replace a mistake; setting right
correctional: Tending to, or intended for, correction; used for correction; as, a correctional institution.
corrections: the department of local government that is responsible for managing the treatment of convicted offenders
correctly: In a correct manner; exactly; acurately; without fault or error.
correctness: The state or quality of being correct; as, the correctness of opinions or of manners; correctness of taste; correctness in writing or speaking; the correctness of a text or copy.
corrector: One who, or that which, corrects; as, a corrector of abuses; acor rector of the press; an alkali is a corrector of acids.
corrects: third-person singular simple present indicative of correct
corregidor: The chief magistrate of a Spanish town.
corregimiento: A historical administrative subdivision of a country in certain parts of Spain and Latin America
correi: A hollow in the side of a hill, where game usually lies. Fleet foot on the correi. " Sir W. Scott.
correlatable: Such as can be correlated; as, correlatable phenomena.
correlate: To have reciprocal or mutual relations; to be mutually related. Doctrine and worship correlate as theory and practice. Tylor.
correlates: third-person singular simple present indicative of correlate
correlating: present participle and gerund of correlate
correlation: Reciprocal relation; corresponding similarity or parallelism of relation or law; capacity of being converted into, or of giving place to, one another, under certain conditions; as, the correlation of forces, or of zymotic diseases. Correlation of energy, the relation to one another of different forms of energy; usually having some reference to the principle of conservation of energy. See conservation of energy, under Conservation. Correlation of forces, the relation between the forces which matter, endowed with various forms of energy, may exert.
correlative: Having or indicating a reciprocal relation. Father and son, prince and subject, stranger and citizen, are correlative terms. Hume.
correption: Chiding; reproof; reproach. Angry, passionate correption being rather apt to provoke, than to amend. Hammond.
corresponded: simple past and past participle of correspond
correspondence: communication by the exchange of letters
correspondency: Same as Correspondence,.The correspondencies of types and antitypes. may be very reasonable confirmations. S. Clarke.
correspondent: Suitable; adapted; fit; corresponding; congruous; conformable; in accord or agreement; obedient; willing. Action correspondent or repugnant unto the law. Hooker. As fast the correspondent passions rise. Thomson. I will be correspondent to command.
correspondential: Relating to a correspondence (congruity or similarity between things).
corresponds: third-person singular simple present indicative of correspond
corrida: a Spanish or Portuguese or Latin American spectacle
corridor: A gallery or passageway leading to several apartments of ah ouse.
corrigibility: Quality of being corrigible; capability of being corrected; corrigibleness.
corrigible: capable of being corrected or set right
corrigibleness: The state or quality of being corrigible; corrigibility.
corrival: A fellow rival; a competitor; a rival; also, a companion.
corrivalship: Co rivalry. By the corrivalship of Sh ager his false friend. Sir T. Herbert.
corroborates: third-person singular simple present indicative of corroborate
corroborating: present participle and gerund of corroborate

corroboratory: Tending to strengthen; corroborative; as, corroboratory facts.
corroboree: A nocturnal festivity with which the Australian aborigines celebrate tribal events of importance. Symbolic dances are given by the young men of the tribe, while the women act as musicians.
corrode: To have corrosive action; to be subject to corrosion. Corroding lead, lead sufficiently pure to be used in making white lead by aprocess of corroding.
corroded: eaten away as by acid or oxidation
corroder: One who or that which corrodes.
corrodes: third-person singular simple present indicative of corrode
corrodibility: The quality of being corrodible. Johnson.
corrodible: Capable of being corroded; corrosible. Sir T. Browne.
corrody: A form of pension or annuity given by a religious institution as provision for maintenance.
corrosion: The action or effect of corrosive agents, or the process of corrosive change; as, the rusting of iron is a variety of corrosion. Corrosion is a particular species of dissolution of bodies, either by an acid or a saline menstruum. John Quincy.
corrosive: a substance having the tendency to cause corrosion (such a strong acids or alkali)
corrosiveness: The quality or property of corroding or being corrosive, of eating away or disintegrating; acrimony.
corroval: A dark brown substance of vegetable origin, allied to curare, and used by the natives of New Granada as an arrow poison.
corrugate: Wrinkled; crumpled; furrowed; contracted into ridges and furrows.
corrugated: shaped into alternating parallel grooves and ridges
corrugating: present participle and gerund of corrugate
corrugation: The act corrugating; contraction into wrinkles or alternate ridges and grooves.
corrugator: A muscle which contracts the skin of the forehead into wrinkles.
corrupter: One who corrupts; one who vitiates or taints; as, a corrupter of morals.
corruptful: Tending to corrupt; full of corruption. Corruptful bribes. " Spenser.
corruptibility: The quality of being corruptible; the possibility or liability of being corrupted; corruptibleness. Burke.
corruptible: That which may decay and perish; the human body.Cor. xv.
corruptibleness: The state or quality of being corruptible.
corruption: decay of matter (as by rot or oxidation)
corruptive: Having the quality of tai ning or vitiating; tending to produce corruption. It should be endued with some corruptive quality for so speedy adissolution of the meat. Ray.
corruptly: In a corrupt manner; by means of corruption or corrupting influences; wronfully.
corruptress: A woman who corrupts. Thou studied old corruptress. Beau & Fl.
corrupts: third-person singular simple present indicative of corrupt

corsair: a pirate along the Barbary Coast
corsak: A small foxlike mammal (Cynalopex corsac), found in Central asia.
corse: an island in the Mediterranean; with adjacent islets it constitutes a region of France
corseque: A pole weapon with a spike and two lateral blades on a shaft.
corsican: of or relating to or characteristic of Corsica or its people
cortege: A train of attendants; a procession.

corticifugal: of a nerve fiber passing outward from the cerebral cortex
corticipetal: of a nerve fiber or impulse originating outside and passing toward the cerebral cortex

corticoid: a steroid hormone produced by the adrenal cortex or synthesized
corticose: Abounding in bark; resembling bark; barky.

cortina: a cobwebby partial veil consisting of silky fibrils

It is the hardest substance found native, next to the diamond.
coruscate: To glitter in flashes; to flash.

coruscation: a sudden or striking display of brilliance
corvee: An obligation to perform certain services, as the repair of roads, for the lord or sovereign.
corvette: a highly maneuverable escort warship; smaller than a destroyer
corvina: Any of various fish, including Cilus gilberti, Larimichthys polyactis, and members of the genera Cynoscion and Isopisthus.
corvine: Of or pertaining to the crow; crow like.
corvus: a small quadrilateral constellation in the southern hemisphere near Virgo
cory: An English surname from Old Norse, a variant of Corey.
corybant: One of the priests of Cybele in Phrygia. The rites of the Corybants were accompanied by wild music, dancing, etc.
corybantic: Of, pertaining to, or resembling, the Corybant es or their rites; frantic; frenzied; as, a corybantic dance.

corylus: deciduous monoecious nut-bearing shrubs of small trees: hazel; sometimes placed in the subfamily or family Corylaceae

corymbose: Consisting of corymbs, or resembling them in form.
corynebacterium: any species of the genus Corynebacterium
corypha: large fan palms of tropical Asia to Australia
coryphaeus: The conductor or leader of the chorus of a drama.
coryphantha: a cactus of the genus Coryphantha
corypheus: The conductor, chief, or leader of the dramatic chorus; hence, the chief or leader of a party or interest. That noted corypheus of the Independent faction. South.

coshering: A feudal prerogative of the lord of the soil entitling him to lodging and food at his tenant's house. Bur rill. Sometimes he contrived, in def lance of the law, to live by coshering, that is to say, by quartering himself on the old tent ants of his family, who, wretched as was their own condition, could not refuse aport ion of their pittance to one whom they still regarded as their rightful lord. Macaulay.
coshers: third-person singular simple present indicative of cosher
cosier: A tailor who botches his work.
cosign: sign and endorse (another person's signature), as for a loan

cosmetology: the practice of beautifying the face and hair and skin
cosmic: of or from or pertaining to or characteristic of the cosmos or universe
cosmine: A continuous layer of dentine, covered by a layer of enamel, that takes the place of scales in some ancient fish.
cosmism: A philosophical and cultural movement in Russia in the early th century, combining elements of religion and ethics with a history of the origin, evolution and future of the cosmos and humankind.
cosmochemistry: The branch of chemistry that deals with the creation of the elements, and their isotopic distribution, in the universe; also with the synthesis and reactions of simple molecules in interstellar space.
cosmogeny: the branch of astrophysics that studies the origin and evolution and structure of the universe
cosmogonist: One who treats of the origin of the universe; one versed in cosmogony.
cosmogony: The creation of the world or universe; a theory or account of such creation; as, the poetical cosmogony of Hesoid; the cosmogonies of Thales, Anaxagoras, and Plato. The cosmogony or creation of the world has puzzled philosophers ofall ages. Goldsmith.
cosmography: A description of the world or of the universe; or the science which teaches the constitution of the whole system of worlds, or the figure, disposition, and relation of all its parts.
cosmolabe: An instrument resembling the astrolabe, formerly used for measuring the angles between heavenly bodies; called also pantacosm.
cosmoline: A substance obtained from the residues of the distillation of petroleum, essentially the same as vaseline, but of somewhat stiffer consistency, and consisting of a mixture of the higher paraffin es; akind of petroleum jelly.
cosmologist: One who describes the universe; one skilled in cosmology.
cosmology: The science of the world or universe; or a treatise relating to the structure and parts of the system of creation, the elements of bodies, the modifications of material things, the laws of motion, and the order and course of nature.
cosmonaut: a person trained to travel in a spacecraft
cosmonautics: The activities of cosmonauts; Soviet/Russian astronautics.
cosmoplastic: Pertaining to a plastic force as operative in the formation of the world independently of God; world-forming. Cosmoplastic and hylozoic atheisms. " Gud worth.
cosmopolis: An important city, such as a capital city, inhabited by people from a diverse range of cultural backgrounds.

The cosmothetic idealists. deny that mind is immediately conscious of matter. Sir W. Hamilton.
cosmozoism: The belief that the cosmos is a living thing.
cosponsorship: joint sponsorship by more than one party
coss: A Hindoo measure of distance, varying from one and a half totwo English miles. Whitworth.
cossack: One of a warlike, pastoral people, skillful as horsemen, inhabiting different parts of the Russian empire and furnishing valuable contingents of irregular cavalry to its armies, those of little Russia and those of the Don forming the principal divisions.
cosset: A lamb reared without the aid of the dam. Hence: A pet, in general.
costa: A rib of an animal or a human being.
costal: Pertaining to the ribs or the sides of the body; as, costal nerves.
costar: A person who shares star billing with another.
costard: An apple, large and round like the head. Some consist more of air than water.; others more of water than wind, as your costards and pome waters. Muffett.
costate: (of the surface) having a rough, riblike texture
costated: simple past and past participle of costate

costiasis: a fatal disease of freshwater fish caused by a flagellated protozoan invading the skin
costive: retarding evacuation of feces; binding; constipating
costliest: superlative form of costly: most costly
costliness: The quality of being costy; expensiveness; sumptuousness.

costotransverse: connecting a rib and the transverse process of a vertebra
costovertebral: Connecting a rib with the body of a vertebra
costrel: A bottle of leather, earthenware, or wood, having ears by which it was suspended at the side. A youth, that, following with a costrel, bore The means of goodly welcome, flesh and wine. Tennyson.
costs: pecuniary reimbursement to the winning party for the expenses of litigation
costumed: dressed in clothing characteristic of a period, country, or class
costumer: One who makes or deals in costumes, as for theaters, fancy balls, etc.
costumier: someone who designs or supplies costumes (as for a play or masquerade)
costuming: present participle and gerund of costume
costusroot: annual herb of the eastern Himalayas (Kashmir) having purple florets and a fragrant root that yields a volatile oil used in perfumery and for preserving furs
cot: A small, rudely-formed boat. Bell cot. (Arch.) See under Bell.
cotan: ratio of the adjacent to the opposite side of a right-angled triangle
cotangent: The tangent of the complement of an arc or angle. See Illust.of Functions.
cote: To go side by side with; hence, to pass by; to outrun and get before; as, a dog cotes a hare. Dray ton. We coted them on the way, and hither are they coming.
coteau: A hilly upland including the divide between two valleys; a divide.
coted: simple past and past participle of cote
cotehardie: A mid to late th century unisex garment tailored to fit the torso and arms, usually with a row of buttons down the front as well as down each fitted sleeve from the elbow to the wrist. Women's coathardies trailed on the floor, but those for men could be cut very short.
cotemporary: Living or being at the same time; contemporary.
cotenant: A tenant in common, or a joint tenant.
coterie: A set or circle of persons who meet familiarly, as for social, literary, or other purposes; a clique. The queen of your coterie. Thackeray.
cothurn: A buskin anciently used by tragic actors on the stage; hence, tragedy in general. The moment had arrived when it was thought that the mask and the cothurn might be assumed with effect. Motley.
cothurnate: Wearing a cothurn, or (by extension) tragic, solemn.
cotidal: Marking an equality in the tides; having high tide at the same time. Cotidal lines (Phys. Geog.), lines on a map passing through places that have high tide at the same time.
cotillion: a ball at which young ladies are presented to society
coting: present participle and gerund of cote
cotingid: Any bird in the family Cotingidae.
coto: A traditional Spanish unit of length, equivalent to about. cm.
cotoneaster: any shrub of the genus Cotoneaster: erect or creeping shrubs having richly colored autumn foliage and many small white to pinkish flowers followed by tiny red or black fruits
cotquean: A man who busies himself with affairs which properly belong to women. Addison.

Cotswold sheep, a long-wooled breed of sheep, formerly common in the counties of Gloucester, Hereford, and Worcester, Eng.; so called from the Cotswold Hills. cotta: A surplice, in England and America usually one shorter and less full than the ordinary surplice and with short sleeves, or sometimes none.
cottabus: An ancient game played by throwing wine at metal disks or pans, trying to knock them down or make them sink in a basin of water.

cottaged: Set or covered with cottages. Even humble Hart ing's cottaged vale. Collins.
cottager: One who lives on the common, without paying any rent, or having land of his own.
cottar: fastener consisting of a wedge or pin inserted through a slot to hold two other pieces together
cottier: In Great Britain and Ireland, a person who hires a small cottage, with or without a plot of land. Cottiers commonly aid in the work of the landlord's farm.
cottise: A diminutive of the bendlet, containing one half its area orone quarter the area of the bend. When a single cottise is used alone it is often called a cost. See also Couple-close.

cottoid: Like a fish of the genus Cottus. n.
cottoned: simple past and past participle of cotton
cottonmouth: venomous semiaquatic snake of swamps in southern United States

cottontail: The American wood rabbit (Lepus sylvatic us); also called molly cottontail.
cottonwood: An American tree of the genus Populus or polar, having the seeds covered with abundant cotton like hairs; esp., the P. moniliferaand P. angustifolia of the Western United States.

cottus: type genus of the Cottidae: sculpins
cotula: cosmopolitan herbs especially southern hemisphere; many used as ground covers

Black stone.

couldst: second-person singular simple past indicative of can

couloir: A dredging machine for excavating canals, etc.
