counsel: Interchange of opinions; mutual advising; consultation. All the chief priest and elders of the people took counsel against Jesus, to put him to death. Matt. xxvii.
counselable: Willing to receive counsel or follow advice. Few men of so great parts were upon all occasions more counselable than he. Clarendon.
counseled: simple past and past participle of counsel
counseling: something that provides direction or advice as to a decision or course of action
counselled: simple past and past participle of counsel
counselling: something that provides direction or advice as to a decision or course of action
counsellor: a lawyer who pleads cases in court
counselor: someone who gives advice about problems
count: To plead orally; to argue a matter in court; to recite a count. Bur rill.
countably: In a countable manner; in a way that can be counted.
countdown: counting backward from an arbitrary number to indicate the time remaining before some event (such as launching a space vehicle)
counted: simple past and past participle of count
countenance: the appearance conveyed by a person's face
countenanced: simple past and past participle of countenance
counter: A prefix meaning contrary, opposite, in opposition; as, counteract, counterbalance, countercheck. See Counter, adv. & a.
counteract: To act in opposition to; to hinder, defeat, or frustrate, by contrary agency or influence; as, to counteract the effect of medicines; to counteract good advice.
counteracted: simple past and past participle of counteract
counteracting: present participle and gerund of counteract
counteraction: Action in opposition; hindrance resistance.do not. overcome the counteraction of a false principle or of stubborn partiality. Johnson.
counteragitation: Agitation (the excitement of public feeling by discussion, appeals, etc.) that opposes agitation by another party.
counterappeal: An appeal lodged in response to an earlier appeal.
counterargument: an argument offered in opposition to another argument
counterbalance: To oppose with an equal weight or power; to counteract the power or effect of; to countervail; to equiponderate; to balance. The remaining air was not able to counterbalance the mercurial cylinder. Boyle. The cstudy of mind is necessary to counterbalance and correct the influence of the study of nature. Sir W. Hamilton.
counterbalanced: brought into equipoise by means of a weight or force that offsets another
counterbalancing: present participle and gerund of counterbalance
counterblow: a return blow; a retaliatory blow
counterbore: To form a counterbore in, by boring, turning, or drilling; to enlarge, as a hole, by means of a counterbore.
counterbrace: To brace in opposite directions; as, to counterbrace the yards, i. e., to brace the head yards one way and the after yards another.
countercathexis: The suppression or repression of mental energy.
counterchanged: Having the tinctures exchanged mutually; thus, if the field is divided palewise, or and azure, and cross is borne counterchanged, that part of the cross which comes on the azure side will be or, and that on the or side will be azure.
countercharm: To destroy the effect of a charm upon.
countercheck: To oppose or check by some obstacle; to check by a return check.
counterclaim: A claim made by a person as an offset to a claim made on him.
counterclockwise: in a direction opposite to the direction in which the hands of a clock move
counterculture: a culture with lifestyles and values opposed to those of the established culture
countered: simple past and past participle of counter
counterextension: The fixation of the upper part of a limb, while extension is practiced on the lower part, as in cases of luxation or fracture.
counterfactual: going counter to the facts (usually as a hypothesis)
counterfeited: simple past and past participle of counterfeit
counterfeiter: One who counterfeits; one who copies or imitates; especially, one who copies or forges bank notes or coin; a forger. The coin which was corrupted by counterfeiters. Camden.
counterfeiting: present participle and gerund of counterfeit
counterflory: Adorned with flowers (usually fleurs-de-lis) so divided that the tops appear on one side and the bottoms on the others; said ofany ordinary.
counterfoil: That part of a tally, formerly in the exchequer, which was kept by an officer in that court, the other, called the stock, being delivered to the person who had lent the king money on the account; - - called also counterstock.
counterfort: A kind of buttress of masonry to strengthen a revetment wall.
countergage: An adjustable gage, with double points for transferring measurements from one timber to another, as the breadth of a mortise to the place where the tenon is to be made. Knight.
counterguerrilla: Opposed to guerrillas and their warfare.
countering: present participle and gerund of counter
counterinsurgency: actions taken by a government to defeat insurgency
counterinsurgent: of or relating or characteristic of actions taken by a government to defeat insurgency
counterintelligence: intelligence activities concerned with identifying and counteracting the threat to security posed by hostile intelligence organizations or by individuals engaged in espionage or sabotage or subversion or terrorism
counterintuitive: contrary to what common sense would suggest
counterion: Any ion of opposite charge to another in a solution or other electrochemical system
counterirritation: The treatment of one diseased area by acting elsewhere.
counterlath: A batten laid lengthwise between two rafters to afford a bearing for laths laid crosswise.
counterman: A man who attends at the counter of a shop to sell goods.
countermand: A contrary order; revocation of a former order or command. Have you no countermand for Claudio yet, But he must die to-morrows hak.
countermandable: Capable of being countermanded; revocable. Bacon.
countermanded: simple past and past participle of countermand
countermarch: To march back, or to march in reversed order. The two armies marched and counter marched, drew near and receded. Macaulay.
countermark: An artificial cavity made in the teeth of horses that have outgrown their natural mark, to disguise their age.
countermeasure: an action taken to offset another action
countermine: An underground gallery excavated to intercept and destroy the mining of an enemy.
countermove: To move in a contrary direction to.
counteroffensive: a large scale offensive (more than a counterattack) undertaken by a defending force to seize the initiative from an attacking force
counteropening: An aperture or vent on the opposite side, or in a different place.
counterpane: A coverlet for a bed, originally stitched or woven in squares or figures. On which a tissue counterpane was cast. Dray ton.
counterpart: One of two corresponding copies of an instrument; a duplicate.
counterpassant: Passant in opposite directions; said of two animals.
counterplay: (chess) an attack that is intended to counter the opponent's advantage in another part of the board
counterplead: To plead the contrary of; to plead against; to deny.
counterplot: To oppose, as another plot, by plotting; to attempt to frustrate, as a stratagem, by stratagem. Every wile had proved abortive, every plot had been counterplotted. De Quins ey.
counterplotted: simple past and past participle of counterplot
counterpoint: An opposite points ir E. Sand ys.
counterpoise: To act against with equal weight; to equal in weght; to balance the weight of; to counterbalance. Weigts, counterpoising one another. Sir K. Digby.
counterpoised: brought into equipoise by means of a weight or force that offsets another
counterpoising: present participle and gerund of counterpoise
counterpoison: a remedy that stops or controls the effects of a poison
counterpole: The exact opposite. The German prose offers the counterpole to the French style. De Quincey.
counterpose: to constitute a counterweight or counterbalance to
counterproductive: tending to hinder the achievement of a goal
counterpropaganda: Propaganda disseminated as a response and opposition to other propaganda.
counterproposal: a proposal offered as an alternative to an earlier proposal
counterquestion: A question that serves as a reply to, or distraction from, another.
counterrevolution: a revolution whose aim is to reverse the changes introduced by a previous revolution
counterrevolutionary: relating to or being a counterrevolution
counterscarp: The outer slope of a defensive or fortified ditch
countershaft: An intermediate shaft; esp., one which receives motion from aline shaft in a factory and transmits it to a machine.
countersign: To sign on the opposite side of (an instrument or writing); hence, to sign in addition to the signature of a principal or superior, in order to attest the authenticity of a writing.
countersignature: a second confirming signature endorsing a document already signed
countersigned: simple past and past participle of countersign
countersink: a hole (usually in wood) with the top part enlarged so that a screw or bolt will fit into it and lie below the surface
counterspy: a spy who works against enemy espionage
counterstand: Resistance; opposition; a stand against. Making counterstand to Robert Gui scard. Longfellow.
counterstimulation: Stimulation in an opposite manner or direction.
countersunk: Chamfered at the top; said of a hole.
countersway: A swaying in a contrary direction; an opposing influence. A countersway of restraint, curbing their wild exorbitance. Milton.
countertenor: of or being the highest male voice; having a range above that of tenor
counterterm: A term or word which is the opposite of, or antithesis to, another; an antonym; the opposite of synonym; as, foe is the counterterm of friend. C. J. Smith.
counterterrorist: someone who attempts to prevent terrorism
countertrippant: Trippant in opposite directions. See Trippant.
counterturn: The critical moment in a play, when, contrary to expectation, the action is embroiled in new difficulties. Dryden.
countervail: To act against with equal force, power, or effect; to thwart or overcome by such action; to furnish an equivalent to or for; to counterbalance; to compensate. Upon balancing the account, the profit at last will hardly countervail the inconveniences that go al long with it. L'Estrange.
countervailed: simple past and past participle of countervail
countervair: A heraldic fur resembling vair, except in the arrangement of the patches or figures: succeeding rows are reversed instead of staggered, so the bases of the panes of each tincture are opposite those of the same tincture in adjoining rows.
counterview: An opposite or opposing view; opposition; a posture in which two persons front each other. Within the gates of hell sat Death and Sin, In counterview. Milton M. Peisse has ably advocated the counterview in his preface and appendixx. Sir W. Hamilton.
counterweight: constitute a counterweight or counterbalance to
counterwill: The instinctive resistance to any coercion.
counterwork: To work in opposite ion to; to counteract. That counterwork sh folly and caprice. Pope.
countess: The wife of an earl in the British peerage, or of a count in the Continental nobility; also, a lady possessed of the same dignity in her own right. See the Note under Count.
countian: An inhabitant of a specified county.
countless: Incapable of being counted; not ascertainable; innumerable.
countor: An advocate or professional pleader; one who counted for his client, that is, orally pleaded his cause. Bur rill.
countretaille: A counter tally; correspondence (in sound).At the countretaille, in return. Chaucer.
countrified: Having the appearance and manners of a rustic; rude. As being one who took no pride, And was a deal too countrified. Lloyd.
country: The rock through which a vein runs. Conclusion to the country. See under Conclusion. To put, or throw, one's self upon the country, to appeal to one'sconstituents; to stand trial before a jury.
countryman: a man from your own country
countryside: A particular rural district; a country neighborhood. W.Black. Black more.
countrywoman: A woman born, or dwelling, in the country, as opposed to the city; a woman born or dwelling in the same country with another native or inhabitant.
county: (United Kingdom) a region created by territorial division for the purpose of local government
coupe: a car with two doors and front seats and a luggage compartment
couped: Cut off smoothly, as distinguished from erased; used especially for the head or limb of an animal. See Erased.
coupled: connected by a link, as railway cars or trailer trucks
couplement: Union; combination; a coupling; a pair. And forth together rode, a goodly couplement. Spenser.
coupler: One who couples; that which couples, as a link, ring, or shackle, to connect cars. Coupler of an organ, a contrivance by which any two or more of the ranks of keys, or keys and pedals, are connected so as to act together when the organ is played.
couplet: Two taken together; a pair or couple; especially two lines of verse that rhyme with each other. A sudden couplet rushes on your mind. Crab be.
coupling: A device or contrivance which serves to couple or connect adjacent parts or objects; as, a belt coupling, which connects the ends of a belt; a car coupling, which connects the cars in a train; as haft coupling, which connects the ends of shafts. Box coupling, Chain coupling. See under Box, Chain. Coupling box, a coupling shaped like a journal box, for clamping together the ends of two shafts, so that they may revolve together. Coupling pin, a pin or bolt used in coupling or joining together railroad cars, etc.
coupon: A certificate of interest due, printed at the bottom of transferable bonds (state, railroad, etc.), given for a term of years, designed to be cut off and presented for payment when the interest is due; an interest warrant.
courage: To inspire with courage. Paul write th unto Timothy. to courage him. Tyndale.
courageous: Possessing, or characterized by, courage; brave; bold. With this victory, the women became most courageous and proud, and the men waxed. fearful and desperate. Stow.
courageousness: The quality of being courageous; courage.
courant: Represented as running; said of a beast borne in a coat of arms.
courante: a court dance of the th century; consisted of short advances and retreats
couranto: A sprightly dance; a coranto; a courant.
courb: Curved; rounded. Her neck is short, her shoulders courb. Gower.
courbette: A movement in dressage in which the horse makes a series of jumps on the hind legs with the forelegs in the air.
courche: A square piece of linen used formerly by women instead of acap; a kerchief. Jamie son.
courier: A messenger sent with haste to convey letters or dispatches, usually on public busuness. The wary Bassa. by speedy couriers, advertised Soly man of the enemy's purpose. Knoll es.
courlan: A South American bird, of the genus Aramus, allied to the rails.
course: A continuous level range of brick or stones of the same height throughout the face or faces of a building. Gwilt.
courser: A grallatorial bird of Europe (Cursorius cursor), remarkable for its speed in running. Sometimes, in a wider sense, applied to running birds of the Ostrich family.
coursing: The pursuit or running game with dogs that follow by sight instead of by scent. In coursing of a deer, or hart, with greyhounds. Bacon
court: an assembly (including one or more judges) to conduct judicial business
courteous: Of courtlike manners; pertaining to, or exxpressive of, courtesy; characterized by courtesy; civil; obliging; well bred; polite; affable; complaisant. A patient and courteous bearing. Prescott. His behavior toward his people is grave and courteous. Fuller.
courteousness: The quality of being courteous; politeness; courtesy.
courtepy: A short coat of coarse cloth. Full threadbare was his overeste courtepy. Chaucer.
courter: One who courts; one who plays the lover, or who solicits inmarriage; one who flatters and cajoles. Sherwood.
courtesan: A woman who prostitutes herself for hire; a prostitute; aharlot. Lasciviously decked like a courtesan. Sir H. Wot ton.
courtesy: An act of civility, respect, or reverence, made by women, consisting of a slight depression or dropping of the body, with bending of the kness. The lady drops a courtesy in token of obedience, and the ceremony proceeds as usual. Golgsmith.
courthouse: a government building that houses the offices of a county government
courtier: an attendant at the court of a sovereign
courting: a man's courting of a woman
courtlike: After the manner of a court; elegant; polite; courtly.
courtliness: The quality of being courtly; elegance or dignity of manners.
courtly: In the manner of courts; politely; gracefully; elegantly. They can produce nothing so courtly writ. Dryden
courtroom: a room in which a lawcourt sits
courtship: a man's courting of a woman; seeking the affections of a woman (usually with the hope of marriage)
courtyard: A court or inclosure attached to a house.
couscous: A kind of food used by the natives of Western Africa, made of millet flour with flesh, and leaves of the baobab; called also lalo.
cousinhood: The state or condition of a cousin; also, the collective body of cousins; kinsfolk.
cousinry: A body or collection of cousins; the whole number of persons who stand in the relation of cousins to a given person or persons.
cousins: The American intelligence services (from a British perspective) or the British intelligence services (from an American perspective).
couter: A piece of armor which covers the elbow.
couth: Could; was able; knew or known; understood. Above all other one Daniel He love th, for he couth well Divine, that none other couth; To him were all thing couth, As he had it of God'sg race. Gower.
coutil: A woven cloth created specifically for making corsets.
couvade: A custom, among certain barbarous tribes, that when a woman gives birth to a child her husband takes to his bed, as if ill. The world-wide custom of the couvade, where at childbirth the husband undergoes medical treatment, in many cases being put to bed for days. Tylor.
covalence: valence characterized by the sharing of electrons in a chemical compound; the number of pairs of electrons an atom can share
covalent: of or relating to or characterized by covalence
covariant: A function involving the coefficients and the variables of aquantic, and such that when the quantic is lineally transformed the same function of the new variables and coefficients shall be equal to the old function multiplied by a factor. An invariant is a like function involving only the coefficients of the quantic.
covariate: A variable that is possibly predictive of the outcome under study.
cove: To arch over; to build in a hollow concave form; to make in the form of a cove. The mosques and other buildings of the Arabians are rounded into domes and coved roofs. H. Swinburne. Coved ceiling, a ceiling, the part of which next the wail is constructed in a cove. Coved vault, a vault composed of four coves meeting in a central point, and therefore the reverse of a groined vault.
coved: simple past and past participle of cove
covellite: A shiny indigo-blue sulfide mineral, CuS, that is an ore of copper.
coven: an assembly of witches; usually witches
covenable: Fit; proper; suitable. A covenable day. " Wyclif (Mark vi. ).
covenably: Fitly; suitably. Well and covenably. " Chaucer.
covenant: An agreement made by the Scottish Parliament in, and by the English Parliament in, to preserve the reformed religion in scotland, and to extirpate popery and prelacy; usually called theSolemn League and Covenant. Hewas born in the days of the Covenant, and was the heir of a covenanted house. Macualay.
covenanted: simple past and past participle of covenant
covenanter: One who subscribed and defended the Solemn League and covenant. " See Covenant.
covenanting: Belonging to a covenant. Specifically, belonging to the Scotch Covenanters. Be they covenanting traitors, Or the brood of false Argyle Aytoun.
covent: A convent or monastery. Bale. Covent Garden, a large square in London, so called because originally it was the garden of amonastery.
coventry: A town in the county of Warwick, England. To send to Coventry, to exclude from society; to shut out from social intercourse, as for ungentlemanly conduct. Coventry blue, blue thread of a superior dye, made at Coventry, England, and used for embroidery.
cover: The woods, underbrush, etc., which shelter and conceal game; covert; as, to beat a cover; to ride to cover.
coverage: The aggregate of risks covered by the terms of a contract of insurance.
coverall: a loose-fitting protective garment that is worn over other clothing
covered: Under cover; screened; sheltered; not exposed; hidden. Covered way (Fort.), a corridor or banquette along the top of the counterscarp and covered by an embankment whose slope forms the glacis. It gives the garrisonn an open line of communication around the works, and a standing place beyond the ditch. See Illust. of ravelin.
coverer: One who, or that which, covers.
covering: Anything which covers or conceals, as a roof, a screen, aw rapper, clothing, etc. Noah removed the covering of the ark. Gen. viii.They cause the naked to lodge without clothing, that they have no covering in the cold. Job. xxiv.A covering over the well's mouth. Sam. xvii.
coverlet: The uppermost cover of a bed or of any piece of furniture. Lay her in lilies and in violets. And odored sheets and arras coverlets. Spenser.
coverlid: A coverlet. All the coverlid was clocth of gold. Tennyson.
covert: Under cover, authority or protection; as, a feme covert, amarried woman who is considered as being under the protection and control of her husband. Covert way, (Fort.) See Covered way, under covered.
coverture: The condition of a woman during marriage, because she is considered under the cover, influence, power, and protection of her husband, and therefore called a feme covert, or femme couverte.
covet: To have or indulge inordinate desire. Which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith. Tim. vi.
coveting: present participle and gerund of covet
covetous: showing extreme cupidity; painfully desirous of another's advantages
covetousness: an envious eagerness to possess something
covets: third-person singular simple present indicative of covet
covey: To brood; to incubate.covey a whole year before they hatch. Holland.
covin: A collusive agreement between two or more persons to prejudicea third.
coving: A cove or series of coves, as the concaved surface under the overhang of a projecting upper story.
coward: Borne in the escutcheon with his tail doubled between his legs; said of a lion.
cowardice: Want of courage to face danger; extreme timidity; pusillanimity; base fear of danger or hurt; lack of spirit. The cowardice of doing wrong. Milton. Moderation was despised as cowardice. Macualay.
cowardish: Cowardly. " A base and a cowardish mind. " Robynson (More's Utopia).
cowardize: To render cowardly. God. cowardize th. insolent spirits. Bp. Hall.
cowardly: In the manner of a coward. Spenser.
cowbane: A poisonous umbelliferous plant; in England, the Cicuta vi rosa; in the United States, the Cicuta macula ta and the Arche mora rig ida. See Water hemlock.
cowbell: a bell hung around the neck of cow so that the cow can be easily located
cowberry: A species of Vaccinium (V. Vitis-id), which bears acid red berries which are sometimes used in cookery; locally called mountain cranberry.
cowbind: Any plant of genus Bryonia, which form dense mats of vines when they are not overgrowing shrubs, trees, and structures, especially white bryony (Bryonia alba).
cowbird: The cow blackbird (Molothrus ater), an American starling. Like the European cuckoo, it builds no nest, but lays its eggs in the nests of other birds; so called because frequently associated with cattle.
cowboy: a hired hand who tends cattle and performs other duties on horseback
cowboys: A pair of kings as a starting hand in Texas hold 'em.
cowcatcher: A strong inclined frame, usually of wrought-iron bars, in front of a locomotive engine, for catching or throwing off obstructions on a railway, as cattle; the pilot.
cower: To stoop by bending the knees; to crouch; to squat; hence, to quail; to sink through fear. Our dame sits cowering o'er a kitchen fire. Dryden. Like falcons, cowering on the nest. Goldsmith.
cowered: simple past and past participle of cower
cowering: present participle and gerund of cower
cowers: third-person singular simple present indicative of cower
cowfish: trunkfish having hornlike spines over the eyes
cowhand: a hired hand who tends cattle and performs other duties on horseback
cowherb: European annual with pale rose-colored flowers; cultivated flower or self-sown grainfield weed; introduced in North America; sometimes classified as a soapwort
cowherd: One whose occupation is to tend cows.
cowinner: A joint winner; somebody who is declared a winner along with somebody else.
cowl: A vessel carried on a pole between two persons, for conveyance of water. Johnson.
cowled: Wearing a cowl; hooded; as, a cowled monk. That cowled churchman. " Emerson.
cowlick: A tuft of hair turned up or awry (usually over the forehead),as if licked by a cow.
cowlike: Resembling a cow. With cowlike udders and with oxlike eyes. Pope.
cowling: protective covering consisting of a metal part that covers the engine
cowman: a hired hand who tends cattle and performs other duties on horseback
coworker: One who works with another; a co
cowpea: The seed of one or more leguminous plants of the genus dolichos; also, the plant itself. Many varieties are cultivated in the southern part of the United States.
cowper: English surgeon who discovered Cowper's gland (-)
cowpoke: a hired hand who tends cattle and performs other duties on horseback
cowpox: A pustular eruptive disease of the cow, which, when communicated to the human system, as by vaccination, protects from the smallpox; vaccinia; called also kinepox, cowpock, andkinepock. Dunglison.
cowpuncher: a hired hand who tends cattle and performs other duties on horseback
cowry: any of numerous tropical marine gastropods of the genus Cypraea having highly polished usually brightly marked shells
cows: domesticated bovine animals as a group regardless of sex or age
cowskin: leather made from the hide of a cow
cowslip: early spring flower common in British isles having fragrant yellow or sometimes purple flowers
cowslipped: Adorned with cowslips. Cowslipped lawns. " Keats.
cox: A coxcomb; a simpleton; a gull. Go; you're a brainless cox, a toy, a fop. Beau. & Fl.
coxa: The first joint of the leg of an insect or crustacean.
coxcomb: A name given to several plants of different genera, but particularly to Celosia crista ta, or garden cockscomb. Same as cockscomb.
coxcombical: Befitting or indicating a coxcomb; like a coxcomb; foppish; conceited. Coxcombically, adv. Studded all over in coxcombical fashion with little brass nails. W.Irving.
coxcombly: like a coxcomb. You coxcombly ass, you!" Beau & Fl.
coxcombry: The manners of a coxcomb; foppishness.
coy: affectedly modest or shy especially in a playful or provocative way
coyly: In a coy manner; with reserve.
coyness: The quality of being coy; feigned o When the kind nymph would coyness feign, And hides but to be found again. Dryden.
coyote: A carnivorous animal (Canis la trans), allied to the dog, found in the western part of North America; called also prairie wolf. Its voice is a snapping bark, followed by a prolonged, shrill howl.
coyotillo: A low rhamnaceous shrub (Karwinskia humboldtiana) of the southwestern United States and Mexico. Its berries are said to be poisonous to the coyote.
coypu: A South American rodent (Myopotamus coypus), allied to the beaver. It produces a valuable fur called nutria.
cozen: To cheat; to def rand; to beguile; to deceive, usually by small arts, or in a pitiful way. He had cozened the world by fine phrases. Macualay. Children may be cozened into a knowledge of the letters. Locke. Goring loved no man so well but that he would cozen him, and expose him to public mirth for having been cozened. Clarendon.
cozenage: The art or practice of cozening; artifice; fraud.
cozened: simple past and past participle of cozen
cozening: present participle and gerund of cozen
coziness: The state or quality of being cozy.
cpt: Initialism of charge, parity, time-reversal (in the phrase CPT symmetry).
crab: One of the brachyuran Crustacea. They are mostly marine, and usually have a broad, short body, covered with a strong shell or carapace. The abdomen is small and curled up beneath the body.
crabbish: Somewhat sour or cross. The wips of the most crabbish Satyristes. Decker.
crabby: Crabbed; difficult, or perplexing. Persius is crabby, because ancient. " Mars ton.
crablike: Having some characteristics of a crab
crabmeat: the edible flesh of any of various crabs
crabs: infestation of the pubic hair by crab lice
crack: Of superior excellence; having qualities to be boasted of. One of our crack speakers in the Commons. Dickens.
crackable: Able to be cracked or fractured.
cracked: Coarsely ground or broken; as, cracked wheat.
crackerberry: creeping perennial herb distinguished by red berries and clustered leaf whorls at the tips of shoots
crackers: informal or slang terms for mentally irregular
cracking: the process whereby heavy molecules of naphtha or petroleum are broken down into hydrocarbons of lower molecular weight (especially in the oil-refining process)
crackle: To make slight cracks; to make small, sharp, sudden noises, rapidly or frequently repeated; to crepitate; as, burning thorns crackle. The unknown ice that crackles underneath them. Dryden.
crackled: Covered with minute cracks in the glaze; said of some kinds of porcelain and fine earthenware.
crackling: Food for dogs, made from the refuse of tallow melting.
cracklings: the crisp residue left after lard has been rendered
cracknel: A hard brittle cake or biscuit. Spenser.
crackup: A crash or wreck, generally involving a car or airplane.
cracovienne: A lively Polish dance, in - time.
cracow: an industrial city in southern Poland on the Vistula
cracowes: Long-toed boots or shoes formerly worn in many parts of Europe; so called from Cracow, in Poland, where they were first worn in the fourteenth century. Fair holt.
cradle: An implement consisting of a broad scythe for cutting grain, with a set of long fingers parallel to the scythe, designed to receive the grain, and to lay it eventlyin a swath.
cradled: simple past and past participle of cradle
cradleman: A member of the navy employed to load projectiles onto a cradle prior to firing.
cradler: An agricultural worker who uses a cradle (a kind of broad scythe).
cradlesong: the act of singing a quiet song to lull a child to sleep
craft: A vessel; vessels of any kind; generally used in acollective sense. The evolutions of the numerous tiny craft moving over the lake. Prof. Wilson. Small crafts, small vessels, as sloops, schooners, ets.
crafter: a creator of great skill in the manual arts. Syn. craftsman.

crinkle: To form with short turns, bends, or wrinkles; to mold intoinequalites or sinuosities; to cause to wrinkle or curl. The houscrinkled to and fro. Chaucer. Her face all bowsy, Comely crinkled, Wondrously wrinkled. Skel ton. The flames through all the casements pushing forth, Like red-not devils crinkled into snakes. Mrs. Browning.
crinkled: Having short bends, turns, or wrinkles; wrinkled; wavy; zigzag. The crinkled lightning. " Lowell.
crinoidal: Of pertaining to crinoids; consisting of, or containing, crinoids.
crinoidea: A large class of Echinodermata, including numerous extinct families and genera, but comparatively few living ones. Most of the fossil species, like some that are recent, were attached by a jointed stem. See Blastoidea, Cystoidea, Comatula.
crinoline: a full stiff petticoat made of crinoline fabric
crinum: A genus of bulbous plants, of the order Amaryllid ace, cultivated as greenhouse plants on account of their beauty.
criollo: a Spanish American of pure European stock (usually Spanish)
criophore: A statue or other representation of a person carrying a ram.
criosphinx: A sphinx with the head of a ram.
cripple: One who creeps, halts, or limps; one who has lost, or never had, the use of a limb or limbs; a lame person; hence, one who is partially disabled. I am a cripple in my limbs; but what decays are in my mind, the reader must determine. Dryden.
crippled: Lamed; lame; disabled; impeded. The crippled crone. Longfellow.
crippler: A wooden tool used in graining leather. Knight.
crippling: Spars or timbers set up as a support against the side of abuilding.
crisis: That change in a disease which indicates whether the result isto be recovery or death; sometimes, also, a striking change of symptoms attended by an outward manifestation, as by an eruption or sweat. Till some safe crisis authorize their skill. Dryden.
crisp: To undulate or ripple. Cf. Crisp, v. t. To watch the crisping ripples on the beach. Tennu son.
crispate: wavy or notched and curled very irregularly
crisped: simple past and past participle of crisp
crispen: make brown and crisp by heating
crisper: One who, or that which, crisps or curls; an instrument for making little curls in the nap of cloth, as in chinchilla.
crispin: patron saint of shoemakers; he and his brother were martyred for trying to spread Christianity (rd century)
crisping: present participle and gerund of crisp
crispy: Formed into short, close ringlets; frizzed; crisp; as, crispy locks.
crissal: Pertaining to the crissum; as, crissal feathers.
crisscross: To mark or cover with cross lines; as, a paper was crisscrossed with red marks.
crissum: That part of a bird, or the feathers, surrounding the cloacal opening; the under tail coverts.
crista: Any of the internal compartments formed by the inner membrane of a mitochondrion, where many chemical reactions take place.
criterion: A standard of judging; any approved or established rule or test, by which facts, principles opinions, and conduct are tried informing a correct judgment respecting them. Of the diseases of the mind there is no criterion. Donne. Inferences founded on such enduring criteria. Sir G. C. Lewis.
crith: The unit for estimating the weight of a
critic: Of or pertaining to critics or criticism; critical. Critic learning. " Pope.
critical: Pertaining to, or indicating, a crisis, turning point, or specially important juncture; important as regards consequences; hence, of doubtful issue; attended with risk; dangerous; as, the critical stage of a fever; a critical situation. Our circumstances are indeed critical. Burke. The small moment, the exact point, the critical minute, on which every good work so much depends. South. Critical angle (Optics), that angle of incidence of a luminous ray at which it is wholly reflected, and no portion of it transmitted. The sine of this angle is the reciprocal of the refractive index of the medium. Critical philosophy, the metaphysical system of Kant; so called from his most important work, the Critique of Pure Reason. " Critical point (Physics), a certain temperature, different for different gases, but always the same for each gas, regarded as the limit above which no amount of pressure can produce condensation to aliquid.
criticaster: A contemptible or vicious critic. The rancorous and reptile crew of poeticules, who decompose intocriticasters. Swinburne.
criticise: To examine and judge as a critic; to pass literary or artistic judgment upon; as, to criticise an author; to criticise a picture.
criticised: simple past and past participle of criticise
criticises: third-person singular simple present indicative of criticise
criticising: present participle and gerund of criticise
criticism: disapproval expressed by pointing out faults or shortcomings
criticized: simple past and past participle of criticize
criticizer: A person who criticizes; a carper or faultfinder.
criticizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of criticize
criticizing: present participle and gerund of criticize
critique: To criticise or pass judgment upon. Pope.
critter: a regional term for creature' (especially for domestic animals)
crix: persons who are professionally engaged in the analysis and interpretation of works of art
croak: To utter in a low, hoarse voice; to announce by croaking; to forebode; as, to croak disaster. The raven himself is hoarse, That croaks the fatal entrance of duncan. Two ravens now began to croak Their nuptial song. Wordsworth.
croaked: simple past and past participle of croak
croaker: the lean flesh of a saltwater fish caught along Atlantic coast of southern U.S.
croaking: a harsh hoarse utterance (as of a frog)
croaks: third-person singular simple present indicative of croak
croaky: like the sounds of frogs and crows
croat: A native of Croatia, in Austria; esp., one of the native Slavic race.
croatan: A member of a small Native American group once living in the coastal areas of what is now North Carolina.
croatia: a republic in the western Balkans in south-central Europe in the eastern Adriatic coastal area; formerly part of the Habsburg monarchy and Yugoslavia; became independent in
croatian: Of or pertaining to Croatia. n.
crocein: A name given to any one of several yellow or scarlet dyestuffs of artificial production and complex structure. In general they are diazo and sulphonic acid derivatives of benzene and naphthol.
crochet: A kind of knitting done by means of a hooked needle, with worsted, silk, or cotton; crochet work. Commonly used adjectively. Crochet hook, Crochet needle, a small hook, or a hooked needle (often of bone), used in crochet work.
crocheted: Made with crochet (needlework made by looping thread with a hooked needle).
crocidolite: A mineral oc curing in silky fibers of a lavender blue color. Itis related to hornblende and is essentially a silicate of iron and soda; called also blue asbestus. crocin: The coloring matter of Chinese yellow pods, the fruit of Gardenia grandiflora. Watts.
crock: The loose black particles collected from combustion, as on pots and kettles, or in a chimney; soot; smut; also, coloring matter which rubs off from cloth.
crockard: A th-century coin minted in Europe as a debased counterfeit copy of the sterling silver penny of King Edward I, at first legally accepted as a halfpenny and then outlawed.
crockery: Earthenware; vessels formed of baked clay, especially the coarser kinds.
crocket: An ornament often resembling curved and bent foliage, projecting from the sloping edge of a gable, spire, etc.

crocodilia: An order of reptiles including the crocodiles, gavials, alligators, and many extinct kinds.

crocoite: Lead chromate oc curing in crystals of a bright hyacinth red color; called also red lead ore.
croconic: Of, pertaining to, or resembling saffron; having the color of saffron; as, croconic acid.
crocosmia: Any of many plants in the genus Crocosmia
crocus: A genus of iridaceous plants, with pretty blossoms rising separately from the bulb or corm. C. vern us is one of the earliest of spring-blooming flowers; C. sativus produces the saffron, and blossoms in the autumn.
croesus: A king of Lydia who flourished in the th century b. c., and was renowned for his vast wealth; hence, a common appellation for avery rich man; as, he is veritable Croesus.
croft: A small, inclosed field, adjoining a house; a small farm. A few small crofts of stone-encumbered ground. Wordsworth.
crofter: One who rents and tills a small farm or hel ding; as, the crofters of Scotland.
croise: A pilgrim bearing or wearing a cross.
crojik: A triangular sail on old sailing ships.

crokinole: A game, popular in Canada, in which wooden discs are flicked towards the centre of a circular board.

cromwell: English general and statesman who led the parliamentary army in the English Civil War (-)
cronartium: rust fungi having aecia produced in raised or swollen sori and teliospores borne in waxy columns
cronus: (Greek mythology) the supreme god until Zeus dethroned him; son of Uranus and Gaea in ancient Greek mythology; identified with Roman Saturn
crony: A crone. Marry not an old crony. " Burton.
cronyism: favoritism shown to friends and associates (as by appointing them to positions without regard for their qualifications)
cronyn: Canadian actor who frequently played character parts with his wife Jessica Tandy (-)
croodle: To cower or cuddle together, as from fear or cold; to lie close and snug together, as pigs in straw. Wright. Forby. A dove to fly home her nest and croodle there. C. King sley.
crook: A small tube, usually curved, applied to a trumpet, horn, etc.,to change its pitch or key.
crookbill: A New Zealand plover (Anarhynchus frontalis), remarkable for having the end of the beak abruptly bent to the right.
crooked: having or marked by bends or angles; not straight or aligned
crookedly: In a curved or crooked manner; in a perverse or untoward manner.
crookedness: The condition or quality of being crooked; hence, deformity of body or of mind; deviation from moral rectitude; perverseness.
crookes: English chemist and physicist; discovered thallium; invented the radiometer and studied cathode rays (-)
crooking: present participle and gerund of crook

The winter crookneck belongs to a distinct species (C. moschata) and is smooth and often striped.
crooning: singing in a soft low tone
crop: A projecting ornament in carved stone. Specifically, a finial.
cropped: (of land or soil) used for growing crops
cropper: A machine for cropping, as for shearing off bolts or rod iron, or for facing cloth.
cropping: present participle and gerund of crop
cropsick: Sick from excess in eating or drinking. Cropsick drunkards. " Tate. Cropsickness, n. Whit lock.
croquet: In the game of croquet, to drive away an opponent's ball, after putting one's own in contact with it, by striking one's own ball with the mallet.
croquette: A ball of minced meat, fowl, rice, or other ingredients, highly seasoned, and fried.
croquis: A quick and sketchy drawing, often of a live model. Croquis drawings are usually made in a few minutes, after which the model changes pose and another croquis is drawn.
crore: Ten millions; as, a crore of rupees (which is nearly$,).Malcolm.
crosier: The pastoral staff of a bishop (also of an archbishop, being the symbol of his office as a shepherd of the flock of God.
crosne: A vegetable, of species Stachys affinis; a Chinese artichoke.
cross: A monument in the form of a cross, or surmounted bu a cross, set up in a public place; as, a market cross; a boundary cross; Charing Cross in London. Dun-Edin's Cross, a pillared stone, Rose on a turret octagon. Sir W.Scott.
crossarm: The horizontal member of a cross-shaped object, such as the horizontal bar of power poles or telephone poles.
crossband: A band going across something, especially:
crossbar: A transverse bar or piece, as a bar across a door, or as the iron bar or stock which passes through the shank of an anchor to insure its turning fluke down. Russell. Crossbar shot, a projectile which folds into a sphere for loading, but on leaving the gun expands to a cross with a quarter ball at the end of each arm; used in naval actions for cutting the enemy's rigging.
crossbarred: Secured by, or furnished with, crossbars. Milton.
crossbill: A bill brought by a defendant, in an equity or chancery suit, against the plaintiff, respecting the matter in question in that suit. Bouvier.
crossbolt: A bolt of the kind fired from a crossbow.
crossbones: A representation of two of the leg bones or arm bones of askeleton, laid crosswise, often surmounted with a skull, and serving as a symbol of death. Crossbones, scythes, hourglasses, and other lugubrios emblems of mortality. Hawthorne.
crossbow: A weapon, used in discharging arrows, formed by placing a bow crosswise on a stock.
crossbowman: One who shoots with a crossbow. See Arbalest.
crossbred: Produced by mixing distinct breeds; mongrel.
crossbreed: breed animals or plants using parents of different races and varieties
crossbreeding: reproduction by parents of different races (especially by white and non-white persons)
crosscheck: an instance of confirming something by considering information from several sources
crosscurrent: actions counter to the main group activity
crosscut: , v. t. To cut across or through; to intersect.
crosse: The implement with which the ball is thrown and caught in the game of lacrosse.
crosser: Someone who crosses; agent noun of cross
crossfire: a lively or heated interchange of ideas and opinions
crossflow: To flow across, or in a contrary direction. His crossflowingcourse. " Milton.

crosshatch: To shade by means of crosshatching.

crosshaul: The transportation of goods away from a locality while similar goods are simultaneously transported into the same locality, often resulting in inefficiencies.

crossness: The quality or state of being cross; peevishness; fretfulness; ill humor.

crosspatch: An ill-natured person. Crosspatch, draw the latch. Mother Goose.
crosspiece: A bar or timber connecting two knight heads or two bitts.
crosspoint: The point at which two things (especially electrical wires) cross.
crossroad: A road that crosses another; an obscure road intersecting or avoiding the main road.
crossroads: a point where a choice must be made
crossrow: The alphabet; called also Christcross-row. And from the crossrow plucks the letter G.
crossruff: The play in whist where partners trump each a different suit, and lead to each other for that purpose; called also seesaw.
crosstie: one of the cross braces that support the rails on a railway track
crosstrees: Pieces of timber at a masthead, to which are attached the upper shrouds. At the head of lower masts in large vessels, they support asemicircular platform called the top. "
crosswalk: a path (often marked) where something (as a street or railroad) can be crossed to get from one side to the other
crosswise: In the form of a cross; across; transversely. Longfellow.
crossword: a puzzle in which words corresponding to numbered clues are to be found and written in to squares in the puzzle
crotalaria: A genus of leguminous plants; rattlebox.
crotalid: A pit viper; any member of the subfamily Crotalinae (formerly the family Crotalidae) in family Viperidae.
crotalus: A genus of poisonous serpents, including the rattlesnakes.
crotch: A stanchion or post of wood or iron, with two arms for supporting a boom, spare yards, etc.; called also crane and crutch. Totten.

crotchety: Given to crotchets; subject to whims; as, a crotchety man.

crotonic: Of or pertaining to, or derived from, a plant of the genus croton, or from croton oil. Crotonic acid (Chem.), a white crystalline organic acid, CH.COH, of the ethylene, or acrylic acid series. It was so named because formerly supposed to exist in croton oil. Also, any acid metameric with crotonic acid proper.
crouch: bend one's back forward from the waist on down
crouched: Marked with the sign of the cross. Crouched friar. See crutched friar, under Crutched.
crouching: present participle and gerund of crouch
croup: The hinder part or buttocks of certain quadrupeds, especially of a horse; hence, the place behind the saddle. So light to the croup the fair lady he swung, So light to the saddle before her he sprung. Sir W. Scott.
croupe: the part of an animal that corresponds to the human buttocks
croupier: someone who collects and pays bets at a gaming table

croupy: Of or pertaining to croup; resembling or indicating croup; as, a croupy cough.

crouton: Bread cut in various forms, and fried lightly in butter or oil, to garnish hashes, etc.

crowbar: A bar of iron sharpened at one end, and used as a lever.
crowberry: A heathlike plant of the genus Empetrum, and its fruit, ab lack, scarcely edible berry; also called crakeberry.
crowd: An ancient instrument of music with six strings; a kind of violin, being the oldest known stringed instrument played with a bow. A lackey that. can warble upon a crowd a little. B. Jonson.
crowder: One who plays on a crowd; a fiddler. Some blind crowder. " Sir P. Sidney.
crowding: a situation in which people or things are crowded together
crowed: simple past and past participle of crow
crower: A bird which, or person who, crows.
crowfoot: The genus Ranunculus, of many species; some are common weeds, others are flowering plants of considerable beauty.
crowkeeper: A person employed to scare off crows; hence, a scarecrow. Scaring the ladies like a crowkeeper.
crowned: having an (artificial) crown on a tooth
crowning: representing a level of the highest possible achievement or attainment
crownland: In Austria-Hungary, one of the provinces, or largest administrative divisions of the monarchy; as, the crownland of Lower austria.
crows: A tribe of Indians of the Dakota stock, living in Montana; also called Upsarokas.
croy: a natural or man-made protrusion or jetty projecting on a river and used to manage river fisheries, providing an obstacle to slow down current, a shelter for fish, a funnel to net them, and a platform to cast from.
croze: A cooper's tool for making the grooves for the heads of casks, etc.; also, the groove itself.
cru: A vineyard or group of vineyards in France, especially one having a high reputation.
crucial: of extreme importance; vital to the resolution of a crisis
crucian: A small greenish-brown carp, Carassius carassius, farmed in parts of Europe.
cruciate: Having the leaves or petals arranged in the form of a cross; cruciform.
crucible: a vessel made of material that does not melt easily; used for high temperature chemical reactions
cruciferae: a large family of plants with four-petaled flowers; includes mustards, cabbages, broccoli, turnips, cresses, and their many relatives
cruciferous: Of, pertaining to, or resembling, a family of plants which have four petals arranged like the arms of a cross, as the mustard, radish, turnip, etc.
crucified: simple past and past participle of crucify
crucifies: third-person singular simple present indicative of crucify
crucifix: representation of the cross on which Jesus died
crucifixion: the act of executing by a method widespread in the ancient world; the victim's hands and feet are bound or nailed to a cross
cruciform: Cross-shaped; (Bot.) having four parts arranged in the form of a cross.
crucify: kill by nailing onto a cross
cruddle: To curdle. See how thy blood cruddles at this. Bea
crude: Harsh and offensive, as a color; tawdry or in bad taste, as acombination of colors, or any design or work of art.
crudeness: A crude, undigested, or unprepared state; rawness; unripeness; immatureness; unfitness for a destined use or purpose; as, the crudeness of iron ore; crudeness of theories or plans.
cruder: comparative form of crude: more crude
crudity: The condition of being crude; rawness.
crudy: Coagulated. His cruel wounds with crudy blood congealed. Spenser.
cruelty: a cruel act; a deliberate infliction of pain and suffering
cruet: A vessel used to hold wine, oil, or water for the service of the altar. Cruet stand, a frame for holding cruets; a caster.
cruiser: One who, or a vessel that, cruises; usually an armed vessel.
cruising: Sailing about without an exact destination, especially for pleasure.
cruller: A kind of sweet cake cut in strips and curled or twisted, and fried crisp in boiling fat.
crumb: To break into crumbs or small pieces with the fingers; as, to crumb bread.
crumbed: simple past and past participle of crumb
crumber: A player who waits around a marking contest aiming to get the ball if it falls down to the ground (because the opposing players leaping for it have spoiled each other's efforts).

crumbled: simple past and past participle of crumble
crumbling: That crumbles; that breaks into small pieces or particles.
crumbly: EAsily crumbled; friable; brittle. The crumbly soil. Hawthorne.
crump: make a noise typical of an engine lacking lubricants
crumpet: A kind of large. thin muffin or cake, light and spongy, and cooked on a griddle or spider.

crunched: simple past and past participle of crunch
cruncher: A person or thing that crunches.
crunching: present participle and gerund of crunch
crunchingly: With a crunching sound or action.
crunchy: Likely to crunch, especially with reference to food when it is eaten.
crunode: A point where one branch of a curve crosses another branch. See double point, under Double, a.
cruor: The coloring matter of the blood; the clotted portion of coagulated blood, containing the coloring matter; gore.
crup: Short; brittle; as, crup cake. Todd.
crupper: To fit with a crupper; to place a crupper upon; as, to cruppera horse.
crural: Of or pertaining to the thigh or leg, or to any of the part scalled crura; as, the crural arteries; crural arch; crural canal; crural ring.
crus: the leg from the knee to foot
crusade: To engage in a crusade; to attack in a zealous or hot-headed manner. Cease crusading against sense. " M. Green.

crusado: An old Portuguese coin, worth about seventy cents.
cruse: small jar; holds liquid (oil or water)
cruset: A goldsmith's crucible or melting pot.
crush: To be or become broken down or in, or pressed into a smaller compass, by external weight or force; as, an eggshell crushes easily.
crushed: treated so as to have a permanently wrinkled appearance
crusher: One who, or that which, crushes. Crusher gauge, an instrument for measuring the explosive force of gunpowder, etc., by its effect in compressing a piece of metal.
crushing: That crushes; overwhelming. The blow must be quick and crushing. " Macualay.
crust: The exterior portion of the earth, formerly universally supposed to inclose a molten interior.
crustacea: One of the classes of the arthropods, including lobsters and crabs; so called from the crustlike shell with which they are covered.
crustacean: Of or pertaining to the Crustacea; crustaceous. n.
crustated: Covered with a crust; as, crustated basalt.
crusted: Incrusted; covered with, or containing, crust; as, old, crusted port wine.
crustlike: having a hardened crust as a covering
crustose: (of lichens) having a thin crusty thallus that adheres closely to the surface on which it is growing
crusty: Having a hard exterior, or a short, rough manner, though kind at heart; snappish; peevish; surly. Thou crusty batch of nature, what's the news.
crutch: To support on crutches; to prop up. Two fools that crutch their feeble sense on verse. Dryden.

cruzeiro: The currency of Brazil from to and to.

crybaby: a person given to excessive complaints and crying and whining
crying: Calling for notice; compelling attention; notorious; heinous; as, a crying evil. Too much fondness for meditative retirement is not the crying sin ofour modern Christianity. I. Taylor.

cryoconite: Dark silt accumulating mainly from airborne volcanic sediment or soot from artificial pollution, or detritus in water of ablation from ice sheets or glaciers. Cryoconite typically appears either as surface discoloration or in cryoconite holes.
cryogen: a liquid that boils at below - C and is used as a refrigerant
cryogenic: of or relating to very low temperatures

cryolite: A fluoride of sodium and aluminum, found in Greenland, in white cleavable masses; used as a source of soda and alumina.

crypt: A simple gland, glandular cavity, or tube; a follicle; as, thecryps of Lie berk.

cryptid: an organism whose existence has been speculated, but has not been discovered by the scientific community
cryptidine: One of the quinoline bases, obtained from coal tar as an oily liquid, CHN; also, any one of several substances metameric with, and resembling, cryptidine proper.

curtailed: simple past and past participle of curtail
curtailing: present participle and gerund of curtail
curtailment: The act or result of curtailing or cutting off. Ban croft.
curtails: third-person singular simple present indicative of curtail
curtain: That part of the rampart and parapet which is between two bastions or two gates. See Illustrations of Ravelin and Bastion.
curtained: furnished or concealed with curtains or draperies
curtal: Curt; brief; laconic. Essays and curtal aphorisms. Milton. Curtal dog. See Curtail dog.
curtana: The pointless sword carried before English monarchs at their coronation, and emblematically considered as the sword of mercy; also called the sword of Edward the Confessor.
curtate: Shortened or reduced; said of the distance of a planet from the sun or earth, as measured in the plane of the ecliptic, or the distance from the sun or earth to that point where a perpendicular, let fall from the planet upon the plane of the ecliptic, meets the ecliptic. Curtate cycloid. (Math.) See Cycloid.
curtilage: A yard, courtyard, or piece of ground, included within the fence surrounding a dwelling house. Bur rill.
curtseying: present participle and gerund of curtsey
curtsy: Same as Courtesy, an act of respect.
curule: Of or pertaining to a kind of chair appropriated to Roman magistrates and dignitaries; pertaining to, having, or conferring, the right to sit in the curule chair; hence, official.
cururo: A Chilian burrowing rodent of the genus Spalacopus.
curvaceous: (of a woman's body) having a large bosom and pleasing curves
curvate: bent in a regular form; curved.
curvature: The amount of degree of bending of a mathematical curve, or the tendency at any point to depart from a tangent drawn to the curve at that point. Aberrancy of curvature (Geom.), the deviation of a curve from a curcular form. -Absolute curvature. See under Absolute. Angle of curvature (Geom.), one that expresses the amount of curvature of a curve. Chord of curvature. See under Chord. Circle of curvature. See Osculating circle of a curve, under Circle. Curvature of the spine (Med.), an abnormal curving of the spine, especially in a lateral direction. Radius of curvature, the radius of the circle of curvature, or osculatory circle, at any point of a curve.
curve: Bent without angles; crooked; curved; as, a curve line; a curve surface.
curved: having or marked by a curve or smoothly rounded bend
curvet: A particular leap of a horse, when he raises both his fore legs at once, equally advanced, and, as his fore legs are falling, raises his hind legs, so that all his legs are in the air at once.
curveting: present participle and gerund of curvet
curvets: third-person singular simple present indicative of curvet
curvilinear: characterized by or following a curved line
curvimeter: A device for measuring the length of curves, such as on a map
curvinerved: Having the ribs or the veins of the leaves curved; called also curvinervate and curve-veined.
curving: having or marked by a curve or smoothly rounded bend
curviserial: Distributed in a curved line, as leaves along a stem.
curvity: The state of being curved; a bending in a regular form; crookedness. Holder.
cusconine: An alkaloid found in cinchona bark.
cuscus: A soft grass (Pennisetum typhoideum) found in all tropical regions, used as food for men and cattle in Central Africa.
cuscuta: genus of twining leafless parasitic herbs lacking chlorophyll: dodder
cusec: A measure of the rate of flow of fluid, especially through a pipeline, equal to one cubic foot per second.
cushat: The ringdove or wood pigeon. Scarce with cushat's homely song can vie. Sir W. Scott.
cushaw: plant bearing squash having globose to ovoid fruit with variously striped grey and green and white warty rinds
cushing: United States neurologist noted for his study of the brain and pituitary gland and who identified Cushing's syndrome (-)
cushion: the layer of air that supports a hovercraft or similar vehicle
cushioned: softened by the addition of cushions or padding
cushionless: Hot furnished with a cushion. Rows of long, cushionless benches, supplying the place of pews. Hawthorne.
cushionlike: Resembling or characteristic of a cushion.
cushiony: Like a cushion; soft; pliable. A flat and cushiony noce. Dickens.
cushitic: a group of languages spoken in Ethiopia and Somalia and northwestern Kenya and adjacent regions
cushy: not burdensome or demanding; borne or done easily and without hardship
cusk: A large, edible, marine fish (Brosmius bros me), allied to the cod, common on the northern coasts of Europe and America; called also tusk and torsk.
cusp: A triangular protection from the intrados of an arch, or from an inner curve of tracery.
cuspid: One of the canine teeth; so called from having but one point or cusp on the crown. See Tooth.
cuspidor: Any ornamental vessel used as a spittoon; hence, to avoid the common term, a spittoon of any sort.
cuss: profane or obscene expression usually of surprise or anger
cusses: third-person singular simple present indicative of cuss
custard: A mixture of milk and eggs, sweetened, and baked or boiled. Custard apple (Bot.), a low tree or shrub of tropical America, including several species of Anona (A. squamosa, reticula ta, etc.),having a roundish or ovate fruit the size of a small orange, containing a soft, yellowish, edible pulp. Custard coffin, pastry, or crust, which covers or coffins acustard.
custodian: One who has care or custody, as of some public building; akee per or superintendent.
custom: Long-established practice, considered as unwritten law, and resting for authority on long consent; usage. See Usage, and prescription.
customary: Holding or held by custom; as, customary tenants; customary service or estate.
customer: someone who pays for goods or services
customhouse: The building where customs and duties are paid, and where vessels are entered or cleared. Customhouse broker, an agent who acts for merchants in the business of entering and clearing goods and vessels.
customized: simple past and past participle of customize
customizer: A person or business that provides customization services
customizing: present participle and gerund of customize
custumal: A survey of a medieval English manor, listing each tenant and the customs under which the tenancy was held.
cut: separated into parts or laid open or penetrated with a sharp edge or instrument
cutaneous: Of pertaining to the skin; existing on, or affecting, the skin; as, a cutaneous disease; cutaneous absorption; cutaneous respiration.
cutaway: Having a part cut off or away; having the corners rounded orcut away. Cutaway coat, a coat whose skirts are cut away in front soas not to meet at the bottom.
cutback: a reduction in quantity or rate
cutchery: A hindoo hall of justice. Mal com.
cutdown: An emergency medical procedure in which the vein is exposed and a cannula is inserted into it.
cutesy: Overly, affectedly or unnecessarily cute; too cute to be taken seriously.
cutgrass: A grass with leaves having edges furnished with very minute hooked prickles, which form a cutting edge; one or more species of leersia.
cuthbert: A male given name from Old English.
cuticle: The scarfskin or epidermis. See Skin.
cuticula: the outer body wall of an insect
cuticular: Pertaining to the cuticle, or external coat of the skin; epidermal.
cuticularization: The growth of new skin over a wound.
cutin: The substance which, added to the material of a cell wall, makes it waterproof, as in cork.
cutinise: to convert into a waxy substance found on the leaves of plants
cutinization: The conversion of cell walls into a material which repels water, as in cork.
cutlas: a short heavy curved sword with one edge; formerly used by sailors
cutlassfish: long-bodied marine fishes having a long whiplike scaleless body and sharp teeth; closely related to snake mackerel
cutler: One who makes or deals in cutlery, or knives and other cutting instruments.
cutlery: tableware implements for cutting and eating food
cutlet: A piece of meat, especially of veal or mutton, cut for broiling.
cutline: In production, a hypothetical line that separates items that will be executed and publicized, versus items that will be cut.
cutling: The art of making edged tools or cutlery. Milton.
cutoff: a designated limit beyond which something cannot function or must be terminated
cutout: a switch that interrupts an electric circuit in the event of an overload
cutpurse: One who cuts purses for the sake of stealing them or their contents (an act common when men wore purses fastened by a string to their girdles); one who steals from the person; a pickpocket to have an open ear, a quick eye, and a nimble hand, is necessary for a cutpurse.
cuttage: The propagation of plants via cuttings.
cutterhead: A rotating cylindrical cutting tool located at the head of a drill, boring machine, or the like.
cutthroat: One who cuts throats; a murderer; an assassin.
cutting: a part (sometimes a root or leaf or bud) removed from a plant to propagate a new plant through rooting or grafting
cuttlefish: ten-armed oval-bodied cephalopod with narrow fins as long as the body and a large calcareous internal shell
cutty: Short; as, a cutty knife; a cutty sark.
cutup: Someone who cuts up; someone who acts boisterously or clownishly, for example, by playing practical jokes.
cutwal: The chief police officer of a large city.
cutwater: A sea bird of the Atlantic (Rhynchops nigra); called also black skimmer, scissorsbill, and razorbill. See Skimmer.
cutwork: An ancient term for embroidery, esp. applied to the earliest form of lace, or to that early embroidery on linen and the like, from which the manufacture of lace was developed.
cuvier: French naturalist known as the father of comparative anatomy (-)
cv: being five more than one hundred
cwm: a steep-walled semicircular basin in a mountain
cwt: a British unit of weight equivalent to pounds
cx: being ten more than one hundred
cxv: being five more than one hundred ten

cyan: a primary subtractive color for light; has a blue-green color
cyanamid: a weak soluble dibasic acid (the parent acid of cyanamide salts)
cyanamide: a weak soluble dibasic acid (the parent acid of cyanamide salts)
cyanate: A salt of cyanic acid. Ammonium cyanate (Chem.), a remarkable white crystalline substance, NH.O.CN, which passes, on standing, to the organic compound, urea, CO.(NH).
cyaneous: Of a deep or dark blue color.
cyanide: A compound formed by the union of cyanogen with an element or radical.
cyanidin: An anthocyanidin pigment, -(,-dihydroxyphenyl) chromenylium-,-triol, found in many red berries.
cyanin: The blue coloring matter of flowers; called also anthokyan and anthocyanin.
cyanine: One of a series of artificial blue or red dyes obtained from quinoline and lepidine and used in calico printing.
cyanite: A mineral oc curing in thin-bladed crystals and crystalline aggregates, of a sky-blue color. It is a silicate of aluminium.

cyano: a univalent functional group, -CN, consisting of a carbon and a nitrogen atom joined with a triple bond; organic compounds containing a cyano group are nitriles

cyanobacterial: relating to or caused by photosynthetic bacteria of the class Cyanobacteria
cyanocobalamin: a B vitamin that is used to treat pernicious anemia
cyanoethylation: Any reaction, or treatment, with acrylonitrile, especially such treatment of cotton fabric to improve its strength and make it easier to dye

The name is also applied to the univalent radical, CN (the half molecule of cyanogen proper), which was one of the first compound radicals recognized.
cyanometer: An instrument for measuring degress of blueness.
cyanometry: The use of the cyanometer to measure the intensity of blue colour.

cyanophil: A cell that is differentially coloured blue by a cytological dye
cyanophyll: A blue coloring matter supposed by some to be one of the component parts of chlorophyll.
cyanopsia: A disorder of the vision causing all objects to appear blue, often the temporary consequence of removal of a cataract.
cyanosis: A condition in which, from insufficient a Cyanopathy.
cyanotic: Relating to cyanosis; affected with cyanosis; as, a cyanotic patient; having the hue caused by cyanosis; as, a cyanitic skin.
cyanotrichite: A rare, blue, orthorhombic copper aluminium sulfate mineral.
cyanuric: Pertaining to, or derived from, cyanic and uric acids.
cyathea: type genus of the Cyatheaceae: tree ferns of the tropical rain forest to temperate woodlands
cyathium: One of the specialised pseudanthia (false flowers), surrounded by involucral bracts, especially those forming the inflorescence of euphorbias.
cybele: great nature goddess of ancient Phrygia in Asia Minor; counterpart of Greek Rhea and Roman Ops
cyberculture: the culture that emerges from the use of computers for communication and entertainment and business
cybernate: control a function, process, or creation by a computer
cybernetic: of or relating the principles of cybernetics
cybernetics: (biology) the field of science concerned with processes of communication and control (especially the comparison of these processes in biological and artificial systems)
cyborg: a human being whose body has been taken over in whole or in part by electromechanical devices

cycadofilicales: fossil gymnospermous trees or climbing plants from the Devonian: seed ferns
cycas: A genus of trees, intermediate in character between the palms and the pines. The pith of the trunk of some species furnishes avaluable kind of sago.
cycasin: A toxin found in certain plants that affects the gastrointestinal tract and nervous system.
cyclades: a group of over islands in the southern Aegean
cyclamate: any salt or ester of cyclamic acid, especially the sodium and calcium salts, which have been used as artificial sweeteners

cyclase: Any enzyme that catalyzes the cyclization of a compound
cycle: One entire round in a circle or a spire; as, a cycle or set of leaves. Gray.

cycler: Anything with a cyclic (repetitious) behaviour. Something that cycles between different states.
cyclically: In a cyclic manner; in cycles; periodically.
cycling: The act, art, or practice, of riding a cycle, esp. a bicycle or tricycle.
cyclism: The existence of a cycle or eternal recurrence, as in some religions.
cyclitol: Any hydroxylated cycloalkane having at least three hydroxy groups attached to different carbon atoms.
cyclization: The process of cyclizing, of becoming or causing to become aromatic.
cyclize: To undergo, or cause to undergo, a reaction resulting in the formation of an aromatic or ring structure.
cyclizing: present participle and gerund of cyclize
cyclodiene: Any of a class of chlorinated polycyclic insecticides derived from cyclopentadiene
cycloganoidei: An order of ganoid fishes, having cycloid scales. The bowfin (Amia calva) is a living example.
cyclohexanol: a colorless oily alcohol that smells like camphor
cycloid: A curve generated by a point in the plane of a circle when the circle is rolled along a straight line, keeping always in the same plane.

cyclometer: A contrivance for recording the revolutions of a wheel, as of abicycle.
cyclometric: Of or pertaining to the inverse trigonometric functions: arcsine, arccosine, arctangent, arccotangent, arcsecant, and arccosecant.
cyclone: A violent storm, often of vast extent, characterized by high winds rotating about a calm center of low atmospheric pressure. This center moves onward, often with a velocity of twenty or thirty miles an hour.
cyclopaedia: a reference work (often in several volumes) containing articles on various topics (often arranged in alphabetical order) dealing with the entire range of human knowledge or with some particular specialty
cyclopean: Pertaining to the Cyclops; characteristic of the Cyclops; huge; gigantic; vast and rough; massive; as, Cyclopean labors; Cyclopean architecture.
cyclopedia: a reference work (often in several volumes) containing articles on various topics (often arranged in alphabetical order) dealing with the entire range of human knowledge or with some particular specialty
cyclopedic: Belonging to the circle of the sciences, or to a cyclopedia; of the nature of a cyclopedia; hence, of great range, extent, or amount; as, a man of cyclopedic knowledge.
cyclopedist: A maker of, or writer for, a cyclopedia.
cyclophoria: A form of strabismus involving a rotating movement of the eye.
cyclopia: a developmental abnormality in which there is only one eye
cycloplegia: paralysis of the ciliary muscle of the eye, resulting in a loss of accommodation
cyclopropane: a colorless flammable gas sometimes used as an inhalation anesthetic
cyclops: One of a race of giants, sons of Neptune and Amphitrite, having but one eye, and that in the middle of the forehead. They were fabled to inhabit Sicily, and to assist in the workshops of Vulcan, under mt. Etna.

The realistic effect is increased by putting, in the space between the spectator and the picture, things adapted to the scene represented, and in some places only parts of these objects, the completion of them being carried out pictorially.
cyclosilicate: Any of several classes of silicate mineral having rings of silicate anions.
cyclosis: The circulation or movement of protoplasmic granules within aliving vegetable cell.

cyclotomy: surgical removal of the ciliary muscle
cyclotron: an accelerator that imparts energies of several million electron-volts to rapidly moving particles
cydippida: ctenophores having two long pinnate tentacles
cygnus: A constellation of the northern hemisphere east of, or following, Lyra; the Swan.
cylinder: a solid bounded by a cylindrical surface and two parallel planes (the bases)
cylindraceous: Cylindrical, or approaching a cylindrical form.
cylindrical: having the form of a cylinder
cylindrically: In the manner or shape of a cylinder; so as to be cylindrical.
cylindroid: A certain surface of the third degree, described by a moving straight line; used to illustrate the motions of a rigid body and also the forces acting on the body.
cylindroma: A tumor with nests of cells that resemble a cylinder in cross section.
cylix: a shallow drinking cup with two handles
cyma: A member or molding of the cornice, the profile of which is wavelike in form.
cymar: A sight covering; a scarf. See Simar. Her body shaded with a light cymar. Dryden.
cymatium: A capping or crowning molding in classic architecture.
cymbal: a percussion instrument consisting of a concave brass disk; makes a loud crashing sound when hit with a drumstick or when two are struck together

cymose: having a usually flat-topped flower cluster in which the main and branch stems each end in a flower that opens before those below it or to its side

cynghanedd: The complex system of internal assonance, alliteration and rhyme in Welsh strict-meter poetry.
cynic: someone who is critical of the motives of others
cynical: believing the worst of human nature and motives; having a sneering disbelief in e.g. selflessness of others
cynicism: The doctrine of the Cynics; the quality of being cynical; the mental state, opnions, or conduct, of a cynic; morose and contemptuous views and opinions.
cynipid: Any member of the family Cynipidae of wasps.
cynips: type genus of the Cynipidae: gall wasps
cynocephalus: type genus of the family Cynocephalidae
cynodon: creeping perennial grasses of tropical and southern Africa
cynoglossum: a large genus of tall rough herbs belonging to the family Boraginaceae
cynomolgus: A long-tailed macaque (Macaca fascicularis), native to Asia, that feeds on shellfish.
cynophile: A person who loves canines; a dog lover.
cynosure: something that provides guidance (as Polaris guides mariners)
cyperus: A large genus of plants belonging to the Sedge family, and including the species called galingale, several bulrushes, and the egyptian papyrus.
cyphella: A break in the lower cortex of a lichen thallus which appears as a cup-like structure or marking.
cypraea: A genus of mollusks, including the cowries. See Cowrie.
cypraeidae: family of marine gastropods comprising the cowries
cypres: A rule for construing written instruments so as to conform as nearly to the intention of the parties as is consistent with law. Mozley & W.

cyprian: of or relating to Cyprus or its people or culture
cyprinid: of or relating to members of fish family Cyprinidae
cyprinidae: a family of fish including: carp; tench; roach; rudd; dace
cypriniform: Any of many ray-finned fish, of the order Cypriniformes, such as the carps, minnows and loaches

cyprinus: type genus of the family Cyprinidae: carp
cypriot: A native or inhabitant of Cyprus.
cypriote: of or relating to Cyprus or its people or culture
cypripedium: A genus of orchidaceous plants including the lady's slipper.

cyril: Greek missionary; the invention of the Cyrillic alphabet is attributed to him (-)

cyrillic: relating to or written in the alphabet used for writing Slavic languages
cyrus: Persian prince who was defeated in battle by his brother Artaxerxes II (- BC)

cysticercus: The larval stage of any of several tapeworms, having a fluid-filled cyst enclosing a scolex.

cystidium: A relatively large cell found on the hymenium of a basidiomycete
cystine: A white crystalline substance, CHNSO, containing sulphur, oc curing as a constituent of certain rare urinary calculi, and occasionally found as a sediment in urine.
cystocarp: A minute vesicle in a red seaweed, which contains the reproductive spores.
cystocele: Hernia in which the urinary bladder protrudes; vesical hernia.
cystopteris: chiefly small perennial rock ferns: bladder ferns; in some classifications placed in Polypodiaceae
cystoscopy: An endoscopy of the urinary bladder via the urethra

cytochemistry: The biochemistry of cells, especially that of the macromolecules responsible for cell structure and function.
