filmland: The industry of films and filmmaking.
filmmaking: The activity of preparing edited video works, formerly principally films, whether for entertainment or other purposes.
filmography: A selective list of movie titles that share a similar characteristic such as the same genre, the same director, the same actor etc.
filmset: To typeset by exposing type characters onto photographic film, which is then used to generate printing plates.
filmsetting: present participle and gerund of filmset
filmstrip: A length of film containing individual photographs or diagrams intended to be shown in sequence as instruction or as a visual aid.
filmy: Composed of film or films. Whose filmy cord should bind the struggling fly. Dryden.
filoplume: A hairlike feather; a father with a slender scape and without aweb in most or all of its length.
filopodium: A slender cytoplasmic projection which extends from the leading edge of a migrating cell
fils: Son; sometimes used after a French proper name to distinguish a son from his father, as, Alex andre Dumas, fils.
filter: Any porous substance, as cloth, paper, sand, or charcoal, through which water or other liquid may passed to cleanse it from the solid or impure matter held in suspension; a chamber or device containing such substance; a strainer; also, a similar device for purifying air. Filter bed, a pond, the bottom of which is a filter composed of sand gravel. Filter gallery, an underground gallery or tunnel, alongside of astream, to collect the water that filters through the intervening sand and gravel; called also infiltration gallery.
filterability: The state or condition of being filterable.
filterable: Able to be separated by filtration
filterer: A person who, or device that, filters
filtering: present participle and gerund of filter
filterman: A man employed to manage a physical process of filtration.
filth: any substance considered disgustingly foul or unpleasant
filthy: Defiled with filth, whether material or moral; nasty; dirty; polluted; foul; impure; obscene. In the filthy-mantled pool. He which is filthy let him be filthy still. Rev. xxii.
filtrate: To filter; to defecate; as liquid, by straining or percolation. Arbuthnot.
filtrated: simple past and past participle of filtrate
filtration: The act or process of filtering; the mechanical separation of aliquid from the undissolved particles floating in it.
filum: a threadlike structure (as a chainlike series of cells)
fimble: To fumble; do (anything) imperfectly or irresolutely.
fimbria: A fringe, or fringed border.(b) A band of white matter bordering the hippocampus in the brain. Fimbrial, a.
fimbriate: Having the edge or extremity bordered by filiform processes thicker than hairs; fringed; as, the fimbriate petals of the pink; the fimbriate end of the Fallopian tube.
fimbriation: The use of a thin stripe of a contrasting tincture (colour) around a charge, ordinary or stripe in order to make it stand out from the background.
fin: To carve or cut up, as a chub.
finable: Liable or subject to a fine; as, a finable person or offense. Bacon.
finagle: achieve something by means of trickery or devious methods
finagler: a deceiver who uses crafty misleading methods
final: the final match between the winners of all previous matches in an elimination tournament
finale: Close; termination; as:(a) (Mus.) The last movement of a symphony, sonata, concerto, or any instrumental composition.(b) The last composition performed in any act of an opera.(c) The closing part, piece, or scene in any public performance or exhibition.
finalist: Any of the players who meet in the final round of a tournament in which the losers in any round do not play again.
finality: the quality of being final or definitely settled
finalize: make final; put the last touches on; put into final form
finalizing: present participle and gerund of finalize
finally: after an unspecified period of time or an especially long delay
financed: simple past and past participle of finance
finances: assets in the form of money
financial: Pertaining to finance. Our financial and commercial system. Macaulay.
finca: A country estate, farm or ranch in Spain or Hispanic America.
finchbacked: Streaked or spotted on the back; said of cattle.
find: To determine an issue of fact, and to declare such ade termination to a court; as, the jury find for the plaintiff. Bur rill.
findable: Capable of beong found; discoverable. Fuller.
finder: One who, or that which, finds; specifically (Astron.), a small telescope of low power and large field of view, attached to a larger telescope, for the purpose of finding an object more readily.
finding: The result of a judicial examination or inquiry, especially into some matter of fact; a verdict; as, the finding of a jury. Bur rill. After his friends finding and his rent. Chaucer.
findings: a collection of tools and other articles used by an artisan to make jewelry or clothing or shoes
findy: Full; heavy; firm; solid; substemtial. A cold May and a windy Makes the barn fat amd findy. Old Prover
fine: To impose a pecuniary penalty upon for an offense or breach oflaw; to set a fine on by judgment of a court; to punish by fine; to mulct; as, the trespassers were fined ten dollars.
fined: simple past and past participle of fine
finedraw: To sew up, so nicely that the seam is not perceived; to renter. Marry at.
finedrawn: Drawn out with too much subtilty; overnice; as, finedrawn speculations.
finely: In a fine or finished manner.
fineness: the quality of being very good indeed
finery: A charcoal hearth or furnace for the conversion of cast iron into wrought iron, or into iron suitable for puddling.
finespun: Spun so as to be fine; drawn to a fine thread; attenuated; hence, unsubstantial; visionary; as, finespun theories.
finesse: The act of finessing. See Finesse, v. i.,.
finessed: simple past and past participle of finesse
finesses: third-person singular simple present indicative of finesse
finessing: present participle and gerund of finesse
finest: superlative form of fine: most fine
finfoot: A South American bird (heliornis fulica) allied to the grebes. The name is also applied to several related species of the genus Podica.
fingal: A male given name from Scottish Gaelic, best known in Scotland.
finger: To use the fingers in playing on an instrument. Busby.
fingerboard: a narrow strip of wood on the neck of some stringed instruments (violin or cello or guitar etc) where the strings are held against the wood with the fingers
fingerfish: Any fish of the family Monodactylidae.
fingering: the placement of the fingers for playing different notes (or sequences of notes) on a musical instrument
fingernail: the nail at the end of a finger
fingerprint: take an impression of a person's fingerprints
finial: The knot or bunch of foliage, or foliated ornament, that forms the upper extremity of a pinnacle in Gothic architecture; sometimes, the pinnacle itself.
finical: Affectedly fine; overnice; unduly particular; fastidious. Finical taste. " Wordsworth. The gross style consists in giving no detail, the finical in giving nothing else. Hazlitt.
finicalness: The state or characteristic of being finical.
finific: A limiting element or quality. The essential finific in the form of the finite. Coleridge.
finikin: Precise in trifles; idly busy. Smart.
finis: An end; conclusion. It is often placed at the end of a book.
finish: The joiner work and other finer work required for the completion of a building, especially of the interior. See Inside finish, and Outside finish.
finished: Polished to the highest degree of excellence; complete; perfect; as, a finished poem; a finished education. Finished work (Mach.), work that is made smooth or polished, though not necessarily completed.
finisher: a racing driver who finishes a race
finishing: The act or process of completing or perfecting; the final work upon or ornamentation of a thing.
finite: Having a limit; limited in quantity, degree, or capacity; bounded; opposed to infinite; as, finite number; finite existence; a finite being; a finite mind; finite duration.
finjan: In the Levant, a small coffee cup without a handle, such as is held in a cup or stand called a zarf.
fink: take the place of work of someone on strike
finland: republic in northern Europe; achieved independence from Russia in
finn: A native of Finland; one of the Finn finns.
finned: Having a fin, or fins, or anything resembling a fin. Mortimer.
finnic: Of or pertaining to the Finns.
finnish: Of or pertaining to Finland, to the Finns, or to their language. n.
finny: Having, or abounding in, fins, as fishes; pertaining to fishes.
fino: The driest and palest type of traditional sherry.
finocchio: aromatic bulbous stem base eaten cooked or raw in salads
finochio: An umbelliferous plant (Foeniculum dulce) having a somewhat tuberous stem; sweet fennel. The blanched stems are used in France and Italy as a culinary vegetable.
fiord: A narrow inlet of the sea, penetrating between high banks or rocks, as on the coasts of Norway and Alaska.
fiorin: A species of creeping bent grass (Agrostis alba); called also fiorin grass.
fioriture: Little flowers of ornament introduced into a melody by a singer or player.
fipple: A stopper, as in a wind instrument of music. Bacon.
fiqh: Jurisprudence in the Islamic law, shari'a.
fique: A natural fiber, similar to hemp, obtained from the leaves of the plant Furcraea andina and certain other plants of the genus Furcraea.
fir: A genus (Abies) of coniferous trees, often of large size an delegant shape, some of them valued for their timber and others for their resin. The species are distinguished as the balsam fir, the silver fir, the red fir, etc. The Scoth fir is a Pinus.
fire: To cauterize. To fire up, to light up the fires of, as of an engine.
firearm: A gun, pistol, or any weapon from a shot is discharged by the force of an explosive substance, as gunpowder.
fireback: One of several species of pheasants of the genus Euplocamus, having the lower back a bright, fiery red. They inhabit Southern Asia and the East Indies.
fireball: a ball of fire (such as the sun or a ball-shaped discharge of lightning)
firebase: an artillery base to support advancing troops
fireboard: A chimney board or screen to close a fireplace when not in use.
fireboat: a boat equipped to fight fires on ships or along a waterfront
firebote: An allowance of fuel. See Bote.
firebox: a furnace (as on a steam locomotive) in which fuel is burned
firebrand: A piece of burning wood. L'Estrange.
firebrat: lives in warm moist areas e.g. around furnaces
firebreak: a narrow field that has been cleared to check the spread of a prairie fire or forest fire
firebrick: brick made of fire clay; used for lining e.g. furnaces and chimneys
firebug: a true bug: brightly colored bug that can exude a stain
firedamp: a mixture of gases (mostly methane) that form in coal mines and become explosive when mixed with air
firedog: A support for wood in a fireplace; an andiron.
firefighter: a member of a fire department who tries to extinguish fires
fireflame: The European band fish (Cep ola rubescens).
firehouse: a station housing fire apparatus and firemen
firelike: Resembling or characteristic of fire; fiery.
firelock: An old form of gunlock, as the flintlock, which ignites the priming by a spark; perhaps originally, a matchlock. Hence, a gun having such a lock.
fireman: play in which children pretend to put out a fire
firepan: A pan for holding or conveying fire, especially (firearms) the receptacle for the priming of a gun.
firepink: Silene virginica, a brilliant red wildflower of eastern North America in the family Caryophyllaceae.
fireplace: The part a chimney appropriated to the fire; a hearth; usually an open recess in a wall, in which a fire may be built.
fireplug: an upright hydrant for drawing water to use in fighting a fire
firepower: (military) the relative capacity for delivering fire on a target
firer: One who fires or sets fire to anything; an incendiary. R.Carew.
firesafe: Designed to reduce the risk of fire.
fireside: A place near the fire or hearth; home; domestic life or retirement.
firetail: The European redstart; called also fireflirt.
firetrap: a building that would be hard to escape from if it were to catch fire
fireweed: tall North American perennial with creeping rootstocks and narrow leaves and spikes of pinkish-purple flowers occurring in great abundance in burned-over areas or recent clearings; an important honey plant
firework: A pyrotechnic exhibition. Night before last, the Duke of Richmond gave a firework. Walpole.
fireworm: The larva of a small tortricid moth which eats the leaves of the cranberry, so that the vines look as if burned; called also cranberry worm.
firk: To beat; to strike; to chastise. I'll fer him, and firk him, and ferret him.
firkin: a British unit of capacity equal to imperial gallons
firlot: A dry measure formerly used in Scotland; the fourth part of aboll of grain or meal. The Linlithgow wheat firlot was to the imperial bushel as to; the barley firlot as to.Br ande & C.
firm: The name, title, or style, under which a company transacts business; a partnership of two or more persons; a commercial house; as, the firm of Hope & Co.
firmament: The orb of the fixed stars; the most rmote of the celestial spheres.
firman: In Turkey and some other Oriental countries, a decree or mandate issued by the sovereign; a royal order or grant; generally given for special objects, as to a traveler to insure him protection and assistance.
firmer: comparative form of firm: more firm
firmless: Detached from substance. Does passion still the firmless mind control Pope.
firmness: The state or quality of being firm.
firms: The principal rafters of a roof, especially a pair of rafters taken together.
firn: A type of old snow which has gone through multiple thaw and refreeze cycles and thus is made of numerous small icy grains, though it is not nearly as saturated with water as snowcone slush is; can be hard or somewhat soft depending on recent and current weather conditions.
firry: Made of fir; abounding in firs. In firry woodlands making moan. Tennyson.
first: Before any other person or thing in time, space, rank, etc.; much used in composition with adjectives and participles. Adam was first formed, then Eve. Tim. ii.At first, At the first, at the beginning or origin. First or last, at one time or another; at the beginning or end. And all are fools and lovers first or last. Dryden.
firstborn: First brought forth; first in the order of nativity; eldest; hence, most excellent; most distinguished or exalted.
firstling: Firstborn. All the firstling males. Deut. xv.
firth: An arm of the sea; a frith.
fisc: A public or state treasury. Burke.
fiscal: Pertaining to the public treasury or revenue. The fiscal arreangements of government. A. Hamilton.
fiscalizing: present participle and gerund of fiscalize
fisetin: A yellow crystalline substance extracted from fustet, and regarded as its essential coloring principle; called also fisetic acid.
fish: A counter, used in various games.
fishberry: The poisonous fruit of Anamirta cocculus.
fishbolt: A bolt used to fasten fishplates.
fishbowl: a transparent bowl in which small fish are kept
fished: simple past and past participle of fish

fishery: The right to take fish at a certain place, or in particular waters. Abbott.
fisheye: of or relating to a fisheye lens
fishful: Abounding with fish. My fishful pond. " R. Carew.
fishgig: A spear with barbed prongs used for harpooning fish. Knight.
fishhook: A hook with a pendant, to the end of which the fish-tackle is hooked. Dana.

Fishing net, a net of various kinds for catching fish; including the bag net, casting net, drag net, landing net, seine, shrimping net, trawl, etc. Fishing rod, a long slender rod, to which is attached the line for angling. Fishing tackle, apparatus used in fishing, as hook, line, rod, etc. Fishing tube (Micros.), a glass tube for selecting a microscopic object in a fluid.
fishlike: Like fish; suggestive of fish; having some of the qualities offish. A very ancient and fishlike smell.
fishmeal: Ground dried fish, used mainly for livestock feed.
fishnet: a net that will enclose fish when it is pulled in

fishtail: slow down by moving the tail sideways

fishyback: A system of transportation in which containers are moved from truck to ship.

fission: A method of asexual reproduction among the lowest (unicellular) organisms by means of a process of self-division, consisting of gradual division or cleavage of the into two parts, each of which then becomes a separate and independent organisms; as when a cell in an animal or plant, or its germ, undergoes a spontaneous division, and the parts again subdivide. fissipalmate: Semipalmate and lob oped, as a grebe's foot. See Illust. unde raves.

fissipedia: A division of the Carnivora, including the dogs, cats, and bears, in which the feet are not webbed; opposed to Pinnipedia.
fissural: Pertaining to a fissure or fissures; as, the fissural pattern of a brain.

Cerebral fissures (Anat.), the furrows or clefts by which the surface of the cerebrum is divided; esp., the furrows first formed by the infolding of the whole wall of the cerebrum. fissured: simple past and past participle of fissure
fissurella: A genus of marine gastropod mollusks, having a conical orlimpetlike shell, with an opening at the apex; called also keyhole limpet.
fist: the index mark [], used to direct special attention to the passage which follows. Hand over fist (Naut.), rapidly; hand overhand.
fisted: Having some specific type of fist.
fistful: the quantity that can be held in the hand
fistic: Pertaining to boxing, or to encounters with the fists; puglistic; as, fistic exploits; fistic heroes.
fisticuff: A cuff or blow with the fist or hand; (pl.)

fistle: To rustle; to make a slight rustling (or whistling sound).
fistnote: A printed note (as in a book) preceded by the fist symbol, depicting a fist with pointed index finger.

fistular: Hollow and cylindrical, like a pipe or reed. Johnson.
fistularia: A genus of fishes, having the head prolonged into a tube, with the mouth at the extremity.

fistulated: simple past and past participle of fistulate
fistuliform: Of a fistular form; tubular; pipe-shaped. Stalactite often occurs fistuliform. W. Phi lips.

fitful: Full of fits; irregularly variable; impulsive and unstable. After life's fitful fever, he sleeps well. Fitfully, adv. Fitfulness, n. The victorius trumpet peal Dies fitfully away. Macaulay.
fitly: In a fit manner; suitably; properly; conveniently; as, a maxim fitly applied.
fitment: The act of fitting; that which is proper or becoming; equipment.
fitness: The state or quality of being fit; as, the fitness of measures or laws; a person's fitness for office.
fitted: being the right size and shape to fit as desired
fitter: A little piece; a flitter; a flinder. Where's the Frenchman Alas, he's all fitters. Beau. & Fl.
fittest: superlative form of fit: most fit
fitting: Anything used in fitting up; especially (pl.),
fittonia: Any of the genus Fittonia of flowering plants.
fitz: A son; used in compound names, to indicate paternity, esp.of the illegitimate sons of kings and princes of the blood; as, Fitzroy, the son of the king; Fitzclarence, the son of the duke of clarence.
five: Four and one added; one more than four.
fivefold: In fives; consisting of five in one; five repeated; quintuple.
fiver: a United States bill worth dollars
fives: A kind of play with a ball against a wall, resembling tennis; so named because three fives, or fifteen, are counted to the game. Smart. Fives court, a place for playing fives.
fixate: attach (oneself) to a person or thing in a neurotic way
fixated: simple past and past participle of fixate
fixation: the activity of fastening something firmly in position
fixative: That which serves to set or fix colors or drawings, as amordant.
fixed: Stable; non-volatile. Fixed air (Old Chem.), carbonic acid or carbon dioxide; so called by Dr. Black because it can be absorbed or fixed by strong bases. See Carbonic acid, under Carbonic. Fixed ammunition (Mil.), a projectile and powder inclosed together in a case ready for loading. Fixed battery (Mil.), a battery which contains heavy guns and mortars intended to remain stationary; distinguished from movable battery. Fixed bodies, those which can not be volatilized or separated by a common menstruum, without great difficulty, as gold, platinum, lime, etc. Fixed capital. See the Note under Capital, n.,. Fixed fact, a well established fact. Fixed light, one which emits constant beams; distinguished from a flashing, revolving, or intermittent light. Fixed oils (Chem.), non-volatile, oily substances, as stearine and olein, which leave a permanent greasy stain, and which can not be distilled unchanged; distinguished from volatile or essential oils. Fixed pivot (Mil.), the fixed point about which any line of troops wheels. Fixed stars (Astron.), such stars as always retain nearly the same apparent position and distance with respect to each other, thus distinguished from planets and comets.
fixedly: In a fixed, stable, or constant manner.
fixedness: the quality of being fixed and unchangeable
fixer: someone who intervenes with authorities for a person in trouble (usually using underhand or illegal methods for a fee)
fixity: Fixedness; as, fixity of tenure; also, that which is fixed.
fixture: Anything of an accessory character annexed to houses and lands, so as to constitute a part of them. In this latter sense, the same things may be fixtures under some circumstances, and not fixtures under others. Wharton (Law Dict. ). Bouvier.
fizz: To make a hissing sound, as a burning fuse.
fjeld: A rocky, barren plateau, especially in Scandinavia.

flabelliform: Having the form of a fan; fan-shaped; flabellate.
flabellum: A fan; especially, the fan carried before the pope on state occasions, made in ostrich and peacock feathers. Shi pley.
flaccid: Yielding to pressure for want of firmness and stiffness; soft and weak; limber; lax; drooping; flabby; as, a flaccid muscle; flaccid flesh. Religious profession. has become flacced. I. Taylor. Flaccidly, adv. Flaccidness, n.
flack: artillery designed to shoot upward at airplanes
flacon: A small glass bottle; as, a flacon for perfume. Two glass flacons for the ink. " Longfellow.
flag: An aquatic plant, with long, ensiform leaves, belonging to either of the genera Iris and Acorus. Cooper's flag, the cat-tail (Typha latifolia), the long leaves of which are placed between the staves of barrels to make the latter water-tight. Corn flag. See under d Corn. Flag broom, a coarse of broom, originally made of flags or rushes. Flag root, the root of the sweet flag. Sweet flag. See Calamus, n.,.
flagellant: One of a fanatical sect which flourished in Europe in the thand th centuries, and maintained that flagellation was of equal virtue with baptism and the sacrament; called also disciplinant.
flagellata: An order of Infusoria, having one or two long, whiplike cilia, at the anterior end. It includes monads. See Infusoria, and Monad.

flagellated: having or resembling a lash or whip (as does a flagellum)
flagellates: third-person singular simple present indicative of flagellate
flagellation: A beating or flogging; a whipping; a scourging. Garth.

flagelliform: Shaped like a whiplash; long, slender, round, flexible, and (com ming) tapering.
flagellum: A young, flexible shoot of a plant; esp., the long trailing branch of a vine, or a slender branch in certain mosses.

flagged: simple past and past participle of flag
flagger: One who uses a flag or signal, as for example to direct traffic or to start a race.
flagging: A pavement or sidewalk of flagstones; flagstones, collectively.
flaggy: Abounding with the plant called flag; as, a flaggy marsh.
flagman: One who makes signals with a flag.
flagon: A vessel with a narrow mouth, used for holding and conveying liquors. It is generally larger than a bottle, and of leather or stoneware rather than of glass. A trencher of mutton chops, and a flagon of ale. Macaulay.
flagpole: a tall staff or pole on which a flag is raised
flagrancy: A burning; great heat; inflammation. Lust cause th a flagrancy in the eyes. Bacon.
flagrant: Flaming; inflamed; glowing; burning; ardent. The beadle's lash still flagrant on their back. Prior. A young man yet flagrant from the lash of the executioner or the beadle. De Quincey. Flagrant desires and affections. Hooker.
flagship: The vessel which carries the commanding officer of a fleet or squadron and flies his distinctive flag or pennant.
flagstaff: A staff on which a flag is hoisted.
flagstone: A flat stone used in paving, or any rock which will split into such stones. See Flag, a stone.
flail: an implement consisting of handle with a free swinging stick at the end; used in manual threshing
flake: A small stage hung over a vessel's side, for workmen to stand on in calking, etc.
flaked: simple past and past participle of flake
flaker: A tool or appliance used to break flakes off a piece of material or something into it.
flaking: Breaking or tending to break into flakes.
flaky: Consisting of flakes or of small, loose masses; lying, or cleaving off, in flakes or layers; flake like. What showers of mortal hail, what flaky fires! Watts. A flaky weight of winter's purest snows. Wordsworth.

floss: The slender styles of the pistillate flowers of maize; also called silk.
flossie: A diminutive of the female given name Florence.
flossy: Pertaining to, made of, or resembling, floss; hence, light; downy.

flotilla: A little fleet, or a fleet of small vessels.

flounces: third-person singular simple present indicative of flounce
floundering: present participle and gerund of flounder

flouring: present participle and gerund of flour
flourished: simple past and past participle of flourish
flourishes: third-person singular simple present indicative of flourish
floury: Of or resembling flour; mealy; covered with flour. Dickens.
flout: To mock or insult; to treat with contempt. Phil lida flouts me. Walton. Three gaudy stan darts lout the pale blue sky. Byron.
flouted: simple past and past participle of flout
flouting: present participle and gerund of flout

flouts: third-person singular simple present indicative of flout
flow: imp. sing. of Fly, v. i. Chaucer.

flowered: resembling or made of or suggestive of flowers

Flowering rush, a European rushlike plant (Butomus umbel latus),with an umbel of rosy blossoms.

flowerlike: Resembling a flower, especially in shape
flowerpot: A vessel, commonly or earthenware, for earth in which plants are grown.
flowery: of or relating to or suggestive of flowers
flowing: That flows or for flowing (in various sense of the verb); gliding along smoothly; copious. flowmeter: Any of various devices used to measure the flow of a fluid through a pipe, etc.
flown: p. p. of Fly; often used with the auxiliary verb to be; as, the birds are flown.

fluctuant: showing undulation or fluctuation; as, a fluctuant tumor.

fluerics: A subfield of fluidics, dealing with fluid components that perform functions not requiring the use of moving parts.
fluff: Nap or down; flue; soft, downy feathers.

fluffiest: superlative form of fluffy: most fluffy

flummox: be a mystery or bewildering to

fluocerite: A cerium fluoride mineral found in Sweden.

fluoric: Pertaining to, obtained from, or containing, fluorine.

If set free it immediately attacks the containing material, so that it was not isolated until. It is a pungent, corrosive, colorless gas. Symbol F. Atomic weight.

footboard: a narrow platform on which to stand or brace the feet
footboy: A page; an attendant in livery; a lackey.
footbreadth: The breadth of a foot; used as a measure. Longfellow. Not so much as a footbreadth. Deut. ii.
footbridge: A narrow bridge for foot passengers only.
footcandle: a unit of illuminance on a surface that is everywhere foot from a point source of candle
footcloth: Formerly, a housing or caparison for a horse. Sir W. Scott.
footer: (used only in combinations) the height or length of something in feet
footfall: A setting down of the foot; a footstep; the sound of afoot step. Seraphim, whose footfalls tinkled on the tufted floor. Poe
foothill: A low hill at the foot of highe
foothold: A holding with the feet; firm L'Estrange.
foothot: Hastily; immediately; instantly; on the spot; hotfloot. Gower. Cust ance have they taken anon, foothot. Chaucer.
footing: The thickened or sloping portion of a wall, or of an embankment at its foot. Footing course (Arch.), one of the courses of masonry at the foot of a wall, broader than the courses above. To pay one's footing, to pay a fee on first doing anything, as working at a trade or in a shop. Wright. Footing beam, the tie beam of a roof.
footle: act foolishly, as by talking nonsense
footler: One who footles; a foolish trifler.
footles: third-person singular simple present indicative of footle
footlights: theater light at the front of a stage that illuminate the set and actors
footlocker: a trunk for storing personal possessions; usually kept at the foot of a bed (as in a barracks)
footmark: A footprint; a track or vestige. Coleridge.
footnote: A note of reference or comment at the foot of a page.
footpad: A highwayman or robber on foot.
footpath: A narrow path or way for pedes trains only; a footway.
footprint: The impression of the foot; a trace or footmark; as,Footprints of the Creator. "
footrest: a low seat or a stool to rest the feet of a seated person
footrope: The rope rigged below a yard, upon which men stand when reefing or furling; formerly called a horse.
foots: The settlings of oil, molasses, etc., at the bottom of a barrel or hogshead. Simmon ds.
footsie: A flirting game where two people touch their feet together, under a table or otherwise concealed, as a romantic prelude.
footslog: walk heavily and firmly, as when weary, or through mud
footstalk: The stalk of a leaf or of flower; a petiole, pedicel, orreduncle.
footstep: the act of taking a step in walking
footstool: A low stool to support the feet of one when sitting.
footwall: the lower wall of an inclined fault
footwarmer: Something used to keep the feet warm, especially during a journey.
footwear: clothing worn on a person's feet
footwork: the manner of using the feet
footworn: Worn by, or weared in, the feet; as, a footworn path; afoot worn traveler.
footy: Having foots, or settlings; as, footy oil, molasses, etc.
foozle: To bungle; to manage awkwardly; to treat or play unskillfully; as, to foozle a stroke in golf.
foozler: One who bungles; a maker of mistakes.
fop: One whose ambition it is to gain admiration by showy dress; acoxcomb; an inferior dandy.
foppery: The behavior, dress, or other indication of a fop; coxcombry; affectation of show; showy folly.
foppish: Fop like; characteristic of a top in dress or manners; making an ostentatious display of gay clothing; affected in manners.
foppishness: the manner and dress of a fop or dandy
for: In the most general sense, indicating that in consideration of, in view of, or with reference to, which anything is done or takes place.
foraged: simple past and past participle of forage
foraging: the act of searching for food and provisions
foram: marine microorganism having a calcareous shell with openings where pseudo pods protrude
foramen: A small opening, perforation, or orifice; a fenestra. Foramen of Monro (Anat.), the opening from each lateral into the third ventricle of the brain. Foramen of Winslow (Anat.), the opening connecting the sac of the omentum with the general cavity of the peritoneum.
foraminifera: An extensive order of rhizopods which generally have achambered calcareous shell formed by several united zooids. Many of them have perforated walls, whence the name. Some species are covered with sand. See Rhizophoda.
foraminiferan: An organism of the phylum Foraminifera; a foraminifer.
foraminous: Having foramina; full of holes; porous. Bacon.
foraneous: Only used in foraneous vicar: translator's error for vicar forane
foray: A sudden or irregular incursion in border warfare; hence, any irregular incursion for war or spoils; a raid. Spenser. The huge Earl Doorm,. Bound on a foray, rolling eyes of prey. Tennyson.
forayer: One who makes or joins in a foray. They might not choose the low and road, For the Merse forayers were abroad. Sir W. Scott.
forb: Any nonwoody flowering plant that is not a graminoid (a grass, sedge, or rush).
forbar: To bar in; to shut up.
forbear: An ancestor; a forefather; usually in the plural. Your forbears of old. " Sir W. Scott.
forbearance: The act of forbearing or waiting; the exercise of patience. He soon shall find forbearance no acquittance ere day end. Milton.
forbearing: Disposed or accustomed to forbear; patient; long-suffering. Forbearingly, adv.
forbid: To utter a prohibition; to prevent; to hinder. I did not or forbid. " Milton.
forbiddance: The act of forbidding; prohibition; command or edict against athing.ow hast thou yield to transgress The strict forbiddance. Milton.
forbidden: Prohibited; interdicted. I kniw no spells, use no forbidden arts. Milton. Forbidden fruit. (a) Any coveted unlawful pleasure, so called with reference to the forbidden fruit of the Garden of Eden. (b) (Bot.) As mall variety of shaddock (Citrus decumana). The name is given indifferent places to several varieties of Citrus fruits.
forbidding: Repelling approach; repulsive; raising abhorrence, aversion, or dislike; disagreeable; prohibiting or interdicting; as, a forbidding aspect; a forbidding formality; a forbidding air.
forbids: third-person singular simple present indicative of forbid
forblack: Very black. As any raven's feathers it shone forblack. Chaucer.
forbode: A forbidding, a prohibition; a command forbidding a thing.
forby: Near; hard by; along; past. To tell her if her child went ought forby. Chaucer. To the intent that ships may pass along forby all the sides of the city without let. Robynson (More's Utopia).
forcarve: To cut completely; to cut off. Chaucer.
force: To stuff; to lard; to farce. Wit larded with malice, and malice forced with wit.
forced: Done or produced with force or great labor, or by extraordinary exertion; hurried; strained; produced by unnatural effort or pressure; as, a forced style; a forced laugh. Forced draught. See under Draught. Forced march (Mil.), a march of one or more days made with all possible speed. Forcedly, adv. Forcedness, n.
forcedly: In a manner that is, or seems, forced.
forceful: Full of or processing force; exerting force; mighty. Forcefully, adv. Against the steed he threw His forceful spear. Dryden.
forceless: Having little or no force; feeble. These forceless flowers like sturdy trees support me.
forcemeat: Meat chopped fine and highly seasoned, either served up alone, or used as a stuffing.
forcement: The act of forcing; compulsion. It was imposed upon us by constraint; And will you count such forcement treachery J. Webster.
forceps: The caudal forceps-shaped appendage of earwigs and some other insects. See Earwig. Dressing forceps. See under Dressing.
forcer: One who, or that which, forces or drives.
forcible: impelled by physical force especially against resistance
forcing: The art of raising plants, flowers, and fruits at an earlier season than the natural one, as in a hit bed or by the use of artificial heat. Forcing bed or pit, a plant bed having an underlayer of fermenting manure, the fermentation yielding bottom heat for forcing plants; a hotbed. Forcing engine, a fire engine. Forcing fit (Mech.), a tight fit, as of one part into a hole in another part, which makes it necessary to use considerable force inputting the two parts together. Forcing house, a greenhouse for the forcing of plants, fruit trees, etc. Forcing machine, a powerful press for putting together or separating two parts that are fitted tightly one into another, as for forcing a crank on a shaft, or for drawing off a car wheel from the axle. Forcing pump. See Force pump (b).
forcipal: Forked or branched like a pair of forceps; constructed so as to open and shut like a pair of forceps. Sir T. Browne.
ford: To pass or cross, as a river or other water, by wading; to wade through. His last section, which is no deep one, remains only to be forted. Milton.
fordable: Capable of being forded. Fordableness, n.
forded: simple past and past participle of ford
fording: the act of crossing a stream or river by wading or in a car or on a horse
fordless: Without a ford. A deep and fordless river. Mal lock.
fordo: To destroy; to undo; to ruin. This is the night That either makes me or fordoes me quite.
fordoes: third-person singular simple present indicative of fordo
fordoing: present participle and gerund of fordo
fordry: Entirely dry; withered. A tree fordry. " Chaucer.
fore: Journey; way; method of proceeding. Follow him and his fore. " Chaucer.
forearm: To arm or prepare for attack or resistance before the time of need. South.
forebay: An artificial pool of water ahead of a larger body of water.
forebode: To for tell; to presage; to augur. If I forebode aright. Hawthorne.
foreboded: simple past and past participle of forebode
forebodes: third-person singular simple present indicative of forebode
foreboding: Presage of coming ill; expectation of misfortune.
forebody: The forepart of a vehicle; foreside.
forebrain: The anterior of the three principal divisions of the brain, including the prosencephalon and thalamencephalon. Sometimes restricted to the prosencephalon only. See Brain.
forecast: To contrive or plan beforehand. If it happen as I did forecast. Milton.
forecasted: simple past and past participle of forecast
forecasting: a statement made about the future
forecastle: living quarters consisting of a superstructure in the bow of a merchant ship where the crew is housed
forecastleman: A crew member whose station is the forecastle, or whose quarters are below it.
forecasts: third-person singular simple present indicative of forecast
foreclose: To shut up or out; to preclude; to stop; to prevent; to bar; to exclude. The embargo with Spain foreclosed this trade. Carew. To foreclose a mortgager (Law), to cut him off by a judgment of court from the power of redeeming the mortgaged premises, termed his equity of redemption. To foreclose a mortgage, (not technically correct, but often used to signify) the obtaining a judgment for the payment of an overdue mortgage, and the exposure of the mortgaged property to sale to meet the mortgage debt. Wharton.
foreclosed: simple past and past participle of foreclose
foreclosing: present participle and gerund of foreclose
foreclosure: The act or process of foreclosing; a proceeding which bars or extinguishes a mortgager's right of redeeming a mortgaged estate.
forecourt: the outer or front court of a building or of a group of buildings
foredate: To date before the true time; to antendate.
foredeck: The fore part of a deck, or of a ship.
foredesign: To plan beforehand; to intend previously. Ch eyne.
foredoom: To doom beforehand; to predestinate. Thou art fore domed to view the Stygian state. Dryden.
foreface: The front portion of a dog's face; the muzzle.
forefather: One who precedes another in the line of genealogy in any degree, but usually in a remote degree; an ancestor. Respecting your forefathers, you would have been taught to respect yourselves. Burke. Forefathers' Day, the anniversary of the day (December ) on which the Pilgrim Fathers landed at Plymouth, Massachusetts. On account of a mistake in reckoning the change from Old Style to New style, it has generally been celebrated on the d.
forefeel: To feel beforehand; to have a presentiment of. As when, with unwieldy waves, the great sea forefeels winds. Chapman.
forefeels: third-person singular simple present indicative of forefeel
forefend: To hinder; to fend off; to avert; to prevent the approach of; to forbid or prohibit. See Forfend. God forefend it should ever be recorded in our history. Land or. It would be a far better work. to forefend the cruelty. I.Taylor.
forefield: The nearest part of a field (as of view or of combat).
forefinger: The finger next to the thumb; the index.
forefoot: A piece of timber which terminates the keel at the fore end, connecting it with the lower end of the stem.
forefront: Foremost part or place. Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle. Sam. xi.Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, standing in the forefront for all time, the masters of those who know. J. C. Sha irp.
foreglimpse: A glimpse or revelation of the future.
forego: To go before; to precede; used especially in the present and past participles. Pleasing remembrance of a thought foregone. Wordsworth. For which the very mother's face forewent The mother's special patience. Mrs. Browning. Foregone conclusion, one which has preceded argument or examination; one predetermined.
foregoing: especially of writing or speech; going before
foreground: On a painting, and sometimes in a bas-relief, mosaic picture, or the like, that part of the scene represented, which is nearest to the spectator, and therefore occupies the lowest part of the work ofart itself. Cf. Distance, n.,.
foregut: The anterior part of the alimentary canal, from the mouth to the intestine, o
forehand: Done beforehand; anticipative. And so extenuate the forehand sin.
forehead: The front of that part of the head which incloses the brain; that part of the face above the eyes; the brow.
foreign: of concern to or concerning the affairs of other nations (other than your own)
foreigner: A person belonging to or owning allegiance to a foreign country; one not native in the country or jurisdiction under consideration, or not naturalized there; an alien; a stranger. Joy is such a foreigner, So mere a stranger to my thoughts. Den ham. Nor could the majesty of the English crown appear in a greater luster, either to foreigners or subjects. Swift.
foreignness: The quality of being foreign; remoteness; want of relation or appropriateness. Let not the foreignness of the subject hinder you from endeavoring toset me right. Locke. A foreignness of complexion. G. Eliot.
forejudge: To judge beforehand, or before hearing the facts and proof; to prejudge.
foreknew: simple past and past participle of foreknow
foreknow: To have previous knowledge of; to know beforehand. Who would the miseries of man foreknow Dryden.
foreknowable: That may be foreknown. Dr. H. More.
foreknowingly: With foreknowledge. He who. foreknowingly loses his life. Jer. Taylor.
foreknowledge: Knowledge of a thing before it happens, or of whatever is to happen; prescience. If I foreknew, Foreknowledge had no influence on their fault. Milton.
foreknows: third-person singular simple present indicative of foreknow
forel: A kind of parchment for book covers. See Forrill.
forelady: a woman who is foreperson of a jury
forelaid: simple past and past participle of forelay
foreland: A piece of ground between the wall of a place and the moat. Farrow.
forelay: To lay down beforehand. These grounds being forelaid and understood. Mede.
forelimb: the front limb (or the homologous structure in other animals, such as a flipper or wing)
forelock: A cotter or split pin, as in a slot in a bolt, to prevent retraction; a linchpin; a pin fastening the cap-square of a gun. Forelock bolt, a bolt retained by a key, gib, or cotter passing through a slot. Forelock hook (Rope Making), a winch or whirl by which a bunch of three yarns is twisted into a standard. Knight. To take time, or occasion, by the forelock, to make prompt use of anything; not to let slip an opportunity. Time is painted with a lock before and bald behind, signifying thereby that we must take time by the forelock; for when it is once past, there is no recalling it. Swift. On occasion's forelock watchful wait. Milton.
foreman: The first or chief man; as:(a) The chief man of a jury, who acts as their speaker.(b) The chief of a set of hands employed in a shop, or on works ofany kind, who superintends the rest; an overseer.
foremast: The mast nearest the bow. Foremast hand or man (Naut.), acommon sailor; also, a man stationed to attend to the gear of the foremast.
foremastman: Any sailor below the rank of petty officer.
foremilk: The milk secreted just before, or directly after, the birth of a child or of the young of an animal; colostrum.
foremost: First in time or place; most advanced; chief in rank or dignity; as, the foremost troops of an army. THat struck the foremost man of all this world.
forename: A name that precedes the family name or surname; a first name. Selden.
forenenst: Over against; opposite to. The land forenenst the Greekish shore. Fair fax.
forenoon: The early part of the day, from morning to meridian, or noon.
forensic: Belonging to courts of judicature or to public discussion and debate; used in legal proceedings, or in public discussions; argumentative; rhetorical; as, forensic eloquence or disputes. Forensic medicine, medical jurisprudence; medicine in its relations to law.
foreordain: To ordain or appoint beforehand; to preordain; to predestinate; to predetermine. Hooker.
foreordaining: present participle and gerund of foreordain
foreordainment: The quality of being foreordained; ordainment of an outcome in advance.
foreordains: third-person singular simple present indicative of foreordain
foreparent: a forefather or foremother (used as a gender-neutral equivalent)
forepart: the side that is forward or prominent
forepaw: front paw; analogous to the human hand
forepeak: The part of the hold of a ship within the angle of the bow.
foreperson: the presiding member of the jury and the one who speaks on their behalf
foreplan: A plan, device, or strategy created in advance.
foreplay: mutual sexual fondling prior to sexual intercourse
forequarter: the front half of a side of meat
forereach: To advance or gain upon; said of a vessel that gains upon another when sailing closehauled.
foreread: To tell beforehand; to signify by tokens; to predestine. Spenser.
forereading: present participle and gerund of foreread
forerecited: Named or recited before. The forerecited practices.
forerib: A cut of beef that includes the rib in front of the sirloin, used especially for roasting.
foreright: Ready; directly forward; going before. A foreright wind. " Chapman.
forerun: To turn before; to precede; to be in advance of (something following).
forerunner: A piece of rag terminating the log line.
forerunning: present participle and gerund of forerun
foresail: the lowest sail on the foremast of a square-rigged vessel
foresay: To foretell. Her danger nigh that sudden change foresaid. Fair fax.
foreseeing: present participle and gerund of foresee
foreseen: , or (strictly) p. p. Provided; in case that; on condition that. One manner of meat is most sure to every complexion, foreseen that itbe alway most commonly in conformity of qualities, with the person that ea teth. Sir T. Elyot.
foresees: third-person singular simple present indicative of foresee
foreshadows: third-person singular simple present indicative of foreshadow
foresheet: one of the sheets (ropes) that controls the foresail
foreshore: the part of the seashore between the highwater mark and the low-water mark
foreshorten: To represent on a plane surface, as if extended in a direction toward the spectator or nearly so; to shorten by drawing in perspective.
foreshortened: simple past and past participle of foreshorten
foreshot: In distillation of low wines, the first portion of spirit that comes over, being a fluid abounding in fusel oil. Knight.
foreshow: To show or exhibit beforehand; to give foreknowledge of; to prognosticate; to foretell. Your looks foreshow You have a gentle heart. Next, like Aurora, Spenser rose, Whose purple blush the day foreshows. Den ham.
foreshowing: present participle and gerund of foreshow
foreside: The front side; the front; esp., a stretch of country fronting the sea.
foresight: Any sight or reading of the leveling staff, except the backsight; any sight or bearing taken by a compass or theodolite in aforward direction.
foresighted: Sagacious; prudent; provident for the future. Bartram.
foreskin: The fold of skin which covers the glans of the penis; the prepuce.
foreskirt: The front skirt of a garment, in distinction from the train. Honor's train Is longer than his foreskirt.
foreslow: To make slow; to hinder; to obstruct. See Forslow, v. t. No stream, no wood, no mountain could foreslow Their hasty pace. Fair fax.
forest: A large extent or precinct of country, generally waste and woody, belonging to the sovereign, set apart for the keeping of game for his use, not inclosed, but distinguished by certain limits, and protected by certain laws, courts, and officers of its own. Bur rill.
forestaff: An instrument formerly used at sea for taking the altitudes of heavenly bodies, now superseded by the sextant; called also cross-staff. Br ande & C.
forestal: Of or pertaining to forests; as, forestal rights.
forestall: To obstruct or stop up, as a way; to stop the passage of on highway; to intercept on the road, as goods on the way to market. To forestall the market, to buy or contract for merchandise or provision on its way to market, with the intention of selling it again at ahigh er price; to dissuade persons from bringing their goods or provisions there; or to persuade them to enhance the price when there. This was an offense at law in England until. Bur rill.
forestalled: simple past and past participle of forestall
forestalling: the act of preventing something by anticipating and disposing of it effectively
forestallment: The act or process of forestalling; a delay; hindrance; prevention; aversion.
forestalls: third-person singular simple present indicative of forestall
forestay: A large, strong rope, reaching from the foremast head to the bowsprit, to support the mast. See Illust. under Ship.
forester: A lepidopterous insect belonging to Aly pia and allied genera; as, the eight-spotted forester (A. octomaculata), which in the larval state is injurious to the grapevine.
forestiera: any plant of the genus Forestiera
forestry: The art of forming or of cultivating forests; the management of growing timber.
foretaste: A taste beforehand; enjoyment in advance; anticipation.
foretell: To predict; to tell before occurence; to prophesy; to foreshow. Deeds then undone my faithful tongue foretold. Pope. Prodigies, foretelling the future eminence and luster of his character. C. Middleton.
foretelling: the art or gift of prophecy (or the pretense of prophecy) by supernatural means
foretells: third-person singular simple present indicative of foretell
forethought: Thought of, or planned, beforehand; aforethought; prepense; hence, deliberate. Forethought malice. " Bacon.
foretime: The past; the time before the present. A very dim foretime. J. C. Sha irp.
foretoken: Prognostic; previous omen. Sir P. Sidney.
foretold: simple past and past participle of foretell
foretop: The platform at the head of the foremast.
foretopman: A sailor who controls the masts in the foretop.
forever: for a very long or seemingly endless time
foreward: The van; the front. My foreward shall be drawn out all in length, Consisting equally of horse and foot.
forewarmer: An apparatus for heating a substance prior to some other process.
forewarn: To warn beforehand; to give previous warning, admonition, information, or notice to; to caution in advance. We were forewarned of your coming.
forewarned: simple past and past participle of forewarn
forewarning: an early warning about a future event
forewarns: third-person singular simple present indicative of forewarn
forewing: either of the anterior pair of wings on an insect that has four wings
forewoman: A woman who is chief; a woman who has charge of the work or workers in a shop or other place; a head woman. Tatler. W. Besant.
foreworn: Worn out; wasted; used up. Old foreworn stories almost forgotten. Brydges.
foreyard: The lowermost yard on the foremast.
forfar: A town in Angus council area, Scotland; it is the administrative centre of Angus, and was the county town of the historic county of Angus (OS grid ref NO).
forfeit: Lost or alienated for an offense or crime; liable to penal seizure. Thy wealth being forfeit to the state. To tread the forfeit paradise. Emerson.
forfeitable: Liable to be forfeited; subject to forfeiture. For the future, uses shall be subject to the statutes of mortmain, and forfeitable, like the lands themselves. Black stone.
forfeiting: present participle and gerund of forfeit
forfeiture: The act of forfeiting; the loss of some right, privilege, estate, honor, office, or effects, by an offense, crime, breach of condition, or other act. Under pain of foreiture of the said goods. Hakluyt.
forfend: To prohibit; to forbid; to avert. Which peril heaven forefend!.
forfered: Excessively alarmed; in great fear. Forfered of hi sdeath. " Chaucer.
forficate: Deeply forked, as the tail of certain birds.
forgather: To convene; to gossip; to meet accidentally. Jamie son. Within that circle he forgathered with many a fool. Wilson.
forgathered: simple past and past participle of forgather
forge: To move heavily and slowly, as a ship after the sails are furled; to work one's way, as one ship in outsailing another; used especially in the phrase to forge ahead. Totten. And off she forged without a shock. De Quincey.
forgeable: That can be forged (shaped under heat and pressure).
forgeman: A skilled smith, who has a hammerer to assist him.
forger: One who forges, makes, of forms; a fabricator; a falsifier.
forgery: criminal falsification by making or altering an instrument with intent to defraud
forget: dismiss from the mind; stop remembering
forgets: third-person singular simple present indicative of forget
forgettable: Liable to be, or that may be, forgotten. Carlyle.
forgetter: One who forgets; a heedless person. Johnson.
forgetting: present participle and gerund of forget
forging: A piece of forged work in metal; a general name for a piece of hammered iron or steel. There are very few yards in the world at which such forgings could be turned out. London Times.
forgivable: Capable of being forgiven; pardonable; venial. Sherwood.
forgiveness: compassionate feelings that support a willingness to forgive
forgives: third-person singular simple present indicative of forgive
forgiving: Disposed to forgive; inclined to overlook offenses; mild; merciful; compassionate; placable; as, a forgiving temper. Forgivingly, adv. Forgivingness, n. J. C. Sha irp.
forgo: To pass by; to leave. See st Forego. For sith I shall for goon my liberty At your request. Chaucer. And four since Florimell the court forwent. Spenser.
forgoes: third-person singular simple present indicative of forgo
forgrow: To grow to excess or out of shape; grow unduly.
forint: the basic unit of money in Hungary
forjudge: To exclude, oust, or dispossess by a judgment; prohibit (from).
forjudgment: The act or result of forjudge.
fork: To raise, or pitch with a fork, as hay; to dig or turn over with a fork, as the soil. Forking the sheaves on the high-laden cart. Prof. Wilson. To fork over or out, to hand or pay over, as money. G. Eliot.
forkbeard: A European fish (Rani ceps rani nus), having a large flat head; also called tadpole fish, and lesser forked beard.
forked: Formed into a forklike shape; having a fork; dividing into two or more prongs or branches; furcated; bifurcated; zigzag; as, the forked lighting. A serpent seen, with forked tongue.
forker: An agricultural laborer who uses a fork.
forkful: The amount that a fork will hold.
forking: the act of branching out or dividing into branches
forklift: a small industrial vehicle with a power operated forked platform in front that can be inserted under loads to lift and move them
forklike: Resembling or characteristic of a fork.
forkman: An agricultural worker who uses a fork.
forky: Opening into two or more parts or shoots; forked; furcated. Forky tongues. " Pope.
forlet: To give up; to leave; to abandon. To forlet sin. Chaucer.
forlore: o Forlese. The beasts their caves, the birds their ne forlore. Fair fax.
form: A suffix used to denote in the form or shape of, resembling, etc.; as, vali form; oviform.
formal: being in accord with established forms and conventions and requirements (as e.g. of formal dress)
formaldehyde: A colorless, volatile liquid, HCO, resembling acetic or ethyl aldehyde, and chemically intermediate between methyl alcohol and formic acid.
formalin: An aqueous solution of formaldehyde, used as a preservative in museums and as a disinfectant.
formalism: The practice or the doctrine of strict adherence to, or dependence on, external forms, esp. in matters of religion. Official formalism. Sir H. Rawlinson.
formalist: One overattentive to forms, or too much confined to them; esp.,one who rests in external religious forms, or observes strictly the outward forms of worship, without possessing the life and spirit of religion. As far a formalist from wisdom sits, In judging eyes, as libertines from wits. Young.
formalistic: concerned with or characterized by rigorous adherence to recognized forms (especially in religion or art)
formalities: a requirement of etiquette or custom
formality: The dress prescribed for any body of men, academical, municipal, or sacerdotal. The doctors attending her in their formalities as far as Shot over. Fuller.
formalization: the act of making formal (as by stating formal rules governing classes of expressions)
formalized: given formal standing or endorsement; made official or legitimate by the observance of proper procedures
formalizer: One who or that which formalizes.
formalizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of formalize
formally: In a formal manner; essentially; characteristically; expressly; regularly; ceremoniously; precisely. That which formally makes thisa Christian grace, is the spring from which it flows.
