fucus: A genus of tough, leathery seaweeds, usually of a dull brownish green color; rockweed.
fud: The tail of a hare, coney, etc. Burns.
fuddle: To make foolish by drink; to cause to become intoxicated. I am too fuddled to take care to observe your orders. Steele.
fudge: A made-up story; stuff; nonsense; humbug; often an exclamation of contempt.
fudged: simple past and past participle of fudge
fuel: provide with a combustible substance that provides energy
fueled: heated, driven, or produced by burning fuel
fueler: One who, or that which, supplies fuel. Donne.
fueling: the activity of supplying or taking on fuel
fuelled: simple past and past participle of fuel
fug: (British informal) an airless smoky smelly atmosphere
fugacious: Fleeting; lasting but a short time; applied particularly to organs or parts which are short-lived as compared with the life of the individual.
fugacity: the tendency of a gas to expand or escape
fugal: of or relating to or in the style of a musical fugue
fugato: in the gugue style, but not strictly like a fugue. n.
fugitive: someone who flees from an uncongenial situation
fugle: To maneuver; to move hither and thither. Wooden arms with elbow joints jerking and fugling in the air. Carlyle.
fugleman: A soldier especially expert and well drilled, who takes his place in front of a military company, as a guide for the others in their exercises; a file leader. He originally stood in front of the right wing.
fugling: present participle and gerund of fugle
fugue: A polyphonic composition, developed from a given theme or themes, according to strict contrapuntal rules. The theme is first given out by one voice or part, and then, while that pursues its way, it is repeated by another at the interval of a fifth or fourth, andso on, until all the parts have answered one by one, continuing their several melodies and interweaving them in one complex progressive whole, in which the theme is often lost and reappears. All parts of the scheme are eternally chasing each other, like the parts of a fugue. Jer. Taylor.
fuguist: A musician who composes or performs fugues. Busby.
fuji: shrubby Japanese cherry tree having pale pink blossoms
fula: a family of languages of the Fulani of West Africa and used as a lingua franca in the sub-Saharan regions from Senegal to Chad; the best known of the West African languages
fulani: a member of a pastoral and nomadic people of western Africa; they are traditionally cattle herders of Muslim faith
fulcrum: That by which a lever is sustained, or about which it turns in lifting or moving a body.
fulfil: fill or meet a want or need
fulfill: To fill up; to make full or complete. Fulfill her week Gen. xxix. Suffer thou that the children be fulfilled first, for it is not good to take the bread of children and give to hounds. Wyclif (Mark vii. ).
fulfilling: Which causes fulfilment; emotionally or artistically satisfying.
fulfillment: a feeling of satisfaction at having achieved your desires
fulfills: third-person singular simple present indicative of fulfill
fulfilment: the act of consummating something (a desire or promise etc)
fulgent: Exquisitely bright; shining; dazzling; effulgent. Other Thracians. fulgent morions wore. Glower.
fulgor: Dazzling brightness; splendor. Sir T. Browne.
fulguration: The sudden brightening of a fused globule of gold or silver, when the last film of the oxide of lead or copper leaves its surface; also called blick. A phenomenon called, by the old chemists, fulguration. Ure.
fulgurite: A vitrified sand tube produced by the striking of lightning on sand; a lightning tube; also, the portion of rock surface fused by alight ning discharge.
fuliginous: Pertaining to soot; sooty; dark; dusky.
full: Complete measure; utmost extent; the highest state or degree. The swan's-down feather, That stands upon the swell at full of tide. Full of the moon, the time of full moon.
fulled: simple past and past participle of full. To make cloth denser and firmer.
fuller: One whose occupation is to full cloth. Fuller's earth, avariety of clay, used in scouring and cleansing cloth, to imbibe grease. Fuller's herb (Bot.), the soapwort (Saponaria officinal is),formerly used to remove stains from cloth. Fuller's thistle or weed (Bot.), the teasel (Dipsacus fullonum) whose burs are used by fullers in dressing cloth. See Teasel.
fullerene: a form of carbon having a large molecule consisting of an empty cage of sixty or more carbon atoms
fullery: The place or the works where the fulling of cloth is carried on.
fullest: superlative form of full: most full.
fulling: The process of cleansing, shrinking, and thickening cloth by moisture, heat, and pressure. Fulling mill, a mill for fulling cloth as by means of pe sties or stampers, which alternately fall into and rise from troughs where the cloth is placed with hot water and fuller's earth, or other cleansing materials.
fullness: The state of being full, or of abounding; abundance; completeness. In thy presence is fullness of joy. " Ps. xvi.
fulls: third-person singular simple present indicative of full
fully: In a full manner or degree; completely; entirely; without lack or defect; adequately; satisfactorily; as, to be fully persuaded of the truth of a proposition. Fully committed (Law), committed to prison for trial, in distinction from being detained for examination.
fulminated: simple past and past participle of fulminate
fulminating: Thundering; exploding in a peculiarly sudden or violent manner.
fulmined: simple past and past participle of fulmine
fulminic: Pertaining to fulmination; detonating; specifically (Chem.),pertaining to, derived from, or denoting, an acid, so called; as, fulminic acid. Fulminic acid (Chem.), a complex acid, HCNO,isomeric with cyanic and cyanuric acids, and not known in the free state, but forming a large class of highly explosive salts, the fulminates. Of these, mercuric fulminate, the most common, is used, mixed with niter, to fill percussion caps, charge cartridges, etc. Fulminic acid is made by the action of nitric acid on alcohol.
fulminuric: Pertaining to fulminic and cyanuric acids, and designating anacid so called. Fulminuric acid (Chem.), a white, crystalline, explosive subatance, HCNO, forming well known salts, and obtained from the fulnunates. It is isomeric with cyanuric acid, and hence is also called isocyanuric acid.
fulsome: Full; abundant; plenteous; not shriveled. His lean, pale, hoar, and withered corpse grew fulsome, fair, and fresh. Golding.
fulvene: the hydrocarbon methylenecyclopentadiene or any of its derivatives
fulvous: Tawny; dull yellow, with a mixture of gray and brown. Lind ley.
fum: To play upon a fiddle. Follow me, and fum as you go. B. Jonson.
fumado: a smoked fish, especially a pilchard
fumage: Hearth money. Fumage, or fuage, vulgarly called smoke farthings. Black stone.
fumarase: An enzyme that in the Krebs cycle acts as a catalyst for the reaction of water and fumarate to form L-malate.
fumaria: annual herbs whose flowers have only one petal spurred at the base
fumariaceae: erect or climbing herbs of the northern hemisphere and southern Africa: bleeding heart; Dutchman's breeches; fumitory; squirrel corn
fumaric: Pertaining to, or derived from, fumitory (Fumaria officinal is).Fumaric acid (Chem.), a widely occurring organic acid, exttractedfrom fumitory as a white crystall line substance, CH(COH), and produced artificially in many ways, as by the distillation of malic acid; boletic acid. It is found also in the lichen, Iceland moss, and hence was also called lichenic acid.
fumarole: A hole or spot in a volcanic or other region, from which fumes issue.
fumarolic: Of or relating to a fumarole or fumaroles.
fumble: To handle or manage awkwardly; to crowd or tumble together.
fumbled: simple past and past participle of fumble
fumbling: showing lack of skill or aptitude
fumes: gases ejected from an engine as waste products
fumet: The dung of deer. B. Jonson.
fumette: The unpleasant odour or taste of old game meat.
fumigate: treat with fumes, expose to fumes, especially with the aim of disinfecting or eradicating pests
fumigated: simple past and past participle of fumigate
fumigates: third-person singular simple present indicative of fumigate
fumigating: present participle and gerund of fumigate
fumigation: the application of a gas or smoke to something for the purpose of disinfecting it
fumigator: One who, or that which, fumigates; an apparattus for fumigating.
fuming: Producing fumes, or vapors. Cadet's fuming liquid (Chem.),alkarsin. Fuming liquor of Libsvius (Old Chem.), stannic chloride; the chloride of tin, Sn Cl, forming a colorless, mobile liquid which fumes in the air. Mixed with water it solidifies to the so-called butter of tin. Fuming sulphuric acid. (Chem.) Same as Disulphuric acid, uder Disulphuric.
fumingly: In a fuming manner; angrily. They answer fumingly. " Hooker.
fumitory: The common uame of several species of the genus Fumaria, annual herbs of the Old World, with finely dissected leaves and small flowers in dense racemes or spikes. F. officinal is is a common species, and was formerly used as an antiscorbutic. Climbing fumitory (Bot.), the Alleghany vine (Adlumia cirrhosa); a biennial climbing plant with elegant feathery leaves and large clusters of pretty white or pinkish flowers looking like grains of rice.
fumose: fumous; of or resembling fumes or smoke
fumulus: A very thin cloud resembling a veil, especially one formed of water droplets from a rising plume (from a cooling tower etc)
fumy: Producing fumes; fumous. Drowned in fumy wine. " H. Brooke.
fun: Sport; merriment; frolicsome amusement. Oddity, frolic, and fun. " Goldsmith. To make fan of, to hold up to, or turn into, ridicule.
funambulate: To walk or to dance on a rope.
funambulism: walking on a tightrope or slack rope
function: The appropriate action of any special organ or part of an animal or vegetable organism; as, the function of the heart or the limbs; the function of leaves, sap, roots, etc.; life is the sum of the functions of the various organs and parts of the body.
functional: Pertaining to the function of an organ or part, or to the functions in general. Functional disease (Med.), a disease of which the symptoms cannot be referred to any appreciable lesion or change of structure; the derangement of an organ arising from a cause, often unknown, external to itself opposed to organic disease, in which the organ itself is affected.
functionalism: a psychology based on the assumption that all mental process are useful to an organism in adapting to the environment
functionality: capable of serving a purpose well
functionalize: To assign to some function or office.
functionally: In a functional manner; as regards normal or appropriate activity. The organ is said to be functionally disordered. Lawrence.
functionary: One charged with the performance of a function or office; as, apublic functionary; secular functionaries.
functioning: performing or able to perform its regular function
functionless: Destitute of function, or of an appropriate organ. Darwin.
fund: The stock of a national debt; public securities; evidences (stocks or bonds) of money lent to government, for which interest is paid at prescribed intervals; called also public funds.
fundable: Capable of being funded, or converted into a fund; convertible into bonds.
fundamental: Pertaining to the foundation or basis; serving for the foundation. Hence: Essential, as an element, principle, or law; important; original; elementary; as, a fundamental truth; afundamental axiom. The fundamental reasons of this war. Some fundamental antithesis in nature. Whew ell. Fundamental bass (Mus.), the root note of a chord; a bass formed of the roots or fundamental tones of the chords. Fundamental chord (Mus.), a chord, the lowest tone of which isits root. Fundamental colors, red, green, and violet-blue. See Primary colors, under Color.
fundamentalism: the interpretation of every word in the sacred texts as literal truth
fundamentalist: of or relating to or tending toward fundamentalism
fundamentally: Primarily; originally; essentially; radically; at the foundation; in origin or constituents. Fundamentally defective. Burke.
fundamentals: principles from which other truths can be derived
fundatrix: A female aphid hatched in the spring from an overwintering egg.
fundi: A master of a particular skill; an expert.
funding: Providing a fund for the payment of the interest or principal of a debt.
fundraiser: a social function that is held for the purpose of raising money
fundraising: The process of collecting money by requesting donations from individuals and businesses.
funds: assets in the form of money
fundus: The bottom or base of any hollow organ; as, the fundus of the bladder; the fundus of the eye.
funebrial: Pertaining to a funeral or funerals; funeral; funereal. Sir T. Browne.
funeral: Per. tai ning to a funeral; used at the interment of the dead; as, funeral rites, honors, or ceremonies. Funeral pile, astructure of combustible material, upon which a dead body is placed to be reduced to ashes, as part of a funeral rite; a pyre. Funerally, adv. Sir T. Browne.
funerary: of or for or relating to a funeral
funereal: Suiting a funeral; pertaining to burial; solemn. Hence: Dark; dismal; mournful. Jer. Taylor. What seem to us but sad funereal tapers May be heaven's distant lamps. Longfellow. Funereally, adv.
funest: Lamentable; doleful. Funest and direful deaths. Coleridge. A forerunner of something very funest. Evelyn.
fungating: present participle and gerund of fungate
fungia: A genus of simple, stony corals; so called because they are usually flat and circular, with radiating plates, like the gills of amushroom. Some of them are eighteen inches in diameter.
fungible: of goods or commodities; freely exchangeable for or replaceable by another of like nature or kind in the satisfaction of an obligation
fungic: Pertaining to, or obtained from, mushrooms; as, fungic acid.
fungicide: Anything that kills fungi. Fungicidal, n.
fungid: Any cnidarian of the family Fungiidae
fungistatic: That inhibits the growth and reproduction of fungi but does not kill off their population.
fungo: A fielding practice drill where a person hits fly balls intended to be caught.
fungosity: The quality of that which is fungous; fungous excrescence. Dunglison.
fungous: Of the nature of fungi; spongy.
fungus: Any one of the Fungi, a large and very complex group of thallophytes of low organization, the molds, mildews, rusts, smuts, mushrooms, toadstools, puff balls, and the allies of each.
funicle: The little stalk that attaches a seed to the placenta.
funicular: Pertaining to a funiculus; made up of, or resembling, afuniculus, or funiculi; as, a funicular ligament. Funicular action (Mech.), the force or action exerted by a rope in drawing together the supports to which its ends are Fastened, when acted upon by forces applied in a direction transverse to the rope, as in the archer's bow. Funicular curve. Same as Catenary. Funicular machine (Mech.), an apparatus for illustrating certain principles in statics, consisting of a cord or chain attached at one end to a fixed point, and having the other passed over a pulley and sustaining a weight, while one or more other weights are suspended from the cord at points between the fixed support and the pulley. Funicular polygon (Mech.), the polygonal figure assumed by a cord fastened at its extremities, and sustaining weights at different points.
funiculus: any of several body structure resembling a cord
funker: One who funks, or backs out of something due to cowardice.
funkia: Any of the plants of the genus Funkia (now Hosta).
funking: present participle and gerund of funk
funky: Pertaining to, or characterized by, great fear, or funking.
funnel: move or pour through a funnel
funnelform: Having the form of a funnel, or tunnel; that is, expanding gradually from the bottom upward, as the corolla of some flowers; infundibuliform.
funnier: comparative form of funny: more funny
funny: Droll; comical; amusing; laughable. Funny bone. See crazy bone, under Crazy.
fur: Articles of clothing made of fur; as, a set of furs for a lady (a collar, tippet, or cape, muff, etc.).Wrapped up in my furs. Lady M. W. Montagu.
furan: a colorless toxic flammable liquid used in the synthesis of nylon
furane: a colorless toxic flammable liquid used in the synthesis of nylon
furanose: any cyclic hemiacetal form of a monosaccharide having a five-membered ring (the tetrahydrofuran skeleton)
furbelow: A plaited or gathered flounce on a woman's garment.
furbelowed: simple past and past participle of furbelow
furbish: To rub or scour to brightness; to clean; to burnish; as, to furbish a sword or spear. Furbish new the name of John a Gaunt.
furbished: simple past and past participle of furbish
furbishes: third-person singular simple present indicative of furbish
furca: A forked structure, a fork-like part.
furcate: divide into two or more branches so as to form a fork
furciferous: Rascally; scandalous. Furciferous knaves. " De Quincey.
furcraea: Any plant of the genus Furcraea.
furcula: A forked process; the wishbone or furculum.
furculum: The wishbone or merrythought of birds, formed by the united clavicles.
furfuraceous: Made of bran; like bran; scurfy.
furfural: a liquid aldehyde with a penetrating odor; made from plant hulls and corncobs; used in making furan and as a solvent
furfuran: A colorless, oily substance, CHO, obtained by distilling certain organic substances, as pine wood, salts of pyromucic acid, etc.; called also tetraphenol.
furfurol: A colorless oily liquid, CHO.CHO, of a pleasant odor, obtained by the distillation of bran, sugar, etc., and regarded as an aldehyde derivative of furfuran; called also furfural.
furfurous: Made of bran; furfuraceous. Furfurous bread. " Sydney smith.
furile: A yellow, crystalline substance, (CHO).CO, obtained by the oxidation of furoin.
furilic: Pertaining to, or derived from, furile; as, furilic acid.
furious: Transported with passion or fury; raging; violent; as, a furious animal.
furiously: (of the elements) in a wild and stormy manner
furiousness: the property of being wild or turbulent
furl: To draw up or gather into close compass; to wrap or roll, as asail, close to the yard, stay, or mast, or, as a flag, close to or around its staff, securing it there by a gasket or line. Totten.
furler: A person or device that furls a flag, a sail, etc.
furling: present participle and gerund of furl
furlong: A measure of length; the eighth part of a mile; forty rods; two hundred and twenty yards.
furlough: Leave of abserice; especially, leave given to an offcer or soldier to be absent from service for a certain time; also, the document granting leave of absence.
furls: third-person singular simple present indicative of furl
furnace: an enclosed chamber in which heat is produced to heat buildings, destroy refuse, smelt or refine ores, etc.
furnaceman: One who operates a furnace in metalworking.
furnarius: type genus of the family Furnariidae: ovenbirds
furnish: That which is furnished as a specimen; a sample; a supply. Greene.
furnished: provided with whatever is necessary for a purpose (as furniture or equipment or authority)
furniture: A mixed or compound stop in an organ; sometimes called mixture.
furoic: Of or pertaining to furoic acid or its derivatives.
furoin: A colorless, crystalline substance, CHO, from furfurol.
furred: covered with a dense coat of fine silky hairs
furrier: A dealer in furs; one who makes or sells fur goods.
furring: Double planking of a ship's side.
furrow: hollow out in the form of a furrow or groove
furrowed: having long narrow shallow depressions (as grooves or wrinkles) in the surface
furrower: A tool for creating furrows in the ground.
furry: Covered with fur; dressed in fur. Furry nations. " Thomson.
further: To a greater distance; in addition; moreover. See Farther. Carries us, I know not how much further, into familiar company. M.Arnold. They sdvanced us far as Eleusis and Thria; but no further. Jowett (Thucyd. ).Further off, not so near; apart by a greater distance.
furtherance: The act of furthering or helping forward; promotion; advancement; progress. I know that I shall abide and continue with you all for yourfurthersnce and joy of faith. Phil. i.Built of furtherance and pursuing, Not of spent deeds, but of doing. Emerson.
furtherer: One who furthers. or helps to advance; a promoter.
furthering: present participle and gerund of further
furthermore: or conj. Moreover; besides; in addition to what has been said.
furthers: third-person singular simple present indicative of further
furthersome: Tending to further, advance, or promote; helpful; advantageous. You will not find it furthersome. Carlyle.
furthest: superl. Most remote; most in advance; farthest. See Further, a.
furtive: Stolen; obtained or characterized by stealth; sly; secret; stealthy; as, a furtive look. Prior. A hasty and furtive ceremony. Hall am.
furuncle: A superficial, inflammatory tumor, suppurating with a central core; a boil.
furuncular: Of or pertaining to a furuncle; marked by the presence of furuncles.
fury: A thief. Have an eye to your plate, for there be furies. J. Flete her.
furzy: bounding in, or overgrown with, furze; characterized by furze. Gay.
fusain: Fine charcoal of willow wood, used as a drawing implement.
fusarium: Any of various fungi, of the genus Fusarium, some of which are pathogenic to plants and animals.
fuscin: A brown, nitrogenous pigment contained in the retinal epithelium; a variety of melanin.
fuscous: Brown or grayish black; darkish. Sad and fuscous colors, as black or brown, or deep purple and the like. Burke.
fuse: A tube or casing filled with combustible matter, by means of which a charge of powder is ignited, as in blasting; called also fuzee. See Fuze. Fuse hole, the hole in a shell prepared for the reception of the fuse. Farrow.
fusee: A small packet of explosive material with wire appendage sallowing it to be conveniently attached to a railroad track. It will explode with a loud report when run over by a train, and is used to provide a warning signal to the engineer.
fusible: Cap abie of being melted or liquefied. Fusible metal, any alloy of different metals capable of being easily fused, especially an alloy of five parts of bismuth, three of lead, and two of tin, which melts at a temperature below that of boiling water. Ure. Fusible plug (Steam Boiler), a piece of easily fusible alloy, placed in one of the sheets and intended to melt and blow off the steam in case of low water.
fusiform: Shaped like a spindle; tapering at each end; as, a fusiform root; a fusiform cell.
fusil: A light kind of flintlock musket, formerly in use.
fusilier: (formerly) a British infantryman armed with a light flintlock musket
fusing: present participle and gerund of fuse
fusion: The union, or binding together, of adjacent parts or tissues.
fusionism: The political practice, principle or theory of forming groups.
fusobacterium: Any bacterium of the genus Fusobacterium
fuss: To be overbusy or unduly anxious about trifles; to make abustle or ado. Sir W. Scott.
fussbudget: One who complains or fusses a great deal, especially about unimportant matters; a fusspot.
fusser: One who fusses; a fussy person.
fussing: present participle and gerund of fuss
fusspot: thinks about unfortunate things that might happen
fussy: Making a fuss; disposed to make an unnecessary ado about trifles; overnice; fidgety. Not at all fussy about his personal appearance. R. G. White.
fustanella: A form of skirt or kilt traditionally worn by men in Albania, Greece and other parts of the Balkans.
fustee: A person who is of / black ancestry, the child of a mustee and a white.
fustet: The wood of the Rhus Cptinus or Venice sumach, a shrub of southern Europe, which yields a fine orange color, which, however, isnot durable without a mordant. Ure.
fustian: a strong cotton and linen fabric with a slight nap
fustic: The wood of the Maclura tinctoria, a tree growing in the West indies, used in dyeing yellow; called also old fustic.
fustigation: A punishment by beating with a stick or club; cudgeling. This satire, composed of actual fustigation. Motley.
fustiness: A fusty state or quality; moldiness; mustiness; an ill smell from moldiness.
futhark: The Germanic runic alphabet; especially specifically the Elder or Younger futhark alphabet (of Scandinavia and the European mainland), as contrasted with the Anglo-Saxon futhorc.
futhorc: The Runic alphabet as used to write Old English and Old Frisian.
futility: uselessness as a consequence of having no practical result
futtock: One of the crooked timbers which are scarfed together to form the lower part of the compound rib of a vessel; one of the crooked transverse timbers passing across and over the keel. Futtock plates (Naut.), plates of iron to which the dead-eyes of the topmast rigging are secured. Futtock shrouds, short iron shrouds leading from the upper part of the lower mast or of the main shrouds to the edge of the top, or through it, and connecting the topmast rigging with the lower mast. Totten.
futurable: Capable of being future; possible to occur. Not only to things future, but futurable. Fuller.
futurama: A palpable depiction of a (usually sensational) vision of the future.
future: That is to be or come hereafter; that will exist at any time after the present; as, the next moment is future, to the present. Future tense (Gram.), the tense or modification of a verb which expresses a future act or event.
futurism: A movement or phase of post-impressionism (which see, below).
futurist: One who believes or maintains that the fulfillment of the prophecies of the Bible is to be in the future.
futurition: The state of being future; futurity. Nothing. can have this imagined futurition, but as it is decreed. Coleridge.
futurity: the quality of being in or of the future
futurology: the study or prediction of future developments on the basis of existing conditions
fuze: A tube, filled with combustible matter, for exploding a shell, etc. See Fuse, n. Chemical fuze, a fuze in which substances separated until required for action are then brought into contact, and uniting chemically, produce explosion. Concussion fuze, a fuze ignited by the striking of the projectile. Electric fuze, a fuze which is ignited by heat or a spark produced by an electric current. Friction fuze, a fuze which is ignited by the heat evolved by friction. Percussion fuze, a fuze in which the ignition is produced by ablow on some fulminating compound. Time fuze, a fuze adapted, either by its length or by the character of its composition, to burn a certain time before producing an explosion.
fuzee: any igniter that is used to initiate the burning of a propellant
fuzzy: confused and not coherent; not clearly thought out
fy: A word which expresses blame, dislike, disapprobation, abhorrence, or contempt. See Fie.
fyke: A long bag net distended by hoops, into which fish can pass easily, without being able to return; called also fyke net. Cozzens.
fylfot: A swastika, especially one with the arms bent in an anticlockwise direction.
g: G is the name of the fifth tone of the natural or model scale; called also sol by the Italians and French. It was also originally used as the treble clef, and has gradually changed into the character represented in the margin. See Clef. G# (G sharp) is a tone intermediate between G and A.
gab: The hook on the end of an eccentric rod opposite the strap. See. Illust. of Eccentric.
gabardine: a firm durable fabric with a twill weave
gabbart: A lighter or barge; a small one-masted sailing or coasting vessel designed for inland navigation.
gabble: To talk fast, or to talk without meaning; to prate; to jabber.
gabbles: third-person singular simple present indicative of gabble
gabbling: present participle and gerund of gabble
gabbro: A name originally given by the Italians to a kind of serpentine, later to the rock called euphotide, and now generally used for a coarsely crystalline, igneous rock consisting of lamellar pyroxene (diallage) and labradorite, with sometimes chrysolite (olivine gabbro).
gabel: A rent, service, tribute, custom, tax, impost, or duty; an excise. Bur rill. He enables St. Peter to pay his gabel by the ministry of a fish. Jer. Taylor.
gabeler: A collector of ga bels or taxes.
gabelle: A tax, especially on salt. Br ande & C.
gabfest: light informal conversation for social occasions
gabion: A hollow cylinder of wickerwork, like a basket without abottom. Gabions are made of various sizes, and filled with earth in building field works to shelter men from an enemy's fire.
gabionade: A traverse made with gabions between guns or on their flanks, protecting them from enfilading fire.
gabled: (of a roof) constructed with a single slope on each side of the ridge supported at the end by a gable or vertical triangular portion of an end wall
gabon: a republic on the west coast of Africa
gabonese: of or relating to Gabon or its inhabitants
gabriel: (Bible) the archangel who was the messenger of God
gaby: A simpleton; a dunce; a lout.
gad: To walk about; to rove or go about, without purpose; hence, torun wild; to be uncontrolled. The gadding vine. " Milton. Why gaddest thou about so much to change thy way Jer. ii.
gadder: One who roves about idly, a rambling gossip.
gaddi: a cushion on a throne for a prince in India
gadding: Going about much, needlessly or without purpose. Envy is a gadding passion, and walk eth the streets. Bacon. The good nuns would check her gadding tongue. Tennyson. Gadding car, in quarrying, a car which carries a drilling machine so arranged as to drill a line of holes.
gaddish: Disposed to gad. Gaddishnes, n. Gaddishness and folly. " Abp. Leighton.
gadfly: Any dipterous insect of the genus Oestrus, and allied genera of botflies.

gadi: A cushioned throne used by Indian princes.
gadic: Pertaining to, or derived from, the cod (Gadus); applied to an acid obtained from cod-liver oil, viz., gadic acid.

gadroon: Any of a series of raised decorative curves used as adornments on the necks of vases, silverware, etc.

gadwall: A large duck (Anas strepera), valued as a game bird, found in the northern parts of Europe and America; called also gray duck.
gadzooks: An expression of surprise, shock, etc.

gael: A Celt or the Celts of the Scotch Highlands or of Ireland; now esp., a Scotch Highlander of Celtic origin.

gaetuli: An ancient Berber tribe inhabiting Gaetulia.
gaetulian: Of or relating to the Gaetuli tribe.

gaffer: an electrician responsible for lighting on a movie or tv set
gafsa: a city in west central Tunisia
gag: restraint put into a person's mouth to prevent speaking or shouting

gagster: someone who writes comic material for public performers
gaia: The ecosystem of the Earth regarded as a self-regulating superorganism.

gain: A square or beveled notch cut out of a girder, binding joist, or other timber which supports a floor beam, so as to receive the endof the floor beam.
gainable: Capable of being obtained or reached. Sherwood.
gained: simple past and past participle of gain

gaining: present participle and gerund of gain

gainly: Handily; readily; dexterously; advantageously. Dr. H.More.
gainsaid: simple past and past participle of gainsay

gainsayer: One who gainsays, contradicts, or denies. To convince the gainsayers. " Tit. i.
gainsays: third-person singular simple present indicative of gainsay
gainstand: To withstand; to resist. Durst. gainstand the force of so many enraged desires. Sir P.Sidney.
gaited: Having (such) a gait; used in composition; as, slow-gaited; heavy-gaited.

gala: Pomp, show, or festivity. Macaulay. Gala day, a day of mirth and festivity; a holiday.

galactocele: a cystic tumor containing milk or a milky substance (especially in the mammary glands)

galactorrhea: Lactation (the secretion of milk from nipples) that is not associated with childbirth or nursing.
galactosamine: an amino derivative of the sugar galactose; found in glycolipids and in mucopolysaccharides

galangal: southeastern Asian perennial with aromatic roots
galantine: A dish of veal, chickens, or other white meat, freed from bones, tied up, boiled, and served cold. Smart.
galatea: A kind of striped cotton fabric, usually of superior quality and striped with blue or red on white.
galatia: an ancient country in central Asia Minor
galatian: Of or pertaining to Galatia or its inhabitants. A native or inhabitant of Galatia, in Asia Minor; a descendant of the Gauls who settled in Asia Minor.
galatians: The ninth book of the New Testament of the Bible, the epistle of Saint Paul to the Galatians.

galliformes: pheasants; turkeys; grouse; partridges; quails; chickens; brush turkeys; curassows; hoatzins
galligaskins: Loose hose or breeches; leather leg quar ds. The word is used loosely and often in a jocose sense.

galloon: A narrow tapelike fabric used for binding hats, shoes, etc., sometimes made ornamental.

galway: a port city in western Ireland on Galway Bay

gandhian: of or relating to Mahatma Gandhi or his teachings

ganef: (Yiddish) a thief or dishonest person or scoundrel (often used as a general term of abuse)
gangbang: An act of two or more people having sex with one person who is the focus of the sexual activity.
ganged: simple past and past participle of gang

ganges: an Asian river; rises in the Himalayas and flows east into the Bay of Bengal; a sacred river of the Hindus

gantline: A line rigged to a mast; used in hoisting rigging; agirtline.
ganymede: (Greek mythology) a Trojan boy who was so beautiful that Zeus carried him away to serve as cupbearer to the gods

gapes: third-person singular simple present indicative of gape

garce: A unit of volume or weight for rice, etc.
garcinia: A genus of plants, including the mangosteen tree (Garcinia Mangostana), found in the islands of the Indian Archipelago; so called in honor of Dr. Garcin.

gardner: United States collector and patron of art who built a museum in Boston to house her collection and opened it to the public in (-)
garefowl: The great auk; also, the razorbill. See Auk.

garrigue: A type of low scrubland found on limestone soils in southern France and other parts of the Mediterranean Basin.
garrison: station (troops) in a fort or garrison
garrot: A stick or small wooden cylinder used for tightening a bandage, in order to compress the arteries of a limb.

garrotte: an instrument of execution for execution by strangulation

garrulus: type genus of the Garrulinae: Old World jays
garrya: Any of the genus Garrya of flowering plants.
garshuni: The Arabic language written in the Syriac alphabet.
garum: A sauce made of small fish. It was prized by the ancients.
garvey: A type of boat which was originally flat-bottomed, reminiscent of a sled, and historically sailed around New Jersey.
garvie: The spart; called also garvie herring, and garvock.
garvock: A fish, garvie or sprat (Sprattus sprattus).
gary: a city in northwest Indiana on Lake Michigan; steel production
gas: attack with gas; subject to gas fumes

gaselier: A chandelier arranged to burn gas.

gaskell: English writer who is remembered for her biography of Charlotte Bronte (-)

gastight: So tightly fitted as to preclude the escape of gas; impervious to gas.

gau: A prayer box or small container worn as jewelry and containing an amulet or similar item.

gebang: Corypha utan, a palm tree native to Asia and Oceania.

geest: Alluvial matter on the surface of land, not of recent origin. R. Jameson.

geezer: A queer old fellow; an old chap; an old woman.
gegenschein: a faint spot of light in the night sky that appears directly opposite the position of the sun
gehenna: The valley of Hin nom, near Jerusalem, where some of the israelites sacrificed their children to Moloch, which, on this account, was afterward regarded as a place of abomination, and made areceptacle for all the refuse of the city, perpetual fires being kept up in order to prevent pestilential effluvia. gelee: Any gelled suspension made for culinary purposes.
gelid: Cold; very cold; frozen. Gelid founts. " Thompson.
gelled: simple past and past participle of gel
gelling: present participle and gerund of gel

glorification: the act of glorifying (as in worship)
glorifier: Agent noun of glorify: one who glorifies.
glorifies: third-person singular simple present indicative of glorify
glorifying: present participle and gerund of glorify
gloriosa: A genus of climbing plants with very showy lilylike blossoms, natives of India.
glorious: having or deserving or conferring glory
gloriousness: glory, the state or quality of being glorious
glorying: present participle and gerund of glory
gloss: To give a superficial luster or gloss to; to make smooth and shining; as, to gloss cloth. The glossed and gleamy wave. J. R. Drake.
glossa: The tongue, or lingua, of an insect. See Hymenoptera.
glossal: Of or pertaining to the tongue; lingual.
glossary: A collection of glosses or explanations of words and passages of a work or author; a partial dictionary of a work, an author, adialect, art, or science, explaining archaic, technical, or other uncommon words.
glossectomy: The surgical removal of all or part of the tongue.
glossematics: A structuralist linguistic theory that defines the glosseme as the most basic unit of language.
glosseme: The smallest irreducible unit of both the content and expression planes of language; the basic unit of language in the theory of glossematics.
glosser: A polisher; one who gives a luster.
glossiness: The condition or quality of being glossy; the luster or brightness of a smooth surface. Boyle.
glossing: The addition of a gloss, or explanatory note.
glossoepiglottic: Pertaining to both tongue and epiglottis; as, glossoepiglottic folds.
glossography: The writing of glossaries, glosses, or comments for illustrating an author.
glossohyal: Pertaining to both the hyoidean arch and the tongue; applied to the anterior segment of the hyoidean arch in many fishes. n. The glossohyal bone or cartilage; lingual bone; entoglossal bone.
glossolalia: repetitive nonmeaningful speech (especially that associated with a trance state or religious fervor)
glossology: The definition and explanation of terms; a glossary.
glossopharyngeal: Pertaining to both the tongue and the pharynx; applied especially to the ninth pair of cranial nerves, which are distributed to the pharynx and tongue. n. One of the glossopharyngeal nerves.
glossy: a photograph that is printed on smooth shiny paper
glottal: Of or pertaining to, or produced by, the glottis; glottic. Glottal catch, an effect produced upon the breath or voice by asudden opening or closing of the glotts. Sweet.
glottalization: The act or process of constricting or closing the glottis during the production of a speech sound that normally does not involve such constriction.
glottalize: To apply glottalization while articulating another sound.
glottic: Of or pertaining to the glottis or the tongue.
glottis: The opening from the pharynx into the larynx or into the trachea. See Larynx.
glottochronology: the determination of how long ago different languages evolved from a common source language
glottogony: The genesis of language, i. e. the emergence of a system of verbal communication from proto-linguistic or non-linguistic means of communication.
glottology: The science of tongues or languages; comparative philology; glossology.
gloucester: a town in northeastern Massachusetts on Cape Ann to the northeast of Boston; the harbor has been a fishing center for centuries
gloucestershire: a county in southwestern England in the lower Severn valley
glout: To pout; to look sullen. Garth.
glove: To cover with, or as with, a glove.
glover: One whose trade it is to make or sell gloves. Glover's suture or stitch, a kind of stitch used in sewing up wounds, in which the thread is drawn alternately through each side from within outward.
glow: To make hot; to flush. Fans, whose wind did seem To glow the delicate cheeks which they did cool.
glowed: simple past and past participle of glow
glower: to look intently; to stare angrily or with a scowl. Thackeray.
glowingly: In a glowing manner; with ardent heat or passion.
glows: third-person singular simple present indicative of glow
gloxinia: American genus of herbaceous plants with very handsome bell-shaped blossoms; named after B. P. Gloxin, a German botanist.
gloze: To smooth over; to palliate. By glozing the evil that is in the world. I. Taylor.
glozed: simple past and past participle of gloze
glozing: present participle and gerund of gloze
glucagon: a hormone secreted by the pancreas; stimulates increases in blood sugar levels in the blood (thus opposing the action of insulin)
glucic: Pertaining to, or obtained from, sugar; as, glucic acid.
glucina: A white or gray tasteless powder, the oxide of the element glucinum; formerly called glucine.
glucine: A monoclinic mineral containing beryllium, calcium, hydrogen, oxygen, and phosphorus.
glucinic: Pertaining to, derived from, or containing, glucinum; as, glucinic oxide.
glucinum: A rare metallic element, of a silver white color, and low specific gravity (.), resembling magnesium. It never occurs naturally in the free state, but is always combined, usually with silica or alumina, or both; as in the minerals phenacite, chrysoberyl, beryl or emerald, euclase, and danalite. It was named from its oxide glucina, which was known long before the element was isolated. Symbol Gl. Atomic weight. Called also beryllium.
glucocorticoid: a steroid hormone that is produced by the adrenal cortex of animals; affects functioning of gonads and has anti-inflammatory activity
glucolipid: Any glycolipid whose carbohydrate component is glucose.
gluconate: Any salt or ester of gluconic acid
gluconeogenesis: The metabolic process in which glucose is formed, mostly in the liver, from non-carbohydrate precursors
gluconic: Pertaining to, or derived from, glucose. Gluconic acid (Chem.),an organic acid, obtained as a colorless, sirupy liquid, by the oxidation of glucose; called also maltonic acid, and dextronic acid.
glucosamine: an amino derivative of glucose that is a component of many polysaccharides
glucose: Any one of a large class of sugars, isometric with glucose proper, and including levulose, galactose, etc.
glucoside: One of a large series of amorphous or crystalline substances, occurring very widely distributed in plants, rarely in animals, and regarded as influent al agents in the formation and disposition of the sugars. They are frequently of a bitter taste, but, by the action of ferments, or of dilute acids and alkalies, always break down into some characteristic substance (acid, aldehyde, alcohol, phenole, or alkaloid) and glucose (or some other sugar); hence the name. They areof the nature of complex and compound ethers, and ethereal salts of the sugar carbohydrates.
glucosidic: Of or pertaining to a glucoside
glucosuria: A condition in which glucose is discharged in the urine; diabetes mellitus.
glucuronic: Of or pertaining to glucuronic acid or its derivatives.
glucuronide: Any of various derivatives of glucuronic acid formed during the metabolism of phenols etc that serve to remove them from the bloodstream.
glue: A hard brittle brownish gelatin, obtained by boiling to a jelly the skins, hoofs, etc., of animals. When gently heated with water, it becomes viscid and tenaceous, and is used as a cement for uniting substances. The name is also given to other adhesive or viscous substances. Bee glue. See under Bee. Fish glue, a strong kind of glue obtained from fish skins and bladders; isinglass. Glue plant (Bot.), a fucoid seaweed (Gloiopeltis tenax). Liquid glue, a fluid preparation of glue and acetic acidoralcohol. Marine glue, a solution of caoutchouc in naphtha, with shellac, used in shipbuilding.
glued: affixed or as if affixed with glue or paste
gluelike: Resembling glue or some aspect of it.
gluey: Viscous; glutinous; of the nature of, or like, glue.
gluing: present participle and gerund of glue
glumal: Characterized by a glume, or having the nature of a glume.
glume: The bracteal covering of the flowers or seeds of grain and grasses; esp., an outer husk or bract of a spike lt. Gray.
glumose: Bearing or relating to a glume.
glumpy: Glum; sullen; sulky. He was glumpy enough. " T. Hook.
glunch: Frowning; sulky; sullen. Sir W. Scott. n.
glut: To eat gluttonously or to satiety. Like three horses that have broken fence, And glutted all night long breast-deep in corn. Tennyson.
glutamate: a salt or ester of glutamic acid
glutamic: Of or pertaining to gluten. Glutamic acid, a nitrogenous organic acid obtained from certain albuminoids, as gluten; called also amido-glutaric acid. CHNO.
glutamine: a crystalline amino acid occurring in proteins; important in protein metabolism
glutaric: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid so called; as, glutaric ethers. Glutaric acid, an organic acid obtained as a white crystalline substance, isomeric with pyrotartaric acid; called also normal pyrotartaric acid.
glutelin: a simple protein found in the seeds of cereals
gluten: The viscid, tenacious substance which gives adhesiveness to dough.
glutinous: Havig a moist and adhesive or sticky surface, as a leaf or gland.
glutting: present participle and gerund of glut
gluttonise: eat a lot and without restraint
gluttonize: To eat to excess; to eat voraciously; to gormandize. Hallywell.
gluttonous: Given to gluttony; eating to excess; indulging the appetite; voracious; as, a gluttonous age. Gluttonously, adv. Gluttonousness, n.
gluttony: Excess in eating; extravagant indulgence of the appetite for food; voracity. Their sumptuous gluttonies, and gorgeous feasts. Milton.
glycan: Any polysaccharide or oligosaccharide, especially one that is part of a glycoprotein or glycolipid.
glycemia: Presence of glucose in the blood (which is always true), and (usually, more specifically) average concentration thereof over time, and its regulation; in this sense, glycemia is hypernymic to euglycemia, hyperglycemia, and hypoglycemia, and a mention of glycemia is a reference to blood sugar regulation and degree or quality thereof.
glycemic: Of, pertaining to or suffering from glycemia.
glyceraldehyde: a sweet crystalline aldehyde formed by the breakdown of sugars
glyceric: Pertaining to, or derived from, glycerin. Glyceric acid (Chem.), an organic acid, obtained by the partial oxidation of glycerin, as a thick liquid. It is a hydroxyl derivative of propionic acid, and has both acid and alcoholic properties.
glyceride: A compound ether (formed from glycerin). Some glycerides exist ready formed as natural fats, others are produced artificially.
glycerin: a sweet syrupy trihydroxy alcohol obtained by saponification of fats and oils
glycerinate: To react or treat with glycerine.
glycerinated: Modified by reaction or treatment with glycerine
glycerine: a sweet syrupy trihydroxy alcohol obtained by saponification of fats and oils
glycerite: A medicinal preparation made by mixing or dissolving asubstance in glycerin.
glycerophosphate: Any salt or ester of glycerophosphoric acid; but especially the phospholipids.
glycerophosphoric: Of or pertaining to glycerophosphoric acid or its derivatives
glyceryl: A compound radical, CH, regarded as the essential radical of glycerin. It is metameric with allyl. Called also propenyl.
glycide: A colorless liquid, obtained from certain derivatives of glycerin, and regarded as a partially dehydrated glycerin; called also glycidic alcohol.
glycidic: Pertaining to, or derived from, glycide; as, glycidic acid.
glycine: the simplest amino acid found in proteins and the principal amino acid in sugar cane
glycocholate: A salt of glycocholic acid; as, sodium glycocholate.
glycocholic: Pertaining to, or composed of, glycocoll and cholic acid. Glycocholic acid (Physiol. Chem.), a conjugate acid, composed of glycocoll and cholic acid, present in bile in the form of a sodium salt. The acid commonly forms a resinous mass, but can be crystallized in long, white needles.
glycocoll: A crystalline, nitrogenous substance, with a sweet taste, formed from hippuric acid by boiling with hydrochloric acid, and present in bile united with cholic acid. It is also formed from gelatin by decomposition with acids. Chemically, it is amido-acetic acid. Called also glycin, and glycocin.
glycogen: A white, amorphous, tasteless substance resembling starch, soluble in water to an opalescent fluid. It is found abundantly in the liver of most animals, and in small quantity in other organs and tissues, particularly in the embryo. It is quickly changed into sugar when boiled with dilute sulphuric or hydrochloric acid, and also by the action of amylolytic ferments.
glycogenesis: the formation in animals of glycogen from glucose
glycogenic: Pertaining to, or caused by, glycogen; as, the glycogenic function of the liver.
glycogenolysis: The production of glucosephosphate by splitting a glucose monomer from glycogen using inorganic phosphate
glycol: A thick, colorless liquid, CH(OH), of a sweetish taste, produced artificially from certain ethylene compounds. It is a diacid alcohol, intermediate between ordinary ethyl alcohol and glycerin.
glycolic: Pertaining to, or derived from, glycol; as, glycolic ether; glycolic acid. Glycolic acid (Chem.), an organic acid, found naturally in unripe grapes and in the leaves of the wild grape (Ampelopsis quinquefolia), and produced artificially in many ways, asby the oxidation of glycol, whence its name. It is a sirupy, or white crystalline, substance, HO.CH.COH, has the properties both of an alcohol and an acid, and is a type of the hydroxy acids; called also hydroxyacetic acid.
glycolide: A white amorphous powder, CHO, obtained by heating and dehydrating glycolic acid.
glycolipid: An association of a carbohydrate and a phospholipid, such as phosphatidylinositol, found in cell membranes
glycoluric: Pertaining to, derived from, glycol and urea; as, glycoluric acid, which is called also hydantoic acid.
glycolyl: A divalent, compound radical, CO.CH, regarded as the essential radical of glycolic acid, and a large series of related compounds.
glycolysis: a metabolic process that breaks down carbohydrates and sugars through a series of reactions to either pyruvic acid or lactic acid and releases energy for the body in the form of ATP
glyconic: Consisting of a spondee, a choriamb, and a pyrrhic; applied to a kind of verse in Greek and Latin poetry. n. (Pros.)
glycoprotein: a conjugated protein having a carbohydrate component
glycose: One of a class of carbohydrates having from three to nine atoms of carbon in the molecules and having the constitution either of an aldehyde alcohol or of a ketone alcohol. Most glyc oses have hydrogen and oxygen present in the proportion to form water, while the number of carbon atoms is usually equal to the number of atoms of oxygen.
glycoside: a group of compounds derived from monosaccharides
glycosidic: Of or pertaining to a glycoside.
glycosyl: Any functional group derived from a sugar (especially from a monosaccharide) by removal of the hemiacetal hydroxy group.
glycyl: The univalent radical obtained by removal of a hydrogen atom from the carboxylic acid group of glycine.
glycyrrhiza: A genus of papilionaceous herbaceous plants, one species of which (G. gl abra), is the licorice plant, the roots of which have abittersweet mucilaginous taste.
glycyrrhizimic: From, or pertaining to, glycyrrhizin; as, glycyrrhizimic acid.
glycyrrhizin: A glucoside found in licorice root (Glycyrrhiza), in monesia bark (Chrysophyllum), in the root of the walnut, etc., and extracted as a yellow, amorphous powder, of a bittersweet taste.
glyoxal: A white, amorphous, deliquescent powder, (CO.H), obtained by the partial oxidation of glycol. It is a double aldehyde, between glycol and oxalic acid.
glyoxaline: A white, crystalline, organic base, CHN, produced by the action of ammonia on glyoxal, and forming the origin of a large class of derivatives hence, any one of the series of which glyoxaline is atype; called also oxaline.
glyoxime: A white, crystalline, nitrogenous substance, produced by the action of hydroxylamine on glyoxal, and belonging to the class of oximes; also, any one of a group of substances resembling glyoxime proper, and of which it is a type. See Oxime.
glyoxylic: Of or pertaining to glyoxylic acid or its derivatives
glyph: A sunken channel or groove, usually vertical. See Triglyph.
glyphography: A process similar to etching, in which, by means of voltaic electricity, a raised copy of a drawing is made, so that it can be used to print from.
glyptodon: An extinct South American quaternary mammal, allied to the armadillos. It was as large as an ox, was covered with tessellated scales, and had fluted teeth. Owen.
glyptography: The art or process of engraving on precious stones.
glyptology: The study of engraving, especially on precious stones.
gm: a metric unit of weight equal to one thousandth of a kilogram
gmelina: Any member of the genus Gmelina.
gnaphalium: A genus of composite plants with white or colored dry and persistent involucres; a kind of everlasting.
gnar: A knot or gnarl in wood; hence, a tough, thickset man; written also gnarr. He was. a thick gnar re. Chaucer.
gnarl: To growl; to snarl. And wolves are gnarling who shall gnaw thee first.
gnarling: present participle and gerund of gnarl
gnarly: Full of knots; knotty; twisted; crossgrained.
gnash: To strike together, as in anger or pain; as, to gnash the teeth.
gnashing: present participle and gerund of gnash
gnat: A blood-sucking dipterous fly, of the genus Culex, undergoing ametamorphosis in water. The females have a proboscis armed with needlelike organs for penetrating the skin of animals. These are wanting in the males. In America they are generally called mosquitoes. See Mosquito.
gnathic: Of or pertaining to the jaw. Gnathic index, in a skull, the ratio of the distance from the middle of the nasofrontal suture to the basion (taken equal to ), to the distance from the basion to the middle of the front edge of the upper jaw; called also alveolar index. Skulls with the gnathic index below are orthognathous, from to mesognathous, and above are prognathous. Flower.
gnathion: the most inferior point of the mandible in the midline
gnathobase: A lower appendage of many arthropods, used to macerate food items.
gnathopod: A gnathopodite or maxilliped. See Maxilliped.
gnathopodite: Any leglike appendage of a crustacean, when modified wholly, orin part, to serve as a jaw, esp. one of the maxillipeds.
gnathostomata: comprising all vertebrates with upper and lower jaws
gnathostome: a vertebrate animal possessing true jaws
gnaw: To use the teeth in biting; to bite with repeated effort, as in eating or removing with the teeth something hard, unwiedly, or unmanageable. I might well, like the spaniel, gnaw upon the chain that ties me. Sir P. Sidney.
gnawed: simple past and past participle of gnaw
gnaws: third-person singular simple present indicative of gnaw
gneiss: A crystalline rock, consisting, like granite, of quartz, feldspar, and mica, but having these materials, especially the mica, arranged in planes, so that it breaks rather easily into coarse slabs or flags. Hornblende sometimes takes the place of the mica, and it is then called hornblendic or syenitic gneiss. Similar varieties of related rocks are also called gneiss.
gnetaceae: plants having small unisexual flowers and fleshy or winged fruit: in some classifications includes the genera Ephedra and Welwitschia as well as genus Gnetum
gnetum: small tropical tree with tiered branches and divaricate branch lets having broad glossy dark green leaves; exploited for its edible young leaves and seeds that provide a fine flour
gnome: A small owl (Glaucidium gnoma) of the Western United States.
gnomological: Relating to, of the nature of, or resembling, a gnomology.
gnomology: A collection of, or a treatise on, maxims, grave sentences, or reflections. Milton.
gnomon: The style or pin, which by its shadow, shows the hour of the day. It is usually set parallel to the earth's axis.
gnomonic: Showing all great circles as straight lines, and thus preserving the shortest distances between any two locations.
gnomonics: The art or science of dialing, or of constructing dials to show the hour of the day by the shadow of a gnomon.
gnosis: The deeper wisdom; knowledge of spiritual truth, such as was claimed by the Gnostics.
gnostic: Of or pertaining to Gnosticism or its adherents; as, the gnostic heresy.
gnosticism: The system of philosophy taught by the Gnostics.
gnotobiology: The study of animals in a microbe-free environment.
gnotobiotics: The science involved with maintaining a microbiologically controlled environment.
gnu: One of two species of large South African antelopes of the genus Catoblephas, having a mane and bushy tail, and curved horns in both sexes.
goa: A species of antelope (Pro capra picticauda), inhabiting Thibet.
goad: A pointed instrument used to urge on a beast; hence, any necessity that urges or stimulates. The daily goad urging him to the daily toil. Macaulay.
goaded: compelled forcibly by an outside agency
goaf: That part of a mine from which the mineral has been partially or wholly removed; the waste left in old workings; called also gob. To work the goaf or gob, to remove the pillars of mineral matter previously left to support the roof, and replace them with props. Ure.
goal: the state of affairs that a plan is intended to achieve and that (when achieved) terminates behavior intended to achieve it
goalie: the defensive position on an ice hockey or soccer or lacrosse team who stands in front of the goal and tries to prevent opposing players from scoring
goalkeeper: the soccer or hockey player assigned to protect the goal
goalpost: one of a pair of posts (usually joined by a crossbar) that are set up as a goal at each end of a playing field
goals: Extremely admirable; worthy of being set as a goal and emulated.
goaltender: the defensive position on an ice hockey or soccer or lacrosse team who stands in front of the goal and tries to prevent opposing players from scoring
goat: A hollow-horned ruminant of the genus Capra, of several species and varieties, esp. the domestic goat (C. hircus), which is raised for its milk, flesh, and skin.
goatee: A part of a man's beard on the chin or lower lip which is allowed to grow, and trimmed so as to resemble the beard of a goat.
goatfish: A fish of the genus Upeneus, inhabiting the Gulf of Mexico. Itis allied to the surmullet.
goatish: Characteristic of a goat; goatlike. Give your chaste body up to the embraces Of goatish lust. Mass inger. Goatishly, adv. Goatishness, n.
goatskin: The skin of a goat, or leather made from it. a.
gobang: A Japanese game, played on a checkerboard, in which the object of the game is to be the first in placing five pieces, or men, in arow in any direction.
gobbet: A mouthful; a lump; a small piece. Spenser.had broken the stocks to small gobbets. Wyclif.
gobble: A noise made in the throat. Ducks and geese. set up a discordant gobble. Mrs. Gore.
gobbledygook: incomprehensible or pompous jargon of specialists
gobbler: A turkey cock; a bubbling Jock.
gobelin: Pertaining to tapestry produced in the so-called Gobelin works, which have been maintained by the French Government since.
gobiiform: Any goby (fish) of the order Gobiiformes
gobioid: Like, or pertaining to, the goby, or the genus Gobi us. n.
goblet: A kind of cup or drinking vessel having a foot or standard, but without a handle. We love not loaded boards and goblets crowned. Den ham.
goblin: An evil or mischievous spirit; a playful or malicious elf; af rightful phantom; a gnome. To whom the goblin, full of wrath, replied. Milton.
gobo: A screen (often in disc form) placed between a light and an illuminated actor or object in order to diffuse the glare.
goby: One of several species of small marine fishes of the genus Gobius and allied genera.
godchild: One for whom a person becomes sponsor at baptism, and whom he promises to see educated as a Christian; a godson or goddaughter. See godfather.
goddamnedest: superlative form of goddamned: most goddamned
goddaughter: A female for whom one becomes sponsor at baptism.
godetia: Any of several flowering plants of the taxonomic section of Clarkia, Clarkia sect. Godetia.
godfather: A man who becomes sponsor for a child at baptism, and makes himself a surety for its Christian training and instruction. There shall be for every Male-child to be baptized, when they can behad, two Godfathers and one Godmother; and for every Female, one godfather and two Godmothers; and Parents shall be admitted as sponsors, if it is desired. Book of Common Prayer (Prot. Episc. Ch.,U. S. ).
godfrey: A male given name from the Germanic languages.
godhead: terms referring to the Judeo-Christian God
godhood: Divine nature or essence; deity; godhead.
godkin: A little god; a minor or inferior deity; godling.
godless: Having, or acknowledging, no God; without reverence for God; impious; wicked. Godlessly, adv. Godlessness, n.
godlike: Resembling or befitting a god or God; divine; hence, preeminently good; as, godlike virtue. Godlikeness, n.
godliness: Careful observance of, or conformity to, the laws of God; the state or quality of being godly; piety. Godliness is profitable unto all things. Tim. iv.
godly: Pious; reverencing God, and his character and laws; obedient to the commands of God from love for, and reverence of, his character; conformed to God's law; devout; righteous; as, a godly life. For godly sorrow work eth repentance. Cor. vii.
godmother: A woman who becomes sponsor for a child in baptism. See godfather
godparent: a person who sponsors someone (the godchild) at baptism
godroon: An ornament produced by notching or carving a rounded molding.
godsend: Something sent by God; an unexpected acquisiton or piece of good fortune.
godship: The rank or character of a god; deity; divinity; a god or goddess. O'er hills and dales their godships came. Prior.
godson: A male for whom one has stood sponsor in baptism. See godfather.
godwin: A surname originating as a patronymic based on a medieval given name.
goer: One who, or that which, goes; a runner or walker; as:(a) A foot. Chapman.(b) A horse, considered in reference to his gait; as, a good goer; asafe goer. This antechamber has been filled with comers and goers. Macaulay.
goes: third-person singular simple present indicative of go
goethe: German poet and novelist and dramatist who lived in Weimar (-)
goethite: a red or yellow or brown mineral; an oxide of iron that is a common constituent of rust
goetic: Pertaining to black magic or necromancy.
gofer: an employee whose duties include running errands
goffer: To plait, flute, or crimp. See Gauffer. Clarke.
goffered: simple past and past participle of goffer
goffers: third-person singular simple present indicative of goffer
gog: Haste; ardent desire to go. Beau. & Fl.
goggle: To roll the eyes; to stare. And wink and goggle like an owl. Hudibras.
goggler: A carangoid oceanic fish (Trachurops crum enophthalmus), having very large and prominent eyes; called also goggle-eye, big-eyed scad, and cichar ra.
goggles: tight-fitting spectacles worn to protect the eyes
goggly: Resembling goggles, used mostly in relation to eyes.
gogmagog: A legendary giant in Welsh and later English folklore, said to have been a giant inhabitant of Albion who was thrown off a cliff during a wrestling match with Corineus, a companion of Brutus of Troy.
going: Course of life; behavior; doings; ways. His eyes are upon the ways of man, and he seeth all his goings. Job xxxiv.Going barrel. (Horology) (a) A barrel containing the mainspring, and having teeth on its periphery to drive the train. (b) A device for maintaining a force to drive the train while the timepiece is being wound up. Going forth. (Script.) (a) Outlet; way of exit. Every going forth of the sanctuary. " Ezek. xliv. (b) A limit; a border. The going forth thereof shall be from the south to Kadesh-barn ea. " Num.xxxiv. Going out, or Goings out. (Script.) (a) The utmost extremity or limit. The border shall go down to Jordan, and the goings out of it shall be at the salt sea. " Num. xxxiv. (b) Departure or journeying. And Moses wrote their goings out according to their journeys. " Num. xxxiii. Goings on, behavior; actions; conduct; usually in a bad sense.
goiter: abnormally enlarged thyroid gland; can result from underproduction or overproduction of hormone or from a deficiency of iodine in the diet
goitrogen: any substance (such as thiouracil) that induces the formation of a goiter
goitrogenic: Of, pertaining to, or being a goitrogen
goitrous: Pertaining to the goiter; affected with the goiter; of the nature of goiter or bronchocele. Let me not be understood as insinuating that the inhabitants in general are either goitrous or idiots. W. Coxe.
golconda: a source of great wealth (especially a mine)
gold: A metallic element, constituting the most precious metal used as a common commercial medium of exchange. It has a characteristic yellow color, is one of the heaviest substances known (specific gravity.), is soft, and very malleable and ductile. It is quite unalterable by heat, moisture, and most corrosive agents, and therefore well suited for its use in coin and jewelry. Symbol Au (Aurum). Atomic weight.
goldbrick: a soldier who performs his duties without proper care or effort
goldcrest: The European golden-crested kinglet (Regulus cristatus, or R.regulus); called also golden-crested wren, and golden wren. The name is also sometimes applied to the American golden-crested kinglet. See Kinglet.
goldenrod: any of numerous chiefly summer-blooming and fall-blooming North American plants especially of the genus Solidago
goldenseal: perennial herb of northeastern United States having a thick knotted yellow rootstock and large rounded leaves
goldeye: A North American freshwater fish of the mooneye family, Hiodon alosoides, usually eaten smoked.
goldfields: small slender woolly annual with very narrow opposite leaves and branches bearing solitary golden-yellow flower heads; southwestern Oregon to Baja California and Arizona; often cultivated
goldfinch: small European finch having a crimson face and yellow-and-black wings
goldfinny: One of two or more species of European labroid fishes (Crenilabrus me lops, and Ctenolabrus rupestris); called also goldsinny, and goldney.
goldfish: small golden or orange-red freshwater fishes of Eurasia used as pond or aquarium fishes
goldhead: A kind of fishing lure, usually bright yellow.
goldsmith: an artisan who makes jewelry and other objects out of gold
goldylocks: A plant of several species of the genus Chrysocoma; so called from the tufts of yellow flowers which terminate the stems; also, the Ranunculus auricomus, a kind of buttercup.
