isoenzyme: Any of a group of enzymes that catalyze the same reaction but have structures that are (minorly or substantially) different and have physical, biochemical, and immunological properties that are (minorly or substantially) different.
isoetaceae: quill worts; coextensive with the genus Isoetes
isoetales: aquatic or marsh-growing fern allies; known to have existed since the Cenozoic; sometimes included in Lycopodiales
isoetes: type and genus of the Isoetaceae and sole extant genus of the order Isoetales
isoflavone: Any of a class of polyphenolic phytoestrogens found in soybeans and similar plants that may have beneficial health properties.
isogamy: (biology) reproduction by the union or fusion of gametes of the same size and structure
isogloss: A line on a map indicating the geographical boundaries of a linguistic feature.
isognathous: Having similar molar teeth in both jaws
isogonal: Describing lines connecting points on the Earth's surface whose magnetic declination is identical.
isogone: an imaginary line connecting points on the Earth's surface where the magnetic declination is the same
isogonic: Pertaining to, or noting, equal angles. Isogonic lines (Magnetism), lines traced on the surface of the globe, or upon ac hart, connecting places at which the deviation of the magnetic needle from the meridian or true north is the same.
isogram: a line drawn on a map connecting points having the same numerical value of some variable
isograph: A line indicating the geographical boundaries within which a particular feature of a written script is used.
isogriv: A line on a map or chart which joins points of equal grivation, that is, equal angle between grid north and magnetic north.
isohaline: An isoline on a map that links places (in water) that have the same salinity.
isohel: an isogram connecting points receiving equal amounts of sunshine
isohyet: A line of equal rainfall on a map or chart, such as a weather map.
isokeraunic: Indicating areas that have the same amount of thunderstorm activity.
isolable: Capable of being isolated, or of being obtained in a pure state; as, gold is isolable.
isolated: Placed or standing alone; detached; separated from others. Isolated point of a curve. (Geom.) See Acnode.
isolating: relating to or being a language in which each word typically expresses a distinct idea and part of speech and syntactical relations are determined almost exclusively by word order and particles
isolation: The act of isolating, or the state of being isolated; insulation; separation; loneliness. Mil man.
isolationism: a policy of nonparticipation in international economic and political relations
isolator: One who, or that which, isolates.
isolde: A female given name from the Celtic languages or the Germanic languages.
isolead: On a ballistic graph, a curve used to calculate the trajectory needed to hit a moving target.
isoline: Any of several types of line on a map, chart or graph that link points having the same value of a parameter.
isologous: Having similar proportions, similar relations, or similar differences of composition; said specifically of groups or series which differ by a constant difference; as, ethane, ethylene, an acetylene, or their analogous compounds, form an isologous series.
isolysin: A hemolysin, in the serum of an animal, that will dissolve the red blood cells of another animal of the same species.
isomer: A body or compound which is isomeric with another body or compound; a member of an isomeric series.
isomerase: an enzyme that catalyzes its substrate to an isomeric form
isomeric: Having the same percentage composition; said of two or more different substances which contain the same ingredients in the same proportions by weight, often used with with. Specif.: (a) Polymeric; i. e., having the same elements united in the same proportion by weight, but with different molecular weights; as, acetylene and benzine are isomeric (polymeric) with each other in this sense. See polymeric. (b) Metameric; i. e., having the same elements united in the same proportions by weight, and with the same molecular weight, but which a different structure or arrangement of the ultimate parts; as, ethyl alcohol and methyl ether are isomeric (metameric) with each other in this sense. See Metameric.
isomerisation: the conversion of a compound into an isomer of itself
isomerization: the conversion of a compound into an isomer of itself
isomerize: cause to change into an isomer
isometry: the growth rates in different parts of a growing organism are the same
isomorph: A substance which is similar to another in crystalline form and composition.
isomorphism: A similarity of crystalline form between substances of similar composition, as between the sulphates of barium (Ba SO) and strontium (Sr SO). It is sometimes extended to include similarity of form between substances of unlike composition, which is more properly called homoeomorphism.
isonandra: A genus of sapotaceous trees of India. Isonandra Gutta is the principal source of gutta-percha.
isonephelic: Having, or indicating, an equal amount of cloudiness for a given period; as, isonephelic regions; an isonephelic line.
isonicotine: A crystalline, nitrogenous base, CHN, isomeric with nicotine.
isonomic: The same, or equal, in law or right; one in kind or origin; analogous; similar. Dana.
isonomy: Equal law or right; equal distribution of rights and privileges; similarity.
isoperimetrical: Having equal perimeters of circumferences; as, isoperimetrical figures or bodies.
isophane: Being of a certain ratio of protamine to insulin.
isophote: A contour of equal luminance in an image.
isophthalic: Of or pertaining to isophthalic acid and its derivatives.
isophyllous: Having leaves of equal size and shape throughout.
isopiestic: Having equal pressure. Isopiestic lines, lines showing, in adiagram, the relations of temperature and volume, when the elastic force is constant; called also isobars.
isopleth: a line drawn on a map connecting points having the same numerical value of some variable
isopleura: A subclass of Gastropoda, in which the body is symmetrical, the right and left sides being equal.
isopod: Having the legs similar in structure; belonging to the Isopoda. n.
isopoda: An order of sessile-eyed Crustacea, usually having seven pairs of legs, which are all similar in structure.
isopodan: Of or relating to the isopods.
isopolity: Equal rights of citizenship in different communities; mutual political rights.
isoporic: Concerning isopors, lines of equal annual change in a geomagnetic property.
isoprene: An oily, volatile hydrocarbon, obtained by the distillation of caoutchouc or guttaipercha. CH unsaturated, and used to make synthetic rubber by polymerization. In organic chemistry, viewed conceptually as the building block of the terpene series of hydrocarbons
isoprenoid: Any compound formally derived from one or more isoprene units.
isopropanol: alcohol used as antifreeze or a solvent
isoptera: order of social insects that live in colonies, including: termites; often placed in subclass Exopterygota
isopycnic: Having equal density, as different regions of a medium; passing through points at which the density is equal; as, an isopycnic line or surface.
isoquinoline: An isomer of quinoline, many of whose derivatives occur as alkaloids and are synthesized for use as dyes, pharmaceuticals etc.
isorcin: A crystalline hydrocarbon derivative, metameric with orcin, but produced artificially; called also cresorcin.
isorhythm: A technique that arranges a fixed pattern of pitches with a repeating rhythmic pattern, used in some medieval motets and in more recent works.
isorropic: Of equal value. Isorropic line (in a diagram) (Geom.), the locus of all the points for which a specified function has a constant value. Newcomb.
isosceles: Having two legs or sides that are equal; said of a triangle.
isoseismal: A line on a map joining points of equal seismic intensity produced by an earthquake.
isosorbide: drug (trade name Isordil) used to treat angina pectoris and congestive heart failure
isospin: A quantum number or symmetry related to the strong interaction.
isospondyli: An extensive order of fishes, including the salmons, herrings, and many allied forms.
isospore: One of the spores produced by an isosporous organism.
isosporous: Producing but one kind of spore, as the ferns.
isostasy: The state or quality of being isostatic. Specif. (Geol.),
isostatic: Subjected to equal pressure from every side; being in hydrostatic equilibrium, as a body submerged in a liquid at rest; pertaining to, or characterized by, isostasy.
isostemonous: Having exactly as many stamens as petals.
isostructural: Having the same, or a corresponding, structure.
isosulphocyanic: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid, HNCS, isomeric with sulphocyanic acid.
isotach: An isoline linking places on a map which have equal wind speed.
isotheral: Having the nature of an isothere; indicating the distribution of temperature by means of an isothere; as, an isotheral chart or line.
isothere: A line connecting points on the earth's surface having the same mean summer temperature.
isotherm: A line connecting or marking points on the earth's surface having the same temperature. This may be the temperature for a given time of observation, or the mean temperature for a year or other period. Also, a similar line based on the distribution of temperature in the ocean.
isothermal: of a process or change taking place at constant temperature
isothermic: of or relating to an isotherm
isothermobath: A line drawn through points of equal temperature in a vertical section of the ocean.
isothiocyanate: a family of compounds derived from horseradish and radishes and onions and mustards
isotome: A line drawn through a joint to indicate which segments are homologous
isotone: Any of a number of nuclides of different elements that have the same number of neutrons.
isotonic: Having or indicating, equal tones, or tension. Isotonic system (Mus.), a system consisting of intervals, in which each concord is alike tempered, and in which there are twelve equal semitones.
isotope: one of two or more atoms with the same atomic number but with different numbers of neutrons
isotopic: of or relating to or having the relation of an isotope
isotopy: A form of homotopy that is always an embedding.
isotrimorphism: Isomorphism between the three forms, severally, of two trimorphous substances.
isotrimorphous: Having the quality of isotrimorphism; isotrimorphic.
isotron: A device that uses an electrical field to separate the isotopes of uranium.
isotropic: Having the same properties in all directions; specifically, equally elastic in all directions.
isotropy: Uniformity of physical properties in all directions in a body; absence of all kinds of polarity; specifically, equal elasticity inall directions.
isotype: A marker corresponding to an antigen found in all members of a subclass of a specific class of immunoglobulins
isotypic: Of, related to, or being an isotype.
isovaleric: Of or pertaining to isovaleric acid or its derivatives
israel: Jewish republic in southwestern Asia at eastern end of Mediterranean; formerly part of Palestine
israeli: of or relating to or characteristic of Israel or its people
israelite: A descendant of Israel, or Jacob; a Hebrew; a Jew.
israelitic: Of or relating to the Israelites; Jewish; Hebrew.
issei: A member of the first generation of Japanese immigrants to North America, South America, or Australia.
issuable: Leading to, producing, or relating to, an issue; capable of being made an issue at law. Bur rill.
issuably: In an issuable manner; by way of issue; as, to plead issuably.
issuance: The act of issuing, or giving out; as, the issuance of an order; the issuance of rations, and the like.
issue: An artificial ulcer, usually made in the fleshy part of the armor leg, to produce the secretion and discharge of pus for the relief of some affected part.
issued: simple past and past participle of issue.
issueless: Having no issue or progeny; childless. The heavens. have left me issueless.
issuer: One who issues, emits, or publishes.
issuing: the act of providing an item for general use or for official purposes (usually in quantity)
ist: A practitioner or supporter of an ism.
istanbul: the largest city and former capital of Turkey; rebuilt on the site of ancient Byzantium by Constantine I in the fourth century; renamed Constantinople by Constantine who made it the capital of the Byzantine Empire; now the seat of the Eastern Orthodox Church
isthmectomy: The surgical removal of the band of tissue (or isthmus) connecting the two lobes of the thyroid gland.
isthmian: Of or pertaining to an isthmus, especially to the Isthmus of corinth, in Greece. Isthmian games (Gr. Antiq.), one of the four great national festivals of Greece, celebrated on the Isthmus of corinth in the spring of every alternate year. They consisted of all kinds of athletic sports, wrestling, boxing, racing on foot and in chariots, and also contests in music and poetry. The prize was agar land of pine leaves.
isthmus: A neck or narrow slip of land by which two continents are connected, or by which a peninsula is united to the mainland; as, the isthmus of Panama; the Isthmus of Suez, etc. Isthmus of the fauces.(Anat.) See Fauces.
isuretine: A synthetic nitrogenous base, isomeric with urea.
it: The neuter pronoun of the third person, corresponding to the masculine pronoun he and the feminine she, and having the same plural (they, their of theirs, them).
ita: A kind of palm tree (Mauritia flexuosa), growing near the Orinoco.
itacism: Pronunciation of e in the English word be. This was the pronunciation advocated by Reu Etacism. In all such questions between a the confusing element of itacism comes in. Al ford.
itaconic: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid, CHO, which is obtained as a white crystalline substance by decomposing aconitic an dother organic acids.
ital: Pure, natural food suiting a Rastafari lifestyle.
italian: Of or pertaining to Italy, or to its people or language. Italian cloth a light material of cotton and worsted; called also farmer's satin. Italian iron, a heater for fluting frills. Italian juice, Calabrian liquorice.
italianate: To render Italian, or conformable to Italian customs; to italianize. Ascham.
italianism: A word, phrase, or idiom, peculiar to the Italians; an Italicism.
italianize: To play the Italian; to speak Italian. Cot grave.
italic: An Italic letter, character, or type (see Italic, a.,.); often in the plural; as, the Italics are the author's. Italic letters are used to distinguish words for emphasis, importance, antithesis, etc. Also, collectively, Italic letters.
italicism: A phrase or idiom peculiar to the Italian language; to Italianism.
italicize: To print in Italic characters; to underline written letters or words with a single line; as, to Italicize a word; Italicizes too much.
italicizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of italicize
italicizing: present participle and gerund of italicize
italy: a republic in southern Europe on the Italian Peninsula; was the core of the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire between the th century BC and the th century AD
itch: An eruption of small, isolated, acuminated vesicles, produced by the entrance of a parasitic mite (the Sarcoptes scabei), and attended with itching. It is transmissible by contact.
itching: an irritating cutaneous sensation that produces a desire to scratch
itchy: Infected with the itch, or with an itching sensation. Cowper.
itemization: the act of making a list of items
itemize: To state in items, or by particulars; as, to itemize the cost of a railroad.
itemized: simple past and past participle of itemize
itemizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of itemize
iter: A passage; esp., the passage between the third and fourth ventricles in the brain; the aqueduct of Sylvius.
iterable: Capable of being iterated or repeated.
iterant: Repeating; iterating; as, an iterant echo. Bacon.
iterate: Uttered or done again; repeated. Bp. Gardiner.
iterated: simple past and past participle of iterate
iterating: present participle and gerund of iterate
iteration: Recital or performance a second time; repetition. Bacon. What needs this iteration, woman.
iterator: One who or that which iterates.
iteroparous: reproducing more than once in a lifetime
ithaca: a college town in central New York on Lake Cayuga
itinerancy: A passing from place to place. Dr. H. More.
itinerant: Passing or traveling about a country; going or preaching on acircuit; wandering; not settled; as, an itinerant preacher; an itinerant peddler. The king's own courts were then itinerant, being kept in the king'spa lace, and removing with his household in those royal progresses which he continually made. Black stone.
itinerarium: An Ancient Roman road map in the form of a listing of cities, villages and other stops, with the intervening distances.
itinerary: Itinerant; traveling; passing from place to place; done on ajourney. It was rather an itinerary circuit of justice than a progress. Bacon.
itinerate: To wander without a settled habitation; to travel from place oron a circuit, particularly for the purpose of preaching, lecturing, etc.
itinerating: present participle and gerund of itinerate
its: Possessive form of the pronoun it. See It.
itself: The neuter reciprocal pronoun of It; as, the thing is good in itself; it stands by itself. Borrowing of foreigners, in itself, makes not the kingdom rich or poor. Locke.
iulus: A genus of chilognathous myriapods. The body is long and round, consisting of numerous smooth, equal segments, each of which bears two pairs of short legs. It includes the galley worms. See chilognatha.
ivan: A male given name from Russian of English speakers.
ives: United States composer noted for his innovative use of polytonality (-)
ivorytype: A picture produced by superposing a very light print, rendered translucent by varnish, and tinted upon the back, upon a stronger print, so as to give the effect of a photograph in natural colors; called also hellenotype. Knight.
iwo: a bloody and prolonged operation on the island of Iwo Jima in which American marines landed and defeated Japanese defenders (February and March )
ix: denoting a quantity consisting of one more than eight and one less than ten
ixia: A South African bulbous plant of the Iris family, remarkable for the brilliancy of its flowers.
ixion: King of Lapiths, who was punished by Zeus for trying to seduce Hera by being bound to a winged fiery wheel that was always spinning.
ixodes: A genus of parasitic Acarina, which includes various species of ticks. See Tick, the insect.
ixodid: ticks having a hard shield on the back and mouth parts that project from the head
ixora: Any of the flowering plants in the genus Ixora.
ixtle: A variety of Agave angustifolia var. angustifolia (syn. Agave rigida), furnishing a strong coarse fiber.
izanami: sister and consort of Izanami; mother of the islands and gods of Japan
izar: a voluminous cotton outer garment (usually white) traditionally worn by Muslim women of northern Africa and the Middle East; covers the entire body
izard: A variety of the chamois found in the Pyrenees.
izedi: One of an Oriental religious sect which worships Satan or the devil. The Izedis or Yez dis, the so-called Devil worshipers, still remain anumerous though oppressed people in Mesopotamia and adjacent countries. Tylor.
izle: A spark, an ember, a hot ash or cinder.
j: . J is the tenth letter of the English alphabet. It is a later variant form of the Roman letter I, used to express a consonantal sound, that is, originally, the sound of English y in yet. The forms J and I have, until a recent time, been classed together, and they have been used interchangeably.
ja: Abbreviation of Japan: a country in East Asia (NATO country code).
jab: To thrust; to stab; to punch. See Job, v. t.
jabber: To talk rapidly, indistinctly, or unintelligibly; to utter gibberish or nonsense; to chatter. Swift.
jabbers: third-person singular simple present indicative of jabber
jabbing: a sharp hand gesture resembling a blow
jabiru: One of several large wading birds of the genera Mycteria and xenorhynchus, allied to the storks in form and habits.
jaborandi: The native name of a South American rutaceous shrub (Pilocarpuspennatifolius). The leaves are used in medicine as an diaphoretic and sialogogue.
jabot: a ruffle on the front of a woman's blouse or a man's shirt
jacal: In Mexico and the southwestern United States, a kind of plastered house or hut, usually made by planting poles or timber in the ground, filling in between them with screen work or wickerwork, and daubing one or both sides with mud or adobe mortar; also, this method of construction.
jacamar: Any one of numerous species of tropical American birds of the genus Galbula and allied genera. They are allied to the kingfishers, but climb on tree trunks like nuthatches, and feed upon insects. Their colors are often brilliant.
jacamin: A bird, the grey-winged trumpeter (Psophia crepitans).
jacana: Any of several wading birds belonging to the genus Jacana and several allied genera, all of which have spurs on the wings. They are able to run about over floating water weeds by means of their very long, spreading toes. Called also surgeon bird.
jacaranda: The native Brazilian name for certain leguminous trees, which produce the beautiful woods called king wood, tiger wood, and violet wood.
jacent: Lying at length; as, the jacent posture. Sir H. Wot ton.
jack: A large tree, the Artocarpus integrifolia, common in the East indies, closely allied to the breadfruit, from which it differs in having its leaves entire. The fruit is of great size, weighing from thirty to forty pounds, and through its soft fibrous matter are scattered the seeds, which are roasted and eaten. The wood is of ayellow color, fine grain, and rather heavy, and is much used in cabinetwork. It is also used for dyeing a brilliant yellow.
jackal: Any one of several species of carnivorous animals inhabiting africa and Asia, related to the dog and wolf. They are cowardly, nocturnal, and gregarious. They feed largely on carrion, and are noted for their piercing and dismal howling.
jackanapes: A young man living as an apprentice on a sheep station, or otherwise engaged in acquainting himself with colonial life.
jackaroo: To be a jackaroo; to pass one's time as a jackaroo.
jackboot: a heavy leather military boot which rises above the knee, primarily worn during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries
jacketed: Wearing, or furnished with, a jacket.
jacketing: The material of a jacket; as, nonconducting jacketing.
jackfish: A jack (in any of the senses referring to types of fish).
jackfruit: East Indian tree cultivated for its immense edible fruit and seeds
jackhammer: a hammer driven by compressed air
jackknife: A large, strong clasp knife for the pocket; a pocket knife.
jackman: See Jack-with-a-lantern, under d Jack. Jackpot jackpot
jackrabbit: go forward or start with a fast, sudden movement
jacks: a game in which jackstones are thrown and picked up in various groups between bounces of a small rubber ball
jackscrew: A jack in which a screw is used for lifting, or exerting pressure. See Illust. of d Jack, n.,.
jacksmelt: a relatively large silversides of the Pacific coast of North America (known to reach inches in length)
jacksnipe: a small short-billed Old World snipe
jackson: English film actress who later became a member of British Parliament (born in )
jacksonian: of or pertaining to Andrew Jackson or his presidency or his concepts of popular democracy
jackstay: A rail of wood or iron stretching along a yard of a vessel, to which the sails are fastened.
jackstones: a game in which jackstones are thrown and picked up in various groups between bounces of a small rubber ball
jackstraw: a thin strip of wood used in playing the game of jackstraws
jackstraws: a game in which players try to pick each jackstraw (or spillikin) off of a pile without moving any of the others
jackwood: Wood of the jack (Artocarpus integrifolia), used in cabinetwork.
jacky: A landsman's nickname for a seaman, resented by the latter.
jackyard: A spar at the top of a mast that supports a topsail
jacob: A Hebrew patriarch (son of Isaac, and ancestor of the Jews),who in a vision saw a ladder reaching up to heaven (Gen. xxviii. ); also called Israel. And Jacob said. with my staff I passed over this Jordan, and now I am become two bands. Gen. xxxii.,.Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel. Gen. xxxii.Jacob's ladder. (a) (Bot.) A perennial herb of the genus Polemonium (P. coeruleum), having corymbs of drooping flowers, usually blue. Gray. (b) (Naut.) A rope ladder, with wooden steps, for going aloft. R. H. Dana, Jr. (c) (Naut.) A succession of short cracks in adefective spar. Jacob's membrane. See Retina. Jacob's staff. (a) A name given to many forms of staff or weapon, especially in the Middle Ages; a pilgrim's staff. Spenser. (b)(Surveying) See under Staff.
jacobean: of or relating to James I or his reign or times
jacobin: A Dominican friar; so named because, before the French revolution, that order had a convent in the Rue St. Jacques, Paris.
jacobinic: of or relating to the Jacobins of the French Revolution
jacobinical: of or relating to the Jacobins of the French Revolution
jacobinism: The principles of the Jacobins; violent and factious opposition to legitimate government. Under this new stimulus, Burn's previous Jacobitism passed towards the opposite, but not very distant, extreme of Jacobinism. J. C.Sha irp.
jacobite: A partisan or adherent of James the Second, after his abdication, or of his descendants, an opposer of the revolution in in favor of William and Mary. Macaulay.
jacobitic: Of or pertaining to the Jacobites.
jacobitish: Of or pertaining to the Jacobites.
jacobitism: The principles of the Jacobites. Mason.
jacobson: An English surname transferred from the given name.
jacobus: An English gold coin, of the value of twenty-five shillings sterling, struck in the reign of James I.
jaconet: A thin cotton fabric, between and muslin, used for dresses, neck cloths, etc.
jacquard: Pertaining to, or invented by, Jacquard, a French mechanician, who died in. Jacquard apparatus or arrangement, a device applied to looms for weaving figured goods, consisting of mechanism controlled by a chain of variously perforated cards, which cause the warp threads to be lifted in the proper succession for producing the required figure. Jacquard card, one of the perforated cards of a Jacquard apparatus. Jackquard loom, a loom with Jacquard apparatus.
jacqueline: A female given name from French.
jacqueminot: A half-hardy, deep crimson rose of the remontant class; so named after General Jacqueminot, of France.
jacques: A male given name from French [in turn from Latin, in turn from Ancient Greek, in turn from Biblical Hebrew], feminine equivalent Jacqueline, equivalent to English Jacob.
jactitate: to move or stir about violently
jaculate: To throw or cast, as a dart; to throw out; to emit.
jaculation: The act of tossing, throwing, or hurling, as spears. Hurled to and fro with jaculation dire. Milton.
jaculatory: Darting or throwing out suddenly; also, suddenly thrown out; uttered in short sentences; ejaculatory; as, jaculatory prayers. Smart.
jade: A stone, commonly of a pale to dark green color but sometimes whitish. It is very hard and compact, capable of fine polish, and is used for ornamental purposes and for implements, esp. in Eastern countries and among many early peoples.
jadish: Vicious; ill-tempered; resembling a jade; applied to a horse.
jag: A cleft or division. Jag bolt, a bolt with a nicked or barbed shank which resists retraction, as when leaded into stone.
jaggary: unrefined brown sugar made from palm sap
jagged: Having jags; having rough, sharp notches, protuberances, or teeth; cleft; laciniate; divided; as, jagged rocks. " Jagged vine leaves' shade. " Trench. Jaggedly, adv. Jaggedness, n.
jagger: One who carries about a small load; a peddler. See d Jag. Sir W. Scott.
jaggery: Raw palm sugar, made in the East Indies by evaporating the fresh juice of several kinds of palm trees, but specifically that of the palmyra (Borassus flabelliform is).
jagghery: unrefined brown sugar made from palm sap
jaggy: Having jags; set with teeth; notched; uneven; as, jaggy teeth. Addison.
jaghir: A village or district the government and revenues of which are assigned to some person, usually in consideration of some service tobe rendered, esp. the maintenance of troops. Whitworth.
jagir: An assignment of the produce and income of a particular district or village to a person or persons, as an annuity
jaguar: A large and powerful feline animal (Felis onca), ranging from texas and Mexico to Patagonia. It is usually brownish yellow, with large, dark, somewhat angular rings, each generally inclosing one ortwo dark spots. It is chiefly arboreal in its habits. Called also the american tiger.
jaguarondi: A South American wild cat (Felis jaguarondi), having a long, slim body and very short legs. Its color is grayish brown, varied with a blackish hue. It is arboreal in its habits and feeds mostly on birds.
jail: A kind of prison; a building for the confinement of person sheld in lawful custody, especially for minor offenses or with reference to some future judicial proceeding. This jail I count the house of liberty. Milton. Jail bird, a prisoner; one who has been confined in prison. Jail delivery, the release of prisoners from jail, either legally or by violence. Jail delivery commission. See under Gaol. Jail fever (Med.), typhus fever, or a disease resembling it, generated in jails and other places crowded with people; called also hospital fever, and ship fever. Jail liberties, or Jail limits, a space or district around a jail within which an imprisoned debtor was, on certain conditions, allowed to go at large. Abbott. Jail lock, a peculiar form of padlock; called also scandinavian lock.
jailbird: a criminal who has been jailed repeatedly
jailer: The keeper of a jail or prison.
jailhouse: a place used to detain persons who are in the lawful custody of the government
jain: relating to or characteristic of Jainism
jainism: The heterodox Hindoo religion, of which the most striking features are the exaltation of saints or holy mortals, called jins, above the ordinary Hindoo gods, and the denial of the divine origin and infallibility of the Vedas. It is intermediate between Brahmanism and Buddhism, having some things in common with each.
jakarta: capital and largest city of Indonesia; located on the island of Java; founded by the Dutch in th century
jako: An African parrot (Psittacus erithacus), very commonly kept as a cage bird; called also gray parrot.
jakob: A male given name, equivalent to English Jacob.
jalap: The tubers of the Mexican plant Ipomoea purga (or Exogonium purga), a climber much like the morning-glory. The abstract, extract, and powder, prepared from the tubers, are well known purgative medicines. Other species of Ipomoea yield several inferior kinds of jalap, as the I. Orizabensis, and I. tube rosa. False jalap, the root of Mirabilis Jalapa, four-o'clock, or marvel of Peru.
jalapa: The convolvulaceous plant Ipomoea purga, whose roots are used to make the drug jalap.
jalapeno: hot green or red pepper of southwestern United States and Mexico
jalapin: A glucoside found in the stems of the jalap plant and scammony. It is a strong purgative.
jalopy: a car that is old and unreliable
jalousie: A Venetian or slatted inside window blind.
jalousied: Furnished with jalousies; as, jalousied porches.
jam: A kind of frock for children.
