keraunophone: A radio-based device that generates sound corresponding to distant lightning flashes.
kercher: A kerchief. He became. white as a kercher. Sir T. North.
kerchief: Dressed; hooded; covered; wearing a kerchief. Milton.
keres: The goddesses of death, specifically cruel and violent deaths, including death in battle, by accident, murder or ravaging disease. They numbered in the thousands and were the daughters of Nyx and Erebus, and the sisters of Thanatos and Hypnos. Their Roman counterparts were the Letum or the Tenebrae.
kerf: A notch, channel, or slit made in any material by cutting or sawing.
kerman: A city in Iran, the seat of Kerman County's Central District and the capital of Kerman Province.
kermanshah: A city in Iran, the seat of Kermanshah County's Central District and the capital of Kermanshah Province.
kermes: The dried bodies of the females of a scale insect (Coccusilicis), allied to the cochineal insect, and found on several species of oak near the Mediterranean. They are round, about the size of apea, contain coloring matter analogous to carmine, and are used in dyeing. They were anciently thought to be of a vegetable nature, and were used in medicine.
kerned: Having part of the face projecting beyond the body or shank; said of type. In Roman, f and j are the only kerned letters. Mac Kellar.
kernel: To harden or ripen into kernels; to produce kernels.
kernish: Clownish; booorish. A petty kernish prince. " Milton.
kernite: a light soft mineral consisting of hydrated sodium borate in crystalline form; an important source of boron
kernos: A pottery ring or stone tray to which are attached several small vessels for holding ritual offerings in Ancient Greece.
kerogen: any organic matter present in a sedimentary rock that is insoluble in organic solvents; the precursor of oil and natural gas
kerosene: An oil used for illuminating purposes, formerly obtained from the distillation of mineral wax, bituminous shale, etc., and hence called also coal oil. It is now produced in immense quantities, chiefly by the distillation and purification of petroleum. It consists chiefly of several hydrocarbons of the methane series.
kerosine: a flammable hydrocarbon oil used as fuel in lamps and heaters
kerria: A deciduous shrub with five-petalled yellow flowers, of species Kerria japonica, sole species in the genus Kerria.
kerry: A county of Ireland. County seat: Tralee.
kersey: A kind of coarse, woolen cloth, usually ribbed, woven from wool of long staple.
kerugma: preaching the gospel of Christ in the manner of the early church
kerygma: preaching the gospel of Christ in the manner of the early church
kerystic: Concerning preaching, particularly preaching of the gospels.
kestrel: A small, slender European hawk (Falco alaudarius), allied to the sparrow hawk. Its color is reddish fawn, streaked and spotted with white and black. Also called windhover and stannel. The name is also applied to other allied species.
keta: A small salmon (Oncorhynchus keta) of inferior value, which in the autumn runs up all the larger rivers between San Francisco and Kamchatka.
ketamine: a general anesthetic and tranquilizer (not a barbiturate) that is administered intravenously or intramuscularly
ketch: An almost obsolete form of vessel, with a mainmast and amizzenmast, usually from one hundred to two hundred and fifty tons burden. Bomb ketch. See under Bomb.
keto: The carbonyl group of a ketone.
ketogenesis: The metabolic breakdown of fatty acids to produce ketone bodies.
ketohexose: a monosaccharide having six carbon atoms and a ketone group
ketone: One of a large class of organic substances resembling the aldehydes, obtained by the distillation of certain salts of organic acids and consisting of carbonyl (CO) united with two hydrocarbon radicals. In general the ketones are colorless volatile liquid shaving a pungent ethereal odor.
ketonemia: an abnormal increase of ketone bodies in the blood as in diabetes mellitus
ketonic: Pertaining to, or derived from, a ketone; as, a ketonic acid.
ketose: any monosaccharide sugar that contains a ketone group or its hemiacetal
ketosis: an abnormal increase of ketone bodies in the blood, as in diabetes mellitus
ketosuccinic: Of or pertaining to ketosuccinic acid or its derivatives
kettle: A metallic vessel, with a wide mouth, often without a cover, used for heating and boiling water or other li guids. Kettle pins, ninepins; skittles. Shel ton. Kettle stitch (Bookbinding), the stitch made in sewing at the head and tail of a book. Knight.
kettledrum: A drum made of thin copper in the form of a hemispherical kettle, with parchment stretched over the mouth of it.
ketu: The descending lunar node. In Hindu mythology, Ketu is generally referred to as a shadow planet, believed to have a tremendous impact on human lives and also the whole creation.
ketubah: A traditional Jewish marriage contract that outlines the rights and responsibilities of the groom in relation to the bride.
keuper: The upper division of the European Triassic. See Chart of geology.
kevel: A strong cleat to which large ropes are belayed.
kevil: A lot (object used to determine a question by chance or independently of human choice).
kevin: A male given name from Irish.
kex: A weed; a kecksy. Bp. Gaud en. Though the rough kex break The starred mosaic. Tennyson.
key: An indehiscent, one-seeded fruit furnished with a wing, as the fruit of the ash and maple; a samara; called also key fruit.
keyboard: The whole arrangement, or one range, of the keys of an organ, typewriter, etc.
keyed: Furnished with keys; as, a keyed instrument; also, set to akey, as a tune. Keyed bugle. See Kent bugle.
keyhole: the hole where a key is inserted
keying: present participle and gerund of key
keynes: English economist who advocated the use of government monetary and fiscal policy to maintain full employment without inflation (-)
keynote: The tonic or first tone of the scale in which a piece or passage is written; the fundamental tone of the chord, to which all the modulations of the piece are referred; called also key tone.
keynoter: A speaker who delivers the keynote speech of a conference.
keypad: a keyboard that is a data input device for computers
keypress: The depression of an input key; a keystroke.
keypunch: A mechanical device whose keys are pressed, individually or in combination, to punch holes in punched cards or paper tape that correspond to particular characters.
keyset: An input device whose few keys can be pressed in many combinations, often simultaneously, to enter different commands or characters.
keystone: The central or topmost stone of an arch. This in some styles is made different in size from the other voussoirs, or projects, or is decorated with carving. See Illust. of Arch. Keystone State, the state of Pennsylvania; so called from its having been the central state of the Union at the formation of the Constitution.
keystroke: the stroke of a key; one depression of a key on a keyboard
keyword: a significant word used in indexing or cataloging
khabarovsk: a city on the Amur River on the border of China and the capital of Khabarovsk
khaddar: a coarse homespun cotton cloth made in India
khadi: a coarse homespun cotton cloth made in India
khaki: Of a dull brownish yellow, or drab color; applied to cloth, originally to a stout brownish cotton cloth, used in making uniforms in the Anglo-Indian army. In the United States service the summer uniform of cotton is officially designated khaki; the winter uniform of wool, olive drab.
khalat: A type of native gown worn in parts of Central Asia, historically awarded as a robe of honor.
khalif: the civil and religious leader of a Muslim state considered to be a representative of Allah on earth
khan: A king; a prince; a chief; a governor; so called among the tartars, Turks, and Persians, and in countries now or formerly governed by them.
khanate: Dominion or jurisdiction of a khan.
khansamah: A house-steward or native servant, being in charge of the kitchen and the food supplies.
kharouba: A fraction of a rural tribe in the Beylik of Constantine.
khartoum: the capital of Sudan located at the confluence of the Blue Nile and White Nile
khat: the leaves of the shrub Catha edulis which are chewed like tobacco or used to make tea
khaya: A lofty West African tree (Khaya Senegalensis), related to the mahogany, which it resembles in the quality of the wood. The bark is used as a febrifuge.
khazar: A member of a semi-nomadic Turkic tribe that occupied a large part of southwestern Russia and Ukraine (Khazaria).
khediva: The female consort of a khedive.
khedivate: The region ruled by a khedive.
khedive: A governor or viceroy; a title granted in by the sultan of Turkey to the ruler of Egypt.
khedivial: Of or relating to a khedive.
khi: the nd letter of the Greek alphabet
khirkah: The robe or mantle worn by Muslim dervishes.
khitan: A member of the Mongolic people who ruled Manchuria, then northern China as the Liao, then Central Asia as the Qara Khitais, from the th to th century C.E.
khitmatgar: A male servant, with responsibility for waiting at table.
khmer: the Mon-Khmer language spoken in Cambodia
khoisan: a family of languages spoken in southern Africa
khoja: A member of a Gujarati-speaking Shiite sect who take the Aga Khan as their religious head.
khond: A Dravidian of a group of tribes of Orissa, India, a section of whom were formerly noted for their cruel human sacrifices to the earth goddess, murder of female infants, and marriage by capture.
khutbah: An address or public prayer read from the steps of the pulpit in Mohammedan mosques, offering glory to God, praising Mohammed and his descendants, and the ruling princes.
ki: goddess personifying earth; counterpart of Akkadian Aruru
kibbeh: A form of dumpling, from the Levant, made of spiced lamb and bulgur wheat.
kibble: To bruise; to grind coarsely; as, kibbled oats. Halliwell.
kibbled: simple past and past participle of kibble
kibbutz: a collective farm or settlement owned by its members in modern Israel; children are reared collectively
kibe: A chap or crack in the flesh occasioned by cold; an ulcerated chilblain. He galls his kibe.
kibed: Chapped; cracked with cold; affected with chilblains; as kibed heels. Beau. & Fl.
kibitzer: (Yiddish) a meddler who offers unwanted advice to others
kick: To strike, thrust, or hit violently with the foot; as, a horse kicks a groom; a man kicks a dog. He kicked the shins of his judges. Macaulay. To kick the beam, to fit up and strike the beam; said of the lighter arm of a loaded balance; hence, to be found wanting inweight. Milton. To kick the bucket, to lose one's life; to die.
kickable: Capable or deserving of being kicked. A kickable boy. " G.Eliot.
kickback: a commercial bribe paid by a seller to a purchasing agent in order to induce the agent to enter into the transaction
kicked: simple past and past participle of kick
kicker: One who, or that which, kicks.
kicking: the act of delivering a blow with the foot
kickoff: (football) a kick from the center of the field to start a football game or to resume it after a score
kickshaws: Something fantastical; any trifling, trumpery thing; a toy. Art thou good at these kicks hawses!.
kickstand: a swiveling metal rod attached to a bicycle or motorcycle or other two-wheeled vehicle; the rod lies horizontally when not in use but can be kicked into a vertical position as a support to hold the vehicle upright when it is not being ridden
kid: A young goat. The. leopard shall lie down with the kid. Is. xi.
kidder: One who kids, or teases light-heartedly.
kidding: present participle and gerund of kid
kiddo: a form of address used for children
kiddush: A blessing recited over wine or grape juice in commemoration of the sanctity of the Shabbat or other Jewish holy day.
kidnap: To take (any one) by force or fear, and against one's will, with intent to carry to another place. Abbott. You may reason or expostulate with the parents, but never attempt to kidnap their children, and to make proselytes of them. Wh ately.
kidnaper: someone who unlawfully seizes and detains a victim, usually for ransom
kidnaping: present participle and gerund of kidnap
kidnapped: simple past and past participle of kidnap
kidnapper: someone who unlawfully seizes and detains a victim (usually for ransom)
kidnapping: (law) the unlawful act of capturing and carrying away a person against their will and holding them in false imprisonment
kidnaps: third-person singular simple present indicative of kidnap
kidney: A glandular organ which excretes urea and other waste products from the animal body; a urinary gland.
kidneywort: A kind of saxifrage (Saxifrage stellar is).
kidskin: soft smooth leather from the hide of a young goat
kielbasa: A spicy, smoked sausage of a particular kind from Eastern Europe.
kier: A large tub or vat in which goods are subjected to the action of hot lye or bleaching liquor; also called keeve.
kierkegaard: Danish philosopher who is generally considered. along with Nietzsche, to be a founder of existentialism (-)
kieselguhr: Siliceous earth; specifically, porous infusorial earth, used as an absorbent of nitroglycerin in the manufacture of dynamite.
kif: A kind of cannabis smoked in Morocco and Algeria, for narcotic or intoxicating effect.
kilim: A flat tapestry-woven carpet or rug from Turkey or Kurdistan.
killable: fit to kill, especially for food
killdeer: American plover of inland waters and fields having a distinctive cry
killed: simple past and past participle of kill
killer: A voracious, toothed whale of the genus Orca, of which several species are known.
killifish: Any one of several small American cyprinodont fishes of the genus Fundulus and allied genera. They live equally well in fresh and brackish water, or even in the sea. They are usually striped or barred with black. Called also minnow, and brook fish. See Minnow.
killing: Literally, that kills; having power to kill; fatal; in acolloquial sense, conquering; captivating; irresistible. Killingly, adv. Those eyes are made so killing. Pope. Nothing could be more killingly spoken. Milton.
killjoy: someone who spoils the pleasure of others
killock: A small anchor; also, a kind of anchor formed by a stone inclosed by pieces of wood fastened together.
kiln: a furnace for firing or burning or drying such things as porcelain or bricks
kilned: simple past and past participle of kiln
kilobar: A unit of pressure equal to, bars (Symbol: kb)
kilobit: a unit of information equal to bits
kilobyte: a unit of information equal to bytes
kilocalorie: a unit of heat equal to the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of water by one degree at one atmosphere pressure
kilogram: one thousand grams; the basic unit of mass adopted under the Syst eme International d'Unites
kiloliter: a metric unit of volume or capacity equal to liters
kilometer: a metric unit of length equal to meters (or. miles)
kilometre: a metric unit of length equal to one thousand meters
kiloparsec: A unit of distance equal to one thousand parsecs.
kilopound: A non-SI unit of force equal to pounds-force.
kilorad: A unit of absorbed radiation dose, equivalent to rads.
kilovolt: A unit of electromotive force equal to one thousand volts.
kiltie: A shoe having a fringed tongue or fringed extra piece that lies over the tongue.
kilting: A perpendicular arrangement of flat, single plaits, each plait being folded so as to cover half the breadth of the preceding one.
kimchi: A Korean dish made of vegetables, such as cabbage or radishes, that are salted, seasoned, and stored in sealed containers to undergo lactic acid fermentation.
kimnel: A tub. See Kemelin. She knew not what a kimnel was Beau. & Fl.
kimono: a loose robe; imitated from robes originally worn by Japanese
kin: A diminutive suffix; as, manikin; lambkin.
kina: the basic unit of money in Papua New Guinea
kinaesthesia: the perception of body position and and movement based on input received by sensory organs in the muscles and joints
kinase: an enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of a proenzyme to an active enzyme
kincob: India silk brocaded with flowers in silver or gold. a.
kindergarten: A school for young children, conducted on the theory that education should be begun by gratifying and cultivating the normal aptitude for exercise, play, observation, imitation, and construction; a name given by Fried rich Froebel, a German educator, who introduced this method of training, in rooms opening on a garden.
kindergartner: One who teaches in a kindergarten.
kindest: superlative form of kind: most kind
kindhearted: having or proceeding from an innately kind disposition
kindle: To bring forth young. The poor beast had but lately kindled. Holland.
kindled: simple past and past participle of kindle
kindler: One who, or that which, kindles, stirs up, or sets on fire. Kindlers of riot. " Gay.
kindless: Destitute of kindness; unnatural. Kindless villain.
kindliness: friendliness evidence by a kindly and helpful disposition
kindling: Materials, easily lighted, for starting a fire.
kindness: the quality of being warmhearted and considerate and humane and sympathetic
kindred: Related; congenial; of the like nature or properties; as, kindred souls; kindred skies; kindred propositions. True to the kindred points of heaven and home. Wordsworth.
kine: Cows. A herd of fifty or sixty kine. " Milton.
kinematic: Of or relating to motion or to kinematics.
kinematics: The science which treats of motions considered in themselves, or apart from their causes; the comparison and relation of motions.
kinescope: a cathode-ray tube in a television receiver; translates the received signal into a picture on a luminescent screen
kinesiatrics: A mode of treating disease by appropriate muscular movements; also termed kinesitherapy, kinesipathy, lingism, and the movement cure.
kinesics: The study of non-verbal communication by means of gestures and/or other body movements.
kinesimeter: An instrument for the quantitative measurement of movements.
kinesiology: the branch of physiology that studies the mechanics and anatomy in relation to human movement
kinesis: a movement that is a response to a stimulus but is not oriented with respect to the source of stimulation
kinesodic: Conveying motion; as; kinesodic substance; applied esp. to the spinal cord, because it is capable of conveying doth voluntary and reflex motor impulses, without itself being affected by motor impulses applied to it directly.
kinesthesia: the perception of body position and movement and muscular tensions etc
kinesthesis: the ability to feel movements of the limbs and body
kinetic: Moving or causing motion; motory; active, as opposed to latent. Kinetic energy. See Energy, n.
kinetin: A tricyclic heterocyclic plant hormone that promotes cell division
kinetogenesis: An instrument for producing curves by the combination of circular movements; called also kinescope.
kinetophone: A machine combining a kinetoscope and a phonograph synchronized so as to reproduce a scene and its accompanying sounds.
kinetoplast: A disk-shaped mass of circular DNA inside a large mitochondrion, found specifically in protozoa of the class Kinetoplastea (kinetoplastids).
kinetoscope: A machine, for the production of animated pictures, in which afilm carrying successive instantaneous views of a moving scene travels uniformly through the field of a magnifying glass. The observer sees each picture, momentarily, through a slit in ar evolving disk, and these glimpses, blended by persistence of vision, give the impression of continuous motion.
kinfolk: people treated as if they were family
king: A Chinese musical instrument, consisting of resonant stones or metal plates, arranged according to their tones in a frame of wood, and struck with a hammer.
kingbolt: A vertical iron bolt, by which the forward axle and wheels of avehicle or the trucks of a railroad car are connected with the other parts.
kingdom: a domain in which something is dominant
kingfish: the lean flesh of any of several fish caught off the Atlantic coast of the United States
kinghead: Ambrosia trifida, a form of ragweed.
kinghood: The state of being a king; the attributes of a king; kingship. Gower.
kingliest: superlative form of kingly: most kingly
kinglike: having the rank of or resembling or befitting a king
kingly: Belonging to, suitable to, or becoming, a king; characteristic of, resembling, a king; directed or administered by a king; monarchical; royal; sovereign; regal; august; noble; grand. Kingly magnificence. " Sir P. Sidney. A kingly government. " Swift. The kingly couch. The kingliest kings are crowned with thorn. G. Mass ey. Leave kingly backs to cope with kingly cares. Cowper.
kingpin: the most important person in a group or undertaking
kingship: The state, office, or dignity of a king; royalty. Land or.
kingside: The side of the chessboard nearest to the king (at the opening position).
kingston: a town on the Hudson River in New York
kingwood: handsome violet-streaked wood of the kingwood tree; used especially in cabinetwork
kinin: any of a class of plant hormones that promote cell division and delay the senescence of leaves
kininogen: Any of a set of proteins defined by their primary role as precursors for kinin
kink: To wind into a kink; to knot or twist spontaneously upon itself, as a rope or thread.
kinky: (used of sexual behavior) showing or appealing to bizarre or deviant tastes
kinnikinic: Prepared leaves or bark of certain plants; used by the indians of the Northwest for smoking, either mixed with tobacco or as a substitute for it. Also, a plant so used, as the osier cornel (Cornus stolonijra), and the bearberry (Arctostaphylus Uva-ursi).
kinnikinnick: A mixture of bark, dried leaves, and often berries and/or tobacco, which is smoked.
kino: The dark red dried juice of certain plants, used variously in tanning, in dyeing, and as an astringent in medicine.
kinoo: A hybrid mandarin citrus fruit from two citrus cultivars, 'King' Citrus nobilis and 'Willow Leaf' of Citrus reticulata (syn. Citrus deliciosa), grown extensively in the Punjab region.
kinoplasm: an active protoplasm used to make filaments and mobile structures.
kinsfolk: Relatives; kindred; kin; persons of the same family or closely or closely related families. They sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintance. Luke ii.
kinshasa: the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo on the Congo river opposite Brazzaville
kinsman: A man of the same race or family; one related by blood.
kinsperson: a person having kinship with another or others
kiosk: A Turkish open summer house or pavilion, supported by pillars.
kiowa: a member of a Tanoan people living in the southwestern United States
kip: The hide of a young or small beef creature, or leather made from it; kipskin. Kip leather. See Kipskin.
kipling: English author of novels and poetry who was born in India (-)
kippen: A piece of small firewood or kindling; dibber
kippernut: A name given to earthnuts of several kinds.
kipskin: Leather prepared from the skin of young or small cattle, intermediate in grade between calfskin and cowhide.
kirchhoff: German physicist who with Bunsen pioneered spectrum analysis and formulated two laws governing electric networks (-)
kirghiz: a member of a people of Turkic speech and Mongolian race inhabiting vast regions of central Siberia
kiribati: an island republic in the west central Pacific just to the south of the equator
kirigami: An art similar to origami, with cutting permitted.
kirk: A church or the church, in the various senses of the word; esp., the Church of Scotland as distinguished from other reformed churches, or from the Roman Catholic Church. Jamie son.
kirkman: A clergyman or officer in a kirk.
kirmess: In Europe, particularly in Belgium and Holland, and outdoor festival and fair; in the United States, generally an indoor entertainment and fair combined.
kirsch: from fermented juice of black morello cherries
kirschwasser: An alcoholic liquor, obtained by distilling the fermented juice of the small black cherry.
kirsome: Christian; christened. I am a true kirsome woman. Beau. & Fl.
kirtle: A garment varying in form and use at different times, and worn doth by men and women. Wearing her Norman car, and her kirtle of blue. Longfellow.
kirundi: The standardized dialect of the Bantu language Rwanda-Rundi which is spoken in Burundi.
kish: A workman's name for the graphite which forms incidentally in iron smelting.
kishke: (Judaism) roasted fowl intestines with a seasoned filling of matzo meal and suet
kiskatom: A stream in New York; a village located near this stream.
kislev: the third month of the civil year; the ninth month of the ecclesiastical year in the Jewish calendar (in November and December)
kiss: the act of caressing with the lips (or an instance thereof)
kissed: simple past and past participle of kiss
kissingcrust: The portion of the upper crust of a loaf which has touched another loaf in baking. Lamb. A massy fragment from the rich kissingcrust that hangs like a fretted cornice from the upper half of the loaf. W. Howitt.
kist: A chest; hence, a coffin. Jamie son. Halliwell.
kistvaen: A Celtic monument, commonly known as a dolmen.
kiswah: The cloth that covers the Kaaba in Mecca, Saudi Arabia.
kitcat: A game played by striking with a stick small piece of wood, called a cat, shaped like two coned united at their bases; tipcat. Cotton. Kitcat roll (Agric.), a roller somewhat in the form of two cones set base to base.
kitchen: To furnish food to; to entertain with the fare of the kitchen.
kitchenette: A room combining a very small kitchen and a pantry, with the kitchen conveniences compactly arranged, sometimes so that they fold up out of sight and allow the kitchen to be made a part of the adjoining room by opening folding doors.
kitchenware: hardware utensils for use in a kitchen
kiter: One who writes a check while there are insufficient funds in the account, hoping it will be able to clear by the time it is cashed.
kith: Acquaintance; kindred. And my near kith for sore me shend. W. Browne. The sage of his kith and the hamlet. Longfellow. Kith and kin, kindred more or less remote.
kitling: A young kitten; a whelp. B. Jonson.
kitsch: excessively garish or sentimental art; usually considered in bad taste
kittenhood: The state or time of being a kitten.
kittenish: Resembling a kitten; playful; as, a kittenish disposition. Richardson.
kittiwake: A northern gull (Rissa tridactyla), inhabiting the coasts of europe and America. It is white, with black tips to the wings, and has but three toes.
kittle: To bring forth young, as a cat; to kitten; to litter.
kitty: informal terms referring to a domestic cat
kiva: A large chamber built under, or in, the houses of a Pueblo village, used as an assembly room in religious rites or as a men'sdormitory. It is commonly lighted and entered from an opening in the roof.
kivu: a lake in the mountains of central Africa between Congo and Rwanda
kiwi: fuzzy brown egg-shaped fruit with slightly tart green flesh
kiwikiwi: The kiwi, a flightless bird of the order Apterygiformes native to New Zealand.
klamath: a river flowing southwest from Oregon through northern California to the Pacific Ocean
klansman: a member of the Ku Klux Klan
klatch: An informal social gathering, especially one held over coffee for the purpose of conversation.
klavern: a local unit of the Ku Klux Klan
klaxon: a kind of loud horn formerly used on motor vehicles
kleagle: A recruiter for the Ku Klux Klan.
klein: German mathematician who created the Klein bottle (-)
kleist: German dramatist whose works concern people torn between reason and emotion (-)
klepht: An anti-Ottoman insurgent living in the mountains when Greece was a part of the Ottoman Empire.
kleptomania: A propensity to steal, claimed to be irresistible. This does not constitute legal irresponsibility. Wharton.
klipdas: A small mammal (Hyrax capensis), found in South Africa, that closely resembles the daman.
klipspringer: A small, graceful South African antelope (Nanotragusoreotragus), which, like the chamois, springs from one crag to another with great agility; called also kainsi.
klismos: A light Ancient Greek chair with curved legs.
klondike: a region in northwestern Canada where gold was discovered in but exhausted by
kloof: A glen; a ravine closed at its upper end.
klootch: klootchman: woman, wife (especially if Native American).
kludge: a badly assembled collection of parts hastily assembled to serve some particular purpose (often used to refer to computing systems or software that has been badly put together)
klystron: an electron tube used to generate or amplify electromagnetic radiation in the microwave region by velocity modulation
km: a metric unit of length equal to meters
knab: To seize with the teeth; to gnaw. Knab bing crusts. L'Estrange.
knabble: To bite or nibble. Horses will knabble at walls, and rats gnaw iron. Sir T. Browne.
knack: To crack; to make a sharp, abrupt noise to chink. Bp. Hall.
knacker: someone who buys old buildings or ships and breaks them up to recover the materials in them
knacky: Having a knack; cunning; crafty; trickish. Halliwell.
knag: A knot in wood; a protuberance. Wright.
knaggy: Knotty; rough; figuratively, rough in temper. Fuller. Knagginess, n.
knaidel: A type of dumpling made of matzo eaten by Ashkenazi Jews during Passover.
knap: A protuberance; a swelling; a knob; a button; hence, rising ground; a summit. See Knob, and Knop. The highest part and knap of the same island. Holland.
knaps: third-person singular simple present indicative of knap
knapsack: A case of canvas or leather, for carrying on the back asoldier's necessaries, or the clothing, etc., of a traveler. And each one fills his knapsack or his scrip With some rare thing that on the field is found. Dray ton.
knapweed: The black centaury (Centaurea nigra); so called from the knoblike heads of flowers. Called also bullweed.
knarred: Knotty; gnarled. The knarred and crooked cedar knees. Longfellow.
knave: A boy; especially, a boy servant. Wyclif. Chaucer. O murderous slumber, Lay'st thou thy leaden mace upon my boy That plays thee music Gentle knave, good night.
knavish: Like or characteristic of a knave; given to knavery; trickish; fraudulent; dishonest; villainous; as, a knavish fellow, or a knavish trick. Knavish politicians. " Macaulay.
knawel: A low, spreading weed (Scleranthus annuus), common in sandy soil.
kneaded: simple past and past participle of knead
kneading: present participle and gerund of knead
kneads: third-person singular simple present indicative of knead
knee: A piece of timber or metal formed with an angle somewhat in the shape of the human knee when bent.
kneecapping: The act of injuring the knees of (a person), usually by shooting at the knees; often a punishment carried out by criminals or terrorists.
kneed: Geniculated; forming an obtuse angle at the joints, like the knee when a little bent; as, kneed grass.
kneehole: A space for the knees (and lower legs), especially under a desk.
kneel: To bend the knee; to fall or rest on the knees; sometime swith down. And he kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. Acts vii.As soon as you are dressed, kneel and say the Lord's Prayer. Jer. Taylor.
kneeled: simple past and past participle of kneel
kneeler: A name given to certain catechumens and penitents who were permitted to join only in parts of church worship.
kneepan: A roundish, flattened, sesamoid bone in the tendon in front of the knee joint; the patella; the kneecap.
knell: The stoke of a bell tolled at a funeral or at the death of apers on; a death signal; a passing bell; hence, figuratively, awarn ing of, or a sound indicating, the passing away of anything. The dead man's knell Is there scarce asked for who. The curfew tolls the knell of parting day. Gray.
knez: A duke or prince in medieval Slavic countries.
knickerbockers: The name for a style of short breeches; smallclothes.
knickknack: A trifle or toy; a bawble; a gewgaw.
knickpoint: Part of a river or channel where there is a sharp change in slope, such as a waterfall or lake.
knifed: Having been cut or stabbed with a knife.
knifelike: cutting or able to cut as if with a knife
knifing: An instance of stabbing with a knife.
knight: To dub or create (one) a knight; done in England by the sovereign only, who taps the kneeling candidate with a sword, saying: Rise, Sir -.A soldier, by the honor-giving hand Of Ck nighted in the field.
knighted: simple past and past participle of knight
knighthead: A bollard timber. See under Bollard.
knighthood: aristocrats holding the rank of knight
knightless: Unbecoming a knight. Knightless guile. " Spenser.
knightly: Of or pertaining to a knight; becoming a knight; chivalrous; as, a knightly combat; a knightly spirit. For knightly jousts and fierce encounters fit. Spenser.full knightly without scorn. Tennyson.
kniphofia: a plant of the genus Kniphofia having long grasslike leaves and tall scapes of red or yellow drooping flowers
knish: (Yiddish) a baked or fried turnover filled with potato or meat or cheese; often eaten as a snack
knittable: That can be knitted or used as material for knitting.
knitted: made by intertwining threads in a series of connected loops rather than by weaving
knitter: One who, or that which, knits, joins, or unites; a knitting machine.
knob: See Knop. Knob latch, a latch which can be operated by turn inga knob, without using a key.
knobbed: Containing knobs; full of knobs; ending in a nob. See Illust of antenna. The horns of a roe deer of Greenland are pointed at the top, and knobbed or tuberous at the bottom. Grew.
knobbiness: The state or condition of being knobby.
knobbing: Rough dressing by knocking off knobs or projections.
knobbler: The hart in its second year; a young deer. Halliwell. He has hallooed the hounds upon a velvet-headed knobbler. Sir W.Scott.
knock: deliver a sharp blow or push:He knocked the glass clear across the room
knockabout: a sloop with a simplified rig and no bowsprit
knockdown: A felling by a knock, as of a combatant, or of an animal.
knocked: simple past and past participle of knock
knocker: One who, or that which, knocks; specifically, an instrument, or kind of hammer, fastened to a door, to be used in seeking for admittance. Shut, shut the door, good John! fatigued, knocker; say I'm sick, I'mdead. Pope.
knocking: A beating; a rap; a series of raps. The. repeated knockings of the head upon the ground by the chinese worshiper. H. Spencer.
knockings: Large lumps picked out of the sieve, in dressing ore.
knockout: a blow that renders the opponent unconscious
knockwurst: a short thick highly seasoned sausage
knoll: A little round hill; a mound; a small elevation of earth; the top or crown of a hill. On knoll or hillock rears his crest, Lonely and huge, the giant oak. Sir W. Scott.
knoller: One who tolls a bell. Sherwood.
knop: Any boldly projecting sculptured ornament; esp., the ornamental termination of a pinnacle, and then synonymous with finial; called also knob, and knosp. Knop sedge (Bot.), the bur reed (Sparganium); so called from its globular clusters of seed vessels. Prior.
knossos: an ancient town on Crete where Bronze Age culture flourished from about BC to BC
knotgrass: low-growing weedy grass with spikelets along the leaf stems
knothole: a hole in a board where a knot came out
knotless: Free from knots; without knots. Silver firs with knotless trunks. " Congreve.
knotted: Characterized by small, detached points, chiefly composed of mica, less decomposable than the mass of the rock, and forming knots in relief on the weathered surface; as, knotted rocks. Percival.
knotting: present participle and gerund of knot
knotwork: A design or pattern of interlocking or overlapping geometric shapes resembling a knot
knout: A kind of whip for flogging criminals, formerly much used in russia. The last is a tapering bundle of leather thongs twisted with wire and hardened, so that it mangles the flesh.
knowable: That may be known; capable of being discovered, understood, or ascertained. Thus mind and matter, as known or knowable, are only two different series of phenomena or qualities. Sir W. Hamilton.
knowing: Knowledge; hence, experience. " In my knowing. This sore night Hath trifled former knowings.
knowingly: With knowledge; in a knowing manner; intelligently; consciously; deliberately; as, he would not knowingly offend. Strype.
knowleche: See Knowl, edge. We consider and knowleche that we have offended. Chaucer.
knowledge: To acknowledge. Sinners which knowledge their sins. Tyndale.
knowledgeableness: wisdom as evidenced by the possession of knowledge
knows: third-person singular simple present indicative of know
knox: Scottish theologian who founded Presbyterianism in Scotland and wrote a history of the Reformation in Scotland (-)
knuckle: The joining pars of a hinge through which the pin or rivet passes; a knuckle joint.
knucklebone: A bone that forms a knuckle in the human hand, in an animal's paw or any bone that forms a similar bump.
knuckleheaded: Stupid or inept, like a knucklehead.
knuckler: a baseball pitch thrown with little speed or spin
knuckles: a small metal weapon that fits over one's knuckles
knurl: A contorted knot in wood; a crossgrained protuberance; anodule; a boss or projection.
knurling: present participle and gerund of knurl
knurly: Full of knots; hard; tough; hence, capable of enduring or resisting much.
ko: a blow that renders the opponent unconscious
koa: A large tree of species Acacia koa (family Fabaceae) which is endemic to and common on the islands of Hawaii; or the wood of this tree.
koala: A tailless marsupial (Phascolarctos ci nereus), found in australia. The female carries her young on the back of her neck. Called also Australian bear, native bear, and native sloth.
koan: a paradoxical anecdote or a riddle that has no solution; used in Zen Buddhism to show the inadequacy of logical reasoning
kob: an orange-brown antelope of southeast Africa
koban: An oval gold coin in the Edo period of feudal Japan.
kobold: A kind of domestic spirit in German mythology, corresponding to the Scottish brownie and the English Robin Good fellow.
koch: German bacteriologist who isolated the anthrax bacillus and the tubercle bacillus and the cholera bacillus (-)
koel: Any one of several species of cuckoos of the genus Eudynamys, found in India, the East Indies, and Australia. They deposit their eggs in the nests of other birds.
koelreuteria: Any plant of the genus Koelreuteria.
kofta: Any of various spicy meatball or meatloaf dishes of the Middle East, Caucasus, South Asia, and the Balkans.
koftgari: Ornamental work produced by inlaying steel with gold, avariety of damascening much used in the arts of India.
kohl: A mixture of soot and other ingredients, used by Egyptian an dother Eastern women to darken the edges of the eyelids.
kohlrabi: plant cultivated for its enlarged fleshy turnip-shaped edible stem
koi: Ornamental domesticated varieties of the Amur carp (Cyprinus rubrofuscus), of Japan and eastern Asia with red-gold or white coloring.
koine: a Greek dialect that flourished under the Roman Empire
kojang: A former unit of weight in Indonesia, varyingly equal to, or pikols.
kokanee: A lacustrine (that is, land-locked, found in lakes and not in the ocean) sockeye.
kokka: of or pertaining to the branch of Shinto recognized as the state religion of Japan
koklass: Any pheasant of the genus Pucras ia. The birds of this genus inhabit India and China, and are distinguished by having a long central and two lateral crests on the head. Called also pucras.
kokum: A plant (Garcinia indica) in the mangosteen family with culinary, pharmaceutical, and industrial uses.
kola: tree bearing large brown nuts containing e.g. caffeine; source of cola extract
koli: A member of an agriculturist caste of India, mostly found in Gujarat.
kolinsky: Among furriers, any of several Asiatic minks; esp., Putoriussibiricus, the yellowish brown pelt of which is valued, esp. for the tail, used for making artists' brushes. Trade names for the fur are red sable and Tatar sable.
kolkhoz: a collective farm owned by the communist state
kolo: A national folk dance common in regions pertaining to South Slavic people, performed in a circle.
komatik: A rawhide-lashed sledge with wooden crossbars and runners, first invented and used by the Inuit of Northern Canada, but since used also by non-Inuit people.
komi: a member of a Finnish people living in the northwestern Urals in Russia
komondor: Hungarian breed of large powerful shaggy-coated white dog; used also as guard dog
komsomol: Young Communist League, the former youth wing of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.
komtok: An African freshwater fish (Protopterus annect ens), belonging to the Dipnoi. It can breathe air by means of its lungs, and when waters dry up, it encases itself in a nest of hard mud, where it remains till the rainy season. It is used as food.
kondo: To tidy up using the methods advocated by Marie Kondo, especially keeping only those things that tokimeku (spark joy).
kongo: the Bantu language spoken by the Kongo living in the tropical forests of Zaire and Congo and Angola
koniology: the study of dust, pollen and other airborne particles.
konkani: A member of the indigenous peoples of the Konkan coast of India.
konrad: A male given name, variant of Conrad
kontakion: A form of hymn or poem recited as a dialogue between a chanter and the choir.
koodoo: A large South African antelope (Strepsiceros kudu). The male shave graceful spiral horns, sometimes four feet long. The general color is reddish or grayish brown, with eight or nine white bands on each side, and a pale dorsal stripe. The old males become dark bluish gray, due to the skin showing through the hair. The females are hornless. Called also nell ut.
kook: someone regarded as eccentric or crazy and standing out from a group
kookaburra: Australian kingfisher having a loud cackling cry
koolokamba: A west African anthropoid ape (Troglodytes koolokamba, or T.Aubryi), allied to the chimpanzee and gorilla, and, in some respects, intermediate between them.
kopeck: A small Russian coin. One hundred kopecks make a rouble, worth about sixty cents.
koppie: a small hill rising up from the African veld
kor: an ancient Hebrew unit of capacity equal to ten baths or ten ephahs
kora: A type of harp or lute played in West Africa.
korah: A biblical character who rebelled against Moses.
koran: The Scriptures of the Mohammed ans, containing the professed revelations to Mohammed; called also Alcoran.
kordofan: a mountainous province of central Sudan
kore: An Ancient Greek statue of a woman, portrayed standing, usually clothed, painted in bright colours and having an elaborate hairstyle.
korea: an Asian peninsula (off Manchuria) separating the Yellow Sea and the Sea of Japan; the Korean name is Dae-Han-Min-Gook or Han-Gook
korean: of or relating to or characteristic of Korea or its people or language
koreshanity: The set of religious and pseudoscientific beliefs put forth by Cyrus Teed (also known as Koresh), including reincarnation, immortality, alchemy, and the idea that the Earth and universe are contained within a concave sphere.
koromiko: A shrub, Hebe stricta, endemic to New Zealand.
korrigum: A West African antelope (Dama lis Senegalensis), allied to the sassaby. It is reddish gray, with a black face, and a black stripe on the outside of the legs above the knees.
koruna: the basic unit of money in Slovakia
korymbos: A jewel-studded globe containing the top hair of the ruler of the Sasanian dynasty of Iran, resting on his crown.
kos: (in India) a unit of length having different values in different localities
kosher: Ceremonially clean, according to Jewish law; applied to food, esp. to meat of animals slaughtered according to the requirements of jewish law. Opposed to tref. Hence, designating a shop, store, house, etc., where such food is sold or used.
koshered: simple past and past participle of kosher
koto: Japanese stringed instrument that resembles a zither; has a rectangular wooden sounding board and usually silk strings that are plucked with the fingers
kotow: The prostration made by mandarins and others to their superiors, either as homage or worship, by knocking the forehead on the ground. There are degrees in the rite, the highest being expressed by three knockings.kowtow S. W. Williams.
koulan: A wild horse (Equus, or Asinus, onager) inhabiting the plants of Central Asia; called also gour, khur, and onager.
koumiss: An intoxicating fermented or distilled liquor originally made by the Tartars from mare's or camel's milk. It can be obtained from any kind of milk, and is now largely made in Europe. Koumiss has from time immemorial served the Tartar instead of wine or spirits. J. H. Newman.
kouprey: A wild, forest-dwelling ox, Bos sauveli, from Cambodia and surrounding countries.
kouros: A sculpture of a naked youth in Ancient Greece, the male equivalent of a kore.
kousso: An Abyssinian rosaceous tree (Brayera anthelmintica), the flowers of which are used as a vermifuge.
kowtow: The same as Kotow. I have salaamed and kowtowed to him. H. James.
kowtowed: simple past and past participle of kowtow
kra: A long-tailed ape (Macacus cynomolgus) of India and Sumatra. Itis reddish olive, spotted with black, and has a black tail.
kraal: a village of huts for native Africans in southern Africa; usually surrounded by a stockade
kraft: strong wrapping paper made from pulp processed with a sulfur solution
krait: A very venomous snake of India (Bungarus coeruleus), allied to the cobra. Its upper parts are bluish or brownish black, often with narrow white streaks; the belly is whitish.
kraken: A fabulous Scandinavian sea monster, often represented as resembling an island, but sometimes as resembling an immense octopus. To believe all that has been said of the sea serpent or kraken, would be credulity; to reject the possibility of their existence, would be presumption. Goldsmith. Like a kraken huge and black. Longfellow.
krameria: A genus of spreading shrubs with many stems, from one species of which (K. triandra), found in Peru, rhatany root, used as amedicine, is obtained.
krameric: Pertaining to, or derived from, Krameria (rhatany); as, krameric acid, usually called ratanhia-tannic acid.
krang: The carcass of a whale after the blubber has been removed.
krantz: An encircling or overhanging wall of rock.
krater: An ancient Greek vessel for mixing water and wine.
kraurosis: atrophy and shriveling of the skin or mucous membrane
kraut: offensive term for a person of German descent
krebs: English biochemist (born in Germany) who discovered the Krebs cycle (-)
kremlin: The citadel of a town or city; especially, the citadel of moscow, a large inclosure which contains imperial palaces, cathedrals, churches, an arsenal, etc.
kremlinology: The study of the internal politics of the high members of the government of the USSR.
krems: A variety of white lead. See Krems lead, under Lead, n.
kreplach: Small dumplings of Eastern European origin, filled with meat or cheese and served usually in soup.
kreutzer: A small copper coin formerly used in South Germany; also, as mall Austrian copper coin.
kreuzer: A small coin of varying value formerly used in parts of Germany and Austria.
krigia: any small branched yellow-flowered North American herb of the genus Krigia
krill: shrimp-like planktonic crustaceans; major source of food for e.g. baleen whales
krishna: The most popular of the Hindoo divinities, usually held to bethe eighth incarnation of the god Vishnu.
krishnaism: worship of Krishna the th avatar of Vishnu
kritarchy: The rule of the judges over Israel. Samson, Jephthah, Gideon, and other heroes of the kritarchy. Southey.
krobylos: An ancient Athenian hairstyle in which the hair was rolled up into a kind of knot on the crown of the head, and fastened with golden clasps in the shape of grasshoppers.
kromesky: A kind of Russian croquette wrapped in bacon before deep-frying.
kromskop: A device used for taking colour photographs of specimens in pathology.
krona: the basic unit of money in Iceland
krone: A coin of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, of the value of about twenty-eight cents. See Crown, n.,.
kroon: the basic unit of money in Estonia
krouchka: An old Russian liquid measure, one tenth of a vedro.
kru: A West African ethnic group who originated in eastern Liberia and migrated and settled along the coast.
krubi: malodorous tropical plant having a spathe that resembles the corolla of a morning glory and attains a diameter of several feet
krubut: Rafflesia arnoldii, a plant with very large flowers.
krummholz: Dense low matted bushes at the tree-line.
krummhorn: a Renaissance woodwind with a double reed and a curving tube (crooked horn)
krupp: German arms manufacturer and son of Fried rich Krupp; his firm provided ordnance for German armies from the s through World War II (-)
krypsis: The doctrine that Christ, during His state of humiliation, continued to possess in a veiled way the divine attributes of omnipotence, omniscience, etc.
kshatriya: a member of the royal or warrior Hindu caste
kuchen: Any of several types of cake, typically eaten with coffee.
kudzu: fast-growing vine from eastern Asia having tuberous starchy roots and hairy trifoliate leaves and racemes of purple flowers followed by long hairy pods containing many seeds; grown for fodder and forage and root starch; widespread in the southern United States
kue: The name of the Latin-script letter Q/q. Alternative form of cue.
kuklux: The name adopted in the southern part of the United States by asecret political organization, active for several years after the close of the Civil War, and having for its aim the repression of the political power of the freedmen; called also Kuklux Klan.
kukri: a curved steel Nepalese knife with a razor-sharp edge used in combat by the Gurk has
kula: A tower, turret or steeple in Southeast Europe erected during the period of Ottoman domination on the area.
kulak: A prosperous peasant in the Russian Empire or the Soviet Union, who owned land and could hire workers.
kultur: German culture or civilization, especially seen as authoritarian or racist during the period of world wars (- and -)
kulturkampf: Lit., culture war; a name, originating with Virchow, given to a struggle between the the Roman Catholic Church and the German government, chiefly over the latter's efforts to control educational and ecclesiastical appointments in the interest of the political policy of centralization. The struggle began with the passage by the Prussian Diet in May, of the so-called May laws, or Falk laws, aiming at the regulation of the clergy. Opposition eventually compelled the government to change its policy, and from to laws virtually nullifying the May laws were enacted.
kummel: A Russian and German liqueur, consisting of a sweetened spirit flavored with caraway seeds.
kumquat: A small tree of the genus Citrus (C. Japonica) growing in China and Japan; also, its small acid, orange-colored fruit used for preserves.
kunzite: a pinkish lilac crystal form of the mineral spodumene that is used as a gemstone
kuomintang: the political party founded in by Sun Yat-sen; it governed China under Chia ng Kai-shek from until when the Communists took power and subsequently was the official ruling party of Taiwan
kura: a river in western Asia; rises in northeast Turkey and flows to the Caspian Sea
kurbash: A whip or strap about a yard in length.
kurd: A native or inhabitant of a mountainous region of Western Asia belonging to the Turkish and Persian monarchies.
kurdish: Of or pertaining to the Kurds.
kurdistan: an extensive geographical region in the Middle East to the south of the Caucasus
kurgan: A prehistoric burial mound once used by peoples in Siberia and Central Asia.
kuri: The kitchen of a Zen monastery.
kurilian: Of or pertaining to the Kuri le Islands, a chain of islands in the Pacific ocean, extending from the southern extremity of Kamschatka to Yesso. n.
kurrajong: widely distributed tree of eastern Australia yielding a tough durable fiber and soft light attractively grained wood; foliage is an important emergency food for cattle
kurta: a loose collarless shirt worn by many people on the Indian subcontinent (usually with a salwar or churidars or pyjama)
kurtosis: A measure of heaviness of the tails of a probability distribution, defined as the fourth cumulant divided by the square of the variance of the probability distribution.
kurukh: A member of a people of eastern India and Bangladesh.
kusimanse: A carnivorous animal (Crossarchus obscurus) of tropical Africa. It its allied to the civets. Called also kusimansel, and mangue.
kutch: The packet of vellum leaves in which the gold is first beaten into thin sheets.
kuvasz: long-established Hungarian breed of tall light-footed but sturdy white dog; used also as a hunting dog
kuwait: a seaport on the Persian Gulf and capital of Kuwait
kuwaiti: of or relating to the kingdom of Kuwait or its people
kvass: fermented beverage resembling beer but made from rye or barley
kvutza: A Jewish communal settlement, primarily in Israel before it became a modern state.
kw: a unit of power equal to watts
kwa: a group of African language in the Niger-Congo group spoken from the Ivory Coast east to Nigeria
kwacha: the basic unit of money in Malawi
kwakiutl: a member of the Wakashan people living around Queen Charlotte Sound and on northern Vancouver Island
kwanza: the basic unit of money in Angola
ky: Kine. See Kee, Kie, and Kine.
kyack: A pack sack to be swung on either side of a packsaddle.
kyanize: To render (wood) proof against decay by saturating with asolution of corrosive sublimate in open tanks, or under pressure.
kyanizing: present participle and gerund of kyanize
kyar: Cocoanut fiber, or the cordage made from it. See Coir.
kyat: the basic unit of money in Myanmar
kyathos: A style of painted Greek vase with a single long flat looping handle resembling a ladle.
kylie: an Australian boomerang; one side flat and the other convex
kylix: a shallow drinking cup with two handles; used in ancient Greece
kymogram: A graphical record produced by a kymograph.
kymograph: An instrument for measuring, and recording graphically, the pressure of the blood in any of the blood vessels of a living animal; called also kymograph ion.
kymographic: Of or pertaining to a kymograph; as, a kymographic tracing.
kyoodle: A mutt, dog of mixed breed of little value; noisy dog.
kyphoscoliosis: Abnormal curvature of the spine in both coronal and sagittal planes; i.e. backward and lateral (sideways) spinal curvature.
kyphosis: an abnormal backward curve to the vertebral column
kyriological: Serving to denote objects by conventional signs or alphabetical characters; as, the original Greek alphabet of sixteen letters was called kyriologic, because it represented the pure elementary sounds. See Curiologic.
kythe: To come into view; to appear. It kythes bright. because all is dark around it. Sir W. Scott.
kythes: third-person singular simple present indicative of kythe
kyushu: the southernmost of the four main islands of Japan; contains coal fields
l: A short right-angled pipe fitting, used in connecting two pipes at right angles.
la: the syllable naming the sixth (submediant) note of a major or minor scale in solmization
laager: A camp, esp. one with an inclosure of travelers' wagons for temporary defense.
lab: To prate; to gossip; to babble; to blab. Chaucer.
labanotation: a system of notation for dance movements that uses symbols to represent points on a dancer's body and the direction of the dancer's movement and the tempo and the dynamics
labarum: The standard adopted by the Emperor Constantine after his conversion to Christianity. It is described as a pike bearing a silk banner hanging from a crosspiece, and surmounted by a golden crown. It bore a monogram of the first two letters (CHR) of the name of christ in its Greek form. Later, the name was given to various modifications of this standard.
labefaction: The act of labefying or making weak; the state of being weakened; decay; ruin. There is in it such a labefaction of all principles as may be injurious to morality. Johnson.
labefying: present participle and gerund of labefy
label: A barrulet, or, rarely, a bendlet, with pendants, or points, usually three, especially used as a mark of cadency to distinguish an eldest or only son while his father is still living.
labeled: bearing or marked with a label or tag
labelled: bearing or marked with a label or tag
labellum: The lower or apparently anterior petal of an orchidaceous flower, often of a very curious shape.
labial: Furnished with lips; as, a labial organ pipe.
labialism: The quality of being labial; as, the labialism of an articulation; conversion into a labial, as of a sound which is different in another language. J. Peile.
labialization: The modification of an articulation by contraction of the lip opening.
labialize: To modify by contraction of the lip opening.
labialized: simple past and past participle of labialize
labiatae: a large family of aromatic herbs and shrubs having flowers resembling the lips of a mouth and four-lobed ovaries yielding four one-seeded nutlets and including mint; thyme; sage; rosemary
labidometer: A forceps with a measuring attachment for ascertaining the size of the fetal head.
labile: Liable to slip, err, fall, or apostatize. Ch eyne.
lability: Liability to lapse, err, or apostatize. Coleridge.
labilize: To make or become labile (i.e. unstable).
labioalveolar: Involving the lip and the alveolar ridge.
labiodental: Formed or pronounced by the cooperation of the lips and teeth, as f and v. n.
labiovelar: co-articulated at the velum and the lips
labiovelarize: To become, or cause to become, labiovelar.
labium: The folds of integument at the opening of the vulva.
lablab: an East Indian name for several twining leguminous plants related to the bean, but commonly applied to the hyacinth bean (Delichos Lablab).
labor: The pitching or tossing of a vessel which results in the straining of timbers and rigging.
laboratory: The workroom of a chemist; also, a place devoted to experiments in any branch of natural science; as, a chemical, physical, or biological laboratory. Hence, by extension, a place where something is prepared, or some operation is performed; as, the liver is the laboratory of the bile.
labored: Bearing marks of labor and effort; elaborately wrought; no teasy or natural; as, labored poetry; a labored style.
laboredly: In a labored manner; with labor.
laborer: One who labors in a toilsome occupation; a person who does work that requires strength rather than skill, as distinguished from that of an artisan.
laboring: That labors; performing labor; esp., performing coarse, heavy work, not requiring skill also, set apart for labor; as, laboring days. The sleep of a laboring man is sweet. eccl. v.
laborious: Requiring labor, perseverance, or sacrifices; toilsome; tiresome. Dost thou love watchings, abstinence, or toil, Laborious virtues all Learn these from Cato. Addison.
laboriousness: the quality of requiring extended effort
laborist: A physician who aids labor and delivery but does not provide prenatal care.
laborite: a supporter of a labor movement
laborless: Not involving labor; not laborious; easy.
laborous: Laborious. Wyatt. Laborously, adv. Sir T. Elyot.
laborsaving: designed to replace or conserve human and especially manual labor
laborsome: Likely or inclined to roll or pitch, as a ship in a heavy sea; having a tendency to labor.
labour: productive work (especially physical work done for wages)
labourer: someone who works with their hands
labourism: Support for the labour movement, the development of a collective organization of working people to campaign for better working conditions and treatment.
labradorite: A kind of feldspar commonly showing a beautiful play of colors, and hence much used for ornamental purposes. The finest specimens come from Labrador. See Feldspar.
labret: A piece of wood, shell, stone, or other substance, worn in aperforation of the lip or cheek by many savages.
labrid: Any of the family Labridae of marine fishes.
labrum: A lip or edge, as of a basin.
labrus: A genus of marine fishes, including the wrasses of Europe. See wrasse.
laburnum: A small leguminous tree (Cytisus Laburnum), native of the Alps. The plant is reputed to be poisonous, esp. the bark and seeds. It has handsome racemes of yellow blossoms.
labyrinth: The internal ear. See Note under Ear.
labyrinthal: Pertaining to, or resembling, a labyrinth; intricate; labyrinthian.
labyrinthian: Intricately winding; like a labyrinth; perplexed; labyrinthal.
labyrinthici: An order of teleostean fishes, including the Anabas, or climbing perch, and other allied fishes.
labyrinthine: Pertaining to, or like, a labyrinth; labyrinthal.
labyrinthodon: A genus of very large fossil amphibians, of the Triassic period, having bony plates on the under side of the body. It is the type of the order Labyrinthodonta. Called also Mastodonsaurus.
labyrinthodont: Of or pertaining to the Labyrinthodonta. n.
labyrinthodonta: An extinct order of Amphibia, including the typical genus labyrinthodon, and many other allied forms, from the Carboniferous, Permian, and Triassic formations. By recent writers they are divided into two or more orders. See Stegocephala.
lac: A resinous substance produced mainly on the banyan tree, but to some extent on other trees, by the Coccus lacca, a scale-shaped insect, the female of which fixes herself on the bark, and exudes from the margin of her body this resinous substance.
laccic: Pertaining to lac, or produced from it; as, laccic acid.
laccolith: A mass of igneous or volcanic rock found within strata which forces the overlaying strata upwards and forms domes.
lace: To be fastened with a lace, or laces; as, these boots lace.
lacebark: small tree or shrub of New Zealand having a profusion of axillary clusters of honey-scented paper-white flowers and whose bark is used for cordage
laceman: A man who deals in lace.
lacer: a workman who laces shoes or footballs or books (during binding)
lacerable: That can be lacerated or torn.
lacerate: To tear; to rend; to separate by tearing; to mangle; as, to lacerate the flesh. Hence: To afflict; to torture; as, to lacerate the heart.
lacerated: having edges that are jagged from injury
lacerating: present participle and gerund of lacerate
lacerative: Lacerating, or having the power to lacerate; as, lacerative humors. Harvey.
lacertian: Like a lizard; of or pertaining to the Lacertilia. n.
lacertilia: An order of Reptilia, which includes the lizards.
lacewood: variably colored and sometimes variegated hard tough elastic wood of a sycamore tree
lachenalia: Any of the genus Lachenalia of bulbs.
lachesis: the Greek goddess of fate who determines the length of the thread of life
lachrymatory: A tear-bottle;" a narrow-necked vessel found in sepulchers of the ancient Romans; so called from a former notion that the tears of the deceased person's friends were collected in it. Called also lachrymal or lacrymal.
lachrymose: Generating or shedding tears; given to shedding tears; suffused with tears; tearful. You should have seen his lachrymose visnomy. Lamb. Lachrymosely, adv.
lacing: A system of bracing bars, not crossing each other in the middle, connecting the channel bars of a compound strut. Wad dell.
laciniate: having edges irregularly and finely slashed
lack: Exclamation of regret or surprise. Cowper.
lackadaisical: Affectedly pensive; languidly sentimental. Lackadaisically, adv.
lacker: One who lacks or is in want.
laconia: an ancient region of southern Greece in the southeastern Peloponnesus; dominated by Sparta
laconian: Of or pertaining to Laconia, a division of ancient Greece; Spartan. n.
laconicum: A hot dry sweating room, next to the caldarium in the Roman baths.
laconize: To imitate the manner of the Laconia ns, especially in brief, pithy speech, or in frugality and austerity.
lacquered: simple past and past participle of lacquer
lacquerer: One who lacquers, especially one who makes a business of lacquering.
lacquering: The act or business of putting on lacquer; also, the coat of lacquer put on.
lacrosse: A game of ball, originating among the North American Indians, now the popular field sport of Canada, and played also in England and the United States. Each player carries a long-handled racket, calle da crosse. The ball is not handled but caught with the crosse and carried on it, or tossed from it, the object being to carry it or throw it through one of the goals placed at opposite ends of the field.
lacrymal: See Lachrymatory, n., and Lachrymal, a.
lactam: One of a series of anhydrides of an amido type, analogous to the lactones, as oxindol.
lactarene: A preparation of casein from milk, used in printing calico.
lactarius: large genus of agarics that have white spore and contain a white or milky juice when cut or broken; includes both edible and poisonous species
lactary: Milky; full of white juice like milk. Lactary or milky plants. " Sir T. Browne.
lactase: any of a group of enzymes (trade name Lactaid) that hydrolyze lactose to glucose and galactose
lactation: A giving suck; the secretion and yielding of milk by the mammary gland.
lacteal: Pertaining to, or containing, chyle; as, the lacteal vessels.
lacteous: Milky; resembling milk. The lacteous circle. " Sir T. Browne.
lactescence: The latex of certain plants. See Latex.
lactescent: Producing milk or a milklike juice or fluid, as the milkweed. See Latex.
lactic: Of or pertaining to milk; procured from sour milk or whey; as, lactic acid; lactic fermentation, etc. Lactic acid (Physiol. Chem.),a sirupy, colorless fluid, soluble in water, with an intensely sour taste and strong acid reaction. There are at least three isomeric modifications all having the formula CHO. Sarcolactic or paralactic acid occurs chiefly in dead muscle tissue, while ordinary lactic acid results from fermentation. The two acids are alike in having the same constitution (expressed by the name ethylidene lactic acid), but the latter is optically inactive, while sarcolactic acid rotates the plane of polarization to the right. The third acid, ethylene lactic acid, accompanies sarcolactic acid in the juice of flesh, and is optically inactive. Lactic ferment, an organized ferment (Bacterium lactic um orlactis), which produces lactic fermentation, decomposing the sugar of milk into carbonic and lactic acids, the latter, of which renders the milk sour, and precipitates the casein, thus giving rise to the so-called spontaneous coagulation of milk. Lactic fermentation. See under Fermentation.
lactiferous: Bearing or containing milk or a milky fluid; as, the lactiferous vessels, cells, or tissue of various vascular plants.
lactim: One of a series of anhydrides resembling the lactams, but of an imido type; as, isatine is a lactim. Cf. Lactam.
lactobacillus: a Gram-positive rod-shaped bacterium that produces lactic acid (especially in milk)
lactometer: An instrument for estimating the purity or richness of milk, as a measuring glass, a specific gravity bulb, or other apparatus.
lactone: One of a series of organic compounds, regarded as anhydrides of certain hydroxy acids. In general, they are colorless liquids, hav inga weak aromatic odor. They are so called because the typical lactone is derived from lactic acid.
lactonize: To convert (a hydroxy acid) into a lactone
lactoprotein: A peculiar albuminous body considered a normal constituent of milk.
lactory: Lactiferous. Lactory or milky plants. " Sir T. Browne.
lactose: Sugar of milk or milk sugar; a crystalline sugar present in milk, and separable from the whey by evaporation and crystallization. It has a slightly sweet taste, is dextrorotary, and is much less soluble in water than either cane sugar or glucose. Formerly called lactin.
lactuca: A genus of composite herbs, several of which are cultivated foe salad; lettuce.
lactucarium: The inspissated juice of the common lettuce, sometimes used as a substitute for opium.
lacuna: A small opening; a small depression or cavity; a space, as ava cant space between the cells of plants, or one of the spaces left among the tissues of the lower animals, which serve in place of vessels for the circulation of the body fluids, or the cavity or sac, usually of very small size, in a mucous membrane.
lacunar: The ceiling or under surface of any part, especially when it consists of compartments, sunk or hollowed without spaces or bands between the panels. Gwilt
lacustrine: of or relating to or living near lakes
ladakhi: A person from Ladakh, or of Ladakhi descent.
ladanum: A gum resin gathered from certain Oriental species of Cistus. It has a pungent odor and is chiefly used in making plasters, and for fumigation.
ladder: come unraveled or undone as if by snagging
ladderman: A casino employee who supervises the baccarat table from a tall chair, watching for cheating etc.
lade: To transfer (the molten glass) from the pot to the forming table.
laden: Loaded; freighted; burdened; as, a laden vessel; a laden heart. Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity. Is. i.A ship laden with gold.
lader: One who loads cargo onto a vessel.
ladied: Ladylike; not rough; gentle. Stroked with a ladied land. " Felt ham.
ladify: To make a lady of; to make ladylike. Mass inger.
ladino: One of the half-breed descendants of whites and Indians; amestizo; so called throughout Central America. They are usually of a yellowish orange tinge. Am. Cyc.
ladle: A vessel to carry liquid metal from the furnace to the mold.
ladleful: A quantity sufficient to fill a ladle.
ladrone: A robber; a pirate; hence, loosely, a rogue or rascal.
ladyfish: game fish resembling the tarpon but smaller
ladyhood: The state or quality of being a lady; the personality of alady.
ladykin: A little lady; applied by the writers of Queen Elizabeth'stime, in the abbreviated form Lakin, to the Virgin Mary.
ladylike: befitting a woman of good breeding
ladyship: The rank or position of a lady; given as a title (preceded by her or your.) Your ladyship shall observe their gravity. B. Jonson.
laelia: any of various spectacular plants of the genus Laelia having showy flowers in many colors
laen: A locality in the Shire of Northern Grampians and the Shire of Yarriambiack, central western Victoria, Australia.
laevoversion: A movement of both eyes to the left.
lafayette: French soldier who served under George Washington in the American Revolution (-)
lag: See Graylag. Lag of the tide, the interval by which the time of high water falls behind the mean time, in the first and third quarters of the moon; opposed to priming of the tide, or the acceleration of the time of high water, in the second and fourth quarters; depending on the relative positions of the sun and moon. Lag screw, an iron bolt with a square head, a sharp-edged thread, and a sharp point, adapted for screwing into wood; a screw for fastening lags.
lagena: The terminal part of the cochlea in birds and most reptiles; an appendage of the sacculus, corresponding to the cochlea, in fishes and amphibians.
lagend: goods (or wreckage) on the sea bed that is attached to a buoy so that it can be recovered
lagerstroemia: shrubs or small trees of tropical Asia and Africa usually with showy white, pink, or purplish flowers
lagging: The clothing (esp., an outer, wooden covering), as of a steam cylinder, applied to prevent the radiation of heat; a covering of lags; called also deading and cleading.
lagniappe: a small gift (especially one given by a merchant to a customer who makes a purchase)
lagomorpha: A group of rodents, including the hares. They have four incisors in the upper jaw. Called also Duplicidentata.
lagomorphic: Shaped like a hare or rabbit.
lagoon: A morbid condition in which the eye stands wide open, giving apeculiar staring appearance.
laguna: a body of water cut off from a larger body by a reef of sand or coral
lai: A mostly North European medieval form of lyrical, narrative poem written in octosyllabic couplets that often deals with tales of adventure and romance, with stanzas that do not repeat.
laical: Of or pertaining to a layperson, layman, laywoman, or laypeople, i.e. the laity in general.
laically: As a layman; after the manner of a layman; as, to treat am atter laically.
laicizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of laicize
laicizing: present participle and gerund of laicize
laid: of Lay. Laid paper, paper marked with parallel lines or watermarks, as if ribbed, from parallel wires in the mold. It is called blue laid, cream laid, etc., according to its color.
laidly: Ugly; loathsome. This laidly and loathsome worm. W. Howitt.
laine: an area of arable land at the foot of a hill
laird: A lord; a landholder, esp. one who holds land directly of the crown.
laitance: A weak, milky layer of cement and aggregate fines on a concrete surface that is usually caused by an overwet mixture, overworking the mixture, improper or excessive finishing or combination thereof. Also, could be caused when a slurry mix is used on a deep foundation, where the slurry mix is not completely removed before placing concrete on top.
laity: in Christianity, members of a religious community that do not have the priestly responsibilities of ordained clergy
laius: (Greek mythology) king of Thebes who was unwittingly killed by his son Oedipus
lake: A pigment formed by combining some coloring matter, usually by precipitation, with a metallic oxide or earth, esp. with aluminium hydrate; as, madder lake; Florentine lake; yellow lake, etc.
lakeland: The Lake District, a rural area in northwest England.
lakeport: A port located on a lake.
laker: One of the poets of the Lake school. See Lake poets, under Lake, n.
lakes: The Lake District, a rural area in northwest England.
lakh: Same as Lac, one hundred thousand.
laking: present participle and gerund of lake
lakota: A member of a Native American tribe, also known as the Sioux, now living primarily on the Rosebud, Pine Ridge, Lower Brule, Standing Rock and Cheyenne River Reservations.
laky: Pertaining to a lake. Sir W. Scott.
lallation: An imperfect enunciation of the letter r, in which it sounds like l.
lalo: The powdered leaves of the baobab tree, used by the Africans tomix in their soup, as the southern negroes use powdered sassafras. Cf. Couscous.
lam: To beat soundly; to thrash. Beau. & Fl.
lamaism: A modified form of Buddhism which prevails in Thibet, Mongolia, and some adjacent parts of Asia; so called from the name of its priests. See d Lama.
lamarck: French naturalist who proposed that evolution resulted from the inheritance of acquired characteristics (-)
lamarckism: The theory that structural variations, characteristic of species and genera, are produced in animals and plants by the direct influence of physical environments, and esp., in the case of animals, by effort, or by use or disuse of certain organs.

lambdoid: Shaped like the Greek letter lambda (as, the lambdoid suture between the occipital and parietal bones of the skull.

lamber: A ewe that gives birth to a lamb.

lambkill: A small American ericaceous shrub (Kalmia angustifolia); called also calfkill, sheepkill, sheep laurel, etc. It is supposed to poison sheep and other animals that eat it at times when the snow is deep and they cannot find other food.
lamblia: Giardia lamblia, an intestinal parasite that causes giardiasis.
lamblike: Like a lamb; gentle; meek; inoffensive.
lambrequin: a scarf that covers a knight's helmet
lambskin: the skin of a lamb with the wool still on
lamby: Resembling or characteristic of a lamb or the meat of a lamb.
lame: To make lame. If you happen to let child fall and lame it. Swift.
lamed: The twelfth letter of many Semitic alphabets/abjads (Phoenician, Aramaic, Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic and others).
lamedh: the th letter of the Hebrew alphabet
lamella: a thin plate or scale of anything, as a thin scale growing from the petals of certain flowers; or one of the thin plates or scales of which certain shells are composed.

lamellate: Composed of, or furnished with, thin plates or scales.
lamellibranch: One of the Lamellibranchia. Also used adjectively.
lamellirostral: Having a lamellate bill, as ducks and geese.
lamellirostres: A group of birds embracing the Anseres and flamingoes, in which the bill is lamellate.
lamely: An a lame, crippled, disabled, or imperfect manner; as, to walk lamely; a figure lamely drawn.
lameness: The condition or quality of being lame; as, the lameness of an excuse or an argument.
lament: To express or feel sorrow; to weep or wail; to mourn. Jeremiah lamented for Josiah. Chron. xxxv.Ye shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice. John xvi.
lamentable: Mourning; sorrowful; expressing grief; as, a lamentable countenance. Lamentable eye. " Spenser.
lamentably: in an unfortunate or deplorable manner
lamentation: A book of the Old Testament attributed to the prophet Jeremiah, and taking its name from the nature of its contents.
lamentations: an Old Testament book lamenting the desolation of Judah after the destruction of Jerusalem in BC; traditionally attributed to the prophet Jeremiah
lamented: Mourned for; bewailed. This humble praise, lamented shade! receive. Pope.
lamenting: Lamentation. Lamentin gs heard i' the air.
lames: Small steel plates combined together so as to slide one upon the form a piece of armor.
lamia: A monster capable of assuming a woman's form, who was said to devour human beings or suck their blood; a vampire; a sorceress; awith.
lamiaceous: Of or relating to the family Lamiaceae of mint and its close relatives.
lamiid: Any member of the family Lamiidae, now considered to be the cerambycid subfamily Lamiinae.
lamin: Any of a class of fibrous proteins that provide structure, and regulate transcription in a cell nucleus
lamina: The blade of a leaf; the broad, expanded portion of a petal or sepal of a flower. Gray.
