monocle: An eyeglass for one eye. Simmon ds.
monoclinal: Having one oblique inclination; applied to strata that dipin only one direction from the axis of elevation.
monoclinic: Having one oblique intersection; said of that system of crystallization in which the vertical axis is inclined to one, but at right angles to the other, lateral axis. See Crystallization.
monoclinous: Hermaphrodite, or having both stamens and pistils in every flower.
monocot: a monocotyledonous flowering plant; the stem grows by deposits on its inside
monocotyledon: A plant with only one cotyledon, or seed lobe.
monocotyledonous: Having only one cotyledon, seed lobe, or seminal leaf. Lind ley.
monocrotic: Of, pertaining to, or showing, monocrotism; as, a monocrotic pulse; a pulse of the monocrotic type.
monocrotism: That condition of the pulse in which the pulse curve or sphygmogram shows but a single crest, the dicrotic elevation entirely disappearing.
monocular: Having only one eye; with one eye only; as, monocular vision.
monoculture: the cultivation of a single crop (on a farm or area or country)
monocyclic: Having a single cycle of development or activity.
monocyte: a type of granular leukocyte that functions in the ingestion of bacteria
monodactylous: Having but one finger or claw.
monodactyly: The presence of a single digit on a limb
monodelphia: The group that includes all ordinary or placental mammals; the placentalia. See Mammalia.
monodelphous: Describing stamens that have filaments united into a single tubelike group
monodrama: A play in the form of a monologue
monodromy: The globalization of local morphisms in category theory
monody: A species of poem of a mournful character, in which a single mourner expresses lamentation; a song for one voice.
monodynamic: Possessing but one capacity or power. Monodynamic men. " De Quincey.
monoecious: Having the sexes united in one individual, as when male and female flowers grow upon the same individual plant; hermaphrodite; opposed to Ant: dioecious.
monoecism: The state or condition of being monoecious.
monoecy: The state of having both male and female sex organs; hermaphrodism.
monoester: An ester of a polyhydric alcohol or a polycarboxylic acid containing only a single ester group.
monofilament: A single strand of man-made fiber
monogamist: One who practices or upholds monogamy. Goldsmith.
monogamy: State of being paired with a single mate.
monogenesis: That form of reproduction which requires but one parent, as in reproduction by fission or in the formation of buds, etc., which drop off and form new individuals; asexual reproduction. Haeckel.
monogenetic: One in genesis; resulting from one process of formation; used of a mountain range. Dana.
monogenist: One who maintains that the human races are all of one species; opposed to polygenist.
monogenous: Of or pertaining to monogenesis; as, monogenous, or asexual, reproduction.
monogeny: The doctrine that the members of the human race have all acommon origin.
monoglyceride: a lipid, an ester of glycerol and one fatty acid (in the - or - positions)
monogram: a graphic symbol consisting of or more letters combined (usually your initials); printed on stationery or embroidered on clothing
monogrammed: simple past and past participle of monogram
monogrammic: Of, pertaining to, or resembling, a monogram.
monograph: A written account or description of a single thing, or class of things; a special treatise on a particular subject of limited range.
monographic: Of or pertaining to a monograph or treatise.
monogynous: Of or pertaining to Monogynia; having only one style or stigma.
monogyny: The state or condition of being monogynous.
monohydric: Having a single replaceable hydrogen atom
monohydroxy: Having a single hydroxy group in a molecule. E.g. a monool is monohydroxy/monohydric alcohol.
monolater: One who worships a single deity (possibly while believing in the existence of others).
monolingual: using or knowing only one language
monolith: A single stone, especially one of large size, shaped into apillar, statue, or monument.
monolithic: Of or pertaining to a monolith; consisting of a single stone.
monologist: One who soliloquizes; esp., one who monopolizes conversation in company. De Quincey.
monologue: a long utterance by one person (especially one that prevents others from participating in the conversation)
monology: The habit of soliloquizing, or of monopolizing conversation. It was not by an insolent usurpation that Coleridge persisted in monology through his whole life. De Quincey.
monomania: Derangement of the mind in regard of a single subject only; also, such a concentration of interest upon one particular subject or train of ideas to show mental derangement.
monomer: a simple compound whose molecules can join together to form polymers
monometallism: The legalized use of one metal only, as gold, or silver, in the standard currency of a country, or as a standard of money values. See bimetallism.
monometallist: One who believes in monometallism as opposed to bimetallism, etc.
monomethyl: A single methyl group in a molecule
monomial: A single algebraic expression; that is, an expression unconnected with any other by the sign of addition, substraction, equality, or inequality.
monomorphic: Having or existing in a single shape or form.
monomyarian: Of or relating to the Monomya, bivalves having only one adductor muscle.
monongahela: a river that rises in northern West Virginia and flows north into Pennsylvania where it joins the Allegheny River at Pittsburgh to form the Ohio River
mononitrate: Any nitrate having a single nitrate anion
mononucleated: Having a single nucleus; mononucleate, mononuclear.
mononucleosis: an acute disease characterized by fever and swollen lymph nodes and an abnormal increase of mononuclear leucocytes or monocytes in the bloodstream
mononym: A single name by which a person, thing, etc., is known.
monoousian: Having one and the same nature or essence, especially with regard to the persons of the Trinity.
monopetalous: Having only one petal, or the corolla in one piece, or composed of petals cohering so as to form a tube or bowl; gamopetalous.
monophagy: The feeding on a single type of food (e.g., a single plant species).
monophasia: A type of aphasia where the sufferer is only able to speak a single word or sentence.
monophonic: Single-voiced; having but one part; as, a monophonic composition; opposed to Ant: polyphonic.
monophony: music consisting of a single vocal part (usually with accompaniment)
monophote: An electric arc-lamp regulator working in single series.
monophthongize: To change to a monophthong (as by removing a vowel).
monophyletic: Of or pertaining to a single family or stock, or to development from a single common parent form; opposed to polyphyletic; as, monophyletic origin.
monophyletism: The property of being monophyletic; monophyly.
monophyllous: One-leaved; composed of a single leaf; as, a monophyllous involucre or calyx.
monophyodont: Having but one set of teeth; opposed to diphyodont.
monophysite: One of a sect, in the ancient church, who maintained that the human and divine in Jesus Christ constituted but one composite nature. Also used adjectively.
monophysitism: a Christian heresy of the th and th centuries that challenged the orthodox definition of the two natures (human and divine) in Jesus and instead believed there was a single divine nature
monoplane: an airplane with a single wing
monoplastic: That has one form, or retains its primary form, as, amonoplastic element.
monopodium: A single and continuous vegetable axis; opposed to sympodium.
monopody: A measure of but a single foot.
monopole: An appellation owned by a single winery.
monopolise: have or exploit a monopoly of
monopolist: One who monopolizes; one who has a monopoly; one who favors monopoly.
monopolistic: Of or pertaining to a monopolist. North Am. Rev.
monopolize: To acquire a monopoly of; to have or get the exclusive privilege or means of dealing in, or the exclusive possession of; to engross the whole of; as, to monopolize the coffee trade; to monopolize land.
monopolized: simple past and past participle of monopolize
monopolizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of monopolize
monopolizing: present participle and gerund of monopolize
monopoly: (economics) a market in which there are many buyers but only one seller
monopolylogue: An exhibition in which an actor sustains many characters.
monoprionidian: Having a polyparium with a single row of cells.
monopropellant: Any propellant that consists of a single substance, or of a mixture of fuel and oxidant in the same container
monopsony: (economics) a market in which goods or services are offered by several sellers but there is only one buyer
monopsychism: The doctrine that there is but one immortal soul or intellect with which all men are endowed.
monopteron: A circular temple consisting of a roof supported on columns, without a cella.
monopteros: A classical temple made up of one circle of columns supporting a roof.
monoptote: A noun having only one case. Andrews.
monorail: a railway having a single track
monorhyme: A composition in verse, in which all the lines end with the same rhyme.
monosaccharide: a sugar (like sucrose or fructose) that does not hydrolyse to give other sugars; the simplest group of carbohydrates
monosemy: having a single meaning (absence of ambiguity) usually of individual words or phrases
monosepalous: Having only one sepal, or the calyx in one piece or composed of the sepals united into one piece; gamosepalous.
monosodium: one atom of sodium in a compound
monosome: The chromosome whose homologous counterpart is missing in monosomy
monosomy: chromosomal abnormality consisting of the absence of one chromosome from the normal diploid number
monostich: A composition consisting of one verse only.
monostrophic: Having one strophe only; not varied in measure; written in unvaried measure. Milton.
monosulphide: A sulphide containing one atom of sulphur, and analogous to amonoxide; contrasted with a Ant: polysulphide; as, galena is amonosulphide.
monosyllabic: Being a monosyllable, or composed of monosyllables; as, amonosyllabic word; a monosyllabic language. Monosyllabically, adv.
monosynaptic: Having, or involving a single synapse
monotelephone: An early telephonic device that transmits only one specific tone.
monotheism: The doctrine or belief that there is but one God.
monotheist: One who believes that there is but one God.
monothelete: Someone who believed Christ had two natures (human and divine), but one single will; a Monothelite.
monothelite: One of an ancient sect who held that Christ had but one will ashe had but one nature. Cf. Monophysite. Gibbon.
monothelitic: Of or pertaining to the Monothelites, or their doctrine.
monothelitism: the theological doctrine that Christ had only one will even though he had two natures (human and divine); condemned as heretical in the Third Council of Constantinople
monotomous: Having a distinct cleavage in a single direction only.
monotone: A single unvaried tone or sound.
monotonic: of a sequence or function; consistently increasing and never decreasing or consistently decreasing and never increasing in value
monotonous: Uttered in one unvarying tone; continued with dull uniformity; characterized by monotony; without change or variety; wearisome. Monotonously, adv. Monotonousness, n.
monotony: the quality of wearisome constancy, routine, and lack of variety
monotremata: A subclass of Mammalia, having a cloaca in which the ducts of the urinary, genital, and alimentary systems terminate, as in birds. The female lays eggs like a bird. See Duck mole, under Duck, and echidna.
monotriglyph: A kind of intercolumniation in an entablature, in which only one triglyph and two metopes are introduced.
monotropa: A genus of parasitic or saprophytic plants including the Indian pipe and pine sap. The name alludes to the dropping end of the stem.
monotropaceae: used in some classification for saprophytic herbs sometimes included in the family Pyrolaceae: genera Monotropa and Sarcodes
monotropic: Describing any material that exists in multiple forms, only one of which is stable at all temperatures and pressures.
monotype: (biology) a taxonomic group with a single member (a single species or genus)
monounsaturated: (of long-chain carbon compounds especially fats) saturated except for one multiple bond
monovalent: Having a valence of one; univalent. See Univalent.
monoxide: An oxide containing one atom of oxygen in each molecule; as, barium monoxide.
monozygotic: derived from a single fertilized egg
monroe: United States film actress noted for sex appeal (-)
monroeism: Synonym of Monroe Doctrine: the United States policy opposing European colonialism in the Americas beginning in.
mons: a mound of fatty tissue covering the pubic area in women
monseigneur: My lord; a title in France of a person of high birth or rank; as, Monseigneur the Prince, or Monseigneur the Archibishop. Itwas given, specifically, to the dauphin, before the Revolution of. (Abbrev. Mgr.)
monsieur: used as a French courtesy title; equivalent to English Mr'
monsignor: (Roman Catholic Church) an ecclesiastical title of honor bestowed on some priests
monsoon: A wind blowing part of the year from one direction, alternating with a wind from the opposite direction; a term applied particularly to periodical winds of the Indian Ocean, which blow from the southwest from the latter part of May to the middle of September, and from the northeast from about the middle of October to the middle of December.
monsoonish: Resembling or characteristic of a monsoon.
monstera: any plant of the genus Monstera; often grown as house plants
monstrance: A transparent pyx, in which the consecrated host is exposed to view.
monstration: The act of demonstrating; proof. A certain monstration. Graft on.
monstrosity: The state of being monstrous, or out of the common order of nature; that which is monstrous; a monster. South. A monstrosity never changes the name or affects the immutability of aspecies. Adanson (Trans. ).
monstrous: Exceedingly; very; very much. A monstrous thick oil on the top. " Bacon. And will be monstrous witty on the poor. Dryden.
monstrously: In a monstrous manner; unnaturally; extraordinarily; as, monstrously wicked. Who with his wife is monstrously in love. Dryden.
montage: a paste-up made by sticking together pieces of paper or photographs to form an artistic image
montagu: United States anthropologist (born in England) who popularized anthropology (-)
montague: A surname from Old French, variant of Montagu.
montana: a state in northwestern United States on the Canadian border
montanan: a native or resident of Montana
montanism: The doctrines of a heretical sect of the second to fifth centuries in Asia Minor, who held millenarian beliefs.
monte: A favorite gambling game among Spaniards, played with dice or cards.
montenegro: a former country bordering on the Adriatic Sea; now part of the Union of Serbia and Montenegro
monterey: a town in western California to the south of San Francisco on a peninsula at the southern end of Monterey Bay
montero: An ancient kind of cap worn by horsemen or huntsmen. Bacon.
monterrey: an industrial city in northeastern Mexico
montessori: Italian educator who developed a method of teaching mentally handicapped children and advocated a child-centered approach (-)
montezuma: evergreen tree with large leathery leaves and large pink to orange flowers; considered a link plant between families Bombacaceae and Sterculiaceae
montgolfier: A balloon which ascends by the buoyancy of air heated by afire; a fire balloon; so called from two brothers, Stephen and joseph Montgolfier, of France, who first constructed and sent up afire balloon.

monthly: A publication which appears regularly once a month.
montia: small genus of densely tufted annual herbs; north temperate regions and South America and tropical Africa and Asia
monticle: A little mount; a hillock; a small elevation or prominence.

montilla: A kind of sweet dessert wine from the Montilla-Moriles region of Spain, made similarly to sherry.
montmartre: the highest point in Paris; famous for its associations with many artists
montmorillonite: Any of a group of soft, clay-like silicate minerals having many industrial and technical uses.
montreal: a city in southern Quebec province on the Saint Lawrence River; the largest city in Quebec and nd largest in Canada; the nd largest French-speaking city in the world
montserrat: a volcanic island in the Caribbean; in the West Indies
monument: an important site that is marked and preserved as public property
monumental: relating or belonging to or serving as a monument
monumentalise: record or memorialize lastingly with a monument
monumentalize: record or memorialize lastingly with a monument
monumentalizing: present participle and gerund of monumentalize
monumented: simple past and past participle of monument
monureid: Any one of a series of complex nitrogenous substances regarded as derived from one molecule of urea; as, alloxan is a monureid.
monzonite: An intrusive igneous rock composed mostly of plagioclase and orthoclase
mooch: ask for and get free; be a parasite
moocher: someone who mooches or cadges (tries to get something free)
mooches: third-person singular simple present indicative of mooch
mood: Manner of conceiving and expressing action or being, as positive, possible, hypothetical, etc., without regard to other accidents, such as time, person, number, etc.; as, the indicative mood; the infinitive mood; the subjunctive mood. Same as Mode.
moodiness: The quality or state of being moody; specifically, liability to strange or violent moods.
moodir: The governor of a province in Egypt, etc.

moonbeam: A ray of light from the moon.
moonbow: A rainbow formed by moonlight diffracted by water droplets in the air, usually fainter than a daytime rainbow and with fewer distinguishable colours.
mooncalf: A monster; a false conception; a mass of fleshy matter, generated in the uterus.
mooned: Of or resembling the moon; symbolized by the moon. Sharpening in mooned horns. " Mooned Ashtaroth. " Milton.
moonfish: any of several silvery marine fishes with very flat bodies
moonish: Like the moon; variable. Being but a moonish youth.
moonless: Being without a moon or moonlight.
moonlet: a very small body orbiting a planet, often as part of a planetary ring system.
moonlight: The light of the moon. a.
moonlighter: a person who holds a second job (usually after hours)
moonlit: Illumined by the moon. The moonlit sea. " Moore. Moonlit dells. " Lowell.
moonrise: The rising of the moon above the horizon; also, the time of its rising.
moonsail: A sail sometimes carried in light winds, above a skysail. R. H.Dana, Jr.
moonscape: A view of an area of the Moon.
moonseed: A climbing plant of the genus Menispermum; so called from the crescentlike form of the seeds.
moonset: The descent of the moon below the horizon; also, the time when the moon sets.

moonshiny: Moonlight. I went to see them in a moonshiny night. Addison.
moonsick: Insane or emotionally deranged, either temporarily or permanently.

moonstruck: Mentally affected or deranged by the supposed influence of the moon; lunatic.
moonwalk: a kind of dance step in which the dancer seems to be sliding on the spot
moonwort: of America and Eurasia and Australia
moony: Of or pertaining to the moon. Soft and pale as the moony beam. J. R. Drake.
moor: Any individual of the swarthy races of Africa or Asia which have adopted the Mohammedan religion. In Spanish history the terms moors, Saracens, and Arabs are synonymous. " Internat. Cyc.
moorburn: The controlled burning of moorland vegetation to encourage new growth (either heather or grassland) for the management of moorland game and wildlife or for improving the grazing potential.
moore: United States composer of works noted for their use of the American vernacular (-)
moored: simple past and past participle of moor
moorfowl: reddish-brown grouse of upland moors of Great Britain
moorhen: black gallinule that inhabits ponds and lakes
mooring: The place or condition of a ship thus confined. And the tossed bark in moorings swings. Moore. Mooring block (Naut.), a heavy block of cast iron sometimes used as an anchor for mooring vessels.
moorish: Having the characteristics of a moor or heath. Moorish fens. Thomson.
moorland: Land consisting of a moor or moors.
moorpan: A clayey layer or pan underlying some moors, etc.
moorwort: wiry evergreen shrub having pendent clusters of white or pink flowers
moory: Of or pertaining to moors; marshy; fenny; boggy; moorish. Mortimer. As when thick mists arise from moory vales. Fair fax.
mooseberry: A pembina or lowbush cranberry (Viburnum edule)
moosewood: maple of eastern North America with striped bark and large two-lobed leaves clear yellow in autumn
mooted: Made, or proven to be, moot.
mooter: A disputer of a mooted case.
mooting: The activity of taking part in a moot court.
mootman: One who argued moot cases in the inns of court.
mop: A made-up face; a grimace. What mops and mowes it makes!Beau. & Fl.
mopane: A tree, Colophospermum mopane, native to southern Africa.
mopboard: A narrow board nailed against the wall of a room next to the floor; skirting board; baseboard. See Baseboard.
mope: To be dull and spiritless. Moping melancholy. " Milton. A sickly part of one true sense Could not so mope.
moped: a motorbike that can be pedaled or driven by a low-powered gasoline engine
moper: One who mopes or is inclined to do so.
mopes: an informal expression for a mildly depressed state
mopey: Given to moping; in a depressed condition, low in spirits; lackadaisical.
moping: present participle and gerund of mope
mopish: Dull; spiritless; dejected. Mopishly, adv. Mopishness, n.
mopped: simple past and past participle of mop
mopper: a worker who uses a mop to clean a surface
mops: third-person singular simple present indicative of mop
mopsy: A nickname for a person with a mop of hair.
moquette: A kind of carpet having a short velvety pile.
mor: A mid-ocean ridge: a submarine volcanic mountain range.
mora: A game of guessing the number of fingers extended in a quick movement of the hand, much played by Italians of the lower classes.
moraceae: trees or shrubs having a milky juice; in some classifications includes genus Cannabis
moraceous: of or pertaining to or characteristic of plants of the family Moraceae
moraine: An accumulation of earth and stones carried forward and deposited by a glacier. Lyell.
morainic: Of or pertaining to a moran ie.
morale: The moral condition, or the condition in other respects, so faras it is affected by, or dependent upon, moral considerations, such as zeal, spirit, hope, and confidence; mental state, as of a body ofmen, an army, and the like.
moralism: A maxim or saying embodying a moral truth. Farrar.
moralist: a philosopher who specializes in morals and moral problems
morality: concern with the distinction between good and evil or right and wrong; right or good conduct
moralization: the act of making moral (or more moral)
moralize: To make moral reflections; to regard acts and events as involving a moral.
moralizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of moralize
moralizing: indulgence in moral pronouncements; the exposition (often superficially) of a particular moral code
morals: motivation based on ideas of right and wrong
moran: A surname from Old French of Old French origin.
morass: A tract of soft, wet ground; a marsh; a fen. Morass ore. (Min.) See Bog ore, under Bog.
moration: A delaying tarrying; delay. Sir T. Browne.
moratorium: A period during which an obligor has a legal right to delay meeting an obligation, esp. such a period granted, as to a bank, by amora tory law.
moravia: a region in the central and eastern part of the Czech Republic; it lies to the east of Bohemia and to the west of the Carpathians
moravian: Of or pertaining to Moravia, or to the United Brethren. See moravian, n.
morbidity: the relative incidence of a particular disease
morbose: Proceeding from disease; morbid; unhealthy. Morbose tumors and excrescences of plants. Ray.
morcellate: To break into small pieces, prior to removal
morcellation: The breaking into small pieces prior to removal.
mordacious: Biting; given to biting; hence, figuratively, sarcastic; severe; scathing. Mordaciously, adv.
mordancy: The state or quality of being mordant.
mordanted: simple past and past participle of mordant
mordecai: One of the main personalities in the Book of Esther. He adopted and raised his cousin Esther and foiled a plot to assassinate the king.
mordenite: An orthorhombic-pyramidal mineral containing aluminum, calcium, hydrogen, oxygen, potassium, silicon, and sodium.
mordent: An ornament consisting of a single alternation between a given pitch and the one immediately below it.
mordicant: Biting; acrid; as, the mordicant quality of a body. Boyle.
moreen: A thick woolen fabric, watered or with embossed figures; used in upholstery, for curtains, etc.
moreish: Causing one to want to have more, addictive.
morel: An edible fungus (Morchella esculenta), the upper part of which is covered with a reticulated and pitted hymenium. It is used as food, and for flavoring sauces.
morello: A kind of nearly black cherry with dark red flesh and juice, used chiefly for preserving.
moreover: Beyond what has been said; further; besides; in addition; furthermore; also; likewise. Moreover, he hath left you all his walks.
mores: Customs; habits; esp., customs conformity to which is more or less obligatory; customary law.
moresque: Of or pertaining to, or in the manner or style of, the Moors; Moorish. n.
morfound: To affect (an animal or person) with catarrh or coldlike illness.
morgan: One of a celebrated breed of American trotting horses; so called from the name of the stud from which the breed originated in vermont.
morganatic: Pertaining to, in the manner of, or designating, a kind of marriage, called also left-handed marriage, between a man of superior rank and a woman of inferior, in which it is stipulated that neither the latter nor her children shall enjoy the rank or inherit the possessions of her husband. Br ande & C. Morganatically, adv.
morgen: a South African unit of measure equal to about acres
morgue: A place where the bodies of persons found dead are exposed, that they may be identified, or claimed by their friends; adead house.
moribund: In a dying state; dying; at the point of death. The patient was comatose and moribund. Copland.

mormaer: A regional or provincial ruler in the mediaeval Kingdom of the Scots.
mormal: A bad sore; a gangrene; a cancer. Chaucer.
mormon: One of a sect in the United States, followers of Joseph Smith, who professed to have found an addition to the Bible, engraved on golden plates, called the Book of Mormon, first published in.The Mormons believe in polygamy, and their hierarchy of apostles, etc., has control of civil and religious matters.
morn: The first part of the day; the morning; used chiefly in poetry. From morn To noun he fell, from noon to dewy eve. Milton.
mornay: Served with a white sauce containing cheese.
morne: Of or pertaining to the morn; morning. White as morne milk. " Chaucer.

She looks as clear As morning roses newly washed with dew. Morning gown, a gown worn in the morning before one is dressed for the day. Morning gun, a gun fired at the first stroke of reveille at military posts. Morning sickness (Med.), nausea and vomiting, usually occurring in the morning; a common sign of pregnancy. Morning star. Since he miscalled the morning star, Nor man nor fiend hath fallen sofar. Byron.(c) A weapon consisting of a heavy ball set with spikes, either attached to a staff or suspended from one by a chain. mornward: Towards the morn. And mornward now the starry hands move on. Lowell.
moro: A small abscess or tumor having a resemblance to a mulberry. Dunglison.
moroccan: Of or pertaining to Morocco, or its inhabitants.
morocco: A fine kind of leather, prepared commonly from goatskin (though an inferior kind is made of sheepskin), and tanned with sumac and dyed of various colors; said to have been first made by the Moors.
moron: A person whose intellectual development proceeds normally up to about the eighth year of age and is then arrested so that there is little or no further development.
morone: Maroon; the color of an unripe black mulberry.
moronic: having a mental age of between eight and twelve years
moronism: The condition of being a moron (person of borderline intelligence).
moros: The Mohammedan tribes of the southern Philippine Islands, said to have formerly migrated from Borneo. Some of them are warlike and addicted to piracy.
morose: Of a sour temper; sullen and austere; ill-humored; severe. A morose and affected taciturnity. " I. Watts.

morphean: Of or relating to Morpheus, to dreams, or to sleep. Keats.

morphic: Of or pertaining to shape or form; morphological.

morphism: Being or having distinct variants of a plant or animal species in the same locale; polymorphism.

morphologic: relating to or concerned with the morphology of plants and animals
morphological: relating to or concerned with the morphology of plants and animals
morphologically: in a morphological manner; with regard to morphology
morphologist: One who is versed in the science of morphology.
morphology: That branch of biology which deals with the structure of animals and plants, treating of the forms of organs and describing their varieties, homologies, and metamorphoses. See Tectology, and promorphology.
morphon: A morphological individual, characterized by definiteness of form bion, a physiological individual. See Tectology. Haeckel.
morphophoneme: (linguistics) the phonemes (or strings of phonemes) that constitute the various allo morphs of a morpheme

morphophyly: The tribal history of forms; that part of phylogeny which treats of the tribal history of forms, in distinction from the tribal history of functions. Haeckel.
morphosis: The order or mode of development of an organ or part.

morristown: a town in northern New Jersey where the Continental Army spent two winters
morro: A round hill or point of land; hence, Morro castle, a castle on a hill.
mort: A great quantity or number. There was a mort of merrymaking. Dickens.

mortarboard: a square board with a handle underneath; used by masons to hold or carry mortar

mosan: a family of Amerindian languages spoken in Washington and British Columbia

mossback: A veteran partisan; one who is so conservative in opinion that he may be likened to a stone or old tree covered with moss.
mossberry: Empetrum nigrum, a species of crowberry.
mosser: A person who gathers Irish moss, a type of seaweed.

motacilla: type genus of the Motacillidae: wagtails

motherhood: The state of being a mother; the character or office of am other.

mothery: Consisting of, containing, or resembling, mother (in vinegar).

motley: having sections or patches colored differently and usually brightly

mousy: Infested with mice; smelling of mice.
