Occipital bone (Anat.), the bone which forms the posterior segment of the skull and surrounds the great foramen by which the spinal cord leaves the cranium. In the higher vertebrates it is usually composed of four bones, which become consolidated in the adult. Occipital point (Anat.), the point of the occiput in the mesial plane farthest from the ophryon.
occipitofrontalis: A large flat muscle on each side of the vertex of the skull, consisting of an occipital portion (arising from the occipital and temporal bones) and a frontal portion that are separated by the epicranial aponeurosis, and serving to draw the scalp backwards, raising the eyebrows and wrinkling the forehead.
occiput: The back, or posterior, part of the head or skull; the region of the occipital bone.
occlude: To take in and retain; to absorb; said especially with respect to gases; as iron, platinum, and palladium occlude large volumes of hydrogen.
occludes: third-person singular simple present indicative of occlude
occlusal: On the side of a tooth which mates with the opposing tooth.
occlusion: The transient approximation of the edges of a natural opening; imperforation. Dunglison. Occlusion of gases (Chem. & Physics), the phenomenon of absorbing gases, as exhibited by platinum, palladium, iron, or charcoal; thus, palladium absorbs, or occludes, nearly athousand times its own volume of hydrogen, and in this case achemical compound seems to be formed.
occult: Hidden from the eye or the understanding; inviable; secret; concealed; unknown. It is of an occult kind, and is so insensible in its advances as to escape observation. I. Taylor. Occult line (Geom.), a line drawn as a part of the construction of afigure or problem, but not to appear in the finished plan. Occult qualities, those qualities whose effects only were observed, but the nature and relations of whose productive agencies were undetermined; so called by the schoolmen. Occult sciences, those sciences of the Middle Ages which related to the supposed action or influence of occult qualities, or supernatural powers, as alchemy, magic, necromancy, and astrology.
occultation: The hiding of a heavenly body from sight by the intervention of some other of the heavenly bodies; applied especially to eclipses of stars and planets by the moon, and to the eclipses of satellites of planets by their primaries.
occulter: Any object, natural or man-made, that blocks the light of an object from an observer, typically used in reference to astronomical events.
occultism: A certain Oriental system of theosophy. A. P. Sin nett.
occupancy: The act of taking or holding possession; possession; occupation. Title by occupancy (Law), a right of property acquired by taking the first possession of a thing, or possession of a thing which belonged to nobody, and appropriating it. Black stone. Kent.
occupant: One who occupies, or takes possession; one who has the actual use or possession, or is in possession, of a thing.
occupation: the principal activity in your life that you do to earn money
occupational: of or relating to the activity or business for which you are trained
occupied: held or filled or in use
occupier: a member of a military force who is residing in a conquered foreign country
occupies: third-person singular simple present indicative of occupy
occupying: present participle and gerund of occupy
occur: come to one's mind; suggest itself
occurred: simple past and past participle of occur
occurring: present participle and gerund of occur
occurs: third-person singular simple present indicative of occur
occursion: A meeting; a clash; a collision. Boyle.
ocean: Of or pertaining to the main or great sea; as, the ocean waves; an ocean stream. Milton.
oceanaut: a skilled worker who can live in underwater installations and participate in scientific research
oceania: a large group of islands in the south Pacific including Melanesia and Micronesia and Polynesia (and sometimes Australasia and the Malay Archipelago)
oceanian: From or relating to Oceania (geographical region or continent).
oceanic: relating to or occurring or living in or frequenting the open ocean
oceanicity: The condition or degree of being oceanic.
oceanographer: a scientist who studies physical and biological aspects of the seas
oceanology: That branch of science which relates to the ocean.
oceanus: The god of the great outer sea, or the river which was believed to flow around the whole earth.
ocellus: A little eye; a minute simple eye found in many invertebrates.
ocelot: An American feline carnivore (Felis pardal is). It ranges from the Southwestern United States to Patagonia. It is covered with blackish ocellated spots and blotches, which are variously arranged. The ground color varies from reddish gray to tawny yellow.
och: general interjection of confirmation, affirmation, and often disapproval.
ochlesis: A general morbid condition induced by the crowding together of many persons, esp. sick persons, under one roof. G. Gregory.
ochlocracy: A form of government by the multitude; a mobocracy. Hare.
ochnaceae: family of tropical evergreen trees and shrubs with thick shining parallel-veined leaves
ochreate: Provided with ocreae, or sheath-formed stipules, such as found in the rhubarb, yellow dock, and knotgrass.
ochronosis: an accumulation of dark pigment in cartilage and other connective tissue; usually a symptom of alkaptonuria or phenol poisoning
ock: A man of Middle Eastern descent that runs a deli or bodega, typically in New York.
ocotillo: desert shrub of southwestern United States and Mexico having slender naked spiny branches that after the rainy season put forth foliage and clusters of red flowers
ocracy: Any of various forms of government or rule as designated by words ending in -ocracy.
octachord: An instrument of eight strings; a system of eight tones.
octad: An atom or radical which has a valence of eight, or is octavalent.
octadecanoic: Of or pertaining to octadecanoic acid or its derivatives
octagon: A plane figure of eight sides and eight angles.
octagonal: Having eight sides and eight angles.
octahedral: Having eight faces or sides; of, pertaining to, or formed in, octahedrons; as, octahedral cleavage. Octahedral borax (Chem.), borax obtained from a saturated solution in octahedral crystals, which contain five molecules of water of crystallization; distinguished from common or prismatic borax. Octahedral iron ore (Min.), magnetite.
octahedrite: Titanium dioxide occurring in acute octahedral crystals.
octahedron: A solid bounded by eight faces. The regular octahedron is contained by eight equal equilateral triangles.
octahydrate: A hydrate whose solid contains eight molecules of water of crystallization per molecule, or per unit cell.
octal: of or pertaining to a number system having as its base
octamerous: Having the parts in eights; as, an octamerous flower; octamerous mesenteries in polyps.
octane: Any one of a group of meta metric hydrocarcons (CH) of the methane series. The most important is a colorless, volatile, inflammable liquid, found in petroleum, and a constituent of benzene or ligroin.
octangle: A geometric figure with eight corners, an octagon.
octangular: Having eight angles; eight-angled. Octangularness, n.
octanol: Any of many isomers of the saturated aliphatic alcohol having eight carbon atoms, but especially the simple primary alcohol n-octanol; its esters are used in perfumery
octant: The eighth part of a circle; an arc of degrees.
octastich: A poem or strophe of eight verses or lines.
octavalent: Having a valence of eight; capable of being combined with, exchanged for, or compared with, eight atoms of hydrogen; said of certain atoms or radicals.
octave: The first two stanzas of a sonnet, consisting of four verses each; a stanza of eight lines. With mournful melody it continued this octave. Sir P. Sidney. Double octave. (Mus.) See under Double. Octave flute (Mus.), a small flute, the tones of which range an octave higher than those of the German or ordinary flute; called also piccolo. See Piccolo.
octavian: A male given name from Latin, notably borne by Augustus (Caesar) between and BCE
octennial: Happening every eighth year; also, lasting a period of eight years. Johnson. Octennially, adv.
octet: A composition for eight parts, usually for eight solo instruments or voices.
octette: a musical composition written for eight performers
octic: Of the eighth degree or order. n. (Alg.)
octillion: According to the French method of numeration (which method is followed also in the United States) the number expressed by a unit with twenty-seven ciphers annexed. According to the English method, the number expressed by a unit with forty-eight ciphers annexed. Se enumeration.
october: the month following September and preceding November
octocerata: A suborder of Cephalopoda including Octopus, Argonauta, an dallied genera, having eight arms around the head; called also octopoda.
octodecimo: Having eighteen leaves to a sheet; as, an octodecimo form, book, leaf, size, etc.
octogenarian: A person eighty years, or more, of age.
octogenary: Of eighty years of age. Being then octogenary. " Aubrey.
octoic: Pertaining to, derived from, or resembling, octane; used specifically, to designate any one of a group of acids, the most important of which is called caprylic acid.
octonary: Of or pertaining to the number eight. Dr. H. More.
octoploid: having eight complete sets of chromosomes in a single cell
octopus: A genus of eight-armed cephalopods, including numerous species, some of them of large size. See Devilfish,
octoroon: The offspring of a quadroon and a white person; a mestee.
octostyle: Having eight columns in the front; said of a temple or portico. The Parthenon is octostyle, but most large Greek temples arehexastele. See Hexastyle. n.
octosyllabic: having or characterized by or consisting of eight syllables
octroi: a tax on various goods brought into a town
octuplet: A group of eight things, particularly
octyl: A hypothetical hydrocarbon radical regarded as an essential residue of octane, and as entering into its derivatives; as, octyl alcohol.
octylene: Any one of a series of metameric hydrocarbons (CH) of the ethylene series. In general they are combustible, colorless liquids.
octylic: Pertaining to, derived from, or containing, octyl; as, octylic ether.
ocular: Of or pertaining to the eye; optic.
oculary: Of or pertaining to the eye; ocular; optic; as, oculary medicines. Holland.
oculiform: In the form of an eye; resembling an eye; as, an oculiform pebble.
oculist: One skilled in treating diseases of the eye.
oculomotor: Of or pertaining to the movement of the eye; applied especially to the common motor nerves (or third pair of cranial nerves) which supply many of the muscles of the orbit. n.
oculonasal: Of or pertaining to the region of the eye and the nose; as, the oculonasal, or nasal, nerve, one of the branches of the ophthalmic.
oculus: A round window, usually a small one.
ocypodian: One of a tribe of crabs which live in holes in the sand along the seashore, and run very rapidly, whence the name.
od: An alleged force or natural power, supposed, by Reichenbach and others, to produce the phenomena of mesmerism, and to be developed by various agencies, as by magnets, heat, light, chemical or vital action, etc.; called also odyle or the odylic force. That od force of German Reichenbach Which still, from female fingertips, burnt blue. Mrs. Browning.
odal: Among the early and medieval Teutonic peoples, esp. Scandinavians, the heritable land held by the various odalmenconstituting a family or kindred of freeborn tribesmen; also, the ownership of such land. The odal was subject only to certain rights of the family or kindred in restricting the freedom of transfer or sale and giving certain rights of redemption in case of change of ownership by inheritance, etc., and perhaps to other rights of the kindred or the tribe. Survivals of the early odal estates and tenure exist in Ork ney and Shetland, where it is usually called by the variant form udal.
odalisque: A female slave or concubine in the harem of the Turkish sultan. Not of those that men desire, sleek Odalisques, or oracles of mode. Tennyson.
odalman: A man having odal, or able to share in it by inheritance.
oddball: a person with an unusual or odd personality
oddity: eccentricity that is not easily explained
oddly: In a manner measured by an odd number.
oddness: the parity of odd numbers (not divisible by two)
odds: the likelihood of a thing occurring rather than not occurring
ode: A short poetical composition proper to be set to music or sung; a lyric poem; esp., now, a poem characterized by sustained noble sentiment and appropriate dignity of style. Hangs odes upon hawthorns and elegies on brambles. O! run; prevent them with thy humble ode, And lay it lowly at his blessed feet. Milton. Ode factor, one who makes, or who traffics in, odes; used contemptuously.
odeon: A kind of theater in ancient Greece, smaller than the dramatic theater and roofed over, in which poets and musicians submitted their works to the approval of the public, and contended for prizes; hence, in modern usage, the name of a hall for musical or dramatic performances.
oder: a European river; flows into the Baltic Sea
odessa: a port city of south central Ukraine on an arm of the Black Sea
odic: Of or pertaining to od. See Od. Odically, adv.
odin: The supreme deity of the Scandinavians; the same as Woden, of the German tribes. There in the Temple, carved in wood, The image of great Odin stood. Longfellow.
odinism: Worship of Odin; broadly, the Teutonic heathenism. Odinist, n.
odinite: A monoclinic-domatic mineral containing aluminum, hydrogen, iron, magnesium, manganese, oxygen, silicon, and titanium.
odious: Hateful; deserving or receiving hatred; as, an odious name, system, vice. All wickedness will be most odious. " Sprat. He rendered himself odious to the Parliament. Clarendon.
odiously: in an offensive and hateful manner
odium: state of disgrace resulting from detestable behavior
odograph: A machine for registering the distance traversed by a vehicle or pedes train.
odometer: An instrument attached to the wheel of a vehicle, to measure the distance traversed; also, a wheel used by surveyors, which registers the miles and rods traversed.
odometrical: Of or pertaining to the odometer, or to measurements made with it.
odometry: Measurement of distances by the odometer.
odonate: large primitive predatory aquatic insect having two pairs of membranous wings
odontoblast: One of the more or less columnar cells on the outer surface of the pulp of a tooth; an odontoplast. They are supposed to be connected with the formation of dentine.
odontocete: A subdivision of Cetacea, including the sperm whale, dolphins, etc.; the toothed whales.
odontogenic: Of or pertaining to the formation and development of teeth
odontoglossum: any of numerous and diverse orchids of the genus Odontoglossum having racemes of few to many showy usually large flowers in many colors
odontoid: Having the form of a tooth; toothlike.
odontology: The science which treats of the teeth, their structure and development.
odontophore: A special structure found in the mouth of most mollusks, except bivalves. It consists of several muscles and a cartilage which supports a chitinous radula, or lingual ribbon, armed with teeth. Also applied to the radula alone. See Radula.
odor: Any smell, whether fragrant or offensive; scent; perfume. Meseemed I smelt a garden of sweet flowers, That dainty odors from them threw around. Spenser. To be in bad odor, to be out of favor, or in bad repute.
odored: Having an odor, especially having a specified odor.
odoriferous: Bearing or yielding an odor; perfumed; usually, sweet of scent; fragrant; as, odoriferous spices, particles, fumes, breezes. Milton. Odoriferously, adv. Odoriferousness, n.
odorize: cause to smell or be smelly
odorometer: A device used to measure the intensity of a smell
odorous: Having or emitting an odor or scent, esp. a sweet odor; fragrant; sweet-smelling. Odorous bloom. " Keble. Such fragrant flowers do give most odorous smell. Spenser. Odorously, adv. Odorousness, n.
odour: any property detected by the olfactory system
ods: A corruption of God's; formerly used in oaths and ejaculatory phrases. Ods bodikin. " Ods pity.
odum: Synonym of mvule (a tree of species Milicia excelsa)
odylic: Of or pertaining to odyle; odic; as, odylic force.
odylism: A belief in a vital force known as od or odyle.
odysseus: (Greek mythology) a famous mythical Greek hero; his return to Ithaca after the siege of Troy was described in the Odyssey
odyssey: An epic poem attributed to Homer, which describes the return of ulysses to Ithaca after the siege of Troy.
oe: a diphthong, employed in the Latin language, and thence in the english language, as the representative of the Greek diphthong oe. In many words in common use, e alone stands instead of oe. Classicists prefer to write the diphthong oe separate in Latin words.
oecology: The various relations of animals and plants to one another andto the outer world.
oecus: An apartment, room, or hall in an ancient Roman dwelling house.
oedema: A swelling from effusion of watery fluid in the cellular tissue beneath the skin or mucous membrance; dropsy of the subcutaneous cellular tissue.
oedipal: Of or relating to the Oedipus complex.
oedipus: (Greek mythology) a tragic king of Thebes who unknowingly killed his father Laius and married his mother Jocasta; the subject of the drama Oedipus Rex' by Sophocles
oeillade: A glance, especially an amorous one; an ogle
oenanthic: Having, or imparting, the odor characteristic of the bouquet of wine; specifically used, formerly, to designate an acid whose ethereal salts were supposed to occasion the peculiar bouquet, or aroma, of old wine. Cf. OEnanthylic. OEnanthic acid, an acid obtained from oenanthic ether by the action of alkalies. OEnanthic ether, an ethereal substance (not to be confused with the bouquet, or aroma, of wine) found in wine lees, and consisting of a complex mixture of the ethereal salts of several of the higher acids of the acetic acid series. It has an ethereal odor, and it used in flavoring artificial wines and liquors. Called also oil of wine. See Essential oil, under Essential.
oenanthyl: A hydrocarbon radical formerly supposed to exist in oenanthic acid, now known to be identical with heptyl.
oenanthylate: A salt of oenanthylic acid; as, potassium oenanthylate.
oenanthylic: Pertaining to, derived from, or containing, oenanthyl; specifically, designating an acid formerly supposed to be identical with the acid in oenanthic ether, but now known to be identical with heptoic acid.
oenochoe: A type of Ancient Greek pottery wine jug.
oenological: Of or pertaining to oenology, the study of wine.
oenology: Knowledge of wine, scientific or practical.
oenothera: chiefly North American herbs with usually nocturnal flowers
oersted: The C.G.S. unit of magnetic reluctance or resistance, equal to the reluctance of a centimeter cube of air (or vacuum) between parallel faces. Also, a reluctance in which unit magnetomotive force sets up unit flux.
oesophagus: the passage between the pharynx and the stomach
oestrogen: a general term for female steroid sex hormones that are secreted by the ovary and responsible for typical female sexual characteristics
oestrone: a naturally occurring weak estrogenic hormone secreted by the mammalian ovary
oestrual: Of or pertaining to sexual desire; mostly applied to brute animals; as, the oestrual period; oestrual influence.
oestruate: To be in heat (state of sexual receptivity).
oestruation: The state of being under oestrual influence, or of having sexual desire.
oestrum: A biting insect; a gadfly or botfly.
oeuvre: the total output of a writer or artist (or a substantial part of it)
of: In a general sense, from, or out from; proceeding from; belonging to; relating to; concerning; used in a variety of applications; as:
off: In a general sense, denoting from or away from; as:
offal: viscera and trimmings of a butchered animal often considered inedible by humans
offend: To oppose or obstruct in duty; to cause to stumble; to cause tosin or to fall. Who hath you misboden or offended. Chaucer. If thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out. And if thy right hand offend thee, cut it off. Matt. v., O.Great peace have they which love thy law, and nothing shall offend them. Ps. cxix.
offender: One who offends; one who violates any law, divine or human; awrong doer. I and my son Solomon shall be counted offenders. Kings i.
offending: offending against or breaking a law or rule
offends: third-person singular simple present indicative of offend
offense: the team that has the ball (or puck) and is trying to score
offenseful: Causing offense; displeasing; wrong; as, an offenseful act.
offensive: The state or posture of one who offends or makes attack; aggressive attitude; the act of the attacking party; opposed to defensive. To act on the offensive, to be the attacking party.
offer: make available or accessible, provide or furnish
offered: simple past and past participle of offer
offerer: One who offers; esp., one who offers something to God in worship. Hooker.
offering: money contributed to a religious organization
offeror: someone who presents something to another for acceptance or rejection
offertory: the offerings of the congregation at a religious service
offhand: Instant; ready; extemporaneous; as, an offhand speech; offhand excuses. adv.
office: The apartments or outhouses in which the domestics discharge the duties attached to the service of a house, as kitchens, pantries, stables, etc. As for the offices, let them stand at distance. Bacon.
officeholder: An officer, particularly one in the civil service; a placeman.
officer: Specifically, a commissioned officer, in distinction from awarrant officer. Field officer, General officer, etc. See under field, General. etc. Officer of the day (Mil.), the officer who, on a given day, has charge for that day of the quard, prisoners, and police of the post or camp. Officer of the deck, or Officer of the watch (Naut.), the officer temporarily in charge on the deck of a vessel, esp. a war vessel.
officered: simple past and past participle of officer
official: Approved by authority; sanctioned by the pharmacopoeia; appointed to be used in medicine; as, an official drug or preparation. Cf. Officinal.
officialdom: people elected or appointed to administer a government
officialism: The state of being official; a system of official government; also, adherence to office routine; red-tapism. Officialism may often drift into blunders. Smiles.
officialization: The process or result of officializing.
officializing: present participle and gerund of officialize
officially: By the proper officer; by virtue of the proper authority; in pursuance of the special powers vested in an officer or office; as, accounts or reports officially vertified or rendered; letters officially communicated; persons officially notified.
officialty: The charge, office, court, or jurisdiction of an official. Ayliffe.
officiant: The officer who officiates or performs an office, as the burial office. Shi pley.
officiate: To act as an officer in performing a duty; to transact the business of an office or public trust; to conduct a public service. Bp. Stilling fleet.
officiated: simple past and past participle of officiate
officiates: third-person singular simple present indicative of officiate
officina: A monetary office that issues coins.
officinal: Kept in stock by apothecaries; said of such drugs and medicines as may be obtained without special preparation or compounding; not magistral.
officious: Pertaining to, or being in accordance with, duty. If there were any lie in the case, it could be no more than as officious and venial one. Note on Gen. xxvii. (Douay version).
offing: That part of the sea at a good distance from the shore, or where there is deep water and no need of a pilot; also, distance from the shore; as, the ship had ten miles offing; we saw a ship in the offing.
offload: transfer to a peripheral device, of computer data
offloaded: simple past and past participle of offload
offscour: To remove by, or as if by, scouring; to scrub away.
offscouring: That which is scoured off; hence, refuse; rejected matter; that which is vile or despised. Lam. iii.
offset: In general, that which is set off, from, before, or against, something; as:
offshoot: That which shoots off or separates from a main stem, channel, family, race, etc.; as, the offshoots of a tree.
offshore: From the shore; as, an offshore wind; an offshore signal.
offside: illegally in advance of the ball or puck
offspring: the immediate descendants of a person
oficina: A nitrate-producing factory in a Spanish-speaking country.
oft: Often; frequently; not rarely; many times. Chaucer. Oft she rejects, but never once offends. Pope.
oftenest: superlative form of often: most often
oftensith: Frequently; often. For whom I sighed have so oftensith. Gas coigne.
ogden: English psychologist who collaborated with I. A. Richards in designing Basic English (-)
ogdoad: A thing made up of eight parts. Mil man.
ogee: A molding, the section of which is the form of the letter S, with the convex part above; cyma re versa. See Illust. under Cyma.
ogham: A particular kind of writing practiced by the ancient Irish, and found in inscriptions on stones, metals, etc.
oghamic: In, of, or pertaining to Ogham.
oghamist: Someone who specialises in the academic study of Ogham inscriptions.
oghuz: A group of south-western Turkic people, including the Turks and Turkmens
ogival: Having the curved, pointed shape of an ogive.
ogive: The arch or rib which crosses a Gothic vault diagonally.
ogle: To view or look at with side glances, as in fondness, or with ade sign to attract notice. And ogling all their audience, ere they speak. Dryden.
ogled: simple past and past participle of ogle
ogling: Action of the verb to ogle.
ogre: An imaginary monster, or hideous giant of fairy tales, who lived on human beings; hence, any frightful giant; a cruel monster. His schoolroom must have resembled an ogre's den. Maccaulay.
ogreish: Resembling an ogre; having the character or appearance of an ogre; suitable for an ogre. An ogreish kind of jocularity. " Dickens.
ogreism: The character or manners of an ogre.
oh: An exclamation expressing various emotions, according to the tone and manner, especially surprise, pain, sorrow, anxiety, or awish. See the Note under O.
ohia: Either of two flowering trees of the myrtle family, especially
ohio: a midwestern state in north central United States in the Great Lakes region
ohioan: a native or resident of Ohio
ohmage: the ohmic resistance of a conductor
ohmic: of or relating to or measured in ohms
ohmmeter: An instrument for indicating directly resistance in ohms.
ohms: Initialism of On Her Majesty's/His Majesty's Service.
oik: a member of the lower classes.
oil: Any one of a great variety of unctuous combustible substances, not miscible with water; as, olive oil, whale oil, rock oil, etc. They are of animal, vegetable, or mineral origin and of varied composition, and they are variously used for food, for solvents, for anointing, lubrication, illumination, etc. By extension, any substance of an oily consistency; as, oil of vitriol.
oilcan: a can with a long nozzle to apply oil to machinery
oilcloth: Cloth treated with oil or paint, and used for marking garments, covering flooors, etc.
oilcup: A device that dispenses oil for lubrication in an engine, etc., without the need for a human operator.
oiled: Covered or treated with oil; dressed with, or soaked in, oil. Oiled silk, silk rendered waterproof by saturation with boiled oil.
oiler: a worker who oils engines or machinery
oilfield: a region rich in petroleum deposits (especially one with producing oil wells)
oiliness: The quality of being oily. Bacon.
oiling: present participle and gerund of oil
oilman: One who deals in oils; formerly, one who dealt in oils and pickles.
oilpaper: paper that has been made translucent and waterproof by soaking in oil
oilseed: any of several seeds that yield oil
oilstone: A variety of hone slate, or whetstone, used for whetting tools when lubricated with oil.
oiltight: So tightly made that oil cannot enter or escape.
oilway: An aperture or conduit for oil.
oink: the short low gruff noise of the kind made by hogs
ointment: That which serves to anoint; any soft unctuous substance used for smearing or anointing; an unguent.
oiticica: The tree Licania rigida, endemic to Brazil and Puerto Rico.
ojibwa: a member of an Algonquian people who lived west of Lake Superior
ok: in a satisfactory or adequate manner
oka: a Turkish unit of weight equal to about. pounds
okanagan: Of or relating to the Syilx people.
okapi: A peculiar mammal (Okapia johnostoni) closely related to the giraffe, discovered in the deep forests of Belgian Kongo in. Itis smaller than an ox, and somewhat like a giraffe, except that the neck is much shorter. Like the giraffe, it has no dewclaws. There is a small prominence on each frontal bone of the male. The color of the body is chiefly reddish chestnut, the cheeks are yellowish white, and the fore and hind legs above the knees and the haunches are striped with purplish black and cream color.
okay: in a satisfactory or adequate manner; (alright' is a nonstandard variant of all right')
oke: A Turkish and Egyptian weight, equal to about
okeechobee: a lake in southeast Florida to the north of the Everglades
okeh: in a satisfactory or adequate manner
oken: German naturalist whose speculations that plants and animals are made up of tiny living infusoria' led to the cell theory (-)
okinagan: A member of a Salishan tribe who once occupied an extensive territory on the Okinagan and Similkameen rivers in northern Washington and the adjacent part of British Columbia.
okinawa: the largest island of the central Ryukyu Islands
oklahoma: a state in south central United States
oklahoman: a native or resident of Oklahoma
okra: An annual plant (Abelmoschus, or Hibiscus, esculent us), whose green pods, abounding in nutritious mucilage, are much used for soups, stews, or pickles; gumbo.
okrug: An administrative division of some Slavic states.
okta: One eighth of the total area of the celestial dome; used as a measure of cloudiness (one okta means that one eighth of the sky is obscured, two oktas that one quarter is obscured, and so on).
oktoberfest: a strong lager made originally in Germany for the Oktoberfest celebration; sweet and copper-colored
ola: leaf or strip from a leaf of the talipot palm used in India for writing paper
olden: Old; ancient; as, the olden time. A minstrel of the olden stamp. " J. C. Sha irp.
oldenburg: United States sculptor (born in Sweden); a leader of the pop art movement who was noted for giant sculptures of common objects (born in )
oldest: superlative form of old: most old
oldie: a song that was formerly popular
oldness: The state or quality of being old; old age.
oldster: An old person. H. King sley.
oldstyle: A traditional style of typeface designed to mimic the handwriting of scribes.
oldwife: a common long-tailed sea duck of the northern parts of the United States
ole: An interjection used to stir up excitement.
olea: A genus of trees including the olive.
oleaceae: trees and shrubs having berries or drupes or capsules as fruits; sometimes placed in the order Ole ales: olive; ash; jasmine; privet; lilac
oleaginous: Having the nature or qualities of oil; oily; unctuous.
oleander: A beautiful evergreen shrub of the Dogbane family, having clusters of fragrant red or white flowers. It is native of the East indies, but the red variety has become common in the south of Europe. Called also rosebay, rose laurel, and South-sea rose.
olearia: large genus of Australian evergreen shrubs or small trees with large daisylike flowers
oleaster: any of several shrubs of the genus Elaeagnus having silver-white twigs and yellow flowers followed by olivelike fruits
oleate: A salt of oleic acid. Some oleates, as the oleate of mercury, are used in medicine by way of inunction.
olecranal: Of or pertaining to the olecranon.
olecranon: The large process at the proximal end of the ulna which projects behind the articulation with the humerus and forms the bony prominence of the elbow.
olefiant: Forming or producing an oil; specifically, designating acolorless gaseous hydrocarbon called ethylene.
olefine: Olefiant gas, or ethylene; hence, by extension, any one of the series of unsaturated hydrocarbons of which ethylene is a type. See ethylene.
oleic: Pertaining to, derived from, or contained in, oil; as, oleic acid, an acid of the acrylic acid series found combined with glyceryl in the form of olein in certain animal and vegetable fats and oils, such as sperm oil, olive oil, etc. At low temperatures the acid is crystalline, but melts to an oily liquid above
olenid: Any member of the family Olenidae of trilobites.
oleo: a spread made chiefly from vegetable oils and used as a substitute for butter
oleograph: The form or figure assumed by a drop of oil when placed upon water or some other liquid with which it does not mix.
oleography: Art or process of producing the pictures known as oleo graphs.
oleomargarine: A liquid oil made from animal fats (esp. beef fat) by separating the greater portion of the solid fat or stearin, by crystallization. It is mainly a mixture of olein and palmitin with some little stearin.
oleometer: An instrument for ascertaining the weight and purity of oil; an elaiometer.
oleoresin: A natural mixture of a terebinthinate oil and a resin.
olericulture: The field of horticulture dealing with the production, storage, processing and marketing of vegetables
oleum: A solution of sulfur trioxide in sulfuric acid.
olfactometry: The study and measurement of smells.
olfactory: Of, pertaining to, or connected with, the sense of smell; as, the olfactory nerves; the olfactory cells. Olfactory organ (Anat.),an organ for smelling. In vertebrates the olfactory organs are more or less complicated sacs, situated in the front part of the head and lined with epithelium innervated by the olfactory (or first cranial) nerves, and sensitive to odoriferous particles conveyed to it in the air or in water.
olibanum: The fragrant gum resin of various species of Boswellia; Oriental frankincense.
olibene: A colorless mobile liquid of a pleasant aromatic odor obtained by the distillation of olibanum, or frankincense, and regarded as aterpene; called also conimene.
oligaemia: The condition of having a low quantity of blood.
oligarch: A member of an oligarchy; one of the rulers in an oligarchical government.
oligarchic: of or relating to or supporting or characteristic of an oligarchy
oligarchical: of or relating to or supporting or characteristic of an oligarchy
oligarchy: A form of government in which the supreme power is placed in the hands of a few persons; also, those who form the ruling few. All oligarchies, wherein a few men domineer, do what they list. Burton.
oligist: Hematite or specular iron ore; prob. so called in allusion to its feeble magnetism, as compared with magnetite.
oligistic: Of or relating to oligist, or hematite.
oligocene: Of, pertaining to, or designating, certain strata which occupy an intermediate position between the Eocene and Miocene periods. n.
oligoclase: A triclinic soda-lime feldspar. See Feldspar.
oligodactyly: congenital condition in which some fingers or toes are missing
oligodendroglia: tissue consisting of glial cells with sheetlike processes that form the myelin sheath of nerve fibers
oligomer: A compound intermediate between a monomer and a polymer, normally having a specified number of units between about five and a hundred.
oligomeric: Of, pertaining to, or being an oligomer.
oligomerous: Having few members in each set of organs; as, an oligomerous flower.
oligonucleotide: A short sequence of nucleotides (RNA or DNA), typically with twenty or fewer base pairs.
oligopoly: (economics) a market in which control over the supply of a commodity is in the hands of a small number of producers and each one can influence prices and affect competitors
oligopsony: An economic condition in which a small number of buyers exert control over the market price of a commodity.
oligosaccharide: any of the carbohydrates that yield only a few monosaccharide molecules on complete hydrolysis
olitory: Of or pertaining to, or produced in, a kitchen garden; used for kitchen purposes; as, olitory seeds. At convenient distance towards the olitory garden. Evelyn.
oliva: A genus of polished marine gastropod shells, chiefly tropical, and often beautifully colored.
olivary: Like an olive. Olivary body (Anat.), an oval prominence on each side of the medulla oblongata; called also olive.
olive: An olivary body. See under Olivary.
olivenite: An olive-green mineral, a hydrous arseniate of copper; olive ore.
olivil: A white crystalline substance, obtained from an exudation from the olive, and having a bitter-sweet taste and acid proporties. Gregory.
olivin: A complex bitter gum, found on the leaves of the olive tree; called also olivite.
olivine: A common name of the yellowish green mineral chrysolite, esp.the variety found in eruptive rocks.
olla: A pot or jar having a wide mouth; a cinerary urn, especially one of baked clay.
ollamh: In Irish history, a man of science or learning, equivalent to a university professor.
ollie: An aerial maneuver in which one catches air by leaping off the ground with the skateboard and into the air.
ologist: One who studies some branch of learning, especially one ending in -ology; a specialist.
ology: A colloquial or humorous name for any science or branch of knowledge. He had a smattering of mechanics, of physiology, geology, mineralogy, and all other ologies whatsoever. De Quincey.
olonets: A variety of the Karelian language mainly spoken in the area between Lake Ladoga and Lake Onega.
olpe: Originally, a leather flask or vessel for oils or liquids; afterward, an earthenware vase or pitcher without a spout.
olusatrum: An umbelliferous plant, the common Alexanders of Western Europe (Smyrnium Olusatrum).
olympia: capital of the state of Washington; located in western Washington on Puget Sound
olympiad: A period of four years, by which the ancient Greeks reckoned time, being the interval from one celebration of the Olympic games to another, beginning with the victory of Coroebus in the foot race, which took place in the year b.c.; as, the era of the olympiads.
olympian: of the region of Olympia in Greece or its inhabitants
olympic: of or relating to the Olympic Games
olynthus: An ancient city in Chalcidice, modern Chalkidiki regional unit, Greece.
om: A mystic syllable or ejaculation used by Hindus and Buddhists in religious rites, orig. among the Hindus an exclamation of assent, like Amen, then an invocation, and later a symbol of the trinity formed by Vishnu, Siva, and Brahma. Om mani padme hun, as acred formula of buddhism (esp. of the La maists) translated O, the jewel in the Lotus, Amen," and referring to Amitabha, who is commonly represented as standing or sitting within a lotus.
omadhaun: A fool, someone who is out of their senses, simpleton.
omaha: a member of the Siouan people formerly living in the Missouri river valley in northeastern Nebraska
oman: a strategically located monarchy on the southern and eastern coasts of the Arabian Peninsula; the economy is dominated by oil
omani: of or relating to Oman or its people
omar: Omar bin al-Khattab, second Sunni Islamic caliph and a companion of Muhammad
omasum: The third division of the stomach of ruminants. See Manyplies, and Illust. under Ruminant.
ombre: A large Mediterranean food fish (Umbrina cirrhosa): called also umbra, and umbrine.
ombrograph: A rain gauge used as an instrument for recording the time of occurrence, quantity, and rapidity of rainfall.
ombrophile: Any plant that flourishes in a rainy environment.
ombrophilous: Capable of thriving in areas of heavy rainfall
ombudsman: a government appointee who investigates complaints by private persons against the government
omega: the ending of a series or sequence
omegoid: Having the form of the Greek capital letter Omega (
omelet: Eggs beaten up with a little flour, etc., and cooked in afrying pan; as, a plain omelet.
omelette: beaten eggs or an egg mixture cooked until just set
omen: An occurrence supposed to portend, or show the character of, some future event; any indication or action regarded as afore showing; a foreboding; a presage; an augury. Bid go with evil omen, and the brand Of infamy upon my name. Milton.
omened: Attended by, or containing, an omen or omens; as, happy-omened day.
omental: Of or pertaining to an omentum or the omenta.
omer: A Hebrew measure, the tenth of an ephah. See Ephah. Ex. xvi.
omicron: Lit., the little, or short, O, o; the fifteenth letter of the greek alphabet.
omikron: Alternative form of omikron; Alternative spelling of omicron.
ominate: To presage; to foreshow; to foretoken. Dr. H. More.
omination: The act of omina ting; presaging. Fuller.
ominous: Of or pertaining to an omen or to omens; being or exhibiting an omen; significant; portentous; formerly used both in a favorable and unfavorable sense; now chiefly in the latter; foreboding or foreshowing evil; inauspicious; as, an ominous dread. He had a good ominous name to have made a peace. Bacon. In the heathen worship of God, a sacrifice without a heart was accounted ominous. South. Ominously, adv. Ominousness, n.
omissible: Capable of being omitted; that may be omitted.
omissive: Leaving out; omitting. Bp. Hall. Omissively, adv.
omit: To let go; to leave unmentioned; not to insert or name; to drop. These personal comparisons I omit. Bacon.
omits: third-person singular simple present indicative of omit
omitted: simple past and past participle of omit
omitting: present participle and gerund of omit
ommastrephes: extremely active cylindrical squid with short strong arms and large rhombic terminal fins
ommateum: A compound eye, as of insects and crustaceans.
ommatidium: One of the single eyes forming the compound eyes of crustaceans, insects, and other invertebrates.
omniarch: A ruler of the world or everything.
omnibenevolent: All-loving, or infinitely good, usually in reference to a deity or supernatural being, for example, God.
omnibus: A sheet-iron cover for articles in a leer or annealing arch, to protect them from drafts. Omnibus bill, a legislative bill which provides for a number of miscellaneous enactments or appropriations. Omnibus box, a large box in a theater, on a level with the stage and having communication with it. Thackeray.
omniety: That which is all-pervading or all-comprehensive; hence, the deity. Omniety formed nullity into an essence. Sir T. Browne.
omnifarious: Of all varieties, forms, or kinds. Omnifarious learning. Coleridge.
omniform: Having every form or shape. Berkeley.
omnify: To render universal; to enlarge. Omnify the disputed point into a transcendent, and you may defy the opponent to lay hold of it. Coleridge.
omniparient: Producing or bringing forth all things; all-producing.
omnipotence: the state of being omnipotent; having unlimited power
omnipotent: Able in every respect and for every work; unlimited in ability; all-powerful; almighty; as, the Being that can create worlds must be omnipotent. God's will and pleasure and his omnipotent power. Sir T. More.
omnipresence: Presence in every place at the same time; unbounded or universal presence; ubiquity. His omnipresence fills Land, sea, and air, and every kind that lives. Milton.
omnipresent: Present in all places at the same time; ubiquitous; as, the omnipresent Jehovah. Prior.
omniscience: The quality or state of being omniscient; an attribute peculiar to God. Dryden.
omniscient: Having universal knowledge; knowing all things; infinitely knowing or wise; as, the omniscient God. Omnisciently, adv. For what can scape the eye Of God all-seeing, or deceive his heart omniscient Milton.
omnispective: Beholding everything; capable of seeing all things; all-seeing. Omnispective Power!" Boyse.
omnivora: A group of ungulate mammals including the hog and the hippopotamus. The term is also sometimes applied to the bears, and to certain passerine birds.
omnivore: a person who eats all kinds of foods
omohyoid: Of or pertaining to the shoulder and the hyoid bone; as, the omohyoid muscle.
omophagic: Eating raw flesh; using uncooked meat as food; as, omophagic feasts, rites.
omophorion: A band of brocade originally of wool decorated with crosses and worn on the neck and around the shoulders as the distinguishing vestment of a bishop and the symbol of his spiritual and ecclesiastical authority in the Eastern Christian liturgical tradition, equivalent to the Western archepiscopal pallium.
omosternum: The anterior element of the sternum which projects forward from between the clavicles in many batrachians and is usually tipped with cartilage.
omphacine: Of, pertaining to, or expressed from, unripe fruit; as, omphacine oil.
omphalode: The central part of the hilum of a seed, through which the nutrient vessels pass into the rhaphe or the chalaza; called also omphalodium.
omphalomesenteric: Of or pertaining to the umbilicus and mesentery; omphalomesaraic; as, the omphalomesenteric arteries and veins of afetus.
omphaloskepsis: literally, the contemplation of one's navel, which is an idiom usually meaning complacent self-absorption
omphalus: a scar where the umbilical cord was attached
on: The general signification of on is situation, motion, or condition with respect to contact or support beneath; as:
onager: A military engine acting like a sling, which threw stones from a bag or wooden bucket, and was operated by machinery. Fair holt.
onagraceae: a large and widely distributed family of plants of the order Myrtales
onappo: A nocturnal South American monkey (Callithrix discolor), noted for its agility; called also ventriloquist monkey.
onboard: Carried or used on or in a vehicle or vessel.
onca: Initialism of Ontario Court of Appeal.
onchocerciasis: infestation with slender threadlike roundworms (filaria) deposited under the skin by the bite of black fleas; when the eyes are involved it can result in blindness; common in Africa and tropical America
oncidium: A genus of tropical orchidaceous plants, the flower of one species of which (O. Papilio) resembles a butterfly.
oncogene: a gene that disposes normal cells to change into cancerous tumor cells
oncology: the branch of medicine concerned with the study and treatment of tumors
oncometer: An instrument for measuring the variations in size of the internal organs of the body, as the kidney, spleen, etc.
oncorhynchus: Pacific salmon including sockeye salmon; chinook salmon; chum salmon; coho salmon
ondograph: An instrument for autographically recording the wave forms of varying currents, esp. rapidly varying alternating currents.
ondoyant: Wavy; having the surface marked by waves or slightly depressed furrows; as, ondoyant glass.
one: Any person, indefinitely; a person or body; as, what one would have well done, one should do one's self. It was well worth one's while. Hawthorne. Against this sort of condemnation one must steel one's self as one best can. G. Eliot.
onefold: Constituting or being indicative of a single aspect or theme.
oneida: a member of the Iroquoian people formerly living east of Lake Ontario
oneirocritic: An interpreter of dreams. Bp. War burton. Addison.
oneness: The state of being one; singleness in number; individuality; unity. Our God is one, or rather very oneness. Hooker.
onerous: Burdensome; oppressive. Too onerous a solicitude. " I. Taylor. Onerous cause (Scots Law), a good and legal consideration; opposed to gratuitous.
oneself: A reflexive form of the indefinite pronoun one. Commonly write nas two words, one's self. One's self (or more properly oneself), is quite a modern form. In elizabethan English we find a man's self=one's self. Morris.
ongoing: The act of going forward; progress; (pl.) affairs; business; current events. The common on goings of this our commonplace world, and everyday life. Prof. Wilson.
oni: A Japanese evil spirit or demon.
oniomania: An abnormal impulse to buy things, or a condition characterised by such impulses.
onionskin: A kind of thin translucent paper with a glossy finish.
oniony: Resembling an onion or onions, especially in terms of smell.
onium: Any cation derived by the addition of a proton to the hydride of any element of the nitrogen, chalcogen or halogen families.
onlay: To lay or place something on a surface.
onloft: Aloft; above ground. She kept her father's life onloft. Chaucer.
only: Save or except (that); an adversative used elliptically with or without that, and properly introducing a single fact or consideration. He might have seemed some secretary or clerk. only that his low, flat, unadorned cap. indicated that he belonged to the city. Sir W. Scott.
onobrychis: genus of Old World herbs having pinnate leaves and pink or whites racemose flowers followed by flat unjointed pods
onoclea: one species: sensitive fern; in some classifications included in Polypodiaceae
onomancy: Divination by the letters of a name; nomancy. Camden.
onomasiology: A branch of lexicology concerned with the names of concepts.
onomastic: Applied to a signature when the body of the instrument is in another's handwriting. Bur rill.
onomatology: The science of names or of their classification.
onomatopoeia: The formation of words in imitation of sounds; a figure of speech in which the sound of a word is imitative of the sound of the thing which the word represents; as, the buzz of bees; the hiss of ag oose; the crackle of fire.
onomatopoetic: Of or pertaining to onomatopoeia; characterized by onomatopoeia; imitative; as, an onomatopoetic writer or word. Earle.
onondaga: a member of the Iroquoian people formerly living between Lake Champlain and the Saint Lawrence River
ononis: genus of European subshrubs or herbs having pink or purple or yellow solitary or clustered flowers: restharrow
onshore: on the edge of the land
onslaught: a sudden and severe onset of trouble
onstead: A single farmhouse; a steading. Grose. Jamie son.
ontario: a prosperous and industrialized province in central Canada
onto: On the top of; upon; on. See On to, under On, prep.
ontogenesis: (biology) the process of an individual organism growing organically
ontogenetic: Of or pertaining to ontogenesis; as, ontogenetic phenomena. Ontogenetically, adv.
ontogeny: (biology) the process of an individual organism growing organically
ontologism: An ideological system which maintains that God and divine ideas are the first object of our intelligence and the intuition of God's existence the first act of our intellect.
ontologize: To convert into ontological entities or express in ontological terms.
ontology: That department of the science of metaphysics which investigates and explains the nature and essential properties and relations of all beings, as such, or the principles and causes of being.
onus: A burden; an obligation. Onus probandi ( Etym:, obligation to furnish evidence to prove a thing; the burden of proof.
onward: Toward a point before or in front; forward; progressively; as, to move onward. Not one looks backward, onward still he goes. Pope.
onychopathy: A disease of the fingernails or toenails.
onyx: Chalcedony in parallel layers of different shades of color. Itis used for making cameos, the figure being cut in one layer with the next as a ground. Onyx marble, a banded variety of marble or calcium carbonate resembling onyx. It is obtained from Mexico.
ooblast: A cell that develops into an ovum; a germinal epithelium giving rise to ova.
oocyesis: Ovarian pregnancy: the type of ectopic pregnancy that occurs within an ovary.
oocyst: A reproductive cell in certain fungi.
oocyte: a female gametocyte that develops into an ovum after two meiotic divisions
ooecium: One of the special zooids, or cells, of Bryozoa, destined to receive and develop ova; an ovicell. See Bryozoa.
oof: A sound mimicking the loss of air, as if someone's solar plexus had just been struck.
oogamete: The female gamete; the egg cell or oosphere.
oogamy: A form of anisogamy (heterogamy) in which the female gamete (e.g. ovum) is significantly larger than the male gamete (sperm) and is non-motile.
oogonium: An immature ovarian egg within a developing fetus.
ooh: express admiration and pleasure by uttering ooh' or aah'
ooid: A small calcium carbonate or iron coated grain found on the seafloor.
oolak: An Indian boat for transporting freight.
oolite: A rock consisting of spherical grains within a mineral cortex accreted around a nucleus, often of quartz grains.
oolith: A spherical granule of which oolite is composed, formed by concentric accretion of thin layers of a mineral (usually calcium carbonate (limestone) but also others such as dolomite and silica) around a core; an ooid.
oologist: a person who studies or specializes in oology
oology: the branch of zoology that studies eggs (especially birds' eggs and their size, shape, coloration, and number)
oolong: A fragrant variety of black tea having somewhat the flavor of green tea.
oomancy: Divination through the use of eggs.
oomph: the activeness of an energetic personality
oomycetes: nonphotosynthetic fungi that resemble algae and that reproduce by forming oospores; sometimes classified as protoctists
oop: To bind with a thread or cord; to join; to unite. Jamie son.
oophore: A form of some ferns and mosses that bear sexual fruit.
oophorectomize: To perform, or to undergo an oophorectomy
oophorectomy: surgical removal of one of both ovaries
oophoridium: The macrosporangium or case for the larger kind of spore in heterosporous flowerless plants.
oosperm: The ovum, after fusion with the spermatozoon in impregnation.
oosphere: a gamete; used especially of lower plants
oospore: a thick-walled sexual spore that develops from a fertilized oosphere in some algae and fungi
oostegite: One of the plates which, in some crustaceans, enclose a cavity in which the eggs are hatched.
ootheca: An egg case of any of the orthopteroid insects (such as cockroaches and mantids).
ootid: mature ovum after penetration by sperm but before the formation of a zygote
ooze: To cause to ooze. Alex. Smith.
oozes: third-person singular simple present indicative of ooze
ooziness: The state or condition of being oozy.
oozooid: A zooid that develops from an egg and reproduces by budding
oozy: Miry; containing soft mud; resembling ooze; as, the oozy bed of a river. Pope.
opacity: the phenomenon of not permitting the passage of electromagnetic radiation
opah: A large oceanic fish (Lam pris quttatus), inhabiting the atlantic Ocean. It is remarkable for its brilliant colors, which are red, green, and blue, with tints of purple and gold, covered with round silvery spots. Called also king of the herrings.
opal: A mineral consisting, like quartz, of silica, but inferior to quartz in hardness and specific gravity.
opalesce: To give forth a play of colors, like the opal.
opalescence: A reflection of a milky or pearly light from the interior of amin eral, as in the moonstone; the state or quality of being opalescent.
opalescent: Reflecting a milky or pearly light from the interior; having an opaline play of colors.
opaline: Of, pertaining to, or like, opal in appearance; having changeable colors like those of the opal.
opalize: To convert into opal, or a substance like opal. Lyell.
opaque: That which is opaque; opacity. Young.
opata: An indigenous people of northern Sonora.
ope: Open. Spenser. On Sunday heaven's gate stands ope. Herbert.
opec: Acronym of Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries.
oped: simple past and past participle of ope
opegrapha: Any lichen species of the genus Opegrapha.
open: Open or unobstructed space; clear land, without trees or obstructions; open ocean; open water. To sail into the open. " Jowett (Thucyd. ).Then we got into the open. W. Black. In open, in full view; without concealment; openly. Beau. &Fl.
opener: One who, or that which, opens. True opener of my eyes. Milton.
openmouthed: with eyes or mouth open in surprise
openness: The quality or state of being open.
openwork: A quarry; an open cut. Raymond.
opera: a drama set to music; consists of singing with orchestral accompaniment and an orchestral overture and interludes
operability: The extent to which a system or device is operable.
operand: The symbol, quantity, or thing upon which a mathematical operation is performed; called also faciend.
operate: To perform some manual act upon a human body in a methodic almanner, and usually with instruments, with a view to restore soundness or health, as in amputation, lithotomy, etc.
operated: simple past and past participle of operate
operates: third-person singular simple present indicative of operate
operatic: of or relating to or characteristic of opera
operating: involved in a kind of operation
operation: Something to be done; some transformation to be made upon quantities, the transformation being indicated either by rules or symbols.
operational: pertaining to a process or series of actions for achieving a result
operationalism: (philosophy) the doctrine that the meaning of a proposition consists of the operations involved in proving or applying it
operationism: The doctrine that the meaning of a term consists of the operation(s) performed in defining it
operations: financial transactions at a brokerage; having to do with the execution of trades and keeping customer records
operative: Based upon, or consisting of, an operation or operations; as, operative surgery.
operativeness: The state or quality of being operative.
operator: One who performs some act upon the human body by means of the hand, or with instruments.
opercle: Any one of the bony plates which support the gill covers of fishes; an opercular bone.
opercular: Of, pertaining to, or like, an operculum.
operculum: a hard flap serving as a cover for (a) the gill slits in fishes or (b) the opening of the shell in certain gastropods when the body is retracted
operon: a segment of DNA containing adjacent genes including structural genes and an operator gene and a regulatory gene
operose: Wrought with labor; requiring labor; hence, tedious; wearisome. Operose proceeding. " Burke. A very operose calculation. " De Quincey. Operosely, adv. Operoseness, n.
ophelia: A female given name from Ancient Greek.
ophelic: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a substance (called ophelic acid) extracted from a plant (Ophelia) of the Gentian family as abit ter yellowish sirup, used in India as a febrifuge and tonic.
ophicleide: A large brass wind instrument, formerly used in the orchestra and in military bands, having a loud tone, deep pitch, and a compass of three octaves; now generally supplanted by bass and contrabass tubas. Moore (Encyc. of Music).
ophidia: The order of reptiles which includes the serpents.
ophidian: One of the Ophidia; a snake or serpent.
ophioglossaceae: a family of succulent ferns of order Ophioglossales; cosmopolitan in distribution
ophioglossum: the type genus of the fern family Ophioglossaceae
ophiology: That part of natural history which treats of the ophidians, or serpents.
ophion: A Titan-king of heaven, before being overthrown by Cronus and Rhea.
ophiophagus: A genus of venomous East Indian snakes, which feed on other snakes. Ophiophagus elaps is said to be the largest and most deadly of poisonous snakes.
ophism: Doctrines and rites of the Ophites.
ophite: Of or pertaining to a serpent.
ophitic: Having crystals of feldspar interspersed with plates of augite.
ophiuchus: A constellation in the Northern Hemisphere, delineated as a man holding a serpent in his hands; called also Serpentarius.
ophiuran: Of or pertaining to the Ophiurioid ea. n.
ophiurioid: Of or pertaining to the Ophiurioid ea. n.
ophthalmia: An inflammation of the membranes or coats of the eye or of the eyeball.
ophthalmite: An eyestalk; the organ which bears the compound eyes of decapod crustacea.
ophthalmologist: One skilled in ophthalmology; an oculist.
ophthalmology: The science which treats of the structure, functions, and diseases of the eye.
ophthalmometer: An instrument devised by Helmholtz for measuring the size of areflected image on the convex surface of the cornea and lens of the eye, by which their curvature can be ascertained.
ophthalmometry: Measurement of the visual acuity and refractive power of the eyes.
ophthalmoplegia: paralysis of the motor nerves of the eye
ophthalmoscope: An instrument for viewing the interior of the eye, particularly the retina. Light is thrown into the eye by a mirror (usually concave) and the interior is then examined with or without the aid of a lens. Ophthalmoscopic, a.
ophthalmoscopic: Of, pertaining to or using an ophthalmoscope.
ophthalmoscopy: examination of the interior of an eye using an ophthalmoscope
opianic: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an organic acid obtained by the oxidation of narcotine.
opiate: Inducing sleep; somniferous; narcotic; hence, anodyne; causing rest, dullness, or inaction; as, the opiate rod of Hermes. Milton.
opificer: An artificer; a workman. The almighty opificer. Bent ley.
opinable: Capable of being opined or thought. Holland.
opinative: Obstinate in holding opinions; opinionated.Opinatively, adv. Burton. Sir T. More.
opine: To have an opinion; to judge; to think; to suppose. South.
opined: simple past and past participle of opine
opines: third-person singular simple present indicative of opine
opiniate: To hold or maintain persistently. Barrow.
opiniative: Opinionative. Glanvill. Opiniatively, adv. Opiniativeness, n.
opinicus: An imaginary animal borne as a charge, having wings, an eagle'shead, and a short tail; sometimes represented without wings.
opinion: The formal decision, or expression of views, of a judge, an umpire, a counselor, or other party officially called upon to consider and decide upon a matter or point submitted. To be of opinion, to think; to judge. To hold opinion with, to agree with.
opinionable: Being, or capable of being, a matter of opinion; that can bethought; not positively settled; as, an opinionable doctrine. C. J.Elli cott.

opinionative: Unduly attached to one's own opinions; opinionated. Milton.

opisthoglyphous: Whose teeth include an enlarged pair at the back of the maxillae which normally angle backwards and are grooved to channel venom into the puncture.
opisthograph: Any early document (such as a roll of papyrus) that has writing on the back as well as the front.
opisthotonos: A tetanic spasm in which the body is bent backwards and stiffened.
opium: The inspissated juice of the Papaver somniferum, or white poppy.
opobalsam: The aromatic resinous juice of Commiphora opobalsamum (balm of Gilead).

opossum: Any American marsupial of the genera Didelphys and Chironectes. The common species of the United States is Didelphys Virginia na.
oppidan: Of or pertaining to a town. Howell.
oppilate: To crowd together; to fill with obstructions; to block up. Cocker am.

opportunist: One who advocates or practices opportunism.
opportunistic: taking immediate advantage, often unethically, of any circumstance of possible benefit
opportunity: a possibility due to a favorable combination of circumstances
opposability: The condition or quality of being opposable. In no savage have I ever seen the slightest approach to opposability of the great toe, which is the essential distinguishing feature of apes. A. R. Wallace.
opposable: capable of being placed opposite to something
opposed: being in opposition or having an opponent
opposeless: Not to be effectually opposed; irresistible. Your great opposeless wills.
opposer: One who opposes; an opponent; an antagonist; an adversary.
opposes: third-person singular simple present indicative of oppose
opposite: being directly across from each other; facing

oppositeness: The quality or state of being opposite.
oppositifolious: Placed at the same node with a leaf, but separated from it by the whole diameter of the stem; as, an oppositifolious peduncle.

oppositive: Capable of being put in opposition. Bp. Hall.

oppressively: in a heavy and oppressive way

opprobriate: To express opprobrium for or to view with opprobrium; to scorn.

opprobrium: Disgrace; infamy; reproach mingled with contempt; abusive language. Being both dramatic author and dramatic performer, he found himself heir to a twofold opprobrium. De Quincey.
oppugn: To fight against; to attack; to be in conflict with; to oppose; to resist. They said the manner of their impeachment they could not but conceived id oppugn the rights of Parliament. Clarendon.
oppugnant: Tending to awaken hostility; hostile; opposing; warring. Oppugnant forces. " I. Taylor. n.
oppugned: simple past and past participle of oppugn
oppugner: One who opposes or attacks; that which opposes. Selden.
oppugning: present participle and gerund of oppugn
ops: (Roman mythology) goddess of abundance and fertility; wife of Saturn; counterpart of Greek Rhea and Cybele of ancient Asia Minor
opsin: retinal protein formed by the action of light on rhodopsin

opsonization: process whereby opsonins make an invading microorganism more susceptible to phagocytosis
opsonize: make (cells) more susceptible to the action of phagocytes
opsonotherapy: treatment by increasing the opsonin levels in the bloodstream

optable: That may be chosen; desirable. Cocker am.
optative: Expressing desire or wish. Fuller. Optative mood (Gram.), that mood or form of a verb, as in Greek, Sanskrit, etc., in which a wish or desire is expressed.

optical: of or relating to or involving light or optics
optically: By optics or sight; with reference to optics. Optically active, Optically inactive (Chem. optician: a worker who makes glasses for remedying defects of vision
optics: That branch of physical science which treats of the nature and properties of light, the laws of its modification by opaque and transparent bodies, and the phenomena of vision.
optimal: most desirable possible under a restriction expressed or implied
optimates: The nobility or aristocracy of ancient Rome, as opposed to the populares.
optime: One of those who stand in the second rank of honors, immediately after the wranglers, in the University of Cambridge, England. They are divided into senior and junior optimes.
optimise: act as an optimist and take a sunny view of the world
optimism: The opinion or doctrine that everything in nature, being the work of God, is ordered for the best, or that the ordering of things in the universe is such as to produce the highest good.

optometrist: One who is skilled in or practices optometry.
opulent: Having a large estate or property; wealthy; rich; affluent; as, an opulent city; an opulent citizen. Opulently, adv. I will piece Her opulent throne with kingdoms.
opuntia: A genus of cactaceous plants; the prickly pear, or Indian fig.
opuntiales: coextensive with the family Cactaceae: cactuses
opus: A work; specif. (Mus.), a musical composition.
oquassa: A small, handsome trout (Salvelinus oquassa), found in some of the lakes in Maine; called also blueback trout.

It often connects a series of words or propositions, presenting a choice of either; as, he may study law, or medicine, or divinity, or he may enter into trade. If man's convenience, health, Or safety interfere, his rights and claims Are paramount. Cowper.
orach: any of various herbaceous plants of the genus Atriplex that thrive in deserts and salt marshes
orache: any of various herbaceous plants of the genus Atriplex that thrive in deserts and salt marshes
oracle: The sanctuary, or Most Holy place in the temple; also, the temple itself. Kings vi.Siloa's brook, that flow'd Fast by the oracle of God. Milton.

orangey: A Protestant, especially one that is a member of the Protestant unionist community of Northern Ireland.

orarion: A deacon's stole in the Eastern Orthodox Church.

oratory: A place of orisons, or prayer; especially, a chapel or small room set apart for private devotions. An oratory. in worship of Dian. Chaucer. oratrix: A woman plaintiff, or complainant, in equity pleading. Bur rill.
orb: A blank window or panel. Oxf. Gloss.

orbit: The path described by a heavenly body in its periodical revolution around another body; as, the orbit of Jupiter, of the earth, of the moon.
orbital: Of or pertaining to an orbit. Orbital revolution. " J. D.For bes. Orbital index (Anat.), in the skull, the ratio of the vertical height to the transverse width of the orbit, which is taken as the standard, equal to.

orbiting: present participle and gerund of orbit

orbitosphenoid: Of or pertaining to the sphenoid bone and the orbit, or to the orbitosphenoid bone. n.
orby: Orblike; having the course of an orb; revolving. Orby hours. " Chapman.

orcadian: Of or pertaining to the Ork ney Islands.
orchardman: A man who owns or tends an orchard.
orchestia: type genus of the family Orchestiidae
orchestra: The instruments employed by a full band, collectively; as, an orchestra of forty stringed instruments, with proper complement of wind instruments.

orchestrates: third-person singular simple present indicative of orchestrate

orchestrator: an arranger who writes for orchestras
orchestrion: A large music box imitating a variety of orchestral instruments.

orchiectomy: surgical removal of one or both testicles
orchiopexy: operation to bring an undescended testicle into the scrotum

ordained: invested with ministerial or priestly functions
ordaining: present participle and gerund of ordain
ordains: third-person singular simple present indicative of ordain

orderer: someone who places an order to buy
orderliness: The state or quality of being orderly.

ordinary: One who has immediate jurisdiction in matters ecclesiastical; an ecclesiastical judge; also, a deputy of the bishop, or a clergyman appointed to perform divine service for condemned criminals and assist in preparing them for death.(c) (Am. ordinate: Well-ordered; orderly; regular; methodical. A life blissful and ordinate. " Chaucer. Ordinate figure (Math.), a figure whose sides and angles are equal; a regular figure.
ordination: The act of setting apart to an office in the Christian ministry; the conferring of holy orders.

ore: Honor; grace; favor; mercy; clemency; happy augry. Chaucer.

oreades: A group of butterflies which includes the satyrs. See Satyr,.
orectic: Of or pertaining to the desires; hence, impelling to gratification; appetitive.

oregonian: a native or resident of Oregon

organised: being a member of or formed into a labor union

organist: One who plays on the organ.

organizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of organize
organizing: present participle and gerund of organize

organoarsenic: Describing any organic compound containing a carbon to arsenic bond

organoid: Resembling an organ of the body.
organoleptic: Making an impression upon an organ; plastic; said of the effect or impression produced by any substance on the organs of touch, taste, or smell, and also on the organism as a whole.

organomercury: Describing any organic compound containing a carbon to mercury bond.
organon: a system of principles for philosophic or scientific investigations; an instrument for acquiring knowledge
organophosphate: an insecticide that interferes with an insect's nervous system
organophosphorus: describing any of a series of derivatives of phosphorus that have at least one alkyl or aryl group, especially one containing at least one carbon-phosphorus bond
organoplastic: Having the property of producing the tissues or organs of animals and plants; as, the organoplastic cells.
organotherapy: The therapeutic use of the endocrine organs (or glandular extracts) of animals.
organotin: Describing any organic compound containing a carbon to tin bond
organotropic: Having an affinity for a particular bodily organ
organotropism: The affinity of certain substances, or of certain microorganisms, for particular tissues or organs.
organs: edible viscera of a butchered animal
organule: One of the essential cells or elements of an organ. See Sense organule, under Sense. Huxley.
organum: A type of medieval polyphony which builds upon an existing plainsong.

original: The natural or wild species from which a domesticated or cultivated variety has been derived; as, the wolf is thought by some to be the original of the dog, the blackthorn the original of the plum.
originality: The quality or state of being original. Macaulay.

originated: simple past and past participle of originate
originates: third-person singular simple present indicative of originate
originating: present participle and gerund of originate
