orison: A prayer; a supplication. Chaucer. Lowly they bowed, adoring, and began Their orisons, each morning duly paid. Milton.
orissa: state in eastern India on the Bay of Bengal
orkneyan: Of or pertaining to the Ork ney islands. Orkneyan skerries. Longfellow.
orlando: a city in central Florida; site of Walt Disney World
orle: A bearing, in the form of a fillet, round the shield, within, but at some distance from, the border.
orleanist: a supporter of the Orleans branch of the Bourbons that was descended from a younger brother of Louis XIV
orleans: a city on the Loire river in north central France; site of the siege of Orleans by the English (-)
orlo: A wind instrument of music in use among the Spaniards.
orlon: an acrylic fiber or the lightweight crease-resistant fabric made with Orlon yarns
orlop: The lowest deck of a vessel, esp. of a ship of war, consisting of a platform laid over the beams in the hold, on which the cables are coiled.
ormolu: A variety of brass made to resemble gold by the use of less zinc and more copper in its composition than ordinary brass contains. Its golden color is often heightened by means of lacquer of some sort, or by use of acids. Called also mosaic gold. Ormolu varnish, avarnish applied to metals, as brass, to give the appearance of gold.
ormuzd: The good principle, or being, of the ancient Persian religion. See Ahriman.
ornament: That which embellishes or adorns; that which adds grace or beauty; embellishment; decoration; adornment. The ornament of a meek and quiet spirit. Pet. iii.Like that long-buried body of the king Found lying with his urns and ornaments. Tennyson.
ornamental: Serving to ornament; characterized by ornament; beautifying; embellishing. Some think it most ornamental to wear their bracelets on their wrists; others, about their ankles. Sir T. Browne.
ornamented: simple past and past participle of ornament
ornamenting: present participle and gerund of ornament
ornate: To adorn; to honor. They may ornate and sanctify the name of God. Latimer.
ornately: In an ornate manner. Sir T. More.
ornery: having a difficult and contrary disposition
ornithic: Of or pertaining to birds; as, ornithic fossils. Owen.
ornithine: an amino acid that does not occur in proteins but is important in the formation of urea
ornithischian: herbivorous dinosaur with a pelvis like that of a bird
ornithologist: One skilled in ornithology; a student of ornithology; one who describes birds.
ornithology: the branch of zoology that studies birds
ornithomancy: Divination by means of birds, their flight, etc. Ornithomancy grew into an elaborate science. De Quincey.
ornithophile: A person who loves birds; a bird-lover.
ornithopoda: An order of herbivorous dinosaurs with birdlike characteristics in the skeleton, esp. in the pelvis and hind legs, which in some genera had only three functional toes, and supported the body in walking as in Iguanodon. See Illust. in Appendix.
ornithopter: heavier-than-air craft that is propelled by the flapping of wings
ornithosauria: An order of extinct flying reptiles; called also pterosauria.
ornithoscelida: A group of extinct Reptilia, intermediate in structure (especially with regard to the pelvis) between reptiles and birds. Ornithoscelidan, a.
ornithosis: an atypical pneumonia caused by a rickettsia microorganism and transmitted to humans from infected birds
ornithotomy: The anatomy or dissection of birds.
orobanchaceae: brown or yellow leafless herbs; sometimes placed in the order Scrophularia les
orogen: Rock deformed by orogeny; a belt of such rock(s).
orogenesis: The process of mountain formation by deformation of the Earth's crust.
orogeny: the process of mountain formation (especially by the upward displacement of the earth's crust)
orographic: Of or pertaining to the physical features of mountains, or to orography.
orography: That branch of science which treats of mountains and mountain systems; orology; as, the orography of Western Europe.
oroide: An alloy, chiefly of copper and zinc or tin, resembling gold in color and brilliancy.
orology: The science or description of mountains.
orometer: An aneroid barometer having a second scale that gives the approximate elevation above sea level of the place where the observation is made.
oronasal: Of or pertaining to the mouth and the nose
oropharyngeal: of or relating to or located near the oropharynx
oropharynx: cavity formed by the pharynx at the back of the mouth
orotund: Characterized by fullness, clearness, strength, and smoothness; ringing and musical; said of the voice or manner of utterance. n.
orphan: A child bereaved of both father and mother; sometimes, also, achild who has but one parent living. Orphans' court (Law), a court in some of the States of the Union, having jurisdiction over the estates and persons of orphans or other wards. Bouvier.
orphanage: the condition of being a child without living parents
orphaned: deprived of parents by death or desertion
orphanhood: The state or condition of being an orphan; orphanage.
orphean: Of or pertaining to Orpheus, the mythic poet and musician; as, Orphean strains. Cowper.
orpheus: The famous mythic Thracian poet, son of the Muse Calliope, and husband of Eurydice. He is reputed to have had power to entrance beasts and inanimate objects by the music of his lyre.
orphic: Pertaining to Orpheus; Orphean; as, Orphic hymns.
orphism: A religious movement in antiquity, supposed to have been founded by Orpheus.
orphrey: A band of rich embroidery, wholly or in part of gold, affixed to vestments, especially those of ecclesiastics. Pugin.
orpiment: Arsenic sesquisulphide, produced artificially as an amorphouslemonyellow powder, and occurring naturally as a yellow crystalline mineral; formerly called auripigment. It is used in king's yellow, in white Indian fire, and in certain technical processes, as indigo printing. Our orpiment and sublimed mer curie. Chaucer. Red orpiment, realgar; the red sulphide of arsenic. Yellow orpiment, king's yellow.
orpine: A low plant with fleshy leaves (Sedum telephium), having clusters of purple flowers. It is found on dry, sandy places, and onold walls, in England, and has become naturalized in America. Called also stonecrop, and live-forever.
orrery: An apparatus which illustrates, by the revolution of balls moved by wheelwork, the relative size, periodic motions, positions, orbits, etc., of bodies in the solar system.
orrice: Obsolete form of orris (the plant or its root).
orris: A plant of the genus Iris (I. Floren tina); a kind of flower-de-luce. Its rootstock has an odor resembling that of violets. Orris pea (Med.), an issue pea made from orris root. Orris root, the fragrant rootstock of the orris.
orsellic: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid found in certain lichens, and called also lecanoric acid.
orsellinic: Pertaining to, or designating, an organic acid obtained by apartial decomposition of orsellic acid as a white crystalline substance, and related to protocatechuic acid.
ort: A morsel left at a meal; a fragment; refuse; commonly used in the plural. Milton. Let him have time a beggar's orts to crave.
ortalid: A fly of the family Ortalidae (now Ulidiidae).
orthicon: a now obsolete picture pickup tube in a television camera; electrons emitted from a photoemissive surface in proportion to the intensity of the incident light are focused onto the target causing secondary emission of electrons
orthis: An extinct genus of Brachiopoda, abundant in the Paleozoic rocks.
orthite: A variety of allanite occurring in slender prismatic crystals.
ortho: An isomer of a benzene derivative having two substituents adjacent on the ring.
orthocenter: That point in which the three perpendiculars let fall from the angles of a triangle upon the opposite sides, or the sides produced, mutually intersect.
orthoceras: An extinct genus of Paleozoic Cephalopoda, having a long, straight, conical shell. The interior is divided into numerous chambers by transverse septa.
orthoceratite: An orthoceras; also, any fossil shell allied to Orthoceras.
orthochromatic: Being uniformly sensitive across the entire visible range, and thus reproducing colours faithfully
orthoclase: Common or potash feldspar crystallizing in the monoclinic system and having two cleavages at right angles to each other. See feldspar.
orthoclastic: Breaking in directions at right angles to each other; said of the monoclinic feldspars.
orthodiagonal: The diagonal or lateral axis in a monoclinic crystal which isat right angles with the vertical axis.
orthodiagraph: An instrument used to determine the true contour and dimensions of any internal organ or other object rendered visible by X-rays, the latter being deflected so as to be made parallel.
orthodiagraphy: Examination by means of an orthodiagraph.
orthodontia: the branch of dentistry dealing with the prevention or correction of irregularities of the teeth
orthodontics: the branch of dentistry dealing with the prevention or correction of irregularities of the teeth
orthodontist: a dentist specializing in the prevention or correction of irregularities of the teeth
orthodox: of or pertaining to or characteristic of Judaism
orthodoxical: Pertaining to, or evincing, orthodoxy; orthodox.
orthodoxly: In an orthodox manner; with soundness of faith. Sir W.Hamilton.
orthodoxness: The quality or state of being orthodox; orthodoxy. Water land.
orthodoxy: the quality of being orthodox (especially in religion)
orthodromy: The act or art of sailing on a great circle.
orthoepic: Of or relating to orthoepy in its various senses:
orthoepy: The art of uttering words corectly; a correct pronunciation of words; also, mode of pronunciation.
orthogamy: Direct fertilization in plants, as when the pollen fertilizing the ovules comes from the stamens of the same blossom; opposed to heterogamy.
orthogenesis: The hypothesis that evolution tends toward a certain goal, at least at some scales.
orthognathous: Having the front of the head, or the skull, nearly perpendicular, not retreating backwards above the jaws; opposed to Ant: prognathous. See Gnathic index, under Gnathic.
orthogonal: Right-angled; rectangular; as, an orthogonal intersection ofone curve with another. Orthogonal projection. See under orthographic.
orthogonality: the relation of opposition between things at right angles
orthogonally: Perpendicularly; at right angles; as, a curve cuts a set of curves orthogonally.
orthographer: One versed in orthography; one who spells words correctly.
orthographic: of or relating to or expressed in orthography
orthographical: Of, or relating to orthography or spelling.
orthographize: To spell correctly or according to usage; to correct in regard to spelling. In the coalesced into ith, which modern reaction has orthographized to i' th'. Earle.
orthographized: simple past and past participle of orthographize
orthography: a method of representing the sounds of a language by written or printed symbols
orthology: The right description of things. Fother by.
orthomorphic: Having the right form. Orthomorphic projection, a projection in which the angles in the figure to be projected are equal to the corresponding angles in the projected figure.
orthomyxovirus: a group of viruses including those causing influenza
orthonormal: Of a set of vectors, both orthogonal and normalized.
orthopedia: The branch of medicine which deals with the prevention and correction of deformities in bodies; orthopedics.
orthopedics: the branch of medical science concerned with disorders or deformities of the spine and joints
orthopedist: One who prevents, cures, or remedies deformities, esp. in children.
orthopedy: The art or practice of curing the deformities of children, or, by extension, any deformities of the human body.
orthophony: The art of correct articulation; voice training.
orthophoria: The normal condition in which the tension of the extrinsic eye muscles is equal, the visual axes being therefore parallel
orthophosphoric: Describing the ordinary form of phosphoric acid and its derivatives
orthophyre: a porphyritic rock that contains phenocrysts of orthoclase embedded in feldspar
orthopinacoid: A name given to the two planes in the monoclinic system which are parallel to the vertical and orthodiagonal axes.
orthopnea: form of dyspnea in which the person can breathe comfortably only when standing or sitting erect; associated with asthma and emphysema and angina pectoris
orthopraxy: The treatment of deformities in the human body by mechanical appliances.
orthopsychiatry: branch of psychiatry concerned with the prevention of mental illness, especially in the young
orthopter: heavier-than-air craft that is propelled by the flapping of wings
orthoptera: An order of mandibulate insects including grasshoppers, locusts, cockroaches, etc. See Illust. under Insect.
orthopteroid: Any of the insects historically included in the order Orthoptera, including the cockroaches, earwigs, praying mantises, etc.
orthopterology: The scientific study of the Orthoptera.
orthopterous: Of or pertaining to the Orthoptera.
orthoptics: treatment of defects of binocular vision (such as strabismus and amblyopia) by nonsurgical measures (especially by exercises to strengthen the eye muscles)
orthopyroxene: Any pyroxene that forms orthorhombic crystals.
orthorhombic: Noting the system of crystallization which has three unequal axes at right angles to each other; trimetric. See Crystallization.
orthoscopic: Giving an image in correct or normal proportions; giving a flat field of view; as, an orthoscopic eyepiece.
orthosilicic: Designating the form of silicic acid having the normal or highest number of hydroxyl groups.
orthostichy: A longitudinal rank, or row, of leaves along a stem.
orthosymmetric: That has equal elements of the secondary diagonal.
orthotics: The design, manufacture and installation of orthopedic appliances to support, straighten or improve the function of a body part
orthotomic: Cutting at right angles. Orthotomic circle (Geom.), that circle which cuts three given circles at right angles.
orthotone: Retaining the accent; not enclitic; said of certain indefinite pronouns and adverbs when used interrogatively, which, when not so used, are ordinar illy enclitic.
orthotropic: Having the longer axis vertical; said of erect stems. Encyc. Brit.
orthotropous: (of a plant ovule) completely straight with the micropyle at the apex
orthotype: The original published name for a group of genetically related organisms.
orthoxylene: That variety of xylene in which the two methyl groups are in the ortho position; a colorless, liquid, combustible hydrocarbon resembling benzene.
ortive: Of or relating to the time or act of rising; eastern; as, the ortive amplitude of a planet.
ortolan: brownish Old World bunting often eaten as a delicacy
orwell: imaginative British writer concerned with social justice (-)
oryctognosy: Mineralogy. Oryctognostic, a. Oryctognostical, a. Oryctognostically, adv.
oryx: A genus of African antelopes which includes the gemsbok, the leucoryx, the bisa antelope (O. beisa), and the beatrix antelope (O.beatrix) of Arabia.
oryza: A genus of grasses including the rice plant; rice.
osage: a member of the Siouan people formerly living in Missouri in the valleys of the Missouri and Osage rivers; oil was found on Osage lands early in the th century
osages: A tribe of southern Sioux Indians, now living in the Indian territory.
osaka: port city on southern Honshu on Osaka Bay; a commercial and industrial center of Japan
osazone: any glycoside of an aldose or -ketose formed by reaction with excess of an aryl-hydrazine
oscan: Of or pertaining to the Osci, a primitive people of Campania, aprovince of ancient Italy. n.
oscar: A male given name from Irish or Old English.
oscillate: move or swing from side to side regularly
oscillates: third-person singular simple present indicative of oscillate
oscillating: That oscillates; vibrating; swinging. Oscillating engine, asteam engine whose cylinder oscillates on trunnions instead of being permanently fixed in a perpendicular or other direction. Weale.
oscillation: the process of oscillating between states
oscillative: Tending to oscillate; vibratory. I. Taylor.
oscillator: Any device for producing electric oscillations; esp., an apparatus for generating electric waves in a system of wireless telegraphy.(b) (Mech.) An instrument for measuring rigidity by the torsional oscillations of a weighted wire.
oscillatory: Moving, or characterized by motion, backward and forward like apendulum; swinging; oscillating; vibratory; as, oscillatory motion.
oscillograph: An apparatus for recording or indicating alternating-current wave forms or other electrical oscillations, usually consisting of agalvanometer with strong field, in which the mass of the moving partis very small and frequency of vibration very high. Oscillographic (#), a.
oscillography: Measurement by means of an oscillograph.
oscilloscope: An instrument for showing visually the changes in a varying current; an oscillograph.
oscines: Singing birds; a group of the Passeres, having numerous syringeal muscles, conferring musical ability.
oscinine: Of or pertaining to the Oscines.
oscitancy: drowsiness and dullness manifested by yawning
osculant: Adhering closely; embracing; applied to certain creeping animals, as caterpillars.
oscular: Of or pertaining to the mouth.
osculate: To touch closely, so as to have a common curvature at the point of contact. See Osculation,.
osculating: present participle and gerund of osculate
osculation: The contact of one curve with another, when the number of consecutive points of the latter through which the former passes suffices for the complete determination of the former curve. Br ande &C.
osculatory: Pertaining to, or having the properties of, an osculatrix; capable of osculation; as, a circle may be osculatory with a curve, at a given point. Osculatory circle. (Geom.) See Osculating circle of a curve, under Circle. Osculatory plane (to a curve of double curvature), a plane which passes through three successive points of the curve. Osculatory sphere (to a line of double curvature), a sphere passing through four consecutive points of the curve.
osculatrix: A curve whose contact with a given curve, at a given point, isof a higher order (or involves the equality of a greater number of successive differential coefficients of the ordinates of the curves taken at that point) than that of any other curve of the same kind.
oscule: One of the excurrent apertures of sponges.
oses: The various sugars ending in -ose, such as sucrose, lactose, glucose, and fructose.
osier: Made of osiers; composed of, or containing, osiers. This osier cage of ours.
osiered: Covered or adorned with osiers; as, osiered banks. Collins.
osierlike: Resembling or characteristic of an osier.
osiris: One of the principal divinities of Egypt, the brother and husband of Isis. He was figured as a mummy wearing the royal cap of upper Egypt, and was symbolized by the sacred bull, called Apis. Cf. Serapis. Osirian, a.
oslo: the capital and largest city of Norway; the country's main port; located at the head of a fjord on Norway's southern coast
osmanthus: widely distributed genus of evergreen shrubs or trees of southern United States and Middle East and China and Japan
osmeterium: One of a pair of scent organs in the larvae of certain swallowtail butterflies.
osmiamic: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a nitrogenous acid of osmium, HNOsO, forming a well-known series of yellow salts.
osmic: Pertaining to, derived from, or containing, osmium; specifically, designating those compounds in which it has a valence higher than in other lower compounds; as, osmic oxide. Osmic acid.(Chem.) (a) Osmic tetroxide.(b) Osmic acid proper, an acid analogous to sulphuric acid, not known in the free state, but form inga well-known and stable series of salts (os mates), which were formerly improperly called os mites. Osmic tetroxide (Chem.), a white volatile crystalline substance, Os O, the most stable and characteristic of the compounds of osmium. It has a burning taste, and gives off a vapor, which is a powerful irritant poison, violently attacking the eyes, and emitting a strongchlorinelike odor. Formerly improperly called osmic acid.
osmina: An old Russian dry measure, approximately litres; half of a tchetvert.
osmious: Denoting those compounds of osmium in which the element has avalence relatively lower than in the osmic compounds; as, osmious chloride. Osmious acid (Chem.), an acid derived from osmium, analogous to sulphurous acid, and forming unstable salts. It is a brown amorphous substance.
osmiridium: a hard and corrosion resistant mineral that is a natural alloy of osmium and iridium (usually containing small amounts of rhodium and platinum); used in needles and pen nibs etc.
osmium: A rare metallic element of the platinum group, found native as an alloy in platinum ore, and in iridosmine. It is a hard, infusible, bluish or grayish white metal, and the heaviest substance known. Its tetroxide is used in histological experiments to stain tissues. Symbol Os. Atomic weight. Specific gravity.
osmolality: The molality of an ideal solution that would exert the same osmotic pressure as the solution being considered.
osmolarity: The osmotic concentration of a solution, normally expressed as osmoles of solute per litre of solution.
osmometer: An instrument for measuring the amount of osmotic action indifferent liquids.
osmometry: The study of osmose by means of the osmometer.
osmoregulation: The homeostatic regulation of osmotic pressure in the body in order to maintain a certain water content (concentration of electrolytes, pH, etc).
osmose: The tendency in fluids to mix, or become equably diffused, when in contact. It was first observed between fluids of differing densities, and as taking place through a membrane or an intervening porous structure. The more rapid flow from the thinner to the thicker fluid was then called endosmose, and the opposite, slower current, exosmose. Both are, however, results of the same force. Osmose may be regarded as a form of molecular attraction, allied to that of adhesion.
osmotaxis: movement of an organism in an osmotic pressure gradient
osmotic: Pertaining to, or having the property of, osmose; as, osmotic force.
osmund: A fern of the genus Osmunda, or flowering fern. The most remarkable species is the osmund royal, or royal fern (Osmundaregalis), which grows in wet or boggy places, and has large bipinnate fronds, often with a panicle of capsules at the top. The rootstock contains much starch, and has been used in stiffening linen.
osmunda: A fern of the genus Osmunda, especially the royal fern, Osmunda regalis.
osmundaceae: large family of ferns widely distributed in temperate and tropical areas
osnaburg: A species of coarse linen, originally made in Osnaburg, Germany.
osoberry: Oemleria cerasiformis, the Indian plum, a shrub native to the Pacific coast and ranges of North America.
osone: any,-ketoaldose, especially one derived by hydrolysis of an osazone
osphradium: The olfactory organ of some Mollusca. It is connected with the organ of respiration.
osprey: large harmless hawk found worldwide that feeds on fish and builds a bulky nest often occupied for years
oss: To prophesy; to presage. R. Edge worth.
osse: A prophetic or ominous utterance. Holland.
ossein: The organic basis of bone tissue; the residue after removal of the mineral matters from bone by dilute acid; in embryonic tissue, the substance in which the mineral salts are deposited to form bone; called also ostein. Chemically it is the same as collagen.
osseous: Composed of bone; resembling bone; capable of forming bone; bony; ossific.
ossete: a northeastern Iranian language spoken in Russia
ossetian: Of or relating to Ossetia or Ossetians.
ossian: A male given name from Irish; rather rare in the Anglo-Saxon world.
ossianic: Of or pertaining to, or characteristic of, Ossian, a legendary erse or Celtic bard. The compositions might be fairly classed as Ossianic. G. Eliot.
ossicle: One of numerous small calcareous structures forming the skeleton of certain echinoderms, as the starfishes.
ossific: Capable of producing bone; having the power to change cartilage or other tissue into bone.
ossification: The formation of bone; the process, in the growth of an animal, by which inorganic material (mainly lime salts) is deposited in cartilage or membrane, forming bony tissue; ostosis.
ossified: Changed to bone or something resembling bone; hardened by deposits of mineral matter of any kind; said of tissues.
ossifier: One who, or that which, ossifies.
ossifies: third-person singular simple present indicative of ossify
ossifluent: Breaking down and softening bony tissue.
ossify: To form into bone; to change from a soft animal substance into bone, as by the deposition of lime salts.
ossifying: Changing into bone; becoming bone; as, the ossifying process.
ossivorous: Feeding on bones; eating bones; as, ossivorous quadrupeds. Derham.
ossuary: A place where the bones of the dead are deposited; a charnel house. Sir T. Browne.
ostariophysi: in some classifications considered a superorder comprising the Cypriniform es and the Siluriformes
ostectomy: Excision of all or part of a bone.
osteectomy: The surgical removal of a bone.
osteichthyes: a class of fish having a skeleton composed of bone in addition to cartilage
ostend: To exhibit; to manifest. Mercy to mean offenders we'll ostend. J. Webster.
ostensibility: The quality or state of being ostensible.
ostensible: represented or appearing as such; pretended
ostensibly: In an ostensible manner; avowedly; professedly; apparently. Walsh. Ostensibly, we were intended to prevent filibustering into Texas, but really as a menace to Mexico. U. S. Grant.
ostensive: Showing; exhibiting. Ostensive demonstration (Math.), a director positive demonstration, as opposed to the apagogical or indirect method.
ostensorium: (Roman Catholic Church) a vessel (usually of gold or silver) in which the consecrated Host is exposed for adoration
ostentatious: Fond of, or evincing, ostentation; unduly conspicuous; pretentious; boastful. Far from being ostentatious of the good you do. Dryden. The ostentatious professions of many years. Macaulay. Ostentatiously, adv. Ostentatiousness, n.
ostentatiously: with ostentation; in an ostentatious manner
osteoarthritis: chronic breakdown of cartilage in the joints; the most common form of arthritis occurring usually after middle age
osteoblast: One of the protoplasmic cells which occur in the osteogenetic layer of the periosteum, and from or around which the matrix of the bone is developed; an osteoplast.
osteocartilaginous: Relating to or composed of bone and cartilage, or of osteocartilage.
osteoclasis: The operation of breaking a bone in order to correct deformity.
osteocomma: A metamere of the vertebrate skeleton; an osteomere; avertebra. Owen.
osteodentine: A hard substance, somewhat like bone, which is sometimes deposited within the pulp cavity of teeth.
osteoderm: A bony deposit in the dermal layers of the skin
osteofibrous: Of combined osseous and fibrous type (within bone or within a tumor elsewhere).
osteogen: The soft tissue, or substance, which, in developing bone, ultimately undergoes ossification.
osteogenesis: The formation and development of bone.
osteogenetic: Connected with osteogenesis, or the formation of bone; producing bone; as, osteogenetic tissue; the osteogenetic layer of the periosteum.
osteoglossidae: a family of large fishes that live in freshwater; includes bandfish and bony tongues
osteologer: One versed in osteology; an osteologist.
osteologist: One who is skilled in osteology; an osteologer.
osteology: The science which treats of the bones of the vertebrate skeleton.
osteolysis: Softening and absorption of bone. Osteolytic (#), a.
osteoma: A tumor composed mainly of bone; a tumor of a bone.
osteomalacia: A disease of the bones, in which they lose their earthy material, and become soft, flexible, and distorted. Also called malacia.
osteometry: The measurement of the bones of the skeleton (both human and animal)
osteomyelitis: an inflammation of bone and bone marrow (usually caused by bacterial infection)
osteopathy: therapy based on the assumption that restoring health is best accomplished by manipulating the skeleton and muscles
osteoplasty: An operation or process by which the total or partial loss of abone is remedied. Dunglison.
osteoporosis: An absorption of bone so that the tissue becomes unusually porous.
osteosarcoma: A tumor having the structure of a sa croma in which there is ade posit of bone; sarcoma connected with bone.
osteosclerosis: Abnormal hardness and density of bone.
osteosuture: A surgery in which fragments of broken bone are sutured together.
osteotomy: The operation of dividing a bone or of cutting a piece out ofit, done to remedy deformity, etc.
ostiary: The mouth of a river; an estuary. Sir T. Browne.
ostinato: a musical phrase repeated over and over during a composition
ostiole: a small pore especially one in the reproductive bodies of certain algae and fungi through which spores pass
ostmark: The currency unit of the former German Democratic Republic (aka GDR, DDR, East Germany) until, abbreviated DDM.
ostomy: surgical procedure that creates an artificial opening for the elimination of bodily wastes
ostosis: Bone formation; ossification. See Ectostosis, and Endostosis.
ostracion: A genus of plectognath fishes having the body covered with solid, immovable, bony plates. It includes the trunkfishes.
ostracism: Banishment by popular vote, a means adopted at Athens to rid the city of a person whose talent and influence gave umbrage.
ostracize: To exile by ostracism; to banish by a popular vote, as at athens. Grote.
ostracized: simple past and past participle of ostracize
ostracizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of ostracize
ostracod: tiny marine and freshwater crustaceans with a shrimp-like body enclosed in a bivalve shell
ostracoidea: An order of Entomostraca possessing hard bivalve shells. The yare of small size, and swim freely about.
ostracon: A piece of pottery or stone, usually broken off from a vase or other earthenware vessel, especially one used to cast a vote during the Ancient Greek process of ostracism.
ostrea: A genus of bivalve Mollusca which includes the true oysters.
ostreaceous: Of or pertaining to an oyster, or to a shell; shelly. The crustaceous or ostreaceous body. Cud worth.
ostrich: A large bird of the genus Struthio, of which Struthio camelus of Africa is the best known species. It has long and very strong legs, adapted for rapid running; only two toes; a long neck, nearly bare of feathers; and short wings incapable of flight. The adult male is about eight feet high.
ostrichlike: Resembling or characteristic of an ostrich; struthian
ostrya: deciduous monoecious trees of Europe and Asia and America; sometimes placed in subfamily or family Car pinaceae
oswald: United States assassin of President John F. Kennedy (-)
oswego: A large village in Kendall County, Illinois, United States.
otacoustic: Assisting the sense of hearing; as, an otacoustic instrument.
otariidae: eared seals: sea lions and fur seals
otarine: Of or relating to the eared seals.
othello: the hero of William Shakespeare's tragedy who would not trust his wife
other: Either; used with other or or for its correlative (as either. or are now used).Other of chalk, other of glass. Chaucer.
othergates: In another manner. He would have tickled you othergates.
otherness: The quality or state of being other or different; alterity; oppositeness.
otherwhere: In or to some other place, or places; elsewhere. Milton. Tennyson.
otherworld: an abstract spiritual world beyond earthly reality

pairing: the act of grouping things or people in pairs
paisa: a fractional monetary unit in Bangladesh and India and Nepal and Pakistan
paisley: a soft wool fabric with a colorful swirled pattern of curved shapes
paiute: a member of either of two Shoshonean peoples (northern Paiute and southern Paiute) related to the Aztecs and living in the southwestern United States
pajama: a pair of loose trousers tied by a drawstring around the waist; worn by men and women in some Asian countries
pajamas: Originally, in India, loose drawers or trousers, such as those worn, tied about the waist, by Mohammedan men and women; by extension, a similar garment adopted among Europeans, Americans, etc., for wear in the dressing room and during sleep; also, a suit consisting of drawers and a loose upper garment for such wear.
pakistan: a Muslim republic that occupies the heartland of ancient south Asian civilization in the Indus River valley; formerly part of India; achieved independence from the United Kingdom in
pakistani: of or relating to Pakistan or its people or language
paktong: An alloy of zinc, copper and nickel, closely resembling silver, of Chinese origin; any of a number of similar alloys developed in imitation of the Chinese product.
pal: A mate; a partner; esp., an accomplice or confederate.
pala: A part of an insect's leg that is spade-shaped and can be used as a scoop for feeding.
paladin: A knight-errant; a distinguished champion; as, the paladins of charlemagne. Sir W. Scott.
palaeobiology: a branch of paleontology that deals with the origin and growth and structure of fossil animals and plants as living organisms
palaeoclimatology: the study of the climate of past ages
palaeoecology: the branch of ecology that studies ancient ecology
palaeoentomologist: A scientist who specializes in palaeoentomology
palaeoentomology: The scientific study of prehistoric insects.
palaeolithic: of or relating to the second period of the Stone Age (following the eolithic)
palaeontography: The description of fossil remains in scientific literature.
palaeontology: the earth science that studies fossil organisms and related remains
palaeosaur: Any of various prehistoric animals that have been named Palaeosaurus.
palaeotropical: Occurring in tropical Africa and Asia, i.e. the tropics of the Old World.
palaeotypic: Relating to the palaeotype phonetic alphabet.
palagonite: A material similar to basalt formed by the action of water on volcanic ash
palankeen: a closed litter carried on the shoulders of four bearers
palanquin: An inclosed carriage or litter, commonly about eight feet long, four feet wide, and four feet high, borne on the shoulders of men by means of two projecting poles, used in India, China, etc., for the conveyance of a single person from place to place.
palaquium: large genus of Malaysian trees with milky juice and leathery leaves
palatable: Agreeable to the palate or taste; savory; hence, acceptable; pleasing; as, palatable food; palatable advice.
palatableness: The quality or state of being agreeable to the taste; relish; acceptableness.
palatal: Uttered by the aid of the palate; said of certain sounds, as the sound of k in kirk.
palatalization: The state or quality of being palatalized, of pronouncing a sound with the tongue against the palate of the mouth that normally is not.
palatalized: produced with the front of the tongue near or touching the hard palate (as y') or with the blade of the tongue near the hard palate (as ch' in chin' or j' in gin')
palatial: Of or pertaining to a palace; suitable for a palace; resemblinga palace; royal; magnificent; as, palatial structures. Palatial style. " A. Drummond.
palatinate: The province or seigniory of a palatine; the dignity of apalatine. Howell.
palative: Pleasing to the taste; palatable. Palative delights. Sir T. Browne.
palatize: To modify, as the tones of the voice, by means of the palate; as, to palatize a letter or sound. Palatization, n. J. Peile.
palatoglossal: relating to the palate and tongue
palatoglossus: A small fleshy muscle, narrower in the middle than at either end, that arises from the soft palate on each side, contributes to the structure of the palatoglossal arch of the fauces, and is inserted into the side and dorsum of the tongue; it serves to raise the back of the tongue and constrict the fauces.
palatography: A technique used to identify which parts of the mouth are used when making a certain sound, by painting a colouring agent on the tongue or roof of a subject's mouth and photographing those areas after the subject has pronounced the sound.
palatopharyngeal: Of, relating to, or involving the palate and the pharynx.
palatopharyngeus: A long, fleshy longitudinal muscle, narrower in the middle than at either end, that arises from the soft palate, contributes with the mucous membrane covering its surface to the structure of the palatopharyngeal arch, and is inserted into the thyroid cartilage and the wall of the pharynx; it serves to constrict the fauces and draw the larynx and pharynx upwards.
palatoplasty: A surgical procedure used to correct or reconstruct a cleft palate
palatopterygoid: Pertaining to the palatine and pterygoid region of the skull; as, the palatopterygoid cartilage, or rod, from which the palatine and pterygoid bones are developed.
palau: a republic in the western central Pacific Ocean in association with the United States
palaver: To make palaver with, or to; to used palaver; to talk idly or deceitfully; to employ flattery; to cajole; as, to palaver artfully. Palavering the little language for her benefit. C. Bront
palavering: gerund of palaver: the act of one who palavers.
palavers: third-person singular simple present indicative of palaver
palazzo: A large, palatial urban building in Italy.
palea: A pendulous process of the skin on the throat of a bird, as in the turkey; a dewlap.
palearctic: Belonging to a region of the earth's surface which includes all europe to the Azores, Iceland, and all temperate Asia.
paled: Striped. paled part per part. " Spenser.
paleencephalon: the more primitive parts of the brain phylogenetically; most structures other than the cerebral cortex
paleface: A white person; an appellation supposed to have been applied to the whites by the American Indians. J. F. Cooper.
palempore: A superior kind of dimity made in India, used for bed coverings. De Co lange.
paleness: The quality or condition of being pale; want of freshness or ruddiness; a sickly whiteness; lack of color or luster; wanness. The blood the virgin's cheek forsook; A livid paleness spreads o'erall her look. Pope.
paleoanthropic: of or pertaining to early forms of fossil humans, as Neanderthal
paleoanthropology: the scientific study of human fossils
paleobiogeography: The scientific study of the prehistoric distribution of plants and animals.
paleobiology: a branch of paleontology that deals with the origin and growth and structure of fossil animals and plants as living organisms
paleobotany: That branch of paleontology which treats of fossil plants.
paleoceanography: The study of the history of the oceans, especially their circulation, chemistry, biogeography, fertility, and sedimentation.
paleocene: from million to million years ago; appearance of birds and earliest mammals
paleoclimatic: Of or pertaining to the climate of a region in the past
paleoclimatology: the study of the climate of past ages
paleocrystic: Of, pertaining to, or derived from, a former glacial formation.
paleoecology: the branch of ecology that studies ancient ecology
paleoencephalon: the more primitive parts of the brain phylogenetically
paleoethnology: The ethnology of cultures from past times.
paleofauna: The animals that were alive in a particular period of geological history, especially those known only as fossils
paleogene: Of a geologic period within the Cenozoic era; comprises the Paleocene, Eocene and Oligocene epochs from about to million years ago.
paleogeography: the study of the geography of ancient times or ancient epochs
paleographer: One skilled in paleography; a paleographist.
paleographically: In terms of or by means of paleography.
paleographist: One versed in paleography; a paleographer.
paleography: the study of ancient forms of writing (and the deciphering of them)
paleoherpetology: The scientific study of extinct reptiles and amphibians.
paleohydrography: The hydrography of ancient rivers or shores
paleolimnology: The study of the paleoenvironments of inland bodies of water
paleolith: A relic of the Paleolithic era.
paleolithic: Of or pertaining to an era marked by early stone implements. The Paleolithic era (as proposed by Lubbock) includes the earlier half of the Stone Age;" the remains belonging to it are for the most part of extinct animals, with relics of human beings.
paleomagnetism: The study of the strength and direction of the Earth's magnetic field as it has changed over geologic time.
paleontologic: Pertaining to paleontology; characteristic of paleontology.
paleontological: Of or pertaining to paleontology. Paleontologically, adv.
paleontology: The science which treats of the ancient life of the earth, orof fossils which are the remains of such life.
paleopathology: the study of disease of former times (as inferred from fossil evidence)
paleophysiology: The scientific study of the evolutionary basis of animal physiology.
paleoplain: A buried erosion plain; a particularly large and flat erosion surface.
paleopsychology: Study of the psychology of ancient cultures.
paleornithology: The branch of paleontology which treats of fossil birds.
paleostriatum: the inner pale yellow part of the lenticular nucleus
paleotechnic: Belonging to, or connected with, ancient art. The paleotechnic men of central France. " D. Wilson.
paleotherium: An extinct genus of herbivorous Tertiary mammals, once supposed to have resembled the tapir in form, but now known to have had a more slender form, with a long neck like that of a llama.
paleovolcanic: Relating to, or formed by a paleovolcano
paleozoic: Of or pertaining to, or designating, the older division of geological time during which life is known to have existed, including the Silurian, Devonian, and Carboniferous ages, and also to the life or rocks of those ages. See Chart of Geology.
paleozoologist: Any zoologist whose speciality is paleozoology
paler: comparative form of pale: more pale
palermo: the capital of Sicily; located in northwestern Sicily; an important port for years
pales: third-person singular simple present indicative of pale
palest: superlative form of pale: most pale
palestine: a former British mandate on the east coast of the Mediterranean; divided between Jordan and Israel in
palestinian: of or relating to the area of Palestine and its inhabitants
palestra: Of or pertaining to the palestra, or to wrestling.
palestrian: Of or relating to the palestra, or to wrestling
palestric: Of or relating to the palestra, or to wrestling.
palette: A thin, oval or square board, or tablet, with a thumb hole atone end for holding it, on which a painter lays and mixes his pigments.
palewise: In the manner of a pale or pales; by perpendicular lines or divisions; as, to divide an escutcheon palewise.
palfrey: especially a light saddle horse for a woman
paliform: Resembling a palus; as, the paliform lobes of the septa in corals.
palimbacchius: A metrical foot composed of two long syllables and one short one.
palimpsest: A parchment which has been written upon twice, the first writing having been erased to make place for the second. Longfellow.
palindrome: A word, verse, or sentence, that is the same when read backward or forward; as, madam; Hannah; or Lewd did I live, & evil I did dwel.
palindromic: Of, relating to, or being a palindrome.
paling: Pales, in general; a fence formed with pales or pickets; a limit; an inclosure. They moved within the paling of order and decorum. De Quincey.
palingenesis: emergence during embryonic development of various characters or structures that appeared during the evolutionary history of the strain or species
palingenetic: Of or pertaining to palingenesis: as, a palingenetic process. Palingenetically, adv.
palinode: An ode recanting, or retracting, a former one; also, a repetition of an ode.
palinurus: An instrument for obtaining directly, without calculation, the true bearing of the sun, and thence the variation of the compass
palisade: A strong, long stake, one end of which is set firmly in the ground, and the other is sharpened; also, a fence formed of such stakes set in the ground as a means of defense.
palisaded: Fortified or surrounded with a palisade.
palisades: A line of steep cliffs along the western bank of the Hudson River in New Jersey.
palissy: Designating, or of the nature of, a kind of pottery made by bernard Palissy, in France, in the th centry. Palissy ware, glazed pottery like that made by Bernard Palissy; especially, that having figures of fishes, reptiles, etc., in high relief.
palla: An oblong rectangular piece of cloth, worn by Roman ladies, and fastened with brooches.
palladian: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a variety of the revived classic style of architecture, founded on the works of Andrea palladio, an Italian architect of the th century.
palladic: Of, pertaining to, or derived from, palladium; used specifically to designate those compounds in which the element has ahigh er valence as contrasted with palladious compounds.
palladio: highly original and much imitated Italian architect (-)
palladious: Of, pertaining to, or containing, palladium; used specifically to designate those compounds in which palladium has al ower valence as compared with palladic compounds.
palladium: Any statue of the goddess Pallas; esp., the famous statue on the preservation of which depended the safety of ancient Troy.
palladiumize: To cover or coat with palladium.
pallas: Pallas Athene, the Grecian goddess of wisdom, called also athene, and identified, at a later period, with the Roman Minerva.
pallbearer: One of those who attend the coffin at a funeral; so called from the pall being formerly carried by them.
palled: simple past and past participle of pall
pallet: A small and mean bed; a bed of straw. Milton.
palletize: To place on a pallet or pallets.
palletizing: present participle and gerund of palletize
pallette: one of the rounded armor plates at the armpits of a suit of armor
palliate: Covered with a mant bp. Hall.
palliated: simple past and past participle of palliate
palliates: third-person singular simple present indicative of palliate
palliating: present participle and gerund of palliate
palliation: easing the severity of a pain or a disease without removing the cause
palliative: Serving to palliate; serving to extenuate or mitigate.
pallid: Deficient in color; pale; wan; as, a pallid countenance; pallid blue. Spenser.
pallidness: The quality or state of being pallid; paleness; pallor; wanness.
pallidum: the inner pale yellow part of the lenticular nucleus
pallium: A large, square, woolen cloak which enveloped the whole person, worn by the Greeks and by certain Romans. It is the Roman name of ag reek garment.
pallograph: An instrument for recording vibrations, as of a ship at sea.
pallone: An Italian game, played with a large leather ball.
pallor: Paleness; want of color; pallidity; as, pallor of the complexion. Jer. Taylor.
pally: (used colloquially) having the relationship of friends or pals
palm: The inner and somewhat concave part of the hand between the bases of the fingers and the wrist. Clench'd her fingers till they bit the palm. Tennyson.
palma: Alternative form of palmo, traditional Portuguese and Spanish units of length.
palmae: chiefly tropical trees and shrubs and vines usually having a tall columnar trunk bearing a crown of very large leaves; coextensive with the order Palm ales
palmar: Pertaining to, or corresponding with, the palm of the hand.
palmate: (Chem.) A salt of palmic acid; a ricinoleate.
palmated: Having digits connected by a thin membrane; webbed.
palmatifid: Palmate, with the divisions separated but little more than halfway to the common center.
palmatipartite: Having lobes with incisions that extend over half-way toward the petiole.
palmatisect: Having lobes with incisions that extend almost up, but not quite to the petiole.
palmella: A soaptree (Yucca elata), of the arid southwestern and south-central US and northern Mexico.
palmer: One who palms or cheats, as at cards or dice.
palmette: A floral ornament, common in Greek and other ancient architecture; often called the honeysuckle ornament.
palmic: Of, pertaining to, or derived from, the castor-oil plant (Ricinus communis, or Palma Chris ti); formerly used to designate an acid now called ricinoleic acid.
palmin: A white waxy or fatty substance obtained from castor oil.
palmiped: Web-footed, as a water fowl. n.
palmist: fortuneteller who predicts your future by the lines on your palms
palmistry: telling fortunes by lines on the palm of the hand
palmitin: A solid crystallizable fat, found abundantly in animals and in vegetables. It occurs mixed with stearin and olein in the fat of animal tissues, with olein and butyrin in butter, with olein in olive oil, etc. Chemically, it is a glyceride of palmitic acid, three molecules of palmitic acid being united to one molecule of glyceryl, and hence it is technically called tripalmitin, or glyceryl tripalmitate.
palmitoleic: Of or pertaining to palmitoleic acid or its derivatives.
palmo: A traditional Spanish unit of length, equivalent to about. cm.
palmy: Bearing palms; abounding in palms; derived from palms; as, a palmy shore. Pope. His golden sands and palmy wine. Goldsmith.
palmyra: A species of palm (Borassus flabelliform is) having a straight, black, upright trunk, with palmate leaves. It is found native along the entire northern shores of the Indian Ocean, from the mouth of the tigris to New Guinea. More than eight hundred uses to which it is put are enumerated by native writers. Its wood is largely used for building purposes; its fruit and roots serve for food, its sap for making toddy, and its leaves for thatching huts.
palmyrene: Of, from or relating to ancient Palmyra or Palmyrena.
palo: A pole or timber of any kind; in the names of trees.
palola: An annelid (Palola virid is) which, at certain seasons of the year, swarms at the surface of the sea about some of the Pcific Islands, where it is collected for food.
palomino: a horse of light tan or golden color with cream-colored or white mane and tail
palosapis: The flowering plant Shorea palosapis, endemic to the Philippines.
palpable: capable of being perceived; especially capable of being handled or touched or felt
palpation: Examination of a patient by touch. Quain.
palpator: One of a family of clavicorn beetles, including those which have very long maxillary palpi.
palpebral: Of or pertaining to the eyelids.
palpiger: That portion of the labium which bears the palpi in insects.
palpitate: To beat rapidly and more strongly than usual; to throb; to bound with emotion or exertion; to pulsate violently; to flutter; said specifically of the heart when its action is abnormal, as from excitement.
palpitating: having a slight and rapid trembling motion
palpitation: A rapid pulsation; a throbbing; esp., an abnormal, rapid beating of the heart as when excited by violent exertion, strong emotion, or by disease.
palpus: A feeler; especially, one of the jointed sense organs attached to the mouth organs of insects, arachnids, crustaceans, and annelids; as, the mandibular palpi, maxillary palpi, and labial palpi. The palpi of male spiders serve as sexual organs. Called also palp. See illust. of Arthrogastra and Orthoptera.
palsgrave: A count or earl who presided in the domestic court, and had the superintendence, of a royal household in Germany.
palsy: Paralysis, complete or partial. See Paralysis. One sick of the palsy. " Mark ii. Bell's palsy, paralysis of the facial nerve, producing distortion of one side of the face; so called from Sir charles Bell, an English surgeon who described it. Scrivener's palsy. See Writer's cramp, under Writer. Shaking palsy, paralysis agit ans, a disease usually occurring inold people, characterized by muscular tremors and a peculiar shaking and tottering gait.
palter: To trifle with; to waste; to squander in paltry ways or on worthless things. Palter out your time in the penal statutes. " Beau. & Fl.
palterly: Paltry; shabby; shabbily; paltrily. In palterly clothes. " Pepys.
palters: third-person singular simple present indicative of palter
paltry: Mean; vile; worthless; despicable; contemptible; pitiful; trifling; as, a paltry excuse; paltry gold. Cowper. The paltry prize is hardly worth the cost. Byron.
paludal: Of or pertaining to marshes or fens; marshy. Paludal fever, malarial fever; so called because generated in marshy districts.
paludamentum: Antiq.) A military cloak worn by a general and his principal officers.
paludicolous: That lives in swamps or marshes.
paludina: Any one of numerous species of freshwater pectinibranchiate mollusks, belonging to Paludina, Melantho, and allied genera. They have an operculated shell which is usually green, often with brown bands. See Illust. of Pond snail, under Pond.
paludism: The morbid phenomena produced by dwelling among marshes; malarial disease or disposition.
palus: One of several upright slender calcareous processes which surround the central part of the calicle of certain corals.
palustral: Of or pertaining to a bog or marsh; boggy.
palustrine: Of, pertaining to, or living in, a marsh or swamp; marshy.
palynology: The scientific study of spores, pollen and particulate organic matter in various matrices including the air (pollen counts), crime scenes, and sedimentary rocks.
pamir: A mountain range in Central Asia.
pamlico: a member of the Algonquian people formerly of the Pamlico river valley in North Carolina
pampanga: A province of Central Luzon, Luzon, Philippines. Capital: San Fernando. Largest city: Angeles City.
pampered: Fed luxuriously; indulged to the full; hence, luxuriant. Pampered boughs. " Milton. Pampered insolence. " Pope. Pamperedness, n. Bp. Hall.
pamperer: One who, or that which, pampers. Cowper.
pampers: A diaper or nappy (an absorbent garment worn by a baby, or by someone who is incontinent).
pamphlet: To write a pamphlet or pamphlets. Howell.
pamphleteer: A writer of pamphlets; a scribbler. Dryden. Macaulay.
pamphletic: Resembling or characteristic of a pamphlet.
pamphletize: To publish and distribute pamphlets as a form of propaganda.
pampootie: A traditional shoe, formerly made and worn on the Aran Islands of County Galway, Ireland, consisting of a single piece of untanned hide folded around the foot and stitched with twine or a leather strap.
pan: The distance comprised between the angle of the epaule and the flanked angle.
panacean: Having the properties of a panacea. Panacean dews. Whitehead.
panache: A plume or bunch of feathers, esp. such a bunch worn on the helmet; any military plume, or ornamental group of feathers. A panache of variegated plumes. Prescott.
panada: A dish made by boiling bread in water and combining the pulp with milk, stock, butter or sometimes egg yolks.
panagia: Synonym of Mary, mother of Jesus, particularly in Greek contexts.
panama: a republic on the Isthmus of Panama; achieved independence from Colombia in
panamanian: Of or pert. to Panama. n.
panarchy: The individual's right to choose any form of government without being forced to move from their current locale.
panary: Of or pertaining to bread or to breadmaking.
panathenaea: The most ancient and important festival of Athens, celebrated in honor of Athena, the tutelary goddess of the city.
panatrophy: atrophy of all parts of a structure or the body; general atrophy
panax: perennial herbs of eastern North America and Asia having aromatic tuberous roots: ginseng
panbabylonism: The idea that all cultures and religions of the Middle East and civilization in general are directly derived from Babylonian mythology.
pancake: A thin cake of batter fried in a pan or on a griddle; agriddlecake; a flapjack. A pancake for Shrove Tuesday.
panchax: Any of various tropical fish in the cyprinodontiform families Aplocheilidae and Nothobranchiidae which were formerly classified in the genus Panchax.
panchayat: a village council in India or southern Pakistan
pancheon: A shallow dish used to stand milk while the cream separates, or in which to bake bread.
pancosmism: The belief that nothing exists except the physical and temporal universe.
pancratic: Having all or many degrees of power; having a great range of power; said of an eyepiece made adjustable so as to give a varying magnifying power.
pancratical: Of or relating to the pancratium; athletic.
pancratium: An athletic contest involving both boxing and wrestling.
pancreas: The sweetbread, a gland connected with the intestine of nearly all vertebrates. It is usually elongated and light-colored, and its secretion, called the pancreatic juice, is discharged, often together with the bile, into the upper part of the intestines, and is apowerful aid in digestion. See Illust. of Digestive apparatus.
pancreatectomy: surgical removal of part or all of the pancreas
pancreatic: Of or pertaining to the pancreas; as, the pancreatic secretion, digestion, ferments. Pancreatic juice (Physiol.), a colorless alkaline fluid secreted intermittently by the pancreatic gland. It isone of the most important of the digestive fluids, containing at least three distinct ferments, trypsin, steapsin and an amylolytic ferment, by which it acts upon all three classes of food stuffs. See pancreas.
pancreatitis: inflammation of the pancreas; usually marked by abdominal pain
pancytopenia: an abnormal deficiency in all cells of the blood, including platelets and both red and white cells
panda: A small Asiatic mammal (Ailurus fulgens) having fine soft fur. It is related to the bears, and inhabits the mountains of Northern india.
pandal: a large temporary structure erected during various Hindu and Buddhist religious festivals
pandanaceae: family of woody plants of the order Pandanales including pandanus
pandanus: A genus of endogenous plants. See Screw pine.
pandar: Same as Pander. Seized by the pandar of Appius. " Macaulay.
pandava: A son of Pandu (used to refer to one of the five heroes of the Mahabharata).
pandean: Of or relating to the god Pan. Pandean pipes, a primitive wind instrument, consisting of a series of short hollow reeds or pipes, graduated in length by the musical scale, and fastened together side by side; a syrinx; a mouth organ; said to have been invented by Pan. Called also Pan's pipes and Panpipes.
pandect: The digest, or abridgment, in fifty books, of the decisions, writings, and opinions of the old Roman jurists, made in the sixth century by direction of the emperor Justinian, and forming the leading compilation of the Roman civil law. Kent.
pandemic: Affecting a whole people or a number of countries; everywhere epidemic. n.
pandemonium: The great hall or council chamber of demons or evil spirits. Milton.
pandemos: An epithet of the goddess Aphrodite, common to all the people, with various interpretations.
panderer: a person who serves or caters to the vulgar passions or plans of others (especially in order to make money)
pandering: present participle and gerund of pander
panderism: The employment, arts, or practices of a pander. Bp. Hall.
panderly: Having the quality of a pander. O, you panderly rascals.
panderous: , Of or relating to a pander; characterizing a pander.
pandora: A beautiful woman (all-gifted), whom Jupiter caused Vulcan to make out of clay in order to punish the human race, because prometheus had stolen the fire from heaven. Jupiter gave Pandora abox containing all human ills, which, when the box was opened, escaped and spread over the earth. Hope alone remained in the box. Another version makes the box contain all the blessings of the gods, which were lost to men when Pandora opened it.
pandore: An ancient musical instrument, of the lute kind; a bandore.
pandour: One of a class of Hungarian mountaineers serving in the austrian army; so called from Pand ur, a principal town in the region from which they originally came. Her whiskered pandours and her fierce hussars. Campbell.
pandowdy: A deep pie or pudding made of baked apples, or of sliced bread and apples baked together, with no bottom crust.
pandura: An Ancient Greek stringed instrument, a kind of lute with three strings that were stopped with a fingerboard to alter the tone, and with either a mandolin- or banjo-like shape.
pane: The narrow edge of a hammer head. See Peen.
paned: Having flat sides or surfaces; as, a six paned nut.
panegyric: An oration or eulogy in praise of some person or achievement; aformal or elaborate encomium; a laudatory discourse; laudation. See synonym of Eulogy.
panegyrist: One who delivers a panegyric; a eulogist; one who extols or praises, either by writing or speaking. If these panegyrists are in earnest. Burke.
panegyrize: To praise highly; to extol in a public speech; to write or deliver a panegyric upon; to eulogize.
panegyrized: simple past and past participle of panegyrize
panegyrizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of panegyrize
panel: A sunken compartment with raised margins, molded or otherwise, as in ceilings, wainscotings, etc.
paneled: fitted or decorated with panels or wainscoting
paneless: Without panes. To patch his paneless window. Shen stone.
panelling: a panel or section of panels in a wall or door
panesthesia: Everything that is felt by a person at one time; totality of sensation.
panettone: A soft Italian sourdough brioche from Milan, with candied fruit, usually prepared for Christmas as a dessert.
paneulogism: Eulogy of everything; indiscriminate praise. Her book has a trace of the cant of paneulogism. National Rev.
panfish: any of numerous small food fishes; especially those caught with hook and line and not available on the market
pang: A paroxysm of extreme pain or anguish; a sudden and transitory agony; a throe; as, the pangs of death.
panga: a large heavy knife used in Central and South America as a weapon or for cutting vegetation
pangamic: Of or pertaining to pangamic acid or its derivatives.
pangasinan: A province of the Ilocos Region, Luzon, Philippines. Capital: Lingayen. Largest city: San Carlos.
pangene: A supposed particle with which heritable character was transmitted during cell division.
pangenesis: An hypothesis advanced by Darwin in explanation of heredity.
pangolin: Any one of several species of Manis, Pholidotus, and related genera, found in Africa and Asia. They are covered with imbricated scales, and feed upon ants. Called also scaly ant-eater.

panhead: A fan of the American Christian rock band Skillet.

panurgic: Skilled in all kinds of work. The panurgic Diderot. " J.Morley.

paracone: A cusp in the buccal corner of an upper molar tooth in mammals
paraconine: A base resembling and isomeric with conine, and obtained as acolorless liquid from butyric aldehyde and ammonia.

paradidymis: A small collection of convoluted tubules situated in front of the lower part of the spermatic cord, above the head of the epididymis.
paradigm: An example of a conjugation or declension, showing a word inall its different forms of inflection.
paradigmatic: A writer of memoirs of religious persona, as examples of christian excellence.
parading: present participle and gerund of parade
paradise: An open space within a monastery or adjoining a church, as the space within a cloister, the open court before a basilica, etc.

paraffin: from crude petroleum; used for candles and for preservative or waterproof coatings

paragraphic: Of, pertaining to, or written in paragraphs.

parail: See Apparel. In the parail of a pilgrim. " Piers plowman.

paraldehyde: A polymeric modification of aldehyde obtained as a white crystalline substance.
paraleipsis: A pretended or apparent omission; a figure by which a speaker artfully pretends to pass by what he really mentions; as, for example, if an orator should say, I do not speak of my adversary'sscandalous venality and rapacity, his brutal conduct, his treachery and malice. "

paralgesia: Disordered sensibility to pain, including absence of sensibility to pain, excessive sensibility to pain, and abnormal painful results of stimuli. Paralgesic (#), a.
parallax: The apparent difference in position of a body (as the sun, or astar) as seen from some point on the earth's surface, and as seen from some other conventional point, as the earth's center or the sun. Annual parallax, the greatest value of the heliocentric parallax, or the greatest annual apparent change of place of a body as seen from the earth and sun; as, the annual parallax of a fixed star. Binocular parallax, the apparent difference in position of an object as seen separately by one eye, and then by the other, the head remaining unmoved. Diurnal, or Geocentric, parallax, the parallax of a body with reference to the earth's center. This is the kind of parallax that is generally understood when the term is used without qualification. Heliocentric parallax, the parallax of a body with reference to the sun, or the angle subtended at the body by lines drawn from it to the earth and sun; as, the heliocentric parallax of a planet. Horizontal parallax, the geocentric parallx of a heavenly body when in the horizon, or the angle subtended at the body by the earth's radius. Optical parallax, the apparent displacement in position undergone by an object when viewed by either eye singly. Br ande & C. Parallax of the cross wires (of an optical instrument), their apparent displacement when the eye changes its position, caused by their not being exactly in the focus of the object glass. Stellar parallax, the annual parallax of a fixed star.

parametrized: simple past and past participle of parametrize
parametrizing: present participle and gerund of parametrize
paramilitary: of or relating to a group of civilians organized to function like or to assist a military unit
paramo: A high, bleak plateau or district, with stunted trees, and cold, damp atmosphere, as in the Andes, in South America.

paranoiac: Of or pertaining to paranoia; affected with, or characteristic of, paranoia.
paranormal: not in accordance with scientific laws
paranymphal: Bridal; nuptial. At some paranymphal feast. Ford.

parapodium: One of the lateral appendages of an annelid; called also foot tubercle.

parapsis: The lateral part(s) of the mesoscutum of certain hymenopteran insects
