peasant: A countryman; a rustic; especially, one of the lowest class of tillers of the soil in European countries.
peascod: The legume or pericarp, or the pod, of the pea.
pease: A pea. A peose. " Bread. of beans and of peses. " Piers Plowman.
peat: A small person; a pet; sometimes used contemptuously.
peatery: A peat bog; an area covered by peat, or from which peat is extracted.
peatman: A man whose occupation is digging peat.
peaty: Composed of peat; abounding in peat; resembling peat.
peavey: a stout lever with a sharp spike; used for handling logs
peavy: a stout lever with a sharp spike
peba: An armadillo (Tatusia novemcincta) which is found from Texas to paraguay; called also tatouhou.
pebble: To grain (leather) so as to produce a surface covered with small rounded prominences.
pebblestone: A pebble; also, pebbles collectively. Chains of pebblestone. Marlowe.
pebbly: Full of pebbles; pebbled. A hard, pebbly bottom. " Johnson.
peccability: The state or quality of being peccable; lability to sin. The common peccability of mankind. Dr. H. More.
peccable: Liable to sin; subject to transgress the divine law. A frail and peccable mortal. " Sir W. Scott.
peccadillo: A slight trespass or offense; a petty crime or fault. Sir W.Scott.
peccancy: The quality or state of being peccant.
peccary: A pachyderm of the genus Dicotyles.
peccavi: I have sinned; used colloquially to express confession or acknowledgment of an offense. Aubrey.
pech: An indigenous Amerindian language spoken in Honduras.
peck: A quick, sharp stroke, as with the beak of a bird or a pointed instrument.
pecked: simple past and past participle of peck
pecker: One who, or that which, pecks; specif., a bird that pecks holes in trees; a woodpecker.
pecking: present participle and gerund of peck
peckish: Inclined to eat; hungry. When shall I feel peckish again Beacons field.
pecksniffery: Hypocritical or sanctimonious behaviour or language.
pecky: Discoloured by fungus growth or insects.
pecos: a tributary of the Rio Grande that flows southeastward from New Mexico through western Texas
pectic: Of or pertaining to pectin; specifically, designating an acid obtained from ordinary vegetable jelly (pectin) as an amorphous substance, tough and horny when dry, but gelatinous when moist.
pectin: One of a series of carbohydrates, commonly called vegetable jelly, found very widely distributed in the vegetable kingdom, especially in ripe fleshy fruits, as apples, cranberries, etc. It is extracted as variously colored, translucent substances, which are soluble in hot water but become viscous on cooling.
pectinesterase: A ubiquitous cell-wall-associated enzyme that presents several isoforms that facilitate plant cell wall modification and subsequent breakdown, found in all higher plants as well as in some bacteria and fungi
pectinibranch: One of the Pectinibranchiata. Also used adjectively.
pectinibranchiata: A division of Gastropoda, including those that have a comblike gill upon the neck.
pectinid: Any member of the Pectinidae; a scallop.
pectize: To congeal; to change into a gelatinous mass. H. Spencer.
pectizing: present participle and gerund of pectize
pectoralis: either of two large muscles of the chest
pectoriloquial: Pertaining to, or of the nature of, pectoriloquy.
pectoriloquy: The distinct articulation of the sounds of a patient's voice, heard on applying the ear to the chest in auscultation. It usually indicates some morbid change in the lungs or pleural cavity.
pectose: An amorphous carbohydrate found in the vegetable kingdom, esp.in unripe fruits. It is associated with cellulose, and is converted into substances of the pectin group.
pectostraca: A degenerate order of Crustacea, including the Rhizocephala and cirripedia.
peculate: To appropriate to one's own use the property of the public; to steal public moneys intrusted to one's care; to embezzle. An oppressive,. rapacious, and peculating despotism. Burke.
peculates: third-person singular simple present indicative of peculate
peculating: present participle and gerund of peculate
peculation: The act or practice of peculating, or of defrauding the public by appropriating to one's own use the money or goods intrusted toone's care for management or disbursement; embezzlement. Every British subject. active in the discovery of peculations has been ruined. Burke.
peculator: One who peculates. Peculators of the public gold. " Cowper.
peculiar: A particular parish or church which is exempt from the jurisdiction of the ordinary. Court of Peculiars (Eng. Law), a branch of the Court of Arches having cognizance of the affairs of peculiars. Black stone. Dean of peculiars. See under Dean,.
peculiarize: To make peculiar; to set ap part or assign, as an exclusive possession. Dr. John Smith.
peculiarizing: present participle and gerund of peculiarize
peculiarly: In a peculiar manner; particulary; in a rare and striking degree; unusually.
peculium: The saving of a son or a slave with the father's or master'sconsent; a little property or stock of one's own; any exclusive personal or separate property. Bur rill.
pecuniarily: In a pecuniary manner; as regards money.
pecuniary: Relating to money; monetary; as, a pecuniary penalty; a pecuniary reward. Burke.
ped: A basket; a hammer; a pannier. Halliwell.
pedagogics: The science or art of teaching; the principles and rules of teaching; pedagogy.
pedagogism: The system, occupation, character, or manner of pedagogues. Milton. Avocation of pedantry and pedagogism. De Foe.
pedagogue: A slave who led his master's children to school, and had the charge of them generally.
pedal: Of or pertaining to a pedal; having pedals. Pedal curve or surface (Geom.), the curve or surface which is the locus of the feet of perpendiculars let fall from a fixed point upon the straight lines tangent to a given curve, or upon the planes tangent to a given surface. Pedal note (Mus.), the note which is held or sustained through an organ point. See Organ point, under Organ. Pedal organ (Mus.), an organ which has pedals or a range of keys moved by the feet; that portion of a full organ which is played with the feet.
pedaled: simple past and past participle of pedal
pedalfer: Soil containing aluminum and iron that lacks a hardened layer of carbonates.
pedaliaceae: the family of plants of order Polemoniales
pedaling: present participle and gerund of pedal
pedalling: present participle and gerund of pedal
pedant: Of or pertaining to a pedant; characteristic of, or resembling, a pedant; ostentatious of learning; as, a pedantic writer; a pedantic description; a pedantical affectation. Figures pedantical.
pedantic: marked by a narrow focus on or display of learning especially its trivial aspects
pedantocracy: The sway of pedants. J. S. Mill.
pedantry: The act, character, or manners of a pedant; vain ostentation of learning. This pedantry of quotation. " Cowl ey.'T is a practice that savors much of pedantry. Sir T. Browne.
pedata: An order of holothuria ns, including those that have ambulacral suckers, or feet, and an internal gill.
pedate: Palmate, with the lateral lobes cleft into two or more segments; said of a leaf. Pedately, adv.
pedatifid: Cleft in a pedate manner, but having the lobes distinctly connected at the base; said of a leaf.
pedatisect: Pedately veined, the divisions nearly reaching the midrib.
peddle: To sell from place to place; to retail by carrying around from customer to customer; to hawk; hence, to retail in very small quantities; as, to peddle vegetables or tinware.
peddled: simple past and past participle of peddle
peddler: One who peddles; a traveling trader; one who travels about, retailing small wares; a hawker. Some vagabond huckster or peddler. " Hakluyt.
peddlery: The trade, or the goods, of a peddler; hawking; small retail business, like that of a peddler.
peddles: third-person singular simple present indicative of peddle
pederast: One guilty of pederasty; a sodomite.
pederero: A term formerly applied to a short piece of chambered ordnance.
pedesis: Same as Brownian movement, under Brownian.
pedestal: The base or foot of a column, statue, vase, lamp, or the like; the part on which an upright work stands. It consists of three parts, the base, the die or dado, and the cornice or surbase molding. See illust. of Column. Build him a pedestal, and say, Stand there!" Cowper.
pedestaled: Placed on, or supported by, a pedestal; figuratively, exalted. Hawthorne. Pedestaled haply in a palace court. Keats.
pedestrial: Of or pertaining to the feet; employing the foot or feet.
pedestrian: Going on foot; performed on foot; as, a pedestrian journey.
pedestrianism: The act, art, or practice of a pedestrian; walking or running; traveling or racing on foot.
pedestrianize: To practice walking; to travel on foot.
pedestrious: Going on foot; not winged. Pedestrious animals. " Sir T.Browne.
pedetentous: Proceeding step by step; advancing cautiously. That pedetentous pace and pedetentous mind in which it behooves the wise and virtuous improver to walk. Sydney Smith.
pedial: Pertaining to the foot, or to any organ called a foot; pedal. Dana.
pediatric: Pertaining to the care and medical treatment of children.
pediatrician: a specialist in the care of babies and young children
pediatrics: That branch of medical science which treats of the hygiene and diseases of children.
pedicab: a tricycle (usually propelled by pedalling); used in the Orient for transporting passengers for hire
pedicel: A slender stem by which certain of the lower animals or their eggs are attached. See Illust. of Aphis lion.
pedicellate: Having a pedicel; supported by a pedicel.
pedicellina: A genus of Bryozoa, of the order Entoprocta, having a bell-shaped body supported on a slender pedicel. See Illust. under entoprocta.
pedicular: Of or pertaining to lice; having the lousy distemper (phthiriasis); lousy. Southey.
pediculati: An order of fishes including the anglers. See Illust. of Angler and Batfish.
pediculidae: true lice: human lice and related forms
pediculus: A genus of wingless parasitic Hemiptera, including the common lice of man. See Louse.
pedicure: care for one's feet by cutting and shaping the nails, etc.
pedigerous: Bearing or having feet or legs.
pedigree: A record of the lineage or strain of an animal, as of a horse.
pedimanous: Having feet resembling hands, or with the first toe opposable, as the opossums and monkeys.
pediment: Originally, in classical architecture, the triangular space forming the gable of a simple roof; hence, a similar form used as adecoration over porticoes, doors, windows, etc.; also, a rounded or broken frontal having a similar position and use. See Temple.
pedipalpi: A division of Arachnida, including the whip scorpions (Thelyphonus) and allied forms. Sometimes used in a wider sense to include also the true scorpions.
pedlar: someone who travels about selling his wares (as on the streets or at carnivals)
pedobaptism: The baptism of infants or of small children.
pedocal: Any of a class of soils that are rich in calcium carbonate.
pedogenesis: Process of the formation of soil.
pedogenic: Pertaining to processes that add, transfer, transform, or remove soil constituents.
pedological: Of or pertaining to pedology (in all senses)
pedologist: A scientist who studies origins, composition and distribution of soils and the materials from which soils are formed.
pedometer: An instrument for including the number of steps in walking, andso ascertaining the distance passed over. It is usually in the form of a watch; an oscillating weight by the motion of the body causes the index to advance a certain distance at each step.
pedometric: Relating to, or measured by, a pedometer
pedomorphism: The retention, by an adult, of juvenile characteristics.
pedophile: an adult who is sexually attracted to children
pedosphere: The outermost layer or skin of the Earth, subject to soil formation processes.
pedotrophy: The art of nourishing children properly.
pedrail: A device intended to replace the wheel of a self-propelled vehicle for use on rough roads and to approximate to the smoothness in running of a wheel on a metal track. The tread consists of a number of rubber shod feet which are connected by ball-and-socket joints to the ends of sliding spokes. Each spoke has attached to it a small roller which in its turn runs under a short pivoted rail controlled by a powerful set of springs. This arrangement permits the feet to accomodate themselves to obstacles even such as steps or stairs. The pedrail was invented by one B. J. Di plock of London, Eng.
pedro: The five of trumps in certain varieties of auction pitch.
peduncle: The stem or stalk that supports the flower or fruit of a plant, or a cluster of flowers or fruits.
pedunculata: A division of Cirripedia, including the stalked or goose barnacles.
pedunculate: having or growing on or from a peduncle or stalk
peek: To look slyly, or with the eyes half closed, or through acre vice; to peep.
peel: A small tower, fort, or castle; a keep.
peele: A graceful and swift South African antelope (Pelea capreola).The hair is woolly, and ash-gray on the back and sides. The horns are black, long, slender, straight, nearly smooth, and very sharp. Called also rheeboc, and rehboc.
peeling: loss of bits of outer skin by peeling or shedding or coming off in scales
peen: To draw, bend, or straighten, as metal, by blows with the peen of a hammer or sledge.
peeper: an informal term referring to the eye
peephole: A hole, or crevice, through which one may peep without being discovered.
peeping: The action of the verb to peep.
peepshow: an exhibition of pictures or objects viewed through a small hole or magnifying glass
peepul: fig tree of India noted for great size and longevity
peer: To look narrowly or curiously or intently; to peep; as, the peering day. Milton. Peering in maps for ports, and piers, and roads. As if through a dungeon grate he peered. Coleridge.
peerage: the peers of a kingdom considered as a group
peered: simple past and past participle of peer
peeress: The wife of a peer; a woman ennobled in her own right, or by right of marriage.
peering: present participle and gerund of peer
peerless: Having no peer or equal; matchless; superlative. Her peerless feature. Un vailed her peerless light. Milton.Peerlessly, adv. Peerlessness, n.
peership: The rank, status, or title of a peer
peeve: cause to be annoyed, irritated, or resentful
peever: a small stone or other small object, used in hopscotch.
peevish: Habitually fretful; easily vexed or fretted; hard to please; apt to complain; querulous; petulant. Her peevish babe. " Wordsworth. She is peevish, sullen, froward.
peevishness: The quality of being peevish; disposition to murmur; sourness of temper.
peewee: small olive-colored woodland flycatchers of eastern North America
peewit: small olive-colored woodland flycatchers of eastern North America
peg: To score with a peg, as points in the game; as, she peggedtwelwe points.
pegasus: A winged horse fabled to have sprung from the body of Medusa when she was slain. He is noted for causing, with a blow of his hoof, Hippocrene, the inspiring fountain of the Muses, to spring from Mount helicon. On this account he is, in modern times, associated with the muses, and with ideas of poetic inspiration. Each spurs his jaded Pegasus apace. Byron.
pegboard: a board perforated with regularly spaced holes into which pegs can be fitted
pegbox: The part of a violin or similar stringed instrument that holds the tuning pegs.
pegging: The act or process of fastening with pegs.
pegleg: a prosthesis that replaces a missing leg
pegmatite: a form of igneous rock consisting of extremely coarse granite resulting from the crystallization of magma rich in rare elements
pehlevi: An ancient Persian dialect in which words were partly represented by their Semitic equivalents. It was in use from the dcentury (and perhaps earlier) to the middle of the th century, and later in religious writings.
pei: United States architect (born in China in )
peignoir: A woman's loose dressing sack; hence, a loose morning gown or wrapper.
peirastic: Fitted for trail or test; experimental; tentative; treating of attempts.
peise: A weight; a poise. To weigh pence with a peise. " Piers plowman.
pejoration: The act or process of becoming worse; worsening or degeneration.
pejorative: Implying or imputing evil; depreciatory; disparaging; unfavorable.
pejorist: One who believes that the world is getting worse.
peking: Dated form of Beijing: a direct-administered municipality, the capital city of China.
pekingese: The Beijing dialect of Chinese, as distinct from standardized Mandarin.
pel: the smallest discrete component of an image or picture on a screen, usually a colored dot; also known as a pixel
pelage: The covering, or coat, of a mammal, whether of wool, fur, or hair.
pelagian: Of or pertaining to the sea; marine; pelagic; as, pelagian shells.
pelagic: Of or pertaining to the ocean; applied especially to animals that live at the surface of the ocean, away from the coast.
pelagius: a British or Irish monk who denied the doctrines of original sin and predestination and defended human goodness and free will; his views were declared heretical by the Council of Ephesus in (circa -)
pelargonic: Pertaining to, or designating, an organic acid (called also nonoic acid) found in the leaves of the geranium (Pelargonium) an dallied plants.
pelargonidin: An anthocyanidin, -(-hydroxyphenyl)chromenylium-,-triol, found in geraniums and several soft berries
pelargonin: An anthocyanin that is a glucoside of pelargonidin
pele: The Hawaiian goddess of fire and volcanos.
pelecoid: A figure, somewhat hatched-shaped, bounded by a semicircle and two inverted quadrants, and equal in area to the square ABCD inclosed by the chords of the four quadrants. Math. Dict.
pelerine: A woman's cape; especially, a fur cape that is longer in front than behind.
peleus: a king of the Myrmidons and father of Achilles
pelf: Money; riches; lucre; gain; generally conveying the idea of something ill-gotten or worthless. It has no plural. Mucky pelf. Spenser. Paltry pelf. " Burke. Can their pelf prosper, not got by valor or industry Fuller.
pelican: Any large webfooted bird of the genus of Pelecanus, of which about a dozen species are known. They have an enormous bill, to the lower edge of which is attached a pouch in which captured fishes are temporarily stored.
pelike: A ceramic container of Ancient Greece, similar to an amphora.
pelisse: An outer garment for men or women, originally of fur, or lined with fur; a lady's outer garment, made of silk or other fabric.
pelite: A sedimentary rock containing very fine particles.
pell: To pelt; to knock about. Holland.
pellagra: An erythematous affection of the skin, with severe constitutional and nervous symptoms, endemic in Northern Italy.
pellagrous: Pertaining to, or affected with, or attendant on, pellagra; as, pellagrous insanity.
pelleted: Made of, or like, pellets; furnished with pellets. This pelleted storm.
pelletierine: An alkaloid obtained from pomegranate bark and used as a taenifuge.
pelletizing: present participle and gerund of pelletize
pellibranchiata: A division of Nudibranchiata, in which the mantle itself serves as a gill.
pellicle: A thin film formed on the surface of an evaporating solution.
pellicularia: genus of fungi having the hymenium in the form of a crust; some species formerly placed in form genus Rhizoctinia
pellitory: The common name of the several species of the genus Parietaria, low, harmless weeds of the Nettle family; also called wall pellitory, and lichwort.
pellmell: In utter confusion; with confused violence. Men, horses, chariots, crowded pellmell. " Milton.
pellucid: Transparent; clear; limpid; translucent; not opaque. Pellucid crystal. " Dr. H. More. Pellucid streams. " Wordsworth.
pellucidness: passing light without diffusion or distortion
pelma: The under surface of the foot.
pelobatidae: the amphibian family of spadefoot toads
peloponnese: the southern peninsula of Greece; dominated by Sparta until the th century BC
peloponnesian: Of or pertaining to the Peloponnesus, or southern peninsula of greece. n.
pelops: A Greek mythological figure, the son of Tantalus, and king of Pisa in the Peloponnesus.
peloria: Abnormal regularity; the state of certain flowers, which, being naturally irregular, have become regular through a symmetrical repetition of the special irregularity.
pelorism: An abnormality in plants where the flower appears to revert to an earlier form.
pelorus: An instrument similar to a mariner's compass, but without magnetic needles, and having two sight vanes by which bearings are taken, esp. such as cannot be taken by the compass.
pelota: A Basque, Spanish, and Spanish-American game played in a court, in which a ball is struck with a wickerwork racket.
peloton: A group of riders formed during a cycling road race; especially, the main group of riders; the pack.
pelt: The body of any quarry killed by the hawk. Pelt rot, a disease affecting the hair or wool of a beast.
pelta: A small shield, especially one of an approximately elliptic form, or crescent-shaped.
peltast: A type of light infantry unit in Ancient Greece who often served as skirmishers.
peltate: (of a leaf shape) round, with the stem attached near the center of the lower surface rather than the margin (as a nasturtium leaf for example)
pelted: simple past and past participle of pelt
peltogaster: Any member of the genus Peltogaster.
peltry: Pelts or skins, collectively; skins with the fur on them; furs.
pelusiac: Of or pertaining to Pelu sium, an ancient city of Egypt; as, the pelusiac (or former eastern) outlet of the Nile.
pelvic: Of, pertaining to, or in the region of, the pelvis; as, pelvic cellulitis. Pelvic arch, or Pelvic girdle (Anat.), the two or more bony or cartilaginous pieces of the vertebrate skeleton to which the hind limbs are articulated. When fully ossified, the arch usually consists of three principal bones on each side, the ilium, ischium, and pubis, which are often closely united in the adult, forming the innominate bone. See Innominate bone, under Innominate.
pelvis: The pelvic arch, or the pelvic arch together with the sacrum. See Pelvic arch, under Pelvic, and Sacrum.
pemican: lean dried meat pounded fine and mixed with melted fat
pemmican: lean dried meat pounded fine and mixed with melted fat; used especially by North American Indians
pemoline: A medication used to treat ADHD and narcolepsy, having similar action to methylphenidate.
pemphigus: A somewhat rare skin disease, characterized by the development of blebs upon different part of the body. Quain.
pen: The internal shell of a squid.
penal: Of or pertaining to punishment, to penalties, or to crimes and offenses; pertaining to criminal jurisprudence: as:(a) Enacting or threatening punishment; as, a penal statue; the penal code.(b) Incurring punishment; subject to a penalty; as, a penal act of offense.(c) Inflicted as punishment; used as a means of punishment; as, apenal colony or settlement. Adamantine chains and penal fire. Milton. Penal code (Law), a code of laws concerning crimes and offenses and their punishment. Penal laws, Penal statutes (Law), laws prohibited certain acts, and imposing penalties for committing them. Penal servitude, imprisonment with hard labor, in a prison, in lieu of transportation. Penal suit, Penal action (Law), a suit for penalties.
penalised: simple past and past participle of penalise
penality: The quality or state of being penal; lability to punishment. Sir T. Browne.
penalize: To put a penalty on. See Penalty,.
penalty: a payment required for not fulfilling a contract
penance: A means of repairing a sin committed, and obtaining pardon forit, consisting partly in the performance of expiatory rites, partly in voluntary submission to a punishment corresponding to the transgression. Penance is the fourth of seven sacraments in the Roman catholic Church. Sc haff-Herzog Encyc. And bitter penance, with an iron whip. Spenser. Quoth he, The man hath penance done, And penance more will do. Coleridge.
penang: A state in western Malaysia. Capital: George Town.
penannular: Nearly annular; having nearly the form of a ring. Penannular relics. " D. Wilson.
penates: The household gods of the ancient Romans. They presided over the home and the family hearth. See Lar.
pencel: A small, narrow flag or streamer borne at the top of a lance; called also pennoncel. Piers Plowman. Chaucer.
penchant: Inclination; decided taste; bias; as, a penchant for art.
pencil: An aggregate or collection of rays of light, especially when diverging from, or converging to, a point.
penciler: In comic book production, a person who develops the plot and creative content, and draws an outline to be filled in by an inker.
pendant: A hanging ornament on roofs, ceilings, etc., much used in the later styles of Gothic architecture, where it is of stone, and an important part of the construction. There are imitations in plaster and wood, which are mere decorative features. with.pendants graven fair. " Spenser.
pendency: The quality or state of being pendent or suspended.
pendicle: An appendage; something dependent on another; an appurtenance; a pendant. Sir W. Scott.
pending: Not yet decided; in continuance; in suspense; as, a pending suit.
pendragon: A chief leader or a king; a head; a dictator; a title assumed by the ancient British chiefs when called to lead other chiefs. The dread Pendragon, Britain's king of kings. Tennyson.
pendulosity: The state or quality of being pendulous. Sir T. Browne.
pendulous: Inclined or hanging downwards, as a flower on a recurved stalk, or an ovule which hangs from the upper part of the ovary.
pendulousness: The quality or state of being pendulous; the state of hanging loosely; pendulosity.
pendulum: A body so suspended from a fixed point as to swing freely toand fro by the alternate action of gravity and momentum. It is used to regulate the movements of clockwork and other machinery.
penelope: A genus of curassows, including the guans.
peneplain: A land surface reduced by erosion to the general condition of ap lain, but not wholly devoid of hills; a base-level plain.
penetrable: Capable of being penetrated, entered, or pierced. Used also figuratively. And pierce his only penetrable part. Dryden. I am not made of stones, But penetrable to your kind entreats. Penetrableness, n. Penetrably, adv.
penetralia: The quality or state of being penetrant; power of entering or piercing; penetrating power of quality; as, the penetrancy of subtile effluvia.
penetrance: The quality or state of being penetrant; power of entering or piercing; penetrating power.
penetrancy: The quality or state of being penetrant; penetrance.
penetrant: Having power to enter or pierce; penetrating; sharp; subtile; as, penetrant cold. Penetrant and powerful arguments. " Boyle.
penetrate: To pass; to make way; to pierce. Also used figuratively. Preparing to penetrate to the north and west. J. R. Green. Born where Heaven's influence scarce can penetrate. Pope. The sweet of life that penetrates so near. Daniel.
penetrated: simple past and past participle of penetrate
penetrates: third-person singular simple present indicative of penetrate
penetrating: Having the power of entering, piercing, or pervading; sharp; subtile; penetrative; as, a penetrating odor.
penetration: an attack that penetrates into enemy territory
penetrative: tending to penetrate; having the power of entering or piercing
penetrator: an intruder who passes into or through (often by overcoming resistance)
penetrometer: A mechanical device that measures the ease of penetration of an object into a semisolid
peneus: type genus of the family Peneid ae
pengo: formerly the basic unit of money in Hungary until it was replaced by the forint in

penicil: A tent or pledget for wounds or ulcers.
penicillate: Having the form of a pencil; furnished with a pencil of fine hairs; ending in a tuft of hairs like a camel's-hair brush, as the stigmas of some grasses.
penicillin: any of various antibiotics obtained from Penicillium molds (or produced synthetically) and used in the treatment of various infections and diseases
penicillinase: enzyme produced by certain bacteria that inactivates penicillin and results in resistance to that antibiotic
penicillium: genus of fungi commonly growing as green or blue molds on decaying food; used in making cheese and as a source of penicillin
penile: of or relating to the penis
peninsula: A portion of land nearly surrounded by water, and connected with a larger body by a neck, or isthmus.
peninsular: Of or pertaining to a peninsula; as, a peninsular form; peninsular people; the peninsular war.
penis: The male member, or organ of generation.
penistone: A coarse woolen material or frieze, used in England during the th and th centuries.
penitence: The quality or condition of being penitent; the disposition of a penitent; sorrow for sins or faults; repentance; contrition. Penitence of his old guilt. " Chaucer. Death is deferred, and penitenance has room To mitigate, if not reverse, the doom. Dryden.
penitent: feeling or expressing remorse for misdeeds
penitential: Of or pertaining to penitence, or to penance; expressing penitence; of the nature of penance; as, the penitential book; penitential tears. Penitential stripes. " Cowper. Guilt that all the penitential fires of hereafter can not cleanse. Sir W. Scott.
penitentiary: used for punishment or reform of criminals or wrongdoers
penknife: A small pocketknife; formerly, a knife used for making and mending quill pens.
penlight: a small flashlight resembling a fountain pen
penman: One who uses the pen; a writer; esp., one skilled in the use of the pen; a calligrapher; a writing master.
penmanship: The use of the pen in writing; the art of writing; style or manner of writing; chirography; as, good or bad penmanship.
penn: Englishman and Quaker who founded the colony of Pennsylvania (-)
pennatula: Any one of numerous species of Pennatula, Pteroid es, and allied genera of Alcyonaria, having a featherlike form; a sea-pen. The zooids are situated along one edge of the side branches.
pennatulacea: A division of alcyonoid corals, including the sea pens and related kinds. They are able to move about by means of the hollow muscular peduncle, which also serves to support them upright in the mud. See Pennatula, and Illust. under Alcyonaria.
penner: One who pens; a writer. Sir T. North.
penni: pennia formerly equaled markka in Finland
penniform: Having the form of a feather or plume.
penniless: Destitute of money; impecunious; poor. Pennilessness, n.
pennines: a system of hills in Britain that extend from the Scottish border in the north to the Trent River in the south; forms the watershed for English rivers
penning: the act of creating written works
pennisetum: a genus of Old World grasses
pennoncel: a small pennant borne on a lance
pennsylvania: a Mid-Atlantic state; one of the original colonies
pennsylvanian: from million to million years ago; warm climate; swampy land
penny: Denoting pound weight for one thousand; used in combination, with respect to nails; as, tenpenny nails, nails of which one thousand weight ten pounds.
pennycress: any of several plants of the genus Thlaspi
pennyroyal: An aromatic herb (Mentha Pulegium) of Europe; also, a North american plant (Hedeoma pulegioides) resembling it in flavor. Bastard pennyroyal (Bot.) See Blue curls, under Blue.
pennyweight: A troy weight containing twenty-four grains, or the twentieth part of an ounce; as, a pennyweight of gold or of arsenic. It was anciently the weight of a silver penny, whence the name.
pennywort: A European trailing herb (Linaria Cymbalaria) with roundish, reniform leaves. It is often cultivated in hanging baskets. March, or water, pennywort. (Bot.) See under March.
pennyworth: the amount that can be bought for a penny
penobscot: a member of the Algonquian people belonging to the Abnaki confederacy and living in the Penobscot valley in northern Maine
penoche: fudge made with brown sugar and butter and milk and nuts
penologist: One versed in, or a student of, penology.
penology: The science or art of punishment.
penoncel: a small pennant borne on a lance
penpoint: The point of a pen (writing implement).
pensile: Hanging; suspended; pendent; pendulous. Bacon. The long, pensile branches of the birches. W. Howitt.
pension: A boarding house or boarding school in France, Belgium, Switzerland, etc.
pensionary: Maintained by a pension; receiving a pension; as, pensionary spies. Donne.
pensioner: In the university of Cambridge, England, one who pays for hi sliving in commons; corresponding to commoner at Oxford. Ld. Lytton.
pensiveness: The state of being pensive; serious thoughtfulness; seriousness. Hooker.
penstemon: large genus of subshrubs or herbs having showy blue or purple or red or yellow or white flowers; mostly western North America
penstock: A close conduit or pipe for conducting water, as, to a water wheel, or for emptying a pond, or for domestic uses.
pent: Penned or shut up; confined; often with up. Here in the body pent. J. Montgomery. No pent-up Utica contracts your powers. J. M. Se wall.
pentachloride: A chloride having five atoms of chlorine in each molecule.
pentacid: Capable of neutralizing, or combining with, five molecules of amonobasic acid; having five hydrogen atoms capable of substitution by acid residues; said of certain complex bases.
pentacle: A figure composed of two equilateral triangles intersecting soas to form a six-pointed star, used in early ornamental art, and also with superstitious import by the astrologers and mystics of the middle Ages.
pentacrinus: A genus of large, stalked crinoids, of which several species occur in deep water among the West Indies and elsewhere.
pentacyclic: Having five rings, especially five fused rings as in many triterpenoids.
pentad: Any element, atom, or radical, having a valence of five, or which can be combined with, substituted for, or compared with, five atoms of hydrogen or other monad; as, nitrogen is a pentad in the ammonium compounds.
pentadactyl: Having five digits on a limb.
pentadactyloid: Having the form of, or a structure modified from, a pentadactyl limb.
pentadecahydrate: A hydrate containing fifteen molecules of water per molecule or unit cell.
pentadecane: A hydrocarbon of the paraffin series, (CH) found in petroleum, tar oil, etc., and obtained as a colorless liquid; so called from the fifteen carbon atoms in the molecule.
pentadic: of, or relating to a pentad
pentadrachm: An ancient Cyrenaic coin that was worth five drachmas.
pentaerythritol: a coronary vasodilator (trade name Perit rate) used to treat angina pectoris
pentaglot: A work in five different tongues.
pentagon: A plane figure having five angles, and, consequently, five sides; any figure having five angles. Regular pentagon, a pentagon in which the angles are all equal, and the sides all equal.
pentagonal: Having five corners or angles. Pentagonal dodecahedron. See dodecahedron, and Pyritohedron.
pentagram: A pentacle or a pentalpha. Like a wizard pentagram. " Tennyson.
pentahedral: Having five sides; as, a pentahedral figure.
pentahedron: A solid figure having five sides.
pentahydroxy: Five hydroxy groups in a molecule.
pentail: A peculiar insectivore (Ptilocercus Lowii) of Borneo; so called from its very long, quill-shaped tail, which is scaly at the base and plumose at the tip.
pentaiodide: Any iodide having five iodine atoms
pentalogy: A set of five works of art that are connected, and that can be seen either as a single work or as five individual works.
pentalpha: A five-pointed star, resembling five alphas joined at their bases; used as a symbol.
pentamera: An extensive division of Coleoptera, including those that normally have five-jointed tarsi. It embraces about half of all the known species of the Coleoptera.
pentamerous: Divided into, or consisting of, five parts; also, arranged insets, with five parts in each set, as a flower with five sepals, five petals, five, or twice five, stamens, and five pistils.
pentamerus: A genus of extinct Paleozoic brachiopods, often very abundant in the Upper Silurian. Pentamerus limestone (Geol.), a Silurian limestone composed largely of the shells of Pentamerus.
pentane: Any one of the three metameric hydrocarbons, CH, of the methane or paraffin series. They are colorless, volatile liquids, twoof which occur in petroleum. So called because of the five carbon atoms in the molecule.
pentanedione: Either of two isomeric aliphatic diketones (,-pentanedione,-pentanedione) derived from pentane
pentanoic: Of or pertaining to pentanoic acid or its derivatives
pentaploid: That has five haploid sets of chromosomes
pentapody: A measure or series consisting of five feet.
pentapolis: A geographic and/or institutional grouping of five cities
pentaquin: An -amino-quinoline derivative used to treat malaria.
pentarchy: A government in the hands of five persons; five joint rulers. P. Fletcher. The pentarchy of the senses. " A. Brewer.
pentastichous: Having, or arranged in, five vertical ranks, as the leaves of an apple tree or a cherry tree.
pentastome: Any tongue worm of the subclass Pentastomida
pentasulphide: any sulphide containing five sulphur atoms in each molecule
pentasyllabic: having or characterized by or consisting of five syllables
pentateuch: The first five books of the Old Testament, collectively; called also the Law of Moses, Book of the Law of Moses, etc.
pentathionic: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid of sulphur obtained by leading hydrogen sulphide into a solution of sulphur dioxide; so called because it contains five atoms of sulphur.
pentathlete: an athlete who competes in a pentathlon
pentathlon: A fivefold athletic performance peculiar to the great national games of the Greeks, including leaping, foot racing, wrestling, throwing the discus, and throwing the spear.
pentavalent: Having a valence of five; said of certain atoms and radicals.
penteconter: A Grecian vessel with fifty oars.
pentecost: seventh Sunday after Easter; commemorates the emanation of the Holy Spirit to the Apostles; a quarter day in Scotland
pentecostal: Of or pertaining to Pentecost or to Whitsuntide.
pentecostalism: the principles and practices of Pentecostal religious groups; characterized by religious excitement and talking in tongues
pentecoster: An officer in the Spartan army commanding fifty men. Mitford.
pentecosty: A troop of fifty soldiers in the Spartan army; called also pentecostys. Jowett (Thucyd. ).
pentelic: Of or relating to Mount Pentelicus (Penteliko Mountain), near Athens, famous for its fine white marble quarries.
penthemimer: A metrical unit equal to half of a pentameter
penthouse: A shed or roof sloping from the main wall or building, as overa door or window; a lean-to. Also figuratively. The penthouse of his eyes. " Sir W. Scott.
pentice: A penthouse. Sir H. Wot ton.
pentimento: the reappearance in a painting of an underlying image that had been painted over (usually when the later painting becomes transparent with age)
pentine: An unsaturated hydrocarbon, CH, of the acetylene series. Same as Valerylene.
pentlandite: a mineral (iron and nickel sulphide) that is the chief ore of nickel
pentobarbital: a barbiturate (trade name Nembutal) used as a sedative and hypnotic and antispasmodic
pentose: Any of a group of sugars of the formula CHO, as arabinose; so called from the five carbon atoms in the molecule. They are not fermented by yeast.
pentoxide: An oxide containing five atoms of oxygen in each molecule; as, phosphorus pentoxide, PO.
pentremites: A genus of crinoids belonging to the Blastoidea. They have five petal-like ambulacra.
pentyl: The hypothetical radical, CH, of pentane and certain of its derivatives. Same as Amyl.
pentylenetetrazol: a drug used as a circulatory and respiratory stimulant; larger doses cause convulsions in shock therapy; Metrazol is a trademark
pentylic: Pertaining to, derived from, or containing, pentyl; as, pentylic alcohol
penuche: fudge made with brown sugar and butter and milk and nuts
penuchle: a card game played with a pack of forty-eight cards (two of each suit for high cards)
penult: The last syllable but one of a word; the syllable preceding the final one.
penultimate: Last but one; as, the penultimate syllable, the last syllable but one of a word.
penumbra: The shadow cast, in an eclipse, where the light is partly, but not wholly, cut off by the intervening body; the space of partial illumination between the umbra, or perfect shadow, on all sides, and the full light. Sir I. Newton.
penurious: Excessively sparing in the use of money; sordid; stingy; miserly. A penurious niggard of his wealth. " Milton.
penuriousness: a disposition to be niggardly with money
penury: Absence of resources; want; privation; indigence; extreme poverty; destitution. A penury of military forces. " Bacon. They were exposed to hardship and penury. Sprat. It arises in neither from penury of thought. Land or.
penutian: a family of Amerindian language spoken in the great interior valley of California
penwoman: A female writer; an authoress. Johnson.
people: To stock with people or inhabitants; to fill as with people; to populate. Peopled heaven with angels. " Dryden. As the gay motes that people the sunbeams. Milton.
peopled: Stocked with, or as with, people; inhabited. The peopled air. Gray.
peopler: A settler; an inhabitant. Peoplers of the peaceful glen. " J.S. Blackie.
peoples: the human beings of a particular nation or community or ethnic group
peoria: a city in central Illinois on the Illinois River
peperino: A light, porous volcanic rock composed of small grains of sand etc.
peperomia: any of various plants of the genus Peperomia; grown primarily for their often succulent foliage
peplos: a garment worn by women in ancient Greece; cloth caught at the shoulders and draped in folds to the waist
peplum: A peplos. Hence: An overskirt hanging like an ancient peplos; also, a short fitted skirt attached to a waist or coat.
peplus: An upper garment worn by Grecian and Roman women.
pepo: Any fleshy fruit with a firm rind, as a pumpkin, melon, or gourd. See Gourd.
peponium: Any of the plants of the genus Peponium.
pepper: The plant which yields pepper, an East Indian woody climber (Piper ni grum), with ovate leaves and apetalous flowers in spikes opposite the leaves. The berries are red when ripe. Also, by extension, any one of the several hundred species of the genus Piper, widely dispersed throughout the tropical and subtropical regions of the earth.
peppercorn: A dried berry of the black pepper (Piper ni grum).
pepperer: A grocer; formerly so called because he sold pepper.
peppergrass: Any herb of the cruciferous genus Lepidium, especially the garden peppergrass, or garden cress, Lepidium sati vum; called also pepperwort. All the species have a pungent flavor.
pepperidge: A North American tree (Nyssa multiflora) with very tough wood, handsome oval polished leaves, and very acid berries, the sour gum, or common tupelo. See Tupelo. Pepperidge bush (Bot.), the barberry.
peppermint: An aromatic and pungent plant of the genus Mentha (M.pipe rita), much used in medicine and confectionery.
pepperoni: a pork and beef sausage (or a thin slice of this sausage)
peppery: having the piquant burning taste of peppers
pepsi: Pepsi Cola is a trademarked cola
pepsin: An unorganized proteolytic ferment or enzyme contained in the secretory glands of the stomach. In the gastric juice it is united with dilute hydrochloric acid (. per cent, approximately) and the two together constitute the active portion of the digestive fluid. Itis the active agent in the gastric juice of all animals.
peptic: Pertaining to pepsin; resembling pepsin in its power of digesting or dissolving albuminous matter; containing or yielding pepsin, or a body of like properties; as, the peptic glands.
peptidase: any enzyme that catalyzes the splitting of proteins into smaller peptide fractions and amino acids by a process known as proteolysis
peptide: amide combining the amino group of one amino acid with the carboxyl group of another; usually obtained by partial hydrolysis of protein
peptidoglycan: A polymer of glycan and peptides found in bacterial cell walls
peptize: disperse in a medium into a colloidal state
peptized: simple past and past participle of peptize
peptizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of peptize
peptogenous: Capable of yielding, or being converted into, peptone.
peptohydrochloric: Designating a hypothetical acid (called peptohydrochloric acid, pepsinhydrochloric acid, and chloropeptic acid) which is supposed tobe formed when pepsin and dilute (.-. per cent) hydrochloric acid are mixed together.
peptone: any of various water-soluble compounds that form by hydrolysis in the digestion of proteins to amino acids
peptonization: The conversion of a protein into peptones under the influence of the enzyme pepsin
peptonize: To convert into peptone; to digest or dissolve by means of aproteolytic ferment; as, peptonized food.
peptonized: simple past and past participle of peptonize
pepys: English diarist whose diary contained detailed descriptions of th century disasters in England (-)
pequot: A member of a tribe of Native Americans who historically inhabited eastern Connecticut and spoke a variety of Mohegan-Pequot.
per: Through; by means of; through the agency of; by; for; for each; as, per annum; per capita, by heads, or according to individuals; per curiam, by the court; per se, by itself, of itself. Per is also sometimes used with English words. Per annum, by the year; in each successive year; annually. Per cent, Per centum, by the hundred; in the hundred; used esp. of proportions of ingredients, rate or amount of interest, and the like; commonly used in the shortened form per cent. Per diem, by the day.
peracetic: Of or pertaining to peracetic acid or its derivatives.
peracid: Any acid that contains a peroxy group - e.g. peracetic acid
peracute: Very sharp; very violent; as, a peracute fever. Harvey.
peradventure: By chance; perhaps; it may be; if; supposing. If peradventure he speak against me. Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city. Gen. xviii.
peragration: The act or state of passing through any space; as, the peragration of the moon in her monthly revolution. Sir T.Browne.
perambulate: To walk through or over; especially, to travel over for the purpose of surveying or examining; to inspect by traversing; specifically, to inspect officially the boundaries of, as of a town or parish, by walking over the whole line.
perambulates: third-person singular simple present indicative of perambulate
perambulation: a walk around a territory (a parish or manor or forest etc.) in order to officially assert and record its boundaries
perameles: Any marsupial of the genus Perameles, which includes numerous species found in Australia. They somewhat resemble rabbits in size and form. See Illust. under Bandicoot.
perbromic: Pertaining to, or designating, the highest oxygen acid, HBr O,of bromine.
percale: A fine cotton fabric, having a linen finish, and often printed on one side, used for women's and children's wear.
percarbide: A compound containing a relatively large amount of carbon.
perceivable: Capable of being perceived; perceptible. Perceivably, adv.
perceivance: Power of perceiving. The senses and common perceivance. " Milton.
perceive: to become aware of through the senses
perceived: detected by means of the senses
perceiver: One who perceives (in any of the senses of the verb). Milton.
perceives: third-person singular simple present indicative of perceive
perceiving: present participle and gerund of perceive
percent: a proportion in relation to a whole (which is usually the amount per hundred)
percentage: A certain rate per cent; the allowance, duty, rate of interest, discount, or commission, on a hundred.
percentile: (statistics) any of the numbered points that divide an ordered set of scores into parts each of which contains one-hundredth of the total
perceptibility: the property of being perceptible by the mind or the senses
perceptible: Capable of being perceived; cognizable; discernible; perceivable. With a perceptible blast of the air. Bacon. Perceptibleness, n. Perceptibly, adv.
perception: The faculty of perceiving; the faculty, or peculiar part, ofman's constitution by which he has knowledge through the medium or instrumentality of the bodily organs; the act of apperhendingmaterial objects or qualities through the senses; distinguished from conception. Sir W. Hamilton. Matter hath no life nor perception, and is not conscious of its own existence. Bent ley.
perceptive: Of or pertaining to the act or power of perceiving; having the faculty or power of perceiving; used in perception. His perceptive and reflective faculties. " Motley.
perceptiveness: the quality of insight and sympathetic understanding
perceptual: of or relating to the act of perceiving
percesoces: An order of fishes including the gray mullets (Mugil), the barracudas, the silversides, and other related fishes. So called from their relation both to perches and to pikes.
perch: To alight or settle, as a bird; to sit or roost. Wrens make prey where eagles dare not perch.
perche: A former province in northwestern France, corresponding to the modern departments of Orne, Eure, Eure-et-Loir, Loir-et-Cher and Sarthe.
perched: simple past and past participle of perch
percher: A Paris candle anciently used in England; also, a large wax candle formerly set upon the altar. Bailey.
percheron: One of a breed of draught horses originating in Perche, an old district of France; called also Percheron-Norman.
perching: present participle and gerund of perch
perchloric: Pertaining to, or designating, the highest oxygen acid (HCl O),of chlorine; called also hyperchloric.
perchlorinate: To chlorinate thoroughly: to add the maximum amount of chlorine to.
perchlorinating: present participle and gerund of perchlorinate
percid: Any fish in the family Percidae, the perches and darters.
percidae: active freshwater fishes; true perches and pike perches
percipient: Having the faculty of perception; perceiving; as, a percipient being. Bent ley. n.
percival: A male given name from the Celtic languages.
percolate: To cause to pass through fine interstices, as a liquor; to filter; to strain. Sir M. Hale.
percolated: simple past and past participle of percolate
percolating: present participle and gerund of percolate
percolation: The act or process of percolating, or filtering; filtration; straining. Specifically (Pharm.), the process of exhausting the virtues of a powdered drug by letting a liquid filter slowly through it.
percolator: One who, or that which, filters. act as percolators. " Hen frey.
percuss: To strike smartly; to strike upon or against; as, to percuss the chest in medical examination. Flame percussed by air giveth a noise. Bacon.
percussed: simple past and past participle of percuss
percussing: present participle and gerund of percuss
percussion: The act of tapping or striking the surface of the body in order to learn the condition of the parts beneath by the sound emitted or the sensation imparted to the fingers. Percussion is said to be immediate if the blow is directly upon the body; if some interventingsubstance, as a pleximeter, is, used, it is called mediate. Center of percussion. See under Center. Percussion bullet, a bullet containing a substance which is exploded by percussion; an explosive bullet. Percussion cap, a small copper cap or cup, containing fulminating powder, and used with a percussion lock to explode gunpowder. Percussion fuze. See under Fuze. Percussion lock, the lock of a gun that is fired by percussion upon fulminating powder. Percussion match, a match which ignites by percussion. Percussion powder, powder so composed as to ignite by slight percussion; fulminating powder. Percussion sieve, Percussion table, a machine for sorting ores by agitation in running water.
percussionist: a musician who plays percussion instruments
percussive: Striking against; percutient; as, percussive force.
percutient: Striking; having the power of striking. n.
percy: United States writer whose novels explored human alienation (-)
perdition: Entire loss; utter destruction; ruin; esp., the utter loss of the soul, or of final happiness in a future state; future misery or eternal death. The mere perdition of the Turkish fleet. If we reject the truth, we seal our own perdition. J. M. Mason.
perdix: A genus of birds including the common European partridge. Formerly the word was used in a much wider sense to include many allied genera.
perdu: One placed on watch, or in ambush.
perdurable: Very durable; lasting; continuing long. Chaucer. Perdurably, adv.
perdure: To last or endure for a long time; to be perdurable or lasting. The mind per dures while its energizing may construct a thousand lines. Hick ok.
perdy: Truly. See Parde. Ah, dame! perdy ye have not done me right. Spenser.
peregal: Fully equal. Chaucer. Peregal to the best. " Spenser.
peregrina: A plant of the spurge family, Jatropha interregima, which is native to the Caribbean but introduced throughout the tropics.
peregrinate: To travel from place to place, or from one country to another; hence, to sojourn in foreign countries.
peregrination: A traveling from one country to another; a wandering; sojourn in foreign countries. His peregrination abroad. " Bacon.
peregrinity: Foreignness; strangeness. Somewhat of a peregrinity in their dialect. " Johnson.
pereion: The thorax of a crustacean, between the head (cephalon) and abdomen (pleon).
peremptorily: In a peremptory manner; absolutely; positively. Bacon.
peremptoriness: The quality of being peremptory; positiveness.
perendinate: To procrastinate for a long time, especially two days.
perennial: Continuing more than two years; as, a perennial steam, or root, or plant.
perf: Abbreviation of perforated; when followed by a number, eg, perf, this indicates the number of perforations per two centimetres.
perfect: Hermaphrodite; having both stamens and pistils; said of flower. Perfect cadence (Mus.), a complete and satisfactory close inharmony, as upon the tonic preceded by the dominant. Perfect chord (Mus.), a concord or union of sounds which is perfectly coalescent and agreeable to the ear, as the unison, octave, fifth, and fourth; a perfect consonance; a common chord in its original position of keynote, third, fifth, and octave. Perfect number (Arith.), a number equal to the sum of all its divisors; as, whose aliquot parts, or divisors, are,,. See Abundant number, under Abundant. Br ande & C. Perfect tense (Gram.), a tense which expresses an act or state completed.
perfecta: a bet that you can pick the first and second finishers in the right order
perfecter: One who, or that which, makes perfect. The. perfecter ofour faith. " Barrow.
perfectible: Capable of becoming, or being made, perfect.
perfecting: present participle and gerund of perfect
perfectionist: One pretending to perfection; esp., one pretending to moral perfection; one who believes that persons may and do attain to moral perfection and sinlessness in this life. South.
perfectionize: To bring to perfection; to perfect.
perfective: Tending or conducing to make perfect, or to bring to perfection; usually followed by of. A perfective alteration. Fuller. Actions perfective of their natures. Ray.
perfectly: In a perfect manner or degree; in or to perfection; completely; wholly; throughly; faultlessly. Perfectly divine. " Milton. As many as touched were made perfectly whole. Matt. xiv.
perfectness: The quality or state of being perfect; perfection. Charity, which is the bond of perfectness. " Col. iii.
perfects: third-person singular simple present indicative of perfect
perfervid: Very fervid; too fervid; glowing; ardent.
perfervor: The state of being perfervid; passion; zealotry.
perfidious: Guilty of perfidy; violating good faith or vows; false to trust or confidence reposed; teache rous; faithless; as, a perfidious friend.
perfidy: The act of violating faith or allegiance; violation of apromise or vow, or of trust reposed; faithlessness; teachery. The ambition and perfidy of tyrants. Macaulay. His perfidy to this sacred engagement. De Quincey.
perfin: Perforated initial; a series of small holes punched into a stamp and forming a letter, series of letters or other design for the purpose of preventing the unauthorized use of the stamps.
perfoliate: Having the basal part produced around the stem; said of leaves which the stem apparently passes directory through.
perforata: A division of corals including those that have a porous texture, as Porites and Madrepora; opposed to Aporosa.
perforate: To bore through; to pierce through with a pointed instrument; to make a hole or holes through by boring or piercing; to pierce or penetrate the surface of. Bacon.
perforated: having a number or series of holes
perforates: third-person singular simple present indicative of perforate
perforating: present participle and gerund of perforate
perforation: a line of small holes for tearing at a particular place
perforator: One who, or that which, perforates; esp., a cephalotome.
perforce: By force; of necessary; at any rate.
perform: To do, execute, or accomplish something; to acquit one's self in any business; esp., to represent sometimes by action; to act apart; to play on a musical instrument; as, the players perform poorly; the musician performs on the organ.
performable: Admitting of being performed, done, or executed; practicable.
performance: The act of performing; the carrying into execution or action; execution; achievement; accomplishment; representation by action; as, the performance of an undertaking of a duty. Promises are not binding where the performance is impossible. Paley.
performative: Being enacted as it is said.
performed: simple past and past participle of perform
performer: One who performs, accomplishes, or fulfills; as, a good promiser, but a bad performer; especially, one who shows skill and training in any art; as, a performer of the drama; a performer on the harp.
performing: the performance of a part or role in a drama
performs: third-person singular simple present indicative of perform
perfume: To fill or impregnate with a perfume; to scent. And Carmel's flowery top perfumes the skies. Pope.
perfumer: a person who makes (and sells) perfumes
perfuming: present participle and gerund of perfume
perfunctorily: In a perfunctory manner; formally; carelessly. Boyle.
perfunctory: Done merely to get rid of a duty; performed mechanically and as a thing of rote; done in a careless and superficial manner; characterized by indifference; as, perfunctory admonitions. Macaulay.
perfuse: To suffuse; to fill full or to excess. Harvey.
perfusing: present participle and gerund of perfuse
pergamene: Of, from or pertaining to Pergamum.
pergamum: an ancient Greek city located in the western part of what is now modern Turkey; the technique of preparing sheepskins as parchment was developed here
pergola: Lit., an arbor or bower; specif.: (Italian art)
perhaps: By chance; peradventure; perchance; it may be. And pray God, if perhaps the thought of thine heart may be forgiven thee. Acts viii.
peri: An imaginary being, male or female, like an elf or fairy, represented as a descendant of fallen angels, excluded from paradise till penance is accomplished. Moore.
perianth: collective term for the outer parts of a flower consisting of the calyx and corolla and enclosing the stamens and pistils
periapsis: (astronomy) the point in an orbit closest to the body being orbited
periapt: A charm worn as a protection against disease or mischief; an amulet. Coleridge. Now help, ye charming spells and periapts.
periastral: Among or around the stars. Comets in periastral passage. " R.A. Proctor.
periastron: That point, in the real or apparent orbit of one star revolving around another, at which the former is nearest to the latter.
periblast: The protoplasmic matter which surrounds the entoblast, or cell nucleus, and undergoes segmentation. Periblastic, a.
periblem: Nascent cortex, or immature cellular bark.
peribolos: In ancient architecture, an inclosed court, esp., one surrounding a temple.

perturbation: A disturbance in the regular elliptic or other motion of aheavenly body, produced by some force additional to that which cause sits regular motion; as, the perturbations of the planets are caused by their attraction on each other. Newcomb.
perturbational: Of or pertaining to perturbation, esp. to the perturbations of the planets. The perturbational theory. " Sir J. Herschel.
perturber: One who, or that which, perturbs, or cause perturbation.
perturbs: third-person singular simple present indicative of perturb
pertusion: The act of punching or piercing with a pointed instrument; as, pertusion of a vein. Arbuthnot.
peru: a republic in western South America; achieved independence from Spain in; was the heart of the Inca empire from the th to th centuries
perula: One of the scales of a leaf bud.
perusal: reading carefully with intent to remember
peruse: examine or consider with attention and in detail
perused: simple past and past participle of peruse
peruses: third-person singular simple present indicative of peruse
peruvian: Of or pertaining to Peru, in South America. n.
pervade: To pass or flow through, as an aperture, pore, or interstice; to permeate. That labyrinth is easily pervaded. Black stone.
pervaded: simple past and past participle of pervade
pervades: third-person singular simple present indicative of pervade
pervading: present participle and gerund of pervade
pervasion: The act of pervading, passing, or spreading through the whole extent of a thing. Boyle.
pervasive: Tending to pervade, or having power to spread throughout; of apervading quality. Civilization pervasive and general. " M. Arnold.
perverse: marked by a disposition to oppose and contradict
perverseness: The quality or state of being perverse. Virtue hath some perverseness. " Donne.
perversion: The act of perverting, or the state of being perverted; at urning from truth or right; a diverting from the true intent or object; a change to something worse; a turning or applying to a wrong end or use. Violations and perversions of the laws. " Bacon.
perversity: The quality or state of being perverse; perverseness.
pervert: To become perverted; to take the wrong course. Testament of Love.
perverted: deviating from what is considered moral or right or proper or good
pervertedly: In a perverted, twisted, or corrupt manner.
perverter: One who perverts (a person or thing). His own parents hisperverters. " South. A perverter of his law. " Bp. Stilling fleet.
perverting: present participle and gerund of pervert
pervicacious: Obstinate; willful; refractory. Pervicaciously, adv. Pervicaciousness, n.
pervious: Open; used synonymously with perforate, as applied to the nostrils or birds.
perviousness: The quality or state of being pervious; as, the perviousness of glass. Boyle.
pes: The distal segment of the hind limb of vertebrates, including the tarsus and foot.
pesade: The motion of a horse when, raising his fore quarters, he keeps his hind feet on the ground without advancing; rearing.
pesanted: Made heavy or dull; debased. Pesanted to each lewd thought's control. " Mars ton.
peseta: A Spanish silver coin, and money of account, equal to about nineteen cents, and divided into centesimos.
pesky: Pestering; vexatious; troublesome. Used also as an intensive. Judd.
peso: A Spanish dollar; also, an Argentine, Chilian, Colombian, etc.,coin, equal to from cents to a dollar; also, a pound weight.
pessary: An instrument or device to be introduced into and worn in the vagina, to support the uterus, or remedy a malposition.
pessimism: The opinion or doctrine that everything in nature is ordered for or tends to the worst, or that the world is wholly evil; opposed to Ant: optimism.
pessimist: One who advocates the doctrine of pessimism; opposed to Ant: optimist.
pessimistically: with pessimism; in a pessimistic manner
pester: To trouble; to disturb; to annoy; to harass with petty vexations. We are pestered with mice and rats. Dr. H. More. A multitude of scribblers daily pester the world. Dryden.
pestered: troubled persistently especially with petty annoyances
pesterment: The act of pestering, or the state of being pestered; vexation; worry. The trouble and pesterment of children. " B. Franklin.
pesters: third-person singular simple present indicative of pester
pestful: Pestiferous. After long and pestful calms. " Coleridge.
pesthole: a breeding ground for epidemic disease
pesticidal: Of, pertaining to, or effective as a pesticide.
pesticide: a chemical used to kill pests (as rodents or insects)
pestiferous: Pest-bearing; pestilential; noxious to health; malignant; infectious; contagious; as, pestiferous bodies. Poor, pestiferous creatures begging alms. " Evelyn. Unwholesome and pestiferous occupations. " Burke.
pestilence: a pernicious and malign influence that is hard to get rid of
pestilent: Pestilential; noxious; pernicious; mischievous. Corrupt and pestilent. " Milton. What a pestilent knave is this same!".
pestilential: Having the nature or qualities of a pestilence. Sends the pestilential vapors. " Longfellow.
pestilently: In a pestilent manner; mischievously; destructively. Above all measure pestilently noisome. " Dr. H. More.
pestillation: The act of pounding and bruising with a pestle in a mortar. Sir T. Browne.
pestis: a serious (sometimes fatal) infection of rodents caused by Yersinia pestis and accidentally transmitted to humans by the bite of a flea that has bitten an infected animal
pestle: To pound, pulverize, bray, or mix with a pestle, or as with apestle; to use a pestle.
pestology: The science of pests and pest control.
pet: A slight fit of peevishness or fretfulness. In a pet shes tarted up. " Tennyson.
petal: One of the leaves of the corolla, or the colored leaves of aflower. See Corolla, and Illust. of Flower.
petaled: Having petals; as, a petaled flower; opposed to Ant: apetalous, and much used in compounds; as, one-petaled, three-petaled, etc.
petaline: Pertaining to a petal; attached to, or resembling, a petal.
petalite: A rare mineral, occurring crystallized and in cleavable masses, usually white, or nearly so, in color. It is a silicate of aluminiaand lithia.
petalody: The metamorphosis of various floral organs, usually stamens, into petals.
petar: See Petard. Hoist with his own petar.
petard: A case containing powder to be exploded, esp. a conical or cylindrical case of metal filled with powder and attached to a plank, to be exploded against and break down gates, barricades, drawbridges, etc. It has been superseded.
petasites: genus of rhizomatous herbs of north temperate regions: butterbur; sweet coltsfoot
petasus: The winged cap of Mercury; also, a broad-brimmed, low-crowned hat worn by Greeks and Romans.
petcock: regulator consisting of a small cock or faucet or valve for letting out air or releasing compression or draining
peterman: A fisherman; so called after the apostle Peter. Chapman.
petersburg: a town in southeastern Virginia (south of Richmond); scene of heavy fighting during the American Civil War
pethidine: A synthetic compound used as a painkilling drug, especially for women in labor.
petiolar: Of or pertaining to a petiole.
petiolate: petiolated (connected to a stem by means of a petiole)
petiole: A leafstalk; the footstalk of a leaf, connecting the blade with the stem. See Illust. of Leaf.
petiolule: A small petiole, or the petiole of a leaflet.
petite: Small, little; of a woman or girl, of small size and trim figure.
petition: To make a prayer or request to; to ask from; to solicit; to entreat; especially, to make a formal written supplication, or application to, as to any branch of the government; as, to petition the court; to petition the governor. You have. petitioned all the gods for my prosperity.
petitioned: simple past and past participle of petition
petitioning: The act of presenting apetition; a supplication.
petitory: Petitioning; soliciting; supplicating. Sir W. Hamilton. Bur rill.
petrarch: an Italian poet famous for love lyrics (-)
petrarchan: Of or relating to Francesco Petrarch, a renowned Renaissance Italian humanist.
petrarchist: A writer in the style of Petrarch.
petrescent: Petrifying; converting into stone; as, petrescent water. Boyle.
petrifaction: the process of turning some plant material into stone by infiltration with water carrying mineral particles without changing the original shape
petrifactive: Having the quality of converting organic matter into stone; petrifying.
petrific: Petrifying; petrifactive. Death with his mace petrific, cold and dry. Milton.
petrified: Having undergone the process of petrification (transformation into a stony substance); turned to stone.
petrifies: third-person singular simple present indicative of petrify
petrify: cause to become stonelike or stiff or dazed and stunned
petrine: Of or pertaining to St. Peter; as, the Petrine Epistles.
petro: In Haitian voodoo, a class of loa of uncertain origin, chiefly associated with fierceness or aggression.
petrochemical: any compound obtained from petroleum or natural gas
petrodollar: Money (either notionally or specifically in dollars or other currencies) earned from the sale of oil, often especially as considered among a national economy's principal revenue streams.
petrogale: Any Australian kangaroo of the genus Petrogale, as the rock wallaby (P. penicil lata).
petrogenesis: Rock formation, especially the formation of igneous or metamorphic rocks.
petroglyphy: The art or operation of carving figures or inscriptions on rock or stone.
petrography: The art of writing on stone.
petrohyoid: Pertaining to petrous, oe periotic, portion of the skull and the hyoid arch; as, the petrohyoid muscles of the frog.

petrolize: To treat (water) with kerosene in order to exterminate mosquitoes.
petrologist: One who is versed in petrology.
petrology: the branch of geology that studies rocks: their origin and formation and mineral composition and classification
petronel: A sort of hand cannon, or portable firearm, used in France in the th century.
petrosal: Hard; stony; petrous; as, the petrosal bone; petrosal part of the temporal bone.
petter: a lover who gently fondles and caresses the loved one
petticoat: A loose under-garment worn by women, and covering the body below the waist. Petticoat government, government by women, whether in politics or domestic affairs. Petticoat pipe (Locomotives), a short, flaring pipe surrounding the blast nozzle in the smoke box, to equalize the draft.
pettifog: To do a petty business as a lawyer; also, to do law business in a petty or tricky way. He takes no money, but pettifogs gratis. " S.Butler.

pettifogs: third-person singular simple present indicative of pettifog

pettiness: The quality or state of being petty or paltry; littleness; meanness.
petting: affectionate play (or foreplay without contact with the genital organs)
pettishness: a disposition to exhibit uncontrolled anger
pettle: To fondle or pet; to pamper.
petto: The breast. In petto, in the breast; hence, in secrecy; in reserve.

petunse: Rock rich in feldspar and/or mica, mixed with kaolin to create hard-paste pottery.

peucil: A liquid resembling camphene, obtained by treating turpentine hydrochloride with lime.
pewee: A common American tyrant flycatcher (Say ornis phoebe, or S.fusc us). Called also pewit, and phoebe.

pewter: any of various alloys of tin with small amounts of other metals (especially lead)
pewterer: One whose occupation is to make utensils of pewter; apewtersmith.
pewtery: Belonging to, or resembling, pewter; as, a pewtery taste.
peyote: the hallucinatory alkaloid that is the active agent in mescal buttons
peytrel: The breastplate of a horse's armor or harness. See Poitrel. Chaucer.

pezizaceae: large family comprising many typical cup fungi

pg: Initialism of parental guidance: suitable for viewing, reading, or listening, by minors.
ph: (from potential of Hydrogen) the logarithm of the reciprocal of hydrogen-ion concentration in gram atoms per liter; provides a measure on a scale from to of the acidity or alkalinity of a solution (where is neutral and greater than is more basic and less than is more acidic);
phacelia: any plant of the genus Phacelia
phacops: A genus of trilobites found in the Silurian and Devonian formations. Phacops bufo is one of the most common species.
phacoscope: An instrument in the form of a dark chamber for observing the changes in the crystalline lens during accommodation.
phaenogamous: Having true flowers with with distinct floral organs; flowering.
phaeophyceae: brown algae; mostly marine and littoral eukaryotic algae

phalacrocorax: type genus: coextensive with the family Phalacrocoracidae
phalaenopsis: genus of ornamental epiphytic orchids of Asia and Australia
phalangeal: of or relating to the bones of the fingers or toes

phalangite: A soldier belonging to a phalanx.
phalangium: type genus of the family Phalangiidae
phalanstery: An association or community organized on the plan of Fourier. See Fourierism.

phalera: In Ancient Greece, a metal medallion worn by men or used to ornament the harness of a horse.

phallism: The worship of the generative principle in nature, symbolized by the phallus.
phallus: The penis or clitoris, or the embryonic or primitive organ from which either may be derived.

phanariote: An inhabitant of Phanar, the historically Greek district of Constantinople; hence, a member of the Greek official class in the Ottoman Empire.
phanerite: Evident; visible. Phanerite series (Geol.), the uppermost part of the earth's crust, consisting of deposits produced by causes inobvious operation.

phanerozoic: the period from about, million years ago until the present
phanotron: A kind of rectifier consisting of a thermionic gas tube.

phantasmagorial: Of, relating to, or resembling phantasmagoria; phantasmagoric.
phantasmagoric: Of or pertaining to phantasmagoria; phantasmagorial. Hawthorne.

phar: Acronym of PHP archive, a file format that contains an entire PHP application.
pharaoh: the title of the ancient Egyptian kings
pharaonic: Of or pertaining to the Pharaohs, or kings of ancient Egypt.
pharisaism: The notions, doctrines, and conduct of the Pharisees, as a sect. Sharp.
pharisean: Following the practice of Pharisees; Pharisaic. Pharisean disciples. " Milton.
pharisee: One of a sect or party among the Jews, noted for a strict and formal observance of rites and ceremonies and of the traditions of the elders, and whose pretensions to superior sanctity led them to separate themselves from the other Jews.
pharm: A site where organisms are produced for the creation of medicine or pharmaceuticals.
pharmaceutical: of or relating to pharmacy or pharmacists

pharmacist: One skilled in pharmacy; a pharmaceutist; a druggist.

pharmacogenetics: the branch of genetics that studies the genetically determined variations in responses to drugs in humans or laboratory organisms

pharmacology: the science or study of drugs: their preparation and properties and uses and effects

pharmacy: the art and science of preparing and dispensing drugs and medicines,
pharmakos: In Ancient Greek religion, the ritualistic sacrifice or exile of a human scapegoat.
pharos: A lighthouse or beacon for the guidance of seamen. He. built a pharos, or lighthouse. Arbuthnot.
pharyngeal: Of or pertaining to the pharynx; in the region of the pharynx.

pharyngognathi: A division of fishes in which the lower pharyngeal bones are united. It includes the scaroid, labroid, and embioticoid fishes.
pharyngology: The science that studies the pharynx and treatment of its diseases.

phase: A particular appearance or state in a regularly recurring cycle of changes with respect to quantity of illumination or form of enlightened disk; as, the phases of the moon or planets. See Illust.under Moon.
phased: simple past and past participle of phase
phasel: The French bean, or kidney bean.
phaseless: Without a phase, or visible form. A phaseless and increasing gloom. " Poe.
phasemeter: A device for measuring the difference in phase of two alternating currents of electromotive forces.
phaseolin: A prenylated pterocarpan found in Phaseolus vulgaris seeds and in the stems of Erythrina subumbrans.
phaseolus: A genus of leguminous plants, including the Lima bean, the kidney bean, the scarlet runner, etc. See Bean.
phaseout: The action of phasing out; an incremental removal or reduction.

phasianid: a kind of game bird in the family Phasianidae
phasianus: type genus of the Phasianidae: the typical pheasants
phasing: Pertaining to phase or differences of phase.
phatic: Pertaining to words used to convey any kind of social relationship and whose meaning is otherwise either deemphasized or absent.
phegopteris: beech ferns: genus is variously classified: considered alternative name for genus Dryopteris or included in genus Thelypteris
phellem: (botany) outer tissue of bark; a protective layer of dead cells
phelloderm: A layer of green parenchimatous cells formed on the inner side of the phellogen.
phellogen: The tissue of young cells which produces cork cells.
phelonion: A liturgical vestment worn by a priest of the Eastern Christian tradition, equivalent to the chasuble of the Western tradition.
phenacaine: A local anesthetic, the only anesthetic other than cocaine that is approved for ophthalmic use.
phenacetin: a white crystalline compound used as an analgesic and also as an antipyretic
phenacite: A glassy colorless mineral occurring in rhombohedral crystals, sometimes used as a gem. It is a silicate of glucina, and receive sits name from its deceptive similarity to quartz.
phenakistoscope: A revolving disk on which figures drawn in different relative attitudes are seen successively, so as to produce the appearance of an object in actual motion, as an animal leaping, etc., inconsequence of the persistence of the successive visual impressions of the retina. It is often arranged so that the figures may be projected upon a screen.
phenanthraquinone: Any quinone derived from phenanthrene, but especially,-phenanthraquinone (,-phenanthrenedione)
phenanthrene: A complex hydrocarbon, CH, found in coal tar, and obtained as a white crystalline substance with a bluish fluorescence.
phenanthrenequinone: Any of several isomeric quinones derived from phenanthrene, but especially,-phenanthrenequinone obtained by oxidation with chromic acid
phenanthridine: A nitrogenous hydrocarbon base, CHN, analogous to phenanthrene and quinoline.
phenazine: any of a class of aromatic tricyclic heterocycles used to make dyestuffs
phenetics: A form of numerical systematics in which organisms are grouped based upon the total or relative number of shared characteristics.
phenetol: The ethyl ether of phenol, obtained as an aromatic liquid, CH.O.CH.
phenic: Of, pertaining to, derived from, or resembling, phenyl or phenol. Phenic acid (Chem.), a phenol.
phenicious: Of a red color with a slight mixture of gray. Dana.
phenix: A bird fabled to exist single, to be consumed by fire by it sown act, and to rise again from its ashes. Hence, an emblem of immortality.
