phenocryst: One of the prominent embedded crystals of a porphyry.
phenol: any of a class of weakly acidic organic compounds; molecule contains one or more hydroxyl groups
phenolate: A compound of phenol analogous to a salt.
phenology: The science of the relations between climate and periodic biological phenomena, as the migrations and breeding of birds, the flowering and fruiting of plants, etc. Phenological (#), a. Phenologically, adv. Phenologist (#), n.
phenolphthalein: a laxative used in many preparations under various trade names; also used as an acid-base indicator in tit rations involving weak acids and strong bases because it is brilliant red at high alkalinity and colorless below p H
phenom: Someone or something that is phenomenal, especially a promising young player in sports like baseball, American football, basketball, tennis, and golf.
phenomenal: Relating to, or of the nature of, a phenomenon; hence, extraordinary; wonderful; as, a phenomenal memory. Phenomenally, adv.
phenomenalism: That theory which limits positive or scientific knowledge to phenomena only, whether material or spiritual.
phenomenalist: One who subscribes to the philosophy of phenomenalism.
phenomenalistic: Of or relating to the philosophy of phenomenalism
phenomenalizing: present participle and gerund of phenomenalize
phenomenize: To bring into the realm of experience.
phenomenological: Of or relating to phenomenology, or consistent with the principles of phenomenology.
phenomenology: A description, history, or explanation of phenomena. The phenomenology of the mind. " Sir W. Hamilton.
phenomenon: any state or process known through the senses rather than by intuition or reasoning
phenose: A sweet amorphous deliquescent substance obtained indirectly from benzene, and isometric with, and resembling, dextrose.
phenothiazine: a compound used primarily in veterinary medicine to rid farm animals of internal parasites
phenotype: what an organism looks like as a consequence of the interaction of its genotype and the environment
phenotypic: of or relating to or constituting a phenotype
phenoxide: any metallic salt of a phenol
phenozygous: Having a narrow cranium as compared with the width of the face, so that when the skull is viewed from above, the zygomatic arches are visible.
phenyl: A hydrocarbon radical (CH) regarded as the essential residue of benzene, and the basis of an immense number of aromatic derivatives. Phenyl hydrate (Chem.), phenol or carbolic acid. phenylacetic: Of or pertaining to phenylacetic acid or its derivatives
phenylalanine: an essential amino acid found in proteins and needed for growth of children and for protein metabolism in children and adults; abundant in milk and eggs; it is normally converted to tyrosine in the human body
phenylene: A hypothetic radical (CH) occurring in certain derivatives of benzene; as, phenylene diamine.

phenylic: Pertaining to, derived from, or containing, phenyl. Phenylic alcohol (Chem.), phenol.

phenylthiocarbamide: The N-phenyl derivative of carbamide; it is either tasteless or has a bitter taste, depending on the genetic makeup of the person tasting it, who is either a nontaster or a taster, respectively.
pheochromocytoma: a vascular tumor of the adrenal gland; hypersecretion of epinephrine results in intermittent or sustained hypertension
pheophytin: A chlorophyll from which the central magnesium atom has been removed
pheromone: a chemical substance secreted externally by some animals (especially insects) that influences the physiology or behavior of other animals of the same species
phi: the st letter of the Greek alphabet
phial: A glass vessel or bottle, especially a small bottle for medicines; a vial.
phialide: A flask-shaped projection from the vesicle of certain fungi.
phil: A short form of the male given name Philip.
philadelphia: the largest city in Pennsylvania; located in the southeastern part of the state on the Delaware river; site of Independence Hall where the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution were signed; site of the University of Pennsylvania
philadelphian: Of or pertaining to Ptolemy Philadelphus, or to one of the cities named Philadelphia, esp. the modern city in Pennsylvania.

philander: To make love to women; to play the male flirt. You can't go philandering after her again. G. Eliot.

philandering: present participle and gerund of philander
philanthropic: of or relating to or characterized by philanthropy
philanthropinism: A system of education on so-called natural principles, attempted in Germany in the last century by Based ow, of Dess au.
philanthropist: One who practices philanthropy; one who loves mankind, and seeks to promote the good of others.
philanthropize: To give charitably to (a person or group).

philatelist: One versed in philately; one who collects postage stamps.
philately: The collection of postage stamps of various issues.
philemon: (Greek mythology) a simple countryman who offered hospitality to Zeus and Hermes when they came to earth without revealing their identities in order to test people's piety
philhellene: A friend of Greece, or of the Greeks; a philhellenist. Emerson.
philhellenist: A friend of Greece; one who supports the cause of the Greeks; particularly, one who supported them in their struggle for independence against the Turks; a philhellene.
philip: Englishman and husband of Elizabeth II (born )
philippi: a city in ancient Macedonia that was important in early Christianity
philippians: The eleventh book of the New Testament of the Bible, the epistle of St Paul to the Philippians.
philippic: Any one of the series of famous orations of Demosthenes, the Grecian orator, denouncing Philip, king of Macedon.
philippine: official language of the Philippines; based on Tagalog; draws its lexicon from other Philippine languages
philippines: a republic on the Philippine Islands; achieved independence from the United States in
philistia: an ancient region on the coast of southwestern Palestine that was strategically located on a trade route between Syria and Egypt; important in biblical times
philistine: of or relating to ancient Philistia or its culture or its people
philistinism: The condition, character, aims, and habits of the class called philistines. See Philistine,.Carlyle. On the side of beauty and taste, vulgarity; on the side of morals and feeling, coarseness; on the side of mind and spirit, unintelligence, this is Philistinism. M. Arnold.
phillip: A male given name from Ancient Greek.
phillis: A female given name from Ancient Greek.
phillyrea: A genus of evergreen plants growing along the shores of the mediterranean, and breading a fruit resembling that of the olive.
phillyrin: A glucoside extracted from Phillyrea as a bitter white crystalline substance. It is sometimes used as a febrifuge.
philological: of or relating to or dealing with philology
philomath: A lover of learning; a scholar. Chesterfield.
philomathy: The love of learning or letters.
philomel: Same as Philomela, the nightingale. Milton. Cowper.
philomela: A genus of birds including the nightingales.
philomot: Of the color of a dead leaf. Addison.
philopena: A present or gift which is made as a forfeit in a social game that is played in various ways; also, the game itself.
philopolemic: Exalting or supporting conflict or war.
philosophaster: A pretender to philosophy. Dr. H. More.
philosopheme: A philosophical proposition, doctrine, or principle of reasoning. This, the most venerable, and perhaps the most ancient, of Grecian myths, is a philosopheme. Coleridge.
philosopher: Of or pertaining to philosophy; versed in, or imbued with, the principles of philosophy; hence, characterizing a philosopher; rational; wise; temperate; calm; cool. Philosophically, adv.
philosophic: of or relating to philosophy or philosophers
philosophical: characterized by the attitude of a philosopher; meeting trouble with level-headed detachment
philosophistic: Exhibiting a love of or tendency toward sophistry; pertaining to spurious philosophy.
philosophize: To reason like a philosopher; to search into the reason and nature of things; to investigate phenomena, and assign rational causes for their existence. Man philosophizes as he lives. He may philosophize well or ill, but philosophize he must. Sir W. Hamilton.
philosophized: simple past and past participle of philosophize
philosophizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of philosophize
philosophizing: the exposition (often superficially) of a particular philosophy
philosophy: the rational investigation of questions about existence and knowledge and ethics
philter: A potion or charm intended to excite the passion of love. Addison.
philtre: a drink credited with magical power
philtrum: The shallow vertical groove running from the nasal septum to the center of the upper lip.
phimosis: A condition of the penis in which the prepuce can not be drawn back so as to uncover the glans penis.
phlebography: An X-ray examination of a system of veins that have been injected with a contrast medium.
phlebolith: A calcareous deposit in a venous wall or thrombus.
phlebology: A branch of anatomy which treats of the veins.
phlebosclerosis: sclerosis of the wall of a vein
phlebostasis: A slowing of the flow of blood through the veins
phlebotomus: small bloodsucking sand flies that resemble moths
phlebotomy: The act or practice of opening a vein for letting blood, in the treatment of disease; venesection; bloodletting.
phlegethon: One of the principal rivers of Hades, in the channel of which fire flowed instead of water.
phlegethontic: Of or relating to the river Phlegethon in the underworld of Ancient Greek mythology.
phlegm: Viscid mucus secreted in abnormal quantity in the respiratory and digestive passages.
phlegmasia: An inflammation; more particularly, an inflammation of the internal organs. Phlegmasia do lens ( Etym:, milk leg.
phlegmon: Purulent inflammation of the cellular or areolar tissue.
phlegmonous: Having the nature or properties of phlegmon; as, phlegmonous pneumonia. Harvey.
phleum: A genus of grasses, including the timothy (Phleum prat ense),which is highly valued for hay; cat's-tail grass. Gray.
phloem: That portion of fibrovascular bundles which corresponds to the inner bark; the liber tissue; distinguished from xylem.
phlogistic: Of or pertaining to phlogiston, or to belief in its existence.
phlogiston: The hypothetical principle of fire, or inflammability, regarded by Stahl as a chemical element.
phlogosis: Inflammation of external parts of the body; erysipelatous inflammation.
phlomis: any of various plants of the genus Phlomis; grown primarily for their dense whorls of lipped flowers and attractive foliage
phloretic: Pertaining to, or derived from, or designating, an organic acid obtained by the decomposition of phloretin.
phloretin: A bitter white crystalline substance obtained by the decomposition of phlorizin, and formerly used to some extent as asubstitute for quinine.
phlorizin: A bitter white crystalline glucoside extracted from the root bark of the apple, pear, cherry, plum, etc.
phloroglucin: A sweet white crystalline substance, metameric with pyrogallol, and obtained by the decomposition of phloretin, and from certain gums, as catechu, kino, etc. It belongs to the class of phenols.
phlorone: A yellow crystalline substance having a peculiar unpleasant odor, resembling the quinones, and obtained from beechwood tar and coal tar, as also by the oxidation of xylidine; called also xyloquinone.
phlyctenular: Characterized by the presence of small pustules, or whitish elevations resembling pustules; as, phlyctenular ophthalmia.
pho: A Vietnamese soup with a beef base, typically served with rice noodles and optionally beef or chicken.
phobia: an anxiety disorder characterized by extreme and irrational fear of simple things or social situations
phoca: A genus of seals. It includes the common harbor seal and allied species. See Seal.
phocenic: Of or pertaining to dolphin oil or porpoise oil; said of anacid (called also delphinic acid) subsequently found to be identical with valeric acid. Watts.
phocid: Any member of the family Phocidae, the true seals
phocodontia: A group of extinct carnivorous whales. Their teeth had compressed and serrated crowns. It includes Squalodon and allied genera.
phocomelia: an abnormality of development in which the upper part of an arm or leg is missing so the hands or feet are attached to the body like stumps; rare condition that results from taking thalidomide during pregnancy
phoenicia: an ancient maritime country (a collection of city states) at eastern end of the Mediterranean
phoenician: Of or pertaining to Phoenica. n.
phoenicopterus: A genus of birds which includes the flamingoes.
phoenix: A genus of palms including the date tree.
pholadid: Any member of the family Pholadidae of certain clam-like molluscs.
pholidota: genus of mostly epiphytic orchids of Indonesia and the western Pacific
phonation: The act or process by which articulate sounds are uttered; the utterance of articulate sounds; articulate speech.
phonautograph: An instrument by means of which a sound can be made to producea visible trace or record of itself. It consists essentially of are sonant vessel, usually of paraboloidal form, closed at one end by aflexible membrane. A stylus attached to some point of the membrane records the movements of the latter, as it vibrates, upon a moving cylinder or plate.
phoneidoscope: An instrument for studying the motions of sounding bodies by optical means. It consists of a tube across the end of which is stretched a film of soap solution thin enough to give colored bands, the form and position of which are affected by sonorous vibrations.
phoneme: (linguistics) one of a small set of speech sounds that are distinguished by the speakers of a particular language
phonemically: By means of, or in terms, of phonemes.
phonemicize: To represent as a phoneme or series of phonemes.
phonemics: the study of the sound system of a given language and the analysis and classification of its phonemes
phonestheme: A sound that, because it appears in a number of words of similar meaning, has a recognizable semantic association.
phonetic: of or relating to speech sounds
phonetician: One versed in phonetics; a phonetist.
phonetics: the branch of acoustics concerned with speech processes including its production and perception and acoustic analysis
phonetist: One versed in phonetics; a phonologist.
phoniatrics: The medical research and treatment of organs involved with speech production.
phonic: Of or pertaining to sound; of the nature of sound; acoustic. Tyndall.
phono: A South American butterfly (Ithonia phono) having nearly transparent wings.
phonocardiograph: A device that records and displays the sounds made by the heart.
phonocardiography: The recording of the sounds of the heart.
phonogram: any written symbol standing for a sound or syllable or morpheme or word
phonogrammatic: Pertaining to or involving a phonogram.
phonograph: An instrument for the mechanical registration and reproduction of audible sounds, as articulate speech, etc. It consists of arotating cylinder or disk covered with some material easily indented, as tinfoil, wax, paraffin, etc., above which is a thin plate carry inga stylus. As the plate vibrates under the influence of a sound, the stylus makes minute indentations or undulations in the soft material, and these, when the cylinder or disk is again turned, set the plate in vibration, and reproduce the sound.
phonographer: One versed or skilled in phonography.
phonographic: of or relating to phonography or to a phonograph
phonography: A description of the laws of the human voice, or sounds uttered by the organs of speech.
phonology: The science or doctrine of the elementary sounds uttered by the human voice in speech, including the various distinctions, modifications, and combinations of tones; phonetics. Also, a treatise on sounds.
phonon: The quantum of acoustic or vibrational energy (sound), considered a discrete particle rather than a wave.
phonophore: The phonetic component of a character in Chinese and related writing systems.
phonotype: A type or character used in phonotypy.
phonotypy: A method of phonetic printing of the English language, as devised by Mr. Pitman, in which nearly all the ordinary letters and many new forms are employed in order to indicate each elementary sound by a separate character.
phormium: A genus of liliaceous plants, consisting of one species (Phormium tenax). See Flax-plant.
phorone: A yellow crystalline substance, having a geranium like odor, regarded as a complex derivative of acetone, and obtained from certain camphor compounds.
phoronis: A remarkable genus of marine worms having tentacles around the mouth. It is usually classed with the gephyrea ns. Its larva (Actinotrocha) undergoes a peculiar metamorphosis.
phoronomics: The science of motion; kinematics. Weisbach.
phosgene: Producing, or produced by, the action of light; formerly used specifically to designate a gas now called carbonyl chloride. See Carbonyl.
phosgenite: A rare mineral occurring in tetragonal crystals of a white, yellow, or grayish color and adamantine luster. It is achlorocarbonate of lead.
phospham: An inert amorphous white powder, PNH, obtained by passing ammonia over heated phosphorus.Phosphamic, a.
phosphatase: any of a group of enzymes that act as a catalyst in the hydrolysis of organic phosphates
phosphatic: Pertaining to, or containing, phosphorus, phosphoric acid, or phosphates; as, phosphatic nodules. Phosphatic diathesis (Med.), ahab it of body which leads to the undue excretion of phosphates with the urine.
phosphatidyl: A radical derived from a phosphatide
phosphatization: the conversion of something into a phosphate
phosphatize: to convert something into a phosphate
phosphatized: simple past and past participle of phosphatize
phosphaturia: The excessive discharge of phosphates in the urine.
phosphene: A luminous impression produced through excitation of the retina by some cause other than the impingement upon it of rays of light, asby pressure upon the eyeball when the lids are closed. Cf. After-image.
phosphine: A colorless gas, PH, analogous to ammonia, and having adisagreeable odor resembling that of garlic. Called also hydrogen phosphide, and formerly, phosphureted hydrogen.
phosphocreatine: an organic compound of creatine and phosphoric acid; found in the muscles of vertebrates where its hydrolysis releases energy for muscular contraction
phosphofructokinase: Any of a group of kinase enzymes that convert fructose phosphates to biphosphates
phosphoglyceric: Relating to phosphoglyceric acids and the phosphoglycerides
phospholipid: any of various compounds composed of fatty acids and phosphoric acid and a nitrogenous base; an important constituent of membranes
phosphomolybdic: Relating to phosphomolybdic acid or its derivatives.
phosphonic: Pertaining to, or designating, certain derivatives of phosphorous acid containing a hydrocarbon radical, and analogous to the sulphonic acid.
phosphor: a synthetic substance that is fluorescent or phosphorescent; used to coat the screens of cathode ray tubes
phosphorate: To impregnate, or combine, with phosphorus or its compounds; as, phosphorated oil.
phosphorated: simple past and past participle of phosphorate
phosphoresce: To shine as phosphorus; to be phosphorescent; to emit aphosphoric light.
phosphorescence: a fluorescence that persists after the bombarding radiation has ceased
phosphorescent: Shining with a phosphoric light; luminous without sensible heat. n.
phosphoric: Phosphorescent. A phosphoric sea. " Byron. Glacial phosphoric acid. (Chem.) (a) Metaphosphoric acid in the form of glassy semitransparent masses or sticks. (b) Pure normal phosphoric acid. Phosphoric acid (Chem.), a white crystalline substance, HPO, which is the most highly oxidized acid of phosphorus, and forms an important and extensive series of compounds, viz., the phosphates. Soluble phosphoric acid, Insoluble phosphoric acid (Agric. Chem.), phosphoric acid combined in acid salts, or in neutral or basic salts, which are respectively soluble and insoluble in water or in plant juices. Reverted phosphoric acid (Agric. Chem.), phosphoric acid changed from acid (soluble) salts back to neutral or basic (insoluble) salts.
phosphorolysis: Any reaction, akin to hydrolysis, in which a bond is broken by the action of phosphoric acid or phosphate.
phosphorous: Of or pertaining to phosphorus; resembling or containing phosphorus; specifically, designating those compounds in which phosphorus has a lower valence as contrasted with phosphoric compounds; as, phosphorous acid, HPO.
phosphoruria: a higher than normal amount of phosphate in the urine; a symptom of renal failure
phosphorus: A poisonous nonmetallic element of the nitrogen group, obtained as a white, or yellowish, translucent waxy substance, having acharacteristic disagreeable smell. It is very active chemically, must be preserved under water, and unites with oxygen even at ordinary temperatures, giving a faint glow, whence its name. It always occurs com pined, usually in phosphates, as in the mineral apatite, in bones, etc. It is used in the composition on the tips of friction matches, and for many other purposes. The molecule contains four atoms. Symbol P. Atomic weight.
phosphorylation: the process of transferring a phosphate group from a donor to an acceptor; often catalysed by enzymes.
phosphotungstic: Of or pertaining to phosphotungstic acid or its derivatives.
phosphureted: Impregnated, or combined, with phosphorus. Phosphureted hydrogen. (Chem.) See Phosphine.
phot: a unit of illumination equal to lumen per square centimeter;, phots equal lux
photic: Relating to the production of light by the lower animals.
photinia: genus of deciduous and evergreen east Asian trees and shrubs widely cultivated as ornament als for their white flowers and red fruits; in some classifications includes genus Heteromeles
photism: A luminous image or appearance of a hallucinatory character.
photius: Patriarch of Constantinople and saint of the Greek Orthodox Church; was condemned by the Fourth Council of Constantinople in but was reinstated by a later pope
photoactivation: The absorption of energy from a photon in raising a molecule (or chromophore) from the ground state; especially the first stage of photosynthesis in which energy is absorbed by chlorophyll
photoactive: Able to convert the energy of light into electricity via photoelectricity
photoautotrophic: Relating to a photoautotroph or to photoautotrophism
photobiology: The study of the effects of light on living organisms, and on biological processes
photobiotic: Requiring light to live; incapable of living without light; as, photobiotic plant cells.
photocatalyst: A substance that absorbs light and, in doing so, catalyzes a reaction.
photocathode: a cathode that emits electrons when illuminated
photocell: a transducer used to detect and measure light and other radiations
photoceramics: Art or process of decorating pottery with photographically prepared designs. Photoceramic (#), a.
photochemical: Of or pertaining to chemical action of light, or produced byit; as, the photochemical changes of the visual purple of the retina.
photochemistry: The branch of chemistry which relates to the effect of light in producing chemical changes, as in photography.
photochromic: Of, related to, or produced by photochromism
photochromism: The reversible transformation of the optical properties of a material when exposed to electromagnetic radiation, especially the reversible darkening of a plastic lens when exposed to sunlight.
photochronograph: (Astron.) An instrument for the photographic recording of star transits.
photochronography: Art of recording or measuring intervals of time by the photochronograph. Photochronographic (#), -graphical (#),a. -graphically, adv.
photocoagulation: surgical procedure that uses an intense laser beam to destroy diseased retinal tissue or to make a scar that will hold the retina in cases of detached retina
photocompose: To use photocomposition to prepare text for printing
photoconductivity: change in the electrical conductivity of a substance as a result of absorbing electromagnetic radiation
photocopier: a copier that uses photographic methods of making copies
photocopying: The process by which photocopies are made.
photodiode: A semiconductor two-terminal component whose electrical characteristics are light-sensitive.
photodisintegration: Any nuclear reaction, especially a nuclear fission, initiated by absorption of high-energy electromagnetic radiation such as a gamma ray.
photodissociation: The dissociation of a molecule following the absorption of a photon
photodynamics: The relation of light to the movements of plants and their organs; the study of the phenomena of curvatures induced by the stimulus of light. Photodynamic (#), Photodynamical (#),a.
photoelectricity: electricity generated by light or affected by light
photoelectronic: Describing any electronic effect or device that is affected by light
photoemission: an emission of photo electrons (especially from a metallic surface)
photoengrave: To make a photoengraving of an image
photoengraving: an engraving used to reproduce an illustration
photoepinasty: A disproportionately rapid growth of the upper surface of dorsiventral organs, such as leaves, through the stimulus of exposure to light.
photoetch: To engrave, or make an engraving of, by any photomechanical process involving etching of the plate.
photoflash: a lamp for providing momentary light to take a photograph
photofluorography: The photographic recording of fluoroscope images
photog: A photographer, especially a professional one.
photogalvanography: The art or process of making photo-electrotypes. Sir D.Brewster.
photogenic: Of or pertaining to photogeny; producing or generating light.
photogeology: The use of aerial photography to interpret geologic features
photoglyphic: Pertaining to the art of engraving by the action of light. Photoglyphic engraving, a process of etching on copper, steel, or zinc, by means of the action of light and certain chemicals, so that from the plate impressions may betaken. Sir D. Brewster.
photogrammetry: A method of surveying or map making by photography, used also in determining the height and motions of clouds, sea waves, and the like.
photograph: A picture or likeness obtained by photography.
photographed: simple past and past participle of photograph
photographer: One who practices, or is skilled in, photography.
photographic: relating to photography or obtained by using photography
photographing: present participle and gerund of photograph
photography: the act of taking and printing photographs
photogravure: A photoengraving; also, the process by which such a picture is produced.
photogravurist: A person who produces photogravure prints.
photoheliograph: A modified kind of telescope adapted to taking photographs of the sun.
photoheliography: Heliography (photography of the sun), especially as undertaken using a photoheliograph.
photoinduction: induction as a result of irradiation by light
photojournalism: journalism that presents a story primarily through the use of pictures
photojournalist: a journalist who presents a story primarily through the use of photographs
photokinesis: Any movement that is in response to light.
photolithograph: A lithographic picture or copy from a stone prepared by the aidof photography.
photolithographic: Of or pertaining to photolithography; produced by photolithography.
photolithography: The art or process of producing photo lithographs.
photology: The doctrine or science of light, explaining its nature and phenomena; optics.
photoluminescent: Luminescent by exposure to light waves. Photoluminescence (#), n.
photolysis: Any chemical reaction in which a compound is decomposed after absorbing a photon
photomagnetism: The branch of science which treats of the relation of magnetism to light.
photomap: a map made by the superimposition of aerial photographs onto grid lines, contours and other normal map features
photomechanical: Pertaining to, or designating, any photographic process in which a printing surface is obtained without the intervention of hand engraving.
photometer: An instrument for measuring the intensity of light, or, more especially, for comparing the relative intensities of different lights, or their relative illuminating power.
photometry: That branch of science which treats of the measurement of the intensity of light.
photomicrograph: a photograph taken with the help of a microscope
photomicroscope: An instrument (microscope plus camera) that is used for making photomicrographs.
photomorphogenesis: the regulatory effect of light on the growth, development and differentiation of plant cells, tissues and organs
photomultiplier: A device, normally in the form of a tube, that uses a photocathode to convert photons into photoelectrons which are then amplified.
photomural: A large photograph (or series of photographs) used as a wall decoration.
photon: a quantum of electromagnetic radiation; an elementary particle that is its own antiparticle
photonuclear: Of or relating to any nuclear reaction involving a photon.
photooxidation: The loss of an electron from a photoexcited species.
photoperiodic: Of, pertaining to, or exhibiting photoperiodism
photoperiodism: The growth, development and other responses of plants and animals according to the length of day and/or night.
photophobic: That thrives at a relatively low light level.
photophone: An apparatus for the production of sound by the action of rays of light. A. G. Bell.
photopia: Normal daylight vision, in which the cone cells are used.
photopigment: a special pigment found in the rods and cones of the retina
photoplay: A play for representation or exhibition by moving pictures; also, the moving-picture representation of a play.
photoprint: Any print made by a photomechanical process.
photopsia: An affection of the eye, in which the patient perceives luminous rays, flashes, coruscations, etc. See phosphene.
photoreceptor: A specialized neuron or other structure able to detect and react to light.
photoscope: Anything employed for the observation of light or luminous effects.
photosculpture: A process in which, by means of a number of photographs simultaneously taken from different points of view on the same level, rough models of the figure or bust of a person or animal may be made with great expedition.
photosensitivity: sensitivity to the action of radiant energy
photosensitize: make (an organism or substance) sensitive to the influence of radiant energy and especially light
photosetting: present participle and gerund of photoset
photosphere: A sphere of light; esp., the luminous envelope of the sun.
photostat: make a copy by means of a Photostat device
photosynthesis: The process of constructive metabolism by which carbohydrates are formed from water vapor and the carbon dioxide of the air in the chlorophyll-containing tissues of plants exposed to the action of light. It was formerly called assimilation, but this is now commonly used as in animal physiology. The details of the process are not yet clearly known. Ba eyer's theory is that the carbon dioxide is reduced to carbon monoxide, which, uniting with the hydrogen of the water in the cell, produces formaldehyde, the latter forming various sugars through polymerization. Vines suggests that the carbohydrates are secretion products of the chloroplasts, derived from decomposition of previously formed proteids. The food substances are usually quickly translocated, those that accumulate being changed to starch, which appears in the cells almost simultaneously with the sugars. The chloroplasts perform photosynthesis only in light and within acer tain range of temperature, varying according to climate. This is the only way in which a plant is able to organize carbohydrates. All plants without a chlorophyll apparatus, as the fungi, must be parasitic or saprophytic. Photosynthetic (#), a. Photosynthetically (#), adv.
photosynthesize: To synthesize carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water using the energy of light by photosynthesis
photosynthetic: relating to or using or formed by photosynthesis
phototachometer: A tachometer that measures revolutions by optical sensing.
phototaxis: The movement of an organism either towards or away from a source of light
phototelegraphy: Telegraphy by means of light, as by the heliograph or the photophone. Also, less properly, telephotography. Phototelegraph (#), n. Phototelegraphic (#), a.
phototelescope: A telescope adapted for taking photographs of the heavenly bodies.
phototheodolite: An arrangement of two photographic cameras, the plates of which may be brought into exactly the same plane, used in surveying and mapmaking. From the differences between two pictures taken at the same moment, measurements in all dimensions of the region may be obtained.
phototherapy: The application of light for therapeutic purposes, esp. for treating diseases of the skin. Phototherapic (#),Phototherapeutic (#), a.
phototonus: A motile condition in plants resulting from exposure to light. Phototonic, a.
phototrophy: The synthesis of an organism's food from inorganic material using light as a source of energy.
phototropism: The tendency of growing plant organs to move or curve under the influence of light. In ordinary use the term is practically synonymous with heliotropism.
phototype: A plate or block with a printing surface (usually in relief) obtained from a photograph; also, any one of the many methods of processes by which such a printing surface is obtained.
phototypesetting: A printing process that generated columns of type on a scroll of photographic paper, using a phototypesetter.
phototypy: The art or process of producing photo types.
photovoltaic: producing a voltage when exposed to radiant energy (especially light)
photozincography: A process, analogous to photolithography, for reproducing photographed impressions transferred to zinc plate.
phots: third-person singular simple present indicative of phot
phragma: A septum, especially on the wall of the thorax of an insect.
phragmocone: The thin chambered shell attached to the anterior end of abelemnite.
phrasal: Of the nature of a phrase; consisting of a phrase; as, aphra sal adverb. Earlc.
phrase: A short clause or portion of a period.
phrased: simple past and past participle of phrase
phrasemonger: One who uses overelaborate or wordy phrases.
phraseology: Manner of expression; peculiarity of diction; style. Most completely national in his. phraseology. I. Taylor.
phrasing: The act or method of grouping the notes so as to form distinct musical phrases.
phratry: A subdivision of a phyle, or tribe, in Athens.
phrenic: Of or pertaining to the diaphragm; diaphragmatic; as, the phrenic nerve.
phrenicocostal: Relating to the ribs and diaphragm.
phrenicosplenic: Relating to the diaphragm and spleen.
phrenitis: Inflammation of the brain, or of the meninges of the brain, attended with acute fever and delirium; called also cephalitis.
phrenological: Of or pertaining to phrenology. Phrenologically, adv.
phrenologist: One versed in phrenology; a craniologist.
phrenology: a now abandoned study of the shape of skull as indicative of the strengths of different faculties
phrenosin: A nitrogenous body, related to cerebrin, supposed to exist in the brain.
phrensy: Violent and irrational excitement; delirium. See Frenzy.
phrontistery: an establishment for study and learning (sometimes including modern universities)
phryganeides: A tribe of neuropterous insects which includes the caddice flies; called also Trichoptera. See Trichoptera.
phrygia: an ancient country in western and central Asia Minor
phrygian: Of or pertaining to Phrygia, or to its inhabitants. Phrygian mode (Mus.), one of the ancient Greek modes, very bold and vehement in style; so called because fabled to have been invented by the phrygian Mars yas. Moore (Encyc. of Music). Phrygian stone, a light, spongy stone, resembling a pumice, used by the ancients in dyeing, and said to be drying and astringent.
pht: Used to signify mild annoyance or disagreement.
phthalazine: A bicyclic heterocycle consisting of a benzene ring fused to pyridazine
phthalic: Pertaining to, or designating, a dibasic acid obtained by the oxidation of naphthalene and allied substances. Phthalic acid (Chem.), a white crystalline substance, CH.(COH), analogous to benzoic acid, and employed in the brilliant dyestuffs called thephthaleins.
phthalide: A lactone obtained by reduction of phthalyl chloride, as awhite crystalline substance; hence, by extension, any one of the series of which phthalide proper is the type.
phthalimide: An imido derivative of phthalic acid, obtained as a white crystalline substance, CH.(CO)NH, which has itself (like succinimide) acid properties, and forms a series of salts. Cf. Imido acid, under Imido.
phthalyl: The hypothetical radical of phthalic acid.
phthiriasis: A disease (morbus pediculous) consisting in the excessive multiplication of lice on the human body.
phthisical: Of or pertaining to phthisis; affected with phthisis; wasting; consumptive.
phthisis: A wasting or consumption of the tissues. The term was formerly applied to many wasting diseases, but is now usually restricted to pulmonary phthisis, or consumption. See Consumption. Fibroid phthisis. See under Fibroid.
phycologist: One who studies algae as a profession.
phycomycete: A member of the obsolete class Phycomycetes, now considered a group of fungi in multiple, unrelated classes.
phycomycetes: A large, important class of parasitic or saprophytic fungi, the algal or alga like fungi. The plant body ranges from an undifferentiated mass of protoplasm to a well-developed and much-branched mycelium. Reproduction is mainly sexual, by the formation of conidia or sporangia; but the group shows every form of transition from this method through simple conjugation to perfect sexual reproduction by egg and sperm in the higher forms. Phycomycetous (#), a.
phycoxanthin: A yellowish colouring matter found in certain algae.
phylactery: (Judaism) either of two small leather cases containing texts from the Hebrew Scriptures (known collectively as tefillin); traditionally worn (on the forehead and the left arm) by Jewish men during morning prayer
phylarch: The chief of a phyle, or tribe.
phylarchy: The office of a phylarch; government of a class or tribe.
phyle: A local division of the people in ancient Athens; a clan; at ribe.
phylesis: A course of evolutionary or phylogenetic development which modifies an organism or group of organisms without leading to the formation of a new species.
phyletic: of or relating to the evolutionary development of organisms
phyllary: An individual bract within an involucre or involucel.
phyllo: tissue thin sheets of pastry used especially in Greek dishes
phylloclad: a flattened stem resembling and functioning as a leaf
phyllocladium: A flattened stem or branch which more or less resembles a leaf, and performs the function of a leaf as regards respiration and assimilation.
phyllodium: A petiole dilated into the form of a blade, and usually with vertical edges, as in the Australian acacias.
phyllody: A retrograde metamorphosis of the floral organs to the condition of leaves.
phyllome: A foliar part of a plant; any organ homologous with a leaf, or produced by metamorphosis of a leaf.
phyllomorph: A leaf that has undergone phyllody
phyllophyte: A plant characterized as structurally based upon or possessing true leaves.
phyllopoda: An order of Entomostraca including a large number of species, most of which live in fresh water. They have flattened or leaflike legs, often very numerous, which they use in swimming. Called also branchiopoda.
phyllosilicate: Any silicate mineral having a crystal structure of parallel sheets of silicate tetrahedra.
phyllosoma: The larva of the spiny lobsters (Palinurus and allied genera).Its body is remarkably thin, flat, and transparent; the legs are very long. Called also glass-crab, and glass-shrimp.
phyllostome: Any bat of the genus Phyllostoma, or allied genera, having large membranes around the mouth and nose; a nose-leaf bat.
phyllotaxis: The arrangement of leaves on a stem, or the mathematical principles governing such arrangement.
phyllous: Homologous with a leaf; as, the sepals, petals, stamens, and pistils are phyllous organs.
phylloxanthin: A yellow coloring matter extracted from chlorophyll.
phylloxera: A small hemipterous insect (Phylloxera vastatrix) allied to the aphids. It attacks the roots and leaves of the grapevine, doing great damage, especially in Europe.
phylogenesis: (biology) the sequence of events involved in the evolutionary development of a species or taxonomic group of organisms
phylogenetic: Relating to phylogenesis, or the race history of a type of organism. Phylogenetically, adv.
phylogeny: (biology) the sequence of events involved in the evolutionary development of a species or taxonomic group of organisms
phylum: One of the larger divisions of the animal kingdom; a branch; agr and division.
phyma: A tubercle on any external part of the body.
physa: A genus of fresh-water Pulmonifera, having reversed spiral shells. See Pond snail, under Pond.
physalia: A genus of large oceanic Siphonophora which includes the portuguese man-of-war.
physeter: The genus that includes the sperm whale.
physic: The art of healing diseases; the science of medicine; the theory or practice of medicine. A doctor of phys ik. " Chaucer.
physical: involving the body as distinguished from the mind or spirit
physicalism: (philosophy) the philosophical theory that matter is the only reality
physicalist: An adherent of physicalism; A cosmological proceduralist.
physicality: preoccupation with satisfaction of physical drives and appetites
physically: In a physical manner; according to the laws of nature or physics; by physical force; not morally. I am not now treating physically of light or colors. Locke.
physician: A person skilled in physic, or the art of healing; one duty authorized to prescribe remedies for, and treat, diseases; a doctor of medicine.
physicianed: Licensed as a physician. A physicianed apothecary. Walpole.
physicism: The tendency of the mind toward, or its preoccupation with, physical phenomena; materialism in philosophy and religion. Anthropomorphism grows into theology, while physicism (if I may so call it) develops into science. Huxley.
physicked: simple past and past participle of physic
physicochemical: Involving the principles of both physics and chemistry; dependent on, or produced by, the joint action of physical and chemical agencies. Huxley.
physicomathematics: An academic subject covering both mathematics and physics.
physicotheology: The view that evidence and sound arguments for God's existence can be derived from a study of the natural world; a study of the natural world intended to provide such evidence.
physics: The science of nature, or of natural objects; that branch of science which treats of the laws and properties of matter, and the forces acting upon it; especially, that department of natural science which treats of the causes (as gravitation, heat, light, magnetism, electricity, etc.) that modify the general properties of bodies; natural philosophy.
physiochemical: Of or pertaining to both physiology and chemistry
physiocrat: One of the followers of Ques nay of France, who, in the thcentury, founded a system of political economy based upon the supremacy of natural order. F. A. Walker. Physiocratic, a.
physiogeny: The germ history of the functions, or the history of the development of vital activities, in the individual, being one of the branches of ontogeny. See Morphogeny. Haeckel.
physiognomy: The art and science of discovering the predominant temper, and other characteristic qualities of the mind, by the outward appearance, especially by the features of the face.
physiography: The science which treats of the earth's exterior physical features, climate, life, etc., and of the physical movements or changes on the earth's surface, as the currents of the atmosphere and ocean, the secular variations in heat, moisture, magnetism, etc.;physical geography.
physiolatry: The worship of the powers or agencies of nature; materialism in religion; nature worship. The physiolatry of the Vedas. " M.Williams.
physiological: Of or pertaining to physiology; relating to the science of the functions of living organism; as, physiological botany or chemistry.
physiologist: One who is versed in the science of physiology; a student of the properties and functions of animal and vegetable organs and tissues.
physiology: the branch of the biological sciences dealing with the functioning of organisms
physiopathological: Pathophysiological: pertaining to the physiological changes caused by disease, or to the study thereof
physiophilosophy: A natural philosophy concerning natural history and relationships.
physiotherapeutic: of or relating to or used in physical therapy
physiotherapist: therapist who treats injury or dysfunction with exercises and other physical treatments of the disorder
physiotherapy: therapy that uses physical agents: exercise and massage and other modalities
physique: The natural constitution, or physical structure, of a person. With his white hair and splendid physique. Mrs. Stowe.
physis: Nature, as contrasted with law or custom.
physitheism: The ascription of physical form and attributes to a deity.
physoclisti: An order of teleost in which the air bladder has no opening.
physostegia: any of various plants of the genus Physostegia having sessile linear to oblong leaves and showy white or rose or lavender flowers
physostigmine: An alkaloid found in the Calabar bean (the seed of Physostigmavenenosum), and extracted as a white, tasteless, substance, amorphous or crystalline; formerly called eserine, with which it was regarded as identical.
physostomous: Having a duct to the air bladder.
phytane: A diterpenoid alkane with one more carbon than pristane.
phytic: Relating to phytic acid or its derivatives
phytivorous: Feeding on plants or herbage; phytophagous; as, phytivorous animals. Ray.
phytobiology: The branch of biology that involves plants.
phytochemistry: Chemistry in its relation to vegetable bodies; vegetable chemistry. R. Hunt.
phytogenesis: The origin and evolutionary development of plants.
phytography: The science of describing plants in a systematic manner; also, a description of plants.
phytohemagglutinin: Any hemagglutinin (lectin) of plant origin, but especially that found in many beans that has a physiological action
phytol: The diterpenoid alcohol (E,R,R)-,,-tetramethylhexadecenol, derived from chlorophyll.
phytolacca: A genus of herbaceous plants, some of them having berries which abound in intensely red juice; poke, or pokeweed.
phytolaccaceae: chiefly tropical herbaceous plants (including shrubs and trees) with racemose flowers: genera Phytolacca, Agdestis, Ercilla, Rivina, Trichostigma
phytolithology: The branch of science which treats of fossil plants; usually called paleobotany, sometimes paleophytology.
phytological: Of or pertaining to phytology; botanical.
phytology: The science of plants; a description of the kinds and properties of plants; botany. Sir T. Browne.
phytometric: Relating to phytometers, phytometry or to phytometrics
phytometry: The measurement of physiological responses of plants.
phyton: One of the parts which by their repetition make up a flowering plant, each being a single joint of a stem with its leaf or leaves; aphytomer.
phytopaleontology: The subdiscipline of paleontology that deals with plants.
phytopathology: The science of diseases to which plants are liable.
phytophagous: Feeding on plants; herbivorous; as, a phytophagous animal.
phytophthora: destructive parasitic fungi causing brown rot in plants
phytoplankton: photosynthetic or plant constituent of plankton; mainly unicellular algae
phytosociology: The study of the ecology, classification and distribution of plant communities
phytosterol: Any of a group of steroid alcohols, phytochemicals naturally occurring in plants. They are white powders with mild, characteristic odor, insoluble in water and soluble in alcohols.
phytotomy: The dissection of plants; vegetable anatomy.
phytotopography: The topography of plant life within a region.
phytotoxin: any substance produced by plants that is similar in its properties to extracellular bacterial toxin
pi: A mass of type confusedly mixed or unsorted.
pia: perennial herb of East Indies to Polynesia and Australia; cultivated for its large edible root yielding Otaheite arrowroot starch
piacular: Expiatory; atoning. Sir G. C. Lewis.
piaffe: a cadenced trot executed by the horse in one spot
piaffer: A dressage movement in which a horse trots in a stationary position while using high lifting of the legs.
piaget: Swiss psychologist remembered for his studies of cognitive development in children (-)
pianism: performance by or technique of a pianist
pianissimo: Very soft; a direction to execute a passage as softly as possible. (Abbrev. pp.)
pianist: A performer, esp. a skilled performer, on the piano.
pianistic: skilled at or adapted for the piano
piano: Soft; a direction to the performer to execute a certain passage softly, and with diminished volume of tone. (Abbrev. p.)
pianoforte: a keyboard instrument that is played by depressing keys that cause hammers to strike tuned strings and produce sounds
pianola: A mechanical piano which uses a roll of perforated paper to operate its keys, instead of being played by a pianist.
piaster: A silver coin of Spain and various other countries. See Peso. The Spanish piaster (commonly called peso, or peso duro) is of about the value of the American dollar. The Italian piaster, or scudo, was worth from to cents. The Turkish and Egyptian piasters are now worth about four and a half cents.
piazza: An open square in a European town, especially an Italian town; hence (Arch.), an arcaded and roofed gallery; a portico. In the united States the word is popularly applied to a veranda. We walk by the obelisk, and meditate in piazzas. Jer. Taylor.
piblokto: A condition affecting dogs or other animals in the Arctic, characterized by aggressive behavior and seizures.
pibroch: A Highland air, suited to the particular passion which the musician would either excite or assuage; generally applied to those airs that are played on the bagpipe before the Highlanders when the ygo out to battle. Jamie son.
pic: A Turkish cloth measure, varying from to inches.
pica: The genus that includes the magpies.
picador: A horseman armed with a lance, who in a bullfight receives the first attack of the bull, and excites him by picking him without attempting to kill him.
picaninny: (ethnic slur) offensive term for a Black child
picard: One of a sect of Ada mites in the fifteenth century; so called from one Picard of Flanders. See Adamite.
picaresque: Applied to that class of literature in which the principal personage is the Spanish picaro, meaning a rascal, a knave, a rogue, an adventurer.
picaroon: One who plunders; especially, a plunderer of wrecks; a pirate; a corsair; a marauder; a sharper. Sir W. Temple.
picayune: A small coin of the value of six and a quarter cents. See Fippenny bit.
picayunish: Petty; paltry; mean; as, a picayunish business.
piccadill: A large, broad lace collar from the th century.
piccadilly: Piccadilly, a street running from Hyde Park Corner to Piccadilly Circus.
piccage: Money paid at fairs for leave to break ground for booths. Ains worth.
piccalilli: A pickle of various vegetables with pungent species, originally made in the East Indies.
piccaninny: (ethnic slur) offensive term for a Black child
piccolo: A small, shrill flute, the pitch of which is an octave higher than the ordinary flute; an octave flute.
pice: A small copper coin of the East Indies, worth less than a cent. Mal com.
picea: A genus of coniferous trees of the northen hemisphere, including the Norway spruce and the American black and white spruces. These trees have pendent cones, which do not readily fall to pieces, in this and other respects differing from the firs.
piceous: Of or pertaining to pitch; resembling pitch in color or quality; pitchy.
pichiciago: A small, burrowing, South American edentate (Chlamyphorustruncatus), allied to the armadillos. The shell is attached only along the back.
pici: A division of birds including the woodpeckers and wrynecks.
piciformes: A group of birds including the woodpeckers, toucans, barbets, colies, kingfishes, hornbills, and some other related groups.
pick: A heavy iron tool, curved and sometimes pointed at both ends, wielded by means of a wooden handle inserted in the middle, used by quarrymen, road makers, etc.; also, a pointed hammer used for dressing millstones.
pickaback: On the back or shoulders; as, to ride pickback. A woman stooping to take a child pickaback. R, Jefferies.
pickaninny: A small child; especially, a negro or mulatto infant.
pickax: a heavy iron tool with a wooden handle and a curved head that is pointed on both ends
pickaxe: a heavy iron tool with a wooden handle and a curved head that is pointed on both ends
picked: Having a pike or spine on the back; said of certain fishes.
pickeer: To make a raid for booty; to maraud; also, to skirmish in advance of an army. See Picaroon.
pickeers: third-person singular simple present indicative of pickeer
picker: A machine for picking fibrous materials to pieces so as to loosen and separate the fiber.
pickerel: flesh of young or small pike
pickerelweed: American plant having spikes of blue flowers and growing in shallow water of streams and ponds
pickering: The sauger of the St. Lawrence River.
picket: A detached body of troops serving to guard an army from surprise, and to oppose reconnoitering parties of the enemy; called also outlying picket.
picketed: simple past and past participle of picket
picketer: Someone who pickets; one participating in a demonstration or posted on a picket line.
picketing: present participle and gerund of picket
picking: The pulverized shells of oysters used in making walks. Simmon ds.
pickling: An instance of processing something in brine or in vinegar.
pickman: A man employed to break ground using a pick.
pickoff: A play in which a pitcher throws a live ball to a fielder so that the fielder can tag out a baserunner who has moved away from the base
pickpocket: One who steals purses or other articles from pockets. Bent ley.
picksome: Characterised by picking and choosing, or by being picky; selective.
pickthank: One who strives to put another under obligation; an officious person; hence, a flatterer. Used also adjectively. Smiling pick thanks, and base news mongers.
pickup: a light truck with an open body and low sides and a tailboard
pickwickian: Arbitrary or meaningless (of the usage of a word or phrase).
picnic: Formerly, an entertainment at which each person contributed some dish to a common table; now, an excursion or pleasure party in which the members partake of a collation or repast (usually in the open air, and from food carried by themselves).
picnicker: One who takes part in a picnic.
picnicking: present participle and gerund of picnic
picofarad: a unit of capacitance equal to one trillionth of a farad
picoline: Any one of three isometric bases (CHN) related to pyridine, and obtained from bone oil, acrolein ammonia, and coal-tar naphtha, as colorless mobile liquids of strong odor; called also methyl pyridine.
picolinic: Related to picolinic acid or its derivatives.
picornavirus: a group of single-strand RNA viruses with a protein coat
picosecond: one trillionth (^-) of a second; one thousandth of a nanosecond
picot: One of many small loops, as of thread, forming an ornamental border, as on a ribbon.
picotee: A flower (such as a carnation) whose margin is a different colour from the flower's basic colour.
picramic: Of or pertaining to picramic acid or its derivatives
picric: Pertaining to, or designating, a strong organic acid (called picric acid), intensely bitter.
picrite: A dark green igneous rock, consisting largely of chrysolite, with hornblende, augite, biotite, etc.
picrotoxin: A bitter white crystalline substance found in the cocculusindicus. It is a peculiar poisonous neurotic and intoxicant, and consists of a mixture of several neutral substances.
pict: A member of an ancient people of northern and central Scotland.
pictish: Of or pertaining to Picts; resembling the Picts. The Pictish peer. " Byron.
pictograph: A picture or hieroglyph representing and expressing an idea. Pictographic, a.
pictographic: consisting of or characterized by the use of pictographs
pictones: A Celtic tribe of Aquitania, whose capital was Limonum.
pictorial: Of or pertaining to pictures; illustrated by pictures; forming pictures; representing with the clearness of a picture; as, apictorial dictionary; a pictorial imagination. Pictorial rhetoric. Ruskin. Pictorially, adv.
pictorialism: A school of artistic photography that emphasized using photography to mimic certain styles of contemporary painting, that flourished in the late th and early th centuries
pictorialization: The process or result of pictorializing.
pictorialize: To make pictorial; to illustrate with pictures.
picts: A race of people of uncertain origin, who inhabited Scotland in early times.
picturable: Capable of being pictured, or represented by a picture.
picture: To draw or paint a resemblance of; to delineate; to represent; to form or present an ideal likeness of; to bring before the mind. I. do picture it in my mind. " Spenser. I have not seen him so pictured.
pictured: Furnished with pictures; represented by a picture or pictures; as, a pictured scene.
picturer: One who makes pictures; a painter. Fuller.
picturesque: Forming, or fitted to form, a good or pleasing picture; representing with the clearness or ideal beauty appropriate to apicture; expressing that peculiar kind of beauty which is agreeable in a picture, natural or artificial; graphic; vivid; as, apicturesque scene or attitude; picturesque language. What is picturesque as placed in relation to the beautiful and the sublime It is. the characteristic pushed into a sensible excess. De Quincey. Picturesquely, adv. Picturesqueness, n.
picul: A commercial weight varying in different countries and for different commodities. In Borneo it is tan.
picunche: A Mapudungun-speaking people living to the north of the Mapuches or Araucanians and south of the Choapa River and the Diaguitas.
picus: A genus of woodpeckers, including some of the common American and European species.
piddle: waste time; spend one's time idly or inefficiently
piddling: Trifling; trivial; frivolous; paltry; applied to persons and things. The ignoble hucksterage of piddling tithes. Milton.
piddock: Any species of Pholas; a pholad. See Pholas.
pidgin: an artificial language used for trade between speakers of different languages
piebald: Having spots and patches of black and white, or other colors; mottled; pied. A piebald steed of Thracian strain. " Dryden.
piece: One of the superior men, distinguished from a pawn.
pieced: simple past and past participle of piece
piecemeal: Made up of parts or pieces; single; separate. These piecemeal guilts. " Gov. of Tongue.
piecework: Work done by the piece or job; work paid for at a rate based on the amount of work done, rather than on the time employed. The reaping was piecework, at so much per acre. R. Jefferies.
pieceworker: A worker who is paid according to the number of units of work produced.
pied: imp. & p. p. of Pi, or Pie, v.
piedfort: An unusually thick coin, often exactly twice the normal weight and thickness of other coins.
piedmont: Noting the region of foothills near the base of a mountain chain.
piedmontese: Of, from or relating to Piedmont in northwest Italy.
pieplant: A plant (Rheum Rhapontic um) the leafstalks of which are acid, and are used in making pies; the garden rhubarb.
piepowder: Chiefly in court of piepowders, etc. (sense ): a traveller, particularly one on foot; a wayfarer; specifically, a travelling merchant.
pier: a platform built out from the shore into the water and supported by piles; provides access to ships and boats
pierce: To enter; to penetrate; to make a way into or through something, as a pointed instrument does; used literally and figuratively. And pierced to the skin, but bit no more. Spenser. She would not pierce further into his meaning. Sir P. Sidney.
piercer: One who, or that which, pierces or perforates; specifically:
pierces: third-person singular simple present indicative of pierce
piercing: Forcibly entering, or adapted to enter, at or by a point; perforating; penetrating; keen; used also figuratively; as, apiercing instrument, or thrust. Piercing eloquence. Piercingly, adv. Piercingness, n.
pierian: Of or pertaining to Pierides or Muses. Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring. Pope.
pieridae: arthropod family including cabbage butterflies; sulphur butterflies
pieris: decorative evergreen shrubs of woody vines
pierre: capital of the state of South Dakota; located in central South Dakota on the Missouri river
pierrot: a male character in French pantomime; usually dressed in white with a whitened face
piers: A male given name from Ancient Greek.
pieta: A representation of the dead Christ, attended by the Virgin mary or by holy women and angels. Mol lett.
pietism: th and th-century German movement in the Lutheran Church stressing personal piety and devotion
pietist: One of a class of religious reformers in Germany in the thcentury who sought to revive declining piety in the Protestant churches; often applied as a term of reproach to those who make adisplay of religious feeling. Also used adjectively.
piety: righteousness by virtue of being pious
piezochemistry: The chemistry of materials at high pressure
piezoelectricity: electricity produced by mechanical pressure on certain crystals (notably quartz or Rochelle salt); alternatively, electrostatic stress produces a change in the linear dimensions of the crystal
piezometer: An instrument for measuring the compressibility of liquids.
piezometric: Of or pertaining to a piezometer or to piezometry
piezometry: The measuring of the compressibility of a liquid.
piffle: To be sequeamish or delicate; hence, to act or talk triflingly or ineffectively; to twaddle; piddle.
pigboat: a submersible warship usually armed with torpedoes
pigeonberry: The red berry of Rivina humilis, a flowering plant in the pigeonberry family Petiveriaceae.
pigeonholes: An outdoor game played in the th and early th centuries in which each player bowls a ball towards targets (probably small compartments).
pigeonite: Any monoclinic pyroxene that is a mixed calcium, magnesium and ferrous silicate.
pigeonwood: Oriental trema, an evergreen tree of species Trema orientalis, widely distributed throughout much of the tropics.
pigfish: found around the Great Barrier Reef
piggery: A place where swine are kept.
piggin: A small wooden pail or tub with an upright stave for a handle, often used as a dipper.
piggish: Relating to, or like, a pig; greedy.
pight: Pitched; fixed; determined.pight him on the pommel of his head. Chaucer. I found him pight to do it.
pightle: A small piece of enclosed land, often by a hedge. Some authorities also indicate that a pightle tends to be associated with a house or messuage.
pigment: Any one of the colored substances found in animal and vegetable tissues and fluids, as bilirubin, urobilin, chlorophyll, etc.
pigmentation: A deposition, esp. an excessive deposition, of coloring matter; as, pigmentation of the liver.
pigmented: Colored; specifically (Biol.), filled or imbued with pigment; as, pigmented epithelial cells; pigmented granules.
pignoration: The taking of cattle doing damage, by way of pledge, till satisfaction is made. Bur rill.
pignoratitious: Of, like, or pertaining to pignoration.
pignut: an American hickory tree having bitter nuts
pigpen: A pen, or sty, for pigs.
pigroot: An area of soil where pigs have turned up the ground with their snouts looking for worms, insects, and plant roots to eat.
pigskin: The skin of a pig, used chiefly for making saddles; hence, acolloquial or slang term for a saddle.
pigsney: A word of endearment for a girl or woman. Chaucer.
pigtail: A cue, or queue. J. & H. Smith.
pigtailed: Having a tail like a pig's; as, the pigtailed baboon.
pigweed: A name of several annual weeds. See Goosefoot, and Lamb's-quarters.
pika: Any one of several species of rodents of the genus Lagomys, resembling small tailless rabbits. They inhabit the high mountains of asia and America. Called also calling hare, and crying hare. See chief hare.
pike: A foot soldier's weapon, consisting of a long wooden shaft or staff, with a pointed steel head. It is now superseded by the bayonet.
pikeblenny: tropical American fishes; males are aggressively defensive of their territory
piked: Furnished with a pike; ending in a point; peaked; pointed. With their piked targets bearing them down. " Milton.
pikeman: A soldier armed with a pike. Knoll es.
piker: A soldier armed with a pike, a pikeman.
pil: A leaflet inserted in a package of medicine, providing information about the drug for the patient.
pilaf: rice cooked in well-seasoned broth with onions or celery and usually poultry or game or shellfish and sometimes tomatoes
pilaff: rice cooked in well-seasoned broth with onions or celery and usually poultry or game or shellfish and sometimes tomatoes
pilar: of or relating to a hair
pilaster: An upright architectural member right-angled in plan, constructionally a pier (See Pier, (b)), but architecturally corresponding to a column, having capital, shaft, and base to agree with those of the columns of the same order. In most cases the projection from the wall is one third of its width, or less.
pilate: the Roman procurator of Judea who ordered that Jesus be crucified (died in AD )
pilaw: rice cooked in well-seasoned broth with onions or celery and usually poultry or game or shellfish and sometimes tomatoes
pilchard: A small European food fish (Clupea pilchard us) resembling the herring, but thicker and rounder. It is sometimes taken in great numbers on the coast of England. Fools are as like husbands as pilchards are to herrings.
pilcher: A scabbard, as of a sword.
pile: A covering of hair or fur.
pilea: low-growing tropical perennials grown for their stingless foliage
piled: Having a pile or point; pointed. Magus threw a spear well piled. " Chapman.
piler: One who places things in a pile.
piles: The small, troublesome tumors or swellings about the anus and lower part of the rectum which are technically called hemorrhoids. See Hemorrhoids.
pileus: A kind of skull cap of felt.
pilfer: To steal in small quantities, or articles of small value; to practice petty theft.
pilferage: the act of stealing small amounts or small articles
pilfered: simple past and past participle of pilfer
pilferer: One who pilfers; a petty thief.
pilfering: Thieving in a small way. n.
pilfers: third-person singular simple present indicative of pilfer
pilgarlic: One who has lost his hair by disease; a sneaking fellow, or one who is hardly used.
pilger: To reduce the diameter of a metal tube in a pilger mill
pilgrim: Of or pertaining to a pilgrim, or pilgrims; making pilgrimages. With pilgrim steps. " Milton. Pilgrim fathers, a name popularly given to the one hundred and two English colonists who landed from the mayflower and made the first settlement in New England at Plymouth in. They were separatists from the Church of England, and most of them had sojourned in Holland.
pilgrimage: a journey to a sacred place
pilgrimlike: Resembling or characteristic of a pilgrim.
piliferous: Bearing a single slender bristle, or hair.
piling: The process of building up, heating, and working, fagots, or piles, to form bars, etc.
pill: The peel or skin. Some be covered over with crusts, or hard pills, as the locusts. " Holland.
pillage: To strip of money or goods by open violence; to plunder; to spoil; to lay waste; as, to pillage the camp of an enemy. Mummius. took, pillaged, and burnt their city. Arbuthnot.
pillaged: having been robbed and destroyed by force and violence
pillages: third-person singular simple present indicative of pillage
pillaging: the act of stealing valuable things from a place
pillar: A portable ornamental column, formerly carried before acardinal, as emblematic of his support to the church. Skel ton.
pillared: Supported or ornamented by pillars; resembling a pillar, or pillars. The pillared arches. " Sir W. Scott. Pillared flame. Thomson.
pillarlike: Resembling or characteristic of a pillar.
pillau: An Oriental dish consisting of rice boiled with mutton, fat, or butter.
pilled: Stripped of hair; scant of hair; bald. Pilled beard. Chaucer.
pillion: A panel or cushion saddle; the under pad or cushion of saddle; esp., a pad or cushion put on behind a man's saddle, on which a woman may ride. Hiss hank pillion without stirrups. Spenser.
pilloried: simple past and past participle of pillory
pillory: A frame of adjustable boards erected on a post, and having holes through which the head and hands of an offender were thrust soas to be exposed in front of it.
pillorying: present participle and gerund of pillory
pillow: A piece of metal or wood, forming a support to equalize pressure; a brass; a pillow block.
pillowcase: A removable case or covering for a pillow, usually of white linen or cotton cloth.
pillowed: Provided with a pillow or pillows; having the head resting on, or as on, a pillow. Pillowed on buckler cold and hard. Sir W. Scott.
pilocarpine: An alkaloid extracted from jaborandi (Pilocarpus pennatifolius) as a white amorphous or crystalline substance which has a peculiar effect on the vasomotor system.
pilose: Clothed thickly with pile or soft down.
pilosity: The quality or state of being pilose; hairiness. Bacon.
pilot: One employed to steer a vessel; a helmsman; a steersman. Dryden.
pilotage: The pilot's skill or knowledge, as of coasts, rocks, bars, and channels. Sir W. Raleigh.
piloted: simple past and past participle of pilot
pilotfish: small pelagic fish often accompanying sharks or mantas
pilothouse: an enclosed compartment from which a vessel can be navigated
pilotry: pilotage; skill in being a pilot
pilpul: Among the Jews, penetrating investigation, disputation, and drawing of conclusions, esp. in Talmudic study. Pilpulist (#),n. Pilpulistic (#), a.
pilsen: a town in Czech Republic where Pilsner beer originated
pilsener: a pale lager with strong flavor of hops
pilsner: a pale lager with strong flavor of hops; first brewed in the Bohemian town of Pilsen
pilus: hairlike structure especially on the surface of a cell or microorganism
pima: a member of the North American Indian people living in southern Arizona and northern Mexico
pimelic: Pertaining to, or designating, a substance obtained from certain fatty substances, and subsequently shown to be a mixture of suberic and adipic acids.
pimento: Allspice; applied both to the tree and its fruit. See allspice.
pimiento: The Spanish sweet pepper, the fruit of which is used as ave getable, to stuff olives, etc.
pimp: One who provides gratification for the lust of others; aprocurer; a pander. Swift.
pimpernel: A plant of the genus Anagallis, of which one species (A.arvensis) has small flowers, usually scarlet, but sometimes purple, blue, or white, which speedily close at the approach of bad weather. Water pimpernel. (Bot.) See Brookweed.
pimple: Any small acuminated elevation of the cuticle, whether going onto suppuration or not. All eyes can see a pimple on her nose. " Pope.
pimpleback: Quadrula pustulosa, an American freshwater mussel.
pinacoid: A plane parallel to two of the crystalline axes.
pinacolin: A colorless oily liquid related to the ketones, and obtained by the decomposition of pinacone; hence, by extension, any one of the series of which pinacolin proper is the type.
pinacone: A white crystalline substance related to the glycols, and made from acetone; hence, by extension, any one of a series of substances of which pinacone proper is the type.
pinafore: An apron for a child to protect the front part of dress; atier.
pinang: A palm of the genus Nenga, endemic to Southeast Asia.
pinard: A surname from French originating in France.
pinaster: A species of pine (Pinus Pinaster) growing in Southern Europe.
pinata: plaything consisting of a container filled with toys and candy; suspended from a height for blindfolded children to break with sticks
pinax: A tablet; a register; hence, a list or scheme inscribed on at ablet. Sir T. Browne.
pinball: a game played on a sloping board; the object is to propel marbles against pins or into pockets
pincer: a hand tool for holding consisting of a compound lever for grasping
pinch: To take hold; to grip, as a dog does.
pinche: South American tamarin with a tufted head
pincheck: A kind of sturdy cotton cloth with a dot pattern.
pincher: One who, or that which, pinches.
pinchers: An instrument having two handles and two grasping jaws working on a pivot; used for griping things to be held fast, drawing nails, etc.
pinching: Compressing; nipping; griping; niggardly; as, pinching cold; ap inching parsimony. Pinching bar, a pinch bar. See Pinch, n.,. Pinching nut, a check nut. See under Check, n.
pincushion: A small cushion, in which pins may be stuck for use.
pindar: Greek lyric poet remembered for his odes (?-? BC)
pindaric: Of or pertaining to Pindar, the Greek lyric poet; after the style and manner of Pindar; as, Pindaric odes. n.
pindarical: Pindaric. Too extravagant and Pindarical for prose. Cowl ey.
pine: Woe; torment; pain. Pyne of hell. " Chaucer.
pineal: Of or pertaining to a pine cone; resembling a pine cone. Pineal gland (Anat.), a glandlike body in the roof of the third ventricle of the vertebrate brain; called also pineal body, epiphysis, conarium. In some animals it is connected with a rudimentary eye, theso-called pineal eye, and in other animals it is supposed to be the remnant of a dorsal median eye.
pineapple: A tropical plant (Ananas sa sativa); also, its fruit; so called from the resemblance of the latter, in shape and external appearance, to the cone of the pine tree. Its origin is unknown, though conjectured to be American.
pinecone: the seed-producing cone of a pine tree
pined: simple past and past participle of pine
pinene: Either of two isomeric bicyclic monoterpene hydrocarbons that are the principal components of pine resin.
pinery: A pine forest; a grove of pines.
pinesap: A reddish fleshy herb of the genus Monotropa (M. hypopitys),formerly thought to be parasitic on the roots of pine trees, but more probably saprophytic.
pinetum: A plantation of pine trees; esp., a collection of living pine trees made for ornamental or scientific purposes.
pinfeather: A feather not fully developed; esp., a rudimentary feather just emerging through the skin.
pinfish: similar to sea bream; small spiny-finned fish found in bays along the southeastern coast of the United States
pinfold: A place in which stray cattle or domestic animals are confined; a pound; a penfold. A parish pinfold begirt by its high hedge. Sir W. Scott.
ping: The sound made by a bullet in striking a solid object or in passing through the air.
pinger: a pulse generator used for echo sounding in sonar
pingo: A conical mound of earth with an ice core caused by permafrost uplift, particularly if lasting more than a year.
pinguid: Fat; unctuous; greasy. Some clays are more pinguid. Mortimer.
pinhole: a small puncture that might have been made by a pin
pinion: A moth of the genus Lithophane, as L. antennata, whose larva bores large holes in young peaches and apples.
pinite: A compact granular cryptocrystalline mineral of a dull grayish or greenish white color. It is a hydrous alkaline silicate, and is derived from the alteration of other minerals, as iolite.
pink: A vessel with a very narrow stern; called also pinky. Sir W.Scott. Pink stern (Naut.), a narrow stern.
pinked: Pierced with small holes; worked in eyelets; scalloped on the edge.
pinker: comparative form of pink: more pink
pinkerton: A habitational surname from Old English.
pinkeye: inflammation of the conjunctiva of the eye
pinking: The act of piercing or stabbing.
pinkness: Quality or state of being pink.
pinko: a person with mildly leftist political views
pinkroot: The root of Spigelia Marilandica, used as a powerful vermifuge; also, that of S. Anthelmia. See definition (below).
pinkster: Whitsuntide. Pinkster flower (Bot.), the rosy flower of the Azalea nudiflora; also, the shrub itself; called also Pinxter blomachee by the New York descendants of the Dutch settlers.
pinna: One of the divisions of a pinnate part or organ.
pinnace: A small vessel propelled by sails or oars, formerly employed as a tender, or for coast defence; called originally, spy nace or spyne.
pinnacle: An architectural member, upright, and generally ending in as mall spire, used to finish a buttress, to constitute a part in aproportion, as where pinnacles flank a gable or spire, and the like. Pinnacles may be considered primarily as added weight, where it is necessary to resist the thrust of an arch, etc. Some renowned metropolis With glistering spires and pinnacles around. Milton.
pinnate: (of a leaf shape) featherlike; having leaflets on each side of a common axis
pinnatifid: Divided in a pinnate manner, with the divisions not reaching to the midrib.
pinnatilobate: Having lobes arranged in a pinnate manner.
pinnatisect: (of a leaf shape) cleft nearly to the midrib in narrow divisions not separated into distinct leaflets
pinned: simple past and past participle of pin
pinner: One who pins or impounds cattle. See Pin, v. t.
pinning: a mutual promise of a couple not to date anyone else; on college campuses it was once signaled by the giving of a fraternity pin
pinniped: One of the Pinnipedia; a seal.
pinnipedia: A suborder of aquatic carnivorous mammals including the seals and walruses; opposed to Fissipedia.
pinnothere: A crab of the genus pinnotheres. See Oyster crab, under Oyster.
pinnotheres: type genus of the family Pinnotheridae: pea crabs
pinnule: One of the small divisions of a decompound frond or leaf. See illust. of Bipinnate leaf, under Bipinnate.
pinochle: a card game played with a pack of forty-eight cards (two of each suit for high cards); play resembles whist
pinocytosis: process by which certain cells can engulf and incorporate droplets of fluid
pinole: meal made of finely ground corn mixed with sugar and spices
pinon: any of several low-growing pines of western North America
pinscher: any of three breeds of dogs whose ears and tail are usually cropped
pinsetter: The person who clears fallen pins and resets them in tenpin bowling or candlepin bowling.
pinstripe: a suit made from a fabric with very thin stripes
pint: A measure of capacity, equal to half a quart, or four gills, used in liquid and dry measures. See Quart.
pintado: Any bird of the genus Numida. Several species are found in africa. The common pintado, or Guinea fowl, the helmeted, and the crested pintados, are the best known. See Guinea fowl, under Guinea.
pintail: A northern duck (Da fila acuta), native of both continents. The adult male has a long, tapering tail. Called also gray duck, piketail, piket-tail, spike-tail, split-tail, springtail, sea pheasant, and gray widgeon.
pintano: Abudefduf saxatilis, a species of damselfish.
