specializes: third-person singular simple present indicative of specialize
specializing: present participle and gerund of specialize
specialty: A contract or obligation under seal; a contract by deed; awriting, under seal, given as security for a debt particularly specified. Chitty. Bouvier. Wharton (Law Dict.).Let specialties be therefore drawn between us.
speciate: evolve so as to lead to a new species or develop in a way most suited to the environment
speciation: the evolution of a biological species
specie: abl. of L. species sort, kind. Used in the phrase in specie, that is, in sort, in kind, in (its own) form. expects a return in specie from them Dryden. In specie (Law), in precise or definite form; specifically; according to the exact terms; of the very thing.
species: A group of individuals agreeing in common attributes, and designated by a common name; a conception subordinated to another conception, called a genus, or generic conception, from which it differs in containing or comprehending more attributes, and extending to fewer individuals. Thus, man is a species, under animal as agen us; and man, in its turn, may be regarded as a genus with respect to European, American, or the like, as species.
specific: clearly defined or identified; particular; precise; relating to a particular subject or thing; not general
specificate: To show, mark, or designate the species, or the distinguishing particulars of; to specify.ir M. Hale.
specificated: simple past and past participle of specificate
specification: a detailed description of design criteria for a piece of work
specificity: the quality of being specific rather than general
specifier: someone who draws up specifications giving details (as for obtaining a patent)
specifies: third-person singular simple present indicative of specify
specify: To mention or name, as a particular thing; to designate in words so as to distinguish from other things; as, to specify the uses of a plant; to specify articles purchased. He has there given us an exact geography of Greece, where the countries and the uses of their soils are specified. Pope.
specifying: The act or process of stating or describing something clearly and exactly.
specimen: A part, or small portion, of anything, or one of a number of things, intended to exhibit the kind and quality of the whole, or of what is not exhibited; a sample; as, a specimen of a man'shandwriting; a specimen of painting; aspecimen of one's art.
specimenize: To collect or prepare as a specimen.
speciosity: The quality or state of being specious; speciousness. Professions built so largely on speciosity, instead of performance. Carlyle.
speciousness: an appearance of truth that is false or deceptive; seeming plausibility
speck: The blubber of whales or other marine mammals; also, the fat of the hippopotamus. Speck falls (Naut.), falls or ropes rove through blocks for hoisting the blubber and bone of whales on board a whaling vessel.
speckle: A little or spot in or anything, of a different substance or color from that of the thing itself. An huge great serpent, all with speckles pied. Spebser.
specs: optical instrument consisting of a frame that holds a pair of lenses for correcting defective vision
spect: Acronym of single-photon emission computed tomography.
spectacle: An optical instrument consisting of two lenses set in a light frame, and worn to assist sight, to obviate some defect in the organs of vision, or to shield the eyes from bright light.
spectacles: optical instrument consisting of a frame that holds a pair of lenses for correcting defective vision
spectate: be a spectator in a sports event
spectator: One who on; one who sees or beholds; a beholder; one who is personally present at, and sees, any exhibition; as, the spectators at a show. Devised and played to take spectators.
specter: a mental representation of some haunting experience
spectrochemistry: The application of spectroscopy to the analysis of chemical compounds.
spectrofluorometer: A spectrometer used in fluorescence spectroscopy
spectrogram: A photograph, map, or diagram of a spectrum.
spectrograph: a spectroscope by which spectra can be photographed
spectrographic: relating to or employing a spectrograph
spectrography: The process of using a spectrometer to produce a spectrograph.
spectroheliograph: An apparatus for making spectroheliograms, consisting of aspectroscopic camera used in combination with a telescope, and provided with clockwork for moving the sun's image across the slit. Spectroheliographic (#), a.
spectrohelioscope: An instrument used for observing solar radiation.
spectrological: Of or pertaining to spectrology; as, spectrological studies or experiments. Spectrologically, adv.
spectrology: The science of spectrum analysis in any or all of its relations and applications.
spectrometer: A spectroscope fitted for measurements of the lu minious spectra observed with it.
spectrometry: Art or process of using the spectrometer, or of measuring wavelengths of rays of a spectrum. Spectrometric (#), a.
spectrophone: An instrument constructed on the principle of the photophone and used in spectrum analysis as an adjunct to the spectroscope. Spectrophonic (#), a.
spectrophotography: photography using a spectrophotometer or similar instrument
spectrophotometer: An instrument for measuring or comparing the intensites of the colors of the spectrum.
spectrophotometric: Of, or relating to spectrophotometry, or measured by a spectrophotometer.
spectrophotometry: The art of comparing, photometrically, the brightness of two spectra, wave length by wave length; the use of the spectrophotometer. Spectrophotometric (#), a.
spectroradiometry: The measurement of the intensity or energy of electromagnetic radiation at different wavelengths
spectroscope: An optical instrument for forming and examining spectra (as that of solar light, or those produced by flames in which different substances are volatilized), so as to determine, from the position of the spectral lines, the composition of the substance.
spectroscopic: of or relating to or involving spectroscopy
spectroscopist: One who investigates by means of a spectroscope; one skilled in the use of the spectroscope.
spectroscopy: The use of the spectroscope; investigations made with the spectroscope.
spectrum: an ordered array of the components of an emission or wave
specular: Of or pertaining to a speculum; conducted with the aid of aspeculum; as, a specular examination.
speculate: To view subjects from certain premises given or assumed, and infer conclusions respecting them a priori.
speculated: simple past and past participle of speculate
speculates: third-person singular simple present indicative of speculate
speculating: present participle and gerund of speculate
speculation: The act or process of reasoning a priori from premises given or assumed.(d) (Com.) The act or practice of buying land, goods, shares, etc.,in expectation of selling at a higher price, or of selling with the expectation of repurchasing at a lower price; a trading on anticipated fluctuations in price, as distinguished from trading in which the profit expected is the difference between the retail and wholesale prices, or the difference of price in different markets. year) is considered investment. Sudden fortunes, indeed, are sometimes made in such places, by what is called the trade of speculation. A. Smith. Speculation, while confined within moderate limits, is the agent for equalizing supply and demand, and rendering the fluctuations of priceless sudden and abrupt than they would otherwise be. F. A. Walker.
speculatist: One who speculates, or forms theories; a speculator; atheorist. The very ingenious speculatist, Mr. Hume. V. Knox.
speculative: Given to speculation; contemplative. The mind of man being by nature speculative. Hooker.
speculatively: with speculation; in a speculative manner
speculator: One who speculates. Specifically: (a) An observer; acontemplator; hence, a spy; a watcher. Sir T. Browne.(b) One who forms theories; a theorist. A speculator who had dared to affirm that the human soul is by nature mortal. Macaulay.(c) (Com.)
speculatory: Intended or adapted for viewing or espying; having oversight. T. Wart on.
speculum: An instrument for dilating certain passages of the body, and throwing light within them, thus facilitating examination or surgical operations.
speech: To make a speech; to harangue.
speechful: Full of speech or words; voluble; loquacious.
speechify: To make a speech; to harangue.
speechifying: The act of making a speech or speeches. The dinner and speechifying. at the opening of the annual season for the buckhounds. M. Arnold.
speeded: simple past and past participle of speed
speeder: A machine for drawing and twisting slivers to form rovings.
speedometer: a meter fixed to a vehicle that measures and displays its speed
speedway: road where high speed driving is allowed
speedwell: Any plant of the genus Veronica, mostly low herbs with pale blue corollas, which quickly fall off.
speedy: Not dilatory or slow; quick; swift; nimble; hasty; rapid in motion or performance; as, a speedy flight; on speedy foot. I will wish her speedy strength. Darts, which not the good could shun, The speedy ould outfly. Dryden.
speering: present participle and gerund of speer
speight: A woodpecker; called also specht, spekt, spight.
speir: To ask. See Spere. Sir W. Scott.
speiss: A regulus consisting essentially of nickel, obtained as aresidue in fusing cobalt and nickel ores with silica and sodium carbonate to make smalt.
speldring: A split dried haddock or other small fish.
spelk: A small stick or rod used as a spike in thatching; a splinter. Grose.
spellbind: To bind or hold by, or as if by, a spell or charm; to fascinate, esp. by eloquence of speech, as in a political campaign. Spellbinder (#), n.
spellbinder: an orator who can hold his listeners spellbound
spellbound: Bound by, or as by, a spell.
spelldown: a contest in which you are eliminated if you fail to spell a word correctly
spelled: simple past and past participle of spell
spellful: Abounding in spells, or charms. Here, while his eyes the learned leaves peruse, Each spellful mystery explained he views. Hoole.
spelling: The act of one who spells; formation of words by letters; orthography.
spellwork: Power or effect of magic; that which is wrought by magic; enchantment. Like those Peri isles of light That hang by spellwork in the air. Moore.
spelt: imp. & p. p. of Spell. Spelled.
spelter: Zinc; especially so called in commerce and arts.
spelterman: A person involved in the manufacture of spelter (type of metal).
spelunking: The practice or hobby of exploring underground caverns.
spence: A place where provisions are kept; a buttery; a larder; a pantry. Chiefly Brit. dial. In. his spence, or pantry were hung the carcasses of a sheep or ewe, and two cows lately slaughtered. Sir W. Scott. Bluff Harry broke into the spence, And turned the cowls adrift. Tennyson.
spencer: One who has the care of the spence, or buttery. Promptorium Parvulorum.
spencerian: Of or relating to Platt Rogers Spencer, US business school activist, or the style of handwriting he developed.
spend: To break ground; to continue working.
spender: One who spends; esp., one who spends lavishly; a prodigal; aspendthrift.
spending: The act of expending; expenditure. Spending money, money seta part for extra (not necessary) personal expenses; pocket money.
spendthrift: One who spends money profusely or improvidently; a prodigal; one who lavishes or wastes his estate. Also used figuratively. A woman who was a generous spendthrift of life. Mrs. R. H. Davis.
spengler: German philosopher who argued that cultures grow and decay in cycles (-)
spenser: English poet who wrote an allegorical romance celebrating Elizabeth I in the Spenserian stanza (-)
spent: Exhausted of spawn or sperm; said especially of fishes. Spent ball, a ball shot from a firearm, which reaches an object without having sufficient force to penetrate it.
spere: To search; to pry; to ask; to inquire. Jamie son.
spergula: small genus of Old World annual herbs: corn spurry
sperm: The male fecundating fluid; semen. See Semen. Sperm cell (Physiol.), one of the cells from which the spermatozoids are developed. Sperm morula. (Biol.) Same as Spermosphere.
spermary: An organ in which spermatozoa are developed; a sperm gland; atesticle.
spermatheca: A small sac connected with the female reproductive organs of insects and many other invertebrates, serving to receive and retain the spermatozoa.
spermatic: Of or pertaining to semen; as, the spermatic fluid, the spermatic vessels, etc. Spermatic cord (Anat.), the cord which suspends the testicle within the scrotum. It is made up of aconnective tissue sheath inclosing the spermatic duct and accompanying vessels and nerves.
spermatid: an immature gamete produced by a spermatocyte; develops into a spermatozoon
spermatium: One of the motionless spermatozoids in the conceptacles of certain fungi. J. H. Balfour.
spermatocele: a swelling on the epididymis or the testis; usually contains spermatozoa
spermatogenetic: Relating to, or connected with, spermatogenesis; as, spermatogenetic function.
spermatogonium: A primitive seminal cell, oc curing in masses in the seminal tubules. It divides into a mass (spermosphere) of small cells (spermoblast), which in turn give rise to spermatozoids.
spermatophorous: Producing seed, or sperm; seminiferous; as, the so-called spermatophorous cells.
spermatophyte: Any plant of the phylum Spermatophyta. Spermatophytic (#), a.
spermatorrhoea: Abnormal emission of the semen without copulation.
spermaturia: presence of sperm in the urine
spermine: A polyamine, N,N'-bis(-aminopropyl) butane-,-diamine, originally extracted from sperm, that is involved in cellular metabolism.
spermist: A believer in the doctrine, formerly current, of encasement in the male (see Encasement), in which the seminal thread, or spermatozoid, was considered as the real animal germ, the head being the true animal head and the tail the body.
spermoblast: One of the cells formed by the diivision of the spermospore, each of which is destined to become a spermatozoid; a spermatocyte; aspermatoblast.
spermogonium: A conceptacle of certain lichens, which contains spermatia.
spermosphere: A mass or ball of cells formed by the repeated division of amale germinal cell (spermospore), each constituent cell (spermoblast) of which is converted into a spermatozoid; a spermatogemma.
spermospore: The male germinal or seminal cell, from the breaking up of which the sperm oblasts are formed and ultimately the spermatozoids; aspermatospore. Balfour.
speronara: A small, usually single-masted, sailing boat, used especially for transport between Sicily and Malta, remaining in use along the coast of Sicily until the mid-th century.
speronaro: A kind of Sicilian open boat.
sperrylite: An arsenide of platinum oc curing in grains and minute isometric crystals of tin-white color. It is found near Sudbury, Ontario canada, and is the only known compound of platinum oc curing in nature.
spewed: simple past and past participle of spew
spews: third-person singular simple present indicative of spew
sphacelate: To die, decay, or become gangrenous, as flesh or bone; to mortify.
sphaeriaceae: parasitic fungi having globose and sometimes necked or beaked perithecia
sphaeridium: A peculiar sense organ found upon the exterior of most kinds ofsea urchins, and consisting of an oval or sh erical head surmounting as hort pedicel. It is generally supposed to be an olfactory organ.
sphaeristerium: A large open space connected with the Ancient Roman thermae, for exercise with balls after the bather had been anointed.
sphaerobolaceae: monotypic family of fungi in which the more or less spherical gleba is forcibly ejected at maturity
sphaerocarpaceae: liverworts with bilaterally symmetrical gametophytes; sometimes placed in the order Jungermanniales
sphagnum: A genus of mosses having white leaves slightly tinged with redor green and found growing in marshy places; bog moss; peat moss.
sphalerite: Zinc sulphide; called also blende, black-jack, false galena, etc. See Blende (a).
sphene: A mineral found usually in thin, wedge-shaped crystals of ayellow or green to black color. It is a silicate of titanium and calcium; titanite.
sphenethmoid: Of or pertaining to both the sphenoidal and the ethmoidal regions of the skull, or the sphenethmoid bone; sphenethmoidal. Sphenethmoid bone (Anat.), a bone of the skull which surrounds the anterior end of the brain in many amphibia; the girdle bone.
sphenethmoidal: Relating to the sphenoethmoid bone; sphenoethmoid.
sphenocephaly: A wedge-shaped deformation of the cranium
sphenographer: One skilled in sphenography; a sphenographist.
sphenography: The art of writing in cuneiform characters, or of deciphering inscriptions made in such characters.
sphenoid: Of or pertaining to the sphenoid bone. Sphenoid bone (Anat.),an irregularly shaped bone in front of the occipital in the base of the skull of the higher vertebrates. It is composed of several fetal bones which become united the adult. See Alisphenoid, Basisphenoid, Orbitosphenoid, Presphenoid.
sphenoidal: Pertaining to, or resembling, a sphenoid.
sphenomaxillary: Relating to the sphenoid bone and the maxilla.
sphenopalatine: Relating to, or connecting, the sphenoid bone and the palatine bone.
sphenotic: Of, pertaining to, or designating, the sphenotic bone. Sphenotic bone (Anat.), a bone on the anterior side of the auditory capsule of many fishes, and connected with, or adjoining, the sphenoid bone.
spheral: Of or pertaining to a sphere or the spheres.
sphere: A body or space contained under a single surface, which in every part is equally distant from a point within called its center.
spherical: of or relating to spheres or resembling a sphere
sphericity: The quality or state of being spherial; roundness; as, the sphericity of the planets, or of a drop of water.
spherics: The doctrine of the sphere; the science of the properties and relations of the circles, figures, and other magnitudes of a sphere, produced by planes intersecting it; spherical geometry and trigonometry.
spheroid: A body or figure approaching to a sphere, but not perfectly spherical; esp., a solid generated by the revolution of an ellipse about one of its axes. Oblate spheroid, Prolate spheroid. See Oblate, Prolate, and Ellipsoid.
spheroidal: Having the form of a spheroid. Spheroidally, adv. Spheroidal state (Physics.), the state of aliquid, as water, when, on being thrown on a surface of highly heated metal, it rolls about in spheroidal drops or masses, at a temperature several degrees below ebullition, and without actual contact with the heated surface, a phenomenon due to the repulsive force of heat, the intervention of a cushion of nonconducting vapor, and the cooling effect of evaporation.
spheromere: Any one of the several symmetrical segments arranged around the central axis and composing the body of a radiate anmal.
spherosiderite: Siderite oc curing in spheroidal masses.
spherule: A little sphere or spherical body; as, quicksilver, when poured upon a plane, divides itself into a great number of minute spherules.
spherulite: A minute spherical crystalline body having a radiated structure, observed in some vitreous volcanic rocks, as obsidian and pearlstone.
spherulitic: Of or pertaining to a spherulite; characterized by the presence of spherulites.
sphery: Round; spherical; starlike. Herm ia's sphery eyne.
sphincter: A muscle which surrounds, and by its contraction tends to close, a natural opening; as, the sphincter of the bladder.
sphincteral: Of or pertaining to the sphincter.
sphingosine: An unsaturated aliphatic amino alcohol associated with the lipids of brain tissue
sphinxian: Of or relating to the mythological sphinx.
sphragistics: The science of seals, their history, age, distinctions, etc.,esp. as verifying the age and genuine ss of documents.
sphygmogram: A tracing, called a pulse tracing, consisting of a series of curves corresponding with the beats of the heart, obtained by the application of the sphygmograph.
sphygmograph: An instrument which, when applied over an artery, indicates graphically the movements or character of the pulse. See Sphygmogram.
sphygmographic: Relating to, or produced by, a sphygmograph; as, asphygmographic tracing.
sphygmomanometer: a pressure gauge for measuring blood pressure
sphygmomanometry: The measurement of blood pressure using a sphygmomanometer
sphygmometer: An instrument for measuring the strength of the pulse beat; asphygmograph.
sphygmophone: An electrical instrument for determining by the ear the rhythm of the pulse of a person at a distance.
sphyraena: type and sole genus of the Sphyraenidae: barracuda
sphyraenidae: monotypic family of large active fishes of tropical and subtropical waters: barracuda
spic: (ethnic slur) offensive term for persons of Latin American descent
spica: A kind of bandage passing, by successive turns and crosses, from an extremity to the trunk; so called from its resemblance to a spike of a barley.
spiccato: Detached; separated; a term indicating that every note is tobe performed in a distinct and pointed manner.
spicewood: An American shrub (Lindera Benzoin), the bark of which has asp icy taste and odor; called also Benjamin, wild allspice, and fever bush.
spiciferous: Bearing ears, or spikes; spicate. Bailey.
spiciness: The quality or state of being spicy.
spick: A spike or nail. Spick and span, quite new; that is, as new as a spike or nail just made and a chip just split; brand-new; as, a spick and span novelty. See Span-new. Howell.
spicose: Having spikes, or ears, like corn spikes.
spiculated: simple past and past participle of spiculate
spicy: Flavored with, or containing, spice or spices; fragrant; aromatic; as, spicy breezes. The spicy nut-brown ale. " Milton. Led by new stars, and borne by spicy gales. Pope.
spider: Any one of numerous species of arachnids comprising the order araneina. Spiders have the mandibles converted into poison fangs, orfalcers. The abdomen is large and not segmented, with two or three pairs of spinnerets near the end, by means of which they spin threads of silk to form cocoons, or nests, to protect their eggs and young. Many species spin also complex webs to entrap the insects upon which they prey. The eyes are usually eight in number (rarely six), and are situated on the back of the cephalothorax. See Illust. under araneina.
spiderweb: The net-like construct of a spider containing sticky strands to catch prey.
spiderwort: An American endogenous plant (Tradescantia Virginica), with long linear leaves and ephemeral blue flowers. The name is sometimes extended to other species of the same genus.
spidery: relating to or resembling a member of the class Arachnida
spiel: plausible glib talk (especially useful to a salesperson)
spiff: attractiveness in appearance or dress or manner
spiffy: marked by up-to-date ness in dress and manners
spiflicated: simple past and past participle of spiflicate
spiflication: The act of spiflicating, or the state of being spiflicated; annihilation.
spignet: An aromatic plant of America. See Spikenard.
spigot: A pin or peg used to stop the vent in a cask; also, the plug of a faucet or cock. Spigot and faucet joint, a joint for uniting pipes, formed by the insertion of the end of one pipe, or pipe fitting, intoa socket at the end of another.
spik: (ethnic slur) offensive term for persons of Latin American descent
spiked: Furnished or set with spikes, as corn; fastened with spikes; stopped with spikes. A youth, leaping over the spiked pales,. was caught by those spikes. Wiseman.
spikelet: A small or secondary spike; especially, one of the ultimate parts of the in florescence of grasses. See Illust. of Quaking grass.
spikemoss: any of numerous fern allies of the genus Selaginella
spikenard: An aromatic plant. In the United States it is the Araliaracemosa, often called spignet, and used as a medicine. The spikenard of the ancients is the Nardo stachys Jatamansi, a native of the himalayan region. From its blackish roots a perfume for the hair is still prepared in India.
spiky: Like a spike; spikelike. These spiky, vivid outbursts of metallic vapors. C. A. Young.
spile: To supply with a spile or a spigot; to make a small vent in, as a cask.
spilikin: One of a number of small pieces or pegs of wood, ivory, bone, or other material, for playing a game, or for counting the score in agame, as in cribbage. In the plural (spilikins), a game played with such pieces; pushpin.
spilite: a very fine-grained igneous rock, resembling an altered basalt, containing feldspar together with chlorite, calcite, and epidote etc.
spill: To cover or decorate with slender pieces of wood, metal, ivory, etc.; to inlay. Spenser.
spilled: simple past and past participle of spill
spiller: A system or method of fishing by means of a number of hooks seton snoods all on one line; in North America, called trawl fishing, bultow, or bultow fishing, and long-line fishing.
spilling: The act of dropping or spreading out of a fluid or particles.
spillway: A sluiceway or passage for superfluous water in a reservoir, to prevent too great pressure on the dam.
spilt: imp. & p. p. of Spill. Spilled.
spilth: Anything spilt, or freely poured out; slop; effusion. With drunken spilth of wine. Choicest cates, and the flagon's best spilth. R. Browning.
spin: To shape, as malleable sheet metal, into a hollow form, by bending or buckling it by pressing against it with a smooth hand to olor roller while the metal revolves, as in a lathe. To spin a yarn (Naut.), to tell a story, esp. a long or fabulous tale. To spin hay (Mil.), to twist it into ropes for convenient carriage on an expedition. To spin street yarn, to gad about gossiping.
spinach: southwestern Asian plant widely cultivated for its succulent edible dark green leaves
spinal: Of, pertaining to, or in the region of, the backbone, or vertebral column; rachidian; vertebral.
spindle: The shaft, mandrel, or arbor, in a machine tool, as a lathe or drilling machine, etc., which causes the work to revolve, or carrie sa tool or center, etc.(b) (Mach.) The vertical rod on which the runner of a grinding mill turns.(c) (Founding) A shaft or pipe on which a core of sand is formed.
spindling: Long and slender, or disproportionately tall and slender; as, as pindling tree; a spindling boy.
spine: A sharp appendage to any of a plant; a thorn.
spinel: Bleached yarn in making the linen tape called inkle; unwrought inkle. Knight.
spinelessness: the quality of lacking a strong character; an irresolute disposition
spinelike: Resembling or characteristic of a spine (spike or bristle).
spinescent: Becoming hard and thorny; tapering gradually to a rigid, leafless point; armed with spines. Gray.
spinet: A keyed instrument of music resembling a harpsichord, but smaller, with one string of brass or steel wire to each note, sounded by means of leather or quill plectrums or jacks. It was formerly much used. Dumb spinet. (Mus.) See Manichordon.
spinifex: Any of several Australian grasses of the genus Tri cuspis, which often form dense, almost impassable growth, their leaves being stiff and sharp-pointed.
spinnaker: A large triangular sail set upon a boom, used when running before the wind.
spinner: A goatsucker; so called from the peculiar noise it makes when darting through the air.
spinneret: One of the special jointed organs situated on the under side, and near the end, of the abdomen of spiders, by means of which they spin their webs. Most spiders have three pairs of spinnerets, but some have only two pairs. The ordinary silk line of the spider is composed of numerous smaller lines jointed after issuing from thespinnerets.
spinnery: A mill or factory where spinning takes place.
spinny: A small thicket or grove with undergrowth; a clump of trees. The downs rise steep, crowned with black fir spinnies. C. King sley.
spinose: Full of spines; armed with thorns; thorny.
spinout: A skid that results in a vehicle rotating such that its longitudinal axis is no longer aligned with its direction of linear motion.
spinoza: Dutch philosopher who espoused a pantheistic system (-)
spinozism: The form of Pantheism taught by Benedict Spinoza, that there isbut one substance, or infinite essence, in the universe, of which theso-called material and spiritual beings and phenomena are only modes, and that one this one substance is God.
spinster: An unmarried or single woman; used in legal proceedings as atitle, or addition to the surname. If a gentlewoman be termed a spinster, she may abate the writ. Coke.
spinsterhood: the state of being a spinster (usually an elderly unmarried woman)
spinsterish: Resembling or characteristic of a spinster.
spinsterlike: Resembling or characteristic of a spinster.
spinthariscope: A small instrument containing a minute particle of a radium compound mounted in front of a fluorescent screen and viewed with magnifying lenses. The tiny flashes produced by the continual bombardment of the screen by the a rays are thus rendered visible. Spinthariscopic (#), a.
spiracle: The nostril, or one of the nostrils, of whales, porpoises, an dallied animals.
spiracular: Of or pertaining to a spiracle.
spiraea: A genus of shrubs or perennial herbs including the meadowsweet and the hardhack.
spiral: Of or pertaining to a spiral; like a spiral. Spiral gear, or spiral wheel (Mach.), a gear resembling in general a spur gear, but having its teeth cut at an angle with its axis, or so that they form small portions of screws or spirals. Spiral gearing, a kind of gearing sometimes used in light machinery, in which spiral gears, instead of bevel gears, are used to transmit motion between shafts that are not parallel. Spiral operculum, an operculum whih has spiral lines of growth. Spiral shell, any shell in which the whorls form a spiral or helix. Spiral spring. See the Note under Spring, n.,.
spiraled: simple past and past participle of spiral
spiraling: in the shape of a coil
spirally: In a spiral form, manner, or direction.
spirant: A term used differently by different authorities; by some as equivalent to fricative, that is, as including all the continuous consonants, except the nasals m, n, ng; with the further exception, by others, of the liquids r, l, and the semivowels w, y; by others limited to f, v, th surd and sonant, and the sound of German ch, thus excluding the sibilants, as well as the nasals, liquids, and semivowels. See Guide to Pronunciation, -.
spiranthes: large cosmopolitan genus of white-flowered terrestrial orchids
spirantize: To change (a consonant) to a spirant sound.
spirea: a Japanese shrub that resembles members of the genus Spiraea; widely cultivated in many varieties for its dense panicles of flowers in many colors; often forced by florists for Easter blooming
spired: Having a spire; being in the form of a spire; as, a spired steeple. Mason.
spireme: The tangled mass of strands of chromatin seen in the early stages of mitosis, originally believed to be a single continuous strand (or two in a diploid cell, etc.)
spirifer: Any one of numerous species of fossil brachipods of the genus spirifer, or Delthyris, and allied genera, in which the long calcareous supports of the arms form a large spiral, or helix, on each side.
spirilla: any flagellated aerobic bacteria having a spirally twisted rodlike form
spiring: Shooting up in a spire or spires. The spiring grass. " Dry ton.
spirit: Rum, whisky, brandy, gin, and other distilled liquors having much alcohol, in distinction from wine and malt liquors.
spiritedly: in a spirited or lively manner; with animation and vivacity
spiritedness: quality of being active or spirited or alive and vigorous
spiritful: Full of spirit; spirited. The spiritful and orderly life of our own grown men. Milton. Spiritfully, adv. Spiritfulness, n.
spiritless: lacking ardor or vigor or energy
spiritlessness: the trait of lacking enthusiasm for or interest in things generally
spiritous: Like spirit; refined; defecated; pure. More refined, more spirituous and pure. Milton.
spirits: an alcoholic beverage that is distilled rather than fermented
spiritual: A spiritual function, office, or affair. See Spirituality,.He assigns supremacy to the pope in spirituals, and to the emperor in temporals. Lowell.
spiritualism: The doctrine, in opposition to the materialists, that all which exists is spirit, or soul that what is called the external world is either a succession of notions impressed on the mind by the Deity, as maintained by Berkeley, or else the mere educt of the mind itself, as taught by Fichte.
spiritualistic: Relating to, or connected with, spiritualism.
spirituality: That which belongs to the church, or to a person as an ecclesiastic, or to religion, as distinct from temporalities. During the vacancy of a see, the archbishop is guardian of the spiritualities thereof. Black stone.
spiritualize: To extract spirit from; also, to convert into, or impregnate with, spirit.
spiritualized: simple past and past participle of spiritualize
spiritualizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of spiritualize
spiritualizing: present participle and gerund of spiritualize
spiritually: In a spiritual manner; with purity of spirit; like a spirit.
spirituous: containing or of the nature of alcohol
spirituousness: The quality or state of being spirituous. Boyle.
spirketing: The planking from the waterways up to the port sills. Totten.
spiro: A polycyclic compound or system that contains a single atom as the only common member of two rings.
spirochaetaceae: large coarsely spiral bacteria; free-living in fresh or salt water or commensal in bodies of oysters
spirochetal: Of or pertaining to a spirochete or spirochetes.
spirochete: parasitic or free-living bacteria; many pathogenic to humans and other animals
spirograph: An instrument for recording the respiratory movements, as the sphygmograph does those of the pulse.
spiroid: Resembling or having the form of a spiral or helix.
spirometer: An instrument for measuring the vital capacity of the lungs, or the volume of air which can be expelled from the chest after the deepest possible inspiration. Cf. Pneumatometer.
spirometry: The act or process of measuring the chest capacity by means of a spirometer.
spirula: A genus of cephalopods having a multilocular, internal, siphunculated shell in the form of a flat spiral, the coils of which are not in contact.
spiry: Of a spiral form; wreathed; curled; serpentine. Hid in the spiry volumes of the snake. Dryden.
spiss: Thick; crowded; compact; dense. This spiss and. copious, yet concise, treatise. Brere wood.
spissated: Rendered dense or compact, as by evaporation; inspissated; thickened. The spissated juice of the poppy. Bp. War burton.
spissitude: The quality or state of being spissated; as, the spissitude of coagulated blood, or of any coagulum. Arbuthnot.
spit: To attend to a spit; to use a spit. She's spitting in the kitchen. Old Play.
spitball: Paper chewed, and rolled into a ball, to be thrown as amis sile.
spitballer: A pitcher who moistens the ball with saliva before throwing it.
spitchcock: To split (as an eel) lengthwise, and broil it, or fry it in hot fat.
spitchcocked: Broiled or fried after being split lengthwise; said of eels.
spite: Ill-will or hatred toward another, accompanied with the disposition to irritate, annoy, or thwart; petty malice; grudge; rancor; despite. Pope. This is the deadly spite that angers.
spited: simple past and past participle of spite
spiteful: Filled with, or showing, spite; having a desire to vex, annoy, or injure; malignant; malicious; as, a spiteful person or act. Spitefully, adv. Spitefulness, n.
spitefully: with spite; in a spiteful manner
spitfire: A violent, irascible, or passionate person. Grose.
spithame: The span of a human hand, as a unit of measure in Ancient Greece.
spiting: present participle and gerund of spite
spitter: One who ejects saliva from the mouth.
spitting: the act of spitting (forcefully expelling saliva)
spittlebug: small leaping herbivorous insect that lives in a mass of protective froth which it and its larvae secrete
spitz: any of various stocky heavy-coated breeds of dogs native to northern regions having pointed muzzles and erect ears with a curled furry tail
spiv: a person without employment who makes money by various dubious schemes; goes about smartly dressed and having a good time
splake: A hybrid fish derived from a male brook trout and a female lake trout.
splanchnic: Of or pertaining to the viscera; visceral.
splanchnology: That part of anatomy which treats of the viscera; also, atreatise on the viscera.
splash: To strike and dash about water, mud, etc.; to dash in such away as to spatter.
splashboard: A guard in the front part of vehicle, to prevent splashing by amud or water from the horse's heels; in the United States commonly called dashboard.
splashdown: a landing of a spacecraft in the sea at the end of a space flight
splashed: (of a fluid) having been propelled about in flying drops or masses
splasher: a protective covering over or beside a wheel to protect the upper part of a vehicle from splashes of mud
splashing: the act of scattering water about haphazardly
splashy: Full of dirty water; wet and muddy, so as be easily splashed about; slushy.
splat: give off the sound of a bullet flattening on impact
splattered: covered with bright patches (often used in combination)
splay: Displayed; spread out; turned outward; hence, flat; ungainly; as, splay shoulders. Sonwthing splay, something blunt-edged, unhandy, and infelicitous. M.Arnold.
splayed: Of a door or a window: bevelled so as to be larger on one side of the wall than on the other.
splayfoot: A foot that is abnormally flattened and spread out; flat foot.
splaymouth: A wide mouth; a mouth stretched in derision. Dryden.
spleen: A peculiar glandlike but ductless organ found near the stomach or intestine of most vertebrates and connected with the vascular system; the milt. Its exact function in not known.
spleenful: Displaying, or affected with, spleen; angry; fretful; melancholy. Myself have calmed their spleenful mutiny. Then rode Geraint, a little spleenful yet, Across the bridge that spann'd the dry ravine. Tennyson.
spleenish: Spleeny; affected with spleen; fretful. Spleenishly, adv. Spleenishness, n.
spleenwort: Any fern of the genus Asplenium, some species of which were anciently used as remedies for disorders of the spleen.
spleeny: Irritable; peevish; fretful. Spleeny Lutheran, and not wholesome to Our cause.
splenalgia: Pain over the region of the spleen.
splendent: Shining; glossy; beaming with light; lustrous; as, splendent planets; splendent metals. See the Note under d Luster,.
splendid: Possessing or displaying splendor; shining; very bright; as, a splendid sun.
splendiferous: Splendor-bearing; splendid. Bale. A splendiferous woman. " Haliburton.
splendour: the quality of being magnificent or splendid or grand
splenetic: Affected with spleen; malicious; spiteful; peevish; fretful. Splenetic guffaw. " G. Eliot. You humor me when I am sick; Why not when I am splenetic Pope.
splenic: Of or pertaining to the spleen; lienal; as, the splenic vein. Splenic apoplexy or fever. (Med.) See Anthrax, n.,.
splenitive: Splenetic. Even and smooth as seemed the temperament of the nonchalant, languid virginian not splenitive or rash. T. N. Page.
splenium: The thickened posterior border of the corpus callosum; so called in allusion to its shape.
splenius: A flat muscle of the back of the neck.
splenomegaly: an abnormal enlargement of the spleen
spleuchan: A pouch, as for tobacco. Sir W. Scott.
splice: A junction or joining made by splicing.
spliced: simple past and past participle of splice
splicer: a woodworker who joins pieces of wood with a splice
splicing: a junction where two things (as paper or film or magnetic tape) have been joined together
spline: a flexible strip (wood or rubber) used in drawing curved lines
splining: Of or pertaining to a spline. Splining machine, a machine tool for cutting grooves, key seats, or slots; a slotting machine.
splint: A thin piece of wood, or other substance, used to keep in place, or protect, an injured part, especially a broken bone when set.
splinter: To become split into long pieces.
splintered: simple past and past participle of splinter
splinters: wood in small pieces or splinters
splintery: Consisting of splinters; resembling splinters; as, the splintery fracture of a mineral.
split: To divide or separate into components; often used with up; as, to split up sugar into alcohol and carbonic acid. To split hairs, to make distinctions of useless nicety.
splitter: One who, or that which, splits.
splitting: resembling a sound of violent tearing as of something ripped apart or lightning splitting a tree
splosh: dash a liquid upon or against
splotch: A spot; a stain; a daub. R. Browning.
splurge: A blustering demonstration, or great effort; a great display. Bartlett.
splutter: To speak hastily and confusedly; to sputter. Carlet on.
spluttering: gerund of splutter: the act of one who splutters.
splutters: third-person singular simple present indicative of splutter
spode: English potter who started a pottery famous for its bone china (-)
spodumene: A mineral of a white to yellowish, purplish, or emerald-green color, oc curing in prismatic crystals, often of great size. It is asilicate of alum inia and lithia. See Hiddenite.
spoffish: Earnest and active in matters of no moment; bustling. Dickens.
spoil: (usually plural) valuables taken by violence (especially in war)
spoiled: having the character or disposition harmed by pampering or oversolicitous attention
spoiler: a candidate with no chance of winning but who may draw enough votes to prevent one of the leading candidates from winning
spoiling: the act of damaging or ruining something
spoils: That which is taken from another by violence; especially, the plunder taken from an enemy; pillage, booty.
spoilsman: One who serves a cause or a party for a share of the spoils; in united States politics, one who makes or recognizes a demand for public office on the ground of partisan service; also, one who sanctions such a policy in appointments to the public service.
spoilsport: someone who spoils the pleasure of others
spokane: a city in eastern Washington near the Idaho border
spoken: uttered through the medium of speech or characterized by speech; sometimes used in combination
spokesman: One who speaks for another. He shall be thy spokesman unto the people. Ex. iv.
spokesperson: an advocate who represents someone else's policy or purpose
spoliary: The place in an Ancient Roman amphitheatre where slaughtered gladiators were dragged and the clothes stripped from their bodies.
spoliate: To plunder; to pillage; to despoil; to rob.
spoliates: third-person singular simple present indicative of spoliate
spoliative: Serving to take away, diminish, or rob; esp. (Med.), serving to diminish sensibily the amount of blood in the body; as, spoliative bloodletting.
spondee: A poetic foot of two long syllables, as in the Latin word leges.
spondyle: A joint of the backbone; a vertebra.
spondylitis: inflammation of a spinal joint; characterized by pain and stiffness
spondylolisthesis: a forward dislocation of one vertebra over the one beneath it producing pressure on spinal nerves
spondylotherapy: A form of therapy involving stimulation by ice, electric currents, etc. of the nerves originating from the spinal cord.
spong: An irregular, narrow, projecting part of a field.
sponged: simple past and past participle of sponge
spongefly: hairy-bodied insect whose larvae feed on freshwater sponges
spongelike: like a sponge in being able to absorb liquids and yield it back when compressed
sponger: a workman employed to collect sponges
spongeware: Traditional pottery decorated by spattering or sponging on colour
spongiform: Resembling a sponge; soft and porous; porous.
spongilla: A genus of siliceous spong ea found in fresh water.
spongillafly: hairy-bodied insect whose larvae feed on freshwater sponges
spongin: The chemical basis of sponge tissue, a nitrogenous, hornlike substance which on decomposition with sulphuric acid yields leucin and glycocoll.
sponging: a. & n. from Sponge, v. Sponging house (Eng. Law), a bailiff'sor other house in which debtors are put before being taken to jail, or until they compromise with their creditors. At these houses extortionate charges are commonly made for food, lodging, etc.
spongioblast: any of various columnar epithelial cells in the central nervous system that develop into neuroglia
spongiole: A supposed spongelike expansion of the tip of a rootlet for absorbing water; called also spongelet.
spongioplasm: A fibrous, spongelike component of a cell's cytoplasm.
spongiose: Somewhat spongy; spongelike; full of small cavities.
spongy: easily squashed; resembling a sponge in having soft porous texture and compressibility
sponsion: An act or engagement on behalf of a state, by an agent not specially authorized for the purpose, or by one who exceeds the limits of authority.
sponsional: Of or pertaining to a pledge or agreement; responsible. He is righteous even in that representative and sponsional person heput on. Abp. Leighton.
sponson: One of the triangular platforms in front of, and abaft, the paddle boxes of a steamboat.
sponsored: simple past and past participle of sponsor
spontaneity: the quality of being spontaneous and coming from natural feelings without constraint
spontaneous: happening or arising without apparent external cause
spontaneousness: the quality of being spontaneous and coming from natural feelings without constraint
spontoon: A kind of half-pike, or halberd, formerly borne by inferior officers of the British infantry, and used in giving signals to the soldiers.
spool: A piece of cane or red with a knot at each end, or a hollow cylinder of wood with a ridge at each end, used to wind thread or yarn upon. Spool stand, an article holding spools of thread, turning on pins, used by women at their work.
spooler: One who, or that which, spools.
spoom: To be driven steadily and swiftly, as before a strong wind; tobe driven before the wind without any sail, or with only a part of the sails spread; to scud under bare poles. When virtue spooms before a prosperous gale, My heaving wishes help to fill the sail. Dryden.
spoon: See Spoom. We might have spooned before the wind as well as they. Pepys.
spoonbill: wading birds having a long flat bill with a tip like a spoon
spoondrift: Spray blown from the tops waves during a gale at sea; also, snow driven in the wind at sea; written also spindrift.
spooned: simple past and past participle of spoon
spoonerism: transposition of initial consonants in a pair of words
spooney: Weak-minded; demonstratively fond; as, spooney lovers.
spoonful: The quantity which a spoon contains, or is able to contain; as, a teaspoonful; a tablespoonful.
spooning: present participle and gerund of spoon
spoons: Foolishly infatuated with; having a romantic crush on (used with on).
spoor: The track or trail of any wild animal; as, the spoor of an elephant; used originally by travelers in South Africa.
sporades: Stars not included in any constellation; called also informed, or unformed, stars.
sporadic: Oc curing singly, or apart from other things of the same kind, or in scattered instances; separate; single; as, a sporadic fireball; a sporadic case of disease; a sporadic example of a flower. Sporadic disease (Med.), a disease which occurs in single and scattered cases. See the Note under Endemic, a.
sporangiophore: The axis or receptacle in certain ferns (as Trichomanes), which bears the sporangia.
sporangium: A spore case in the cryptogamous plants, as in ferns, etc.
spore: a small usually single-celled asexual reproductive body produced by many nonflowering plants and fungi and some bacteria and protozoans and that are capable of developing into a new individual without sexual fusion
sporidium: A secondary spore, or a filament produced from a spore, in certain kinds of minute fungi.
sporoblast: A sporozoan cell, found in the oocyst of the malarial parasite in the mosquito, that produces spores and sporozoites.
sporobolus: cosmopolitan annual and perennial grasses (as dropseed or rush grass)
sporocarp: specialized leaf branch in certain aquatic ferns that encloses the sori or clusters of sporangia
sporoderm: The wall or covering of a spore.
sporodochium: A small, compact stroma (mass of hyphae) usually formed on host plants parasitized by mitosporic fungi of the form order Tuberculariales (Deuteromycota, Hyphomycetes). It bears the conidiophores on which the asexual spores or conidia are formed
sporogenous: producing spores or reproducing by means of spores
sporogonium: The sporophyte of a bryophyte (moss, liverwort or hornwort), generally consisting of a foot, seta and capsule.
sporogony: The growth or development of an animal or a zooid from anon sexual germ.
sporophore: a spore-bearing branch or organ: the part of the thallus of a sporophyte that develops spores; in ferns and mosses and liverworts is practically equivalent to the sporophyte
sporophyl: leaf in ferns and mosses that bears the sporangia
sporophyll: leaf in ferns and mosses that bears the sporangia
sporophyte: In plants exhibiting alternation of generations, the generation which bears asexual spores; opposed to gametophyte. It is not clearly differentiated in the life cycle of the lower plants. Sporophytic (#), a.
sporotrichosis: a chronic fungal infection of the skin and lymph nodes
sporozoa: An extensive division of parasitic Protozoa, which increase by sporulation. It includes the Gregarinida.
sporran: A large purse or pouch made of skin with the hair or fur on, worn in front of the kilt by Highlanders when in full dress.
sport: A plant or an animal, or part of a plant or animal, which has some peculiarity not usually seen in the species; an abnormal variety or growth. See Sporting plant, under Sporting.
sported: simple past and past participle of sport
sporter: One who sports; a sportsman. As this gentleman and I have been old fellow sporters, I have afrienship for him. Goldsmith.
sportfishing: the act of someone who fishes as a diversion
sportful: Full of sport; merry; frolicsome; full of jesting; indulging in mirth or play; playful; wanton; as, a sportful companion. Down he alights among the sportful herd. Milton.
sporting: Of pertaining to, or engaging in, sport or sporrts; exhibiting the character or conduct of one who, or that which, sports. Sporting book, a book containing a record of bets, gambling operations, and the like. C. King sley. Sporting house, a house frequented by sportsmen, gamblers, and the like. Sporting man, one who practices field sports; also, a horse racer, a pugilist, a gambler, or the like. Sporting plant (Bot.), a plant in which a single bud or offset suddenly assumes a new, and sometimes very different, character from that of the rest of the plant. Darwin.
sportingly: In sport; sportively. The question you there put, you do it, I suppose, but sportingly. Hammond.
sportive: Tending to, engaged in, or provo cate of, sport; gay; froliscome; playful; merry. Is it I That drive thee from the sportive court. Sportively, adv. Sportiveness, n.
sportscaster: an announcer who reads sports news or describes sporting events
sportsman: One who pursues the sports of the field; one who hunts, fishes, etc.
sportsmanlike: exhibiting or calling for sportsmanship or fair play
sportsmanly: Befitting a sportsman; being or demonstrating the conduct expected of players of sport.
sportsmanship: The practice of sportsmen; skill in field sports.
sportswear: attire worn for sport or for casual wear
sportswriter: a journalist who writes about sports
sportula: A gift; a present; a prize; hence, an alms; a largess. To feed luxuriously, to frequent sports and theaters, to run for the sportula. South.
sporty: appropriate for sport or engagement in a sport
sporulation: The act or process of forming spores; spore formation. See illust. of Bacillus, b.
spot: A variety of the common domestic pigeon, so called from a spot on its head just above its beak.
spotless: Without a spot; especially, free from reproach or impurity; pure; untained; innocent; as, a spotless mind; spotless behavior. A spotless virgin, and a faultless wife. Waller.
spotlessness: the state of being spotlessly clean
spotlight: The projected spot or circle of light used to illuminate brilliantly a single person or object or group on the stage; leaving the rest of the stage more or less unilluminated; hence, conspicuous public notice.
spots: spots before the eyes caused by opaque cell fragments in the vitreous humor and lens
spotsman: A smuggler responsible for selecting a suitable place on shore to land the smuggled goods.
spotted: Marked with spots; as, a spotted garment or character. The spotted panther. " Spenser. Spotted fever (Med.), a name applied to various eruptive fevers, esp. to typhus fever and cere bro-spinal meningitis. Spotted tree (Bot.), an Australian tree (Flindersia maculosa); so called because its bark falls off in spots.
spotty: Full of spots; marked with spots.
spousal: Of or pertaining to a spouse or marriage; nuptial; matrimonial; conjugal; bridal; as, spousal rites; spousal ornaments. Wordsworth.
spouse: To wed; to espouse. This markis hath her spoused with a ring. Chaucer. Though spoused, yet wanting wedlock's solemnize. Spenser. She was found again, and spoused to Mari nell. Spenser.
spoused: simple past and past participle of spouse
spout: an opening that allows the passage of liquids or grain
spouter: One who, or that which, spouts.
spouting: propelled violently in a usually narrow stream
spp: Initialism of statutory paternity pay - payments made by an employer to a father who is absent from work after the birth of a child.
sprain: To weaken, as a joint, ligament, or muscle, by sudden and excessive exertion, as by wrenching; to overstrain, or stretch injuriously, but without luxation; as, to sprain one's ankle.
sprained: simple past and past participle of sprain
sprat: small fatty European fish; usually smoked or canned like sardines
sprauchle: To move in a clumsy manner; to stumble or sprawl; to clamber up with difficulty.
sprawl: go, come, or spread in a rambling or irregular way
sprawls: Small branches of a tree; twigs; sprays. Halliwell.
spray: be discharged in sprays of liquid
sprayed: simple past and past participle of spray
sprayer: One that sprays; any instrument for vaporizing and spraying liquids.
spraying: the application of a liquid in the form of small particles ejected from a sprayer
spread: An unlimited expanse of discontinuous points.
spreader: a hand tool for spreading something
spreading: act of extending over a wider scope or expanse of space or time
spreadingly: , adv. Increasingly. The best times were spreadingly infected. Milton.
spreadsheet: a screen-oriented interactive program enabling a user to lay out financial data on the screen
spree: A merry frolic; especially, a drinking frolic; a carousal.
sprenge: To sprinkle; to scatter. Wyclif ( Pet. i. ).
sprent: p. p. of Sprenge. Sprinkled. All the ground with purple blood was sprent. Spenser.
spreynd: p. p. of Sprenge. Sprinkled. When spreynd was holy water. Chaucer.
sprig: A small eyebolt ragged or barbed at the point.
sprigger: a worker who strips the stems from moistened tobacco leaves and binds the leaves together into books
spriggy: Full of sprigs or small branches.
sprightful: Full of spirit or of life; earnest; vivacious; lively; brisk; nimble; gay. Sprightfully, adv. Sprightfulness, n. Spoke like a sprightful gentlemen. Steeds sprightful as the light. Cowl ey.
sprightliness: The quality or state of being sprightly; liveliness; life; briskness; vigor; activity; gayety; vivacity. In dreams, observe with what a sprightliness and alacrity does she exert herself! Addison.
sprightly: Spright like, or spiritlike; lively; brisk; animated; vigorous; airy; gay; as, a sprightly youth; a sprightly air; a sprightly dance. Sprightly wit and love inspires. " Dryden. The sprightly Sylvia trips along the green. Pope.
spring: An active, springly young man. There came two springals of full tender years. " Spenser. Joseph, when he was sold to Poti phar, that great man, was a fair young spring all. Latimer.
springal: An ancient military engine for casting stones and arrows by means of a spring.
springboard: An elastic board, secured at the ends, or at one end, often by elastic supports, used in performing feats of agility or in exercising.
springbok: a South African gazelle noted for springing lightly into the air
springbuck: a South African gazelle noted for springing lightly into the air
springe: A noose fastened to an elastic body, and drawn close with asudden spring, whereby it catches a bird or other animal; a gin; as nare. As a woodcock to mine own springe.
springfield: capital of the state of Illinois
springfish: Any of the fish in the goodeid genus Crenichthys.
springhalt: A kind of lameness in horse. See Stringhalt.
springing: The act or process of one who, or that which, springs.
springlet: A little spring. But yet from out the little hill Oozes the slender springlet still. Sir W. Scott.
springlike: resembling a spring or the action of a spring
springly: Pertaining to or characteristic of spring; vernal
springtail: Any one of numerous species of small apterous insects belonging to the order Thysanura. They have two elastic caudal stylets which can be bent under the abdomen and then suddenly extended like aspring, thus enabling them to leap to a considerable distance. See collembola, and Podura.
springtide: The time of spring; springtime. Thomson.
sprinkle: cause (a liquid) to spatter about, especially with force
sprinkled: simple past and past participle of sprinkle
sprinkler: mechanical device that attaches to a garden hose for watering lawn or garden
sprinkles: bits of sweet chocolate used as a topping on e.g. ice cream
sprinkling: The act of one who, or that which, sprinkles. Baptism may well enough be performed by sprinkling or effusion of water. Ayliffe.
sprint: To run very rapidly; to run at full speed. A runner should be able to sprint the whole way. Encyc. Brit.
sprinter: One who sprints; one who runs in sprint races; as, a champion sprinter.
sprinting: present participle and gerund of sprint
sprit: To throw out with force from a narrow orifice; to eject; to spurt out. Sir T. Browne.
spritely: Of or relating to a sprite.
spritsail: a fore-and-aft sail extended by a sprit
sprocket: roller that has teeth on the rims to pull film or paper through
sprout: Young coleworts; Brussels sprouts. Johnson. Brussels sprouts (Bot.) See under Brussels.
sprouted: (of growing vegetation) having just emerged from the ground
sprouting: the process whereby seeds or spores sprout and begin to grow
spruce: Any coniferous tree of the genus Picea, as the Norway spruce (P. excel sa), and the white and black spruces of America (P. alba and P. nigra), besides several others in the far Northwest. See Picea.
spruced: simple past and past participle of spruce
spruceness: the state of being neat and smart and trim
sprucing: present participle and gerund of spruce
sprucy: Resembling or characteristic of the spruce tree.
sprunt: To spring up; to germinate; to spring forward or outward. To sprunt up, to draw one's self up suddenly, as in anger or defiance; to bristle up.
spry: Having great power of leaping or running; nimble; active. She is as spry as a cricket. S. Judd (Margaret).If I'm not so large as you, You are not so small as I, And not half so spry. Emerson.
spud: a sharp hand shovel for digging out roots and weeds
spudder: One who digs up weeds with a spud.
spume: Frothy matter raised on liquids by boiling, effervescence, or agitation; froth; foam; scum. Materials dark and crude, Of spiritous and fiery spume. Milton.
spumed: simple past and past participle of spume
spumescence: The state of being foamy; frothiness.
spumoni: An Italian style of ice cream dessert made with layers of different colors and flavors (typically cherry, pistachio, and vanilla or chocolate) and usually containing candied fruits and nuts.
spumy: emitting or filled with bubbles as from carbonation or fermentation
spun: imp. & p. p. of Spin. Spun hay, hay twisted into ropes for convenient carriage, as on a military expedition. Spun silk, a cheap article produced from floss, or short-fibered, broken, and waste silk, carded and spun, in distinction from the long filaments wound from the cocoon. It is often mixed with cotton. Spun yarn (Naut.), a line formed of two or more rope-yarns loosely twisted.
spunk: Wood that readily takes fire; touchwood; also, a kind of tinder made from a species of fungus; punk; amadou. Sir T. Browne.
