strontia: An earth of a white color resembling lime in appearance, and baryta in many of its properties. It is an oxide of the metal strontium.
strontianite: Strontium carbonate, a mineral of a white, greenish, or yellowish color, usually occurring in fibrous massive forms, but sometimes in prismatic crystals.
strontic: Of or pertaining to strontium; containing, or designating the compounds of, strontium.
strontium: A metallic element of the calcium group, always naturally occurring combined, as in the minerals strontianite, celestite, etc. It is isolated as a yellowish metal, somewhat malleable but harder than calcium. It is chiefly employed (as in the nitrate) to color pyrotechnic flames red. Symbol Sr. Atomic weight. A radioactive isotope of strontium produced by certain nuclear reactions, and constituting one of the prominent harmful components of radioactive fallout from nuclear explosions; also called radiostrontium. It has ahalf-life of years.
strop: A strap; specifically, same as Strap,.
strophanthin: a bitter and very toxic glycoside derived from plants of the genus Strophanthus; in moderate doses it is a cardiac stimulant but in larger doses it is a powerful poison; used in Africa as an arrow poison
strophanthus: A genus of tropical apocynaceous shrubs having singularly twisted flowers. One species (Strophanthus hispid us) is used medicinally as a cardiac sedative and stimulant.
strophe: In Greek choruses and dances, the movement of the chorus while turning from the right to the left of the orchestra; hence, the strain, or part of the choral ode, sung during this movement. Also sometimes used of a stanza of modern verse. See the Note under antistrophe.
strophic: Pertaining to, containing, or consisting of, strophes.
strophiole: A crest like excrescence about the hilum of certain seeds; acaruncle.
stropping: present participle and gerund of strop
stroud: A kind of coarse blanket or garment used by the North American indians.
strow: Same as Strew. Thick as autumnal leaves that strow the brooks In Vallombrosa. Milton. A manner turbid. and strown with blemished. M. Arnold.
strows: third-person singular simple present indicative of strow
struck: imp. & p. p. of Strike. Struck jury (Law), a special jury, composed of persons having special knowledge or qualifications, selected by striking from the panel of jurors a certain number for each party, leaving the number required by law to try the cause.
struct: A data structure, especially one that serves to group a number of fields (in contrast to an object-oriented class with methods) or one that is passed by value rather than by reference.
structural: Of or pertaining to organ it structure; as, a structural element or cell; the structural peculiarities of an animal or a plant. Structural formula. (Chem.) See Rational formula, under Formula.empirical formula.
structuralism: linguistics defined as the analysis of formal structures in a text or discourse
structure: Manner of organization; the arrangement of the different tissues or parts of animal and vegetable organisms; as, organic structure, or the structure of animals and plants; cellular structure.
structured: Having a definite organic structure; showing differentiation of parts. The passage from a structureless state to a structured state is itself a vital process. H. Spencer.
structureless: Without a definite structure, or arrangement of parts; without organization; devoid of cells; homogeneous; as, a structureless membrane.
strude: A stock of breeding mares. Bailey.
strudel: thin sheet of filled dough rolled and baked
struggle: an energetic attempt to achieve something
struggled: simple past and past participle of struggle
struggling: engaged in a struggle to overcome especially poverty or obscurity
strum: To play on an instrument of music, or as on an instrument, in an unskillful or noisy way; to thrum; as, to strum a piano.
strummer: One who strums a stringed musical instrument.
strums: third-person singular simple present indicative of strum
strut: In general, any piece of a frame which resists thrust or pressure in the direction of its own length. See Brace, and Illust.of Frame, and Roof.
struthio: A genus of birds including the African ostriches.
struthiones: A division, or order, of birds, including only the African ostriches.
struthioniformes: a ratite bird order: ostriches and related extinct birds; known from the Pleistocene onward
struthious: Of or pertaining to the Struthiones, or Ostrich tribe.
strychnic: Of or pertaining to strychnine; produced by strychnine; as, strychnic compounds; strychnic poisoning; specifically (Chem.),
strymon: large and widely distributed genus of hairstreak butterflies
stu: A diminutive of the male given name Stuart.
stuart: United States painter best known for his portraits of George Washington (-)
stubbed: Reduced to a stub; short and thick, like something truncated; blunt; obtuse.
stubbled: Covered with stubble. A crow was strutting o'er the stubbled plain. Gay.
stubborn: Firm as a stub or stump; stiff; unbending; unyielding; persistent; hence, unreasonably obstinate in will or opinion; not yielding to reason or persuasion; refractory; harsh; said of persons and things; as, stubborn wills; stubborn ore; a stubborn oak; as stubborn as a mule. Bow, stubborn knees. Stubborn attention and more than common application. " Locke. Stubborn stoics. " Swift. And I was young and full of ragerie Stubborn and strong, and jolly as a pie. Chaucer. These heretics be so stiff and stubborn. Sir T. More. Your stubborn usage of the pope.
stubbornness: the trait of being difficult to handle or overcome
stubbs: English historian noted for his constitutional history of medieval England (-)
stucco: To overlay or decorate with stucco, or fine plaster.
stuccoed: simple past and past participle of stucco
stud: A collection of breeding horses and mares, or the place where they are kept; also, a number of horses kept for a racing, riding, etc. In the studs of Ireland, where care is taken, we see horses bred of excellent shape, vigor, and size. Sir W. Temple. He had the finest stud in England, and his delight was to win plates from Tories. Macaulay.
studbook: A genealogical register of a particular breed or stud of horses, esp. thoroughbreds.
studded: dotted or adorned with or as with studs or nailheads; usually used in combination
studdery: A stud, or collection of breeding horses and mares; also, aplace for keeping a stud. King Henry the Eighth erected a noble studdery. Holinshed.
studding: Material for studs, or joists; studs, or joists, collectively; studs.
student: a learner who is enrolled in an educational institution
studfish: Any one of several species of small American minnows of the genus Fundulus, as F. cate natus.
studhorse: adult male horse kept for breeding
studied: produced or marked by conscious design or premeditation
studier: A student. W. Irving. Lipsius was a great studier of the stoical philosophy. Tillot son.
studio: The working room of an artist.
studwork: Upright timbers forming the framework of a wall.
study: A representation or rendering of any object or scene intended, not for exhibition as an original work of art, but for the information, instruction, or assistance of the maker; as, a study of heads or of hands for a figure picture.
studying: reading carefully with intent to remember
stuff: A melted mass of turpentine, tallow, etc., with which the masts, sides, and bottom of a ship are smeared for lubrication. Ham. Nav. Encyc.
stuffer: One who, or that which, stuffs.
stuffing: Any seasoning preparation used to stuff meat; especially, acomposition of bread, condiments, spices, etc.; forcemeat; dressing.
stuffy: affected with a sensation of stoppage or obstruction
stull: A framework of timber covered with boards to support rubbish; also, a framework of boards to protect miners from falling stones.
stultified: simple past and past participle of stultify
stultifies: third-person singular simple present indicative of stultify
stultify: To allege or prove to be of unsound mind, so that the performance of some act may be avoided.
stultifying: present participle and gerund of stultify
stultiloquent: Given to, or characterized by, silly talk; babbling. Stultiloquently, adv.
stum: To renew, as wine, by mixing must with it and raising a new fermentation. We stum our wines to renew their spirits. Fl oyer.
stumbling: present participle and gerund of stumble
stump: The legs; as, to stir one's stumps.
stumpage: Timber in standing trees, often sold without the land at a fixed price per tree or per stump, the stumps being counted when the land is cleared. Only trees above a certain size are allowed to be cut by loggers buying stumpage from the owners of land. C. S. Sargent.
stunned: in a state of mental numbness especially as resulting from shock
stunsail: A contraction of Studding sail. With every rag set, stunsails, sky scrapers and all. Lowell.
stunt: To hinder from growing to the natural size; to prevent the growth of; to stint, to dwarf; as, to stunt a child; to stunt ap lant. When, by a cold penury, I blast the abilities of a nation, and stunt the growth of its active energies, the ill or may do is beyond all calculation. Burke.
stunting: the performance of stunts while in flight in an aircraft
stunty: Stunted, tending to stunt or be stunted.
stupa: A mound or monument commemorative of Buddha.
stupe: Cloth or flax dipped in warm water or medicaments and applied to a hurt or sore.
stupefaction: The act of stupefying, or the state of being stupefied. Resistance of the dictates of conscience brings a hardness and stupefaction upon it. South.
stupefies: third-person singular simple present indicative of stupefy
stupefy: To make stupid; to make dull; to blunt the faculty of perception or understanding in; to deprive of sensibility; to make torpid. The fumes of drink discompose and stupefy the brain. South.
stupefying: making physically stupid or dull or insensible
stupendous: Astonishing; wonderful; amazing; especially, astonishing in magnitude or elevation; as, a stupendous pile. A stupendous sum. Macaulay. All are but parts of one stupendous whole. Pope. Stupendously, adv. Stupendousness, n.
stupeous: Resembling tow; having long, loose scales, or matted filaments, like tow; stupose.
stupid: lacking or marked by lack of intellectual acuity
stupidity: a poor ability to understand or to profit from experience
stupor: Great diminution or suspension of sensibility; suppression of sense or feeling; lethargy.
stuporous: stunned or confused and slow to react (as from blows or drunkenness or exhaustion)
stupose: Composed of, or having, tufted or matted filaments like tow; stupeous.
stuprate: To ravish; to debauch. Hey wood.
stupration: Violation of chastity by force; rape. Sir T. Browne.
sturdier: comparative form of sturdy: more sturdy
sturdy: A disease in sheep and cattle, marked by great nervousness, orby dullness and stupor.
sturnus: type genus of the Sturnidae: common starlings
sturt: To vex; to annoy; to startle.
stutter: To hesitate or stumble in uttering words; to speak with spasmodic repetition or pauses; to stammer. Trembling, stuttering, calling for his confessor. Macaulay.
stuttering: The act of one who stutters; restricted by some physiologists to defective speech due to inability to form the proper sounds, the breathing being normal, as distinguished from stammering.
sty: To shut up in, or as in, a sty.
styan: See Sty, a boil. De quincey.
stygian: Of or pertaining to the river Styx; hence, hellish; infernal. See Styx. At that so sudden blaze, the Stygian throng Bent their aspect. Milton.
stylagalmaic: Performing the office of columns; as, Atlantes and Caryatides are stylagalmaic figures or images.
stylaster: Any one of numerous species of delicate, usually pink, calcareous hydroid corals of the genus Stylaster.
style: The pin, or gnomon, of a dial, the shadow of which indicates the hour. See Gnomon. (f) Etym: [Probably fr. Gr. (Bot.)
stylebook: A manual containing an organization's standardized usage conventions for how to write.
styler: someone who cuts or beautifies hair
styliform: Having the form of, or resembling, a style, pin, or pen; styloid.
styling: Any form of decoration or stylistic approach.
stylise: to represent according to a conventional style
stylish: Having style or artistic quality; given to, or fond of, the display of style; highly fashionable; modish; as, a stylish dress, house, manner. Stylishly, adv. Stylishness, n.
stylishness: elegance by virtue of being fashionable
stylist: One who is a master or a model of style, especially in writing or speaking; a critic of style. Distinguished as a stylist, for ease. Fitz ed. Hall.
stylistic: Of or pertaining to style in language. Stylistic trifles. " J. A. Symonds. The great stylistic differences in the works ascribed to him G. P. Marsh.
stylite: One of a sect of anchorites in the early church, who lived on the tops of pillars for the exercise of their patience; called also pillarist and pillar saint.
stylize: represent according to a conventional style
stylized: using artistic forms and conventions to create effects
stylizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of stylize
stylizing: present participle and gerund of stylize
stylobate: The uninterrupted and continuous flat band, coping, or pavement upon which the bases of a row of columns are supported. See Sub-base.
stylographic: Of or pertaining to stylography; used in stylography; as, stylographic tablets.
stylography: A mode of writing or tracing lines by means of a style on cards or tablets.
stylohyal: A segment in the hyoidean arch between the epihyal and tympanohyal.
stylohyoid: Of or pertaining to the styloid process and the hyoid bone.
styloid: Of or pertaining to the styloid process. Styloid process (Anat.), a long and slender process from the lower side of the temporal bone of man, corresponding to the tympanohyal and stylohyal of other animals.
stylomastoid: Of or pertaining to the styloid and mastoid processes of the temporal bone.
stylomaxillary: Of or pertaining to the styloid process and the maxilla.
stylommatophora: A division of Pulmonata in which the eyes are situated at the tips of the tentacles. It includes the common land snails and slugs. See Illust. under Snail.
stylopharyngeus: A slender muscle in the head that arises from the base of the styloid process of the temporal bone, inserts into the side of the pharynx, and acts with the contralateral muscle in swallowing to increase the transverse diameter of the pharynx by drawing its sides upward and laterally.
stylopize: Of a strepsipteran insect: to parasitize.
stylopodium: An expansion at the base of the style, as in umbelliferous plants.
stylops: A genus of minute insects parasitic, in their larval state, on bees and wasps. It is the typical genus of the group Strepsiptera, formerly considered a distinct order, but now generally referred to the Coleoptera. See Strepsiptera.
stylospore: A spore that has a thin stalk.
stylus: An instrument for writing. See Style, n.,. That needle-shaped part at the tip of the playing arm of phonograph which sits in the groove of a phonograph record while it is turning, to detect the undulations in the phonograph groove and convert them into vibrations which are transmitted to a system (since electronic) which converts the signal into sound; also called needle. The stylus is frequently composed of metal or diamond. The needle-like device used to cut the grooves which record the sound on the original disc during recording of a phonograph record. (Computers)
stymie: a situation in golf where an opponent's ball blocks the line between your ball and the hole
styphnic: Pertaining to, or designating, a yellow crystalline astringent acid, (NO).CH.(OH), obtained by the action of nitric acid on resorcin. Styphnic acid resembles picric acid, but is not bitter. It acts like a strong dibasic acid, having a series of well defined salts.
stypsis: the ability to contract or draw together soft body tissues to check blood flow or restrict secretion of fluids
styptic: Producing contraction; stopping bleeding; having the quality of restraining hemorrhage when applied to the bleeding part; astringent. Styptic weed (Bot.), an American leguminous herb (Cassia occidental is) closely related to the wild senna.
styracaceae: a widely distributed family of shrubs and trees of order Ebenales
styracin: A white crystalline tasteless substance extracted from gum storax, and consisting of a salt of cinnamic acid with cinnamic alcohol.
styrax: A genus of shrubs and trees, mostly American or Asiatic, abounding in resinous and aromatic substances. Styrax officinalisyields storax, and S. Benzoin yields benzoin.
styrene: a colorless oily liquid; the monomer for polystyrene
styrolene: An unsaturated hydrocarbon, CH, obtained by the distillation of storax, by the decomposition of cinnamic acid, and by the condensation of acetylene, as a fragrant, aromatic, mobile liquid; called also phenyl ethylene, vinyl benzene, styrol, styrene, and cinnamene.
styryl: A hypothetical radical found in certain derivatives of styrolene and cinnamic acid; called also cinnyl, or cinnamyl.
styx: The principal river of the lower world, which had to be crossed in passing to the regions of the dead.
suant: Spread equally over the surface; uniform; even. Suantly, adv.
suasible: Capable of being persuaded; easily persuaded.
suasion: The act of persuading; persuasion; as, moral suasion.
suasive: Having power to persuade; persuasive; suasory. South. Genial and suasive satire. " Earle. Suasively, adv.
suave: Sweet; pleasant; delightful; gracious or agreeable in manner; bland. Suavely, adv.
suavely: with suavity; in a suave manner
suavity: the quality of being bland and gracious or ingratiating in manner
subabbot: an abbot with another abbot as their superior
subability: An ability making up part of a greater ability.
subacetate: An acetate containing an excess of the basic constituent.
subacid: Moderately acid or sour; as, some plants have subacid juices. n.
subadar: A surname from India of Indian origin.
subadditive: Such that the image of a sum is at most the sum of the images of the summands.
subadministrative: Describing a smaller part of an administrative region.
subaerial: Beneath the sky; in the open air; specifically (Geol.), taking place on the earth's surface, as opposed to subaqueous.
subaffluent: Between the poverty line and affluence.
subagent: A person employed by an agent to transact the whole, or a part, of the business intrusted to the latter. Bouvier. Chitty.
subah: A province; a government, as of a viceroy; also, a subahdar.
subahdar: A viceroy; a governor of a subah; also, a native captain in the british native army.
subalgebra: A closed subset of an algebra.
subalpine: Inhabiting the somewhat high slopes and summits of mountains, but considerably below the snow line.
subaltern: Asserting only a part of what is asserted in a related proposition. Subaltern genus. (Logic) See under Genus.
subalternate: A particular proposition, as opposed to a universal one. See subaltern,.
subangulate: Almost angulate; having a suggestion of corners or angles.
subantique: Relating to, or exhibiting, an antique classical style imitated by a non-classical culture.
subapical: Being under the apex; of or pertaining to the part just below the apex.
subapparent: Less than apparent; not readily visible.
subarachnoid: Located or occurring below the arachnoid mater, often specifically between the arachnoid membrane and the pia mater.
subarctic: Approximately arctic; belonging to a region just without the arctic circle.
subarcuate: Having a figure resembling that of a bow; somewhat curved or arched.
subarea: A physical region that makes up part of an area.
subarytenoid: Situated under the arytenoid cartilage of the larynx.
subassembly: An assembly that is assembled with others to form a larger assembly.
subassociation: A subset of a larger association
subatom: A hypothetical component of a chemical atom, on the theory that the elements themselves are complex substances; called alsoatomicule.
subatomic: of or relating to constituents of the atom or forces within the atom
subaudition: The act of understanding, or supplying, something not expressed; also, that which is so understood or supplied. Trench.
subbase: the lowest molding of an architectural base or of a baseboard
subbasement: A basement located beneath another basement
subbing: working as a substitute for someone who is ill or on leave of absence
subbrachiales: A division of soft-finned fishes in which the ventral fins are situated beneath the pectorial fins, or nearly so.
subbranch: A branch that is itself an offshoot of a branch of something.
subbreed: A race or strain differing in certain characters from the parent breed; an incipient breed.
subbronchial: Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the bronchi; as, the subbronchial air sacs of birds.
subbureau: A district-level public security bureau in China.
subcaliber: Smaller than the caliber of a firearm. Subcaliber projectile, a projectile having a smaller diameter than the caliber of the arm from which it is fired, and to which it is fitted by means of a sabot. Knight.
subcarboniferous: Of or pertaining to the lowest division of the Carboniferous formations underlying the proper coal measures. It was a marine formation characterized in general by beds of limestone. n.
subcasino: A casino forming part of a larger casino.
subcategory: With respect to a given category; a narrower category.
subcaudal: Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the tail; as, the subcaudal, or chevron, bones.
subcause: A cause forming part of a larger cause.
subcavity: a cavity within a larger one
subcelestial: Being beneath the heavens; as, subcelestial glories. Barrow.
subcellar: A cellar beneath another story wholly or partly underground; usually, a cellar under a cellar.
subcenter: A local center in a larger network
subchannel: A distinct division of a channel or frequency band.
subchanter: An underchanter; a precentor's deputy in a cathedral; asuccentor.
subchronic: That repeats over a relatively short period.
subcinctorium: An ornamental vestment reserved for the pope, resembling a maniple and worn at a solemn pontifical Mass.
subcivilization: A civilization forming part of a larger civilization.
subclan: A branch of a larger clan.
subclass: One of the natural groups, more important than an order, into which some classes are divided; as, the angiospermous subclass of exogens.
subclavian: Situated under the clavicle, or collar bone; as, the subclavian arteries.
subclavius: A muscle which (in humans) originates from the first costal cartilage and inserts on to the undersurface of the clavicle, acting to elevate the first rib or fix the clavicle.
subclimate: A local climate that makes up part of a larger climate.
subclinical: relating to the stage in the development of a disease before the symptoms are observed
subcollege: A college making up part of a larger institution such as a university.
subcolumnar: Having an imperfect or interrupted columnar structure.
subcommander: A commander who is subordinate in rank.
subcommittee: An under committee; a part or division of a committee. Yet by their sequestra tors and subcommittees abroad. those orders were commonly disobeyed. Milton.
subcompact: a car smaller than a compact car
subcomputation: A computation making up part of a larger computation.
subconscious: just below the level of consciousness
subcontinent: a large and distinctive landmass (as India or Greenland) that is a distinct part of some continent
subcontract: A contract under, or subordinate to, a previous contract.
subcontracting: present participle and gerund of subcontract
subcontractor: One who takes a portion of a contract, as for work, from the principal contractor.
subcontrary: Having, or being in, a contrary order; said of a section of an oblique cone having a circular base made by a plane not parallel to the base, but so inclined to the axis that the section is acircle; applied also to two similar triangles when so placed as to have a common angle at the vertex, the opposite sides not being parallel. Br ande & C.
subcontrol: A control making up part of a larger control.
subcool: To cool (a saturated liquid refrigerant) below the saturation temperature.
subcoracoid: Situated under the coracoid process of the scapula; as, the subcoracoid dislocation of the humerus.
subcordate: Somewhat cordate; somewhat like a heart in shape.
subcortex: The part of the brain that lies directly below the cortex.
subcortical: of or relating to or being or involving nerve centers below the cerebral cortex
subcosta: The first major vein behind the costa on an insect wing
subcostal: Situated below the cost as, or ribs; as, the subcostal muscles.
subcranial: Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the cranium; facial.
subcrenate: Having a notched or scalloped margin
subcriminal: Less than criminal; not serious enough to count as a crime or a criminal.
subcrustaceous: Occurring beneath a crust or scab; as, a subcrustaceous cicatrization.
subcultrate: Having a form resembling that of a coulter, or straight on one side and curved on the other.
subculture: a social group within a national culture that has distinctive patterns of behavior and beliefs
subcutaneous: Situated under the skin; hypodermic. Subcutaneously, adv. Subcutaneous operation (Surg.), an operation performed without opening that part of the skin opposite to, or over, the internal section.
subcutis: subcutaneous tissue: the lowermost layer of the integumentary system in vertebrates
subcycle: A smaller or shorter-term cycle within a larger or longer-term cycle
subdeacon: One belonging to an order in the Roman Catholic Church, next interior to the order of deacons; also, a member of a minor order in the Greek Church.
subdean: An under dean; the deputy or substitute of a dean. Ayliffe.
subdebutante: A young woman who has not yet made her formal appearance in society.
subdelegate: A subordinate delegate, or one with inferior powers.
subdelegating: present participle and gerund of subdelegate
subdepartment: A subordinate department; a bureau. See the Note under Bureau.
subdepository: A depository forming part of a larger depository.
subdepot: A lesser depot that is part of a larger one.
subderivative: A word derived from a derivative, and not directly from the root; as, friendliness is a subderivative, being derived fromfriendly, which is in turn a derivative from friend. "
subdevil: A lesser devil: one subordinate to an archdevil.
subdiaconate: Of or pertaining to a subdeacon, or to the office or rank of asubdeacon.
subdichotomy: A subordinate, or inferior, division into parts; a subdivision. Many subdichatomies of petty schisms. Milton.
subdirector: A director who reports to another director.
subdirectory: (computer science) a directory that is listed in another directory
subdiscipline: A field of study or work that is related to one aspect, but not the whole, of a broader field of study or work.
subdistinguish: To distinguish or differentiate as a subtype.
subdistrict: A district forming part of a larger district.
subdititious: Put secretly in the place of something else; foisted in.
subdivide: To divide the parts of (anything) into more parts; to part into smaller divisions; to divide again, as what has already been divided. The progenies of Cham and Jap het swarmed into colonies, and those colonies were subdivided into many others. Dryden.
subdivided: Having divisions that are themselves divided into smaller divisions
subdivides: third-person singular simple present indicative of subdivide
subdividing: present participle and gerund of subdivide
subdivine: Partaking of divinity; divine in a partial or lower degree. Bp. Hall.
subdivision: an area composed of subdivided lots
subdominant: The fourth tone above, or fifth below, the tonic; so called as being under the dominant.
subdual: Act of subduing. Bp. War burton.
subducted: simple past and past participle of subduct
subdue: To bring under; to conquer by force or the exertion of superior power, and bring into permanent subjection; to reduce under dominion; to vanquish. I will subdue all thine enemies. Chron. xvii.
subduer: One who, or that which, subdues; a conqueror. Spenser.
subdues: third-person singular simple present indicative of subdue
subduing: present participle and gerund of subdue
subduple: Indicating one part of two; in the ratio of one to two. Subduple ratio, the ratio of to: thus,: is a subduple ratio, as: is a duple ratio.
subduplicate: Expressed by the square root; said of ratios. Subduplicate ratio, the ratio of the square roots, or the square root of a ratio; thus, the subduplicate ratio of a to b is a to b, or a/b.
subdural: Situated under the dura mater, or between the dura mater and the arachnoid membrane.
subecho: A minor echo or the echo of an echo
subedit: edit and correct (written or printed material)
subeditor: An assistant editor, as of a periodical or journal.
subeffective: Below the threshold where an effect would be produced.
subemployment: The situation where too few people are employed in jobs, or where they have too few hours.
subepoch: A geochronologic unit comprising one or more ages, being a period of generally agreed significance within an epoch.
suber: Cork, or the corresponding layer of woody tissue below the epidermis of a plant.
suberic: Of or pertaining to cork; specifically, designating an acid, C
suberin: A material found in the cell walls of cork. It is amodification of lignin.
suberite: Any sponge of the genus Suberites and allied genera. These sponges have a fine and compact texture, and contain minute siliceous spicules.
suberization: Conversion of the cell walls into cork tissue by development of suberin; commonly taking place in exposed tissues, as when acallus forms over a wound. Suberized cell walls are impervious to water.
suberized: simple past and past participle of suberize
subexpression: An expression that is a part of a larger expression.
subfamily: One of the subdivisions, of more importance than genus, into which certain families are divided.
subfield: A smaller, more specialized area of study or occupation within a larger one
subfigure: a figure that is a part of another figure
subfile: A file organised within another file.
subfix: One or more letters or sounds added at the bottom of a word to modify its meaning, found in Maya script.
subfloor: The floor structure supporting and underlying the visible flooring or other finishing surface such as a carpet
subfoliate: Shaped almost like a leaf; not quite foliate.
subfraction: The result of fractionating a fraction into smaller components
subfreshman: A student preparing for the freshman year.
subgeneric: Of or pertaining to a subgenus.
subgens: The sociological division of a people next below the gens or clan.
subgenus: A subdivision of a genus, comprising one or more species which differ from other species of the genus in some important character or characters; as, the azaleas now constitute a subgenus of rhododendron.
subgeometric: A style of ancient Greek pottery from to BC, bearing simplified geometric designs.
subgiant: A star that has left the main sequence but has not yet become a true giant star.

symposion: A drinking together; a symposium. Our symposion last night. Sir W. Scott.
symposium: a meeting or conference for the public discussion of some topic especially one in which the participants form an audience and make presentations
symptom: Any affection which accompanies disease; a perceptible change in the body or its functions, which indicates disease, or the kind or phases of disease; as, the causes of disease often lie beyond our sight, but we learn their nature by the symptoms exhibited. Like the sick man, we are expiring with all sorts of good symptoms. Swift.
symptomatic: relating to or according to or affecting a symptom or symptoms
symptomatize: To be a symptom of (a named condition)
symptomatology: The doctrine of symptoms; that part of the science of medicine which treats of the symptoms of diseases; semeiology.
synadelphite: An orthorhombic-dipyramidal mineral containing arsenic, calcium, hydrogen, lead, magnesium, manganese, and oxygen.
synaeresis: the separation of liquid from a gel that is caused by contraction (as in cheese making)
synagogue: (Judaism) the place of worship for a Jewish congregation
synalepha: A contraction of syllables by suppressing some vowel or diphthong at the end of a word, before another vowel or diphthong; as, th' army, for the army.
synangium: The divided part beyond the pylangium in the aortic trunk of the amphibian heart. Synangial, a.
synantherous: Having the stamens united by their anthers; as, synantherous flowers.
synanthesis: The simultaneous maturity of the anthers and stigmas of ablossom. Gray.
synanthous: Having flowers and leaves which appear at the same time; said of certain plants.
synaphea: The metrical continuity between one colon and another.
synapse: the junction between two neurons (axon-to-dendrite) or between a neuron and a muscle
synapsed: simple past and past participle of synapse
synapsis: the side by side pairing of homologous maternal and paternal chromosomes at the start of meiosis
synapte: A litany in the Greek church.
synapticula: One of numerous calcareous processes which extend between, an dunite, the adjacent septa of certain corals, especially of the fungian corals.
synaptosome: A structure containing vesicles and mitochondria of a synapse that is obtained when brain tissue is homogenized.
synarchy: Joint rule or sovereignity. Stack house.
synartesis: A fastening or knitting together; the state of being closely jointed; close union. Coleridge.
synarthrosis: Immovable articulation by close union, as in sutures. It sometimes includes symphysial articulations also. See the Note under articulation, n.,.
synaxarion: A compilation of hagiographies in the Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Churches, corresponding roughly to the martyrology of the Roman Church.
synaxis: A congregation; also, formerly, the Lord's Supper. Jer. Taylor.
sync: make synchronous and adjust in time or manner
syncarp: A kind of aggregate fruit in which the ovaries cohere in as olid mass, with a slender receptacle, as in the magnolia; also, asimilar multiple fruit, as a mulberry.
syncarpous: Composed of several carpels consolidated into one ovary.
syncategorematic: Not capable of being used as a term by itself; said of words, as an adverb or preposition.
synchondrosis: An immovable articulation in which the union is formed by cartilage. Synchondrosial, a.
synchro: a system consisting of a generator and a motor so connected that the motor will assume the same relative position as the generator
synchronic: concerned with phenomena (especially language) at a particular period without considering historical antecedents
synchronicity: the relation that exists when things occur at the same time
synchronism: A representation, in the same picture, of two or events whichoccured at different times.
synchronistic: Of or pertaining to synchronism; arranged according to correspondence in time; as, synchronistic tables.
synchronization: The act of synchronizing; concurrence of events in respect to time.
synchronize: To agree in time; to be simultaneous. The path of this great empire, through its arch of progress, synchronized with that of Christianity. De Quincey.
synchronizer: an instrument that indicates whether two periodic motions are synchronous (especially an instrument that enables a pilot to synchronize the propellers of a plane that has two or more engines)
synchronizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of synchronize
synchronizing: coordinating by causing to indicate the same time
synchronous: Happening at the same time; simultaneous. Synchronously, adv.
synchrony: The concurrence of events in time; synchronism. Geological contemporaneity is the same as chronological synchrony. Huxley.
synchrotron: cyclotron in which the electric field is maintained at a constant frequency
synchysis: A derangement or confusion of any kind, as of words in asentence, or of humors in the eye. Sparkling synchysis (Med.), acondition in which the vitreous humor is softened and contains sparkling scales of cholesterin.
synchytriaceae: a fungus family of order Chytridiales
synclastic: Curved toward the same side in all directions; said of surfaces which in all directions around any point bend away from atangent plane toward the same side, as the surface of a sphere; opposed to anticlastic. Sir W. Thomson.
synclinal: Formed by strata dipping toward a common line or plane; as, asynclinal trough or valley; a synclinal fold; opposed to anticlinal.
syncopal: Of or pertaining to syncope; resembling syncope.
syncopate: To contract, as a word, by taking one or more letters or syllables from the middle; as, Glost er is a syncopated form ofGloucester. "
syncopates: third-person singular simple present indicative of syncopate
syncopating: present participle and gerund of syncopate
syncopation: The act of syncopating; the contraction of a word by taking oneor more letters or syllables from the middle; syncope.
syncope: An elision or retrenchment of one or more letters or syllables from the middle of a word; as, ne'er for never, ev'ry for every.
syncranterian: Having teeth in one continuous row.
syncretic: Uniting and blending together different systems, as of philosophy, morals, or religion. Smart.
syncretism: Attempted union of principles or parties irreconcilably at variance with each other. He is plotting a carnal syncretism, and attempting the reconcilement of Christ and Belial. Baxter. Syncretism is opposed to eclecticism in philosophy. Kr auth-Fleming.
syncretistic: Pertaining to, or characterized by, syncretism; as, a syncretistic mixture of the service of Jehovah and the worship of idols.
syncytium: Tissue in which the cell or partition walls are wholly wanting and the cell bodies fused together, so that the tissue consists of acontinuous mass of protoplasm in which nuclei are imbedded, as inordinary striped muscle.
syndactyly: birth defect in which there is partial or total webbing connecting two or more fingers or toes
syndesis: Synonym of arthrodesis, the artificial fusion of a joint between two or more bones.
syndesmology: That part of anatomy which treats of ligaments.
syndesmosis: An articulation formed by means of ligaments.
syndet: A synthetic detergent, as opposed to a natural soap.
syndeton: The use of conjunctions or conjunctive structures to connect words, phrases, etc.
syndic: An agent of a corporation, or of any body of men engaged in abusiness enterprise; an advocate or patron; an assignee.
syndicalist: One who advocates or practices syndicalism. Syndicalistic (#), a.
syndicated: simple past and past participle of syndicate
syndicating: present participle and gerund of syndicate
syndication: Act or process of syndicating or forming a syndicate.
synecdoche: A figure or trope by which a part of a thing is put for the whole (as, fifty sail for fifty ships), or the whole for a part (as, the smiling year for spring), the species for the genus (as, cutthroat for assassin), the genus for the species (as, a creature for a man), the name of the material for the thing made, etc. Bain.
synecdochical: Expressed by synecdoche; implying a synecdoche. Isis is used for Themes is by a synecdochical kind of speech, or by apoetical liberty, in using one for another. Dray ton.
synechia: A disease of the eye, in which the iris adheres to the cornea or to the capsule of the crystalline lens.
synechology: The metaphysical doctrine of the connection of things by causation.
synecology: One of two broad subdivisions of ecology (the other being autecology), meaning the study of groups of organisms associated as a unit (essentially a biological community).
synecphonesis: A contraction of two syllables into one; synizesis.
synectics: A problem-solving methodology that stimulates thought processes of which the subject may be unaware.
synedrion: An assembly that holds formal sessions.
synergic: Of or pertaining to synergy; synergistic
synergid: Either of two naked nucleated cells at the top of the embryo sac that cooperate with the oosphere in the production of the embryo.
synergist: A remedy which has an action similar to that of another remedy, and hence increases the efficiency of that remedy when combined with it.
synergistic: used especially of drugs or muscles that work together so the total effect is greater than the sum of the two (or more)
synesis: A construction in which adherence to some element in the sense causes a departure from strict syntax, as in Philip went down to samaria and preached Christ unto them. "
synesthesia: a sensation that normally occurs in one sense modality occurs when another modality is stimulated
synesthetic: relating to or experiencing synesthesia; involving more than one sense
synfuel: Any of several fuels synthesized from coal or shale etc, or fermented from grain etc.
syngamy: The fusion of two gametes to form a zygote.
syngeneic: Genetically identical, or sufficiently identical and immunologically compatible as to allow for transplantation.
syngenesis: A theory of generation in which each germ is supposed to contain the germs of all subsequent generations; the opposite of epigenesis.
syngnathi: A suborder of lophobranch fishes which have an elongated snout and lack the ventral and first dorsal fins. The pipefishes and sea horses are examples. Syngnathous, a.
syngnathus: type genus of the family Syngnathidae
synizesis: An obliteration of the pupil of the eye.
synkaryon: A cell nucleus formed by the fusion of two preexisting nuclei (such as in an egg and a sperm cell)
synkinesis: The involuntary movement of one body part when moving another.
synnema: A large, erect reproductive structure in some fungi, bearing compact conidiophores that fuse together to form a strand with conidia at the end or on the edges.
synochal: Of or pertaining to synocha; like synocha.
synod: An ecclesiastic council or meeting to consult on church matters.
synodic: Of, related to or produced by a synod; synodal.
synodically: In a synodical manner; in a synod; by the authority of a synod. Synodically agreed upon. " R. Nelson.
synodsman: A member of a church synod.
synoecious: Having stamens and pistil in the same head, or, in mosses, having antheridia and archegonia on the same receptacle.
synoicous: having male and female reproductive organs mixed in the same gametoecium
synonym: One of two or more words (commonly words of the same language) which are equivalents of each other; one of two or more words which have very nearly the same signification, and therefore may often be used interchangeably. See under Synonymous. All languages tend to clear themselves of synonyms as intellectual culture advances, the superfluous words being taken up and appropriated by new shades and combinations of thought evolved in the progress of society. De Quincey. His name has thus become, throughout all civilized countries, asynonym for probity and philanthropy. Macaulay. In popular literary acceptation, and as employed in special dictionaries of such words, synonyms are words sufficiently alike in general signification to be liable to be confounded, but yet so different in special definition as to require to be distinguished. G.P. Marsh.
synonymic: The science, or the scientific treatment, of synonymous words.
synonymize: To express by a synonym or synonyms; to give the synonym or synonyms corresponding to. This word fortis we may synonymize after all these fashions: stout, hardy, valiant, doughty, courageous, adventurous, brave, bold, daring, intrepid. Camden.
synonymizing: present participle and gerund of synonymize
synonymous: Having the character of a synonym; expressing the same thing; conveying the same, or approximately the same, idea. Synonymously, adv. These words consist of two propositions, which are not distinct insense, but one and the same thing variously expressed; for wisdom and understanding are synonymous words here. Tillot son.
synonymy: A figure by which synonymous words are used to amplify adiscourse.
synopsis: A general view, or a collection of heads or parts so arranged as to exhibit a general view of the whole; an abstract or summary of a discourse; a syllabus; a conspectus. That the reader may see in one view the exactness of the method, aswell as force of the argument, I shall here draw up a short synopsis of this epistle. Bp. War burton.
synoptic: One of the first three Gospels of the New Testament. See synoptist.
synoptist: Any one of the authors of the three synoptic Gospels, which give a history of our Lord's life and ministry, in distinction from the writer of John's Gospel, which gives a fuller record of his teachings.
synorchism: Union or fusion of the testes.
synosteosis: Union by means of bone; the complete closing up and obliteration of sutures.
synovia: A transparent, viscid, lubricating fluid which contains mucin and secreted by synovial membranes; synovial fluid.
synovial: Of or pertaining to synovia; secreting synovia. Synovial capsule, a closed sac of synovial membrane situated between the articular surfaces at diarthrodial joints. Synovial fluid, synovia. Synovial membrane, the dense and very smooth connective tissue membrane which secretes synovia and surrounds synovial capsules an dother synovial cavities.
synovium: a thin membrane in synovial (freely moving) joints that lines the joint capsule and secretes synovial fluid
synsacrum: The bone in birds composed of the sacrum and some lumbar or caudal vertebrae fused together.
syntactic: of or relating to or conforming to the rules of syntax
syntactical: of or relating to or conforming to the rules of syntax
syntagma: a syntactic string of words that forms a part of some larger syntactic unit
syntality: The collective psychological traits of a group, analogous to the personality of an individual.
syntax: the grammatical arrangement of words in sentences
syntexis: A change in the structure of magma by melting or the assimilation of a different type of rock.
synthesis: The art or process of making a compound by putting the ingredients together, as contrasted with analysis; thus, water is made by synthesis from hydrogen and oxygen; hence, specifically, the building up of complex compounds by special reactions, whereby their component radicals are so grouped that the resulting substances are identical in every respect with the natural articles when such occur; thus, artificial alcohol, urea, indigo blue, alizarin, etc., are made by synthesis.
synthesist: One who employs synthesis, or who follows synthetic methods.
synthesized: simple past and past participle of synthesize
synthesizer: (music) an electronic instrument (usually played with a keyboard) that generates and modifies sounds electronically and can imitate a variety of other musical instruments
synthesizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of synthesize
synthesizing: present participle and gerund of synthesize
synthetase: Any enzyme that catalyzes the synthesis of a biological compound.
synthetic: a compound made artificially by chemical reactions
synthetical: of a proposition whose truth value is determined by observation or facts
synthetize: To combine; to unite in regular structure.
synthronos: The bishop's throne in the apse of an Eastern Orthodox church.
syntonic: Of or pert. to syntony; specif., designating, or pert. to, asystem of wireless telegraphy in which the transmitting and receiving apparatus are in syntony with, and only with, one another. Syntonical (#), a. Syntonically, adv.
syntonin: A proteid substance (acid albumin) formed from the albuminous matter of muscle by the action of dilute acids; formerly called musculin. See Acid albumin, under Albumin.
syntonize: To adjust or devise so as to emit or respond to electric oscillations of a certain wave length; to tune; specif., to put (twoor more instruments or systems of wireless telegraphy) in syntony with each other. Syntonization (#), n.
syntonizing: present participle and gerund of syntonize
syntony: State of being adjusted to a certain wave length; agreement or tuning between the time period of an apparatus emitting electric oscillations and that of a receiving apparatus, esp. in wireless telegraphy.
syntropy: A tendency towards complexity, structure, order, organization of ever more advantageous and orderly patterns. Originally coined as a synonym for negentropy
syntype: Any one of two or more specimens specified in the description of a species (or lower-order taxon), where no specimen has been designated as holotype.
sypher: To lap the chamfered edges of planks to make a smooth surface, as for a bulkhead.
syphilis: The pox, or venereal disease; a chronic, specific, infectious disease, usually communicated by sexual intercourse or by hereditary transmission, and occurring in three stages known as primary, secondary, and tertiary syphilis. See under Primary, Secondary, and tertiary. Treponema pallidum. Usu. tretable with penicillin or other beta-lactam antibiotics.
syphilitic: Of or pertaining to syphilis; of the nature of syphilis; affected with syphilis. n.
syphilization: Inoculation with the syphilitic virus, especially when employed as a preventive measure, like vaccination.
syphilology: That branch of medicine which treats of syphilis.
syria: an Asian republic in the Middle East at the east end of the Mediterranean; site of some of the world's most ancient centers of civilization
syriac: Of or pertaining to Syria, or its language; as, the Syriac version of the Pentateuch. n.
syrian: Of or pertaining to Syria; Syriac. n.
syrianism: A Syrian idiom, or a peculiarity of the Syrian language; a Syriacism. Paley.
syringa: genus of Old World shrubs or low trees having fragrant flowers in showy panicles: lilacs
syringe: A kind of small hand-pump for throwing a stream of liquid, orfor purposes of aspiration. It consists of a small cylindrical barrel and piston, or a bulb of soft elastic material, with or without valves, and with a nozzle which is sometimes at the end of a flexible tube; used for injecting animal bodies, cleansing wounds, etc. Garden syringe. See Garden.
syringeal: Of or pertaining to the syrinx; as, the syringeal muscle.
syringed: simple past and past participle of syringe
syringin: A glucoside found in the bark of the lilac (Syringa) and extracted as a white crystalline substance; formerly called also lilacin.
syringomyelia: A disorder in which a cyst or cavity forms within the spinal cord, possibly leading to stiffness or paralysis.
syringotomy: The operation of cutting for anal fistula.
syrinx: A wind instrument made of reeds tied together; called also pandean pipes.
syrphid: Of or pertaining to flies of the family Syrphidae.
syrphus: A fly of the genus Syrphus or the family Syrphidae.
syrtis: A quicksand. Quenched in a boggy syrtis, neither sea Nor good dry land. Milton.
syrupy: having a relatively high resistance to flow
systaltic: Capable of, or taking place by, alternate contraction and dilatation; as, the systaltic action of the heart.
system: The collection of staves which form a full score. See Score, n.
systematise: arrange according to a system or reduce to a system
systematist: One who forms a system, or reduces to system.
systematization: The act or operation of systematizing.
systematize: To reduce to system or regular method; to arrange methodically; to methodize; as, to systematize a collection of plants or minerals; to systematize one's work; to systematize one's ideas. Diseases were healed, and buildings erected, before medicine and architecture were systematized into arts. Harris.
systematized: simple past and past participle of systematize
systematizer: One who systematizes. Aristotle may be called the systematizer of his master's doctrines. Harris.
systematizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of systematize
systematizing: present participle and gerund of systematize
systemic: Of or pertaining to the general system, or the body as a whole; as, systemic death, in distinction from local death; systemic circulation, in distinction from pulmonic circulation; systemic diseases. Systemic death. See the Note under Death, n.,.
systemise: arrange according to a system or reduce to a system
systemization: The act or process of systematizing; systematization.
systemize: To reduce to system; to systematize.
systemized: simple past and past participle of systemize
systemizes: third-person singular simple present indicative of systemize
systole: The shortening of the long syllable.
systolic: Of or pertaining to systole, or contraction; contracting; esp.,ralating to the systole of the heart; as, systolic murmur. Dunglison.
syzygium: a tropical evergreen tree of the myrtle family native to the East Indies but cultivated elsewhere
syzygy: The point of an orbit, as of the moon or a planet, at which itis in conjunction or opposition; commonly used in the plural.
t: the th letter of the Roman alphabet
tab: a short strip of material attached to or projecting from something in order to facilitate opening or identifying or handling it
tabanid: Of or pertaining to species of the horsefly family, Tabanidae.
tabard: A sort of tunic or mantle formerly worn for protection from the weather. When worn over the armor it was commonly emblazoned with the arms of the wearer, and from this the name was given to the garment adopted for heralds.
tabaret: A stout silk having satin stripes, used for furniture.
tabasco: a Mexican state on the Gulf of Campeche
tabasheer: A concretion in the joints of the bamboo, which consists largely or chiefly of pure silica. It is highly valued in the East indies as a medicine for the cure of bilious vomitings, bloody flux, piles, and various other diseases.
tabber: A device for applying an adhesive tab.
tabbinet: A fabric like poplin, with a watered surface.
tabby: a cat with a grey or tawny coat mottled with black
tabebuia: Any of the plants in the genus Tabebuia.
tabernacle: To dwell or reside for a time; to be temporary housed.
tabes: Progressive emaciation of the body, accompanied with hectic fever, with no well-marked local symptoms.
tabetic: Of or pertaining to tabes; of the nature of tabes; affected with tabes; tabid. n.
tabla: A pair of tuned hand drums, used in various musical genres of the Indian subcontinent, that are similar to bongos.
table: To insert, as one piece of timber into another, by alternate scores or projections from the middle, to prevent slipping; to scarf.
tableau: a group of people attractively arranged (as if in a painting)
tablebook: A tablet; a notebook. Put into your tablebook whatever you judge worth ly. Dryden.
tablecloth: A cloth for covering a table, especially one with which a table is covered before the dishes, etc., are set on for meals.
tabled: simple past and past participle of table
tableful: As much as fills a table.
tablespoon: A spoon of the largest size commonly used at the table; distinguished from teaspoon, dessert spoon, etc.
tablespoonful: As much as a tablespoon will hold; enough to fill a tablespoon. It is usually reckoned as one half of a fluid ounce, or four fluid drams.
tablet: A kind of pocket memorandum book.
tableting: The manufacture of tablets by compacting a powder using a punch and die; used especially for pharmaceuticals
tabletop: the top horizontal work surface of a table
tableware: Ware, or articles collectively, for table use.
tablinum: An anteroom in a house of ancient Rome, opening out of the atrium opposite the main entry and often containing the family statues and archives.
tabloid: A compressed portion of one or more drugs or chemicals, or of food, etc.
taboo: A total prohibition of intercourse with, use of, or approach to, a given person or thing under pain of death, an interdict of religious origin and authority, formerly common in the islands of polynesia; interdiction.
tabor: A small drum used as an accompaniment to a pipe or fife, both being played by the same person.
taborer: One who plays on the tabor.
taborine: A small, shallow drum; a tabor.
tabula: One of the transverse plants found in the calicles of certain corals and hydroids. Tabula rasa ( Etym:, a smoothed tablet; hence, figuratively, the mind in its earliest state, before receiving impressions from without; a term used by Hobbes, Locke, and others, in maintaining a theory opposed to the doctrine of innate ideas.
tabular: Having the form of, or pertaining to, a table (in any of the uses of the word). Specifically: (a) Having a flat surface; as, a tabular rock.(b) Formed into a succession of flakes; laminated. Nodules. that are tabular and plated. Woodward.
tabularise: arrange or enter in tabular form
tabularium: A central calicle of a coral or hydroid.
tabularization: The act of tabularizing, or the state of being tabularized; formation into tables; tabulation.
tabularized: simple past and past participle of tabularize
tabularizing: present participle and gerund of tabularize
tabulate: shape or cut with a flat surface
tabulated: simple past and past participle of tabulate
tabulating: present participle and gerund of tabulate
tabulation: The act of forming into a table or tables; as, the tabulation of statistics.
tabulator: a calculator that keeps a record of the number of times something happens
tac: A kind of customary payment by a tenant; a word used in old records. Co well. Bur rill.
tacamahac: A bitter balsamic resin or resinous exudation obtained from tropical American trees of the family Burseraceae (Bursera tomentosa and Icica tacamahaca), from East Indian trees of the genus Calophyllum, or from the balsam poplar (Populus balsamifera).
tacana: An ethnic group inhabiting the Beni department of Bolivia.
tacca: genus of tropical plants with creeping rootstocks and small umbellate flowers
tace: The cross, or church, of St. Antony. See Illust., under cross, n. Mol lett.
tach: measuring instrument for indicating speed of rotation
tache: Something used for taking hold or holding; a catch; a loop; abut ton. Ex. xxvi.
tachinid: Any of the family Tachinidae of tachina flies.
tachism: A French style of abstract painting popular in the s and s.
tachiste: An artist working in the style of tachism.
tachograph: A recording or registering tachometer; also, its autographic record.
tachometry: Measurement by a tachometer; the science or use of tachometers.
tachycardia: abnormally rapid heartbeat (over beats per minute)
tachygraphic: Of or relating to tachygraphy; written in shorthand.
tachygraphy: The art or practice of rapid writing; shorthand writing; stenography. I. Taylor (The Alphabet).
tachylyte: A vitreous form of basalt; so called because decompposableby acids and readily fusible.
tachymeter: a theodolite designed for rapid measurements
tachymetry: The science or use of the tachymeter. Tachymetric (#), a.
tachyphemia: rapid speech, often having erratic rhythm and grammar and mixed with irrelevant words.
tachyphylaxis: A rapidly decreasing response to a drug following administration of the initial doses.
tacit: Done or made in silence; implied, but not expressed; silent; as, tacit consent is consent by silence, or by not interposing an objection. Tacitly, adv. The tacit and secret theft of abusing our brother in civil contracts. Jer. Taylor.
tacitly: in a tacit manner; by unexpressed agreement
taciturn: Habitually silent; not given to converse; not apt to talk or speak. Taciturnly, adv.
taciturnity: Habilual silence, or reserve in speaking. The cause of Addison's taciturnity was a natural diffidence in the company of strangers. V. Knox. The taciturnity and the short answers which gave so much offense. Macaulay.
tacitus: Roman historian who wrote major works on the history of the Roman Empire (-)
tack: A peculiar flavor or taint; as, a musty tack. Dray ton.
tacked: simple past and past participle of tack
tacket: A small, broad-headed nail. Jamie son.
tackiness: tastelessness by virtue of being cheap and vulgar
tacking: A union of securities given at different times, all of which must be redeemed before an intermediate purchaser can interpose his claim. Bouvier.
tackle: The rigging and apparatus of a ship; also, any purchase where more than one block is used. Fall and tackle. See the Note under pulley. Fishing tackle. See under Fishing, a. Ground tackle (Naut.), anchors, cables, etc. Gun tackle, the apparatus or appliances for hauling cannon in orout. Tackle fall, the rope, or rather the end of the rope, of atackle, to which the power is applied. Tack tackle (Naut.), a small tackle to pull down the tacks of the principal sails. Tackle board, Tackle post (Ropemaking), a board, frame, or post, at the end of a ropewalk, for supporting the spin dels, or whirls, for twisting the yarns.
tackled: Made of ropes tacked together. My man shall be with thee, And bring thee cords made like a tackled stair.
tackler: a football player who tackles the ball carrier
tackling: Furniture of the masts and yards of a vessel, as cordage, sails, etc.
tacksman: One who holds a tack or lease from another; a tenant, or lessee. Sir W. Scott. The tacksmen, who formed what may be called the peerage of the little community, must be the captains. Macaulay.
tacky: Sticky; adhesive; raw; said of paint, varnish, etc., when not well dried.
tacnode: A point of a curve where two or more osculating circles to the curve at that point are tangent, so that two branches of the curve have ordinary tangency at the double point.
taco: a tortilla rolled cupped around a filling
taconic: Designating, or pertaining to, the series of rocks forming the taconic mountains in Western New England. They were once supposed tobe older than the Cambrian, but later proved to belong to the Lower silurian and Cambrian.
taconite: a variety of chert containing magnetite and hematite; mined as a low-grade iron ore
tactable: Capable of being touched; tangible. Theybeingcreated to be both tractable and tactable. " Mass inger.
tactful: Full of tact; characterized by a discerning sense of what is right, proper, or judicious.
tactfulness: consideration in dealing with others and avoiding giving offense
tactical: of or pertaining to tactic or tactics
tactician: One versed in tactics; hence, a skillful maneuverer; an adroit manager.
tactics: the branch of military science dealing with detailed maneuvers to achieve objectives set by strategy
tactile: Of or pertaining to the organs, or the sense, of touch; perceiving, or perceptible, by the touch; capable of being touched; as, tactile corpuscles; tactile sensations. Tactile sweets. Beaumont. Tactile qualities. " Sir M. Hale. Tactile sense (Physiol.),the sense of touch, or pressure sense. See Touch. The delicacy of the tactile sense varies on different parts of the skin; it is geat est on the forehead, temples and back of the forearm. H. N. Martin.
tactility: The quality or state of being tactile; perceptibility by touch; tangibleness.
taction: The act of touching; touch; contact; tangency. External taction. " Chesterfield.
tactual: Of or pertaining to the sense, or the organs, of touch; derived from touch. In the lowest organisms we have a kind of tactual sense diffused over the entire body. Tyndall.
tactuality: The quality of being tactual (relating to the sense of touch); that which concerns or is characterized by touch.
tad: a slight amount or degree of difference
tadpole: The young aquatic larva of any amphibian. In this stage it breathes by means of external or internal gills, is at first destitute of legs, and has a finlike tail. Called also polliwig, polliwog, por wiggle, or pur wiggy.
tadpolehood: The state or period of being a tadpole.
tael: A denomination of money, in China, worth nearly six shillings sterling, or about a dollar and forty cents; also, a weight of one ounce and a third.
taenia: A genus of intestinal worms which includes the common tapeworms of man. See Tapeworm.
taeniasis: An infection of tapeworms of the genus Taenia that does not usually cause any disease.
taenifuge: A medicine to expel tapeworms from a body.
taffia: Any group of Welsh people who practice nepotism or live in an ethnic enclave.
taffrail: The upper part of a ship's stern, which is flat like a table on the top, and sometimes ornamented with carved work; the rail around a ship's stern.
taffy: chewy candy of sugar or syrup boiled until thick and pulled until glossy
tag: A sale of usually used items (such as furniture, clothing, household items or bric-a-brac), conducted by one or a small group of individuals, at a location which is not a normal retail establishment.
tagalog: a member of a people native to the Philippines chiefly inhabiting central Luzon around and including Manila
tagalong: someone who persistently (and annoyingly) follows along
tagboard: A small message board on a webpage, usually located in the sidebar, where visitors can leave a name and short message.
tagetes: Any plant of the genus Tagetes.
tagged: bearing or marked with a label or tag
tagger: Sheets of tin or other plate which run below the gauge. Knight.
tagging: The act by which something is tagged.
taglioni: A kind of outer coat, or overcoat; said to be so named af tera celebrated Italian family of professional dancers. He ought certainly to exchange his taglioni, or comfortable greatcoat, for a cuirass of steel. Sir W. Scott.
taglock: An entangled lock, as of hair or wool. Nares.
tagmeme: The smallest functional element in the grammatical structure of a sentence.
tagmemics: A theory of discourse that considers context-selected semantically equivalent elements and structures to be different instances of single underlying tagmemes.
tagsore: Adhesion of the tail of a sheep to the wool from excoriation produced by contact with the feces; called also tagbelt.
tagua: The fruit of the tagua palm. When dried, it can be carved like ivory, and is used for beads, buttons, etc.
tagus: a European river; flows into the North Atlantic
tahini: a thick Middle Eastern paste made from ground sesame seeds
tahiti: an island in the south Pacific; the most important island in French Polynesia; made famous by Robert Louis Stevenson and Paul Gauguin
tahitian: Of or pertaining to Tahiti, an island in the Pacific Ocean. n.
tahsil: An administrative division in India and Pakistan.
tai: Designating, or pertaining to, the chief linguistic stock of Indo-China, including the peoples of Siamese and Shan speech.
taiga: A subarctic zone of evergreen coniferous forests situated south of the tundras and north of the steppes in the Northern Hemisphere.
tail: Limitation; abridgment. Bur rill. Estate in tail, a limited, abridged, or reduced fee; an estate limited to certain heirs, and from which the other heirs are precluded; called also estate tail. Black stone.
tailback: (American football) the person who plays tailback
tailboard: The board at the rear end of a cart or wagon, which can be removed or let down, for convenience in loading or unloading.
tailbone: The final fused vertebrae at the base of the spine; the coccyx.
tailcoat: formalwear consisting of full evening dress for men
tailed: Having a tail; having (such) a tail or (so many) tails; chiefly used in composition; as, bobtailed, long tailed, etc. Snouted and tailed like a boar. Grew.
tailer: One who follows or tails surreptitiously, as an investigator.
tailfin: one of a pair of decorations projecting above the rear fenders of an automobile
tailgate: follow at a dangerously close distance
tailing: The part of a projecting stone or brick inserted in a wall. Gwilt.
taille: Any imposition levied by the king, or any other lord, upon his subjects. The taille, as it still subsists in France, may serve as an example of those ancient tallages. It was a tax upon the profits of the farmer, which they estimate by the stock that he has upon the farm. A. Smith.
taillight: lamp (usually red) mounted at the rear of a motor vehicle
tailored: severely simple in line or design
tailoring: The business or the work of a tailor or a tailoress.
tailorlike: Resembling or characteristic of a tailor.
tailpipe: a pipe carrying fumes from the muffler to the rear of a car
tailrace: The channel in which tailings, suspended in water, are conducted away.
tails: formalwear consisting of full evening dress for men
tailskid: A piece of metal or wood used, like a tailwheel, to support the tail of an aircraft on the ground.
tailspin: loss of emotional control often resulting in emotional collapse
tailstock: The sliding block or support, in a lathe, which carries the dead spindle, or adjustable center. The headstock supports the live spindle.
tailwind: wind blowing in the same direction as the path of a ship or aircraft
tailzie: An entailment or deed whereby the legal course of succession iscut off, and an arbitrary one substituted.
taimen: A species of salmon (Hucho taimen), living in Siberia.
tain: Thin tin plate; also, tin foil for mirrors. Knight.
taino: A member of a group of pre-Columbian indigenous inhabitants of the Bahamas, Greater Antilles, and some of the Lesser Antilles.
taint: To thrust ineffectually with a lance.
tainting: present participle and gerund of taint
taintless: Free from taint or infection; pure.
taipan: large highly venomous snake of northeastern Australia
taiping: The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, a rebel state in southern, eastern, and central China during the mid-th century.
taisch: second sight; the involuntary ability of seeing the future or distant events.
tait: A small nocturnal and arboreal Australian marsupial (Tarsipesrostratus) about the size of a mouse. It has a long muzzle, a long tongue, and very few teeth, and feeds upon honey and insects. Called also noolbenger.
taiwan: a government on the island of Taiwan established in by Chia ng Kai-shek after the conquest of mainland China by the Communists led by Mao Zedong
taj: A tall brimless hat, usually conical or curved on top, worn in Muslim countries as a sign of distinction and prestige.
tajik: a native or inhabitant of Tajiki stan and neighboring areas of Uzbekistan and Afghanistan and China
tajiki: the Iranian language of the Tajik that is closely related to Farsi; spoken in Iran and Tajiki stan
tajikistani: of or relating to or characteristic of Tajiki stan or it people or culture
takahe: flightless New Zealand birds similar to gallinules
takedown: (amateur wrestling) being brought to the mat from a standing position
takelma: a member of a North American Indian people of southwestern Oregon
takeout: of or involving food to be taken and eaten off the premises
takeover: a change by sale or merger in the controlling interest of a corporation
taker: One who takes or receives; one who catches or apprehended.
takes: third-person singular simple present indicative of take
taketh: third-person singular simple present indicative of take
takin: large heavily built goat antelope of eastern Himalayan area
taking: Apt to take; alluring; attracting. Subtile in making his temptations most taking. Fuller.
tal: A male given name from Hebrew.
tala: the basic unit of money in Western Samoa
talapoin: A small African monkey (Cercopithecus, or Miopithecus, talapoin) called also mela rhine.
talbot: A sort of dog, noted for quick scent and eager pursuit of game. Wase.
talc: A soft mineral of a soapy feel and a greenish, whitish, or grayish color, usually occurring in foliated masses. It is hydrous silicate of magnesia. Steatite, or soapstone, is a compact granular variety. Indurated talc, an impure, slaty talc, with a nearly compact texture, and greater hardness than common talc; called also talc slate.
talebearer: One who officiously tells tales; one who impertinently or maliciously communicates intelligence, scandal, etc., and makes mischief. Spies and talebearers, encouraged by her father, did their best to inflame her resentment. Macaulay.
talegalla: A genus of Australian birds which includes the brush turkey. See Brush turkey.
talent: a person who possesses unusual innate ability in some field or activity
talented: Furnished with talents; possessing skill or talent; mentally gifted. Abp. Abbot.
tales: Persons added to a jury, commonly from those in or about the courthouse, to make up any deficiency in the number of jurors regularly summoned, being like, or such as, the latter. Blount. Black stone. (b) syntactically sing.
talesman: A person called to make up a deficiency in the number of jurors when a tales is awarded. Wharton.
taliation: Retaliation. Just heav'n this taliation did decree. Beaumont.
talinum: genus of mainly American more-or-less succulent herbs
talipes: The deformity called clubfoot. See Clubfoot.
talipot: A beautiful tropical palm tree (Corypha umbraculifera), anat ive of Ceylon and the Malabar coast. It has a trunk sixty or seventy feet high, bearing a crown of gigantic fan-shaped leaves which are used as umbrellas and as fans in ceremonial processions, and, when cut into strips, as a substitute for writing paper.
talisman: Of or pertaining to a talisman; having the properties of atalisman, or preservative against evils by occult influence; magical.
talismanic: possessing or believed to possess magic power especially protective power
talitha: A female given name from Aramaic of biblical origin.
talkable: Capable of being talked (to or about) (construed with a preposition).
talkativeness: the quality of being wordy and talkative
talked: simple past and past participle of talk
talker: One who talks; especially, one who is noted for his power of conversing readily or agreeably; a conversationist. There probably were never four talkers more admirable in four different ways than Johnson, Burke, Beauclerk, and Garrick. Macaulay.
talkie: a movie with synchronized speech and singing
talking: That talks; able to utter words; as, a talking parrot.
talks: a discussion intended to produce an agreement
tall: A certain rate or tax paid by barons, knights, and inferior tenants, toward the public expenses.
tallage: To lay an impost upon; to cause to pay tallage.
tallageable: On which a tallage must be paid.
tallages: third-person singular simple present indicative of tallage
tallapoosa: river that rises in northwestern Georgia and flows southwest through central Alabama to join the Coosa River near Montgomery and form the Alabama River
tallboy: A kind of long-stemmed wineglass or cup.
taller: comparative form of tall: more tall
tallest: superlative form of tall: most tall
tallied: simple past and past participle of tally
tallit: A traditional Jewish prayer shawl with tassels which covers the chest and upper part of the back.
tallith: An undergarment worn by orthodox Jews, covering the chest and the upper part of the back. It has an opening for the head, and has tassels, called zizith, on its four corners.
tallness: The quality or state of being tall; height of stature.
tallow: obtained from suet and used in making soap, candles and lubricants
tallowy: Of the nature of tallow; resembling tallow; greasy.
tallwood: Firewood cut into billets of a certain length.
tally: To check off, as parcels of freight going inboard or outboard. W. C. Russell. Tally on (Naut.), to dovetail together.
tallyho: The huntsman's cry to incite or urge on his hounds.
tallyman: one who sells goods on the installment plan
tallywoman: A woman who conducts the tally trade.
talma: A kind of large cape, or short, full cloak, forming part of the dress of ladies.
talmud: The body of the Jewish civil and canonical law not comprised in the Pentateuch.
talmudic: Of or relating to the Talmud.
talmudist: One versed in the Talmud; one who adheres to the teachings of the Talmud.
talocalcaneal: Relating to the talus and the calcaneus.
talon: One of certain small prominences on the hind part of the face of an elephant's tooth.
talonic: Of or relating to talonic acid.
talpa: A genus of small insectivores including the common European mole.
talpacoti: The ruddy ground dove, Columbina talpacoti, found from Mexico to Brazil and Argentina.
taluk: A hereditary estate in parts of India; subsequently, an administrative subdivision of a district.
talukdar: An Indian landholder in the Mughal Empire and British Raj, responsible for collecting taxes from a taluk.
tam: a woolen cap of Scottish origin
tama: A form of votive offering in the Eastern Orthodox Church, particularly the Greek Orthodox Church, usually in the form of a small metal plaque with an embossed image symbolizing the subject of prayer for which it is offered.
tamable: Capable of being tamed, subdued, or reclaimed from wildness or savage ferociousness. Tamableness, n.
tamal: Alternative form of tamale (Mexican food dish).
tamale: A Mexican dish made of crushed maize mixed with minced meat, seasoned with red pepper, dipped in oil, and steamed.
tamandu: A small ant-eater (Tamandua tetradactyla) native of the tropical parts of South America.
tamandua: small toothless anteater with prehensile tail and four-clawed forelimbs; of tropical South America and Central America
tamarack: The American larch; also, the larch of Oregon and British Columbia (Larix occidental is). See Hackmatack, and Larch.
tamarao: small buffalo of Mindoro in the Philippines
tamarau: small buffalo of Mindoro in the Philippines
tamaric: A shrub or tree supposed to be the tamarisk, or perhaps some kind of heath. He shall be like tamaric in the desert, and he shall not see when good shall come. Jer. xvii. (Douay version).
tamaricaceae: family of desert shrubs and trees (mostly halophytes and xerophytes)
tamarin: Any one of several species of small squirrel-like South american monkeys of the genus Midas, especially M. urs ulus.
