toparchy: A small state, consisting of a few cities or towns; a petty country governed by a toparch; as, Judea was formerly divided into ten toparchies. Fuller.
topaz: A mineral occurring in rhombic prisms, generally yellowish and pellucid, also colorless, and of gree nesh, bluish, or brownish shades. It sometimes occurs massive and opaque. It is a fluosilicate of alumina, and is used as a gem.
topcross: A hybrid produced by crossing a superior or purebred male with an inferior female.
tope: A mound like Buddhist sepulcher, or memorial monument. often erected over a Buddhi sh relic.
topectomy: The excision of parts of the frontal cortex of the brain, typically for the relief of epilepsy.
topee: a lightweight hat worn in tropical countries for protection from the sun
toper: One who topes, or drinks frequently or to excess; a drunkard; asot.
topful: Full to the top, ore brim; brimfull. Topful of direst cruelty. " was so topful of himself, that he let it spill on all the company. I. Watts.
topgallant: Situated above the topmast and below the royal mast; designatb, or pertaining to, the third spars in order from the deck; as, the topgallant mast, yards, braces, and the like. See Illustration of ship.
tophet: A place lying east or southeast of Jerusalem, in the valley of Hinnom. And he defiled Tophe th, which is in the valley of the children of Hinnom. Kings xxiii.
tophetic: Of or relating to Tophet; hellish; burning.
tophus: One of the mineral concretions about the joints, and in other situations, occurring chiefly in gouty persons. They consist usually of urate of sodium; when occurring in the internal organs they are also composed of phosphate of calcium.
topi: An antelope (Damaliscus corrigum ji mela) having a glossy purplish brown coat. It is related to the blesbok and is native of british East Africa. Also, any of various related varieties of other districts south of the Sahara.
topia: A kind of mural decoration common in Ancient Roman houses, usually featuring landscapes.
topiarian: Of or pertaining to the ornamental cutting and trimming of trees, hedges, etc.; practicing ornamental gardening. The topiarian artist. " Sir W. Scott. All the pedantries of the topiarian art. C. King sley.
topiary: Of or pertaining to ornamental gardening; produced by cutting, trimming, etc.; topiarian. Topiary work, arbors, shrubbery, hedges, or the like, cut and trimmed into fanciful forms, as of animals, building, etc.
topic: A treatise on forms of argument; a system or scheme of forms or commonplaces of argument or oratory; as, the Topics of Aristotle. These topics, or loci, were no other than general ideas applicable to a great many different subjects, which the orator was directed to consult. Blair. In this question by I do not mean a distinct topic, but atranscendent that runs through all topics. Jer. Taylor.
topical: Pertaining to, or consisting of, a topic or topics; according to topics.
topicality: the attribute of being of interest at the present time
topically: In a topical manner; with application to, or limitation of, ap articular place or topic.
topknot: A small Euro pen flounder (Rhoumbus punctatus). The name is also applied to allied species.
topless: Having no top, or no visble fop; hence, fig.: very lofty; supreme; unequaled. " The topless Apennines. " Topless fortunes. Beau. & Fl.
topmaking: The processing of wool into top (bundles of combed slivers with the noils removed).
topman: A man stationed in the top.
topmast: The second mast, or that which is next above the lower mast, and below the topgallant mast.
topminnow: small usually brightly-colored viviparous surface-feeding fishes of fresh or brackish warm waters; often used in mosquito control
topmost: Highest; uppermost; as, the topmost cliff; the topmost branch of a tree. The nightngale may claim the topmost bough. Cowper.
topognosia: recognition of the location of a stimulus on the skin
topography: The description of a particular place, town, manor, parish, or tract of land; especially, the exact and scientific delineation and description in minute detail of any place or region.
topologically: from the point of view of topology
topology: The art of, or method for, assisting the memory by associating the thing or subject to be remembered with some place.
toponym: A name of a place; more broadly, a name, as in the binomial name of a plant, based on, or derived from, a place name, or based on the location of the thing named.
toponymic: Of, relating to, or being a toponym, as:
toponymy: A system of toponyms; the use of toponyms. Toponymal (#),Toponymic (#), Toponymical (#), a.
topos: a traditional theme or motif or literary convention
topped: having a top of a specified character
topper: a worker who makes or adds the top to something
topping: The act of raising one extremity of a spar higher than the other.
topple: To fall forward; to pitch or tumble down. Though castles topple on their warders' heads.
toppled: simple past and past participle of topple
topples: third-person singular simple present indicative of topple
toppling: present participle and gerund of topple
topsail: In a square-rigged vessel, the sail next above the lowermost sail on a mast. This sail is the one most frequently reefed or furled in working the ship. In a fore-and-aft rigged vessel, the sail setup on and above the gaff. See Cutter, Schooner, Sail, and Ship. Topsail schooner. (Naut.) See Schooner, and Illustration in Appendix.
topside: (usually plural) weather deck; the part of a ship's hull that is above the waterline
topsman: The chief drover of those who drive a herd of cattle. P. Cyc.
topsoil: The upper layer of soil; surface soil.
topstone: A stone that is placed on the top, or which forms the top.
topsy: Something or someone who figuratively grows without control or intention.
topwork: To perform a graft on a fruit tree to change it to a more popular or profitable cultivar.
toque: A variety of the bonnet monkey.
torah: the whole body of the Jewish sacred writings and tradition including the oral tradition
toran: A gateway consisting of two upright pillars carrying one to three transverse lintels, often minutely carved with symbolic sculpture, and serving as a monumental approach to a Buddhist temple.
torbanite: A variety of coal, derived from colonial algae, that resembles carbonaceous shale.
torbernite: A mineral occurring in emerald-green tabular crystals having amicaceous structure. It is a hydrous phosphate of uranium and copper. Called also copper uranite, and chalcolite.
torch: A light or luminary formed of some combustible substance, as of resinous wood; a large candle or flambeau, or a lamp giving a large, flaring flame. They light the nuptial torch. Milton. Torch thistle. (Bot.) See under Thistle.
torchbearer: One whose office it is to carry a torch.
torcher: One who gives light with a torch, or as if with a torch.
torchlit: Lit by one or more torches.
torchy: Having the character of a torch song.
torero: a matador or one of the supporting team during a bull fight
toreumatography: A description of sculpture such as bas-relief in metal.
torment: An engine for casting stones. Sir T. Elyot.
tormented: experiencing intense pain especially mental pain
tormenter: a flat at each side of the stage to prevent the audience from seeing into the wings
tormentil: A rosaceous herb (Potentilla Tormentilla), the root of which is used as a powerful astringent, and for alleviating gripes, or tormina, in diarrhea.
tormenting: Causing torment; as, a tormenting dream. Tormentingly, adv.
tormentor: An implement for reducing a stiff soil, resembling a harrow, but running upon wheels. He bert.
tormentress: A woman who torments. Fortune ordinarily cometh after to whip and punish them, as the scourge and tormentress of glory and honor. Holland.
torments: third-person singular simple present indicative of torment
tormentum: An ancient engine for hurling missiles.
tornado: A violent whirling wind; specifically (Meteorol.), a tempest distinguished by a rapid whirling and slow progressive motion, usually accompaned with severe thunder, lightning, and torrents of rain, and commonly of short duration and small breadth; a small cyclone.
tornaria: The peculiar free swimming larva of Balanoglossus. See Illust.in Append.
tornillo: shrub or small tree of southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico having spirally twisted pods
tornus: The bottom corner of a wing.
toroid: the doughnut-shaped object enclosed by a torus
toroidal: of or relating to or shaped like a toroid; doughnut shaped
toronto: the provincial capital and largest city in Ontario (and the largest city in Canada)
torose: Cylindrical with alternate swellings and contractions; having the surface covered with rounded prominences.
torosity: The quality or state of being torose.
torpedinous: Of or pertaining to a torpedo; resembling a torpedo; exerting abe numbing influence; stupefying; dull; torpid. Fishy were his eyes; torpedinous was his manner. De Quincey.
torpedo: Any one of numerous species of elasmobranch fishes belonging to torpedo and allied genera. They are related to the rays, but have the power of giving electrical shocks. Called also crampfish, and numbfish. See Electrical fish, under Electrical.
torpedoed: simple past and past participle of torpedo
torpedoman: A person in charge of the torpedoes on a military vessel.
torpescent: Becoming torpid or numb. Shen stone.
torpid: Having lost motion, or the power of exertion and feeling; numb; benumbed; as, a torpid limb. Without heat all things would be torpid. Ray.
torpidness: The qualityy or state of being torpid.
torpify: To make torpid; to numb, or benumb.
torpitude: Torpidness. In a kind of torpitude, or sleeping state. Derham.
torpor: a state of motor and mental inactivity with a partial suspension of sensibility
torque: That which tends to produce torsion; a couple of forces. J.Thomson.
torquer: A magnetic device that generates torque.
torques: A cervical ring of hair or feathers, distinguished by its color or structure; a collar.
torrefaction: The act or process of torrefying, or the state of being torrefied. Bp. Hall.
torrefied: simple past and past participle of torrefy
torrefy: To subject to scorching heat, so as to drive off volatile ingredients; to roast, as ores.
torrefying: present participle and gerund of torrefy
torrent: Rolling or rushing in a rapid stream. Waves of torrent fire. Milton.
torrential: relating to or resulting from the action of a torrent
torricelli: Italian physicist who invented the mercury barometer (-)
torricellian: Of or pertaining to Torricelli, an Italian philosopher and mathematician, who, in, discovered that the rise of a liquid in a tube, as in the barometer, is due to atmospheric pressure. See barometer. Torricellian tube, a glass tube thirty or more inches in length, open at the lower end and hermetically sealed at the upper, such as is used in the barometer. Torricellian vacuum (Physics), a vacuum produced by filling with a fluid, as mercury, a tube hermetically closed at one end, and, after immersing the other end in a vessel of the same fluid, allowing the inclosed fluid to descend till it is counterbalanced by the pressure of the atmosphere, as in the barometer. Hutton.
torridness: The quality or state of being torrid or parched.
torsade: A twisted cord; also, a molded or worked ornament of similar form.
torsel: A plate of timber for the end of a beam or joist to rest on. Gwilt
torsion: That force with which a thread, wire, or rod of any material, returns, or tends to return, to a state of rest after it has been twisted; torsibility. Angle of torsion (of a curve) (Geom.), the indefinitely small angle between two consecutive osculating planes of a curve of double curvature. Moment of torsion (Mech.) the moment of a pair of equal and opposite couples which tend to twist a body. Torsion balance (Physics.), an instrument for estimating very minute forces, as electric or magnetic attractions and repulsions, by the torsion of a very slender wire or fiber having at its lower extremity a horizontal bar or needle, upon which the forces act. Torsion scale, a scale for weighing in which the fulcra of the levers or beams are strained wires or strips acting by torsion.
torsional: Of or pertaining to torsion; resulting from torsion, or the force with which a thread or wire returns to a state of rest after having been twisted round its axis; as, torsional force.
torso: The human body, as distinguished from the head and limbs; insculpture, the trunk of a statue, mutilated of head and limbs; as, the torso of Hercules.
tort: Any civil wrong or injury; a wrongful act (not involving ab reach of contract) for which an action will lie; a form of action, in some parts of the United States, for a wrong or injury. Executor de son tort. See under Executor. Tort feasor (Law), a wrongdoer; a trespasser. Wharton.
torta: a flat heap of moist, crushed silver ore, prepared for the patio process.
torte: rich cake usually covered with cream and fruit or nuts; originated in Austria
torteau: A roundel of a red color.
tortfeasor: a party who has committed a tort
tortilla: An unleavened cake, as of maize flour, baked on a heated iron or stone.
tortoise: Any one of numerous species of reptiles of the order testudinata.
tortoiseshell: the mottled horny substance of the shell of some turtles
tortoni: Any of several sorts of ice-cream flavoured with rum or sherry, often containing chopped cherries and topped with almonds, crumbled macaroons, etc.
tortuosity: a tortuous and twisted shape or position
tortuous: Oblique; applied to the six signs of the zodiac (from capricorn to Gemini) which ascend most rapidly and obliquely. Skeat. Infortunate ascendent tortuous. Chaucer.Tortuously, adv. Tortuousness, n.
tortured: experiencing intense pain especially mental pain
torturous: Involving, or pertaining to, torture. The torturous crucifixion. " I. Disraeli.
torula: A chain of special bacteria. (b) A genus of budding fungi. Same as Saccharomyces. Also used adjectively.
torulaform: Having the appearance of a torula; in the form of a little chain; as, a torulaform string of micrococci.
toruloid: Minutely torose; shaped like a small torus.
torus: A lage molding used in the bases of columns. Its profile is semicircular. See Illust. of Molding. Br ande&C.
torved: Stern; grim. See Torvous. But yesterday his breath Awed Rome, and his least torved frown was death. J. Webster.
torvous: Sour of aspect; of a severe countenance; stern; grim. That torvous, sour look produced by anger. Derham.
tory: A member of the conservative party, as opposed to the progressive party which was formerly called the Whig, and is now called the Liberal, party; an earnest supporter of ex sisting royal and ecclesiastical authority.
tosk: the dialect of Albanian spoken in southern Albania and in areas of Greece and Italy
tossed: simple past and past participle of toss
tossing: The act of throwing upward; a rising and falling suddenly; a rolling and tumbling.
tosspot: A toper; one habitually given to strong drink; a drunkard.
tossy: Tossing the head, as in scorn or pride; hence, proud; contemptuous; scornful; affectedly indifferent; as, a tossy commonplace. C. King sley.
tosto: Quick; rapid. Pui tosto ( Etym:(Mus.), faster; more rapid.
tot: a small amount (especially of a drink)
total: Whole; not divided; entire; full; complete; absolute; as, atotal departure from the evidence; a total loss. " Total darkness. "To undergo myself the total crime. " Milton. Total abstinence. See abstinence, n.,. Total depravity. (Theol.) See Original sin, under Original.
totalism: the principle of complete and unrestricted power in government
totalitarian: characterized by a government in which the political authority exercises absolute and centralized control
totalitarianism: the principle of complete and unrestricted power in government
totality: the quality of being complete and indiscriminate
totalizator: A machine for registering and indicating the number and nature of bets made on horse races, as in Australia and South Africa. Called also totalizer.
totalize: To make total, or complete; to reduce to completeness. Coleridge.
totalized: simple past and past participle of totalize
totalizing: present participle and gerund of totalize
totalled: simple past and past participle of total
totaller: That which counts items to produce a total.
totalling: present participle and gerund of total
totally: In a total manner; wholly; entirely.
totaquina: A quinine derivative used to treat malaria, consisting of a minimum of % crystallizable alkaloids, of which at least % are quinine, and with not more than % amorphous alkaloids.
totara: A coniferous tree (Podocarpus totara), next to the kauri the most valuable timber tree of New Zel and. Its hard reddish wood is used for furniture and building, esp. in wharves, bridges, etc. Also mahogany pine.
tote: To carry or bear; as, to tote a child over a stream; acolloquial word of the Southern States, and used esp. by negroes.
toted: simple past and past participle of tote
totem: A rude picture, as of a bird, beast, or the like, used by then ord American Indians as a symbolic designation, as of a family or aclan. And they painted on the grave posts Of the graves, yet unforgotten, Each his own ancestral totem Each the symbol of his household; Figures of the bear and reindeer, Of the turtle, crane, and beaver. Longfellow. The totem, the clan deity, the beast or bird who in some supernatural way attends to the clan and watches over it. Bagehot.
totemic: Of or pertaining to a totem, or totemism.
totemism: belief in the kinship of a group of people with a common totem
totemist: One belonging to a clan or tribe having a totem. Totemistic, a.
totemite: A member of a totemic group; a totemist.
toter: The stone roller. See Stone roller (a), under Stone.
totipalmate: Having all four toes united by a web;-said of certain seabirds, as the pelican and the gannet. See Illust. under Aves.
totipalmi: A division of swimming birds including those that have totipalmate feet.
totipotency: the ability of a cell to give rise to unlike cells and so to develop a new organism or part
totipotent: having the ability to give rise to unlike cells
totoaba: The marine fish Totoaba macdonaldi, the largest member of the drumfish family Sciaenidae, endemic to the Gulf of California, Mexico.
totonac: A member of a people who resided in the eastern coastal and mountainous regions of Mexico at the time of the Spanish arrival in, and who now reside in the states of Veracruz, Puebla, and Hidalgo.
totten: A surname transferred from the nickname.
totter: move without being stable, as if threatening to fall
tottering: unsteady in gait as from infirmity or old age
tottery: Trembling or vaccilating, as if about to fall; unsteady; shaking. Johnson.
totty: Unsteady; dizzy; tottery. Sir W. Scott. For yet his noule was totty of the must. Spenser.
touch: To be tangent to. See Tangent, a.
touchable: Capable of being touched; tangible. Touchableness, n.
touchback: The act of touching the football down by a player behind hi sown goal line when it received its last impulse from an opponent; distinguished from safety touchdown.
touchdown: The act of touching the football down behind the opponents'goal. Safety touchdown. See under Safety.
toucher: a person who causes or allows a part of the body to come in contact with someone or something
touchhole: The vent of a cannot or other firearm, by which fire iscommunicateed to the powder of the charge.
touching: Affecting; moving; pathetic; as, a touching tale. Touchingly, adv.
touchline: either of the sidelines in soccer or rugby
touchstone: Lydian stone; basanite; so called because used to test the purity of gold and silver by the streak which is left upon the stone when it is rubbed by the metal. See Basanite.
touchwood: Wood so decayed as to serve for tinder; spunk, or punk.
touchy: Peevish; irritable; irascible; techy; apt to take fire. It may be said of Dryden that he was at no time touchy about personal attacks. Saints bury.
tough: not given to gentleness or sentimentality
toughen: To grow or make tough, or tougher.
tougher: comparative form of tough: more tough
toughie: a particularly difficult or baffling question or problem
toughness: The quality or state of being tough.

toupee: a small hairpiece to cover partial baldness
toured: simple past and past participle of tour
tourer: large open car seating four with folding top
touring: Working for a short time in different places.
tourism: the business of providing services to tourists
tourist: One who makes a tour, or performs a journey in a circuit.

Black tourmaline (schorl) is the most common variety, but there are also other varieties, as the blue (indicolite), red (rubellite), also green, brown, and white. The red and green varieties when transparent are valued as jewels.
tournai: A city in Hainaut, Wallonia, Belgium.
tournament: a sporting competition in which contestants play a series of games to decide the winner

tours: an industrial city in western France on the Loire River
tousle: To put into disorder; to tumble; to touse.
tout: One who secretly watches race horses which are in course of training, to get information about their capabilities, for use in betting.
touter: One who seeks customers, as for an inn, a public conveyance, shops, and the like: hence, an obtrusive candidate for office. The prey of ring droppers,. duffers, touters, or any of those bloodless sharpers who are, perhaps, better known to the police. Dickens.
tovarish: Comrade, especially with reference to the former USSR.
tow: The coarse and broken part of flax or hemp, separated from the finer part by the hatchel or swingle.
toward: Approaching; coming near. His toward peril. " Spenser.
towardliness: The quality or state of being towardly; docility; tractableness. The beauty and towardliness of these children moved her brethren to envy. Sir W. Raleigh.
towardly: Same as Toward, a.,.He's towardly and will come on apace. Dryden.
towaway: The process of towing away a vehicle.
towboat: A vessel constructed for being towed, as a canal boat.
towed: simple past and past participle of tow
toweling: Cloth for towels, especially such as is woven in long pieces tobe cut at will, as distinguished from that woven in towel length swith borders, etc.
towelling: any of various fabrics (linen or cotton) used to make towels
tower: To rise and overtop other objects; to be lofty or very high; hence, to soar. On the other side an high rock towered still. Spenser. My lord protector's hawks do tower so well.
towered: Adorned or defended by towers. Towered cities please us then. Milton.
towering: Very high; elevated; rising aloft; as, a towering height. Pope.
towerman: a person employed in a railroad switch tower to control and direct the movement of cars and trains.
towery: Having towers; adorned or defended by towers. Towery cities. " Pope.
towhead: a person with light blond hair
towie: The Only Way Is Essex, a television reality show based in Essex, England.
towing: present participle and gerund of tow
towline: A line used to tow vessels; a towrope.
town: an urban area with a fixed boundary that is smaller than a city
townee: townsman unacquainted with country life especially a slick and flashy male city dweller
townhall: A public hall or building, belonging to a town, where the public offices are established, the town council meets, the people assemble in town meeting, etc.
townhouse: A building devoted to the public used of a town; a townhall.
townie: resident of a college town not affiliated with the college
townify: To turn into a town, or adapt for a town; to make urban.
townish: Of or pertaining to the inhabitants of a town; like the town. Turbervile.
townlet: A small town. North Brit. Rev.
townlike: Resembling or characteristic of a town.
townsend: United States social reformer who proposed an old-age pension sponsored by the federal government; his plan was a precursor to Social Security (-)
townsfolk: The people of a town; especially, the inhabitants of a city, indistinction from country people; townspeople.
township: an administrative division of a county
townsman: a person from the same town as yourself
townspeople: The inhabitants of a town or city, especially in distinction from country people; townsfolk.
townswoman: A woman who is a resident of a town, especially of one's own town.
townwear: Everyday clothing suitable for wearing in a town, as opposed to activewear.
towny: resident of a college town not affiliated with the college
towpath: A path traveled by men or animals in towing boats; called also towing path.
towrope: A rope used in towing vessels.

toyer: One who toys; one who is full of trifling tricks; a trifler.

traceable: Capable of being traced. Traceableness, n. Tracea/bly, adv.
traced: simple past and past participle of trace
tracer: One who, or that which, traces.
tracery: Ornamental work with rambled lines. Especially: (a) The decorative head of a Gothic window.
tracey: A surname from Old French, a spelling variant of Tracy.

tractableness: the trait of being easily persuaded

tractarianism: The principles of the Tractarians, or of those persons accepting the teachings of the Tracts for the Times. "

tractile: Capable of being drawn out in length; ductile. Bacon.

tractive: Serving to draw; pulling; attracting; as, tractive power.

tracy: United States film actor who appeared in many films with Katharine Hepburn (-)
trademarked: (of goods and merchandise) labeled with proprietary (and legally registered) identification guaranteeing exclusive use
tradeoff: an exchange that occurs as a compromise

tradesmanlike: Resembling or characteristic of a tradesman.

traducianism: The doctrine that human souls are produced by the act of generation; opposed to creationism, and infusionism.
traducianist: One who subscribes to the religious theory of traducianism.
traducing: present participle and gerund of traduce

tragopogon: genus of Old World herbs with linear entire leaves and yellow or purple flower heads
tragus: The prominence in front of the external opening of the ear. See illust. under Ear.

trailed: simple past and past participle of trail
trailer: One who, or that which, trails.
trailing: a. & vb. n. from Trail. Trailing arbutus. (Bot.) See under arbutus. trailsman: A person skilled in outdoor survival on the trail.

Cowper.

trainer: one who trains other persons or animals

traipse: To walk or run about in a slatternly, careless, or thoughtless manner. Pope.
trait: a distinguishing feature of your personal nature
traiteur: The keeper of an eating house, or restaurant; a restaurateur. Simmon ds.

trammed: simple past and past participle of tram

tramway: a conveyance that transports passengers or freight in carriers suspended from cables and supported by a series of towers
tramwayman: A man who works on a tramway.

trangram: Something intricately contrived; a contrived; a puzzle. Arbuthnot.
trank: An oblong piece of skin from which the pieces for a glove are cut.

Called also Trematoda, and Trematoid ea. See Fluke, Tristoma, and Cercaria.
trematoid: f or pertaining to the Trematodea. See Illustration in appendix.
tremble: An involuntary shaking or quivering. I am all of a tremble when I think of it. W. Black.
trembles: disease of livestock and especially cattle poisoned by eating certain kinds of snakeroot
trembling: Shaking; tottering; quivering. Tremblingly, adv. Trembling poplar (Bot.), the aspen.
trembly: In a trembling or shaking state
tremellaceae: a family of basidiomycetous fungi of the order Tremellales that have the basidium divided longitudinally
tremellales: fungi varying from gelatinous to waxy or even horny in texture; most are saprophytic
tremendous: Fitted to excite fear or terror; such as may astonish or terrify by its magnitude, force, or violence; terrible; dreadful; as, a tremendous wind; a tremendous shower; a tremendous shock or fall. A tremendous mischief was a foot. Motley.
tremex: A genus of large hymenopterous insects allied to the sawflies. The female lays her eggs in holes which she bores in the trunks of trees with her large and long ovipositor, and the larva bores in the wood. See Illust. of Horntail.
tremolite: A white variety of amphibole, or hornblende, occurring in long, bladelike crystals, and coarsely fibrous masses.
tremolo: (music) a tremulous effect produced by rapid repetition of a single tone or rapid alternation of two tones
tremor: A trembling; a shivering or shaking; a quivering or vibratory motion; as, the tremor of a person who is weak, infirm, or old. He fell into an universal tremor of all his joints. Harvey.
tremulous: Shaking; shivering; quivering; as, a tremulous limb; a tremulous motion of the hand or the lips; the tremulous leaf of the poplar.
trench: To fortify by cutting a ditch, and raising a rampart or breastwork with the earth thrown out of the ditch; to intrench. Pope. No more shall trenching war channel her fields.
trenchant: Fitted to trench or cut; gutting; sharp. " Trenchant was the blade. " Chaucer.
trencherman: a person who is devoted to eating and drinking to excess
trenching: present participle and gerund of trench
trenchmore: A kind of lively dance of a rude, boisterous character. Also, music in triple time appropriate to the dance. All the windows in the town dance new trenchmore. Beau. & Fl.
trend: To have a particular direction; to run; to stretch; to tend; as, the shore of the sea trends to the southwest.
trendiness: The state or quality of being trendy.
trending: present participle and gerund of trend
trendle: A wheel, spindle, or the like; a trundle. The shaft the wheel, the wheel, the trendle turns. Sylvester.
trendy: in accord with the latest fad
trent: a river in central England that flows generally northeastward to join with the Ouse River and form the Humber
trental: An office and mass for the dead on the thirtieth day afterdeath or burial. Their trent als and their shrifts. " Spenser.
trento: a city in northern Italy (northwest of Venice) on the River Adige; the site of the Council of Trent
trenton: capital of the state of New Jersey; located in western New Jersey on the Delaware river
trepan: A crown-saw or cylindrical saw for perforating the skull, turned, when used, like a bit or gimlet. See Trephine.
trepanation: The practice of drilling a hole in the skull as a physical, mental, or spiritual treatment.
trepanned: simple past and past participle of trepan
trepanner: One who trepans. " Pitiful trepanners and impostors. " Gaud en.
trepanning: present participle and gerund of trepan
trephine: An instrument for trepanning, being an improvement on the trepan. It is a circular or cylindrical saw, with a handle like that of a gimlet, and a little sharp perforator called the center pin.
trephining: present participle and gerund of trephine
trepidation: A libration of the starry sphere in the Ptolemaic system; amotion ascribed to the firmament, to account for certain small changes in the position of the ecliptic and of the stars.
treponema: spirochete that causes disease in humans (e.g. syphilis and yaws)
tres: A three-course stringed instrument similar to a guitar; the Cuban variant has six strings, and the Puerto Rican has nine.
tresayle: A grandfather's grandfather. Writ of tresayle (O. Eng. Law), a writ which lay for a man claiming as heir to his grandfather's grandfather, to recover lands of which he had been deprived by an abatement happening on the ancestor's death. Mozley &W.
trespass: To commit a trespass; esp., to enter unlawfully upon the land of another.
trespassed: simple past and past participle of trespass
trespasser: One who commits a trespass; as:(a) (Law) One who enters upon another's land, or violates his rights.(b) A transgressor of the moral law; an offender; a sinner.
trespassing: gradually intrusive without right or permission
tress: A braid, knot, or curl, of hair; a ringlet. Her yellow hair was braided in a tress. Chaucer. Fair tresses man's imperial race insnare. Pope.
tressure: A kind of border similar to the orle, but of only half the breadth of the latter.
tressured: Provided or bound with a tressure; arranged in the form of atressure. The tressured fleur-de-lis he claims To wreathe his shield. Sir W.Scott.
trestle: a supporting tower used to support a bridge
trestlework: A viaduct, pier, scaffold, or the like, resting on trestles connected together.
tret: d pers. sing. pres. of Tread, for tread eth. Chaucer.
tretable: Tractable; moderate. By nature debonaire and tretable. Chaucer.
trevally: Any of certain fishes of the family Carangidae, especially of the genera Caranx and Pseudocaranx.
trevelyan: English historian and son of Sir George Otto Trevelyan whose works include a social history of England and a biography of Garibaldi (-)
trevet: A stool or other thing supported by three legs; a trivet.
trews: Trowsers; especially, those of the Scotch Highlanders. He wore the trews, or close trowsers, made of tartan. " Sir W. Scott.
trey: Three, at cards, dice, or dominoes; a card, die, or domino of three spots or pips. Seven is my chance and thine is cinq and trey. Chaucer.
triable: Liable to undergo a judicial examination; properly coming under the cognizance of a court; as, a cause may be triable before one court which is not triable in another.
triac: A three-terminal electronic component that conducts current in either direction when triggered; a bidirectional triode thyristor.
triacid: Capable of neutralizing three molecules of a monobasic acid or the equivalent; having three hydrogen atoms which may be acid radicals; said of certain bases; thus, glycerin is a triacid base.
triad: An element or radical whose valence is three. Triads of the welsh bards, poetical histories, in which the facts recorded are grouped by threes, three things or circumstances of a kind being mentioned together. Hindoo triad. See Trimurti.
triadic: Having the characteristics of a triad; as, boron is triadic.
triage: sorting and allocating aid on the basis of need for or likely benefit from medical treatment or food
trial: The formal examination of the matter in issue in a cause beforea competent tribunal; the mode of determining a question of fact in acourt of law; the examination, in legal form, of the facts in issue in a cause pending before a competent tribunal, for the purpose of determining such issue.
trialism: A union of three states or political entities.
triamide: An amide containing three amido groups.
triamine: An amine containing three amido groups.
triandrian: Of or relating to the former Triandria; having three distinct and equal stamens in the same flower.
triangle: A figure bounded by three lines, and containing three angles.
triangulate: composed of or marked with triangles
triangulates: third-person singular simple present indicative of triangulate
triangulation: The series or network of triangles into which the face of acountry, or any portion of it, is divided in a trigonometrical survey; the operation of measuring the elements necessary to determine the triangles into which the country to be surveyed is supposed to be divided, and thus to fix the positions and distances of the several points connected by them.
triangulum: a small northern constellation near Perseus between Andromeda and Aries
trianon: Either of the Grand Trianon and Petit Trianon, two royal palaces constructed in Versailles, France, in the th and th centuries.
triarchy: Government by three persons; a triumvirate; also, a country under three rulers. Holland.
trias: The formation situated between the Permian and Lias, and so named by the Germans, because consisting of three series of strata, which are called in German the Bunter sand stein, Muschelkalk, and keuper.
triassic: Of the age of, or pertaining to, the Trias. n.
triatic: A term used in the phrase triatic stay. See under Stay.
triatomic: Having three atoms; said of certain elements or radicals.
triaxon: A triaxonal spicule of a sponge.
triazine: any of three isomeric compounds having three carbon and three nitrogen atoms in a six-membered ring
triazole: Either of two isomeric heterocyclic compounds having a five-membered ring with three nitrogen atoms and two double bonds in the ring; any organic derivative of these compounds.
trib: To sexually stimulate one's vulva against another person's; to scissor.
tribadism: a form of lesbianism that simulates heterosexual intercourse
tribal: Of or pertaining to a tribe or tribes; as, a tribal scepter. Bp. War burton.
tribally: In a tribal manner or context.
tribasic: Capable of neutralizing three molecules of a monacid base, or their equivalent; having three hydrogen atoms capable of replacement by basic elements on radicals; said of certain acids; thus, citric acid is a tribasic acid.
tribe: A number of species or genera having certain structural characteristics in common; as, a tribe of plants; a tribe of animals.
tribesman: someone who lives in a tribe
tribespeople: The people who belong to a tribe.
tribeswoman: A female member of a tribe.
triblet: A tapering cylinder used in metalcraft, usually made of steel, used to expand or measure a ring or hole in another piece of metal up to a desired size.
tribology: the branch of engineering that deals with the interaction of surfaces in relative motion (as in bearings or gears): their design and friction and wear and lubrication
triboluminescence: The production of light by friction.
tribual: Of or relating to a tribe; tribal.
tribulation: That which occasions distress, trouble, or vexation; severe affliction. When tribulation or persecution arise th because of the word, by andby he is offended. Matt. xiii.In the world ye shall have tribulation. John. xvi.
tribulus: annual or perennial herbs or subshrubs of warm regions
tribunal: The seat of a judge; the bench on which a judge and his associates sit for administering justice.
tribunary: Of or pertaining to tribunes; as, tribunary powers or authority.
tribune: An officer or magistrate chosen by the people, to protect them from the oppression of the patricians, or nobles, and to defend their liberties against any attempts that might be made upon them by the senate and consuls.
tribuneship: The office or power of a tribune.
tributary: (of a stream) flowing into a larger stream
tribute: A certain proportion of the ore raised, or of its value, given to the miner as his recompense. Pryce. Tomlinson. Tribute money, money paid as a tribute or tax. Tribute pitch. (Mining) See under Tributer.
tributer: One who works for a certain portion of the ore, or its value.
trica: An apothecium in certain lichens, having a spherical surface marked with spiral or concentric ridges and furrows.
tricalcium: Three atoms of calcium in a chemical compound.
trice: To haul and tie up by means of a rope.
tricenary: Of or related to the number thirty.
tricennial: Of or pertaining to thirty years; consisting of thirty years; occurring once in every thirty years.
tricentennial: of or relating to or completing a period of years
triceps: A muscle having three heads; specif., the great extensor of the forearm, arising by three heads and inserted into the olecranon at the elbow.
triceratops: huge ceratopsian dinosaur having three horns and the neck heavily armored with a very solid frill
tricerion: A candlestick with three lights, signifying the trinity.
trichechus: type and sole genus of the Trichechidae
trichiasis: A disease of the eye, in which the eyelashes, being turned in upon the eyeball, produce constant irritation by the motion of the lids.
trichinella: Any of the genus Trichinella of parasitic roundworms.
trichinized: simple past and past participle of trichinize
trichion: point where the hairline meets the midpoint of the forehead
trichite: A kind of crystallite resembling a bunch of hairs, common in obsidian. See Illust. of Crystallite.
trichiurid: Any member of the Trichiuridae; a cutlassfish.
trichiurus: A genus of fishes comprising the hair tails. See Hairtail.
trichloride: A chloride having three atoms of chlorine in the molecule.
trichloroacetic: Of or pertaining to trichloroacetic acid or its derivatives
trichloroethylene: a heavy colorless highly toxic liquid used as a solvent to clean electronic components and for dry cleaning and as a fumigant; causes cancer and liver and lung damage
trichoclasis: A brittle condition of the hair.
trichogramma: Any of the tiny insect-egg-parasitizing wasps in the genus Trichogramma, which are widely used as for biological control.
trichogyne: The slender, hairlike cell which receives the fertilizing particles, or antherozoids, in red seaweeds. Trichogynic, a.
trichology: The science or study of hair.
tricholoma: agarics with white spores and a fleshy stalk and notched gills; of various colors both edible and inedible
trichomanes: Any fern of the genus Trichomanes. The fronds are very delicate and often translucent, and the sporangia are borne on threadlike receptacles rising from the middle of cup-shaped marginal involucres. Several species are common in conservatories; two are native in the united States.
trichome: A hair on the surface of leaf or stem, or any modification of ahair, as a minute scale, or star, or gland. The sporangia of ferns are believed to be of the nature of trichomes. Trichomatous, a.
trichomonad: cause of trichomoniasis in women and cattle and birds
trichophyton: a genus of fungus of the family Moniliaceae; causes ringworm and favus
trichoptera: A suborder of Neuroptera usually having the wings covered with minute hairs. It comprises the caddice flies, and is considered by some to be a distinct order.
trichostema: genus of North American aromatic herbs or subshrubs: blue curls
trichotomous: Divided into three parts, or into threes; three-forked; as, atrichotomous stem. Martyn.
trichroism: The quality possessed by some crystals of presenting different colors in three different directions.
trichromacy: the normal ability to see colors
trichromat: One who has trichromatic vision; one whose vision exhibits trichromacy; one who can distinguish three primary colors.
trichromatic: Having or existing in three different phases of color; having three distinct color varieties; said of certain birds and insects.
trichuriasis: infestation by a roundworm; common in tropical areas with poor sanitation
tricipital: Having three heads, or three origins; as, a tricipital muscle.
trick: The whole number of cards played in one round, and consisting of as many cards as there are players. On one nice trick depends the general fate. Pope.
tricked: simple past and past participle of trick
trickery: The art of dressing up; artifice; stratagem; fraud; imposture.
trickish: Given to tricks; artful in making bargains; given to deception and cheating; knavish. Trickishly, adv. Trickishness, n.
trickle: To flow in a small, gentle stream; to run in drops. His salt tears trickled down as rain. Chaucer. Fast beside there trickled softly down A gentle stream. Spenser.
trickled: simple past and past participle of trickle
trickling: present participle and gerund of trickle
trickster: One who tricks; a deceiver; a tricker; a cheat.
tricksy: Exhibiting artfulness; trickish. My tricksy spirit!" he tricksy policy which in the seventeenth century passed for state wisdom. Coleridge.
tricky: Given to tricks; practicing deception; trickish; knavish.
triclad: Any of the turbellarian flatworms of order Tricladida.
triclinic: Having, or characterized by, three unequal axes intersecting at oblique angles. See the Note under crystallization.
triclinium: a dining room (especially a dining room containing a dining table with couches along three sides)
tricolor: a flag having three colored stripes (especially the French flag)
tricorn: cocked hat with the brim turned up to form three points
tricorne: cocked hat with the brim turned up to form three points
tricot: A fabric of woolen, silk, or cotton knitted, or women to resemble knitted work.
tricrotic: Of or pertaining to tricrotism; characterized by tricrotism.
tricrotism: That condition of the arterial pulse in which there is a triple beat. The pulse curve obtained in the sphygmographic tracing characteristic of tricrotism shows two secondary crests in addition to the primary.
tricurvate: Curved in three directions; as, a tricurvate spicule (see illust. of Spicule).
tricuspid: Of or pertaining to the tricuspid valves; as, tricuspid obstruction. Tricuspid valve (Anat.), the valve, consisting of three triangular membranous flaps, at the opening of the right auricle into the right ventricle in the heart of most mammals; sometimes called the tricuspid valves, each flap being regarded as a valve.
tricuspidate: Three-pointed; ending in three points; as, a tricuspidate leaf.
tricycle: A three-wheeled velocipede. See Illust. under Velocipede. Cf. Bicycle.
tricyclic: an antidepressant drug that acts by blocking the reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin and thus making more of those substances available to act on receptors in the brain
tricyclist: A person who rides a tricycle.
tridacna: A genus of very large marine bivalve shells found on the coral reefs of the Indian and Pacific Oceans. One species (T. gigas) often weighs four or five hundred pounds, and is sometimes used for baptismal fonts. Called also paw shell, and fountain shell.
tridactyl: Having three digits on a limb.
tride: Short and ready; fleet; as, a tride pace; a term used by sportsmen. Bailey.
tridecane: A hydrocarbon, CH, of the methane series, which is aprobable ingredient both of crude petroleum and of kerosene, and is produced artificially as a light colorless liquid.
tridecene: Any aliphatic hydrocarbon having a chain of thirteen carbon atoms and containing one double bond.
trident: A kind of scepter or spear with three prongs, the common attribute of Neptune.
tridented: Having three prongs; trident; tridentate; as, a tridented mace. Quarles.
tridentine: Of or pertaining to Trent, or the general church council held in that city.
tridimensional: Having three dimensions; extended in three different directions.
triduum: A period of three days (especially in Roman Catholic liturgy).
tried: imp. & p. p. of Try. Also adj.
triene: Any alkene that has three double bonds
triennial: Something which takes place or appears once in three years.
triens: A Roman copper coin, equal to one third of the as. See d As,.
trier: A person appointed according to law to try challenges of jurors; a trior. Bur rill.
trierarchy: The office duty of a trierarch.
trifallow: To plow the third time before sowing, as land. Mortimer.
trifid: Cleft to the middle, or slightly beyond the middle, into three parts; three-cleft.
trifle: To act or talk without seriousness, gravity, weight, or dignity; to act or talk with levity; to indulge in light or trivial amusements. They trifle, and they beat the air about nothing which touche th us. Hooker. To trifle with, to play the fool with; to treat without respect or seriousness; to mock; as, to trifle with one's feelings, or with sacred things.
trifled: simple past and past participle of trifle
trifling: Being of small value or importance; trivial; paltry; as, at rifling debt; a trifling affair. Triflingly, adv. Triflingness, n.
triflorous: Having or bearing three flowers or blooms.
trifluctuation: A concurrence of three waves. A trifluctuation of evils. " Sir T. Browne.
trifluoride: any chloride containing three fluorine atoms in each molecule
trifoliate: (of a leaf shape) having three leaflets
trifolium: A genus of leguminous herbs with densely spiked flowers and usually trifoliate leaves; trefoil. There are many species, all of which are called clover. See Clover.
trifoly: Sweet trefoil. She was crowned with a chaplet of trifoly. B. Jonson.
triforium: The gallery or open space between the vaulting and the roof of the aisles of a church, often forming a rich arcade in the interior of the church, above the nave arches and below the clearstory windows.
triform: Having a triple form or character. This triform antagonism. I. Taylor. Goddess Triform, I own thy triple spell. Lowell.
trig: To fill; to stuff; to cram. Dr. H. More.
trigeminal: Of, pertaining to, or designating, the fifth pair of cranial nerves, which divide on each side of the head into three main branches distributed to the orbits, jaws, and parts of the mouth; trifacial.
trigeminus: the main sensory nerve of the face and motor nerve for the muscles of mastication
triggered: Having a trigger that reacts to some specific condition.
triggerfish: any of numerous compressed deep-bodied tropical fishes with sandpapery skin and erectile spines in the first dorsal fin
triggering: present participle and gerund of trigger
triglidae: in some classifications restricted to the gurnards and subdivided into the subfamilies Triglinae (true sea robins) and Peristediinae (armored sea robins)
triglochin: perennial or annual bog or marsh plants; includes arrow grass
triglyceride: A glyceride formed by the replacement of three hydrogen atoms in glycerin by acid radicals.
triglyph: An ornament in the frieze of the Doric order, repeated at equal intervals. Each triglyph consists of a rectangular tablet, slightly projecting, and divided nearly to the top by two parallel and perpendicular gutters, or channels, called glyphs, into three parts, or spaces, called femora. A half channel, or glyph, is also cut upon each of the perpendicular edges of the tablet. See Illust. of entablature.
triglyphic: Consisting of, or relating to, triglyphs.
trigness: The quality or state of being trig; smartness; neatness. Their spars had no man-of-war trigness. Kane.
trigon: The cutting region of the crown of an upper molar, usually the anterior part. That of a lower molar is the Trigonid.
trigonal: Having three angles, or corners; triangular; as, a trigonal stem, one having tree prominent longitudinal angles.
trigone: A smooth triangular area on the inner surface of the bladder, limited by the apertures of the ureters and urethra.
trigonella: Old World genus of frequently aromatic herbs
trigonid: The shearing end of a tribosphenic molar.
trigonocephaly: A congenital condition of premature fusion of the metopic suture leading to a triangular-shaped forehead.
trigonometric: of or relating to or according to the principles of trigonometry
trigonometrical: Of, pertaining to, or obtained using trigonometry
trigonometry: the mathematics of triangles and trigonometric functions
trigrammatic: Containing three letters or characters, or three sets of letters or characters.
trigraph: Three letters united in pronunciation so as to have but one sound, or to form but one syllable, as -ieu in adieu; a triphthong.
trihedral: Having three sides or faces; thus, a trihedral angle is a soli dangle bounded by three plane angles.
trihydrate: A hydrate whose solid contains three molecules of water of crystallization per molecule, or per unit cell.
trijet: An aircraft powered by three jet engines.
trijugate: In three pairs; as, a trijugate leaf, or a pinnate leaf with three pairs of leaflets.
trikaya: A fundamental doctrine within Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism that delineates the multidimensional nature of a Buddha's existence in three distinct bodies or aspects.
trilateral: Having three sides; being three-sided; as, a trilateral triangle. Trilaterally, adv. Trilateralness, n.
trilby: singer in a novel by George du Mauri er who was under the control of the hypnotist Svengali
trilingual: Containing, or consisting of, three languages; expressed in three languages. The much-noted Rosetta stone. bears upon its surface atrilingual inscription. I. Taylor.
triliteral: Consisting of three letters; trigrammic; as, a triliteral root or word. n.
trilithon: A monument consisting of three stones; especially, such amonument forming a kind of doorway, as among the ancient Celts.
trill: To flow in a small stream, or in drops rapidly succeeding each other; to trickle. Sir W. Scott. And now and then an ample tear trilled down Her delicate cheek. Whispered sounds Of waters, trilling from the riven stone. Glover.
triller: A small passerine bird of the genus Lalage belonging to the cuckooshrike family Campephagidae, so called because of the loud trilling calls of the male birds.
trilliaceae: small family of herbs having flowers with petals and sepals; in some classification systems considered a subfamily of the Liliaceae
trilling: A compound crystal, consisting of three individuals.
trillion: According to the French notation, which is used upon the continent generally and in the United States, the number expressed by a unit with twelve ciphers annexed; a million millions; according to the English notation, the number produced by involving a million to the third power, or the number represented by a unit with eighteen ciphers annexed. See the Note under Numeration.
trillionth: the ordinal number of one trillion in counting order
trillium: A genus of liliaceous plants; the three-leaved nightshade; so called because all the parts of the plant are in threes.
trillo: A trill or shake. See Trill.
trilobita: An extinct order of arthropods comprising the trilobites.
trilobite: Any one of numerous species of extinct arthropods belonging to the order Trilobita. Trilobites were very common in the Silurian and devonian periods, but became extinct at the close of the Paleozoic. So named from the three lobes usually seen on each segment.
trilobitic: Of, pertaining to or containing, trilobites; as, trilobitic rocks.
trilocular: Having three cells or cavities; as, a trilocular capsule; atrilocular heart.
trilogical: Pertaining to or organized into a trilogy.
trilogy: A series of three dramas which, although each of them is in ones ense complete, have a close mutual relation, and form one historical and poetical picture. Shakespeare's " Henry VI. " is an example. On the Greek stage, a drama, or acted story, consisted in reality of three dramas, called together a trilogy, and performed consecutively in the course of one day. Coleridge.
trim: To dress, as timber; to make smooth.
trimaran: a fast sailboat with parallel hulls
trimer: a polymer (or a molecule of a polymer) consisting of three identical monomers
trimera: A division of Coleoptera including those which have but three joints in the tarsi.
trimeric: Of or pertaining to a trimer
trimesic: Of or pertaining to trimesic acid or its derivatives.
trimesitic: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a tribasic acid, CH.(CO), of the aromatic series, obtained, by the oxidation of mesitylene, as a white crystalline substance.
trimester: A term or period of three months.
trimestrial: Of or pertaining to a trimester, or period of three months; occurring once in every three months; quarterly.
trimetallism: The use of a monetary standard based upon three different metals, typically gold, silver, and copper.
trimeter: Consisting of three poetical measures. n.
trimethoxy: Three methoxy groups in a molecule
trimethyl: (Chem.) A prefix or combining form (also used adjectively) indicating the presence of three methyl groups.
trimethylamine: A colorless volatile alkaline liquid, N.(CH), obtained from herring brine, beet roots, etc., with a characteristic herringlike odor. It is regarded as a substituted ammonia containing three methyl groups.
trimethylbenzene: Any of three isomeric chemical compounds:,-trimethylbenzene,,-trimethylbenzene (pseudocumene), and,-trimethylbenzene (mesitylene).
trimethylene: A gaseous hydrocarbon, CH, isomeric with propylene and obtained from it indirectly. It is the base of a series of compounds analogous to the aromatic hydrocarbons.
trimethylglycine: An organic compound related to choline, with the difference that the terminal carboxylic acid group of trimethylglycine has been reduced to a hydroxyl group in choline.
trimmed: made neat and tidy by trimming
trimmer: A beam, into which are framed the ends of headers in floor framing, as when a hole is to be left for stairs, or to avoid bringing joists near chimneys, and the like. See Illust. of Header.
trimming: a. from Trim, v. The Whigs are, essentially, an inefficient, trimming, halfway sort of a party. Jeffrey. Trimming joist (Arch.), a joist into which timber trimmers are framed; a header. See Header. Knight.
trimmings: the accessories that normally accompany (something or some activity)
trimness: The quality or state of being trim; orderliness; compactness; snugness; neatness.
trimorph: A substance which crystallizes in three distinct forms, or which has three distinct physical states; also, any one of these distinct forms. See Trimorphism,.
trimorphism: The property of crystallizing in three forms fundamentally distinct, as is the case with titanium dioxide, which crystallizes in the forms of rutile, octahedrite, and brookite. See Pleomorphism.
trimorphous: trimorphic; having, or relating to, three forms
trimotor: That has three motors, especially an aircraft with three piston engines.
trimurti: The triad, or trinity, of Hindoo gods, consisting of Brahma, the Creator, Vishnu, the Preserver, and Siva, the Destroyer.
trinal: Threefold. Trinal unity. " Milton. In their trinal triplicities on high. Spenser.
trine: Threefold; triple; as, trine dimensions, or length, breadth, and thickness.
trinervate: Having three ribs or nerves extending unbranched from the base to the apex; said of a leaf. Gray.
tringa: A genus of limicoline birds including many species of sandpipers. See Dunlin, Knot, and Sandpiper.
trinidad: an island in West Indies just off the northeastern coast of Venezuela
trining: present participle and gerund of trine
trinitarian: Of or pertaining to the Trinity, the doctrine of the Trinity, or believers in that doctrine.
trinitarianism: The doctrine of the Trinity; the doctrine that there are three distinct persons in the Godhead.
trinitro: Three nitro groups in a compound
trinitrobenzene: Any derivative of benzene containing three nitro groups, but especially the explosive,-trinitrobenzene.
trinitrocresol: Any of several isomeric trinitro derivatives of cresol; the commercial mixture was once used as an antiseptic
trinitroglycerin: a heavy yellow poisonous oily explosive liquid obtained by nitrating glycerol
trinitrotoluene: explosive consisting of a yellow crystalline compound that is a flammable toxic derivative of toluene
trinity: The union of three persons (the Father, the Son, and the Holy ghost) in one Godhead, so that all the three are one God as to substance, but three persons as to individuality.
triniunity: Triunity; trinity. As for terms of trinity, triniunity,. and the like, they reject them as scholastic notions. Milton.
trinket: A three-cornered sail formerly carried on a ship's foremast, probably on a lateen yard. Sailing always with the sheets of mainsail and trinket warily in our hands. Hakluyt.
trinketry: Ornaments of dress; trinkets, collectively. No trinketry on front, or neck, or breast. Southey.
trinodal: Having three knots or nodes; having three points from which aleaf may shoot; as, a trinodal stem.

trinovantes: A Celtic tribe of pre-Roman Britain, holding territory on the north side of the Thames estuary in current Essex and Suffolk.
trio: Of the value of three oboli; hence, mean; worthless. It may pass current. for a trio bolar ballad. Ch eyne.
triobol: An ancient coin worth three obols.
trioctile: An aspect of two planets with regard to the earth when they are three octants, or three eighths of a circle, that is, degrees, distant from each other. Hutton.
triode: a thermionic vacuum tube having three electrodes; fluctuations of the charge on the grid control the flow from cathode to anode which makes amplification possible
triodia: Any grass of the genus Triodia native to Australia.
trioecious: Having three sorts of flowers on the same or on different plants, some of the flowers being staminate, others pistillate, and others both staminate and pistillate; belonging to the order trioecia.
triolet: A short poem or stanza of eight lines, in which the first line is repeated as the fourth and again as the seventh line, the second being, repeated as the eighth. Br ande & C.
trionychoid: Any of the Trionychoidea, a group of turtles.
trionychoidea: A division of chelonia ns which comprises Trionyx and allied genera; called also Trionychoid es, and Trionychina.
trionyx: A genus of fresh-water or river turtles which have the shell imperfectly developed and covered with a soft leathery skin. They are noted for their agility and rapacity. Called also soft tortoise, soft-shell tortoise, and mud turtle.
triose: any monosaccharide sugar containing three atoms of carbon per molecule
trioxide: An oxide containing three atoms of oxygen; as, sulphur trioxide, SO; formerly called tritoxide.
trip: To release, let fall, or see free, as a weight or compressed spring, as by removing a latch or detent.
tripack: Film that has three emulsions sensitive to red, green, or blue stacked on top of one another.
tripalmitate: A palmitate derived from three molecules of palmitic acid.
triparted: Parted into three piece; having three parts or pieces; said of the field or of a bearing; as, a cross triparted.
tripe: lining of the stomach of a ruminant (especially a bovine) used as food
tripeptide: An organic compound formed from three amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
tripery: A place where tripe is prepared or sold. London Quart. Rev.
triphase: Of, pertaining to, or having three phases
triphosphate: Any salt or ester containing three phosphate groups.
triphthong: A combination of three vowel sounds in a single syllable, forming a simple or compound sound; also, a union of three vowel characters, representing together a single sound; a trigraph; as, eye, -ieu in adieu, -eau in beau, are examples of triphthongs.
triphylite: A mineral of a grayish-green or bluish color, consisting of the phosphates of iron, manganese, and lithia.
tripinnate: Having bipinnate leaflets arranged on each side of a rhachis.
tripinnatifid: Thrice pinnately cleft; said of a pinnatifid leaf when its segments are pinnatifid, and the subdivisions of these also are pinnatifid.
triplane: Composed of, or relating to, three planes (flat surfaces extending infinitely in all directions).
triple: To make threefold, or thrice as much or as many; to treble; as, to triple the tax on coffee.
tripled: simple past and past participle of triple
tripletail: large food fish of warm waters worldwide having long anal and dorsal fins that with a caudal fin suggest a three-lobed tail
triplex: Having three principal operative parts or motions, so as to produce a three-fold effect.
triplicate: Made thrice as much; threefold; tripled. Triplicate ratio (Math.), the ratio of the cubes of two quantities; thus, the triplicate ratio of a to b is a: b.
triplice: A defensive military alliance between Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy, formed on May and renewed periodically until.
triplicity: The quality or state of being triple, or threefold; trebleness. In their trinal triplicities on high. Spenser.
triplite: A mineral of a dark brown color, generally with a fibrous, massive structure. It is a fluophosphate of iron and manganese.
triploid: of a cell or organism having three complete sets of chromosomes
triplopia: An ophthalmologic or neurologic condition where one perceives three images.
tripod: a three-legged rack used for support
tripody: Three metrical feet taken together, or included in one measure.
tripoli: An earthy substance originally brought from Tripoli, used in polishing stones and metals. It consists almost wholly of the siliceous shells of diatoms.
tripoline: Of or pertaining to Tripoli or its inhabitants; Tripolitan.
tripolitan: Of or pertaining to Tripoli or its inhabitants; Tripoline. n.
tripos: final honors degree examinations at Cambridge University
tripped: simple past and past participle of trip
tripper: (slang) someone who has taken a psychedelic drug and is undergoing hallucinations
trippet: A cam, wiper, or projecting piece which strikes another piece repeatedly.
tripping: Having the right forefoot lifted, the others remaining on the ground, as if he were trotting; trippant; said of an animal, as ahart, buck, and the like, used as a bearing.
trippingly: In a tripping manner; with a light, nimble, quick step; with agility; nimbly. Sing, and dance it trippingly. Speak the speech. trippingly on the tongue.
trips: The Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights.
tripsome: Characterised or marked by tripping (light stepping); light-footed; nimble
triptych: Anything in three parts or leaves. Specifically: (a) A writing tablet in three parts, two of which fold over on the middle part.(b) A picture or altarpiece in three compartments.
tripudiary: Of or pertaining to dancing; performed by dancing. Tripudiary augurations. " Sir T. Browne.
tripudium: A solemn religious dance of the Ancient Romans, performed in triple time.
triquadrantal: Having three quadrants; thus, a triquadrantal triangle is one whose three sides are quadrants, and whose three angles are consequently right angles.
triquetrous: Three sided, the sides being plane or concave; having three salient angles or edges; trigonal.
triquetrum: One of the bones of the carpus; the cuneiform. See Cuneiform (b).
triradiate: Having or consisting of three rays; radiating in three directions from a central point; three-rayed, trifurcate.
triradius: A group of three ridges forming a Y shape at the base of each finger on the palm of the hand.
trireme: An ancient galley or vessel with tree banks, or tiers, of oars.
trisagion: An ancient anthem, usually known by its Latin name tersanctus. See Tersanctus.
trisect: To cut or divide into three equal parts.
trisecting: present participle and gerund of trisect
trisection: The division of a thing into three parts, Specifically: (Geom.) the division of an angle into three equal parts.
trisects: third-person singular simple present indicative of trisect
trisetum: Any of various grasses of the genus Trisetum.
triskaidekaphobia: a morbid fear of the number
triskele: a figure consisting of three stylized human arms or legs (or three bent lines) radiating from a center
triskelion: a figure consisting of three stylized human arms or legs (or three bent lines) radiating from a center
trisnitrate: A nitrate formed from three molecules of nitric acid; also, less properly, applied to certain basic nitrates; as, trisnitrate of bismuth.
trisoctahedron: A solid of the isometric system bounded by twenty-four equal faces, three corresponding to each face of an octahedron. Tetragonal trisoctahedron, a trisoctahedron each face of which is aquadrilateral; called also trapezohedron and icositetrahedron. Trigonal trisoctahedron, a trisoctahedron each face of which is an isosceles triangle.
trisome: A chromosome which is represented three times instead of the usual two.
trisomic: Having three copies of a given chromosome in each somatic cell instead of the usual number of two
trisomy: chrosomal abnormality in which there is one more than the normal number of chromosomes in a cell
trispast: A machine with three pulleys which act together to raise great weights.
trispermous: Containing three seeds; three-seeded; as, a trispermous capsule.
tristan: (Middle Ages) the nephew of the king of Cornwall who (according to legend) fell in love with his uncle's bride (Iseult) after they mistakenly drank a love potion that left them eternally in love with each other
tristeza: A damaging viral disease of citrus plants, caused by Closterovirus.
tristful: Sad; sorrowful; gloomy. Eyes so tristful, eyes so tristful, Heart so full of care and cumber. Longfellow.
tristimulus: A set of three stimuli, especially the red, green and blue components of colour vision.
tristoma: Any one of numerous species of trematode worms belonging to tristoma and allied genera having a large posterior sucker and twos mall anterior ones. They usually have broad, thin, and disklike bodies, and are parasite on the gills and skin of fishes.
tristram: A male given name from the Celtic languages, variant of Tristan.
trisula: A trident, seen as a religious symbol of Hinduism and Buddhism.
trisulc: Something having three forks or prongs, as a trident. Jupiter's trisulc. " Sir T. Browne.
trisulcate: Having three furrows, forks, or prongs; having three grooves or sulci; three-grooved.
trisulfate: Any compound containing three sulfate groups or ions
trisulphide: A sulphide containing three atoms of sulphur.
trit: The ternary equivalent of a bit; a fundamental unit of information that may take any of three distinct states.
tritangent: A line that is tangent to a curve at three points.

tritheism: The opinion or doctrine that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three distinct Gods.
trithing: One of three ancient divisions of a county in England; now called riding. Black stone.
trithionic: Of or pertaining to, or designating, a certain thionic acid, HSO which is obtained as a colorless, odorless liquid.
tritical: Trite. T. Wart on. Tritically, adv. Triticalness, n.
triticum: A genus of grasses including the various species of wheat.
tritium: a radioactive isotope of hydrogen; atoms of tritium have three times the mass of ordinary hydrogen atoms
tritocerebrum: The third set of fused ganglia comprising the insect brain.
tritoma: A flowering plant of the genus Kniphofia.
triton: A fabled sea demigod, the son of Neptune and Amphitrite, and the trumpeter of Neptune. He is represented by poets and painters as having the upper part of his body like that of a man, and the lower part like that of a fish. He often has a trumpet made of a shell. Have sight of Proteus rising from the sea, Or hear old Triton blow his wreathed horn. Wordsworth.
tritonia: Any of the genus Tritonia of flowering plants in the iris family.
tritonymph: The instar between deutonymph and adult in some organisms.
tritoxide: trioxide; the third of a series of oxides of a particular metal
tritubercular: Having or designating teeth with three cusps or tubercles; tricuspid.
trituberculy: A theory of the development of mammalian molar teeth. The primitive stage is that of simple cones, as in reptiles. The simple cone then developed a smaller cone in front and another behind. Next, a cingulum was developed, and the three cones became arranged in atriangle, the two smaller cusps having moved to the outer side in upper and to the inner in lower molars. This primitive triangle is called the trigon or trigonid and this stage the tritubercular or trigonodont. The trigon being a cutting apparatus, an extension of the posterior part of the crown was developed in lower molars for crushing, and a smaller corresponding part appeared in upper molars. Another large cone then arose, usually from the cingulum. In more complex forms, smaller intermediate cusps appeared.
triturate: To rub, grind, bruise, or thrash.
triturating: present participle and gerund of triturate

triture: A rubbing or grinding; trituration. Ch eyne.
triturium: A vessel for separating liquids of different densities.
triumph: A magnificent and imposing ceremonial performed in honor of agen eral who had gained a decisive victory over a foreign enemy.

triumphancy: The quality of being triumphant; triumph.
triumphing: Having or celebrating a triumph; victorious; triumphant. Triumphingly, adv.
triumvir: One of tree men united in public office or authority.
triumvirate: a group of three men responsible for public administration or civil authority
triune: Being three in one; an epithet used to express the unity of a trinity of persons in the Godhead.
triungulin: The first-instar planidial larva of certain species of parasitoidal beetle; so named because the triungulin has three claws on each foot.
triunity: The quality or state of being triune; trinity. Dr. H. More.
trivalence: The quality or state of being trivalent.

trivet: a three-legged metal stand for supporting a cooking vessel in a hearth

trivialism: A trivial matter or method; a triviality. Carlyle.

trivium: The three anterior ambulacra of echinoderms, collectively.
triweekly: Occurring or appearing three times a week; thrice weekly; as, atriweekly newspaper. adv.
trix: A female given name, variant of Trixie.
trixie: A diminutive of the female given names Beatrix or Beatrice.
trizone: The combination of the American, British and French occupation zones in Germany after World War II.
troak: To barter or trade, especially outside a government monopoly.

trochaic: A trochaic verse or measure. Dryden.
trochanter: One of two processes near the head of the femur, the outer being called the great trochanter, and the inner the small trochanter.
troche: A medicinal tablet or lozenge; strictly, one of circular form.
trochee: A foot of two syllables, the first long and the second short, as in the Latin word ante, or the first accented and the second unaccented, as in the English word motion; a choreus.
trochid: Any sea snail of the family Trochidae.
trochil: The crocodile bird. The crocodile. opens his chaps to let the trochil in to pick his teeth, which gives it the usual feeding. Sir T. Herbert.
trochilic: OF or pertaining to rotary motion; having power to draw out or turn round. By art trochilic. " Camden.
trochilus: An annular molding whose section is concave, like the edge of apulley; called also scotia.
trochiscus: A kind of tablet or lozenge; a troche.

Cycloids, epi cycloids, hypo cycloids, cardioids, etc., are all trochoids.
trochoidal: Of or pertaining to a trochoid; having the properties of atrochoid.

trock: A genre of music produced by fans of the British science-fiction television series Doctor Who, characterized by lyrics about its characters, settings, and plot elements.
troctolite: A rare type of ultramafic intrusive rock, consisting primarily of olivine and calcic plagioclase
trode: imp. of Tread. On burnished hooves his war-horse trode. Tennyson.
troffer: A rectangular, trough-shaped light fixture, typically for mounting in or on a ceiling to light the area below, and usually containing two or three fluorescent bulbs.
troglodytes: A genus of apes including the chimpanzee.
troglodytic: Of or pertaining to troglodytes, or dwellers in caves.
troika: a Russian carriage pulled by three horses abreast
troilite: Native iron protosulphide, Fe S. It is known only in meteoric irons, and is usually in imbedded nodular masses of a bronze color.
troilus: A large, handsome American butterfly (Euphoeades, or Papilio, troilus). It is black, with yellow marginal spots on the front wings, and blue spots on the rear wings.

trolley: a wheeled vehicle that runs on rails and is propelled by electricity
trolling: angling by drawing a baited line through the water
trollius: perennial herbs of north temperate regions: globe flowers
trollop: A stroller; a loiterer; esp., an idle, untidy woman; asl attern; a slut; a whore.
trombone: A powerful brass instrument of the trumpet kind, thought by some to be the ancient sackbut, consisting of a tube in three parts, bent twice upon itself and ending in a bell. The middle part, bent double, slips into the outer parts, as in a telescope, so that by change of the vibrating length any tone within the compass of the instrument (which may be bass or tenor or alto or even, in rare instances, soprano) is commanded. It is the only member of the family of wind instruments whose scale, both diatonic and chromatic, is complete without the aid of keys or pistons, and which can slide from note to note as smoothly as the human voice or a violin. Softly blown, it has a rich and mellow sound, which becomes harsh and blatant when the tones are forced; used with discretion, its effect is often solemn and majestic.
trombonist: a musician who plays the trombone
trommel: A revolving buddle or sieve for separating, or sizing, ores. Raymond.
tromometer: An instrument for measuring slight earthquake shocks.

trona: A native double salt, consisting of a combination of neutral and acid sodium carbonate, NaCO.HNa CO.HO, occurring as a white crystalline fibrous deposit from certain soda brine springs and lakes; called also urao, and by the ancients nitrum.

trooping: present participle and gerund of troop

trophesy: Malnourishment due to a disorder of the nervous system.

trophied: Adorned with trophies. The trophied arches, storied halls, invade. Pope.

trophophore: The sterile part of a fern's leaf, as opposed to the sporophore.

trophy: A sign or memorial of a victory raised on the field of battle, or, in case of a naval victory, on the nearest land. Sometimes trophies were erected in the chief city of the conquered people.
tropic: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid obtained from atropine and certain other alkaloids, as a white crystalline substance slightly soluble in water.
tropical: Rhetorically changed from its exact original sense; being of the nature of a trope; figurative; metaphorical. Jer. Taylor. Tropic year, the solar year; the period occupied by the sun in passing from one tropic or one equinox to the same again, having amean length of days, hours, minutes,. seconds, which is minutes,. seconds shorter than the sidereal year, on account of the precession of the equinoxes.
tropicalize: To modify something (such as electronic equipment) for use in the tropics, especially by making it resistant to heat and humidity
tropicalizing: present participle and gerund of tropicalize
tropicbird: mostly white web-footed tropical seabird often found far from land
tropics: the part of the Earth's surface between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn
tropin: any of the tropic hormones; one that is secreted by an endocrine gland and targets another such gland
tropine: A white crystalline alkaloid, CHNO, produced by decomposing atropine.
tropism: Modification of the direction of growth.
tropological: Relating to or involving the interpretation of literature focusing on the ethical lesson or moral of the story.
tropologize: To use in a tropological sense, as a word; to make a trope of. If. Minerva be tropologized into prudence. Cud worth.
tropologized: simple past and past participle of tropologize
tropology: A rhetorical mode of speech, including tropes, or changes from the original import of the word. Sir T. Browne.

troposphere: the lowest atmospheric layer; from to miles high (depending on latitude)
troppo: Too much; as, allegro ma non troppo, brisk but not too much so.

troth: Belief; faith; fidelity. Bid her alight And hert roth plight.
trothless: Fait less; false; treacherous. Thrall to the faithless waves and trothless sky. Fair fax.
trotline: a long fishing line with many shorter lines and hooks attached to it (usually suspended between buoys)
trotsky: Russian revolutionary and Communist theorist who helped Lenin and built up the army; he was ousted from the Communist Party by Stalin and eventually assassinated in Mexico (-)
trotted: simple past and past participle of trot
trotter: foot of a pig or sheep especially one used as food
trottoir: Footpath; pavement; sidewalk. Headless bodies trailed along the trottoirs. Froude.

troublemaker: someone who deliberately stirs up trouble

troubles: The continued violence and terrorist, military and paramilitary activity in Northern Ireland that happened from the mid s to the late s.
troubleshooter: a worker whose job is to locate and fix sources of trouble (especially in mechanical devices)

troublous: Full of trouble; causing trouble. In doubtful time of troublous need. " Byron. A tall ship tossed in troublous seas. Spenser.

trounced: simple past and past participle of trounce
trounces: third-person singular simple present indicative of trounce
troupe: A company or troop, especially the company pf performers in aplay or an opera.
