whom: The objective case of who. See Who.
whomever: Whatever person or persons (as object of verb or preposition).
whomsoever: The objective of whosoever. See Whosoever. The Most High rule th in the king dow of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will. Dan. iv.
whoo: An expression of delight and excitement.
whooplike: Resembling or characteristic of a whooping sound.
whooshing: present participle and gerund of whoosh
whopper: a gross untruth; a blatant lie
whore: A woman who practices unlawful sexual commerce with men, especially one who prostitutes her body for hire; a prostitute; aharlot. Wyclif.
whoredom: The sin of worshiping idols; idolatry. O Ephraim, thou commit test whoredom, and Israel is defiled; they will not. turn unto their God. Hos. v.,.
whorehouse: a building where prostitutes are available
whoremonger: A whoremaster; a lecher; a man who frequents the society of whores.
whoremongering: The behaviour of a whoremonger; lewd licentiousness; pimping.
whoreson: A bastard; colloquially, a low, scurvy fellow; used generally in contempt, or in coarse humor. Also used adjectively.
whorish: Resembling a whore in character or conduct; addicted to unlawful pleasures; incontinent; lewd; unchaste. Whorishly, adv. Whorishness, n.
whorl: A circle of two or more leaves, flowers, or other organs, about the same part or joint of a stem.
whorled: Furnished with whorls; arranged in the form of a whorl or whorls; verticillate; as, whorled leaves.
whort: The whortleberry, or bilberry. See Whortleberry (a).
whortle: The whortleberry, or bilberry.looked ahead of him from behind a tump of whortles. R. D.Black more.
whortleberry: In England, the fruit of Vaccinium Myrt illus; also, the plant itself. See Bilberry,.
whose: The possessive case of who or which. See Who, and Which. Whose daughter art thou tell me, I pray thee. Gen. xxiv.The question whose solution I require. Dryden.
whoso: Whosoever. Piers Plowman. Whoso shrinks or falters now,. Brand the craven on his brow!Whittier.
whosoever: Whatsoever person; any person whatever that; whoever. Whosoever will, let him take. freely. Rev. xxii.
whurry: To whisk along quickly; to hurry. Whurry ing the chariot with them to the shore. Vicars.
wi: Abbreviation of Wisconsin: a state of the United States.
wicca: a community of followers of the Wicca religion
wichitas: A tribe of Indians native of the region between the Arkansas and Red rivers. They are related to the Pawnees. See Pawnees.
wick: A bundle of fibers, or a loosely twisted or braided cord, tape, or tube, usually made of soft spun cotton threads, which by capillary attraction draws up a steady supply of the oil in lamps, the melted tallow or wax in candles, or other material used for illumination, in small successive portions, to be burned. But true it is, that when the oil is spent The light goes out, and wick is thrown away. Spenser.
wicked: Having a wick; used chiefly in composition; as, a two-wicked lamp.
wickedly: In a wicked manner; in a manner, or with motives and designs, contrary to the divine law or the law of morality; viciously; corruptly; immorally. I have sinned, and I have done wickedly. Sam. xxiv.
wickedness: The quality or state of being wicked; departure from the rules of the divine or the moral law; evil disposition or practices; immorality; depravity; sinfulness. God saw that the wickedness of man was great. Gen. vi. Their inward part is very wickedness. Ps. v.

wickerwork: A texture of osiers, twigs, or rods; articles made of such atexture.
wicket: The space between the pillars, in post and-stall working. Raymond. Wicket door, Wicket gate, a small door or gate; a wicket. See def., above. Bunyan. Wicket keeper (Cricket), the player who stands behind the wicket to catch the balls and endeavor to put the batsman out.
wicking: the material of which wicks are made; esp., a loosely braided or twisted cord or tape of cotton.
wickiup: a lodge consisting of a frame covered with matting or brush; used by nomadic American Indians in the southwestern United States
widdy: A rope or halter made of flexible twigs, or withes, as of birch.
widen: To make wide or wider; to extend in breadth; to increase the width of; as, to widen a field; to widen a breach; to widen astocking.
widened: simple past and past participle of widen
widener: Any device used to widen something; especially a drill designed to produce a hole greater than its own diameter.
wideness: the property of being wide; having great width
widens: third-person singular simple present indicative of widen
wider: comparative form of wide: more wide
widespread: Spread to a great distance; widely extended; extending far and wide; as, widespread wings; a widespread movement.
widest: superlative form of wide: most wide

The common european widgeon (Anas penelope) and the American widgeon (A.Americana) are the most important species. The latter is called also baldhead, baldpate, bald face, baldcrown, smoking duck, wheat, duck, and whitebelly. Bald-faced, or Green-headed, widgeon, the American widgeon. Black widgeon, the European tufted duck. Gray widgeon. (a) The gadwall. (b) The pintail duck. Great headed widgeon, the poachard. Pied widgeon. (a) The poachard. (b) The goosander. Saw-billed widgeon, the merganser. Sea widgeon. See in the Vocabulary. Spear widgeon, the goosander. Spoonbilledwidgeon, the shoveler. White widgeon, the smew. Wood widgeon, the wood duck.
widget: a device or control that is very useful for a particular job
widowed: single because of death of the spouse
widower: A man who has lost his wife by death, and has not married again.
widowerhood: The state of being a widower.
widowhood: the time of a woman's life when she is a widow
widowman: a man whose wife is dead especially one who has not remarried
width: The quality of being wide; extent from side to side; breadth; wideness; as, the width of cloth; the width of a door.
widthways: widthwise The direction of the width of an object or place.
widthwise: directed across the width of an object or place.
wieldance: The act or power of wielding. Our weak wieldance. " Bp. Hall.
wielded: simple past and past participle of wield

wielding: Power; authority; rule. To have them in your might and in your wielding. Chaucer.
wieldless: Not to be wielded; unmanageable; unwieldy. Wieldless might. " Spenser.
wields: third-person singular simple present indicative of wield
wieldy: Capable of being wielded; manageable; wieldable; opposed to unwieldy. Johnson.
wiener: United States mathematician and founder of cybernetics (-)
wife: a married woman; a man's partner in marriage
wifedom: The condition of marriage for a woman.

wiggery: A wig or wigs; false hair. A. Trollope.
wiggish: Resembling or characteristic of a wig.

wiggling: present participle and gerund of wiggle
wiggly: moving in a twisting or snake-like or wormlike fashion
wigmaker: someone who makes and sells wigs
wigwag: To signal by means of a flag waved from side to side according to a code adopted for the purpose.
wigwam: An Indian cabin or hut, usually of a conical form, and made of a framework of poles covered with hides, bark, or mats; called also tepee. Very spacious was the wigwam, Made of deerskin dressed and whitened, With the gods of the Dacotahs Drawn and painted on its curtains. Longfellow.
wikiup: The hut used by the nomadic Indian tribes of the arid regions of the west and southwest United States, typically elliptical inform, with a rough frame covered with reed mats or grass or brushwood.
wilbur: A surname originating as a matronymic.
wild: Hard to steer; said of a vessel.
wildcat: (of a mine or oil well) drilled speculatively in an area not known to be productive

wildest: superlative form of wild: most wild

wildfowl: flesh of any of a number of wild game birds suitable for food
wildgrave: A waldgrave, or head forest keeper. See Waldgrave. The wildgrave winds his bugle horn. Sir W. Scott.

wildish: Somewhat wild; rather wild. A wildish destiny. " Wordsworth.
wildlife: all living things (except people) that are undomesticated
wildling: A wild, i.e. not cultivated, plant.
wildly: In a wild manner; without cultivation; with disorder; rudely; distractedly; extravagantly.
wildness: The quality or state of being wild; an uncultivated or untamed state; disposition to rove or go unrestrained; rudeness; savageness; irregularity; distraction.
wildwood: A wild or unfrequented wood. Also used adjectively; as, wildwood flowers; wildwood echoes. Burns.

wiles: A surname transferred from the nickname. A patronymic form of Wile.
wilful: habitually disposed to disobedience and opposition
wilhelm: A male given name from German, equivalent to English William.
wilhelmina: A female given name from German, masculine equivalent Wilhelm.
wiliness: The quality or state of being wily; craftiness; cunning; guile.
wilkinson: English chemist honored for his research on pollutants in car exhausts (born in )
will: The legal declaration of a person's mind as to the manner in which he would have his property or estate disposed of after hi sdeath; the written instrument, legally executed, by which a man makes disposition of his estate, to take effect after his death; testament; devise. See the Note under Testament,.
willamette: a river in western Oregon that flows north into the Columbia River near Portland
willard: United States advocate of temperance and women's suffrage (-)
willemite: A silicate of zinc, usually occurring massive and of a greenish yellow color, also in reddish crystals (troostite) containing manganese.

willfulness: the trait of being prone to disobedience and lack of discipline
william: radiotelephony clear-code word for the letter W.
williams: United States country singer and songwriter (-)
willier: One who works at a willying machine.
willingly: In a willing manner; with free will; without reluctance; cheerfully. Chaucer. The condition of that people is not so much to be envied as some would willingly represent it. Addison.
willingness: The quality or state of being willing; free choice or consent of the will; freedom from reluctance; readiness of the mind to do or forbear. Sweet is the love which comes with willingness. Dryden.
willis: English physician who was a pioneer in the study of the brain (-)
williwaw: A strong gust of cold wind.
willow: Any tree or shrub of the genus Salix, including many species, most of which are characterized often used as an emblem of sorrow, desolation, or desertion. A wreath of willow to show my forsaken plight. " Sir W. Scott. Hence, a lover forsaken by, or having lost, the person beloved, is said to wear the willow. And I must wear the willow garland For him that's dead or false tome. Campbell.
willowed: Abounding with willows; containing willows; covered or overgrown with willows. Willowed meads. " Collins.
willowlike: Resembling or characteristic of a willow tree.
willowy: Abounding with willows. Where willowy Camus lingers with delight. Gray.
willpower: the trait of resolutely controlling your own behavior
willying: The process of cleansing wool, cotton, or the like, with aw illy, or willow. Willying machine. Same as st Willow,
wilne: To wish; to desire. He will neth no destruction. Chaucer.
wilson: author of the first novel by an African American that was published in the United States (-)
wilting: causing to become limp or drooping
wilton: a carpet woven on a Jacquard loom with loops like a Brussels carpet but having the loops cut to form a close velvety pile
wiltshire: An inland county of England bordered by Gloucestershire, Somerset, Dorset, Oxfordshire, Hampshire and Berkshire.
wily: Full of wiles, tricks, or stratagems; using craft or stratagem to accomplish a purpose; mischievously artful; subtle. Wily and wise. " Chaucer. The wily snake. " Milton. This false, wily, doubling disposition of mind. South.
wimble: An instrument for boring holes, turned by a handle. Specifically:(a) A gimlet. " It is but like the little wimble, to let in the greater auger. " Selden.(b) A stonecutter's brace for boring holes in stone.(c) An auger used for boring in earth.
wimbledon: a suburb of London and the headquarters of the club where annual international tennis championships are played on grass courts
wimp: a person who lacks confidence, is irresolute and wishy-washy

wimpling: present participle and gerund of wimple
win: To extract, as ore or coal. Raymond.
wince: The act of one who winces.
winced: simple past and past participle of wince
wincer: One who, or that which, winces, shrinks, or kicks.
winch: To wince; to shrink; to kick with impatience or uneasiness.
winchester: a city in southern England; administrative center of Hampshire
winchman: A man who operates a winch.
wincing: The act of washing cloth, dipping it in dye, etc., with awin ce. Wincing machine. (a) A wince. Ure. (b) A succession of winces. See Wince. Knight.
winckelmann: German archaeologist and art historian said to be the father of archaeology (-)
wincopipe: A little red flower, no doubt the pimpernel, which, when it opens in the morning, is supposed to bode a fair day. See Pimpernel. There is small red flower in the stubble fields, which country people call the wincopipe; which if it opens in the morning, you may be surea fair day will follow. Bacon.
wind: The act of winding or turning; a turn; a bend; a twist; awin ding.
windage: The difference between the diameter of the bore of a gun and that of the shot fired from it.
windbag: a boring person who talks a great deal about uninteresting topics
windbreak: hedge or fence of trees designed to lessen the force of the wind and reduce erosion
windburn: redness and irritation of the skin caused by exposure to high-velocity wind
windcatcher: A traditional Persian architectural element for creating natural ventilation in buildings.
windcheater: a kind of heavy jacket (windcheater' is a British term)
windedness: The state of being winded, the temporary inability to breathe
winder: One in a flight of steps which are curved in plan, so that each tread is broader at one end than at the other; distinguished from flyer.
windfall: fruit that has fallen from the tree
windflaw: A sudden, strong current of wind; flaw.
windflower: The anemone; so called because formerly supposed to open only when the wind was blowing. See Anemone.
windgall: A soft tumor or synovial swelling on the fetlock joint of ahorse; so called from having formerly been supposed to contain air.
windhover: The kestrel; called also windbibber, windcuffer, windfanner.
windiness: The quality or state of being windy or tempestuous; as, the windiness of the weather or the season.
winding: A call by the boatswain's whistle.
windlass: A winding and circuitous way; a roundabout course; a shift.
windless: A grass used for making ropes or for plaiting, esp. Agrostis spica-vent is. Shelley.
windlestraw: A grass used for making ropes or for plaiting, especially Apera spica-venti.
windling: present participle and gerund of windle
windmill: A mill operated by the power of the wind, usually by the action of the wind upon oblique vanes or sails which radiate from ahorizontal shaft. Chaucer.
windmills: A plant of the genus Allionia.
window: The shutter, casement, sash with its fittings, or other framework, which closes a window opening.
windowed: Having windows or openings. Looped and windowed raggedness.
windowlike: Resembling a window (an opening in the wall).
windows: (trademark) an operating system with a graphical user interface
windowsill: the sill of a window; the horizontal member at the bottom of the window frame
windpipe: The passage for the breath from the larynx to the lungs; the trachea; the weasand. See Illust. under Lung.
windrow: To arrange in lines or windrows, as hay when newly made. Forby.
windrowing: present participle and gerund of windrow
windsail: A wide tube or funnel of canvas, used to convey a stream of air for ventilation into the lower compartments of a vessel.
windscreen: transparent screen (as of glass) to protect occupants of a vehicle
windshield: transparent screen (as of glass) to protect occupants of a vehicle
windsock: a truncated cloth cone mounted on a mast; used (e.g., at airports) to show the direction of the wind
windsor: A town in Berkshire, England. Windsor bean. (Bot.) See under bean. Windsor chair, a kind of strong, plain, polished, wooden chair. Simmon ds. Windsor soap, a scented soap well known for its excellence.
windstorm: A storm characterized by high wind with little or no rain.
windward: The point or side from which the wind blows; as, to ply to the windward; opposed to Ant: leeward. To lay an anchor to the windward, a figurative expression, signifying to adopt precautionary or anticipatory measures for success or security.
windway: The portion of a wind instrument through which the air is blown.
windy: resembling the wind in speed, force, or variability
wineberry: raspberry of China and Japan having pale pink flowers grown for ornament and for the small red acid fruits
winebibber: One who drinks much wine. Prov. xxiii. Winebibbing, n.
wineglass: A small glass from to drink wine.
wineglassful: As much as a wineglass will hold; enough to fill a wineglass. It is usually reckoned at two fluid ounces, or four tablespoonfuls.
winegrower: A person or company that owns a vineyard and produces wine, a vinedresser.
wineless: destitute of wine; as, wineless life.
winemaking: the craft and science of growing grapes and making wine
winepress: a press that is used to extract the juice from grapes
winery: A place where grapes are converted into wine.
wineskin: an animal skin (usually a goatskin) that forms a bag and is used to hold and dispense wine
winesop: A piece of bread soaked in wine; a small cake made with grapes or wine.
wing: One of the broad, thin, anterior lobes of the foot of apteropod, used as an organ in swimming.(b) (Bot.) Any membranaceous expansion, as that along the sides of certain stems, or of a fruit of the kind called samara.(c) (Bot.) Either of the two side petals of a papilionaceous flower.
winged: Furnished with a leaflike appendage, as the fruit of the elm and the ash, or the stem in certain plants; alate.
winger: One of the casks stowed in the wings of a vessel's hold, being smaller than such as are stowed more amidships. Totten.

winglike: resembling a wing in shape or position
wingman: the pilot who positions his aircraft outside and behind (on the wing of) the leader of a flying formation
wingover: An aerobatic maneuver in which an airplane makes a steep climb followed by a vertical flat-turn (the plane turns to its side, without rolling) and a short dive, levelling out to fly in the opposite direction from which the maneuver began.
wings: a means of flight or ascent
wingspan: linear distance between the extremities of an airfoil
wingspread: distance between the tips of the wings (as of a bird or insect) when fully extended
wingy: Having wings; rapid. With wingy speed outstrip the eastern wind. Addison.
winifred: A female given name from Welsh.
winkers: blocked leather eye shields attached to a (usually) harness bridle for horses, to prevent them from seeing backwards, and partially sideways; blinders in (USA).
winking: closing the eyes intermittently and rapidly
winkle: remove or displace from a position
winnebagoes: A tribe of North American Indians who originally occupied the region about Green Bay, Lake Michigan, but were driven back from the lake and nearly exterminated in by the IIlinnois.
winned: simple past and past participle of win
winner: One who wins, or gains by success in competition, contest, or gaming.
winning: Attracting; adapted to gain favor; charming; as, a winning address. Each mild and winning note. " Keble.
winningness: The quality or state of being winning. Winningness in style. J. Morley.
winnow: To separate chaff from grain. Winnow not with every wind. Eccl us. v.
winnowed: simple past and past participle of winnow
winnower: One who, or that which, winnows; specifically, a winnowing machine.
winnowing: The act of one who, or that which, winnows.
winnows: third-person singular simple present indicative of winnow
winona: A female given name from Dakota, used mainly in the United States.
winslow: English colonial administrator who traveled to America on the Mayflower and served as the first governor of the Plymouth Colony (-)
winsome: charming in a childlike or naive way
winston: A male given name derived from the place name.
winter: To pass the winter; to hibernate; as, to winter in Florida. Because the haven was not commodious to winter in, the more part advised to depart thence. Acts xxvii.
wintered: simple past and past participle of winter
winterer: Any person or animal (but especially a bird) that visits or resides in a specified location during the winter
wintergreen: A plant which keeps its leaves green through the winter.
wintering: present participle and gerund of winter
winterkill: To kill by the cold, or exposure to the inclemency of winter; as, the wheat was winterkilled.
winterkilled: simple past and past participle of winterkill
winterly: Like winter; wintry; cold; hence, disagreeable, cheerless; as, winterly news. The sir growing more winterly in the month of April. Camden.
wintry: Suitable to winter; resembling winter, or what belongs to winter; brumal; hyemal; cold; stormy; wintery. Touch our chilled hearts with vernal smile, Our wintry course do thou beguile. Keble.
winy: Having the taste or qualities of wine; vinous; as, grapes of awiny taste. Dam pier.
winze: A small shaft sunk from one level to another, as for the purpose of ventilation.
winzeman: A man in charge of a winze in a mine.
wiped: simple past and past participle of wipe
wipeout: a spill in some sport (as a fall from a bicycle or while skiing or being capsized on a surfboard)
wiper: A piece generally projecting from a rotating or swinging piece, as an axle or rock shaft, for the purpose of raising stampers, lifting rods, or the like, and leaving them to fall by their own weight; a kind of cam.
wiping: present participle and gerund of wipe
wired: equipped with wire or wires especially for electric or telephone service
wiredraw: To pass, or to draw off, (as steam) through narrow ports, or the like, thus reducing its pressure or force by friction.
wireman: a worker who installs and repairs electric wiring
wirepull: To exert an influence on (others) that is felt but not seen.
wiretap: tap a telephone or telegraph wire to get information
wiretapper: someone who wiretaps a telephone or telegraph wire
wireway: A system for transporting or transmitting by means of wires.
wirework: Work, especially openwork, formed of wires.
wireworm: wormlike larva of various elaterid beetles; feeds on roots of many crop plants
wiring: a circuit of wires for the distribution of electricity
wis: Certainly; really; indeed. As wis God helpe me. Chaucer.
wisconsin: a tributary of the Mississippi River in Wisconsin
wisconsinite: a native or resident of Wisconsin
wisdom: accumulated knowledge or erudition or enlightenment
wise: Way of being or acting; manner; mode; fashion. All armed incomplete wise. " Spenser. To love her in my beste wyse. Chaucer. This song she sings in most commanding wise. Sir P. Sidney. Let not these blessings then, sent from above, Abused be, or spilt in profane wise. Fair fax.
wiseacre: A learned or wise man. Pythagoras learned much. becoming a mighty wiseacre. Le land.
wiseacred: simple past and past participle of wiseacre
wiseacreish: Resembling or characteristic of a wiseacre.
wisecracker: A person who makes wisecrack remarks; a smart aleck.
wisely: In a wise manner; prudently; judiciously; discreetly; with wisdom. And wisely learn to curb thy sorrows wild. Milton.
wisenheimer: an upstart who makes conceited, sardonic, insolent comments
wisent: European bison having a smaller and higher head than the North American bison
wiser: comparative form of wise: more wise
wishbone: The forked bone in front of the breastbone in birds; called also merrythought, and wishing bone. See Merrythought, and Furculum.
wished: simple past and past participle of wish
wisher: One who wishes or desires; one who expresses a wish.
wishful: Having desire, or ardent desire; longing.
wishing: a. & n. from Wish, v. t. Wishing bone. See Wishbone. Wishing cap, a cap fabled to give one whatever he wishes for when wearing it.
wishram: A Chinook Indian tribe from the Columbia River in Oregon.
wisly: Certainly. God so wisly have mercy on me. " Chaucer.
wispen: Formed of a wisp, or of wisp; as, a wispen broom.
wisse: To show; to teach; to inform; to guide; to direct. Ere we depart I shall thee so well wisse That of mine house ne shalt thou never misse. Chaucer.
wistaria: A genus of climbing leguminous plants bearing long, pendulous clusters of pale bluish flowers.
wisteria: any flowering vine of the genus Wisteria
wistful: Longing; wishful; desirous. Lifting up one of my sashes, I cast many a wistful, melancholy look towards the sea. Swift.
wisting: present participle and gerund of wist
wistit: A small South American monkey; a marmoset.
wit: To know; to learn. I wot and wist alway. " Chaucer.
witch: A cone of paper which is placed in a vessel of lard or other fat, and used as a taper.
witchery: Sorcery; enchantment; witchcraft. Great Comus, Deep skilled in all his mother's witcheries. Milton. A woman infamous. for witcheries. Sir W. Scott.
witching: That witches or enchants; suited to enchantment or witchcraft; bewitching. The very witching time of night. Witchingly, adv.
witchlike: being or having the character of witchcraft
witchy: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of witches; witchlike.
wite: To reproach; to blame; to censure; also, to impute as blame. Spenser. Though that I be jealous, wite me not. Chaucer. There if that I misspeak or say, Wite it the ale of South wark, I you pray. Chaucer.
witenagemote: A meeting of wise men; the national council, or legislature, of england in the days of the Anglo-Saxons, before the Norman Conquest.
withal: With; put after its object, at the end of sentence or clause in which it stands. This diamond he greets your wife withal. Whatsoever uncleanness it be that a man shall be defiled withal. Lev.v.
withdraw: To retire; to retreat; to quit a company or place; to go away; as, he withdrew from the company. When the sea withdrew. " King Horn.
withdrawal: The act of withdrawing; withdrawment; retreat; retraction. Fielding.
withdrawing: present participle and gerund of withdraw
withdrawment: The act of withdrawing; withdrawal. W. Bel sham.
withdraws: third-person singular simple present indicative of withdraw
withe: An iron attachment on one end of a mast or boom, with a ring, through which another mast or boom is rigged out and secured; awythe. R. H. Dana, Jr.
wither: To fade; to lose freshness; to become sapless; to become sapless; to dry or shrivel up. Shall he hot pull up the roots thereof, and cut off the fruit thereof, that it wither Ezek. xvii.

witherer: One who or that which withers.

witherite: Barium carbonate occurring in white or gray six-sided twin crystals, and also in columnar or granular masses.
withernam: A second or reciprocal distress of other goods in lieu of goods which were taken by a first distress and have been eloigned; a taking by way of reprisal; chiefly used in the expression capias in withernam, which is the name of a writ used in connection with the action of replevin (sometimes called a writ of reprisal), which issues to a defendant in replevin when he has obtained judgment for are turn of the chattels replevied, and fails to obtain them on the writ of return. Black stone.
withers: The ridge between the shoulder bones of a horse, at the base of the neck. See Illust. of Horse. Let the galled jade wince; our withers are unwrung.

withinside: In the inner parts; inside. Graves.

withset: To set against; to oppose. Their way he them withset. R. of Brun ne.

withstands: third-person singular simple present indicative of withstand

withy: The osier willow (Salix viminal is). See Osier, n. (a).
witing: Knowledge. Withouten witing of any other wight. Chaucer.

witling: A person who has little wit or understanding; a pretender towit or smartness. A beau and witing perished in the forming. Pope. Ye newspaper witlings! ye pert scribbling folks! Goldsmith.
witloof: young broad-leaved endive plant deprived of light to form a narrow whitish head
witness: To see the execution of, as an instrument, and subscribe it for the purpose of establishing its authenticity; as, to witness a bond or a deed.
witnessed: simple past and past participle of witness
witnessing: present participle and gerund of witness
wits: the basic human power of intelligent thought and perception

witter: To speak at length on a trivial subject.

wive: To marry, as a man; to take a wife. Wherefore we pray you hastily to wive. Chaucer.
wivern: a fire-breathing dragon used in medieval heraldry
wiyot: An indigenous people of Humboldt Bay, California, USA and surrounding regions.
wiz: someone who is dazzlingly skilled in any field

wokas: A large yellow water lily (Nuphar polysepala) found in the northwestern United States.

womanizer: a man who likes many women and has short sexual relationships with them
womankind: The females of the human race; women, collectively. A sanctuary into which womankind, with her tools of magic, the broom and mop, has very infrequent access. Hawthorne.
womanlike: Like a woman; womanly. Womanlike, taking revenge too deep. Tennyson.
womanliness: The quality or state of being womanly. There is nothing wherein their womanliness is more honestly garnished than with silence. Udall.

wonderland: A land full of wonders, or marvels. M. Arnold.

wonders: See Wondrous. They be wonders glad thereof. Sir T. More.

woodcarving: a carving created by carving wood

wooden: made or consisting of (entirely or in part) or employing wood

woodhouse: A house or shed in which wood is stored, and sheltered from the weather.
woodland: Land covered with wood or trees; forest; land on which trees are suffered to grow, either for fuel or timber. Here hills and vales, the woodland and the plain, Here earth and water seem to strive again. Pope. Woodlands and cultivated fields are harmoniously blended. Ban croft.
woodlark: A lark, Lullula arborea, the only member of the genus Lullula, found in western Eurasia and northern Africa.
woodlike: Resembling wood, such as in color or texture
woodlore: Skills relating to living in a woodland environment; woodcraft.
woodlouse: any of various small terrestrial isopods having a flat elliptical segmented body; found in damp habitats
woodman: A forest officer appointed to take care of the king's woods; a forester.
woodness: Anger; madness; insanity; rage. Spenser. Woodness laughing in his rage. Chaucer.
woodnote: A natural musical sound, like birdsong in a forest.

woodrow: A topographic surname from Middle English for a dweller in a row of houses near a wood.
woodruff: any plant of the genus Asperula

woodwind: any wind instrument other than the brass instruments
woodwork: Work made of wood; that part of any structure which is wrought of wood.
woodworking: the craft of a carpenter: making things out of wood
woody: made of or containing or resembling wood
wooed: simple past and past participle of woo

woofed: simple past and past participle of woof
woofell: The European blackbird. The woofell near at hand that hath ag olden bill. " Dray ton.

wooing: a man's courting of a woman

(b) One who sorts wool according to its staple, or its adaptation to different manufacturing purposes. Wool winder, a person employed to wind, or make up, wool into bundles to be packed for sale.

wop: (ethnic slur) offensive term for a person of Italian descent
worcester: United States lexicographer who was accused of plagiarism by Noah Webster (-)
worcestershire: A midland county of England bordered by Shropshire, Staffordshire, Warwickshire, Gloucestershire, Herefordshire and West Midlands.

wordier: comparative form of wordy: more wordy

wordy: Of or pertaining to words; consisting of words; verbal; as, a wordy war. Cowper.
work: Structures in civil, military, or naval engineering, as docks, bridges, embankments, trenches, fortifications, and the like; also, the structures and grounds of a manufacturing establishment; as, ironworks; locomotive works; gas works. (d) pl.
workability: The ease with which something can be worked or fashioned.
workable: Capable of being worked, or worth working; as, a workable mine; workable clay.
workableness: The quality or state of being workable, or the extent to which a thing is workable.
workaholic: person with a compulsive need to work
workbag: A bag for holding implements or materials for work; especially, a reticule, or bag for holding needlework, and the like.
workbasket: A basket for holding materials for needlework, or the like.
workbench: A bench on which work is performed, as in a carpenter's shop.
workboat: A boat used for purposes other than recreation, passenger transport, or combat.
workbook: a student's book or booklet containing problems with spaces for solving them
workbox: A box for holding instruments or materials for work.
workday: A day on which work is performed, as distinguished from Sunday, festivals, etc., a working day.
worked: simple past and past participle of work
worker: One of the neuter, or sterile, individuals of the social ants, bees, and white ants. The workers are generally females having the sexual organs imperfectly developed. See Ant, and White ant, under white.
workhorse: machine that performs dependably under heavy use
workhouse: a poorhouse where able-bodied poor are compelled to labor
working: a & n. from Work. The word must cousin be to the working. Chaucer. Working beam. See Beam, n. Working class, the class of people who are engaged in manual labor, or are dependent upon it for support; laborers; operatives; chiefly used in the plural. Working day. See under Day, n. Working drawing, a drawing, as of the whole or part of astructure, machine, etc., made to a scale, and intended to be followed by the workmen. Working drawings are either general or detail drawings. Working house, a house where work is performed; a workhouse. Working point (Mach.), that part of a machine at which the effect required; the point where the useful work is done.
workingman: A laboring man; a man who earns his daily support by manual labor.
workings: a mine or quarry that is being or has been worked
workingwoman: A woman who works in exchange for payment, especially one who does manual labour
workless: Without work; not laboring; as, many people were still workless.
workload: work that a person is expected to do in a specified time
workman: an employee who performs manual or industrial labor
workmanlike: Becoming a workman, especially a skillful one; skillful; well performed.
workmanly: Becoming a skillful workman; skillful; well performed; workmanlike.
workmanship: The art or skill of a workman; the execution or manner of making anything. Due reward For her praiseworthy workmanship to yield. Spenser. Beauty is nature's brag, and must be shown. Where most may wonder at the workmanship. Milton.
workmaster: The performer of any work; a master workman. Spenser.
workout: the activity of exerting your muscles in various ways to keep fit
workpiece: work consisting of a piece of metal being machined
workplace: a place where work is done
workroom: Any room or apartment used especially for labor.
works: performance of moral or religious acts
worksheet: a sheet of paper with multiple columns; used by an accountant to assemble figures for financial statements
workshop: A shop where any manufacture or handiwork is carried on.
workspace: space allocated for your work (as in an office)
workstation: a desktop digital computer that is conventionally considered to be more powerful than a microcomputer
worktable: A table for holding working materials and implements; esp., as mall table with drawers and other conveniences for needlework, etc.
workup: A general medical examination to assess a person's health and fitness.
workweek: hours or days of work in a calendar week
workwoman: A woman who performs any work; especially, a woman skilled in needlework.
workyday: A week day or working day, as distinguished from Sunday or aholiday. Also used adjectively. Prithee, tell her but a workyday fortune.
world: people in general; especially a distinctive group of people with some shared interest
worldliness: The quality of being worldly; a predominant passion for obtaining the good things of this life; covetousness; addictedness to gain and temporal enjoyments; worldly-mindedness.
worldling: A person whose soul is set upon gaining temporal possessions; one devoted to this world and its enjoyments. A foutre for the world and worldlings base. If we consider the expectations of futurity, the worldling gives upthe argument. Rogers. And worldlings blot the temple's gold. Keble.
worldly: With relation to this life; in a worldly manner. Subverting worldly strong and worldly wise By simply meek. Milton.
worldwide: spanning or extending throughout the entire world
wormed: Penetrated by worms; injured by worms; worm-eaten; as, wormed timber.
wormer: Dewormer, medicine used in deworming an animal.
wormfish: Any of the family Microdesmidae of small goby-like fish which often burrow in estuarine mud.
wormhole: A burrow made by a worm.
wormian: Discovered or described by Ol anus Wormius, a Danish anatomist. Wormian bones, small irregular plates of bone often interposed in the sutures between the large cranial bones.
wormil: Any botfly larva which burrows in or beneath the skin of domestic and wild animals, thus producing sores. They belong to various species of Hypoderma and allied genera. Domestic cattle are often infested by a large species. See Gadfly. Called also warble, and worble.
wormling: A little worm. O dusty wormling! dost thou strive and stand With heaven's high monarch Sylvester.
worms: An independent town in Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany.
wormseed: Any one of several plants, as Artemisia santonica, and chenopodium anthelmintic um, whose seeds have the property of expelling worms from the stomach and intestines. Wormseed mustard, as lender, cruciferous plant (Erysinum cheiranthoides) having small lanceolate leaves.
wormwood: A composite plant (Artemisia Absinthium), having a bitter and slightly aromatic taste, formerly used as a tonic and a vermifuge, and to protect woolen garments from moths. It gives the peculiar flavor to the cordial called absinthe. The volatile oil is a narcotic poison. The term is often extended to other species of the same genus.
wormy: Containing a worm; abounding with worms. Wormy beds.
worn: p. p. of Wear. Worn land, land that has become exhausted by tillage, or which for any reason has lost its fertility.
worral: a monitor lizard of Egypt, either a Nile monitor (Varanus niloticus) or a desert monitor (Varanus griseus).
worried: mentally upset over possible misfortune or danger etc
worrisome: Inclined to worry or fret; also, causing worry or annoyance.
worry: To feel or express undue care and anxiety; to manifest disquietude or pain; to be fretful; to chafe; as, the child worries; the horse worries.
worrying: the act of moving something by repeated tugs or pushes
worrywart: thinks about unfortunate things that might happen
worse: Bad, ill, evil, or corrupt, in a greater degree; more bad or evil; less good; specifically, in poorer health; more sick; used both in a physical and moral sense. Or worse, if men worse can devise. Chaucer.was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse. Mark v.Evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse. Tim. iii.There are men who seem to believe they are not bad while another canbe found worse. Rambler. But I love him. " Love him Worse and worse. " Gay.
worsen: To grow or become worse. De Quincey. Indifferent health, which seemed rather to worsen than improve. Carlyle.
worsening: changing something with the result that it becomes worse
worsens: third-person singular simple present indicative of worsen
worser: Worse. Thou dost deserve a worser end. Beau. & Fl. From worser thoughts which make me do amiss. Bunyan. A dreadful quiet felt, and, worser far Than arms, a sullen interval of war. Dryden.
worship: To perform acts of homage or adoration; esp., to perform religious service. Our fathers worshiped in this mountain; and ye say that in Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship. John iv.Was it for this I have loved. and worshiped in silence longfellow.
worshiped: simple past and past participle of worship
worshiper: One who worships; one who pays divine honors to any being or thing; one who adores.
worshipful: Entitled to worship, reverence, or high respect; claiming respect; worthy of honor; often used as a term of respect, sometimes ironically. This is worshipful society. " so dear and worshipful. Chaucer. Worshipfully, adv. Worshipfulness, n.
worshiping: present participle and gerund of worship
worshipped: regarded with deep or rapturous love (especially as if for a god)
worshipper: a person who has religious faith
worshipping: present participle and gerund of worship
worst: Bad, evil, or pernicious, in the highest degree, whether in aphysical or moral sense. See Worse. Heard so oft in worst extremes. Milton. I have a wife, the worst that may be. Chaucer. If thou hadst not been born the worst of men, Thou hadst been a knave and flatterer.
worsted: a woolen fabric with a hard textured surface and no nap; woven of worsted yarns he wore a worsted suit
worth: To be; to become; to betide; now used only in the phrases, woe worth the day, woe worth the man, etc., in which the verb is in the imperative, and the nouns day, man, etc., are in the dative. Woebe to the day, woe be to the man, etc., are equivalent phrases. I counsel. to let the cat wort he. Piers Plowman. He worth upon his steed gray. Chaucer.
worthful: Full of worth; worthy; deserving. Mars ton.
worthily: In a worthy manner; excellently; deservedly; according to merit; justly; suitably; becomingly. You worthily succeed not only to the honors of your ancestors, but also to their virtues. Dryden. Some may very worthily deserve to be hated. South.
worthiness: The quality or state of being worthy; desert; merit; excellence; dignity; virtue; worth. Who is sure he hath a soul, unless It see, and judge, and follow worthiness Donne. She is not worthy to be loved that hath not some feeling of her own worthiness. Sir P. Sidney. The prayers which our Savior made were for his own worthiness accepted. Hooker.
worthing: present participle and gerund of worth
worthless: Destitute of worth; having no value, virtue, excellence, dignity, or the like; undeserving; valueless; useless; vile; mean; as, a worthless garment; a worthless ship; a worthless man or woman; a worthless magistrate.'T is a worthless world to win or lose. Byron. Worthlessly, adv. Worthlessness, n.
worthlessness: having no qualities that would render it valuable or useful
worthwhileness: value sufficient to repay time or effort spent
worthy: A man of eminent worth or value; one distinguished for useful and estimable qualities; a person of conspicuous desert; much used in the plural; as, the worthies of the church; political worthies; military worthies. The blood of ancient worthies in his veins. Cowper.
wost: d pers. sing. pres. of Wit, to know. Spenser.
wot: st & d pers. sing. pres. of Wit, to know. See the Note under Wit, v. Brethren, I wot that through ignorance ye did it. Acts iii.
wottest: second-person singular simple present indicative of wit, wot, wott, and wotte
would: Commonly used as an auxiliary verb, either in the past tense orin the conditional or optative present. See d & d Will.
wouldst: second-person singular simple past indicative of will
wound: imp. & p. p. of Wind to twist, and Wind to sound by blowing.
woundable: Capable of being wounded; vulnerable. Fuller.
wounding: causing physical or especially psychological injury
woundless: Free from wound or hurt; exempt from being wounded; invulnerable. Knights whose woundless armor rusts. " Spenser.may miss our name, And hit the woundless air.
woundy: Excessive. Such a world of holidays, that 't a woundy hindrance to a poor man that lives by his labor. L'Estrange.
wove: p. pr. & rare vb. n. of Weave.
woven: p. p. of Weave. Woven paper, or Wove paper, writing paper having an even, uniform surface, without watermarks.
wovoka: A Paiute religious leader, also known as Jack Wilson (c. - ), who founded a second episode of the Ghost Dance movement.
wowser: One with strong moral views against excessive consumption of alcohol, gambling, pornography, etc., who seeks to promulgate those views.
wowserish: Resembling or characteristic of wowsers (moral crusaders).
wrack: A thin, flying cloud; a rack.
wraith: An apparition of a person in his exact likeness, seen before death, or a little after; hence, an apparition; a specter; a vision; an unreal image. She was uncertain if it were the gypsy or her wraith. Sir W. Scott. O, hollow wraith of dying fame. Tennyson.
wrangle: To involve in a quarrel or dispute; to embroil. Bp. Sanders on.
wrangler: someone who argues noisily or angrily
wrangling: an instance of intense argument (as in bargaining)
wrap: To snatch up; transport; chiefly used in the p. p. wrapt. Lo! where the stripling, wrapt in wonder, roves. Beat tie.
wraparound: a garment (as a dress or coat) with a full length opening; adjusts to the body by wrapping around
wrapped: enclosed securely in a covering of paper or the like
wrapper: One who, or that which, wraps.
wrapping: the covering (usually paper or cellophane) in which something is wrapped
wrasse: Any one of numerous edible, marine, spiny-finned fishes of the genus Labrus, of which several species are found in the Mediterranean and on the Atlantic coast of Europe. Many of the species are bright-colored.
wrastle: To wrestle. Who wrastle th best naked, with oil enoint. Chaucer.
wrathfulness: The quality of being wrathful; wrath
wraw: Angry; vexed; wrathful. With this speech the cock wex wroth and wraw. Chaucer.
wrawl: To cry, as a cat; to waul. Spenser.
wray: To reveal; to disclose. To no wight thou shalt this counsel wray. Chaucer.
wreaked: simple past and past participle of wreak
wreaker: Avenger. The stork, the wrekere of avouter ye Chaucer.
wreaking: present participle and gerund of wreak
wreath: An appendage to the shield, placed above it, and supporting the crest (see Illust. of Crest). It generally represents a twist of two cords of silk, one tinctured like the principal metal, the other like the principal color in the arms.
wreathe: To be intewoven or entwined; to twine together; as, a bower of wreathing trees. Dryden.
wreathed: simple past and past participle of wreath
wreathen: Twisted; made into a wreath. Wreathen work of pure gold. " Ex.xxviii.
wreathing: present participle and gerund of wreath
wreathy: Wreathed; twisted; curled; spiral; also, full of wreaths. Wreathy spires, and cochleary turnings about. " Sir T. Browne.
wreckage: the remaining parts of something that has been wrecked
wrecker: someone who demolishes or dismantles buildings as a job
wreckful: Causing wreck; involving ruin; destructive. By wreckful wind. Spenser.
wrecking: a. & n. from Wreck, v. Wrecking car (Railway), a car fitted upwith apparatus and implements for removing the wreck occasioned by an accident, as by a collision. Wrecking pump, a pump especially adapted for pumping water from the hull of a wrecked vessel.
wrench: The system made up of a force and a couple of forces in a plane perpendicular to that force. Any number of forces acting at any points upon a rigid body may be compounded so as to be equivalent to a wrench. Carriage wrench, a wrench adapted for removing or tightening the nuts that confine the wheels on the axles, or for turning the other nuts or bolts of a carriage or wagon. Monkey wrench. See under Monkey. Wrench hammer, a wrench with the end shaped so as to admit of being used as a hammer.
wrenched: simple past and past participle of wrench
wrenching: causing great physical or mental suffering
wrenlike: Resembling or characteristic of a wren.
wrest: obtain by seizing forcibly or violently, also metaphorically
wrested: simple past and past participle of wrest
wresting: present participle and gerund of wrest
wrestle: To wrestle with; to seek to throw down as in wrestling.
wrestled: simple past and past participle of wrestle
wrestler: One who wrestles; one who is skillful in wrestling.
wrestling: Act of one who wrestles; specif., the sport consisting of the hand-to-hand combat between two unarmed contestants who seek to throw each other. The various styles of wrestling differ in their definition of a fall and in the governing rules. In Greco-Roman wrestling, tripping and taking hold of the legs are forbidden, and afall is gained (that is, the bout is won), by the contestant who pins both his opponent's shoulders to the ground. In catch-as-catch-can wrestling, all holds are permitted except such as may be barred by mutual consent, and a fall is defined as in Greco-Roman style. Lancashire style wrestling is essentially the same as catch-as-catch-can. In Cumberland and West morland wrestling the contestants stand chest to chest, grasping each other around the body. The one first losing his hold, or touching the ground with any part of his body except his feet, loses the bout. If both fall to the ground at the same time, it is a dogfall, and must be wrestled over. In the cornwall and Devon wrestling, the wrestlers complete in strong loose linen jackets, catching hold of the jacket, or anywhere above the waist. Two shoulders and one hip, or two hips and one shoulder, must touch the ground to constitute a fall, and if a man is thrown otherwise than on his back the contestants get upon their feet and the bout recommences.
wrests: third-person singular simple present indicative of wrest
wretched: Very miserable; sunk in, or accompanied by, deep affliction or distress, as from want, anxiety, or grief; calamitous; woeful; very afflicting. To what wretched state reserved!" Milton. O cruel! Death! to those you are more kind Than to the wretched mortals left behind. Waller. The wretched refuse of your teeming shore.
wretchedly: In a wretched manner; miserably; despicable.
wretchedness: the character of being uncomfortable and unpleasant
wretchless: Reckless; hence, disregarded. Wretchlessly, adv. Wretchlessness, n. Bk. of Com. Prayer. Your deaf ears should listen Unto the wretchless clamors of the poor. J. Webster.
wrick: a painful muscle spasm especially in the neck or back (rick' and wrick' are British)
wriggle: To move the body to and fro with short, writhing motions, likea worm; to squirm; to twist uneasily or quickly about. Both he and successors would often wriggle in their seats, as long as the cushion lasted. Swift.
wriggler: One who, or that which, wriggles. Cowper.
wriggles: third-person singular simple present indicative of wriggle
wriggling: moving in a twisting or snake-like or wormlike fashion
wriggly: moving in a twisting or snake-like or wormlike fashion
wright: One who is engaged in a mechanical or manufacturing business; an artificer; a workman; a manufacturer; a mechanic; esp., a worker in wood; now chiefly used in compounds, as in millwright, wheelwright, etc. He was a well good wright, a carpenter. Chaucer.
wring: To bend or strain out of its position; as, to wring a mast.
wringbolt: A bolt used by shipwrights, to bend and secure the planks against the timbers till they are fastened by bolts, spikes, or treenails; not to be confounded with ringbolt.
wringer: a clothes dryer consisting of two rollers between which the wet clothes are squeezed
wringing: a. & n. from Wring, v. Wringing machine, a wringer. See wringer,.
wrinkling: present participle and gerund of wrinkle
wrinkly: Full of wrinkles; having a tendency to be wrinkled; corrugated; puckered. G. Eliot. His old wrinkly face grew quite blown out at last. Carlyle.
wrist: The joint, or the region of the joint, between the hand and the arm; the carpus. See Carpus. He took me by the wrist, and held me hard.
wristband: The band of the sleeve of a shirt, or other garment, which covers the wrist.
wristlet: An elastic band worn around the wrist, as for the purpose of securing the upper part of a glove.
wristwatch: a watch that is worn strapped to the wrist
wristy: Characterised by marked or exaggerated movement of the wrist; involving deft wrist movements.
writ: d pers. sing. pres. of Write, for write th. Chaucer.
writable: Capable of, or suitable for, being written down.
writer: writes (books or stories or articles or the like) professionally (for pay)
writes: third-person singular simple present indicative of write
writhe: To twist or contort the body; to be distorted; as, to writhe with agony. Also used figuratively. After every attempt, he felt that he had failed, and writhed with shame and vexation. Macaulay.
writhed: twisted (especially as in pain or struggle)
writhen: Having a twisted distorted from. A writhen staff his step unstable guides. Fair fax.
writhing: moving in a twisting or snake-like or wormlike fashion
writing: the act of creating written works
wrongdoer: One who commits a tort or trespass; a trespasser; a tortfeasor. Ayliffe.
wrongdoing: Evil or wicked behavior or action.
wronged: simple past and past participle of wrong
wronger: One who wrongs or injures another. Wrongers of the world. " Tennyson.
wrongful: Full of wrong; injurious; unjust; unfair; as, a wrongful taking of property; wrongful dealing. Wrongfully, adv. Wrongfulness, n.
wrongfully: in an unjust or unfair manner
wrongfulness: that which is contrary to the principles of justice or law
wrongheaded: Wrong in opinion or principle; having a perverse understanding; perverse. Wrongheadedly, adv. Wrongheadedness, n. Macaulay.
wrongless: Not wrong; void or free from wrong. Wronglessly, adv. Sir P. Sidney.
wrongly: In a wrong manner; unjustly; erroneously; wrong; amiss; as, he judges wrongly of my motives. And yet wouldst wrongly win.
wrongness: The quality or state of being wrong; wrongfulness; error; fault. The best great wrong nesses within themselves. Bp. Butler. The rightness or wrongness of this view. Latham.
wrongous: Not right; illegal; as, wrongous imprisonment. Craig.
wrote: To root with the snout. See st Root. Chaucer.
wroth: Full of wrath; angry; incensed; much exasperated; wrathful. Wroth to see his kingdom fail. " Milton. Revel and truth as in a low degree, They be full wroth all day. Chaucer. Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell. Gen. iv.
wrought: imp. & p. p. of Work. Alas that I was wrought! Chaucer.
wry: To cover. Wrie you in that mantle. Chaucer.
wrymouth: Any one of several species of large, elongated, marine fishes of the genus Crypt acanthodes, especially C. maculatus of the American coast. A whitish variety is called ghostfish.
wryneck: Any one of several species of Old World birds of the genus jynx, allied to the woodpeckers; especially, the common European species (J. torguilla); so called from its habit of turning the neck around in different directions. Called also cuckoo's mate, snakebird, summer bird, tonguebird, and writheneck.
wryness: The quality or state of being wry, or distorted. W. Montagu.
wudu: A ritual washing of the forearms, head, and feet, required after minor impurity, frequently performed immediately before prayer.
wulfenite: Native lead molybdate occurring in tetragonal crystals, usually tabular, and of a bright orange-yellow to red, gray, or brown color; also called yellow lead ore.
wull: See d Will. Pour out to all that wull. Spenser.
wurley: An Australian indigenous shelter made from small branches with the leaves still attached.
wurtzite: a brownish-black mineral consisting of zinc sulfide
wurzburg: a city of south central Germany
wurzel: A rural, unsophisticated person; a bumpkin.
wuss: a person who is physically weak and ineffectual
wy: Initialism of Wyoming: a state of the United States.
wyandot: A member of a Native American people, formed from the Huron confederacy, that lived in and around Ohio.
wycherley: English playwright noted for his humorous and satirical plays (-)
wycliffe: English theologian whose objections to Roman Catholic doctrine anticipated the Protestant Reformation (-)
wynd: A narrow lane or alley. Jamie son. The narrow wynds, or alleys, on each side of the street. Bryant.
wynn: A kind of timber truck, or carriage.
wyoming: a state in the western United States; mountainous in the west and north with the Great Plains in the east
wyrd: fate personified; any one of the three Weird Sisters
x: X, the twenty-fourth letter of the English alphabet, has three sounds; a compound nonvocal sound (that of ks), as in wax; a compound vocal sound (that of gz), as in example; and, at the beginning of aword, a simple vocal sound (that of z), as in xanthic. See Guide to pronunciation,,.
xanthamide: An amido derivative of xanthic acid obtained as a white crystalline substance, CHO.CS.NH; called also xanthogen amide.
xanthan: A polysaccharide, consisting of galactose and mannose residues, produced by the bacterium Xanthomonas campestris
xanthate: A salt of xanthic; a xanthogenate.
xanthein: The water-soluble part of the yellow carotenoid pigment present in the cell sap of some plants.
xanthelasmoidea: A disease resembling xanthelasma, which leaves yellowish or brownish patches on the skin.
xanthene: Any of a group of tricyclic heterocycles (dibenzopyrans) that are the basis for a range of dyes such as fluorescein and eosin.
xanthic: Tending toward a yellow color, or to one of those colors, green being excepted, in which yellow is a constituent, as scarlet, orange, etc.
xanthin: A white microcrystalline nitrogenous compound, CHON,present in muscle tissue, in the liver, spleen, pancreas, and other organs, and also in urine (in small quantities) and some urinary calculi, and in the juices of certain plants; so called because it leaves a yellow residue when evaporated to dryness with nitric acid. Xanthine is closely related to uric acid.
xanthine: crystalline oxidation product of the metabolism of nucleoproteins; precursor of uric acid; found in many organs and in urine
xanthinuria: An abnormally high level of xanthine in one's urine.
xanthium: A genus of composite plants in which the scales of the involucre are united so as to form a kind of bur; cocklebur; clotbur.
xanthochroi: A division of the Caucasian races, comprising the lighter-colored members.
xanthoconite: A mineral containing silver, arsenic, and sulphur.
xanthoderma: A yellow coloration of the skin.
xanthogen: The hypothetical radical supposed to be characteristic of xanthic acid.
xanthoma: A skin disease marked by the development or irregular yellowish patches upon the skin, especially upon the eyelids; called also xanthelasma.
xanthomelanous: Of or pertaining to the lighter division of the Melanochroi, orthose races having an olive or yellow complexion and black hair.
xanthomonas: a genus of bacteria similar to Pseudomonas but producing a yellow pigment that is not soluble in water
xanthone: An aromatic ketone, -oxo-xanthene, that is used as an insecticide.
xanthophore: A xanthochrome-containing chromatophore, frequently a lipophore.
xanthophyll: A yellow coloring matter found in yellow autumn leaves, and also produced artificially from chlorophyll; formerly called also phylloxanthin.
xanthoproteic: Pertaining to, or derived from, xanthoprotein; showing the characters of xanthoprotein; as, xanthoproteic acid; the xanthoproteic reaction for albumin.
xanthoprotein: A yellow acid substance formed by the action of hot nitric acid on albuminous or proteid matter. It is changed to a deep orange-yellow color by the addition of ammonia.
xanthopsia: visual defect in which objects appear to have a yellowish hue; sometimes occurs in cases of jaundice
xanthorhiza: A genus of shrubby ranunculaceous plants of North America, including only the species Xanthorhiza apii folia, which has roots of a deep yellow color; yellowroot. The bark is intensely bitter, and is sometimes used as a tonic.
xanthorrhoea: Any of the genus Xanthorrhoea of grass trees.
xanthosis: The yellow discoloration often observed in cancerous tumors.
xanthoxylum: A genus of prickly shrubs or small trees, the bark and rots of which are of a deep yellow color; prickly ash.
xaverian: A member of the Xaverian Brothers, a religious order founded in Bruges, Belgium and dedicated to Catholic education.
xebec: A small three-masted vessel, with projecting bow stern and convex decks, used in the Mediterranean for transporting merchandise, etc. It carries large square sails, or both. Xebecs were formerly armed and used by corsairs.
xenia: The concept of hospitality to strangers.
xenial: Hospitable, especially to visiting strangers or foreigners.
xenicidae: alternative names for the family comprising the New Zealand wrens
xenobiology: The speculative biology of extraterrestrial life forms.
xenodiagnosis: The diagnosis of an infectious disease (especially of trypanosomiasis) by exposure to a vector of that disease, incubating the vector and examining it for the presence of the disease.
xenodochium: A house for the reception of strangers.(b) In the Middle Ages, a room in a monastery for the reception and entertainment of strangers and pilgrims, and for the relief of paupers.
xenogenetic: Of or pertaining to xenogenesis; as, the xenogenetic origin ofmicrozymes. Huxley.
xenogenic: Originating outside an organism and being introduced.
xenolith: (geology) a piece of rock of different origin from the igneous rock in which it is embedded
xenomania: A mania for, or an inordinate attachment to, foreign customs, institutions, manners, fashions, etc. Saints bury.
xenophobe: One who hates or fears strangers or foreigners.
xenophobia: a fear of foreigners or strangers
xenophobic: suffering from xenophobia; having abnormal fear or hatred of the strange or foreign
xenophon: Greek general and historian; student of Socrates (- BC)
xenophora: Any mollusk of the genus Xenophora.
xenopodidae: in some classifications the family of the genus Xenopus which is otherwise included in the family Pipidae
xenopus: an African clawed frog; in some classifications made the type genus of a separate family Xenopodidae
xenotransplantation: a surgical procedure in which tissue or whole organs are transfer ed from one species to another species
xenylic: Pertaining to, derived from, designating, certain amido compounds obtained by reducing certain nitro derivatives of diphenyl.
xeranthemum: any plant of the genus Xeranthemum native to southern Europe having chaffy or silvery flower heads with purplish tubular flowers
xeraphim: An old money of account in Bombay, equal to three fifths of aru pee.
xeroderma: a mild form of ichthyosis characterized by abnormal dryness and roughness of the skin
xerographically: In a xerographic way; by xerography.
xerography: forming an image by the action of light on a specially coated charged plate; the latent image is developed with powders that adhere only to electrically charged areas
xeromorphic: Of, relating to, or characteristic of the xerophytes, especially having the ability to store water in leaves and stems.
xeronic: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid, CHO, related to fumaric acid, and obtained from citraconic acid as an oily substance having a bittersweet taste; so called from its tendency to form its anhydride.
xerophagy: Among the primitive Christians, the living on a diet of dry food in Lent and on other fasts.
xerophile: plant adapted for life with a limited supply of water
xerophilous: Drought-loving; able withstand the absence or lack of moisture. Plants which are peculiarly adapted to dry climates are termed by De Candolle xerophilous. Goo dale.
xerophthalmia: An abnormal dryness of the eyeball produced usually by long-continued inflammation and subsequent atrophy of the conjunctiva.
xerophyte: plant adapted for life with a limited supply of water
xerophytic: adapted to a xeric (or dry) environment
xerosere: The succession of ecological communities which originated in an extremely dry habitat such as a desert or sand dunes.
xerox: a copy made by a xerographic printer
xhosa: a member of the Negroid people of southern South Africa
xi: the th letter of the Greek alphabet
xian: a city of central China; capital of ancient Chinese empire - BC
xiphias: A genus of fishes comprising the common swordfish.
xiphiid: A fish in the family Xiphiidae; a swordfish.
xiphiplastron: The posterior, or fourth, lateral plate in the plastron of turtles; called also xiphisternum.
xiphisternum: The posterior segment, or extremity, of the sternum; sometimes called metasternum, ensiform cartilage, ensiform process, or xiphoid process.
xiphius: A genus of cetaceans having a long, pointed, bony beak, usually two tusklike teeth in the lower jaw, but no teeth in the upper jaw.
xiphosuran: Any member of the order Xiphosura, including horseshoe crabs.
xiphura: Same as Limuloidea. Called also Xiphosura. X ray. See under ray.
xoanon: A wooden statue used as a cult image in Ancient Greece.
xs: Initialism of extra small (the manufactured size or an item of that size).
xu: A former unit of currency in Vietnam, equivalent to a hundredth of a dong.
xx: (genetics) normal complement of sex chromosomes in a female
xxx: (genetics) abnormal complement of three X chromosomes in a female
xylan: A gummy substance of the pentosan class, present in woody tissue, and yielding xylose on hydrolysis; wood gum.
xylaria: type genus of Xylariaceae; fungi with perithecia in the upper part of erect black woody stromata
xylariaceae: family of fungi characterized by dark brown to black spores
xylene: Any of a group of three metameric hydrocarbons of the aromatic series, found in coal and wood tar, and so named because found in crude wood spirit. They are colorless, oily, inflammable liquids, CH.(CH), being dimethyl benzenes, and are called respectively orthoxylene, metaxylene, and paraxylene. Called also xylol.
xylenol: Any one of six metameric phenol derivatives of xylene, obtained as crystalline substances, (CH).CH.OH.
xylic: Pertaining to, derived from, or related to, xylene; specifically, designating any one of several metameric acids produced by the partial oxidation of mesitylene and pseudo-cumene.
xylidine: Any one of six metameric hydrocarbons, (CH).CH.NH,resembling aniline, and related to xylene. They are liquids, or easily fusible crystalline substances, of which three are derived from metaxylene, two from orthoxylene, and one from paraxylene. The yare called the amido xylenes.
xylite: A liquid hydrocarbon found in crude wood spirits.
xylograph: An engraving on wood, or the impression from such an engraving; a print by xylography.
xylography: The art of engraving on wood.
xyloidin: A substance resembling pyroxylin, obtained by the action of nitric acid on starch; called also nitramidin.
xyloma: A tumour on the woody part of a plant.
xylon: A unit of length in Ancient Greece.
xylonic: Relating to xylonic acid or its derivatives
xylophone: An instrument common among the Russians, Poles, and Tartars, consisting of a series of strips of wood or glass graduated in length to the musical scale, resting on belts of straw, and struck with twos mall hammers. Called in Germany strohfiedel, or straw fiddle.
xylopia: tropical evergreen trees or shrubs; chiefly African
xyloquinone: Any one of a group of quinone compounds obtained respectively by the oxidation of certain xylidine compounds. In general they are yellow crystalline substances.
xylose: An unfermentable sugar of the pentose class, CHO, formed by the hydrolysis of xylan; wood sugar.
xylostroma: The felted stroma of various wood-destroying fungi.
xylotomy: Art of preparing sections (transverse, tangential, or radial) of wood, esp. by means of a microtome, for microscopic examination.
xylotrya: A genus of marine bivalves closely allied to Teredo, and equally destructive to timber. One species (Xylotrya fimbria ta) is very common on the Atlantic coast of the United States.
xylotypography: Printing using the medium of wooden blocks.
xylyl: Any one of three metameric radicals which are characteristic respectively of the three xylenes.
xylylene: Any one of three metameric radicals, CH.CH.CH, derived respectively from the three xylenes. Often used adjectively; as, xylylene alcohol.
xyris: A genus of endogenous herbs with grassy leaves and small yellow flowers in short, scaly-bracted spikes; yellow-eyed grass. There are about seventeen species in the Atlantic United States.
xystus: A long and open portico within the gymnasium.
y: Y, the twenty-fifth letter of the English alphabet, at the beginning of a word or syllable, except when a prefix (see Y-), is usually a fricative vocal consonant; as a prefix, and usually in the middle or at the end of a syllable, it is a vowel. See Guide to pronunciation, -,.
yabby: Any of various freshwater crayfish, typically of the genus Cherax, valued as food, especially Cherax destructor of southeastern Australia.
yaboo: An Afghan pony used as a beast of burden.
yacare: A South American crocodilian (Jacare scler ops) resembling the alligator in size and habits. The eye orbits are connected together, and surrounded by prominent bony ridges. Called also spectacled alligator, and spectacled cayman.
yacht: A light and elegantly furnished vessel, used either for private parties of pleasure, or as a vessel of state to convey distinguished persons from one place to another; a seagoing vessel used only for pleasure trips, racing, etc. Yacht measurement. See the Note under tonnage,.
yachter: One engaged in sailing a jacht.
yachting: Sailing for pleasure in a yacht.
yachtsman: One who owns or sails a yacht; a yachter.
yachtsmanlike: Resembling or characteristic of a yachtsman.
yachtsmanship: The skill or art of sailing a yacht.
yachtswoman: A woman who sails a yacht.
yad: A pointer used in the ritual of Torah-reading.
yaffle: The European green woodpecker (Picus, or Genius, virid is). Itis noted for its loud laugh like note. Called also eccle, hewhole, high hoe, laughing bird, popinjay, rain bird, yaffil, yaffler, yaffingale, yapping ale, yack el, and woodhack.
yaffler: the European green woodpecker, Picus viridis
yager: In the German army, one belonging to a body of light infantry armed with rifles, resembling the chasseur of the French army.
yagua: A Central American palm tree, Roystonea dunlapiana
yahgan: An indigenous people of the Southern Cone.
yahoo: A modern transliteration of the Hebrew word translated Jehovah in the Bible; used by some critics to discriminate the tribal godof the ancient Hebrews from the Christian Jehovah. Yahweh or Yahwe is the spelling now generally adopted by scholars.
yahooism: The behaviour or attitudes of yahoos; ignorant boorishness.
yahrzeit: The anniversary of a person's death, usually a parent's, often marked by the lighting of a memorial candle and other rituals.
yahweh: a name for the God of the Old Testament as transliterated from the Hebrew consonants YHVH
yahwism: A religion of Iron Age Israel, believing in a pantheon of gods headed by Yahweh.
yaka: An African ethnic group of the southwestern Democratic Republic of the Congo.
yakitori: A Japanese shish kebab-type dish made with small pieces of chicken or other ingredients cooked on skewers, often marinated in soy sauce or seasoned with salt.
yakker: One who yaks; a chatterbox or motormouth.
yaksha: A kind of demigod attendant on Kuvera, the god of wealth.
yale: English philanthropist who made contributions to a college in Connecticut that was renamed in his honor (-)
yall: second person plural pronoun, contraction of you all
yam: A large, esculent, farinaceous tuber of various climbing plants of the genus Dioscorea; also, the plants themselves. Mostly natives of warm climates. The plants have netted-veined, petioled leaves, and pods with three broad wings. The commonest species is D. sativa, but several others are cultivated. Chinese yam, a plant (Dioscorea batatas) with a long and slender tuber, hardier than most of the other species. Wild yam. (a) A common plant (Dioscorea villosa) of the Eastern united States, having a hard and knotty rootstock. (b) An orchidaceous plant (Gastrodia sesamoid es) of Australia and Tasmania.
yamamai: Antheraea yamamai, the Japanese oak silkmoth.
yamen: In China, the official headquarters or residence of a mandarin, including court rooms, offices, gardens, prisons, etc.; the place where the business of any public department is transcated.
yammerer: One who complains or whines peevishly or whimperingly.
yamstchik: In th-century Russia, someone who delivered post by means of a horse-drawn carriage.
yan: One in Cumbrian sheep counting rhyme.
yana: a member of an extinct North American Indian people who lived in northern California
yang: The cry of the wild goose; a honk.
yangtze: The chief river of central China and the third longest river in the world, flowing a total of km.
yankee: A nickname for a native of citizen of New England, especially one descended from old New England stock; by extension, an inhabitant of the Northern States as distinguished from a Southerner; also, applied sometimes by foreigners to any inhabitant of the United states. From meanness first this Portsmouth Yank ey rose, And still to meanness all his conduct flows. Oppression, A poem by an American (Boston, ).
yankton: A city, the county seat of Yankton County, South Dakota, United States.
yanqui: A citizen of the United States of America, as opposed to a Latin American.
yantra: A geometrical diagram used as a meditation aid in tantric worship.
yao: A Bantu people living in Malawi, Mozambique and Tanzania in Africa.
yaourt: A fermented drink, or milk beer, made by the Turks.
yapock: A South American aquatic opossum (Chironectes variegatus) found in Guiana and Brazil. Its hind feet are webbed, and its fore feet donot have an opposable thumb for climbing. Called also water opossum.
yapper: A person's mouth, especially one that gossips or talks too much.
yapping: present participle and gerund of yap
yappy: Of a dog, yapping in an annoying manner.
yaquina: A Native American people from Oregon.
yard: A long piece of timber, nearly cylindrical, tapering toward the ends, and designed to support and extend a square sail. A yard is usually hung by the center to the mast. See Illust. of Ship. Golden yard, or Yard and Ell (Astron.), a popular name the three stars in the belt of Orion. Under yard, under contract. Chaucer.
yardage: distance measured in the aggregate number of yards
yardarm: Either half of a square-rigged vessel's yard, from the center or mast to the end.
yardbird: a person serving a sentence in a jail or prison
yardland: A measure of land of uncertain quantity, varying from fifteen to forty acres; a virgate.
yardmaster: a railroad employer who is in charge of a railway yard
yardstick: A stick three feet, or a yard, in length, used as a measure of cloth, etc.
yardwork: Work done in maintaining a lawn, and related landscaping activities
yare: Ready; dexterous; eager; lively; quick to move. Be yare in thy preparation. The lesser will come and go, leave or take, and is yare; whereas the greater is slow. Sir W. Raleigh.
yareta: Azorella compacta, a South American flowering cushion plant in the family Apiaceae.
yarmelke: a skullcap worn by Jews, especially at prayer
yarmulke: a skullcap worn by religious Jews (especially at prayer)
yarn: One of the threads of which the strands of a rope are composed.
yarnen: Made of yarn; consisting of yarn. A pair of yarnen stocks. " Turbervile.
yarner: One who tells yarns or stories.
yarrow: An American and European composite plant (Achillea Mille folium) with very finely dissected leaves and small white corymbed flowers. It has a strong, and somewhat aromatic, odor and taste, and is sometimes used in making beer, or is dried for smoking. Called also milfoil, and nosebleed.
yarwhip: The European bar-tailed godwit; called also yardkeep, and yarwhelp. See Godwit.
yashmac: the face veil worn by Muslim women in Turkish
yashmak: the face veil worn by Muslim women
yataghan: A long knife, or short saber, common among Mohammedan nations, usually having a double curve, sometimes nearly straight. Chaucer.
yaup: To cry out like a child; to yelp.
yauper: One who, or that which, yaups.
yaupon: A shrub (Ilex Cassine) of the Holly family, native from virginia to Florida. The smooth elliptical leaves are used as asubstitute for tea, and were formerly used in preparing the black drink of the Indians of North Carolina. Called also South-Sea tea.
yautia: In Porto Rico, any of several araceous plants or their starchy edible roots, which are cooked and eaten like yams or potatoes, as the taro.
yavapai: a member of a North American Indian people of central Arizona
yaw: To rise in blisters, breaking in white froth, as cane juice in the clarifiers in sugar works.
yawd: A jade; an old horse or mare. Grose.
yawl: A small ship's boat, usually rowed by four or six oars.
yawmeter: An instrument that measures an aircraft's yaw.
yawn: utter a yawn, as from lack of oxygen or when one is tired
yawned: simple past and past participle of yawn
yawning: gaping open as if threatening to engulf someone or something
yawns: third-person singular simple present indicative of yawn
yawper: A person who yawps; one who cries vigorously.
yawping: present participle and gerund of yawp
yaws: A disease, occurring in the Antilles and in Africa, characterized by yellowish or reddish tumors, of a contagious character, which, in shape and appearance, often resemble currants, strawberries, or raspberries. There are several varieties of this disease, variously known as framboesia, pian, verrugas, and crab-yaws.
yawy: Pertaining to, or afflicted with, the disease yaws.
yazoo: a river that rises in west central Mississippi and flows southwest to empty into the Mississippi River above Vicksburg
ycleped: Called; named; obsolete, except in archaic or humorous writings. It is full fair to ben yclept madame. Chaucer. But come, thou goddess fair and free. In heaven ycleped Euphrosyne. Milton. Those charming little missives ycleped valentines. Lamb.
ydrad: Dreaded. Yet nothing did he dread, but ever was ydrad. Spenser.
yea: An affirmative vote; one who votes in the affirmative; as, avote by yeas and nays.
yead: Properly, a variant of the defective imperfect yode, but sometimes mistaken for a present. See the Note under Yede. Years yead away and faces fair deflower. Drant.
yealing: Someone who is the same age as oneself.
yean: To bring forth young, as a goat or a sheep; to ean.
yeaned: simple past and past participle of yean
yeanling: A lamb or a kid; an eanling.
year: Age, or old age; as, a man in years. Anomalistic year, the time of the earth's revolution from perihelion to perihelion again, which is days, hours, minutes, and seconds. A year's mind (Eccl.), a commemoration of a deceased person, asby a Mass, a year after his death. Cf. A month's mind, under Month. Bissextile year. See Bissextile. Canicular year. See under Canicular. Civil year, the year adopted by any nation for the computation of time. Common lunar year, the period of lunar months, or days. Common year, each year of days, as distinguished from leap year. Embolismic year, or Intercalary lunar year, the period of lunar months, or days. Fiscal year (Com.), the year by which accounts are reckoned, or the year between one annual time of settlement, or balancing of accounts, and another. Great year. See Platonic year, under Platonic. Gregorian year, Julian year. See under Gregorian, and Julian. Leap year. See Leap year, in the Vocabulary.
